Work in four steps. First, compute each student's gain. The raw gain is the post-test minus the pre-test. The normalized gain is (post − pre) ÷ (100 − pre), which accounts for room to improve. Second, find the mean gain for each group. Third, subtract: the difference of means is the treatment mean minus the control mean. Fourth, divide that difference by the pooled standard deviation to get Cohen's d.

Compare gains and not post-test means alone, because the groups may have started at different levels.

Example: In the pilot, the control mean gain is 15.0 and the treatment mean gain is 22.0, a difference of 7.0. The pooled standard deviation is about 6.78, so d is about 1.03. The conventions call 0.2 small, 0.5 medium, and 0.8 large, and they are rules of thumb. Impressive pilot estimates tend to shrink when repeated.

See Chapter 16 and Chapter 17.

docs.title: How do I make A/B test data anonymous?
docs.text:
Coded data replaces names with codes but keeps a key, so it is not anonymous. Anonymized data has every link to a person removed, so no one, including the teacher, can tell whose scores they are. Start by collecting little: the version label, the pre-test, the post-test, and the grade level, with a code such as S01 and the key in a separate locked file.

To anonymize, drop columns you do not need, generalize details such as grade level instead of birthdate, hide results for groups smaller than your district's reporting size, and clean the comments of identifying detail. Destroy the key on the deletion date you stated in the consent letter, and make sure nothing else in the table points to a person.

Example: A class of 24 with gender, class period, and teacher name in the table can single out one student, even without names.

The test: could someone who knows the class pick out a single student? See Chapter 16 and Chapter 17.

docs.title: How do I get a resource to work in my learning management system?
docs.text:
A teacher can bring an OER into a learning management system (LMS) four ways: a link, an embed, an upload of the files, or an import of a package. A reviewer tests at least link and embed. An iframe embed uses a source address, a width, a height, and a title. It fails for three common reasons: the server forbids framing, an insecure page sits inside a secure one, or the platform strips frames.

Two standards from 1EdTech help. Common Cartridge packages a course into one compressed file with a manifest that other systems can import. Learning Tools Interoperability (LTI) lets an outside tool open inside a course and can send scores to the gradebook, which raises privacy questions. Both are pluses and not requirements.

Example: Open the page in a private window with no login, paste the iframe into a blank test page, and then repeat on a second platform such as Moodle or Canvas.

See Chapter 10 and Chapter 9.

docs.title: How do the 3-point flag and the 1-point calibration threshold relate?
docs.text:
They serve different purposes. The 3-point flag from Chapters 3 and 11 is for finding disagreements worth discussing. Two reviewers agree on a metric if their scores differ by 3 or fewer, and a metric is flagged if they differ by more than 3. The workshop's calibration exercise uses the same flag between a teacher and an agent.

Chapter 14 uses a threshold of 1 for deciding whether an agent can be trusted as a first pass, and labels it a provisional teaching choice. Bands are two points wide, so a difference of 2 or more always moves a score into a different band. A loose threshold also fails to separate agents.

Example: In the book's three-agent comparison, all three agents agree on 10 of 10 metrics at a threshold of 3. At a threshold of 1, one of them agrees on only 4 of 10.

Set the threshold before you look at the numbers, so it cannot be bent to fit the results. See Chapter 14.

docs.title: How does sample size relate to the size of effect I can detect?
docs.text:
Larger groups smooth out chance differences, and a smaller effect is harder to tell from chance, so it needs many more students. The book gives rule-of-thumb group sizes: 5 to 10 per group for a pilot only, about 25 per group for a large difference, about 65 for a medium one, and about 400 for a small one.

The planning rule is students per group ≈ 16 ÷ d², rounded up. An effect size d of 0.8 needs 25 per group, 0.5 needs 64, and 0.2 needs 400. Do not plan on the pilot's own d, since pilot estimates tend to shrink. Plan on about half of it, close to 0.5, which means about 64 per group.

Example: A pilot with d about 1.03 would suggest 16 students per group. Planning on roughly half that effect size gives about 64 per group instead.

These are rules of thumb, and a statistician should confirm them. A pilot of about 12 per group is not enough to prove an effect. Its job is to decide whether a larger test is worth running. See Chapter 16 and Chapter 17.

docs.title: The agent cited a source I can't find. What should I do?
docs.text:
Treat it as a possible invented citation: a reference to a source that does not exist, or one that exists and does not say what the agent claims. Run four checks:

  1. Search for the exact title.
  2. Confirm that the journal exists and has the issue cited.
  3. Resolve the identifier or link. A DOI that leads nowhere, or to a different article, is a strong sign of a problem, and a missing identifier is a weaker one.
  4. Open the source and read the passage that is supposed to support the claim.

If you cannot find the source, reject the claim, record the decision and the reason in the findings log, and rescore without it. Never accept a claim you could not verify in time. Mark it "not verified." To prevent a repeat, add a rule to the prompt: cite only sources that appear in the resource or that you supplied, and write "no source found" otherwise.

Example: An agent cites a journal article with a believable title that no library holds. The reviewer rejects the claim, and the accuracy score is recomputed without it.

See Chapter 14 and Chapter 5.

docs.title: Why do agents misread licenses, and how do I catch it?
docs.text:
A license is a short, formal statement, and the neighboring licenses look alike. The book lists five predictable errors: treating one license as covering every item, confusing neighboring licenses such as reading CC BY-NC as CC BY, ignoring a restriction such as NoDerivatives, equating public with free, and missing ShareAlike. A related trap is reading the license of the site template instead of the content.

A misread license can lead to an unsafe adoption, so go to the source. Open the page and read the license statement itself. A good prompt asks the agent to quote the statement word for word, name each item it covers, and write "not stated" for anything the page does not mention. Then compare the quote with the page.

Example: An agent calls a resource CC BY because a link says "Creative Commons," although the terms say NonCommercial. Reading the statement catches it in seconds.

See Chapter 14 and Chapter 2.

docs.title: How can I tell whether an agent's score is overconfident?
docs.text:
An overconfident score is higher or more certain than its evidence supports. It is the quietest agent error because nothing is invented. Four signs give it away: a high score with no quoted evidence, a pass on a check that needs a tool but has no tool log, an empty "checks not verified" list, and round 9s and 10s across many metrics.

Use the quick test. Recompute the band from the agent's own ten checks by dividing the passes by ten, and compare it with the reported score. Then add rules to the prompt: a check that was not tested counts as failed, a check that cannot be verified is marked "not checkable" and listed, and a 10 requires every check to pass.

Example: An agent reports an 8, but its own table shows 6 of 10 checks passed. Sixty percent falls in the Adequate band of 5 to 6, so the 8 is overconfident by at least two points.

See Chapter 14.

docs.title: My score and the agent's score differ by more than 3 points. What now?
docs.text:
The worksheet flags every metric where the two scores differ by more than 3, and the calibration exercise asks you to explain which score you trust and why. A disagreement is information. It points to unclear evidence, a possible agent error, or an ambiguous check in the rubric.

Use the reconciliation steps. Each side states its evidence, you repeat the check that the evidence rests on, and you choose the score the checked evidence supports. If neither side has enough evidence, gather more. Do not average the two scores, because an average is a number neither reviewer found.

Example: You scored accessibility 5 and the agent scored it 9. The agent said contrast was fine but attached no tool log, and the video has no captions. You keep your 5 and record why.

See Chapter 11, Chapter 14, and Chapter 19.

docs.title: The resource is CC BY-ND or has no license. Can I still improve it?
docs.text:
Read the license before the first edit, because an agent's edited version is a derivative work and the license decides what you may do with it. With CC BY-ND you may share only the unchanged work. You can make private changes, but you cannot publish an improved version. Adding alt text, lowering the reading level, and fixing errors are all changes. A resource with no license, or marked all rights reserved, cannot be published in a changed form either.

Your options are to ask the owner for written permission, or to choose another resource. Do not add a license yourself, since only the owner can grant one. If the license allows changes, the rules are simple: with CC BY credit the author and say you changed it, with CC BY-SA also release under CC BY-SA, and with a NonCommercial license avoid commercial use.

Example: A teacher can post a CC BY-ND article for a class as it is, but cannot share a translated version.

See Chapter 15 and Chapter 2.

docs.title: The resource is only a PDF. What can I do?
docs.text:
A CC BY textbook that exists only as a PDF can be revised legally, and not practically. Start by asking the author for the Markdown, HTML, or word processing source. If none exists, you have two choices. You can convert the PDF to Markdown with a tool or an agent, or you can score the editable source metric low and note why. A PDF-only resource usually lands in the low bands of that metric.

Conversion needs careful review, because tables and equations convert poorly. The book lists six common errors: wrong column order, a flattened table, a lost heading, a garbled equation, a lost image, and a split word. Each has a quick check, such as reading a paragraph from each column and comparing every table and formula with the original.

Example: A tool converts a PDF chapter into Markdown, and a teacher repairs a broken table and a lost heading before publishing.

See Chapter 4 and Chapter 15.

docs.title: My accessibility checker reports no errors. Is the resource accessible?
docs.text:
Not necessarily. A clean scan is a starting point and never a pass. Checkers find missing alt attributes, weak contrast, unlabeled form fields, and some heading problems. They cannot judge whether alt text is useful, whether captions are accurate, or whether a heading describes its section.

Add the human checks. Read the alt text, listen to the page with a screen reader such as NVDA (free, for Windows) or VoiceOver (built into Apple devices), and put the mouse aside and press Tab through the page to see whether every function works by keyboard. Check captions on any video.

Example: In Watershed Basics, two of four alt texts are the single word "photo." A checker accepts them, and a reader using a screen reader learns nothing from them.

A Green Report Is Not a Pass

Scanners approve alt text that says only "photo," because the attribute is present. Spend two minutes with the mouse set aside, pressing Tab through the page, and listen with a screen reader before you trust the score.

See Chapter 7 and Chapter 13.

docs.title: The agent's rewrite changed the meaning of a passage. How do I catch that?
docs.text:
An agent can quietly alter what a passage says while it improves how it reads. The book lists five meaning-changing edits:

  • A changed quantity, such as "about 6,000" becoming "more than 6,000."
  • A changed strength, such as "can" becoming "always."
  • A dropped qualifier, such as "most rain" becoming "rain."
  • An added claim that the source never made.
  • A dropped item, such as "the river and its tributaries" becoming "the river."

Do not rely on the agent's own summary, because it can leave a change out. Open a side-by-side difference view and ask the agent to list every claim it changed, added, or removed. Treat an added claim as rejected unless a source supports it, and log corrections separately from plain rewrites.

Example: Rewriting "may reduce" as "reduces" turns a possibility into a certainty and fails the check.

See Chapter 15.

docs.title: The agent gives a different score each time I run it. What should I do?
docs.text:
Language models do not always give the same answer twice, so measure the variation and do not guess at it. Run the same prompt on the same resource five times. Record the lowest score, the highest, the range (highest minus lowest), and the median. The book's illustrative rule is that a range of 1 or less is stable, and a range of 2 or more is unstable. An unstable metric goes to a person.

A median that matches the human score does not make an unstable metric trustworthy. If a metric is unstable, tighten the prompt by asking for a pass or fail on each of the ten checks, move exact checks to tools, and measure again.

Example: Five runs give accessibility scores of 5, 6, 5, 7, and 5, a range of 2 with a median of 5, so it is unstable. Practice scores of 4, 7, 6, 5, and 8 have a range of 4.

See Chapter 14.

docs.title: My A/B test groups aren't comparable. What went wrong?
docs.text:
Most likely a confounding variable crept in, which is a second difference between the groups besides the version. Common ones are different teachers, different times of day, extra help for one group, different tests, and students choosing their own version. If the treatment group had a different teacher, you cannot tell whether the version or the teacher made the difference.

Defend against them with the one-difference rule: the groups differ in the version and nothing else. Assign students by chance. Simple random assignment can still be unlucky in a small class, so the book also teaches blocked assignment. Give the pre-test, sort by score, pair neighbors, and flip a coin within each pair. Also watch for sampling bias, such as only volunteers taking part.

Example: In a simulation on the book's class of 24, letting students choose built in a 23.8-point gap between groups. Simple random assignment had a median gap of about 4 points. Blocked assignment had a median of about 0.6.

See Chapter 16.

docs.title: My class is small. Can I still learn anything from an A/B test?
docs.text:
Yes, if you call it a pilot and read the result as suggestive and not conclusive. A pilot of about 12 students per group is not enough to prove an effect. Its job is to check the procedure and the measures, to estimate the spread of the scores and the size of the effect, and to decide whether a larger test is worth running.

Pilots surface practical problems. In the book's pilot, the original version's quiz would not load for two students on school tablets, and three students scored 95 to 98, so the test had little room to show growth. Both findings improved the next round. Report the limits honestly: one class, a bundle of fixes tested together, and an effect size that often shrinks when repeated.

Example: The book's pilot found a 7-point difference in mean gain. The summary recommended a larger test and did not claim proof.

See Chapter 16 and Chapter 17.

docs.title: How do I handle third-party images with unclear licenses?
docs.text:
A resource's overall license may not cover an image, chart, or quotation that someone else made. A caption that says "used with permission" gives a separate right that does not travel with the rest. The phrase "except where otherwise noted" is a warning to check every image caption.

For each third-party item, find its own notice and record the title, author, source, and license. If you cannot find the terms, replace the item. An image whose terms forbid changes must be replaced and not edited. Also remember that someone who copied an image from a publisher cannot grant you a Creative Commons license for it, so trace it to the original creator. When two items carry licenses that cannot be satisfied together, you can pick a different resource, ask an owner in writing, or keep the works separate with their own notices.

Example: A photo in a CC BY chapter that is labeled "used with permission" has rights separate from the chapter's.

See Chapter 2 and Chapter 9.

docs.title: How do I decide which metric to improve first?
docs.text:
Start with the lowest-scoring metric, unless fixing it is too costly or needs the author's decision. There are three reasons. The adoption floor means any metric under 5 blocks adoption. The lowest scores are often the cheapest to raise. And the total hides the weakest area. If the lowest metric is expensive, do the cheaper fixes first and flag the expensive one.

Then write an improvement plan with five parts: the baseline, the gaps, the fixes, the order and budget in human hours, and the target. The plan is a forecast, written before the work and compared with the result afterward.

Example: For Watershed Basics, the plan starts with metadata (4 to 8, half an hour, +4), then accessibility (5 to 8, two hours, +3), then modularity, practice, and accuracy. It totals 7.5 hours, a projected gain of 14, and a target of 79. Accessibility goes before the cheaper modularity fix because a barrier to learners matters more.

See Chapter 15.

docs.title: How do I review a change an agent made before I publish it?
docs.text:
A named person examines each change in a difference view and decides whether to keep it. Nothing goes live on the agent's say-so, and the agent's own summary is not enough, because an agent can leave a change out. Match the depth of the check to the risk. High-risk changes, such as facts, numbers, quotations, citations, captions, license statements, and anything that touches meaning, get a full check. Low-risk changes, such as heading levels and formatting, get a spot check.

Record each decision in a change log entry with seven fields: when, where, what changed, why, who or what made it, who reviewed it, and the decision. Reusers need the log, since CC BY asks you to indicate changes. Future reviewers and your own re-score need it too.

Example: "May 3, section 2: shortened sentences; made by agent; reviewed by T. Nguyen; accepted."

See Chapter 15.

docs.title: How much of an agent's output should I verify?
docs.text:
Match the checking to the risk, because the two extremes both fail. With no oversight, a blind learner meets an uncaptioned video. Checking everything is accurate but saves no time. Risk-matched oversight catches errors where they occur and keeps most of the time saving.

Send the report back when it breaks a rule, such as a total that does not equal the sum of the scores. Check every claim when the claims rest on the agent's memory with no source. Spot-check when the report follows the rules and carries tool logs. A good sample includes at least one claim from each metric, every claim that decides a band or the floor of 5, and a few at random. Widen the sample if you find an error, and record which claims you checked.

Check the Decisive Claims First

Before anything else, find the claims that decide a band or the floor of 5. A mistake there flips the decision, while a mistake in a claim that moves no threshold costs you very little.

Example: A reviewer verifies 12 of 40 claims and records which ones were checked.

See Chapter 13 and Chapter 14.

docs.title: Which license should I choose for what I publish?
docs.text:
Ask three questions: do you allow commercial reuse, do you allow shared changes, and must changes carry the same license? The answers map to the license:

  • Yes, yes, no: CC BY.
  • Yes, yes, yes: CC BY-SA.
  • No, yes, no: CC BY-NC.
  • No, yes, yes: CC BY-NC-SA.
  • Choose CC0 if you want no conditions at all.

The book favors CC BY for the components teachers publish, because it grants all five permissions with a single condition. The trade-offs are real. ShareAlike keeps adaptations open but limits what a remix can be combined with. NonCommercial blurs at the edges, such as a paid class, and it lowers the open license score. A published CC BY cannot be taken back for copies already out. Also check ownership, funders' requirements, third-party content, and, for software, use a license designed for code.

Example: An author who wants adaptations to stay open picks CC BY-SA, while one who wants the widest reuse picks CC BY.

See Chapter 2. The capstone expects CC BY.

docs.title: How should I run a calibration session?
docs.text:
Have the reviewers score the same sample resources alone, then compare metric by metric, discuss every flagged metric until the evidence settles it, and record how to score similar cases in the future. That is consensus scoring, and it is not averaging. A suggested goal, which a team may change, is agreement within 3 points on at least 8 of 10 metrics. If a team misses it, repeat with a new sample.

To calibrate an agent, follow six steps. Build a calibration set of 10 to 20 resources, scored to consensus by two or more trained humans and hidden from the agent. Run the agent. Compute agreement rate, mean absolute difference, and bias. Trace the largest disagreements to causes by error type. Refine the prompt, one change per observed error, and rerun. Then confirm on a fresh set, because a prompt tuned on one set learns that set's quirks.

Example: Four reviewers each score two sample resources alone, then meet to discuss every metric on which they differ.

See Chapter 11 and Chapter 14.

docs.title: How big should a reusable component be?
docs.text:
Usually one idea or one learning objective, with its explanation, an example, and a check question. A piece that is too big cannot be partly reused, and one that is too small is not worth finding. Apply the lift test: copy the piece somewhere new, and it must still make sense and work.

Search the text for words that depend on the rest of the resource, such as "above," "below," "earlier," "next section," and "the figure." Phrases like these break when the piece is moved. Fix them by restating the idea or linking to the other piece by its own address. Giving a piece its own file does not make it standalone.

Example: A 12-page chapter split into six two-page lessons, each with its own objective and quiz, is far easier to reuse than the whole chapter. A quiz that says "use the table from Chapter 2" fails the lift test.

See Chapter 9 and Chapter 15.

docs.title: How do I keep student data away from AI services?
docs.text:
Reviewing a resource needs no student data, so never paste student names, grades, or private records into an assistant. Student data covers names, ID numbers, grades, test results, written work, photographs, attendance, health and disability information, and anything identifying when combined with other details. Pasted text cannot be pulled back, and a deletion request may not undo it, because the service may store the text, staff may read it, and some services use it to improve models.

In the United States, FERPA restricts disclosure of identifiable student education records, and sending them to an AI company can be such a disclosure. The book gives no legal advice, so ask your school's privacy officer or technology office. Give agents the least file access they need, read-only if possible, and keep student records out of the folder.

Example: A published textbook chapter can go to an AI service. A grade spreadsheet with student IDs, a student photo, or a parent email thread cannot.

An A/B test does involve student data, so it needs consent, anonymizing, and an approved way to handle the data. See Chapter 13 and Chapter 16.

docs.title: When does a second agent add value, and when does it only add cost?
docs.text:
A second agent helps when it narrows what a person must check, and it adds only cost when it is treated as proof. In multi-agent review, several agents score the same resource independently. The spread is the highest score minus the lowest, and a triage rule sorts the results. A spread over 3 is flagged. Otherwise, if any agent quoted no evidence, check anyway. Otherwise accept for a spot check.

The cost multiplies, since three agents cost three times as much as one. Agreement among agents is not truth, because similar models share blind spots, and unanimous agreement with no evidence is especially suspect. A second-agent cross-check, in which the second agent hunts for faults in the first report instead of producing a fresh score, is a cheap first filter. It can miss errors and raise false alarms.

Example: In a test with 5 planted errors, a cross-check flagged 3 of 5, missed 2, and raised 1 false alarm.

See Chapter 13 and Chapter 14.

docs.title: How do changes in one metric affect the others when I improve a resource?
docs.text:
Fixes can have side effects, so re-score all ten metrics and not only the ones you touched. Re-scoring only the metrics you changed hides what else moved. Use the same rubric, evidence rules, prompt, and tools as the first scoring, and use a fresh agent session, because an agent that edited the resource scores it generously. Have a person verify every changed score and sample the rest.

Example: The improved Watershed Basics gained on five metrics, and its portability score fell from 7 to 6, because the new simulation's script is blocked on 1 of 3 test platforms. A partial re-score would have missed the drop. The total rose from 65 to 78, a gain of 13 against a projected 14.

The book's success test for an improvement is that at least two quality and two reusability metrics rise, every change is reviewed and logged, and no metric falls without a stated reason. See Chapter 15.

docs.title: How do I judge whether an improvement actually helped learners?
docs.text:
A score gain is not a learning gain. The score gain is the new total minus the old total, and it shows that the resource passes more of the rubric's checks. Whether students learn more is a different question that only a student test can answer. The book's example gains 13 points, which is 13 for 7.5 hours of work, or about 1.7 points per hour. A gain from better metadata may change nothing a student notices.

Then test. The A/B test compares gains between a control and a treatment group, and it can show only whether the whole bundle of fixes helped, not which fix did the work. Testing one fix at a time takes more students and time. Over many resources, the rubric-outcome correlation shows whether higher-scoring resources tend to produce larger gains.

Example: In the pilot, the improved version's mean gain was 22.0 against 15.0 for the original, a difference of 7.0 points.

See Chapter 15, Chapter 16, and Chapter 17.

docs.title: How would I build a reusable component from a lesson I already teach?
docs.text:
Work in six steps:

  1. Pick one idea or objective, and remove references that depend on the rest of the lesson, such as "as shown above."
  2. Give it a descriptive name, such as watershed-quiz, and not a name like final-v2.
  3. Put everything in one folder: the content, a README, a license file, a metadata file, and any images or scripts, with links that stay inside the folder.
  4. Add the license in three places, the visible page footer, the license file, and the metadata record, and list every third-party item with its title, author, source, and license.
  5. Write a one- or two-sentence description that starts with what the component does, and record subject, grade level, and keywords.
  6. Test it. Apply the lift test, then embed it by iframe on at least two platforms.

Finally, list it in an index page or catalog so teachers can find it.

Example: A folder with index.html, quiz.js, README.md, LICENSE.txt, metadata.json, and an img folder holds one packaged quiz.

See Chapter 18 and Chapter 9.

docs.title: How do I use student surveys and comments alongside test scores?
docs.text:
Test scores say what students learned, and a survey and comments say what they experienced, including barriers. Follow five rules for the survey: ask the same questions of both groups, keep them neutral, put one idea in each, make them specific, and keep responses anonymous. A common format rates each statement from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree). Avoid leading questions such as "Did you enjoy the great new simulation?", double-barreled ones such as "clear and fair," and vague ones such as "The lesson was good."

Ratings report opinion and not learning, and novelty can inflate them. For comments, code them into themes and count the students in each theme. Have two people code independently and resolve differences, and remove identifying detail before you quote anyone. Comments hint at causes without proving them.

Example: In the pilot, "helped me understand" averaged 3.5 for the control group and 4.3 for the treatment group. Seven of the 12 treatment students said the simulation helped. Two control students could not get the original quiz to load on school tablets, which explained a completion rate of 10 of 12, against 12 of 12 for treatment.

See Chapter 17.

docs.title: How do I publish an improved resource so others can find and reuse it?
docs.text:
Publishing means a stable public address, an open license, and complete metadata. A file on a shared drive may be visible, and it is not open. The book gives eight steps in order: confirm the license, finish the metadata, freeze the tested version with release notes, package each component, build the site, deploy it, open the feedback channel and publish the maintenance plan, and list the resource in a clearinghouse and tell colleagues. Listing comes last, so a reader who arrives finds a finished resource.

A static site generator turns Markdown files and a settings file into finished web pages. MkDocs, Jekyll, and Hugo are examples. This book uses MkDocs with the Material theme, and GitHub Pages serves such a site at an address of the form username.github.io/repository. The first page should show the title, the license with a link, a citation, the version, a link to the source, and a contact for the author. Release notes use four headings: Added, Changed, Fixed, and Removed.

Example: A teacher publishes a library of four items, a reading, a quiz, a simulation, and a glossary, each as its own component under CC BY 4.0, and submits it to a catalog such as OER Commons or MERLOT.

A clearinghouse listing points to your site and does not move the resource. See Chapter 18.

docs.title: How do I find out whether anyone is reusing what I published?
docs.text:
An open license lets people reuse a resource without asking or telling you, so the picture is always partial. Read the signals by strength. Strong signals are a course page that links to you and credits you, a fork with changes, and a teacher's message. Weak signals are downloads, page views, and a star. Your own visits and automated crawlers are not evidence at all. Search for the resource's title and your attribution line.

Choose an analytics tool that records counts and not individuals, and remember that a page view is not a reader and a reader is not a learner. A drop over a holiday reflects the calendar. Combine four kinds of evidence in an impact report, keep them apart, and say how strong each is: reach (analytics), reuse (reuse tracking), learning (the A/B test), and experience (surveys, comments, and the issue list).

Example: A sample report cites about 3,500 page views in six months, reuse by at least three teachers, a learning gain of 22.0 against 15.0 in a pilot of 24, and 11 issues of which 7 are fixed, and it notes that the pilot was small and that a larger test is planned.

See Chapter 18.

docs.title: Why does a published resource need a maintenance plan and a feedback channel?
docs.text:
Without a maintenance plan, a resource drifts out of date, and a reuser cannot tell whether it is still safe to trust. A plan states who is responsible, what is checked, how often, and when the resource will be retired. The book's sample schedule runs the link checker every three months, checks changeable facts once a year, runs an accessibility scan once a year and after any large change, reviews open issues at every release, and decides once a year whether to retire the resource. Retiring is part of maintaining: mark the resource archived, with a note on its first page.

Offer more than one feedback channel, such as an issue tracker, a plain email address, and a short form, because a required account excludes some teachers. Never ask for student information, and state how quickly you will reply. A channel that is promised and then ignored is worse than none.

See Chapter 18.

docs.title: Does a higher rubric score predict more student learning?
docs.text:
That is the question of rubric validity, and the book answers it with a method and an illustration, not a finding. The method compares each resource's rubric total with the mean normalized gain its students achieved in an A/B test, using the normalized gain because pilots use different tests. A Pearson correlation near 1 would mean higher-scoring resources tend to produce larger gains.

In the chapter's illustration of seven resources, r is about 0.93, which means roughly 87 percent of the variation in gains goes with the rubric score. Read that number with care. Only two of the seven points, the original and improved Watershed Basics, come from the real pilot, and the other five are made-up pilots. With the weakest resource removed, r is still 0.92. A serious check needs 20 or more resources. And correlation does not show cause.

The illustration also teaches a habit: among three resources with the same total of 65, the gains differ, so read the lowest metric before the total.

See Chapter 17 and Chapter 3.

docs.title: Should an AI agent's score ever replace a human review?
docs.text:
The book's answer is no. The agent drafts and a person verifies, because accountability cannot be delegated and because even a well-calibrated agent makes errors that only checking finds. What calibration can earn is a more limited role: the agent becomes a first pass, with a person still verifying the claims that decide the outcome.

The book offers an illustrative first-pass standard, which each team should reset after its own pilot:

  • Agreement rate at a threshold of 1: 80 percent or more.
  • Absolute bias: 0.5 or less.
  • Mean absolute difference: 1.0 or less.
  • Kappa on the adoption decision: 0.61 or more.
  • Run-to-run range per metric: 1 or less, or that metric goes to a person.

An agent that misses the standard only drafts evidence for a person. In the book's example, the first-draft agent has perfect agreement and correlation but a bias of +1.0, so it fails, because that bias turns a revise decision into adopt. Metrics that rest on exact checks suit a first pass best, and judgment metrics need close human checking.

See Chapter 14 and Chapter 12.

docs.title: What patterns do AI agent errors follow, and how does each type point to a fix?
docs.text:
Agent errors fall into four types, and each type tells you both how to catch it and how to change the prompt.

  • Factual error: the report says something the resource does not. Catch it by opening the resource and checking the claim. Fix the prompt by demanding a quotation or location for every claim and a tool log for every measurement.
  • License error: the license is misread. Compare the claim with the statement itself. Require the agent to quote the statement word for word.
  • Citation error: the source is invented or does not support the claim. Look up the source and read the passage. Allow only sources that appear in the resource or that you supplied.
  • Scoring error: the arithmetic or the band is wrong. Recount the passes, recompute the band, and re-add the total. Ask for a pass or fail on each of the ten checks, and let a spreadsheet or script add the total.

The patterns across types are telling. Errors cluster where a check needs a tool but no tool ran, where the agent relies on memory, and where scores run high with no evidence beside them. A small positive bias on every metric is score inflation, which no single claim check will reveal.

Example: A count that is off by one is a factual error, while a total that does not add up is a scoring error.

Track the types in the findings log, because a type that keeps recurring tells you which prompt rule to add next. See Chapter 14.

docs.title: What are the trade-offs between automated checks and manual review?
docs.text:
Automation gives speed, repeatability, and low cost on exact tasks. It lacks context and judgment, so each tool has a blind spot. The book names four checks worth automating, and what each cannot find:

  • Link checker: finds links that fail or have moved. It cannot tell that a working link leads to the wrong content.
  • Accessibility scan: finds missing alt attributes and weak contrast. It cannot judge whether alt text is useful or captions are accurate.
  • License detection: finds a missing license or a mismatch between page and metadata. It cannot tell whether the claim is true, and it can miss a license that appears only in an image.
  • Readability scan: gives a reading level for sampled passages. It cannot see undefined terms or audience fit.

Manual review is slow, and it is the reference that software is measured against. It brings context, judgment, and real-world tests such as embedding a resource on a platform. The practical split is that tools take the exact checks, the model drafts judgments about text, and a person takes the real-world tests and verifies what decides the outcome. Cost also matters, and batches multiply it.

See Chapter 13 and Chapter 12.

docs.title: How does the rubric specification differ from the ten-metric rubric?
docs.text:
They are two different documents, and the book does not yet reconcile them. The ten-metric rubric in Chapter 3 is the one every chapter teaches. It scores a resource on ten metrics from 0 to 10, adds them to a total out of 100, and ends in an adopt, revise, or reject decision.

The rubric specification is marked as a draft, version 0.4, a design specification that has not yet been implemented or tested. It describes an evaluator for LLM agent skills with a 0 to 3 scale, 22 scripted checks, and 17 judgment indicators. Its two headline numbers, one for overall quality and one for reusable content, are deliberately never combined into a single total, and it sets no adopt or reject rule. It builds on a review of 14 earlier rubrics by Yuan and Recker (2015), which found, among other things, that 5 of the 14 had no rating scale and only 3 had a detailed scoring guide.

For anything you do with this book, such as scoring by hand, writing a prompt, or preparing for the certificate, use the Chapter 3 rubric. Treat the specification as a draft for the automated evaluator.

docs.title: How would I design a calibration and certification program for my district?
docs.text:
Combine the book's pieces into one loop. Train reviewers first: they read Chapters 3 to 10, score two samples with evidence, compare their scores with an experienced reviewer, and join a calibration session. Build a calibration set of 10 to 20 resources scored to consensus by trained humans, and use it to check both new reviewers and any agent. Run a workshop of about 20 teachers, with a facilitator guide for each session that gives the time, goal, materials, steps, and the common problems with their fixes, so a colleague who did not write the workshop can run it. Use the certificate requirements, which tie each requirement to evidence, as the standard. Have a reviewer who did not take part in the work check each submission.

Certified teachers can then serve as local reviewers, the first reviewers for a school or district. The role has limits: they flag license problems without ruling on legal questions, never send student information to an agent, advise and do not make adoption decisions, and do not certify other teachers. They repeat the calibration on a reference set at least once a year.

To grow the program, use train-the-trainer: co-facilitate, then lead with an experienced facilitator watching, then lead alone. Keep quality by using the same kit and reference set, observing every new trainer's first session, and having trainers repeat calibration. Evaluate the program at four levels: reaction, learning, behavior, and results. Do not rely on the exit survey, which measures reaction only.

See Chapter 19, Chapter 11, and Chapter 14.

docs.title: How would I build an agent skill that evaluates OER automatically?
docs.text:
Package the book's method as a skill: a folder with an instructions file whose top description says when it applies. It carries five parts.

  1. A rubric prompt with the role, the ten checks for each metric, the rules (evidence for every check, "not checkable" instead of guessing, no invented quotations, untested checks count as failed), and the output format. Mark the resource as material, not instructions.
  2. Tools for the exact checks: a link checker, a readability calculator, an accessibility checker, and a metadata validator. Record the tool and version in the report.
  3. Structured output with a check-by-check result, passes, band, score, and a list of checks not verified, plus a script that recounts passes, recomputes bands, and re-adds the total.
  4. Human checkpoints: risk-matched oversight and a findings log that records what was accepted, corrected, or rejected.
  5. Calibration: run it on a set of 10 to 20 hand-scored resources, measure against the first-pass standard, refine the prompt one change per observed error, and confirm on a fresh set.

Set safe defaults. Give the agent read-only file access, keep student data out, and record the model, date, and prompt version with every run. Never let it change the resource it reviews.

See Chapter 12, Chapter 13, and Chapter 14.

docs.title: How do I appraise whether my A/B test design is fair?
docs.text:
Apply a checklist drawn from Chapter 16, and treat any failure as a reason to revise the plan before collecting data.

  • Hypothesis: written before the test, and specific, measurable, directional, sized, and falsifiable.
  • Versions: both frozen and labeled, with the change log listing the differences.
  • One difference: the groups differ in the version and nothing else, with the same teacher, instructions, time, and test.
  • Outcome measure: one primary outcome, from a separate test and not the resource's own quiz.
  • Assignment: by chance, blocked by pre-test score if the class is small.
  • Sample size: stated honestly. A group of about 12 is a pilot, and its result is suggestive.
  • Consent and privacy: consent before any data is collected, a real choice to decline at no cost, little data collected, and codes with a separate key.
  • Equity: both versions work for every student, including those using assistive technology and those without a fast home connection, and the report says who took part.

Remember that a bundle of fixes shows only whether the bundle helped. For red flags, look at the book's own failures: students choosing their own version, a pre-test given before consent, and a small test claimed as proof.

See Chapter 16 and Chapter 17.

docs.title: Glossary of Terms
docs.text: This glossary defines the terms used in this book. Each entry gives a short definition, a note on why the term matters when you evaluate or improve an open educational resource (OER), and, for many terms, an example and related terms. Terms are listed alphabetically.

docs.title: A/B Test
docs.text:
A comparison of two versions of something, A and B, in which comparable groups of people use each version at the same time and the results are compared.

The book teaches a manual A/B test with students, original version against improved version, and uses its results to calibrate automated scores.

Example: One class uses the original lesson and another uses the improved lesson, and both take the same post-test.

See also: Control Group, Treatment Group

docs.title: Accept Correct or Reject
docs.text:
The three outcomes of checking one claim from an agent's report: accepted when true as stated, corrected when right in substance but wrong in a detail, and rejected when false, invented, or impossible to verify.

Every checked claim lands in one of the three, and the findings log records the choice.

Example: A claim of "12 images" is corrected to 13 after a count, and a citation that cannot be found is rejected.

docs.title: Accessibility
docs.text:
The degree to which a resource can be used by people with a wide range of abilities, including those who rely on assistive technology.

Accessibility is a learning, ethical, and legal concern. The book uses WCAG 2.1 AA as its working standard.

Example: A page with real headings and image descriptions works for a student who uses a screen reader.

See also: WCAG 2.1 AA, Universal Design for Learning

docs.title: Accessibility Checker
docs.text:
A software tool that scans a page or document for accessibility defects, such as missing alt text, low contrast, or skipped heading levels.

Automated checkers find only part of the problems, so a human check completes the work.

docs.title: Accessibility Metric
docs.text:
A rubric metric, worth up to 10 points, that scores whether people with disabilities can perceive, operate, and understand a resource, using checks drawn from the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.1 level AA.

It is a quality metric, and a low score blocks adoption because barriers keep learners out.

See also: WCAG 2.1 AA, Accessibility Checker

docs.title: Accessible Math
docs.text:
Mathematical notation presented in a form, such as MathML or readable text, that assistive technology can read aloud and navigate, and not as a picture alone.

Equations saved as images are unreadable to screen readers, so math-heavy OER need this check.

docs.title: Accuracy Metric
docs.text:
A rubric metric, worth up to 10 points, that scores whether the facts, figures, and claims in a resource are correct and traceable to credible sources.

It is one of the five quality metrics. Evidence includes checked facts, the quality of citations, and expert comments.

Example: A biology page that names the wrong organ for a function loses points on this metric.

See also: Factual Error, Fact Checking

docs.title: Adopt Revise or Reject
docs.text:
The three decisions a review can lead to: use the resource now, improve it first, or set it aside, chosen by applying the adoption threshold to its scores.

The OER Evaluator's output ends in one of these three outcomes, with reasons.

Example: A total of 82 with every metric at 5 or more supports adopt, a total of 62 supports revise, and a total of 41 supports reject.

See also: Adoption Threshold, Adoption Decision

docs.title: Adoption Decision
docs.text:
The formal choice, made by a person or group with authority, whether to use a resource in a course or school, after weighing a review and local needs.

A review informs the decision and does not make it, because a department or committee also weighs things the rubric does not measure.

Example: A district committee reads a review report and votes to pilot a resource.

See also: Adoption Recommendation, Adopt Revise or Reject

docs.title: Adoption Recommendation
docs.text:
A reviewer's written advice to decision-makers that states which decision the scores support, gives reasons in plain words, and names the strongest and weakest metrics.

It is the part of the review that busy readers actually read.

See also: Review Report, Adoption Decision

docs.title: Adoption Threshold
docs.text:
A decision rule that turns scores into one of three outcomes; in this book's starting values, adopt when the total is at least 75 and every metric is at least 5, reject when the total is under 50, and revise otherwise.

These values are the book's starting rule and not a standard, so a department may set its own. The floor of 5 stops one failed metric from hiding inside a high total.

Example: A resource with a total of 80 but an accessibility score of 3 is revised and not adopted.

See also: Adopt Revise or Reject, Total Score

docs.title: Agent Disagreement
docs.text:
A difference in the scores or findings of two agents, or of an agent and a human, on the same metric.

A disagreement is information. It points to unclear evidence, a possible agent error, or an ambiguous check in the rubric.

Example: One agent scores metadata 8 and another scores it 4, so a reviewer opens the metadata record.

docs.title: Agent Error Rate
docs.text:
The share of an agent's checked claims that were corrected or rejected, found by dividing the number not accepted as stated by the number verified.

It gives a plain number for how far an agent can be trusted on a given task.

Example: If a reviewer verified 40 claims and 6 were corrected or rejected, the rate is 6 divided by 40, or 15 percent.

docs.title: Agent Error Type
docs.text:
A category of mistake that an agent makes, such as a factual, license, citation, or scoring error, used to organize what a reviewer finds.

Naming the type tells the reviewer how to catch it and tells the prompt writer how to fix it.

Example: A count that is off by one is a factual error, while a total that does not add up is a scoring error.

See also: Hallucination, Findings Log

docs.title: Agent Evaluation Report
docs.text:
The document an agent produces from a scoring run, giving for each metric the score, checks, and evidence, plus subtotals, total, band, unverified checks, and a recommendation.

It is what a human reviewer reads and verifies, so its structure is designed to make checking easy.

See also: Agent Scoring, Verification Step

docs.title: Agent Scoring
docs.text:
The use of an AI agent to assign the ten metric scores to a resource, with evidence, by following the rubric.

Agent scoring is fast and repeatable but needs checking, so the book pairs it with verification and calibration.

Example: An agent scores a chapter and returns a total of 71 with evidence for each metric.

See also: Rubric Prompt, Agent Evaluation Report

docs.title: Agent Skill
docs.text:
A packaged set of instructions, and sometimes helper scripts and reference files, that an agent loads when a task matches it.

A skill lets someone write down a procedure once and reuse it. The book's evaluation procedure can be packaged this way.

Example: A folder with a text file of scoring instructions and a short description telling the agent when to use it.

docs.title: Agent Workflow
docs.text:
The designed sequence of steps, tools, and human checkpoints that an agent and its human partner follow to produce a trustworthy evaluation.

It is the agent's version of the review workflow and ends with a person.

Example: The agent reads files, runs link and accessibility tools, drafts scores, and hands a report to a reviewer who verifies it.

See also: Human in the Loop, Review Workflow

docs.title: Agreement Rate
docs.text:
The share of metrics on which an agent's score falls within the score difference threshold of the human score, written as a percentage.

It summarizes human and agent agreement in one percentage that teachers can read at a glance.

Example: If 8 of 10 metrics agree, the agreement rate is 80 percent.

See also: Score Difference Threshold, Inter-Rater Agreement

docs.title: AI Agent
docs.text:
A software system built on a language model that carries out multi-step tasks toward a goal by reading files, using tools, and making decisions with limited human direction at each step.

The OER Evaluator uses agents to draft scores and improvements, and a person verifies the results.

Example: An agent reads a folder of lesson files, runs a link checker, and fills in the rubric worksheet.

See also: Agent Skill, Agent Workflow

docs.title: AI Alt Text Generation
docs.text:
The use of an AI model to draft text descriptions for images in a resource, which a person then checks and corrects.

It makes a tedious job quick, but drafts can be wrong, so each one is accepted, corrected, or rejected.

Example: An agent drafts descriptions for 20 images, and a reviewer corrects 4 of them.

See also: Alt Text, Accept Correct or Reject

docs.title: AI Assistant
docs.text:
A software program that uses artificial intelligence, usually a large language model, to answer questions and complete tasks in a conversation with a person.

An assistant answers when asked, while an agent works through several steps. The book starts with assistants and moves to agents.

Example: A teacher asks an assistant to explain the difference between CC BY and CC BY-SA.

See also: AI Agent, Large Language Model

docs.title: AI Cost
docs.text:
The money a service charges for a language model's work, usually calculated from the number of tokens sent and received.

Cost shapes how many resources a department can score with agents, and prices change often, so reviewers look up current rates.

Example: A batch of fifty chapters costs more than a single chapter because it processes far more tokens.

See also: Token, Batch Evaluation

docs.title: Alignment Metric
docs.text:
A rubric metric, worth up to 10 points, that scores how well a resource's content, activities, and assessments match its stated learning outcomes and relevant standards.

Alignment links a resource to what a course is trying to achieve. A resource can be accurate and still not useful if it is poorly aligned.

See also: Learning Outcome, Outcome Coverage

docs.title: All Rights Reserved
docs.text:
A phrase in a copyright notice indicating that the rights holder keeps every right and grants no permissions beyond those given by law.

It signals that reuse requires asking the owner. The OER Evaluator treats it as the opposite of an open license.

Example: A footer reading "© 2022 Example Press. All rights reserved."

docs.title: Alt Text
docs.text:
A short written description of an image, stored in the page code, that a screen reader speaks aloud when it reaches the image.

Missing or poor alt text is a leading accessibility defect. AI agents can draft it, and people check it for accuracy.

Example: For a bar chart: "Bar chart showing quality scores rising from 62 to 81 after revision."

See also: Decorative Image, AI Alt Text Generation

docs.title: Anonymized Data
docs.text:
Data from which every link to a particular person has been removed, so that no one, including the teacher, can tell whose scores they are.

It differs from coded data, which replaces names with codes but keeps a key. Anonymized data gives stronger privacy.

Example: A score table lists "Student 1, Student 2, and so on" with no key kept anywhere.

docs.title: Answer Key
docs.text:
A list of the correct answers to a set of questions, often with a brief explanation of why each answer is right.

Without a key, a teacher cannot check work quickly or trust that an item is right, so the practice metric looks for one.

Example: "Question 4: B. CC BY-NC restricts commercial use."

See also: Feedback Message, Worked Solution

docs.title: ARIA Labels
docs.text:
Attributes from the Accessible Rich Internet Applications specification that give interactive page elements a name or description for assistive technology.

They help screen reader users with custom controls such as simulation buttons. They patch gaps, and plain HTML elements need them less.

docs.title: Assessment Alignment
docs.text:
The degree to which quiz and test questions measure the same knowledge and level of thinking as the stated learning objectives.

Misaligned assessments reward the wrong learning. The OER Evaluator checks whether each objective has matching questions.

Example: An objective to "design a lesson" paired with a multiple-choice recall quiz is misaligned.

See also: Bloom Cognitive Levels, Learning Objective

docs.title: Attribution Requirement
docs.text:
A condition in many open licenses under which anyone using a work credits its creator and notes the license, the source, and any changes.

Attribution is the one condition of CC BY and appears in most other Creative Commons licenses. The OER Evaluator checks that a resource credits its own borrowed materials correctly.

Example: A reused diagram carries a line naming its creator, the source link, and the license.

See also: Attribution Statement, TASL Attribution Format

docs.title: Attribution Statement
docs.text:
A written credit line placed with a reused work that names its creator, gives its source, and states its license.

A complete credit line is what a reuser needs to follow the license, and a missing one is a common license error. Agents can draft these, and a person checks them against the source.

Example: "Prairie Dawn" by A. Writer, from example.org, licensed under CC BY 4.0.

docs.title: Audience Fit
docs.text:
The degree to which a resource matches its intended users' reading level, prior knowledge, language, culture, and purpose, taken together.

A grade number alone cannot capture fit, so a human check completes the readability score.

docs.title: Audio Description
docs.text:
A spoken narration added to a video that describes important visual content, such as actions, scenes, and on-screen text, for viewers who cannot see it.

Without it, a blind learner misses what is shown. A video whose normal narration already explains every visual needs less.

Example: A narrator says "The graph line climbs steeply after year three" when the speaker only points at the screen.

See also: Transcript, Captions

docs.title: Author Field
docs.text:
The metadata field that names the person or organization responsible for creating a resource, so reusers can give credit and contact the source.

Credit lines depend on it, so the OER Evaluator checks that it is filled and matches the visible byline.

docs.title: Automated Accessibility Scan
docs.text:
A tool-driven test that examines a page's code for known accessibility problems and produces a list of defects for a person to review.

Scans find only part of the problems, so a person completes the check with a screen reader or keyboard test.

Example: A scan reports missing alt text, low contrast, and an empty link.

docs.title: Automated License Detection
docs.text:
A tool or agent step that finds license statements and markings in a resource and identifies which license each one names.

It saves time but can misread vague or conflicting notices, so a person confirms it against the statement.

Example: A detector reports "CC BY 4.0" from a footer link.

docs.title: Automated Link Checker
docs.text:
A program that visits every link in a resource and reports which links work, which redirect to another address, and which fail.

It supplies fast, objective evidence for the currency metric and is the first automated check the book teaches.

Example: A tool lists 4 dead links among 60 and records the date of the test.

docs.title: Automated Readability Scan
docs.text:
A tool-driven test that computes readability formula results, such as grade level, for a resource's text, usually page by page.

It shows where text is too hard, though only a person can judge audience fit.

Example: A scan flags three pages above grade 12 in a seventh-grade unit.

docs.title: Batch Evaluation
docs.text:
The running of the same rubric prompt over many resources, one after another, so that a whole collection can be scored.

It saves time for a department or repository, but errors repeat across the batch, so spot checks matter.

Example: A librarian has an agent score thirty open textbooks and ranks them by total.

docs.title: Before-and-After Comparison
docs.text:
A study design that compares one group's scores before and after using a single version of a resource, with no second group.

It is weak evidence, because anything that happened between the two tests can explain a gain. The book prefers a controlled A/B test.

Example: A teacher gives a pre-test, teaches the improved lesson, gives a post-test, and sees a gain of 18 points, which other factors could also explain.

See also: A/B Test, Control Group

docs.title: Bloom Cognitive Levels
docs.text:
The six ordered categories of thinking named in the 2001 revision of the taxonomy first developed by Benjamin Bloom and colleagues: Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyze, Evaluate, and Create.

Matching the level of an objective to the level of its practice items is a key alignment check.

docs.title: Bloom's Taxonomy
docs.text:
A classification of thinking skills, in its 2001 revised form, arranged from simpler to more complex: Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyze, Evaluate, and Create.

The book uses these levels to set outcomes and to check whether practice questions ask for the same level of thinking as the objectives.

Example: A question asking learners to list the 5Rs is at Remember, while one asking them to judge a resource is at Evaluate.

See also: Bloom Cognitive Levels, Measurable Verb

docs.title: Broken Link Check
docs.text:
A test that follows each link in a resource and records whether it reaches a working page, an error, or a redirect.

It gives hard evidence for the currency metric. Results change over time, so the date of the check is recorded.

Example: A checker reports that 6 of 80 links return errors.

See also: Automated Link Checker, Link Rot

docs.title: Browser Compatibility
docs.text:
The ability of a web resource to display and work correctly in the major web browsers and on the different devices that learners use.

A resource that fails in a student's browser fails for that student. The portability metric checks several browsers.

Example: A simulation that runs in Chrome, Firefox, Safari, and Edge.

docs.title: Calibration Against Humans
docs.text:
The process of testing an agent's scores against careful human scores on a set of resources, then adjusting the prompt until the two agree well enough for the agent's purpose.

It is how an agent earns the trust a teacher is asked to place in it.

Example: A team compares an agent's scores with consensus human scores on twenty resources and finds a bias of +1.0.

docs.title: Calibration Exercise
docs.text:
The workshop session in which each teacher scores a sample resource by hand, runs an agent on the same resource, and compares the two sets of scores.

It is the teaching version of calibration against humans, and it shows teachers directly where an agent errs.

Example: Teachers find that the agent scored accessibility two points higher than their own scores.

See also: Calibration Session, Calibration Against Humans

docs.title: Calibration Session
docs.text:
A meeting in which reviewers score the same sample resources, compare scores metric by metric, and discuss differences until they apply the rubric in the same way.

Calibration is what turns a written rubric into a shared one, because two reviewers can read the same descriptor differently.

Example: Four reviewers each score two sample resources alone, then meet to discuss every metric on which they differ.

See also: Consensus Scoring, Score Reconciliation

docs.title: Capstone Project
docs.text:
The culminating work of the book, in which a person evaluates one open resource from their own subject, improves it with AI agents on at least two quality and two reusability metrics, tests the change with students, and publishes it under CC BY.

It applies every skill in the book to a resource that matters to the learner.

Example: A teacher improves a unit on fractions, runs a small A/B test, and posts the new version.

See also: Improvement Challenge, Professional Development

docs.title: Caption Generation
docs.text:
The use of speech-to-text software or an AI model to draft synchronized captions for a video or audio recording, which a person then corrects.

Automatic captions often misspell names and technical terms, so human correction is part of the process.

Example: A tool drafts captions for a lecture, and a teacher fixes three misspelled terms.

docs.title: Captions
docs.text:
Text synchronized with the audio of a video that shows spoken words and important sounds, for viewers who cannot hear or choose to watch without sound.

WCAG 2.1 AA expects captions on prerecorded video with sound. Speech-to-text software can draft them, and a person corrects them.

Example: A lecture video shows each sentence as it is spoken, plus "[applause]" for the sound.

See also: Transcript, Caption Generation

docs.title: CC BY
docs.text:
A Creative Commons license that permits anyone to copy, adapt, and distribute a work for any purpose, including commercial use, provided the creator is credited.

CC BY is the least restrictive Creative Commons license and the one this book favors for the components teachers publish. It grants all five permissions with a single condition, attribution.

Example: A photograph under CC BY can appear in a school textbook with a credit line naming its creator.

See also: Attribution Requirement, TASL Attribution Format

docs.title: CC BY-NC
docs.text:
A Creative Commons license that permits copying and adapting a work with credit to the creator, but only for noncommercial purposes.

The NonCommercial limit restricts some permissions, so this book does not treat a CC BY-NC resource as open in the full 5R sense. The OER Evaluator notes the limit on the open license metric.

Example: A free workshop can reuse a CC BY-NC worksheet, while a company selling a paid course with it raises a question.

docs.title: CC BY-NC-ND
docs.text:
The most restrictive of the six main Creative Commons licenses, permitting others only to copy and share a work unchanged, with credit, and for noncommercial purposes.

It allows use but not revision or remixing, so a resource under it scores low on the open license metric. Improving it would first require the owner's separate permission.

Example: An article under this license can be handed out as is, but not edited into a new handout.

See also: CC BY-NC, CC BY-ND

docs.title: CC BY-NC-SA
docs.text:
A Creative Commons license that combines credit to the creator, a noncommercial-use limit, and a requirement that adapted versions carry the same license.

It stacks two restrictions, so remixing is possible only with works under compatible terms. The OER Evaluator reads both limits when scoring the open license metric.

Example: A teacher adapts a CC BY-NC-SA worksheet and shares the new version under the same terms for noncommercial use.

See also: ShareAlike Requirement, NonCommercial Requirement

docs.title: CC BY-ND
docs.text:
A Creative Commons license that permits copying and sharing a work in unchanged form, with credit to the creator, but does not permit sharing adapted versions.

NoDerivatives blocks revision and remixing, the permissions that improvement work needs. The OER Evaluator records it as a restriction on the open license metric.

Example: A teacher can post a CC BY-ND article for a class but cannot share a translated version.

See also: NoDerivatives Requirement, Revise Permission

docs.title: CC BY-SA
docs.text:
A Creative Commons license that permits copying and adapting a work, including for commercial use, if the creator is credited and adapted versions carry the same license.

ShareAlike keeps adaptations open but limits what a remix can be combined with. The OER Evaluator checks compatibility when a resource mixes sources.

Example: A teacher who adapts CC BY-SA text shares the adapted version under CC BY-SA too.

See also: ShareAlike Requirement, License Compatibility

docs.title: CC0 Dedication
docs.text:
A Creative Commons tool by which a creator gives up copyright and related rights as far as the law allows, placing a work as close to the public domain as possible.

CC0 is a dedication and not a license in the strict sense, and it attaches no conditions, not even credit. The OER Evaluator treats it as the most open status a resource can have.

Example: A data table released under CC0 can be used in a lesson without a credit line.

See also: Public Domain, CC BY

docs.title: Certificate
docs.text:
A record issued by a program to show that a person has completed defined work to a defined standard; in this book, the credential for evaluating OER quality with AI agents.

Earning it shows that a teacher attended training, calibrated against an agent, evaluated a real resource, and improved it.

Example: A teacher receives the certificate after a reviewer approves the submission.

See also: Certificate Requirements, Certificate Submission

docs.title: Certificate Requirements
docs.text:
The conditions a teacher meets to earn the certificate, each linked to the evidence that shows the condition has been met.

Clear conditions let a teacher plan the work and let a reviewer judge it fairly.

Example: One requirement calls for an evaluation scored on all ten metrics with evidence.

See also: Certificate, Certificate Submission

docs.title: Certificate Submission
docs.text:
The package of evidence a teacher sends to earn the certificate, including the worksheet, the agent's scores, the findings log, and a link to the published improved component.

It lets a reviewer judge the work without being present.

Example: A teacher uploads a worksheet, a findings log with five entries, and the link to a CC BY component.

See also: Submission Review, Findings Log

docs.title: Change Log Entry
docs.text:
The record of one change to a resource, answering when it was made, where, what changed, why, who or what made it, who reviewed it, and what was decided.

The log serves reusers, reviewers, and the agent's own checkers, and CC BY asks reusers to indicate changes.

Example: "May 3, section 2: shortened sentences; made by agent; reviewed by T. Nguyen; accepted."

See also: Changelog, Human Review of Changes

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text:
A dated list of the notable changes made in each version of a resource, written for the people who use it and wish to know what is new.

A changelog tells reusers what is new and what has been fixed. It is also the record behind release notes.

Example: "v1.2: Added alt text to all figures; fixed two broken links."

docs.title: Chapter Splitting
docs.text:
The division of a long resource into smaller, self-contained pieces, each with its own title, purpose, and objective, so they can be used separately.

Splitting raises modularity and lets teachers reuse one part.

Example: A 40-page chapter becomes five lessons that each have an objective and a quiz.

docs.title: Chapter Structure
docs.text:
The division of a textbook's concepts into chapters in an order that places every concept after the concepts it depends on.

A structure that breaks the order makes readers meet a term before it is defined.

Example: A chapter on re-scoring comes after the chapter that defines improvement plans.

See also: Concept Dependency, Learning Graph

docs.title: Citation Quality
docs.text:
The degree to which a resource's references are real, complete, relevant to the claims they support, and drawn from credible sources.

Citation quality is part of the accuracy evidence. It is also where AI agents often fail, by inventing sources that do not exist.

docs.title: Cohen's Kappa
docs.text:
A statistic that measures how well two raters agree on categories after correcting for the agreement expected by chance alone.

It guards against false confidence, since two raters who both say "adopt" most of the time will agree often by luck.

Example: If a human and an agent each say "adopt" for most resources, kappa shows whether they agree more than chance would predict.

docs.title: Color Contrast
docs.text:
The difference in brightness between text or graphics and their background, which determines how easily people can see them in different lighting.

Low contrast shuts out learners with low vision and anyone reading in bright light.

docs.title: Color Independence
docs.text:
A design property in which meaning is carried by more than color alone, through added text, labels, patterns, or icons.

Learners with color blindness would otherwise miss information. Reviewers check charts and instructions for it.

Example: A chart marks passing and failing bars with green and red and also with the words "pass" and "fail."

docs.title: Commercial Textbook
docs.text:
A textbook sold by a publisher for profit under traditional copyright, with most rights kept by the publisher, usually in print or as a paid digital edition.

Commercial textbooks are the cost and rights baseline against which OER are compared. A teacher can still score one with the rubric to see what a switch would gain or lose.

Example: A calculus text bundled with a single-use online homework code is a commercial textbook.

docs.title: Common Cartridge
docs.text:
An IMS Global (1EdTech) standard file format that packages course content, such as pages, quizzes, and links, so it can move between learning management systems.

Exporting to it is a sign of portability. The OER Evaluator notes whether a resource offers it.

Example: A teacher exports a unit as a Common Cartridge file from one system and imports it into another.

docs.title: Community Contribution
docs.text:
A change, correction, or addition to a shared resource that is proposed by someone outside the original author team, such as a reader or a colleague.

Contributions are a benefit of open resources, and on GitHub they arrive as pull requests that the owner reviews.

Example: A reader fixes a typo in a lesson and sends a pull request.

See also: Pull Request, Feedback Channel

docs.title: Completion Rate
docs.text:
The share of students who finished an activity out of all those who started it, usually written as a percentage.

It shows whether a version is usable. A low rate can signal confusion or technical trouble.

docs.title: Complex Image Description
docs.text:
A longer text explanation of a chart, diagram, or map that holds too much detail for alt text, placed near the image or linked from it.

Complex visuals carry lessons that a short description cannot. The accessibility metric checks that they have fuller descriptions.

docs.title: Component Discoverability
docs.text:
The degree to which the people who need a component can find it, through its name, description, metadata, and the places where it is listed.

A component no one can find is not reused. Discoverability comes from a clear name, a complete metadata record, a plain-language description, and listing in places teachers look.

Example: A component named "Hands-On Fractions Quiz, Grade 4" with keywords and a description appears in search results.

See also: Metadata Completeness, OER Clearinghouse

docs.title: Component Granularity
docs.text:
The size of a component, in terms of how much content one piece contains, ranging from a single idea to a whole book.

A piece that is too big cannot be partly reused, and one that is too small is not worth finding. About one idea or objective with its explanation and practice is usually a good size.

Example: A 12-page chapter split into six two-page lessons.

See also: Chapter Splitting, Modular Content

docs.title: Component Library
docs.text:
An organized collection of reusable components, with an index that lets a visitor see what is there and choose what they need.

A library turns a pile of packages into something a teacher can browse.

Example: A website lists forty components by subject, each in its own folder.

See also: Reusable Component, Component Discoverability

docs.title: Component Licensing
docs.text:
The practice of giving each component its own license statement and credit lines, so it keeps its terms when it travels alone.

A reuser who copies only a quiz still sees its license, its author, and what it adapted.

Example: A quiz page shows "CC BY 4.0" in its footer, in its folder, and in its metadata.

See also: License Statement, Attribution Statement

docs.title: Component Packaging
docs.text:
The gathering of everything a component needs into one folder that can be copied, downloaded, or embedded as a unit.

A package holds the content, a short README, a license file, a metadata file, and any images or scripts, with links that work inside it.

Example: A folder holding a simulation, its README, license file, and metadata record.

docs.title: Concept Dependency
docs.text:
A link between two concepts showing that a learner needs to understand one of them first, which places that concept earlier in a learning sequence.

In this book's graph each link points from a concept to its prerequisite, so the arrow reads "needs."

Example: Score Band depends on Total Score, because a band is read from the total.

See also: Learning Graph, Chapter Structure

docs.title: Confounding Variable
docs.text:
A factor other than the version being tested, such as teacher, time of day, or prior knowledge, that differs between groups and could explain the result.

If the treatment group had a different teacher, one cannot tell whether the version or the teacher made the difference.

Example: A morning class and an afternoon class differ in alertness as well as in which version they used.

docs.title: Consensus Scoring
docs.text:
A process in which two or more reviewers each score alone, compare their scores, and discuss each difference until they agree on one final score per metric.

Consensus works when the decision rests on evidence and not on seniority or persistence.

Example: Two reviewers differ on accessibility, 4 and 7; after checking the images together, both agree on 5.

docs.title: Content Gap
docs.text:
A topic, skill, or explanation that a course's learning outcomes call for but that a given resource leaves out or covers too thinly.

Gaps explain why a good resource may still not fit a course. The OER Evaluator lists them in the review report.

docs.title: Content Update
docs.text:
A revision that brings out-of-date facts, examples, or data in a resource up to date with current information from reliable sources.

It is a high-risk change because it affects meaning, so it gets a full check against the source.

Example: Replacing a ten-year-old statistic with a recent one from the same agency.

docs.title: Context Window
docs.text:
The maximum amount of text, measured in tokens, that a language model can consider at one time, including the prompt and its own reply.

Long resources may not fit, which is one reason to split them into smaller pieces.

Example: A 300-page book may exceed the window, so an agent reads it chapter by chapter.

See also: Token, Chapter Splitting

docs.title: Contrast Ratio
docs.text:
A number from 1:1 to 21:1 that compares the relative brightness of two colors, with higher values meaning greater separation.

WCAG 2.1 AA sets minimums of 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text, and free tools compute the ratio instantly.

Example: Black text on white measures 21:1, the highest possible value.

See also: Color Contrast, WCAG 2.1 AA

docs.title: Control Group
docs.text:
