Every later chapter relies on these terms, because the book's rubric scores a resource on two things at once: how well it teaches and how freely it can be reused.

docs.title: Educational Resources: Everything You Teach With
docs.text:
An educational resource is any material that a teacher or learner uses to support teaching and learning. The definition depends on purpose, not on format. A photograph of a canyon is a family snapshot in an album, and it becomes an educational resource when a teacher uses it to explain erosion.

Educational resources fall into five broad groups. Texts include textbooks, articles, and readings. Media include images, audio, and video. Tools include interactive simulations, spreadsheets, and data sets that learners work with. Assessments include quizzes, tests, and scoring rubrics. Plans include syllabi, lesson plans, and unit outlines. Most real lessons mix several groups at once.

The following table summarizes the five groups with examples.

Group What it does for learning Examples Texts Present explanations and information Textbook chapter, article, reading list Media Show or tell what words alone cannot Photograph, diagram, podcast, video Tools Let learners work with something Simulation, spreadsheet, data set Assessments Check what learners know Quiz, test, scoring rubric Plans Organize the teaching Syllabus, lesson plan, unit outline

Worked example: inventorying a unit. A seventh-grade science teacher is planning a two-week unit on erosion, and her draft materials list has eight items. Step 1 sorts each item into one of the five groups. Step 2 asks a question that the rest of this chapter teaches you to answer: what can she see about who holds the right to copy and change this item?

Item Group What she can see about its rights Chapter 6 of the district's textbook Texts A copyright notice on the title page: "All rights reserved" A video about the Grand Canyon from a streaming site Media Nothing, apart from the site's terms of use Her own slide deck Plans She wrote it; her district's policy may say who owns it A soil-erosion simulation from a university project Tools A footer line: "CC BY 4.0" A county soil data set Tools A statement that the data is in the public domain A vocabulary quiz she wrote Assessments She wrote it A photograph of a gully from a blog Media Nothing A reading on the Dust Bowl from an online encyclopedia Texts A footer line: "CC BY-SA 4.0"

Sorting the items took a minute. Reading the right-hand column is the skill that matters. Three items state a clear permission, one states a clear restriction, two are the teacher's own work, and two state nothing at all.

Two Questions, Not One

Every resource answers two separate questions: how well does it teach, and what may I do with it? A lesson that teaches beautifully but cannot be adapted is still a problem for your classroom. This book scores both.

docs.title: Copyright: The Default Rule
docs.text:
Copyright is a legal protection that gives the creator of an original work the exclusive right to control how the work is copied and used. In the United States, protection begins automatically the moment a work is fixed in a tangible form: typed, saved to a file, recorded, or drawn. No registration and no © symbol are required. Other countries follow similar rules under international agreements, so this chapter uses U.S. law as its example. Check your own country's law before you rely on any detail here.

Copyright gives the owner five exclusive rights. Three of them matter most to teachers:

  • Reproduce: make copies, whether on a copier or as a saved file.
  • Adapt: make a changed version, such as a translation or a rewrite at a lower reading level. The law calls this a derivative work.
  • Distribute: give or sell copies to others, including by posting a file online.

The other two rights are to perform the work in public and to display it in public.

For a work by an individual author, U.S. protection lasts for the author's life plus 70 years, so most resources a teacher meets today are still protected. The default rule is often summed up as all rights reserved: anyone other than the owner needs permission before doing any of the five things. Permission arrives as a license, a statement from the owner of what others may do.

Exceptions exist. U.S. fair use, for example, allows limited use of a work for purposes such as teaching or commentary. Courts weigh each case separately, and fair use does not give you a blanket right to copy, revise, and share someone's whole resource. This book explains only the parts of copyright you need to read and apply open licenses, and it is not legal advice.

The table below applies the default rule to four everyday actions.

What you want to do Under the default rule Rights involved Read a book you own or borrowed Allowed None Save a copy of a worksheet to your class site Needs permission or a legal exception Reproduce, distribute Translate a reading for your students Needs permission or a legal exception Adapt Post your edited version of a lesson for other schools Needs permission or a legal exception Adapt, distribute

Worked example: a worksheet with no license. A teacher finds a fraction worksheet on a blog. The page shows no license statement.

  1. Is it protected? Yes. Copyright began when the author wrote the worksheet, and a missing notice does not remove it.
  2. What is the default? All rights reserved.
  3. What can she do? She can link to the page, read it, and ask the author for permission. She should not post an edited copy for other teachers.
  4. What is the better route? She can look for a similar worksheet that carries an open license, which the following sections explain.

Public Is Not the Same as Free to Reuse

A page being easy to see does not mean the owner gave permission to copy it. If you cannot find a license statement in the footer, on an "about" page, or in the file itself, treat the work as all rights reserved. Then link to it, ask the owner, or look for an open alternative.

docs.title: Public Domain
docs.text:
The public domain is the set of creative works that no one owns, so anyone may use them in any way without asking. A work reaches the public domain in one of three ways:

  • Expiration: the term of copyright ends. A nineteenth-century novel is in the public domain.
  • Ineligibility: the work was never protected. In the United States, works that federal employees create as part of their official duties are not eligible for copyright, so many federal reports, maps, and images are in the public domain. Most images on NASA's websites fall into this group, but a page may credit a partner who keeps its copyright, so read the credit line.
  • Dedication: the owner gives up their rights on purpose, for example with the Creative Commons CC0 dedication, which Chapter 2 describes.

Write Down Why It Is Public Domain

When you decide a work is public domain, record the reason beside it: the expiry date, the agency that made it, or the CC0 notice. Next semester you or a colleague will ask for that evidence, and the work will not announce it.

docs.title: Commercial Textbooks
docs.text:
A commercial textbook is a textbook that a company publishes to sell, usually under all rights reserved. Students buy, rent, or license it, and they receive a copy to read but not the right to change or share it. Many commercial textbooks come bundled with an access code, a one-time key that unlocks an online homework system for a single term.

These books bring real strengths: professional editing, teacher resources, and tested homework platforms. They also carry limits that matter to this book's topic. A teacher cannot fix an error in the text, replace an example, or post a chapter for students, because each of those uses needs permission the publisher has not granted. New editions arrive every few years, and a used copy of the previous edition may no longer match the course.

Worked example: a bundled text. A community-college biology course requires a commercial textbook bundled with an access code.

  • A student buys the bundle new, rents the book and buys the code, or goes without. The code works for one term and cannot be resold.
  • The instructor finds that chapter 4 uses an outdated classification. She can tell students about the error in class, but she cannot publish a corrected chapter.
  • When the department moves to the next edition, students repeat the purchase.

docs.title: Course Material Affordability
docs.text:
Course material affordability is whether students can pay for the materials a course requires without giving up other needs or skipping the materials. Textbook price is only one part of it, because access codes, lab manuals, and software add to the total. Surveys of college students repeatedly find that many have delayed buying, shared a copy, or gone without a required text because of the price. A student who lacks the text in the first weeks starts the course behind.

Worked example: one course, one section. The figures below are illustrative, not a real price list. A section of 30 students requires a $120 textbook and a $40 access code.

Item Per student 30 students Textbook $120 $3,600 Access code $40 $1,200 Total $160 $4,800

If the course switches to an open textbook with free practice problems, the digital cost is $0 per student. An optional printed copy sold at cost might add $15 for a student who wants one, or $450 if all 30 students chose it. The price changes because the permissions changed: an open license lets a campus print shop make copies without asking the publisher.

docs.title: Free Does Not Mean Open
docs.text:
A free resource is one that costs the user nothing. That statement is only about price. A publisher's sample chapter, a video on a streaming site, and a library e-book are all free to read, yet each may forbid copying, editing, and sharing. People use free to mean two different things: free of charge, and free of restrictions. Open education cares about the second.

The table below compares four resources on both questions.

Resource Costs the user nothing? May the user edit and share it? A publisher's sample chapter marked "All rights reserved" Yes No A lesson plan with a CC BY license Yes Yes, with credit to the author A commercial textbook from the campus store No No An open textbook that a print shop sells at cost Digital copy yes; printed copy no Yes, with credit to the author

Price and Permission Are Separate

Price and permission are two separate dials. A zero on the price dial says nothing about the permission dial, so ask what it costs and what you may do.

docs.title: Open Educational Resources
docs.text:
Open educational resources (OER) are educational resources that are in the public domain or carry an open license. An open license is a copyright license through which the owner gives everyone advance permission to use, adapt, and share the work, so no one has to ask first. The Creative Commons family is the most widely used set of open licenses, and Chapter 2 explains how to read them.

The term open educational resources was adopted at a 2002 UNESCO forum on open courseware. It built on projects such as MIT's OpenCourseWare, announced in 2001, which put course materials online for anyone to use. Today OER include textbooks, lesson plans, quizzes, images, videos, and simulations.

An OER is defined by its permissions, not by its quality, format, or price. A resource is OER when it passes two tests: it is an educational resource, and it is in the public domain or under an open license. Some OER are excellent, some are poor, and some resources that are not OER are excellent. That is why this book teaches evaluation. The word open tells you what you may do, not whether the resource is good.

Worked example: three resources, two tests. The table applies both tests to three resources.

Resource Educational resource? Open license or public domain? OER? A publisher's free sample chapter marked "All rights reserved" Yes No No A lesson plan on a teacher's blog with the notice "Licensed CC BY 4.0" Yes Yes, an open license Yes An image on a federal agency's website, made by the agency's employees Yes, when used to teach Yes, public domain Yes

The third row carries a caution. An agency's page may include images from partners who keep their copyright, so confirm the status of each image you reuse.

Three misunderstandings are common:

  • "OER must be digital." An open license applies to a printed book as well as to a file. Openness is about permission, not medium.
  • "OER must cost nothing." A printed copy costs money to produce, and many open licenses allow a print shop to charge for it.
  • "OER are low quality." OER range from a single teacher's worksheet to full textbooks produced by university projects with peer review. The license tells you nothing about quality, which is why Chapter 3 introduces a rubric.

The MicroSim below gives you practice with the same two tests. It shows 11 resource cards and three bins. Open (OER) holds any resource in the public domain or under an open license, whatever its price. Free but not open holds resources that cost nothing but have no open license. Not free and not open holds resources that cost money and have no open license.

docs.title: Diagram: OER or Not Classifier
docs.text:
Run the OER or Not Classifier MicroSim Fullscreen

OER or Not Classifier

Type: microsim sim-id: oer-or-not-classifier Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: classify Learning Objective: The learner will classify each of 11 described resources as open (OER), free but not open, or not free and not open, by checking its license and public-domain status rather than its price.

Prerequisites: educational resource, copyright, license, public domain, open license, free resource, open educational resource (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of the 11 resource cards the learner commits one of three bins. A placement is correct when it matches the Correct bin column in Content. Mastery is at least 9 of 11 correct on the first run. Only the first committed placement of each card on the first run counts as evidence; replays are practice.

Misconceptions: (1) A resource that is free to download is OER. (2) A resource must be free of charge to be open. (3) A resource posted publicly with no license statement may be reused.

Instructional Rationale: Classifying is an Understand-level action: the learner must apply the definition of open to a concrete case instead of recalling it. Three bins separate price from permission, so a learner who sorts by price alone is shown, case by case, where that rule fails.

Content:

The three bins, shown to the learner at all times:

  • Open (OER): the resource is in the public domain or carries an open license, whatever its price.
  • Free but not open: the resource costs the user nothing but is neither in the public domain nor under an open license.
  • Not free and not open: the resource costs money and is neither in the public domain nor under an open license.

The 11 cards:

# Description shown to the learner Correct bin Why (shown as feedback) 1 A lesson plan on fractions on a teacher's blog, with the notice "Licensed CC BY 4.0" Open (OER) The CC BY license gives advance permission to retain, reuse, revise, remix, and redistribute. 2 A publisher's sample chapter, free to download, stamped "All rights reserved" Free but not open It costs nothing, but all rights are reserved, so no permissions are granted. 3 A commercial biology textbook sold in the campus bookstore Not free and not open It costs money and the publisher reserves all rights. 4 A photograph taken by a NASA employee as part of their job and posted on NASA's website Open (OER) Works made by U.S. federal employees as part of their duties are in the public domain. 5 A video on a streaming site, free to watch, with no license statement Free but not open With no license, the default is all rights reserved. A zero price does not grant permission. 6 An open textbook from a university press under a CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license Open (OER) An open license grants the permissions, with conditions: credit, non-commercial use, and share-alike. 7 An online homework system that requires a $45 access code and forbids copying its questions Not free and not open It costs money and its terms forbid reuse. 8 A quiz bank that its author dedicated to the public domain with CC0 Open (OER) CC0 gives up the owner's rights in advance, so anyone may use the quiz bank. 9 A free online course whose terms say "personal use only; do not copy or share" Free but not open It costs nothing, but the terms forbid copying and sharing. 10 The text of an online encyclopedia article released under CC BY-SA 4.0 Open (OER) The CC BY-SA license permits reuse, revision, remixing, and sharing, with credit and share-alike. 11 An open textbook that is free online under CC BY and also sold in print at cost for $15 by a campus print shop Open (OER) Openness comes from the license, not the price. The printed copy costs money, but the license still grants the permissions.

Provenance: The 11 cards are illustrative cases written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The bin definitions follow the chapter sections "Free Does Not Mean Open" and "Open Educational Resources". The rule about federal works follows the chapter section "Public Domain". The license abbreviations (CC BY, CC BY-NC-SA, CC BY-SA, CC0) are explained in the Why text of each card, and Chapter 2 defines them in full.

Rules: Each card has exactly one correct bin. A resource with no license statement is treated as all rights reserved. Price never moves a resource out of the Open bin: a resource that is in the public domain or under an open license belongs in Open (OER) even when a copy costs money. A resource whose terms forbid copying or sharing is not open, whatever its price.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one card at a time, with the three bins and their definitions.
  2. The learner places the card in a bin. The placement is committed and cannot be changed.
  3. The sim shows whether the placement was correct, moves the card to its correct bin, and shows the Why text.
  4. After the 11th card the sim shows the number of cards placed correctly on the first run, and lists each missed card with its Why text.
  5. The learner may replay with a new shuffle. Replays show the same feedback but do not change the recorded first-run score.

Feedback: 11 cards, shuffled at the start of each run, one attempt per card. Correct: "Correct: [bin]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. This belongs in [correct bin]. [Why]". The correct bin is revealed immediately after each placement. The summary shows "[n] of 11 correct on the first run". At 9 or more it adds "You can tell open from free." Below 9 it lists the Why text of each missed card.

Starting State: The first card and the three empty bins with their definitions. The question shown is "Which bin does this resource belong in?"

Chapter Anchors: The bin names are "Open (OER)", "Free but not open" and "Not free and not open". The chapter defines OER as an educational resource that is in the public domain or carries an open license. The chapter's worked-example table (a publisher's free sample chapter, a CC BY lesson plan, and a federal agency image) matches cards 2, 1 and 4 and their bins.

docs.title: Open Textbooks
docs.text: An open textbook is a complete textbook that carries an open license, so a teacher may adopt, revise, and share it. Most are free to read online, and many offer a printed copy sold at cost. OpenStax, based at Rice University, publishes open textbooks for high-enrollment college courses and some high school courses. The Open Textbook Library, run by the Center for Open Education at the University of Minnesota, catalogs open textbooks together with reviews from faculty.

docs.title: Zero Textbook Cost Courses
docs.text: A zero textbook cost (ZTC) course is a course in which students pay nothing for required learning materials. Colleges often flag ZTC sections in the class schedule so that students can see the cost before they register. A ZTC course often relies on OER, but it need not: a course built on e-books that the library licenses is also ZTC, even though those e-books are free but not open. ZTC describes price. OER describes permissions.

docs.title: The 5R Permissions
docs.text: An open license grants permission for five kinds of actions. Open-education researcher David Wiley named them the 5R permissions: retain, reuse, revise, remix, and redistribute. His first version of the framework had four Rs, and he later added retain. A resource that grants all five is open in the fullest sense. Most open licenses attach conditions, such as giving credit to the author, and Chapter 2 sorts those out. In this section the only question is what each R lets you do.

docs.title: Retain Permission
docs.text:
The retain permission lets you make, own, and control copies of the resource: download it, duplicate it, store it, and manage your own copy. Retain matters because websites change and disappear. A teacher who keeps a copy still has the lesson next year.

Keep the file, not just a link. A bookmark is not a copy: if the site disappears, the bookmark goes with it. Download the document and, when the author offers them, the editable source files.

docs.title: Reuse Permission
docs.text:
The reuse permission lets you use the resource in its original, unaltered form in many settings: a class, a study group, a workshop, a website, or a video.

Reuse stops where change begins. The moment you alter the resource, even to fix a typo, you have moved from reuse to revise, the next permission.

docs.title: Revise Permission
docs.text:
The revise permission lets you adapt, adjust, modify, or alter the resource itself. Typical revisions fix an error, update a statistic, translate the text, lower the reading level, or add local examples. Revise is the permission that separates an open resource from a merely free one. A free resource lets you read it, but only revise lets you improve it for your students. Revision is not limited to text: adding captions to a video, describing an image in alt text, and correcting a spreadsheet formula are all revisions.

Worked example: revising a reading. A teacher uses an openly licensed reading about watersheds.

  1. She saves a copy of the original, which exercises the retain permission.
  2. She replaces a river from another state with the river in her own county.
  3. She corrects an outdated population figure and adds alt text to the two maps.
  4. She records each change, and the original author's credit, at the end of the document.

The result is a revised version, also called an adaptation: a new work derived from the original.

docs.title: Remix Permission
docs.text:
The remix permission lets you combine the original or a revised copy with other open material to create something new, such as a unit built from chapters of two open textbooks plus a public-domain map. Revise changes one work, and remix joins two or more. Remixing requires that the licenses of the parts are compatible, which Chapter 2 explains.

Revise and Remix Blur Together

If revise and remix blur together, that is normal, because most newcomers blur them. You already do both with documents: editing one file is revising, and pasting two files into one is remixing. Ask one question: did I change one work, or combine several?

docs.title: Redistribute Permission
docs.text:
The redistribute permission lets you share copies of the original, revised, or remixed work with others: post it on a website, email it to colleagues, or upload it to a repository. Redistribution is what lets one teacher's improvement reach every other teacher.

Worked example: sharing the revised reading. The teacher has finished the watershed revision.

  1. She uploads the file to her district's shared site and to a public repository.
  2. She adds the license notice that the original requires, so the next teacher knows the permissions.
  3. She credits the original author and labels the file "revised version".
  4. She tells her colleagues where to find it.

Keep a Credit Note With Every File

Keep a one-line credit note with every open file: title, author, license, and where you found it. When you pass the file on, the note travels with it. Credit it, share it, pass it on.

docs.title: Putting the Five Together
docs.text:
The permissions build on one another. You need a copy to use it (retain), you use it before you change it (reuse), and you change it before you combine it or share the result (revise, remix, redistribute). The table below gives each permission a test question that you can ask of any resource.

Permission Plain-language meaning Test question Retain Make and keep your own copy Can I make and keep my own copy? Reuse Use the work as it is Can I use it as it is? Revise Change the work Can I change it? Remix Combine the work with other open work Can I combine it with other open work? Redistribute Share copies with others Can I share copies with others?

Worked example: two resources, five questions. Ask the five test questions of a lesson plan licensed CC BY 4.0 and of the publisher's free sample chapter marked "All rights reserved". The CC BY license attaches one condition, credit to the author.

Test question CC BY 4.0 lesson plan Free sample chapter, all rights reserved Can I make and keep my own copy? Yes Only as far as the site's terms allow Can I use it as it is? Yes Only as far as the site's terms allow Can I change it? Yes No Can I combine it with other open work? Yes No Can I share copies with others? Yes No

Both resources cost nothing, yet they differ on every row. That difference is what the word open measures.

The MicroSim below uses the five test questions. It presents 10 everyday teacher actions, and you name the one permission that each action uses.

docs.title: Diagram: Five R Scenario Matcher
docs.text:
Run the Five R Scenario Matcher MicroSim Fullscreen

Five R Scenario Matcher

Type: microsim sim-id: five-r-scenario-matcher Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: apply Learning Objective: The learner will apply the definitions of the five R permissions to name the one permission that each of 10 classroom actions exercises, with at least 8 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: open license, retain permission, reuse permission, revise permission, remix permission, redistribute permission (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of the 10 scenarios the learner chooses one of the five permissions. A choice is correct when it matches the Correct permission column in Content. Mastery is at least 8 of 10 scenarios answered correctly on the first attempt. Viewing a hint is not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Reuse covers any use, including after changes. (2) Retain means keeping a link to a resource online. (3) Revise and remix are the same permission. (4) Sharing an unchanged copy is reuse.

Instructional Rationale: Apply-level practice needs new situations and a check. Each scenario is worded as a teacher action, so the learner must map the action to a permission rather than recall a definition. The hint models the test question the learner should ask, so the question becomes a habit.

Content:

The five permissions and their test questions:

Permission Test question Retain Can I make and keep my own copy? Reuse Can I use it as it is? Revise Can I change it? Remix Can I combine it with other open work? Redistribute Can I share copies with others?

The 10 scenarios:

# Scenario shown to the learner Correct permission Why (shown as feedback) 1 You download an openly licensed textbook's PDF and its editable source files to your own laptop, so you still have them if the website goes offline. Retain Making and keeping your own copy is the retain permission. 2 You show an openly licensed diagram, unchanged, on the projector during your lesson. Reuse Using a work as it is, in your class, is reuse. 3 You replace a U.S.-only example in an openly licensed science reading with an example from your own watershed. Revise Changing the content of a single work is revising it. 4 You combine two chapters from different open textbooks and a public-domain map into one unit packet. Remix Combining two or more works into something new is remixing. 5 A colleague asks for the open worksheet you use, and you email them an unchanged copy. Redistribute Sharing copies with others is redistributing. 6 You embed an unchanged open video on your course web page. Reuse Using a work as it is, on a website, is reuse. 7 You add alt text to every image in an openly licensed chapter. Revise Adding alt text changes the work, and changing a work is revising it. 8 You merge the terms from two open glossaries into one list and add 20 terms of your own. Remix Merging works into a new one is remixing. 9 You copy the full set of source files of an open lab manual to an external drive for safekeeping. Retain Keeping your own copy for safekeeping is retaining. 10 You have already corrected the errors in an open lab handout. Now you post the corrected handout in a repository so that any teacher can download it. Redistribute Sharing the corrected version with others is redistributing. The correcting was revising, and it is already done.

Provenance: The scenarios are illustrative cases written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The permission names and test questions are those in the chapter sections "The 5R Permissions" and "Putting the Five Together".

Rules: Each scenario has exactly one correct permission, two scenarios per permission. Where a scenario says a step is already done, only the action described as happening now counts. The sim does not test license conditions (credit, share-alike).

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees the five permission names, without their definitions, and the first scenario.
  2. The learner chooses the permission that the action uses.
  3. If the choice is correct, the sim shows the Why text and moves to the next scenario.
  4. If the choice is wrong on the first attempt, the sim shows the test question for the correct permission without naming it, and the learner chooses again.
  5. If the second choice is also wrong, the sim reveals the correct permission and the Why text, and the scenario counts as missed.
  6. After scenario 10 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 10 scenarios, shuffled once per session, two attempts each. First-attempt correct answers count as evidence. Correct: "Correct: [permission]. [Why]". First wrong attempt: "Not yet. Ask yourself: [test question for the correct permission]". Second wrong attempt: "The answer is [permission]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 10 correct on the first attempt". At 8 or more it adds "You can match actions to permissions." Below 8 it lists each missed scenario with its Why text.

Starting State: The five permission names in the order retain, reuse, revise, remix, redistribute, with no definitions, and the first scenario in the shuffled order. The question shown is "Which permission does this action use?"

Chapter Anchors: The five permissions are retain, reuse, revise, remix, and redistribute, in that order. The test questions match the chapter table "Putting the Five Together" word for word. The chapter says the sim presents 10 everyday teacher actions.

Remember that these are permissions, not duties. An open license says what you may do, and you decide what is worth doing. The next section looks at the three ways teachers decide.

docs.title: Adopt, Adapt, or Create
docs.text: Teachers put OER to work in three ways, listed here from least to most effort: adopt, adapt, and create. Sometimes none of them is the right first move, and the right decision is to keep searching. Each way relies on different permissions, and each trades effort against control.

docs.title: OER Adoption
docs.text:
OER adoption means choosing an existing OER and using it as it is for a course. In higher education the word often means selecting an open textbook as the required text, and in K-12 it may mean using an open curriculum for a unit. Adoption relies on the retain and reuse permissions.

Worked example: adopting a statistics textbook. A college instructor wants an open text for introductory statistics.

  1. She compares the table of contents with her course outcomes and lists the gaps.
  2. She reads the license on the title page or the book's website.
  3. She downloads her own copy of the file, which exercises the retain permission.
  4. She gives students the link and tells them the cost: nothing.
  5. She plans short supplements for the gaps she found in step 1.

Adoption is the fastest route, and it gives up control. She gets the text as the authors wrote it.

Adoption still needs evaluation. An open text may be out of date, may assume different prior knowledge than her students have, or may lack practice problems. The question "may I use it?" is answered by the license, and the question "is it good?" stays open until someone checks.

docs.title: OER Adaptation
docs.text:
OER adaptation means changing an existing OER to fit your course, using the revise permission and often the remix permission. Typical adaptations lower the reading level, add local examples, translate the text, add practice questions, or repair accessibility problems such as missing alt text. The adapted version is a new version, and the original stays available.

Worked example: adapting a history chapter. A tenth-grade teacher adopts an open history chapter whose vocabulary is too hard for her class.

  1. She checks that the license allows revised versions to be shared.
  2. She rewrites two dense paragraphs in plainer language and defines four terms.
  3. She adds a local example and alt text for the chapter's three images.
  4. She credits the original author, notes "adapted by" with her name, and shares the new version under the terms the original license requires.

Check the License Before You Edit

Some licenses let you share a resource but not a changed version of it, so check before you edit. Read the license name on the resource, and if you are unsure, ask the owner or choose another resource. Chapter 2 shows how to read each license.

docs.title: OER Creation
docs.text:
OER creation means writing or producing a new educational resource and releasing it under an open license, so that others may use the 5R permissions on your work. It takes the most time and gives the most control. Many teachers start by adapting and remixing existing OER, and create a resource from scratch only when nothing fits.

The table below summarizes the three pathways.

Pathway What you do Permissions it relies on Control you keep Adopt Use an existing OER as it is Retain, reuse Little Adapt Change an existing OER to fit Revise, often remix Some Create Make a new resource and open-license it You hold the rights and choose the license Most

The MicroSim below practices the choice. It uses three facts about a candidate resource and a simple rule of thumb that this chapter proposes. The rule is a heuristic, not an official standard. In four teacher cases you predict the pathway first, and then you explore how the three facts change the answer.

docs.title: Diagram: Adopt Adapt Create Pathway Chooser
docs.text:
Run the Adopt, Adapt, or Create Pathway Chooser MicroSim Fullscreen

Adopt Adapt Create Pathway Chooser

Type: microsim sim-id: adopt-adapt-create-pathway-chooser Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: use Learning Objective: The learner will use a three-fact decision rule (fit to the course, whether revision is permitted, and time available) to choose adopt, adapt, create, or keep searching for four teacher cases, with at least 3 of 4 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: OER adoption, OER adaptation, OER creation, revise permission (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of four cases the learner commits one of four pathways before the rule is shown. A choice is correct when it matches the Correct pathway column in Content. Mastery is at least 3 of 4 correct on the first attempt. Setting the three facts in exploration mode is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Creating a resource is always the best choice because you control everything. (2) Any free resource may be adapted. (3) A partial fit can always be fixed.

Instructional Rationale: Applying a rule to new situations is the Apply-level action. Predicting before the rule is shown makes the learner commit to a pathway, and the exploration afterward shows which of the three facts change the answer and which do not.

Content:

The three facts, each set to one of its values:

Fact Values Meaning Fit to course outcomes Full, Partial, None Full: the resource covers what the course needs. Partial: it covers some of it and needs changes. None: it does not match. Revision permitted Yes, No Yes: the license grants the revise permission. No: it does not. Time available Little, Much Little: fewer than 40 hours of preparation. Much: 40 hours or more. (The 40-hour threshold is illustrative.)

The four pathways: Adopt, Adapt, Create, Keep searching.

The rule, applied in this order:

  1. Fit is Full: the pathway is Adopt, whatever the other two facts are.
  2. Fit is Partial and revision is permitted: the pathway is Adapt.
  3. Fit is Partial and revision is not permitted: the pathway is Keep searching, because a partial fit that may not be changed cannot be fixed.
  4. Fit is None and time is Much: the pathway is Create.
  5. Fit is None and time is Little: the pathway is Keep searching.

All 12 combinations:

Fit Revision permitted Time Pathway Rule Full Yes Little Adopt 1 Full Yes Much Adopt 1 Full No Little Adopt 1 Full No Much Adopt 1 Partial Yes Little Adapt 2 Partial Yes Much Adapt 2 Partial No Little Keep searching 3 Partial No Much Keep searching 3 None Yes Little Keep searching 5 None Yes Much Create 4 None No Little Keep searching 5 None No Much Create 4

The four prediction cases, in this order:

Case Situation shown to the learner Fit Revision permitted Time Correct pathway A An open course packet covers exactly what the unit needs, and its license forbids changes. The teacher has three evenings. Full No Little Adopt B An open reading covers most of a unit but is too hard for the class, its license allows changes, and the teacher has one evening. Partial Yes Little Adapt C An open lab guide covers half of a unit, its license forbids changes, and the teacher has the whole summer. Partial No Much Keep searching D Nothing found matches a unit on local water quality, and the teacher has a full summer. None Yes Much Create

Provenance: The rule is a heuristic written for this chapter, and the sim labels it "a simple rule of thumb, not a standard". The cases are illustrative, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples".

Rules: The pathway for any combination of the three facts is given by the rule above and the 12-row table. Revision permission has no effect when fit is Full or None, and time has an effect only when fit is None. In exploration mode the sim names the rule number that produced the pathway.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads case A and chooses one of the four pathways. The rule is hidden.
  2. The sim shows the correct pathway, the three facts for the case, and the rule that applies. The learner moves on to cases B, C and D in the same way.
  3. After case D, exploration mode opens. The learner sets each of the three facts to any of its values, and the sim shows the pathway and the rule number at once.
  4. The learner should notice that changing revision permission has no effect when fit is Full or None, and that time matters only when fit is None.

Feedback: 4 cases in fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [pathway]. Rule [n]: [rule text]." Incorrect: "Rule [n] applies: [rule text]. So the pathway is [pathway]." The summary shows "[n] of 4 correct on the first attempt". At 3 or more it adds "You can use the rule." Below 3 it lists each missed case with its rule.

Starting State: Case A with the three facts shown and four pathway choices. The question shown is "Which pathway should this teacher take?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter names three pathways in order of effort (adopt, adapt, create) and says that sometimes the right decision is to keep searching. The chapter says the rule is a heuristic, not an official standard, and that the sim uses four cases.

docs.title: Finding OER
docs.text:
An OER repository is an online collection of OER that people can search and browse. A good repository records each resource's subject, grade level, and license, so you can filter before you read. Repositories differ in focus, and the table below summarizes four well-known ones.

Collection Focus OER Commons A public digital library of OER of many types for K-12 and higher education MERLOT A curated collection for higher education, with peer reviews and ratings Open Textbook Library Open textbooks with faculty reviews, from the Center for Open Education at the University of Minnesota LibreTexts A platform of open textbooks that teachers can remix in a browser and export

Worked example: finding a ratios lesson. A sixth-grade teacher wants a lesson on ratios.

  1. She searches for "ratios" and filters by subject, grade level, and an open license.
  2. She opens three results and reads the license statement on each resource, not only in the listing.
  3. She checks the date of each and discards the one that has not been updated in many years.
  4. She downloads the best match, which exercises the retain permission, and records its title, author, and license.

A listing is not an endorsement. A repository holds resources of uneven quality, and the license shown in a listing was entered by a person, so confirm it on the resource itself.

docs.title: Open Pedagogy
docs.text: Open pedagogy is a way of teaching that relies on the 5R permissions, usually by having students create or improve resources that others can use. A disposable assignment is written, graded, and thrown away. A renewable assignment adds lasting value: students in an anatomy course each write and illustrate one section of an open textbook, and later cohorts revise it. Students gain a real audience, and their work outlives the course. Students own the copyright to their own work, so they must choose to release it under an open license, and a teacher should offer a non-public alternative to any student who prefers one.

docs.title: Resource Selection
docs.text:
Resource selection is the process of choosing which resource to use in a course. A first pass often asks five questions:

  • Does it match the course outcomes, meaning what learners should be able to do?
  • What is its license, and does the license permit what I plan to do?
  • Is it accurate and current?
  • Can every learner use it, including learners who use assistive technology?
  • Can I get the editable source so that I can improve it?

Most teachers answer these questions informally, and informal answers vary from one person to the next. Chapter 3 introduces a rubric that scores a resource on ten metrics and records the evidence for each score.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• An educational resource is any material used to support teaching and learning, and every one is protected by copyright unless it is in the public domain or released under an open license.
  • A free resource costs nothing, but only an open license or the public domain makes a resource an open educational resource (OER). Price and permission are separate questions.
  • The 5R permissions are retain, reuse, revise, remix, and redistribute, each answered by a short test question.
  • Teachers adopt, adapt, or create OER, and sometimes the right move is to keep searching. Repositories help you search, and a listing is not an endorsement.
  • Open pedagogy invites students to create resources that others can reuse, with their consent.
  • Resource selection needs a repeatable method, which Chapter 3 begins to supply.

You Have the Vocabulary

You can now define an OER, tell open from merely free, name the 5R permissions, and choose between adopting, adapting, and creating. That vocabulary is the base every later chapter stands on.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Foundations of Open Educational Resources
docs.text: Test your understanding of open educational resources, the 5R permissions, and the ways teachers adopt, adapt, and create OER with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. Which statement best defines an open educational resource (OER)?
docs.text:
1. Any educational resource that the user can read or download without paying
  2. Any complete textbook that a university makes available to read online
  3. Any educational resource that has passed a peer review by its publisher
  4. An educational resource that is in the public domain or carries an open license
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. An OER is an educational resource that is in the public domain or carries an open license, so anyone may use, adapt, and share it without asking first. Option A describes a free resource, which may still forbid copying and editing. Options B and C describe a source and a quality check, and the definition requires neither. Openness is about permission, not about price, publisher, or approval.

Concept Tested: Open Educational Resource

See: Open Educational Resources

docs.title: 2. Under U.S. law, when does copyright protection for a new work begin?
docs.text:
1. When the creator registers the work with the Copyright Office
  2. Automatically, when the work is fixed in a tangible form such as a saved file
  3. When the creator adds a © symbol and an "all rights reserved" notice
  4. When the creator publishes the work for sale or posts it online
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Protection begins the moment a work is fixed in a tangible form, such as a typed document, a saved file, or a recording. Registration, a © symbol, and publication are not required. This is why a worksheet on a blog with no license statement is still protected, and why a teacher should treat it as all rights reserved unless the owner grants permission.

Concept Tested: Copyright

See: Copyright: The Default Rule

docs.title: 3. Which list names the 5R permissions that an open license can grant?
docs.text:
1. Read, reuse, rewrite, resell, redistribute
  2. Retain, reproduce, revise, resell, redistribute
  3. Retain, reuse, revise, remix, redistribute
  4. Reproduce, adapt, distribute, perform, display
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. David Wiley named the 5R permissions retain, reuse, revise, remix, and redistribute. Option D is a tempting mix-up because it lists the five exclusive rights that copyright gives an owner: reproduce, adapt, distribute, perform, and display. Those are what an owner controls by default, while the 5Rs are what an open license hands to everyone else. Options A and B swap in words that are not part of the framework.

Concept Tested: The 5R Permissions

See: The 5R Permissions

docs.title: 4. What makes a material an educational resource?
docs.text:
1. Its format, because only textbooks, articles, and readings count as resources
  2. Its price, because a resource must be free of charge to be used in teaching
  3. Its purpose, because any material that supports teaching and learning counts, whatever its format
  4. Its publisher, because the material must come from a school or a university
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. An educational resource is any material that a teacher or learner uses to support teaching and learning. The definition depends on purpose and not on format: a photograph of a canyon is a family snapshot in an album, and it becomes an educational resource when a teacher uses it to explain erosion. Texts, media, tools, assessments, and plans all qualify, so format (A), price (B), and publisher (D) do not decide it.

Concept Tested: Educational Resource

See: Educational Resources: Everything You Teach With

docs.title: 5. Why is a publisher's free sample chapter marked "All rights reserved" not an OER?
docs.text:
1. It is only an excerpt, and OER must be complete books
  2. It costs nothing but grants no permission to edit or share it
  3. It comes from a company, and OER must come from universities
  4. It is protected by copyright, and OER cannot be copyrighted by their creators
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The sample chapter passes the price test but fails the permission test, because "All rights reserved" grants no permission to revise, remix, or redistribute it. OER can be a single worksheet, so length and source do not matter (A and C). OER are usually copyrighted too: an open license is a permission the owner grants on a protected work, so D reverses how openness works.

Concept Tested: Free Resource

See: Free Does Not Mean Open

docs.title: 6. Under the 5R framework, how does the revise permission differ from the remix permission?
docs.text:
1. Revise lets you share a work with others, while remix allows private use only
  2. Revise applies to text only, while remix applies to images and video
  3. Revise requires the author's approval each time, while remix does not
  4. Revise changes a single work, while remix combines two or more works into something new
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Revising means adapting one work: fixing an error, translating it, or adding alt text. Remixing means joining the work with other open material, such as a unit built from chapters of two open textbooks. Echo's rule of thumb is to ask whether you changed one work or combined several. Sharing copies is the redistribute permission, so option A confuses two of the five. Neither permission is limited by media type or needs fresh approval.

Concept Tested: Remix Permission

See: Remix Permission

docs.title: 7. A teacher downloads an openly licensed textbook's PDF and its editable source files to her own laptop so that she still has them if the website goes offline. Which of the 5R permissions is she using?
docs.text:
1. Retain, because she is making and keeping her own copy
  2. Reuse, because she is using the work in its original form
  3. Revise, because the source files let her change the work
  4. Redistribute, because she is moving copies between devices
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The retain permission covers downloading, duplicating, storing, and managing your own copy. Websites change and disappear, and a bookmark is not a copy, so keeping the files protects next year's lesson. She has not yet changed the work (revise), taught with it (reuse), or given copies to others (redistribute). The test question for retain is, "Can I make and keep my own copy?"

Concept Tested: Retain Permission

See: Retain Permission

docs.title: 8. Why does the chapter say that adopting an open textbook still requires evaluating it?
docs.text:
1. The license shows whether you may use the book, but not whether the book is good
  2. Adopted resources must be revised before any student is allowed to read them
  3. Open licenses expire unless the adopter checks the resource and renews the license each year
  4. Adopting an open textbook transfers its copyright to the adopting teacher
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The license answers "may I use it?", while the question "is it good?" stays open until someone checks. An open text may be out of date, may assume prior knowledge that your students lack, or may have no practice problems. Adoption means using the resource as it is, so revision is optional (B). Open licenses do not expire when unchecked (C), and adoption never transfers copyright (D). This gap is why the book teaches a rubric.

Concept Tested: OER Adoption

See: OER Adoption

docs.title: 9. In open pedagogy, how does a renewable assignment differ from a disposable assignment?
docs.text:
1. A renewable assignment is repeated every term by the same teacher, while a disposable one is given only once and never again
  2. A renewable assignment is graded by classmates, while a disposable assignment is graded by the teacher alone
  3. A renewable assignment uses a commercial textbook for its readings, while a disposable assignment uses an open textbook
  4. A renewable assignment creates lasting value that others can reuse, while a disposable one is written, graded, and discarded
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. A disposable assignment is written, graded, and thrown away. A renewable assignment adds lasting value: for example, each anatomy student writes and illustrates one section of an open textbook that later cohorts revise. The word "renewable" refers to the work's lasting life, not to repeating the task (A) or to who grades it (B). Because students own their work, they must choose to release it openly.

Concept Tested: Open Pedagogy

See: Open Pedagogy

docs.title: 10. A department announces, "Our course is a zero textbook cost course because the library licenses the e-books, so it is built on OER." What is wrong with this reasoning?
docs.text:
1. Zero textbook cost describes price and OER describes permissions, so free library e-books can be zero cost without being open
  2. Zero textbook cost courses may use only printed books and never e-books, because e-books always carry a fee
  3. Library e-books are always in the public domain, so they need no license and no permission at all
  4. OER must carry a price so that the open license can be funded, and a free course cannot be built on OER
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. A ZTC course means students pay nothing for required materials, and it often relies on OER, but it need not. Library-licensed e-books are free to read yet typically forbid copying, editing, and sharing, so they are free but not open. The department has confused the price dial with the permission dial. E-books are allowed in ZTC courses (B), library e-books are rarely public domain (C), and OER have no price requirement (D).

Concept Tested: Zero Textbook Cost Course

See: Zero Textbook Cost Courses

docs.title: References: Foundations of Open Educational Resources
docs.text:
1. Open educational resources - Wikipedia - Defines OER, traces the movement's history, and lists the 5R permissions with examples of repositories and national policies. Anchors this chapter's definition of an OER and its distinction between open and merely free materials.

  2. Copyright - Wikipedia - Explains how copyright arises automatically, how long it lasts, and which exclusive rights it gives creators. Supplies the default rule that makes an explicit open license necessary before a teacher may copy, change, or share a resource.

  3. Free content - Wikipedia - Surveys definitions of free and open content, separating works that merely cost nothing from works that grant freedoms to reuse and modify. Supports the chapter's section explaining why free does not mean open.

  4. Free Culture: How Big Media Uses Technology and the Law to Lock Down Culture and Control Creativity - Lawrence Lessig - Penguin Press (2004) - Lessig's contrast between a "free culture" and a "permission culture" shows why restrictive copyright is the default and why openly licensed work matters. His story-driven framing helps teachers see what the 5R permissions release.

  5. Open: The Philosophy and Practices that are Revolutionizing Education and Science (2017) - Rajiv Jhangiani and Robert Biswas-Diener (eds.) - Ubiquity Press - Includes Robin DeRosa and Scott Robison's chapter "From OER to Open Pedagogy," which argues that students should help build open resources, not only consume them. That idea underlies this chapter's short section on open pedagogy.

  6. Definition of Open - opencontent.org - David Wiley's own statement of the 5R permissions (retain, reuse, revise, remix, redistribute) and why a license must grant all five. This is the source of the 5R framework used throughout the book.

  7. Open Educational Resources - UNESCO - UNESCO's OER hub, including the 2019 Recommendation on OER, the first international standard-setting instrument for openly licensed materials. Shows how governments define OER and why they encourage adoption.

  8. OER Resources for Educators - Creative Commons - A teacher's guide to finding openly licensed images, video, audio, textbooks, simulations, and courses, with pointers to OpenStax, PhET, and OER Commons. Supports the chapter's section on finding OER.

  9. A Guide to Making Open Textbooks with Students - Rebus Community - An open guide in which instructors describe having students create open textbooks and renewable assignments. A practical follow-up to the chapter's discussion of open pedagogy and of creating OER.

  10. OpenStax - Rice University - A nonprofit publisher of free, peer-reviewed college and high-school textbooks under open licenses. A well-known example of an adoptable OER collection, useful for practicing the adopt-adapt-create decision.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Explains the Creative Commons license family, its elements, attribution, and compatibility, so teachers can read a license, give correct credit, and choose a license for their own work. It builds on the 5R permissions and is needed before any chapter scores reusability. After this chapter you can read a Creative Commons license, write a correct attribution statement, and spot a license conflict that blocks reuse.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 23 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Open License 295 License Statement 189 Creative Commons 65 CC0 Dedication 1 Attribution Requirement 21 CC BY 18 ShareAlike Requirement 10 CC BY-SA 5 NonCommercial Requirement 8 CC BY-NC 7 CC BY-NC-SA 4 NoDerivatives Requirement 6 CC BY-ND 4 CC BY-NC-ND 1 License Compatibility 3 License Conflict 1 Attribution Statement 2 TASL Attribution Format 1 Third-Party Content 1 Fair Use 1 Proprietary License 2 All Rights Reserved 1 License Selection 1

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Foundations of Open Educational Resources

Read the Fine Print Without Fear

A license is only a few lines long, but it decides whether the lesson you love can travel to your classroom. By the end of this chapter you will read any Creative Commons license in under a minute, credit it correctly, and spot a conflict before it costs you a week of work. Let's dive in and check the evidence!

Chapter 1 gave you the five permissions and the idea that an open license grants them in advance. This chapter looks at the licenses themselves. Open licenses do not all grant the same freedoms, and the differences decide whether you can translate a reading, sell a printed copy, or combine two resources into one packet.

You will learn the Creative Commons family of licenses, how to read a license statement, how to credit a creator correctly, how to tell when two licenses cannot be combined, and how to choose a license for your own work. Later chapters score how reusable a resource is, and every one of those scores starts from the vocabulary in this chapter.

docs.title: What an Open License Grants
docs.text:
An open license is a license in which the owner of a work gives everyone permission, in advance and at no charge, to do things that copyright would otherwise reserve to the owner. Chapter 1 defined a license as a statement of what others may do. An open license is one that grants the five R permissions (retain, reuse, revise, remix, and redistribute) to the whole public instead of to one person who asked.

Three features separate an open license from a one-time permission:

  • Public: the owner offers it to everyone, not to a named person.
  • In advance: the owner grants it before anyone asks, usually by posting a notice on the work.
  • Standing: people who received the work under the license keep their rights, even if the owner later stops offering the work.

Open licenses attach conditions. Every Creative Commons license except the public domain dedication, for example, requires credit to the creator. Conditions differ from license to license, and they decide how much you can do with a resource. A condition that asks something of you, such as giving credit, costs little. A condition that takes a freedom away, such as banning commercial use or banning changes, makes a license less open, and people disagree about how much less.

Some definitions of openness are strict. The Open Definition published by the Open Knowledge Foundation, for example, accepts only licenses that allow commercial use and changes. Many OER programs accept licenses that restrict commercial use, and fewer accept licenses that forbid changes. This book treats openness as a spectrum, and Chapter 9 shows how the rubric scores a resource's license along it.

Standard licenses also beat homemade ones. Anyone can write "free to use for education" on a page, but the sentence leaves open whether it covers translation, sale, or sharing with a colleague. A standard license answers those questions in advance, it has been tested in courts, and search tools recognize it.

Worked example: three notices. Read each notice below and decide what kind of license it is.

Text found on a page What it is Why "This lesson plan is licensed under CC BY 4.0." Open license It grants permissions to everyone, with one stated condition: credit. "You may view this document for personal use. Copying, editing, or sharing requires written permission." Proprietary license Permission is narrow, and every other use needs a request. "© 2025 Example Press. All rights reserved." All rights reserved No license is granted, and every right is kept.

Look in Three Places

Look for a license in the page footer or "about" page, on the first or last page of the file, and in the file's properties. If all three are silent, treat the work as all rights reserved.

docs.title: Proprietary License
docs.text: A proprietary license is a license that an owner writes to keep control of a work. It grants narrow permission, usually to view or use the work under stated terms, and reserves everything else. Common examples are a publisher's terms of use for a digital textbook, a software end-user license agreement, and a streaming site's terms of service. Proprietary does not mean unfair, and a publisher may have good reasons for its terms. For evaluation the point is practical: a proprietary license permits only the uses it lists, so read it before you assume anything else.

docs.title: All Rights Reserved
docs.text: All rights reserved is a notice that the owner keeps every right that copyright gives and has granted no license. In most countries a work is protected whether or not the notice appears, so a work with no notice at all is treated the same way. A work marked all rights reserved is the opposite of an open resource, because it grants none of the five R permissions in advance. You may still link to it, read it, and ask the owner for permission.

docs.title: Creative Commons
docs.text:
Creative Commons (CC) is a nonprofit organization, founded in 2001, that publishes a standard set of open licenses anyone may apply to their own work. Before CC, an owner who wanted to share generously had to write a custom license and hope it held up. Now the owner picks one of the standard licenses and adds a notice. CC licenses work for text, images, audio, and video.

Every CC license has three layers, so that people, lawyers, and software can each read it:

  • Commons Deed: a short plain-language summary that people can read in a minute.
  • Legal code: the full license text that a court would read.
  • Machine-readable code: metadata that lets search engines and software recognize the license.

CC licenses also have versions, and the current one is 4.0. Terms differ slightly between versions, so a careful credit names the version.

Worked example: finding the three layers. A teacher opens a lesson page whose footer says "CC BY 4.0".

  1. She clicks the footer link and reaches the Commons Deed, the plain-language summary.
  2. At the bottom of the Deed she finds a link to the legal code, the full text.
  3. She views the page source and finds a link marked rel="license", which is the machine-readable layer that search tools use to filter by license.

docs.title: The Four License Elements
docs.text:
Every CC license is built from four elements. Attribution (BY) appears in six of the seven CC tools, and the other three, ShareAlike (SA), NonCommercial (NC), and NoDerivatives (ND), can be added to it. To read a CC license, read which elements it has. The sections below take the elements one at a time and then show how they combine into six licenses.

Think of Switches

Picture the elements as switches on a panel. BY is always on, and each other switch you turn on takes a freedom away from the person who receives the work.

The MicroSim below puts three of these switches in your hands: flip ShareAlike and NonCommercial to watch the license name change and see which freedom each one takes away, and try to turn Attribution off.

docs.title: Diagram: Creative Commons License Switches
docs.text: Run the Creative Commons License Switches MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: Attribution Requirement
docs.text:
The attribution requirement means that anyone who shares the work must give credit to its creator. Under the 4.0 licenses, credit includes the creator's name, any copyright notice the creator supplied, a statement of which license applies and a link to it, a link to the work where practical, and a note of any changes you made. You may give credit in any reasonable way for your medium, such as a caption under an image, a credits slide, or a references page. Credit must not suggest that the creator endorses you or your use.

Credit works in both directions. A creator may ask you to remove their name from a work you have adapted, and the license requires you to do so as far as is reasonably practicable. Credit also does not require the creator's approval. The license grants permission in advance, so you do not need to email the author before you reuse the work.

Worked example: crediting a diagram. A teacher puts an openly licensed diagram of the water cycle on a slide.

  1. She keeps the creator's name, the title, and the link to the original.
  2. She writes the license name and version, with a link to the license.
  3. She places all of this in a small caption under the diagram, because that is where a viewer looks for it.

docs.title: CC BY
docs.text:
CC BY, the Attribution license, has one element: BY. It lets anyone retain, reuse, revise, remix, and redistribute the work, including for money, as long as they credit the creator. It is the most open of the six licenses. Many open textbooks and publicly funded projects choose it, and some funders require it. Choose it when you want your work to travel as far as possible and you accept that others will profit from it and change it. Anyone who adapts the work must note their changes, so readers can tell your words from theirs.

Worked example: commercial reuse of a CC BY worksheet. A district posts a revised CC BY worksheet, and a for-profit tutoring company puts it into a paid course. The license allows this. The company must credit the district and note its changes, but the district cannot stop the sale or demand payment. A creator who is uncomfortable with that outcome should pick a different license before sharing, because the choice cannot be reversed later for copies already out in the world.

docs.title: ShareAlike Requirement
docs.text:
The ShareAlike requirement means that if you share an adaptation, you must license it under the same license, or under one that the license lists as compatible. The aim is to keep improvements open: each new version carries the same freedoms as the one before it. The requirement applies only when you adapt the work. Sharing an unchanged copy brings no extra burden beyond credit. People call this approach copyleft, a play on the word copyright: the license uses copyright law to keep a work free instead of to restrict it. The trade-off is that a ShareAlike work cannot move to a less restrictive license, even to another open license that lacks the ShareAlike condition.

Worked example: translating a ShareAlike reading. A teacher translates a CC BY-SA reading into Spanish and posts it.

  1. She credits the original creator and notes that she translated it.
  2. She marks the translation CC BY-SA, because ShareAlike requires the same license.
  3. She cannot relabel the translation as CC BY, since that would remove the ShareAlike condition from the original.

docs.title: CC BY-SA
docs.text: CC BY-SA combines BY and SA. It allows all five R permissions, including commercial use, and requires every adaptation to carry CC BY-SA too. The text of Wikipedia uses this license, which is why many remixes of Wikipedia text must also be CC BY-SA. The trade-off is compatibility: a ShareAlike work cannot be blended with works whose licenses demand something different, as the section on combining works shows.

docs.title: NonCommercial Requirement
docs.text:
The NonCommercial requirement means that you may not use the work in a way that is primarily intended for commercial advantage or monetary compensation. The words sound clear, but their edges are not. Creative Commons itself has found that people disagree about whether a use is commercial. The table below gives a likely reading for four uses of a CC BY-NC worksheet, and it is a guide rather than legal advice.

Use of the worksheet Likely reading Reason A teacher hands it out in a public school class Allowed No one earns money from it. A blog with paid advertising posts it Not allowed The advertising income makes the use commercial. A tutoring company uses it in paid sessions Not allowed The company earns money from the use. A nonprofit workshop charges $20 to cover room and printing costs Unclear Cost recovery is a gray area, so ask the owner.

NonCommercial Is Blurrier Than It Sounds

Advertising, cost recovery, and paid workshops are gray areas that even experts argue about. If your use touches money in any way, ask the owner in writing before you rely on the work, or choose a resource under a more open license.

docs.title: CC BY-NC
docs.text:
CC BY-NC combines BY and NC. It allows all five R permissions for noncommercial use and requires credit. Teachers like it because it feels protective, but it limits reuse in ways that surprise people. A paid course, a publisher, and a school that sells materials to families may all fall outside it, and a work under CC BY-NC cannot be blended into a resource that allows commercial use. NC can exclude more than people expect: a private school that charges tuition, or a district vendor that bundles materials, may fall outside the license. When you cannot tell whether your setting counts as noncommercial, ask the owner.

Worked example: adapting a CC BY-NC reading. A teacher wants to rewrite a CC BY-NC reading and publish the result as a CC BY resource.

  1. She checks the original license and finds NC.
  2. She sees that releasing her version as CC BY would let anyone sell it, which the original forbids.
  3. She decides to publish her version under CC BY-NC, or CC BY-NC-SA, so that the noncommercial limit stays in place.

The MicroSim below tests your judgment on ten uses of a CC BY-NC worksheet. For each use you decide whether it is clearly allowed, unclear, or likely not allowed. The goal is to learn where the clear cases end and the gray area begins, so that you know when to ask the owner.

docs.title: Diagram: NonCommercial Gray Area Sorter
docs.text:
Run the NonCommercial Gray Area Sorter MicroSim Fullscreen

NonCommercial Gray Area Sorter

Type: microsim sim-id: noncommercial-gray-area-sorter Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: judge Learning Objective: The learner will judge whether each of ten uses of a CC BY-NC resource is clearly allowed, unclear, or likely not allowed, with at least 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: NonCommercial Requirement, CC BY-NC, Attribution Requirement (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each use the learner commits one of three bins. A placement is correct when it matches the Correct bin column in Content. Mastery is at least 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt. Reading the bin definitions is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) NonCommercial means free of charge. (2) A nonprofit is always noncommercial. (3) Selling at cost is always noncommercial. (4) Advertising on a free page does not count as commercial.

Instructional Rationale: Judging a use against a criterion is an Evaluate-level action, and the NonCommercial criterion is vague enough to need judgment. Three bins, including an explicit "unclear" bin, teach the learner that ask-the-owner is a valid answer and not a failure to decide.

Content:

The criterion, shown at all times: a use is noncommercial when it is not primarily intended for or directed toward commercial advantage or monetary compensation.

The three bins:

  • Clearly allowed: no one earns money from the use.
  • Unclear: ask the owner: the use touches money in a way reasonable people disagree about.
  • Likely not allowed: the use earns money or is directed toward earning it.

The ten uses of a CC BY-NC worksheet:

# Use shown to the learner Correct bin Why (shown as feedback) 1 A public-school teacher hands the worksheet out in class. Clearly allowed No one earns money from the use. 2 A teacher posts the worksheet on a free class website with no advertising. Clearly allowed No payment or advertising income is involved. 3 A blog with paid advertising posts the worksheet. Likely not allowed The advertising income makes the use commercial. 4 A tutoring company uses the worksheet in sessions that parents pay for. Likely not allowed The company earns money from sessions that use the worksheet. 5 A nonprofit workshop charges $20 to cover room and printing costs. Unclear: ask the owner Cost recovery is a gray area, because the charge is not profit but is still payment. 6 A university department prints copies and sells them at cost in its bookstore. Unclear: ask the owner Selling at cost is a gray area, because the sale is not for profit but is still a sale. 7 A publisher sells a printed edition for profit. Likely not allowed Sale for profit is commercial advantage. 8 A teacher places the worksheet in a paid online course on a marketplace. Likely not allowed The course earns money from learners who pay for it. 9 Teachers exchange the worksheet through a free file-sharing group, with no payment. Clearly allowed An exchange with no payment is noncommercial. 10 A school district uses the worksheet in free training for its own teachers. Clearly allowed No one is charged, and the use is not directed toward earning money.

Provenance: The criterion is the Creative Commons definition of NonCommercial, paraphrased in the chapter section "NonCommercial Requirement". The ten uses are illustrative cases written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The sim states that the bins are a likely reading and not legal advice.

Rules: Each use has exactly one correct bin. Only the "Clearly allowed" bin means no permission is needed. The "Unclear" bin is a valid answer, and it is correct for exactly the uses marked Unclear in the table.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one use at a time, with the criterion and the three bins.
  2. The learner places the use in a bin, and the placement is committed.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text.
  4. After the 10th use the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 10 uses in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [bin]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. This is [bin]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 10 correct on the first attempt". At 8 or more it adds "You can spot when to ask the owner." Below 8 it lists the Why text of each missed use.

Starting State: The first use, the criterion, and the three empty bins. The question shown is "Is this use allowed under CC BY-NC?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's table of four uses agrees with this sim: the classroom handout is allowed (use 1), the advertising blog is not allowed (use 3), the tutoring company is not allowed (use 4), and the $20 nonprofit workshop is unclear (use 5).

docs.title: CC BY-NC-SA
docs.text: CC BY-NC-SA adds ShareAlike to CC BY-NC. Credit is required, use must be noncommercial, and every adaptation must carry CC BY-NC-SA. It is a common choice for course materials from universities. It is also easy to get stuck with, because it cannot be combined with a CC BY-SA work: one requires noncommercial use and the other requires that commercial use remain possible.

docs.title: NoDerivatives Requirement
docs.text:
The NoDerivatives requirement means that you may share the work only as it is. You may not share a version that you have changed. The license does not forbid private changes, so you may adjust a copy for your own study, but sharing that adjusted copy is not allowed. In an OER setting this limit is severe, because it blocks the revise and remix permissions for anyone who wants to share the result.

Worked example: alt text on an ND chapter. A teacher finds a CC BY-ND chapter whose images lack alt text.

  1. She may add alt text to a copy for her own reading.
  2. Giving that changed copy to students or colleagues counts as sharing, and the license does not allow it.
  3. She can ask the owner for permission to share the improved version, or she can choose a resource that allows changes.

ND Blocks the Fixes This Book Teaches

Adding alt text, lowering a reading level, and fixing an error all change the work, so an ND license stops you from sharing any of them. If sharing the improved version matters to you, ask the owner for written permission or pick a different resource.

docs.title: CC BY-ND
docs.text: CC BY-ND combines BY and ND. You may share the unchanged work, including commercially, with credit. You may not share any changed version, whether it is a translation, a summary, or a remix. It suits a creator who wants wide distribution of a finished piece, such as a report, and no variations.

docs.title: CC BY-NC-ND
docs.text: CC BY-NC-ND combines all three restrictions. You may share the unchanged work, for noncommercial purposes only, with credit. It is the most restrictive of the six licenses and the one that gives teachers the least to work with. A resource under it can be read, assigned, and passed along, but it cannot be improved and shared.

docs.title: CC0 Dedication
docs.text: The CC0 dedication, written CC0 1.0 Universal, is a Creative Commons tool for placing a work in the public domain. It is not a license that adds conditions. The creator gives up copyright and related rights as far as the law of their country allows, and where the law does not allow giving them up, CC0 acts as a license with no conditions. Credit is not legally required for CC0 work, though giving credit is good practice and helps readers find the source. Creators use CC0 for data sets, quiz banks, and other material where they want no friction at all.

docs.title: The Six Licenses Together
docs.text:
