The four elements combine into six licenses. ShareAlike and NoDerivatives never appear together, because ShareAlike governs adaptations that NoDerivatives forbids you to share. The table summarizes what each license allows, with CC0 added for comparison.

License Elements Share unchanged Share a changed version Commercial use Rule for changed versions CC0 None Yes Yes Yes None CC BY BY Yes Yes Yes Keep the credit and note changes CC BY-SA BY, SA Yes Yes Yes Same license, CC BY-SA CC BY-NC BY, NC Yes Yes No Stay noncommercial CC BY-NC-SA BY, NC, SA Yes Yes No Same license, CC BY-NC-SA CC BY-ND BY, ND Yes No Yes Sharing a changed version is not allowed CC BY-NC-ND BY, NC, ND Yes No No Sharing a changed version is not allowed

Creative Commons orders the licenses from most to least permissive: CC0, CC BY, CC BY-SA, CC BY-NC, CC BY-NC-SA, CC BY-ND, and CC BY-NC-ND. Each step down takes away a freedom from the person receiving the work. The first MicroSim below makes this concrete. You switch elements on and off, predict what a license allows, and check your prediction against the license's actual terms.

docs.title: Diagram: Creative Commons Element Explorer
docs.text:
Run the Creative Commons Element Explorer MicroSim Fullscreen

Creative Commons Element Explorer

Type: microsim sim-id: cc-element-explorer Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: infer Learning Objective: The learner will infer whether each of five actions is allowed under a given Creative Commons license by reasoning from its elements, with at least 7 of 8 predictions correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Attribution Requirement, ShareAlike Requirement, NonCommercial Requirement, NoDerivatives Requirement, CC BY, CC BY-SA, CC BY-NC, CC BY-NC-SA, CC BY-ND, CC BY-NC-ND (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: The learner commits a Yes or No for each of 8 prompts before the answer is shown. A prediction is correct when it matches the Correct answer column in Content. Mastery is at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Switching elements on and off in explore mode is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) NoDerivatives forbids all changes, including private ones. (2) NonCommercial only forbids selling the exact file. (3) ShareAlike applies to unchanged copies. (4) Any element can be combined with any other.

Instructional Rationale: Inferring is an Understand-level action, so the learner must reason from the elements to a result instead of reading it from a chart. Explore mode lets the learner build the mental model first, and committed predictions afterward make them test it before the answer appears.

Content:

The four elements: BY (Attribution), SA (ShareAlike), NC (NonCommercial), ND (NoDerivatives). BY is always on. SA and ND cannot both be on, and the sim explains why: ShareAlike governs adaptations that NoDerivatives forbids anyone to share.

The five actions:

  • A1: Post an unchanged copy on your website, with credit.
  • A2: Post a translated version.
  • A3: Sell printed copies for profit.
  • A4: Publish a remix of it under CC BY.
  • A5: Change it privately for your own use and do not share it.

The result for each license and action:

License A1 A2 A3 A4 A5 CC BY Yes Yes Yes Yes Yes CC BY-SA Yes Yes (translation must be CC BY-SA) Yes No (remix must be CC BY-SA) Yes CC BY-NC Yes Yes (noncommercial only) No No (CC BY would allow commercial use) Yes CC BY-NC-SA Yes Yes (must be CC BY-NC-SA) No No Yes CC BY-ND Yes No (ND forbids sharing changes) Yes No Yes CC BY-NC-ND Yes No No No Yes

The eight predictions, in this order:

# License Action Correct answer Why (shown as feedback) 1 CC BY-SA A2 Yes Translations are allowed, and the translation must carry CC BY-SA. 2 CC BY-ND A2 No ND forbids sharing a changed version, and a translation is a change. 3 CC BY-NC A3 No NC forbids use directed toward monetary compensation. 4 CC BY A3 Yes BY allows commercial use with credit. 5 CC BY-NC-ND A5 Yes ND blocks sharing changed versions, not private changes. 6 CC BY-SA A4 No SA requires the remix to carry CC BY-SA, not CC BY. 7 CC BY-NC-SA A2 Yes A translation is allowed if it is noncommercial and carries CC BY-NC-SA. 8 CC BY-ND A1 Yes ND allows sharing the unchanged work with credit.

Provenance: The result table applies the element definitions in the chapter sections "The Four License Elements" and "The Six Licenses Together". The actions are illustrative cases written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples".

Rules: A license is the set of elements switched on, and only the six valid combinations exist. A1 is Yes for every license because every license allows sharing the unchanged work with credit. A5 is Yes for every license because no license forbids private changes. For every other cell, apply the result table. The sim states that the table follows the 4.0 licenses and is a study aid, not legal advice.

Learner Activity:

  1. In explore mode the learner switches NC, SA, and ND on or off. BY stays on, and turning on SA while ND is on, or the reverse, shows the explanation instead of a change.
  2. After each switch the sim shows the license name and the Yes or No result for all five actions, with the reason for each No.

  4. The learner commits an answer, and the sim shows the correct answer with the Why text.
  5. After prediction 8 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 8 predictions in the fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [answer]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. The answer is [answer]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 8 correct on the first attempt". At 7 or more it adds "You can read a license from its elements." Below 7 it lists the Why text of each missed prediction.

Chapter Anchors: The chapter says the elements combine into six licenses and that SA and ND never appear together. The chapter's table "The Six Licenses Together" agrees with this result table for sharing unchanged copies, sharing changed versions, and commercial use.

The second MicroSim is a comparison poster. A poster suits the six licenses because the reader's question is "which license is which?", and a labeled picture with hover zones answers it faster than a paragraph.

docs.text:

Six Creative Commons Licenses Poster

The poster is a flat comparison illustration with six equal panels in two rows of three. Each panel prints the license's short name and shows the license's icons, and each carries a simple pictogram that suggests its main rule. The printed text is limited to the six license names. All other words come from the explore and quiz data. The six zones, one per panel:

Zone id Label Summary Facts shown on hover or click cc-by CC BY Credit is the only condition. Credit the creator and link to the license. Share, adapt, and sell, including for profit. All five R permissions remain. The most open of the six. cc-by-sa CC BY-SA Credit, and keep adaptations open the same way. Credit the creator. Commercial use is allowed. Every adaptation must carry CC BY-SA. Wikipedia text uses it. cc-by-nc CC BY-NC Credit, and no commercial use. Credit the creator. Adaptations are allowed. Use must be noncommercial. Adaptations must stay noncommercial. cc-by-nc-sa CC BY-NC-SA Credit, noncommercial, and the same license on adaptations. Credit the creator. Use must be noncommercial. Every adaptation must carry CC BY-NC-SA. cc-by-nd CC BY-ND Credit, and share the work unchanged only. Credit the creator. Commercial use is allowed. You may not share a changed version. Private changes are allowed. cc-by-nc-nd CC BY-NC-ND Credit, noncommercial, unchanged only. Credit the creator. Use must be noncommercial. You may not share a changed version. The most restrictive of the six.

The six quiz questions, in this order:

# Question Correct zone Why (shown as feedback) 1 Which license allows commercial use and requires every adaptation to carry the same license? cc-by-sa SA keeps adaptations open, and without NC, commercial use stays allowed. 2 Which license allows noncommercial use only and forbids sharing changed versions? cc-by-nc-nd It combines NC and ND. 3 Which license allows commercial use but forbids sharing changed versions? cc-by-nd ND blocks changed versions, and there is no NC element. 4 Which license requires noncommercial use and the same license on every adaptation? cc-by-nc-sa It combines NC and SA. 5 Which license places no condition on the work beyond credit? cc-by BY is the only element. 6 Which license allows noncommercial adaptations and does not dictate the adaptation's license? cc-by-nc NC without SA lets adapters choose, as long as use stays noncommercial.

Provenance: The facts follow the chapter sections "The Four License Elements" and "The Six Licenses Together". The statement that Wikipedia text uses CC BY-SA follows the chapter section "CC BY-SA". The illustration is synthetic, and it carries no statistics.

Rules: Each question has exactly one correct zone. Zones are distinct regions of the poster, so a click belongs to at most one zone. Because the poster prints its own panel titles, the sim does not add its own zone labels over the image.

Learner Activity:

  1. In explore mode the learner hovers or clicks a panel and reads its summary and facts.
  2. In quiz mode the sim shows question 1 above the poster.
  3. The learner clicks the panel they think matches.
  4. The sim shows the Why text and moves to the next question, until question 6 is done.

Feedback: 6 questions in the fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [label]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. The answer is [label]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 6 correct on the first attempt". At 5 or more it adds "You can tell the six licenses apart." Below 5 it lists the Why text of each missed question.

Starting State: The poster with no zone selected, explore mode active, and the prompt "Hover a panel to learn what the license allows."

Chapter Anchors: The chapter says there are six licenses, lists them as CC BY, CC BY-SA, CC BY-NC, CC BY-NC-SA, CC BY-ND, and CC BY-NC-ND, and states that Wikipedia text uses CC BY-SA.

docs.title: License Statement
docs.text:
A license statement is the notice that tells readers which license applies to a work. A complete statement does four things. It names the license and its version, it links to the license text, it identifies the owner, and it says what the statement covers. The standard Creative Commons wording is short, such as "This work is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License", followed by a link to the license page.

Place the statement where readers will meet it: the footer of every page, the title page of a book, the last slide of a deck, or the description of a video. A statement that sits only on the home page leaves a reader on page 40 guessing. For readers who use search tools, add machine-readable marking as well, such as a link marked rel="license" in the page's code, so that a filter for "reusable" resources can find the work.

A statement is a claim, and claims need checking. A page can show a license icon that its owner never intended, or a site can copy a work and add a license that the original never carried. The reliable check is to follow the link back to the original source and confirm the license there. When the statement and the source disagree, the source wins.

Only an owner can grant a license. Suppose a teacher-sharing site marks a worksheet CC BY, but the worksheet's own pages say the uploader copied it from a publisher's book. The marking is worthless, because the uploader never held the rights to give away. This is why you trace a resource to its original creator before you rely on its statement, and why Chapter 14 asks you to check an AI agent's reading of a license the same way.

Before you look at an annotated example, three terms need defining. The scope is what the statement covers: this page, the whole book, or only the text. The version is the release of the license, such as 4.0. The holder is the person or organization that owns the copyright. The table below applies the four-part test to four statements.

Worked example: grading four statements. The statements are made-up examples.

Statement Verdict What to do "Licensed under CC BY 4.0, https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/. © 2025 Maria Lopez. Applies to all text on this page." Complete License, version, link, holder, and scope are all present. "Some rights reserved." Incomplete No license is named. Look for the source or ask the owner. "Free to use." Not a license The words do not say which uses are allowed. Ask, or treat the work as all rights reserved. "Licensed under Creative Commons." Incomplete Which of the six, and which version? Check the source before you reuse it.

docs.title: Third-Party Content
docs.text:
Third-party content is material inside a resource that someone other than the resource's owner created, such as a photograph, a chart, or a quotation. A page's license statement usually covers only what the page's owner made. Phrases like "except where otherwise noted" warn you that some items carry other licenses. Before you reuse a page, check the caption or credit line of each image and figure.

For example, suppose a CC BY textbook includes a photo credited "Used with permission of Example Agency." The textbook's license covers the author's own text and diagrams. The photo is not covered, so you may not copy it into your remix without the agency's permission.

Follow the Link Back

If you find a license statement on a copy, follow its link back to the original and read the license there. Copies can lose a statement or change it, and the original is the evidence.

The MicroSim below puts a license statement under a magnifying glass. The illustration shows the footer of an open lesson page, and its seven numbered markers point to the parts of a complete statement. In explore mode you read what each part does. In quiz mode you match a visual clue to its marker.

docs.title: Diagram: Anatomy of a License Statement
docs.text:
Run the Anatomy of a License Statement MicroSim Fullscreen

Anatomy of a License Statement

Type: infographic sim-id: license-statement-anatomy Library: html Status: Specified Bloom Level: Remember Bloom Verb: identify Learning Objective: The learner will identify the seven parts of a complete license statement on an annotated page footer from a description of each part, with at least 6 of 7 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: License Statement, Open License, Creative Commons, Third-Party Content (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: In quiz mode the learner clicks the marker that matches a visual hint. A click is correct when it matches the marker named in the Hint column of Content. Mastery is at least 6 of 7 correct on the first attempt. Hovering markers in explore mode is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) The license icons alone are the license. (2) "CC BY" without a version is a complete statement. (3) A license statement on a page covers every image on it.

Instructional Rationale: Identifying the parts of a statement is a Remember-level task, and an annotated illustration places each part where it appears on a real page. The quiz asks the learner to recognize a part from how it looks, which is how they will find it on real pages.

Content:

The illustration is a text-free flat drawing of the bottom of a lesson web page inside a simple browser frame. Across the footer bar, left to right, are a row of four small round badge icons, two short stacked lines of text, an underlined link-shaped bar, and a copyright symbol beside a short name line. Above the footer is a framed picture thumbnail with a thin caption strip beneath it. At the far right of the footer is a small code-bracket icon, drawn as a shape. The seven markers:

# Label Hint (describes the look, not the name) Description Tip 1 License badge icons A row of four small round icons at the left of the footer. The icons show at a glance which license elements apply. They are a hint, not the license itself. Icons are easy to copy onto a page with no license, so always confirm the written statement. 2 License name and version Two short stacked lines of text beside the icons. The exact license name, for instance Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International. The version matters because terms differ between versions. "CC BY" alone leaves the version open. Write the full name or the version number. 3 Link to the license An underlined bar that looks like a hyperlink. A link to the license page, so readers can check the real terms. Check that the link goes to the Creative Commons site and not to a copy. 4 Copyright holder and year A copyright symbol beside a short name line. Names who holds the copyright and when. This is the person to credit and the person to ask for permission. The work of a school employee may belong to the school, so the named holder is the one to ask. 5 Scope of the license A thin line directly under the license name. States what the license covers: this page, the whole book, or only the text. A missing scope is a question to ask the owner, not an assumption. 6 Notice for third-party content The thin caption strip beneath the picture thumbnail. Marks material that someone else owns or that carries a different license, for instance a photo used with permission. Treat each image as separately licensed until its caption says otherwise. 7 Machine-readable license marking The small code-bracket icon at the far right of the footer. Hidden markup, like a link marked rel="license", lets search tools filter by license. Readers cannot see it on the page. Look in the page source, or use a search tool's license filter.

Provenance: The seven parts follow the chapter section "License Statement" and its example statements. The illustration is synthetic, and the sim labels the page "illustrative example".

Rules: Each hint matches exactly one marker. The illustration contains no text, so every label comes from the table above. Markers are numbered 1 to 7 in the order of the table.

Learner Activity:

  1. In explore mode the learner hovers or clicks a marker and reads its label, description, and tip.
  2. In quiz mode the sim shows a hint, for instance "A row of four small round icons at the left of the footer".
  3. The learner clicks the marker they think the hint describes.
  4. If the first click is wrong, the sim says the click was wrong and lets the learner try once more. If the second click is also wrong, the sim reveals the marker and its description.
  5. After all 7 hints the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 7 hints in a shuffled order, two attempts each. Only a correct first click counts as evidence. Correct: "Correct: [label]. [Description]". First wrong click: "Not quite. Look again at the hint: [hint]". Second wrong click: "This is [label]. [Description]". The summary shows "[n] of 7 correct on the first attempt". At 6 or more it adds "You can find every part of a license statement." Below 6 it lists the labels of the missed parts.

Starting State: The illustration with seven numbered markers, explore mode active, and the prompt "Hover a marker to see what it is."

Chapter Anchors: The chapter says a complete license statement names the license and its version, links to the license text, identifies the owner, and says what the statement covers. The illustration shows seven parts, and the chapter's text mentions the scope, version, and holder.

docs.title: Attribution Statement
docs.text: An attribution statement is the credit line that meets the attribution requirement. It tells readers who made the work, where it came from, and under which license it may be used. A good attribution statement is short, sits next to the item it credits, and gives the reader enough to find the original in a minute. If you changed the work, the statement also says what you changed, such as "translated into Spanish" or "reading level lowered." A statement that only says "image from the internet" gives no usable credit.

docs.title: TASL Attribution Format
docs.text:
The TASL attribution format is a four-part pattern that Creative Commons recommends for credit lines. TASL stands for Title, Author, Source, and License. Writing the four parts in order makes a statement hard to get wrong. The table shows what each part contains, using a made-up resource.

Part What to write Example Title The work's name, in quotation marks "Watershed Basics" Author The creator, and the organization if one is named Maria Lopez Source A link to the work https://example.org/watershed-basics License The license name and version, linked to the license CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)

Joined together, the credit reads: "Watershed Basics" by Maria Lopez, https://example.org/watershed-basics, licensed under CC BY 4.0. If you adapted it, add a sentence such as "Adapted: reading level lowered and two examples localized."

The MicroSim below gives you eight credit lines to inspect. For each one you decide which TASL parts are missing, and whether a change note is also needed.

docs.title: Diagram: Attribution Statement Checker
docs.text:
Run the Attribution Statement Checker MicroSim Fullscreen

Attribution Statement Checker

Type: microsim sim-id: attribution-statement-checker Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: assess Learning Objective: The learner will assess whether each of eight attribution statements is complete by identifying exactly which of the five checked parts are missing, with at least 7 of 8 judged correctly on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Attribution Requirement, Attribution Statement, TASL Attribution Format, CC BY (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each statement the learner marks which of five parts are missing, or marks none. A judgment is correct when the marked set equals the Missing parts column in Content exactly. Mastery is at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the checklist definitions is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) "CC BY" without a version is a complete license part. (2) A copyright line with no license counts as credit. (3) A change note is needed even when the work is unchanged. (4) A site name is a source link.

Instructional Rationale: Assessing a credit line against a criterion list is an Evaluate-level action, and the checklist makes the criteria explicit so the learner judges against standards, not impressions. Eight statements with different mixes of gaps force the learner to apply each criterion separately.

Content:

The resource record that every statement refers to (a made-up resource): Title "Watershed Basics", Author Maria Lopez, Source https://example.org/watershed-basics, License CC BY 4.0, license link https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/.

The five checked parts and when each counts as present:

Part Counts as present when Title The work's name appears. Author The creator's name appears. Source A link to the work appears. A site name alone does not count. License A specific license with its version, or a link to it, appears. "Creative Commons" alone or "CC BY" with no version or link does not count. Change note A sentence says what was changed. Required only when the use changed the work.

The eight statements:

# Use Statement shown Missing parts Why (shown as feedback) 1 Unchanged "Watershed Basics" by Maria Lopez, https://example.org/watershed-basics, licensed under CC BY 4.0. None All four TASL parts are present, and no change note is needed. 2 Unchanged Maria Lopez, Watershed Basics. Source, License The link and the license are missing. 3 Unchanged "Watershed Basics", https://example.org/watershed-basics, licensed CC BY. Author, License The creator is not named, and "CC BY" has no version or link. 4 Unchanged "Watershed Basics" by Maria Lopez, https://example.org/watershed-basics, licensed under a Creative Commons license. License The statement does not say which license or version. 5 Unchanged Image courtesy of Maria Lopez. Title, Source, License The work is not named, linked, or licensed. 6 Changed: reading level lowered, two examples localized "Watershed Basics" by Maria Lopez, https://example.org/watershed-basics, licensed under CC BY 4.0. Adapted: reading level lowered and two examples localized. None The four TASL parts and the change note are all present. 7 Changed: translated into Spanish "Watershed Basics" by Maria Lopez, https://example.org/watershed-basics, licensed under CC BY 4.0. Change note The work was translated, and the statement does not say so. 8 Changed: shortened © Maria Lopez. All rights reserved. Title, Source, License, Change note The statement claims all rights reserved, which contradicts the CC BY license, and it omits the title, link, and change note.

Provenance: The resource, creator, and URL are made up, and the sim labels them "illustrative example". The checked parts follow the chapter sections "Attribution Requirement", "Attribution Statement", and "TASL Attribution Format".

Rules: Each statement has a fixed set of missing parts, and the empty set is valid. A part is present only when it meets the "Counts as present when" rule. Change note is checked only for statements 6, 7, and 8, where the use column says the work was changed. For statements 1 to 5, Change note is not offered as a choice.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees the resource record, the use, and the statement.
  2. The learner marks each missing part, or marks "None missing".
  3. The learner presses Check. The sim shows the correct set and the Why text.
  4. The learner moves to the next statement, until statement 8 is done.

Feedback: 8 statements in the fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. Missing: [missing parts, or none]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 8 correct on the first attempt". At 7 or more it adds "You can check a credit line." Below 7 it lists the Why text of each missed statement.

Starting State: The resource record, the five parts and their rules, and statement 1 with all five parts unmarked. The question shown is "Which parts are missing?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter says TASL stands for Title, Author, Source, and License, and its example credit line matches statement 1. The chapter says that a statement for an adapted work adds a change note.

docs.title: License Compatibility
docs.text:
License compatibility is whether the licenses of two or more sources can all be satisfied at once by a single license on the combined work. You need it whenever you remix: a unit built from a CC BY chapter and a CC BY-SA chapter must carry one license, and that license must honor both sources. A simple method works for the six licenses. For each source, write what it requires of the combined work, then look for a license that meets every requirement. If more than one qualifies, use the first in the order CC BY, CC BY-SA, CC BY-NC, CC BY-NC-SA.

Source license What it requires of the combined work CC0 Nothing. CC BY Credit, and any CC license that keeps the credit. CC BY-SA The combined work must be CC BY-SA. CC BY-NC The combined work must be noncommercial. CC BY-NC-SA The combined work must be CC BY-NC-SA. Any ND license The source cannot be changed or blended and then shared.

Worked example: three combinations. Apply the table to three pairs of sources.

  1. CC BY with CC BY-SA: the second source requires CC BY-SA, and CC BY accepts it, so the result is CC BY-SA.
  2. CC BY-NC with CC BY-NC-SA: the first needs noncommercial use, the second requires CC BY-NC-SA, and that satisfies both, so the result is CC BY-NC-SA.
  3. CC BY-ND with any other source: the ND source cannot be changed or blended and then shared, so the combination cannot be shared at all.

This is a rule of thumb for study. Creative Commons publishes its own compatibility chart, and you should check it for any real combination.

docs.title: License Conflict
docs.text:
A license conflict is a case where no single license satisfies all the sources, so the combined work cannot legally be shared. CC BY-SA and CC BY-NC conflict: one requires the whole work to be CC BY-SA, which allows commercial use, and the other requires noncommercial use. CC BY-SA and CC BY-NC-SA also conflict, because each demands that the work carry its own license. When you face a conflict you have three choices. You can pick a different resource for one of the parts. You can ask an owner in writing to permit different terms. Or you can keep the works separate, each with its own license notice, so that you are not blending them into one work. Whether a packet counts as blended can be a judgment call, so ask the owners if you are unsure.

Compatibility Trips Up Almost Everyone

If license compatibility feels slippery, that is normal, because even experienced reviewers check a chart. You already solve problems like this when you match two schedules, and the same method works here. List what each source requires, then look for one license that meets all of it.

The MicroSim below gives you ten pairs of sources to combine. For each pair you choose the license the combined work may carry, or you recognize a conflict or a blocked combination.

docs.title: Diagram: License Compatibility Checker
docs.text:
Run the License Compatibility Checker MicroSim Fullscreen

License Compatibility Checker

Type: microsim sim-id: license-compatibility-checker Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: solve Learning Objective: The learner will solve ten license-combination problems by finding the license a combined work may carry, or by recognizing a conflict or a blocked combination, with at least 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: License Compatibility, License Conflict, CC BY, CC BY-SA, CC BY-NC, CC BY-NC-SA, CC BY-ND, CC BY-NC-ND, CC0 Dedication (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each pair the learner chooses one of six outcomes. A choice is correct when it matches the Correct outcome column in Content. Mastery is at least 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt. Viewing the requirements table is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Any two Creative Commons licenses can be combined. (2) The more restrictive license always wins. (3) CC BY-SA and CC BY-NC can be combined if the author gives credit. (4) An ND source can be remixed if the remix is credited.

Instructional Rationale: Solving combination problems is an Apply-level task, and ten pairs of increasing difficulty make the learner execute the same procedure repeatedly: write each source's requirement, intersect them, and choose the first qualifying license. Immediate feedback with the worked reasoning builds the habit.

Content:

The six outcomes the learner can choose: CC BY, CC BY-SA, CC BY-NC, CC BY-NC-SA, Conflict (no license satisfies both), Blocked (an ND source cannot be shared in a combined work).

What each source requires of the combined work, written as the set of licenses it allows:

Source Licenses the combined work may carry CC0 CC BY, CC BY-SA, CC BY-NC, CC BY-NC-SA CC BY CC BY, CC BY-SA, CC BY-NC, CC BY-NC-SA CC BY-SA CC BY-SA CC BY-NC CC BY-NC, CC BY-NC-SA CC BY-NC-SA CC BY-NC-SA CC BY-ND, CC BY-NC-ND None: the combination is Blocked

The ten pairs:

# Source A Source B Correct outcome Why (shown as feedback) 1 CC BY CC BY CC BY Both allow any of the four licenses, and CC BY is first in the order. 2 CC BY CC BY-SA CC BY-SA Only CC BY-SA satisfies the second source, and CC BY accepts it. 3 CC BY CC BY-NC CC BY-NC The second source needs a noncommercial license, and CC BY-NC comes first among those. 4 CC BY-SA CC BY-NC Conflict CC BY-SA allows only CC BY-SA, and CC BY-NC allows only noncommercial licenses, so there is no overlap. 5 CC BY-NC CC BY-NC-SA CC BY-NC-SA CC BY-NC-SA is the only license that satisfies both. 6 CC BY-SA CC BY-NC-SA Conflict Each requires its own license, and the two are different. 7 CC BY CC BY-ND Blocked The ND source cannot be changed or blended and then shared. 8 CC0 CC BY-SA CC BY-SA CC0 allows any of the four, and CC BY-SA is the only one that satisfies the other source. 9 CC0 CC BY CC BY Both allow any of the four, and CC BY is first. 10 CC BY-NC CC BY-NC-ND Blocked The ND source cannot be changed or blended and then shared.

Provenance: The requirements table is this chapter's rule of thumb, written for study and consistent with the chapter sections "License Compatibility" and "License Conflict". The sim labels it "a study aid, not a legal chart" and links to the Creative Commons compatibility chart as the authority.

Rules: The correct outcome for a pair is the first license, in the order CC BY, CC BY-SA, CC BY-NC, CC BY-NC-SA, that appears in the allowed set of both sources. If the two allowed sets share no license the outcome is Conflict. If either source is an ND license the outcome is Blocked, whatever the other source is. Each pair has exactly one correct outcome.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees a pair of sources and the six outcomes.
  2. The learner may open the requirements table. Opening it does not change the score.
  3. The learner chooses an outcome.
  4. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text, then presents the next pair.
  5. After pair 10 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 10 pairs in the fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [outcome]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. The answer is [outcome]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 10 correct on the first attempt". At 8 or more it adds "You can combine licenses." Below 8 it lists the Why text of each missed pair.

Starting State: Pair 1 with the six outcomes and the requirements table closed. The question shown is "Which license may the combined work carry?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter says CC BY-SA and CC BY-NC conflict, CC BY-SA and CC BY-NC-SA conflict, CC BY with CC BY-SA gives CC BY-SA, CC BY-NC with CC BY-NC-SA gives CC BY-NC-SA, and any ND source blocks sharing the combination. The chapter's first-in-order rule uses the order CC BY, CC BY-SA, CC BY-NC, CC BY-NC-SA.

docs.title: Fair Use
docs.text:
Fair use is a U.S. legal doctrine that lets people use copyrighted work without permission in some situations, such as teaching, criticism, and news reporting. A court weighs four factors:

  • Purpose and character: whether the use is educational and transformative or commercial.
  • Nature of the work: whether the work is factual or creative.
  • Amount used: how much of the work is used, and whether it is the heart of the work.
  • Market effect: whether the use harms the owner's ability to sell the work.

Fair use is decided case by case, usually after a dispute has begun, so you cannot know in advance how a court would rule. It is a defense, not a license. For OER work, that has two consequences. Fair use does not let you share a changed copy of a whole resource, and it does not replace a license that already covers your use. If a license covers what you want to do, rely on the license. Keep fair use in reserve for small excerpts, such as quoting a paragraph in a review, and note that other countries have different rules. This is general information, not legal advice.

docs.title: License Selection
docs.text:
License selection is the choice of which license to put on a work you own. Three questions drive the choice: will you allow commercial reuse, will you allow others to share changed versions, and must changed versions carry the same license? The table maps the answers to a license.

Allow commercial reuse? Allow shared changes? Same license on changes? License Yes Yes No CC BY Yes Yes Yes CC BY-SA No Yes No CC BY-NC No Yes Yes CC BY-NC-SA Yes No Not applicable CC BY-ND No No Not applicable CC BY-NC-ND

If you want no conditions at all, CC0 does that. Five practical points apply before you decide:

  • Ownership: check who owns the work. A school's policy or your employment contract may give the school the right to choose.
  • Funders: some grants require a specific license, so read the grant terms first.
  • Third-party content: you can license only what you own, so replace or credit any item that belongs to someone else.
  • Permanence: you can stop offering a work, but people who already received it keep their rights.
  • Software: Creative Commons recommends licenses designed for software when you share code, not CC licenses.

Choosing Is Giving

Choosing a license is choosing which freedoms to give away. Each condition you add protects something you care about and removes a use someone else could have made.

The default advice in OER work is CC BY for the widest reuse, or CC BY-SA when you want improvements to stay open. NC and ND licenses reduce reuse, so choose them for a reason you can state. Chapter 9 shows how the rubric scores that choice. The last MicroSim of the chapter is a practice round. You read a teacher's goal and choose the license that serves it.

docs.title: Diagram: License Selection Advisor
docs.text:
Run the License Selection Advisor MicroSim Fullscreen

License Selection Advisor

Type: microsim sim-id: license-selection-advisor Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: apply Learning Objective: The learner will apply the three license-selection questions to choose the license that serves each of seven stated goals, with at least 6 of 7 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: License Selection, CC0 Dedication, CC BY, CC BY-SA, CC BY-NC, CC BY-NC-SA, CC BY-ND, CC BY-NC-ND (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each goal the learner chooses one of seven licenses. A choice is correct when it matches the Correct license column in Content. Mastery is at least 6 of 7 correct on the first attempt. Opening the question table is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) NonCommercial protects a creator without limiting reuse much. (2) NoDerivatives and ShareAlike can be combined. (3) CC BY is the only open choice.

Instructional Rationale: Choosing a license for a goal is an Apply-level task that uses the three questions as a procedure. One goal per license makes the learner discriminate between neighboring options.

Content:

The seven license choices: CC0, CC BY, CC BY-SA, CC BY-NC, CC BY-NC-SA, CC BY-ND, CC BY-NC-ND.

The three questions, shown on request: Will you allow commercial reuse? Will you allow others to share changed versions? Must changed versions carry the same license?

The seven goals:

# Goal shown to the learner Correct license Why (shown as feedback) 1 "I want no friction at all. Anyone may do anything." CC0 CC0 gives up all conditions, including credit. 2 "Anyone may use, change, and sell my worksheet. I only need credit." CC BY BY is the only condition, and commercial reuse and changes are allowed. 3 "Anyone may use and sell my unit, but every changed version must stay open under the same terms." CC BY-SA SA keeps changed versions under the same license, and commercial use stays allowed. 4 "Others may change my lesson, but they may not make money from it, and I do not mind which license their changes use." CC BY-NC NC blocks commercial use, and without SA, adapters choose their license. 5 "Others may change my lesson noncommercially, and every changed version must carry my license." CC BY-NC-SA NC blocks commercial use, and SA requires the same license on changes. 6 "Anyone may share my finished report, even for sale, but nobody may share a changed version." CC BY-ND ND forbids changed versions, and there is no NC element. 7 "Anyone may share my unchanged handout, but not for money, and nobody may share a changed version." CC BY-NC-ND It combines NC and ND.

Provenance: The goals are illustrative cases written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The mapping follows the chapter's license-selection table.

Rules: Each goal has exactly one correct license, one per license. The three questions determine the choice as shown in the chapter's table. CC0 applies only when the goal asks for no conditions.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads a goal.
  2. The learner may open the three questions.
  3. The learner chooses one of the seven licenses.
  4. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text, then presents the next goal.
  5. After goal 7 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 7 goals in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [license]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. The answer is [license]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 7 correct on the first attempt". At 6 or more it adds "You can pick a license for a goal." Below 6 it lists the Why text of each missed goal.

Starting State: Goal 1 or the first goal in the shuffled order, with the seven licenses and the question "Which license fits this goal?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's table maps three yes-or-no answers to six licenses, and says CC0 applies when you want no conditions at all.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• An open license gives everyone permission in advance. A proprietary license and all rights reserved grant little or nothing, so read them before you assume.
  • Creative Commons offers six licenses built from four elements: attribution (BY), ShareAlike (SA), NonCommercial (NC), and NoDerivatives (ND). SA and ND never appear together, and CC0 is a dedication with no conditions.
  • NC is blurrier than it sounds, and ND blocks the improvements this book teaches you to make.
  • A complete license statement names the license and version, links to it, names the owner, and says what it covers. Third-party content may be licensed separately.
  • Credit with TASL: Title, Author, Source, License, plus a note of any change.
  • License compatibility asks whether one license satisfies every source. A license conflict means none does, and an ND source blocks sharing entirely.
  • Fair use is a case-by-case defense and not a license. License selection is a choice of which freedoms to give.

You Can Read a License

You can now tell the six Creative Commons licenses apart, write a TASL credit line, and check whether two licenses can be combined. That is the reading skill every reusability score in this book depends on.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Open Licenses and Attribution
docs.text: Test your understanding of Creative Commons licenses, license statements, attribution, and license compatibility with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. What are the three layers that every Creative Commons license provides?
docs.text:
1. A plain-language summary, a court ruling, and a registration record
  2. A Commons Deed, the legal code, and machine-readable code
  3. A license name, a version number, and an author credit
  4. A badge icon, a legal notice, and a copyright symbol
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Every CC license comes in three layers so that people, lawyers, and software can each read it. The Commons Deed is a short plain-language summary, the legal code is the full text a court would read, and the machine-readable code is metadata that lets search tools recognize the license. Options A, C, and D mix in items such as a court ruling, a version number, and a copyright symbol, which are not license layers.

Concept Tested: Creative Commons

See: Creative Commons

docs.title: 2. Which Creative Commons element requires that anyone who shares an adaptation must license it under the same license or a compatible one?
docs.text:
1. Attribution (BY)
  2. ShareAlike (SA)
  3. NonCommercial (NC)
  4. NoDerivatives (ND)
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. ShareAlike (SA) keeps improvements open by requiring each adaptation to carry the same license, or one that the license lists as compatible. It applies only when you adapt the work, so sharing an unchanged copy needs only credit. Attribution (A) requires credit, NonCommercial (C) limits commercial use, and NoDerivatives (D) forbids sharing changed versions altogether. People call the ShareAlike approach copyleft.

Concept Tested: ShareAlike Requirement

See: ShareAlike Requirement

docs.title: 3. Which statement best describes an open license?
docs.text:
1. A license in which the owner gives one named person permission to use a work after that person asks
  2. A license in which the owner keeps every right and allows the work to be viewed online
  3. A license in which the owner gives everyone permission in advance, at no charge, to do things that copyright would otherwise reserve
  4. A license in which the owner sells the right to change a work to anyone who pays a fee
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. An open license is public, in advance, and standing. The owner offers it to everyone and not to a named person, grants it before anyone asks, and people who received the work keep their rights even if the owner later stops offering it. It grants the five R permissions to the whole public, usually with conditions such as credit. Option A describes a one-time permission, and option B describes all rights reserved.

Concept Tested: Open License

See: What an Open License Grants

docs.title: 4. What does TASL stand for in the credit-line format that Creative Commons recommends?
docs.text:
1. Title, Author, Source, License
  2. Title, Attribution, Statement, License
  3. Type, Author, Scope, Link
  4. Title, Adaptation, Source, Link
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. TASL stands for Title, Author, Source, and License. Writing the four parts in order makes a credit line hard to get wrong: for example, "Watershed Basics" by Maria Lopez, a link to the work, licensed under CC BY 4.0. If you changed the work, add a sentence naming the change, such as "Adapted: reading level lowered." The other options mix in terms that are not part of the format.

Concept Tested: TASL Attribution Format

See: TASL Attribution Format

docs.title: 5. A teacher-sharing site marks a worksheet CC BY, but the worksheet's own pages say the uploader copied it from a publisher's book. What is the best conclusion?
docs.text:
1. The marking is worthless, because only an owner can grant a license and the uploader did not hold the rights
  2. The marking is valid, because a license statement always overrides what the original source says
  3. The marking is valid, because the license icon on the site proves the creator's intent
  4. The marking is valid, but only after the uploader adds a version number and a link
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Only an owner can grant a license, and the uploader never held the rights to give away, so the marking carries no weight. This is why you trace a resource to its original creator and follow the license link back to the source. When a statement and its source disagree, the source wins. Icons and markings are easy to copy onto pages that never carried a license.

Concept Tested: License Statement

See: License Statement

docs.title: 6. Why can a CC BY-NC-SA work not be combined with a CC BY-SA work?
docs.text:
1. ShareAlike licenses may never be combined with any other Creative Commons license, whatever its elements
  2. CC BY-NC-SA works are in the public domain, so they cannot be mixed with licensed works of any kind
  3. Only works from the same creator can be combined under a ShareAlike license, so remixes need one author
  4. One requires noncommercial use while the other keeps commercial use possible, so no single license satisfies both
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. CC BY-SA requires the combined work to be CC BY-SA, which allows commercial use, while CC BY-NC-SA requires the combined work to be CC BY-NC-SA, which does not. No single license meets both demands, so this is a license conflict. Option A is too broad, because a CC BY work combines with a CC BY-SA work. When you face a conflict, choose a different resource, ask an owner in writing, or keep the works separate.

Concept Tested: License Conflict

See: License Conflict

docs.title: 7. A teacher adds alt text to the images of a CC BY-ND chapter. What does the NoDerivatives requirement allow her to do with the changed copy?
docs.text:
1. She may not add alt text even to a private copy, because any change is forbidden
  2. She may share the changed copy, but only if she keeps the use noncommercial
  3. She may use the changed copy for her own reading, but she may not share it
  4. She may share the changed copy as long as she credits the original author
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. NoDerivatives lets you share the work only as it is. It does not forbid private changes, so she may adjust a copy for her own study, but giving the changed copy to students or colleagues counts as sharing, and the license does not allow that. She can ask the owner for permission to share the improved version, or choose a resource that allows changes. Credit alone (D) does not lift the restriction.

Concept Tested: NoDerivatives Requirement

See: NoDerivatives Requirement

docs.title: 8. Which statement correctly describes fair use in OER work?
docs.text:
1. It is a Creative Commons license that allows classroom copying of any work, with credit to the author
  2. It guarantees that any educational use of a work is allowed without permission, whatever the amount copied
  3. It lets you share a changed version of a whole textbook as long as you credit the author and keep the use educational
  4. It is a case-by-case defense, not a license, and it does not cover sharing a changed copy of a whole resource
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Fair use is a U.S. legal doctrine that a court weighs case by case, usually after a dispute has begun, using four factors: purpose, nature of the work, amount used, and market effect. It is a defense, not a license, so you cannot know in advance how a court would rule. If a license already covers your use, rely on the license, and keep fair use in reserve for small excerpts.

Concept Tested: Fair Use

See: Fair Use

docs.title: 9. A teacher combines a chapter licensed CC BY with a chapter licensed CC BY-SA into one unit. Which license may the combined unit carry?
docs.text:
1. CC BY-SA, because the ShareAlike source requires it and CC BY accepts it
  2. CC BY, because the more open license always governs the combined work
  3. CC BY-NC, because mixing two licenses makes the combined work noncommercial
  4. No license, because the two sources conflict and cannot be combined
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The method is to write what each source requires of the combined work, then look for a license that satisfies every requirement. CC BY accepts any of the four licenses in the order CC BY, CC BY-SA, CC BY-NC, CC BY-NC-SA, while CC BY-SA requires CC BY-SA, so CC BY-SA is the only license that meets both. This pair does not conflict. Option B reverses the logic, since the ShareAlike source sets the requirement.

Concept Tested: License Compatibility

See: License Compatibility

docs.title: 10. A teacher reviews three uses of a CC BY-NC worksheet: handing it out in a public-school class, posting it on a blog that earns paid advertising income, and using it in a $20 nonprofit workshop that charges to cover room and printing costs. Which reading matches the chapter's guidance?
docs.text:
1. All three are allowed, because none of the uses sells the worksheet itself for profit to a customer
  2. Only the class handout is allowed, because charging any fee at all makes a use commercial and so forbidden
  3. The class handout is allowed, the advertising blog is not, and the $20 workshop is unclear, so ask the owner
  4. The class handout and the workshop are allowed, and the advertising blog is unclear because blogs are public
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Nobody earns money from the classroom handout, so it is allowed. Advertising income makes the blog's use commercial, so it is not allowed. Cost recovery is a gray area, so the workshop is unclear and the teacher should ask the owner in writing. NonCommercial is blurrier than it sounds, and the table in the chapter is a guide rather than legal advice. Option B treats every fee as commercial, which overstates the rule.

Concept Tested: NonCommercial Requirement

See: NonCommercial Requirement

docs.title: References: Open Licenses and Attribution
docs.text:
1. Creative Commons license - Wikipedia - Describes the six main Creative Commons licenses, the BY, SA, NC, and ND conditions they combine, and the history of the license suite. Background for reading and comparing the licenses taught in this chapter.

  2. License compatibility - Wikipedia - Explains why works under different licenses cannot always be combined, with examples drawn mainly from open-source software. The same share-alike logic underlies this chapter's rules for combining openly licensed works.

  3. Fair use - Wikipedia - Covers the four-factor test in U.S. law, landmark cases, and the limits of the doctrine. Clarifies why fair use is a separate permission from an open license, which the chapter treats only briefly.

  4. Copyright Law for Librarians and Educators: Creative Strategies and Practical Solutions (4th ed.) - Kenneth D. Crews - ALA Editions (2020) - Crews co-created the widely copied Fair Use Checklist, which turns the four statutory factors into a balance of reasons for and against. His book teaches teachers to reason through permissions step by step.

  5. Made with Creative Commons - Paul Stacey and Sarah Hinchliff Pearson - Ctrl+Alt+Delete Books (2017) - Teaches licensing through case studies of creators and organizations that chose Creative Commons licenses, illustrated by Bryan Mathers. It shows how license choice follows from a creator's goals, as in this chapter's license selection section.

  6. About CC Licenses - Creative Commons - Official overview of the six licenses, with plain-language summaries of the conditions each carries. The authoritative reference for what BY, SA, NC, and ND permit and require.

  7. Recommended Practices for Attribution - CC Public Wiki - Official guidance on crediting a CC-licensed work with its title, author, source, and license, with examples of good and weak credit lines. The model for the credit lines taught in the giving credit section.

  8. Compatible Licenses - Creative Commons - Explains which Creative Commons licenses may be combined in an adaptation and which license the result may carry. Direct support for checking whether two licenses allow a remix.

  9. License Chooser - Creative Commons - An interactive questionnaire that leads a creator to a suitable license and produces the license statement. Good practice for the chapter's license selection exercise.

  10. Measuring Fair Use: The Four Factors - Stanford Copyright & Fair Use Center - Rich Stim's plain-English guide to the purpose, nature, amount, and market-effect factors, with examples from court decisions. Helps teachers see where fair use ends and open licenses begin.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Introduces the rubric that scores an OER on five quality and five reusability metrics, including score scales, evidence, subtotals, reviewers, and what makes a rubric reliable and valid. It sets up the scoring framework that the following metric chapters apply one at a time. After this chapter you can explain how a rubric score, its evidence, and its subtotals fit together, and how to judge whether a rubric is reliable.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Foundations of Open Educational Resources

Turn Opinion Into a Score

Every teacher has said "this resource is good" and then struggled to say why. In this chapter you build the habit that replaces that feeling with ten numbers and the evidence behind each one. Let's dive in and check the evidence!

Chapters 1 and 2 answered one question about a resource: what may I do with it? A second question is still open: is it any good? Teachers answer that question by instinct every day, and instinct varies. Two careful teachers can read the same textbook and disagree about whether to adopt it, with no way to tell who is right.

This chapter introduces the scoring method that the rest of the book applies. You will learn what quality means for a learner, how a rubric turns that meaning into ten scored metrics, how to attach evidence to every score, how the scores add up, who does the scoring, and how to tell whether the rubric itself can be trusted. Chapters 4 through 10 then teach the ten metrics one at a time.

docs.title: OER Quality
docs.text:
OER quality is the degree to which an open educational resource helps its intended learners reach its intended learning outcomes. Notice what the definition leaves out: how polished the resource looks, what awards it won, and what it cost. Quality describes a relationship between a resource and a learner. A resource that a graduate student finds excellent can be poor quality for a sixth grader, and the reverse is also true.

OER quality varies more than the quality of commercial textbooks, for reasons that are easy to see:

  • No editorial gate: anyone can publish an OER, so no editor or review board need approve it.
  • Uneven funding and review: some OER come from funded projects with peer review, and others from one teacher's spare evenings.
  • Age: facts, links, and software versions go out of date, and a resource that was right five years ago may be wrong now.
  • Uneven skills: an author who knows the subject may not know how to make a resource accessible to a blind learner.
  • Remixing: each copy and revision can add errors or drop credit, and no one is required to check.

None of this makes OER worse than other materials. It means the label open tells you nothing about quality, which is why a reviewer needs a method. Quality also has parts. A resource can fail a learner in several different ways, and a single "good" or "bad" hides which one.

Worked example: three resources, three blocked learners. Each resource below has a strength and a failure, and the failure blocks a different learner.

Resource Its failure Learner it blocks Part of quality that failed A chemistry reading with correct facts, written at a university level Words and sentences are too hard A grade 8 student who quits after two paragraphs Readability A well-written history unit that cites a 1990s source for current data Figures are out of date Students who memorize outdated numbers Accuracy and currency A clear science lab page whose diagrams have no text descriptions Diagrams cannot be read by a screen reader A blind student who cannot do the lab Accessibility

The same word, quality, covers all three failures. A star rating would give the three resources similar scores and hide what to fix.

Quality also depends on the learner. The same chemistry reading can be excellent for a first-year college class and poor for a grade 8 class, because the words, the pace, and the background it assumes fit one audience and not the other. A reviewer therefore starts every review by writing down the intended audience and the intended outcomes, and scores the resource against those. A resource that never states its audience or its outcomes has a quality problem before the review begins, because no one can say what it was built to do.

docs.title: Quality Rubric
docs.text:
A rubric is a scoring guide that lists the criteria for judging a piece of work and describes what each level of performance looks like. A quality rubric applies that idea to the quality of a resource. It replaces "this seems good" with named criteria, a scale, and rules about what counts as proof.

A quality rubric has five parts:

  • Criteria: the specific things to be judged, such as accuracy or accessibility.
  • A scale: the numbers a reviewer may assign.
  • Descriptors: short statements of what each score level looks like.
  • Evidence rules: what a reviewer must record to support a score.
  • A way to combine scores: how single scores become a summary and a decision.

Rubrics come in two broad kinds. A holistic rubric gives one overall rating for a piece of work, such as "excellent" or "four stars". An analytic rubric scores several criteria separately and then combines them. Holistic rubrics are fast, but they hide what to fix and are hard to compare between reviewers. Analytic rubrics take longer and repay the time with detail, which is why this book uses one.

A rubric helps in four ways. It makes two reviewers look at the same things. It makes a score explainable, because the criteria are visible. It points to what to improve, because a low score names a specific metric. And it makes a decision defensible to a department or a district. Published rubrics do not always supply these parts. A 2015 review of 14 OER rubrics by Yuan and Recker, summarized in this book's rubric specification, reported that 5 of the 14 gave no rating scale and only 3 offered a detailed scoring guide.

Worked example: two reviews of one resource. A teacher reviews the reading Watershed Basics, the CC BY resource from Chapter 2, and a colleague reviews it with a rubric. The table shows what each review tells the next teacher.

Unstructured review Rubric review What it says "Looks good. Clear and useful. Four stars." Ten metrics, each scored from 0 to 10, each with evidence What the next teacher learns That one person liked it That facts are mostly current, the video has no captions, and the metadata is nearly empty Can another reviewer repeat it? No: there is nothing to check Yes: each score names where to look What to fix first Unknown The lowest-scoring metrics

docs.title: Ten-Metric Rubric
docs.text:
The ten-metric rubric is the quality rubric this book uses. It scores a resource on ten metrics. Each metric is worth 10 points, five metrics measure quality, five measure reusability, and the ten scores add up to a total of 100. Reviewers score each metric separately and record evidence for each score. The table lists the ten metrics in the order the worksheet uses, with the question each one answers and the chapter that teaches it.

# Metric The question it answers Half Chapter 1 Accuracy and currency Are the facts correct and up to date? Quality 5 2 Alignment Do the activities and tests match the stated learning outcomes? Quality 6 3 Readability Do the words fit the audience? Quality 6 4 Accessibility Can learners with disabilities use it? Quality 7 5 Practice with feedback Can learners try things and learn how they did? Quality 8 6 Open license Does a clear license say what others may do? Reusability 9 7 Modularity Can each part stand alone? Reusability 9 8 Metadata Can others find it and tell what it is? Reusability 9 9 Editable source Can others change it? Reusability 4 10 Portability Does it work in other places without a login? Reusability 10

The numbers show the order on the worksheet and do not rank importance, because every metric carries the same 10 points. Ten is a compromise. One review of published rubrics found indicator counts ranging from 3 to 42, and a long rubric costs reviewers time that they stop spending. Ten metrics cover both halves of a resource and stay short enough for a careful reviewer to finish.

The rubric also leaves things out on purpose. It does not measure whether students learn more from the resource, because a rubric looks at the resource and not at its results. It does not measure fit with your particular students, your school's schedule, or your budget. And it does not replace your professional judgment about what to teach. Chapters 16 and 17 test the one claim a rubric cannot make for itself, which is that higher-scoring resources help learners more.

Worked example: which metric? A complaint about a resource usually points at one metric. Match each complaint below to the metric it tests.

Complaint Metric it tests "The quiz won't load in our learning management system." Portability "I can't tell whether I may translate this." Open license "I only have a PDF, and I need to change one sentence." Editable source "A screen reader reads the picture names as 'image1.png'." Accessibility

The first MicroSim below shows the whole structure as a map. The rubric is at the center, the two halves branch from it, and each half branches into its five metrics. In explore mode you click each node to read what it means. In quiz mode you read a teacher's complaint and click the metric it points to.

Can each part stand alone? 9 Metadata Reusability dimension Title, author, subject, grade level, license, and description are recorded. Can others find it and tell what it is? 9 Editable source Reusability dimension The source is in an editable open format, not only PDF. Can others change it? 4 Portability Reusability dimension The resource runs in a browser without a login and embeds elsewhere. Does it work in other places without a login? 10

The ten complaints, in this order:

# Complaint shown to the learner Correct metric Why (shown as feedback) 1 "The page gives a river's length that does not match its own cited source." Accuracy and currency A fact that disagrees with its source is an accuracy problem. 2 "The quiz asks about topics the unit never teaches." Alignment Assessment that does not match the outcomes is an alignment problem. 3 "My students stop at the second paragraph because the words are too hard." Readability Wording that does not fit the audience is a readability problem. 4 "A screen reader reads the picture names as 'image1.png'." Accessibility Missing text descriptions block learners who use screen readers. 5 "Students read it, but have nothing to try and no way to know if they are right." Practice with feedback The resource offers no practice and no feedback. 6 "I cannot tell whether I may translate this." Open license The reuse permissions are not stated. 7 "I want just the quiz, but it is built into the middle of the chapter." Modularity The quiz cannot stand alone. 8 "Search cannot tell me the subject or grade level." Metadata The descriptive fields are missing. 9 "I only have a PDF, and I need to change one sentence." Editable source There is no editable file. 10 "It needs a login before it will open." Portability A login blocks use in other places.

Provenance: The ten metrics and their questions follow the chapter section "Ten-Metric Rubric" and the project's sample rubric worksheet. The complaints are illustrative cases written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". Chapter numbers follow this book's table of contents.

Rules: Each complaint has exactly one correct metric, and each metric is the answer to exactly one complaint. Clicking a dimension node or the root node during the quiz counts as a wrong attempt. The sim offers buttons to zoom and does not zoom with the mouse wheel.

Learner Activity:

  1. In explore mode the learner clicks each node and reads its definition, question, and chapter.
  2. In quiz mode the sim shows complaint 1 above the map.
  3. The learner clicks the metric node that the complaint tests.
  4. If the first click is wrong, the sim says so and the learner tries once more. If the second click is also wrong, the sim reveals the metric and the Why text.
  5. After complaint 10 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 10 complaints in a shuffled order, two attempts each. Only a correct first click counts as evidence. Correct: "Correct: [metric]. [Why]". First wrong click: "Not quite. Think about what the complaint says is broken." Second wrong click: "This is [metric]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 10 correct on the first attempt". At 9 or more it adds "You can match a problem to its metric." Below 9 it lists the metrics the learner missed.

Starting State: The map with all 13 nodes visible, explore mode active, and the prompt "Click a node to see what it means."

Chapter Anchors: The chapter says the rubric has ten metrics worth 10 points each, five for quality and five for reusability, totaling 100. The chapter's table lists the metrics in the order accuracy and currency, alignment, readability, accessibility, practice with feedback, open license, modularity, metadata, editable source, portability, with chapters 5, 6, 6, 7, 8, 9, 9, 9, 4, and 10.

docs.title: Rubric Metric
docs.text:
A rubric metric is one measurable aspect of a resource that the rubric scores. Every metric in this book has the same five parts: a name, a question, a list of what to check, the score scale, and the rules for evidence. Keeping the parts the same lets a reviewer move from one metric to the next without learning a new procedure. A metric also measures one thing. A metric that mixes two ideas, such as "clear and accessible", cannot be scored, because a resource can be clear and inaccessible at once.

Worked example: taking apart readability. The table shows the five parts for the readability metric.

Part Readability Name Readability Question Do the words fit the audience? What to check The reading level fits the audience, and terms are defined before use. Scale Whole numbers from 0 to 10. Evidence rule Record the measured reading level of sampled passages and list any terms used before they are defined.

Every metric is scored on its own, and the ten scores are never averaged into a single judgment before they are recorded. Chapters 4 through 10 give the what-to-check list and the evidence rule for each of the ten.

Metrics fail in predictable ways, and a good one avoids them. The table shows four common problems, with a weak metric and a better one for each.

Problem Weak metric Better metric Two ideas in one "Clear and accessible" Readability and accessibility, as two separate metrics No way to check "Is engaging" Practice with feedback: count the practice items and the feedback messages Vague words "Has good images" Accessibility: every image has a useful text description Judges the author "Written by an expert" Accuracy and currency: facts match the cited sources

Every metric in this rubric is also worth the same 10 points. Equal weights are a choice. Some reviewers will feel that accuracy matters more than metadata, and in a classroom decision it often does. The rubric keeps the weights equal so that scores are easy to compare between resources and reviewers, and it protects the most important metrics with a floor in the adoption threshold, described later in this chapter.

docs.title: Quality Dimension
docs.text:
A quality dimension is a group of rubric metrics that measure one side of a resource. The rubric has two dimensions, and the quality dimension is the group of five metrics that measure how well the resource helps learners learn. Its subtotal is worth 50 points.

  • Accuracy and currency asks whether the content is correct and up to date. A learner who studies a wrong fact has learned something false.
  • Alignment asks whether the activities and tests match the stated learning outcomes. A resource can teach well and still fail a course if it teaches the wrong thing.
  • Readability asks whether the wording fits the audience, including whether terms are defined before they are used.
  • Accessibility asks whether learners with disabilities can use the resource, following the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.1 at level AA.
  • Practice with feedback asks whether learners can try something and learn how they did, through quizzes, worked examples, or interactive simulations.

Worked example: five learners, five metrics. Each learner in the table below meets a quality failure, and each failure belongs to a different metric.

Learner What goes wrong Metric that would catch it A student relies on a figure from an old source The figure is out of date Accuracy and currency A teacher builds a unit around the resource The test measures skills the reading never teaches Alignment A grade 6 student reads the passage The vocabulary is far above grade level Readability A student with low vision enlarges the page Text is part of an image and cannot be enlarged Accessibility A student finishes the chapter There is nothing to try and no way to check understanding Practice with feedback

The five quality metrics do not overlap. Each picks out a way a learner can be let down, so a resource must be checked against all five before anyone calls it good.

The five metrics do touch each other. Readability and accessibility both depend on plain, well-structured writing, and alignment and practice both depend on clear learning outcomes, so a weak outcome statement can lower two scores at once. The metrics stay separate because each asks a different question and has a different fix: a readability problem is fixed by rewriting, and an accessibility problem by adding descriptions, captions, and structure.

docs.title: Reusability Dimension
docs.text:
A reusability dimension is the second group of rubric metrics, and it measures how easily other people can find, change, and reuse the resource. It also has five metrics and a 50-point subtotal.

  • Open license asks whether a clear license states what others may do and whether attribution is complete.
  • Modularity asks whether each section, quiz, or simulation stands alone and can be embedded elsewhere.
  • Metadata asks whether the title, author, subject, grade level, license, and description are recorded so that others can find the resource and know what it is.
  • Editable source asks whether the source is in a format others can change, such as Markdown or HTML, and not only a locked PDF.
  • Portability asks whether the resource runs in a browser with no login and can be linked or embedded elsewhere.

These five connect to the 5R permissions from Chapter 1. A license grants the permissions, and the other four metrics decide whether you can use them in practice. An editable source makes revising and remixing possible. Modularity makes it possible to reuse one part without taking the rest. Metadata helps others find the work and credit it. Portability lets the work move to a new platform for use or redistribution.

Worked example: five obstacles. A teacher tries to reuse a chapter that scores poorly on reusability. Each obstacle she meets maps to one metric.

What the teacher tries What stops her Metric She looks for the license No license is stated anywhere Open license She wants one quiz from the chapter The quiz is woven into the chapter text Modularity She searches for the chapter by topic Nothing records its subject or grade level Metadata She tries to change an example Only a PDF is available Editable source She embeds the chapter in her course The page asks visitors to log in Portability

The five reusability metrics depend on each other in a rough order. A reader cannot reuse what they cannot find, so metadata comes first. They cannot reuse what they may not use, so the license comes next. Then the work has to run in the new place (portability), be separable (modularity), and be changeable (editable source). A resource that fails an early step makes the later ones moot: the best-structured module in the world is no use if no one can find it or know whether they may use it.

docs.title: Quality Versus Reusability
docs.text:
Quality versus reusability names the idea that the two halves of the rubric are independent. A resource can be strong on one half and weak on the other, and any of the four combinations occurs in practice. The table shows the four combinations and where to spend effort.

Reusability high Reusability low Quality high Strong and open: adopt it Good but locked: improve license, metadata, source, or portability Quality low Open but weak: improve accuracy, readability, accessibility, or practice Weak and locked: look elsewhere

Two Scoreboards, Never Merged

A resource can win one scoreboard and lose the other, so keep two subtotals and read them side by side. A merged number would tell you how good it is on average and hide what to fix.

The second MicroSim is a sorting practice with eight resource profiles. For each profile you decide which of the four combinations it belongs to, and then the sim shows its two subtotals so you can check your reading.

docs.title: Diagram: Quality and Reusability Quadrant Sorter
docs.text:
Run the Quality and Reusability Quadrant Sorter MicroSim Fullscreen

Quality and Reusability Quadrant Sorter

Type: microsim sim-id: quality-reusability-quadrant Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: differentiate Learning Objective: The learner will differentiate resources that need quality work from resources that need reusability work by placing each of eight profiles in the correct one of four quadrants, with at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Quality Dimension, Reusability Dimension, Quality Versus Reusability (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each profile the learner commits one of four quadrants before the subtotals are shown. A placement is correct when it matches the Correct quadrant column in Content. Mastery is at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the quadrant definitions is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A resource that is free to read is high in reusability. (2) A high total means both halves are strong. (3) An open resource is a high-quality resource.

Instructional Rationale: Differentiating two kinds of weakness is an Analyze-level action. Eight profiles that pair the same kinds of strength with different weaknesses force the learner to read each description for what it says about quality and what it says about reuse, instead of reacting to a single impression.

Content:

The four quadrants, shown at all times:

  • Strong and open: quality subtotal >= 25 and reusability subtotal >= 25.
  • Good but locked: quality subtotal >= 25 and reusability subtotal < 25.
  • Open but weak: quality subtotal < 25 and reusability subtotal >= 25.
  • Weak and locked: quality subtotal < 25 and reusability subtotal < 25.

The eight profiles:

# Profile shown to the learner Quality subtotal Reusability subtotal Correct quadrant Why (shown as feedback) 1 A peer-reviewed algebra text under CC BY, with HTML and Markdown source and complete metadata. 42 46 Strong and open Both subtotals are at least 25. 2 A polished chemistry e-book, free to read, all rights reserved, PDF only, behind a login. 44 12 Good but locked Quality is high, and the license, source, and login pull reusability less than 25. 3 A teacher's CC BY worksheet set with no answer key, outdated links, and images with no text descriptions. 18 38 Open but weak Reusability is high, and the errors, links, and missing descriptions pull quality less than 25. 4 A scanned 1998 handout with no source file and no license. 15 8 Weak and locked Both subtotals are less than 25. 5 An open history reading with a clear license and editable source but several factual errors and dense prose. 20 40 Open but weak Reusability is high, and the errors and dense prose pull quality less than 25. 6 A commercial platform with excellent practice quizzes and accessibility, but no reuse license and no export. 41 10 Good but locked Quality is high, and the missing license and export pull reusability less than 25. 7 A university's CC BY-SA physics module collection that is accurate, accessible, well structured, and fully described. 38 44 Strong and open Both subtotals are at least 25. 8 A free video series on a streaming site with no license, no transcripts, and broken links. 22 9 Weak and locked Both subtotals are less than 25.
