The scoring rules from Chapter 3 then apply: count the passed checks, find the band that holds that share, and choose the lower number in the band when a failed check blocks revision.

# Check Blocks revision if it fails? 1 An editable source file is offered, not only a PDF Yes 2 The source is in an open format Yes 3 The source holds all of the content: text, headings, tables, and equations Yes 4 The source can be downloaded with no login or payment Yes 5 Images have their original or vector source files No 6 Interactive parts supply their code Yes 7 A short note explains how the pieces fit together No 8 A record of changes is available No 9 The reviewer opened the source in a free tool and it displayed correctly Yes 10 Editing needs no paid software or special template Yes

A check that does not apply, such as the interactive-parts check for a resource with no simulations, counts as passed. The check list is this book's starting list, and a team may adjust it.

Worked example: Watershed Basics. The reviewer applies the ten checks to the reading from Chapter 3.

# Result Evidence 1 Pass HTML and Markdown source files are linked from the page. 2 Pass Both formats are open. 3 Pass The source holds all text, headings, and the quiz. 4 Pass The files download with no login. 5 Fail The five images are PNG files, and no source files are offered. 6 Pass The quiz script is included in the HTML source. 7 Pass A short note lists the files and how they connect. 8 Fail No list of changes is offered. 9 Pass The reviewer opened both files in a free editor, and they displayed correctly. 10 Pass No paid software is needed.

Eight of ten checks pass, a share of 80 percent, which falls in the 7 to 8 band. Neither failed check blocks revision, because a reviser can still change every word and replace any picture. The reviewer therefore chooses the higher number, 8. The Chapter 3 worksheet recorded the image gap only. A fuller check also finds that no change record is offered, and that second gap is why the score is not higher.

docs.title: Source Format
docs.text:
A source format is the file format in which a resource is authored and can be edited. It differs from a delivery format, which is the form meant for reading, printing, or showing, and which is usually hard to change. A recipe and a cake make a useful comparison. The recipe is the source: you can change an ingredient and bake again. The cake is the delivered result: you can eat it, but you cannot take the sugar out. A source format keeps the structure of the content, such as headings, lists, links, and images, so a reviser can change it. A delivery format often keeps only the appearance.

Kind Purpose Typical files Source Authoring and editing Markdown, HTML, word processing files, vector drawings, spreadsheets Delivery Reading, printing, projecting PDF, scanned pages, flattened images, exported slides

A resource often exists in several files at once. The same lesson can be a Markdown file, a web page built from it, and a PDF made for printing.

Worked example: one lesson, four files.

File Source or delivery? Can a reviser change the content? Why lesson.md Source Yes Plain text that any editor can open lesson.html Source and delivery Yes The web page is readable and editable text lesson.docx Source Yes An editable word processing file lesson.pdf Delivery Only with difficulty The file records how pages look, not how the content is built

A reviewer scores the editable source metric on the source files and does not count the delivery file. A resource that offers four formats but only a PDF as source has one useful file.

Recipe, Not Cake

A source is the recipe and a delivery file is the cake. Ask whether you could change the recipe, and a PDF alone will fail that test.

docs.title: Open File Format
docs.text:
An open file format is a file format whose specification is public and can be used without paying a fee or asking permission, so that anyone can write software that reads and writes it. Three questions test a format. Is the specification published? Can anyone implement it without paying? Does free software exist that opens it? A format that passes all three will still be readable when a company changes its products or closes. Files in a closed format may become unreadable, or readable only with software you must buy.

The table lists common formats. "Open" here means the specification is public. The last column says whether the format is a good source for editing.

Format Open? A good source? Markdown (.md) and plain text (.txt) Yes, plain text Yes HTML (.html) Yes, public web standards Yes OpenDocument text (.odt) Yes, an international standard Yes Word document (.docx) A published standard, but full fidelity depends on particular software Usually acceptable CSV (.csv) Yes, plain text table Yes, for data SVG (.svg) Yes, a web standard for drawings Yes, for diagrams PDF (.pdf) An open international standard Poor, because it is built for reading A page layout or design-program file Closed Poor, unless you own the program

Worked example: choosing a format. A teacher wants to share a worksheet so that colleagues can change it. She weighs three options. Saving it as a design-program file would keep her layout, but only people with that program could edit it. Saving it as a PDF would look identical everywhere, but no one could easily change a question. Saving it as an OpenDocument or Word document, with a Markdown or HTML copy beside it, lets nearly everyone open and change it. She picks the last option and keeps the PDF only as a printing copy.

docs.title: Common Source Formats
docs.text: Four kinds of file account for most editable sources in OER. Two of them, Markdown and HTML, are open formats designed for the web. A third, the word processing file, is the format most teachers already use. The fourth, the PDF used alone, is the one that causes the problem.

docs.title: Markdown
docs.text:
Markdown is a way of writing structured text using plain keyboard symbols, such as a pound sign for a heading and a hyphen for a list item. A Markdown file is plain text, so any editor can open it, and a program converts it into a formatted web page. This book is written in Markdown. Markdown files are small, they work well with version control, and a reviewer can read the source and understand it. The trade-off is limited layout control, which helps accessibility and portability because the structure stays simple.

Before the example, here is what the symbols do. A line that starts with ## becomes a second-level heading. A line that starts with a hyphen and a space becomes a bullet. Text in square brackets followed by an address in parentheses becomes a link. The same pattern with an exclamation mark in front becomes an image, and the square brackets then hold the alt text, the text description of the picture.

## Water Cycle

Water moves between the sea, the air, and the land.

- evaporation
- condensation
- precipitation

Read more in [Watershed Basics](https://example.org/watershed-basics).

![A river flowing through a valley](https://example.org/images/river.png)

Worked example: reading the Markdown. The first line is a heading. The sentence below it is an ordinary paragraph, set off by a blank line. The three hyphen lines are a bulleted list. The sentence with square brackets and parentheses contains a link whose visible text is "Watershed Basics". The last line is an image, and its alt text is "A river flowing through a valley". Every piece of structure is visible in the text, which is exactly what a reviser needs.

Many tools read Markdown. GitHub shows a Markdown file as a formatted page, MkDocs (the tool that builds this book) turns Markdown files into a website, and free converters change Markdown into Word, HTML, or PDF files. That makes Markdown a good first-draft format: write once, and produce the other formats from the same source.

Write Once, Export Many

Draft your own materials in Markdown or HTML first. Then export the PDF or Word copies you need, so that the editable source always exists.

The MicroSim below lets you practice. It shows a plain-text editor next to a live preview, and it sets four small tasks. Each task asks for one piece of structure: a heading, a list, a link, and an image with alt text.

docs.title: Diagram: Markdown Practice Lab
docs.text:
Markdown Practice Lab

Type: microsim sim-id: markdown-practice-lab Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: practice Learning Objective: The learner will practice writing Markdown for four structures (a heading, a list, a link, and an image with alt text), with at least 3 of 4 tasks passing on the first Check.

Prerequisites: Markdown, Source Format, Open File Format (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each task the learner edits the text and presses Check. A task passes when the live preview contains the required structure exactly as described in the Requirement column of Content. Mastery is at least 3 of 4 tasks passing on the first Check. Using the hint is allowed and is shown in the score.

Misconceptions: (1) Markdown needs special software to write. (2) The square brackets in an image hold the file name. (3) Alt text is optional because the image is already on the page.

Instructional Rationale: Practice with immediate feedback is the right pattern for an Apply-level skill. A live preview shows each symbol's effect as the learner types, so the learner links the symbol to the structure instead of memorizing a list.

Content:

The four tasks, in this order:

# Task Starting text Requirement Hint (shown on request) Message when it fails 1 Make a heading Water Cycle The preview contains a level-2 heading whose text is exactly "Water Cycle". Start the line with two pound signs and a space. "The heading needs two pound signs, a space, and the text Water Cycle." 2 Make a list evaporation, condensation, and precipitation, one per line The preview contains a bulleted list of exactly three items, in the order evaporation, condensation, precipitation. Start each line with a hyphen and a space. "Each item needs a hyphen and a space at the start of its own line." 3 Add a link The words Watershed Basics and the address https://example.org/watershed-basics The preview contains a link whose visible text is exactly "Watershed Basics" and whose address is https://example.org/watershed-basics. Put the visible text in square brackets and the address in parentheses right after it. "The link needs square brackets around the words and parentheses around the address." 4 Add an image with alt text The address https://example.org/images/river.png and the words A river flowing through a valley The preview contains an image whose address is https://example.org/images/river.png and whose alt text is exactly "A river flowing through a valley". Write an exclamation mark, then square brackets holding the alt text, then the address in parentheses. "The image needs an exclamation mark first, then the alt text in brackets, then the address in parentheses."

The Markdown symbols the lab teaches: two pound signs and a space for a level-2 heading, a hyphen and a space for a bullet, square brackets then parentheses for a link, and an exclamation mark before that pattern for an image.

Provenance: The tasks are illustrative cases written for this chapter, and the sim labels the addresses "example addresses". The symbols follow the chapter section "Markdown".

Rules: A task passes only when the preview shows the required structure with the exact text or address. Extra text elsewhere in the editor does not fail a task. The learner may press Check as many times as they like. Only a pass on the first Check counts toward mastery, and later passes are shown as passed with hint or retry.

Learner Activity:

  1. The sim shows task 1, with the starting text in the editor and the live preview beside it.
  2. The learner edits the text and watches the preview change.
  3. The learner presses Check. The sim shows pass or fail with the message.
  4. The learner may open the hint at any time.
  5. After a pass the sim shows task 2, and so on through task 4.

Feedback: 4 tasks in the fixed order. Pass: "Task passed: the preview shows [requirement]". Fail: the message in the table for that task. The summary shows "[n] of 4 tasks passed on the first Check, and [m] needed a retry or a hint". At 3 or more first-Check passes it adds "You can write the four Markdown structures." Below 3 it lists the tasks that needed a retry.

Starting State: Task 1 with the text Water Cycle in the editor and an empty-structure preview. The question shown is "Make this line a level-2 heading."

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's Markdown example uses the heading "Water Cycle", a list of evaporation, condensation, and precipitation, the link text "Watershed Basics" with the address https://example.org/watershed-basics, and an image with the alt text "A river flowing through a valley".

docs.title: HTML
docs.text:
HTML, short for HyperText Markup Language, is the language of web pages. An HTML file is plain text in which tags, written in angle brackets, mark the parts of a page: a heading, a paragraph, a picture, a link. Every web page you read is HTML. Because browsers have to read it, HTML is an open standard, and a web resource in HTML needs no special software to open or edit. The accessibility chapter and the portability chapter both depend on HTML, since a screen reader reads HTML tags and an embed runs HTML.

Before the example, here is what the tags do. The heading tag marks a title, and the digit says how important the heading is. The paragraph tag marks a block of text. The image tag shows a picture, and its alt attribute holds the alt text. The link tag turns text into a link, and its href attribute holds the address.

<h1>Watershed Basics</h1>
<p>Water moves between the sea, the air, and the land.</p>
<img src="river.png" alt="A river flowing through a valley">
<p>Read more in <a href="https://example.org/watershed-basics">Watershed Basics</a>.</p>

Worked example: view the source. Any browser can show the HTML of a page. Open a web page, right-click, and choose the option to view the page source. The page you read is built from the text you now see. A reviewer who wants to know whether the images have alt text, or whether the headings are in order, can look at the source and check each tag. That inspection is the basis of the accessibility checks in Chapter 7.

The next MicroSim shows the parts of a web page with an illustration. Each of its eight numbered markers points at one part and names the HTML tag that makes it.

docs.title: Diagram: Anatomy of a Web Page
docs.text:
Anatomy of a Web Page

Type: infographic sim-id: html-page-anatomy Library: html Status: Specified Bloom Level: Remember Bloom Verb: identify Learning Objective: The learner will identify the HTML tag behind each of eight parts of a web page from a description of how the part looks, with at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: HTML, Markdown, Source Format (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: In quiz mode the learner clicks the marker that matches a visual hint. A click is correct when it matches the marker named in the Hint column of Content. Mastery is at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Hovering in explore mode is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) The picture's alt text is shown on the page. (2) Any large text is a heading tag. (3) A link needs no address.

Instructional Rationale: Identifying the parts of a page is a Remember-level task, and an illustration links each visible part to the tag that creates it. The quiz asks the learner to go from the look to the tag, which is the direction a reviewer works when inspecting a source.

Content:

The illustration is a text-free flat drawing of a simple lesson web page inside a browser frame. A small tab sits at the upper left of the frame. On the page, from top to bottom, are a large bar of heading text, a block of several thin text lines, a landscape picture box with a thin strip beneath it, a short list of three lines each with a dot at its left, an underlined bar of link text, and a small grid of two columns and three rows. The eight markers:

# Label Hint (describes the look, not the name) Description Tip 1 Page title (title tag) A small tab at the upper left of the browser frame. The title tag holds the text that appears in the browser tab and in search results. Give each page its own title. 2 Main heading (h1 tag) The largest bar of text at the top of the page. The h1 tag marks the page's main heading. A page usually has one. Use heading tags in order, with no skipped levels. 3 Paragraph (p tag) A block of several thin lines under the heading. The p tag marks a paragraph of text. Keep one idea in each paragraph. 4 Image (img tag) The landscape picture box in the middle of the page. The img tag shows a picture. Its alt attribute holds the text description for people who cannot see it. Write alt text for every image that carries meaning. 5 Caption (figcaption tag) The thin strip directly beneath the picture. The figcaption tag holds the caption for a figure, which is a good place to credit the image. Put the image credit in the caption. 6 Bulleted list (ul and li tags) Three short lines, each with a dot at its left. The ul tag marks a bulleted list, and each li tag is one item. Use a real list tag, not dots typed by hand. 7 Link (a tag) An underlined bar of text. The a tag makes a link, and its href attribute holds the address. Write link text that says where the link goes. 8 Table (table tag) A small grid with two columns and three rows. The table tag marks a table, and header cells use the th tag. Mark header cells so screen readers can read the table.

Provenance: The tags follow the chapter section "HTML". The illustration is synthetic, and the sim labels the page "illustrative example".

Rules: Each hint matches exactly one marker. The illustration contains no text, so every label comes from the table above. Markers are numbered 1 to 8 in the order of the table.

Learner Activity:

  1. In explore mode the learner hovers or clicks a marker and reads its label, description, and tip.
  2. In quiz mode the sim shows a hint.
  3. The learner clicks the marker they think the hint describes.
  4. If the first click is wrong, the sim says so and lets the learner try once more. If the second click is also wrong, the sim reveals the marker and its description.
  5. After all 8 hints the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 8 hints in a shuffled order, two attempts each. Only a correct first click counts as evidence. Correct: "Correct: [label]. [Description]". First wrong click: "Not quite. Look again at the hint: [hint]". Second wrong click: "This is [label]. [Description]". The summary shows "[n] of 8 correct on the first attempt". At 7 or more it adds "You can read the parts of a page." Below 7 it lists the labels of the missed parts.

Starting State: The illustration with eight numbered markers, explore mode active, and the prompt "Hover a marker to see which tag makes it."

Chapter Anchors: The chapter says the heading tag marks a title, the paragraph tag marks text, the image tag has an alt attribute, and the link tag has an href attribute. The chapter's HTML example uses h1, p, img, and a.

docs.title: Word Processing File
docs.text: A word processing file is a document made in a program such as a word processor, saved as an editable file with a name ending in .docx or .odt. It is the format most teachers already use, and it is a reasonable source format: anyone with a word processor can open it, change it, and save it. Two cautions apply. A .docx file is a published standard but is built around one family of programs, and complex layouts may shift in another program. An .odt file uses an international open standard and opens consistently in free software. When you share a word processing file as a source, keep the layout simple, use real headings and lists, and describe images with alt text.

docs.title: PDF-Only Distribution
docs.text:
PDF-only distribution means that the only file a resource offers is a PDF. A PDF records how each page looks, so a person can read and print it with confidence. It does not record the structure, so changing a sentence means copying text out of the page, losing headings and tables, and rebuilding the layout by hand. PDF-only distribution fails the editable source checks that matter most, and it usually leaves the metric in the low bands. A PDF alongside editable sources is fine. A PDF in place of them is a locked file.

A PDF Is Not a Source

A PDF looks finished, so it is easy to mistake it for a source. If a resource offers only a PDF, you may have the legal right to change it and no practical way to do so. Ask the author for the Markdown, HTML, or word processing file, or score the metric low.

The next MicroSim puts the formats together. It shows ten files you might find with a resource, and for each one you judge whether it is a good source, an acceptable source, or a poor source.

docs.title: Diagram: File Format Triage
docs.text:
File Format Triage

Type: microsim sim-id: file-format-triage Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: judge Learning Objective: The learner will judge whether each of ten files is a good source, an acceptable source, or a poor source for revising a resource, with at least 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Source Format, Open File Format, Markdown, HTML, Word Processing File, PDF-Only Distribution (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each file the learner commits one of three bins. A placement is correct when it matches the Correct bin column in Content. Mastery is at least 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt. Reading the format table is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A PDF is a good source because it is an open standard. (2) A picture of text can be edited. (3) A word processing file is always a poor source.

Instructional Rationale: Judging a file against criteria is an Evaluate-level action. Ten files that mix open and closed formats, text and pictures, and editable and locked files make the learner apply the same criteria each time: can the structure be changed with free tools?

Content:

The three bins: Good source (open format that keeps structure and opens in free tools), Acceptable source (editable, but depends on particular software or loses some structure), and Poor source (cannot be edited as structured content with free tools).

The ten files:

# File shown to the learner Correct bin Why (shown as feedback) 1 lesson.md, a Markdown text file Good source Plain text in an open format that any editor opens. 2 lesson.odt, an OpenDocument text file Good source An international open standard that free software opens. 3 lesson.docx, a Word document Acceptable source Editable in many programs, though full fidelity depends on particular software. 4 slides.pptx, a slide file Acceptable source Editable, but it depends on particular software to display exactly. 5 diagram.svg, a vector drawing Good source An open web standard, and shapes and text stay editable. 6 diagram.png, a picture with no original drawing file Poor source A flat picture of a diagram, so its shapes and words cannot be edited. 7 data.csv, a table saved as plain text Good source Plain text that any spreadsheet or editor opens. 8 sim.html with sim.js, a simulation's web code Good source Readable, editable web code in open formats. 9 lesson.pdf, offered with no other file Poor source A PDF records how pages look, not how the content is built. 10 scan.jpg, a photo of a printed page Poor source It is a picture of text and not text, so no structure exists to edit.

Provenance: The files are illustrative cases written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The format judgments follow the chapter sections "Open File Format" and "Common Source Formats".

Rules: Each file has exactly one correct bin. Five files are Good, two are Acceptable, and three are Poor. A file offered alongside editable sources would be judged differently, and the sim states that these files are offered without other sources.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one file at a time, with the three bin definitions.
  2. The learner places the file in a bin, and the placement is committed.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text.
  4. After file 10 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 10 files in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [bin]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. This is [bin]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 10 correct on the first attempt". At 8 or more it adds "You can judge a source." Below 8 it lists the Why text of each missed file.

Starting State: The first file, the three bin definitions, and three empty bins. The question shown is "Is this file a good source for revising the resource?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's format table lists Markdown, HTML, OpenDocument, Word, CSV, SVG, and PDF, and says a PDF alone is a poor source.

docs.title: Version Control
docs.text:
Version control is a system that records every change made to a set of files, along with who made it, when, and why, so that any earlier state can be viewed or restored. Most people have met the problem it solves: a folder holding lesson_final.docx, lesson_final2.docx, and lesson_FINAL_really.docx, with no way to tell which differs from which. A version control system replaces that folder with one set of files and a recorded history.

The history gives an open resource four things that copies cannot. A reviser can see exactly what changed between two versions. A mistake can be undone by returning to an earlier state. Several people can work on the same resource at once and combine their changes. And a reuser can judge a resource's health by looking at when it was last changed and by whom.

Without version control With version control Many copies of the same file with confusing names One set of files with a recorded history No record of who changed what Every change carries an author, a date, and a message Two people editing at once overwrite each other Changes are combined, and conflicts are shown An error cannot be reliably undone Any earlier version can be restored

Worked example: a history instead of a pile of copies. A teacher fixes a wrong answer in a practice set on 12 September and adds alt text on 13 September. With copies, a colleague must open both files and compare them by eye. With version control, the history lists the two changes, each with a date and a one-line message, and shows the exact lines that differ.

docs.title: Git
docs.text:
Git is the most widely used version control software. It is free and open source, and its creator, Linus Torvalds, released it in 2005 to manage the Linux kernel project. Git keeps the whole history on your own computer, so you can work without a network connection and share your work later. It uses four ideas, and the table defines them before they appear in any example.

Term Meaning Repository The project folder together with its full recorded history Commit A saved snapshot of the changes, with an author, a date, and a message Branch A separate line of work that does not disturb the main line until you are ready Merge Combining the changes from one branch into another

You can use Git without typing commands, because GitHub and several desktop programs provide buttons for each step. For readers who want to see the commands, four of them cover most of a teacher's work. The command git clone copies a repository from the web to your computer. The command git add marks a changed file for the next snapshot. The command git commit saves the snapshot, and the text after -m is its message. The command git push sends your new commits to the shared copy on the web.

git clone https://github.com/example-school/fraction-practice-set.git
git add problems.md
git commit -m "Add alt text to the two number-line images"
git push

Worked example: one improvement, start to finish. A teacher wants to add alt text to a practice set. She runs the four commands in order. The clone gives her a working copy. She edits problems.md in a text editor. The add command selects that file, the commit command saves the change with a message that says what she did, and the push command publishes it. The history now shows her change, her name, and the date.

The Words Are the Hard Part

Commit, branch, and merge sound strange at first, and nearly everyone stumbles on them. You already keep a history when you save a document under a new name, and Git does the same with a message attached. Start with the four terms in the table and the rest follows.

The MicroSim below shows a small repository's history as a graph. Each circle is a commit, and the lines show which commit came before which. In explore mode you click a commit to read its message. In quiz mode you answer questions about the history by clicking the right commit.

docs.title: Diagram: Git History Explorer
docs.text:
Git History Explorer

Type: graph-model sim-id: git-history-explorer Library: vis-network Status: Specified Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: examine Learning Objective: The learner will examine the history of a small repository to find the commit that answers each of six questions, with at least 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Version Control, Git (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: In quiz mode the learner clicks the commit that answers a question. A click is correct when it matches the Correct commit column in Content. Mastery is at least 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Clicking commits in explore mode is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A merge commit is the same as the changes it combines. (2) A branch is a separate copy of the files. (3) The history cannot show who made a change.

Instructional Rationale: Examining a history is an Analyze-level action, because the learner must read the parts, the messages and the structure, to find which one answers a question. A graph shows the branch and the merge as shape, so the learner sees what the words describe.

Content:

The graph has 8 nodes, one per commit, and 8 edges. Each edge points from a commit to its parent, the commit that came before it. Commit c7 is a merge commit and has two parents, c6 and c5. The repository is a made-up practice set called Fraction Practice Set, and the authors are made up. Clicking a node highlights its parents and children and shows its details.

Commit Author Date Message Files changed Branch Parents c1 Priya Shah 2026-09-01 Add first draft of the fraction problems problems.md main none c2 Priya Shah 2026-09-03 Add an answer key answers.md main c1 c3 Sam Okafor 2026-09-10 Fix the answer to problem 7 answers.md main c2 c4 Dana Reyes 2026-09-12 Start alt text work: describe the two number-line images problems.md alt-text c3 c5 Dana Reyes 2026-09-13 Add alt text to two more images problems.md alt-text c4 c6 Priya Shah 2026-09-14 Define denominator where it first appears problems.md main c3 c7 Priya Shah 2026-09-15 Merge the alt-text branch into main problems.md main c6 and c5 c8 Priya Shah 2026-09-16 Add CHANGELOG.md listing the changes CHANGELOG.md main c7

The six questions, in this order:

# Question shown to the learner Correct commit Why (shown as feedback) 1 Which commit first added an answer key? c2 Its message says it added an answer key, and it changed answers.md. 2 Which commit corrected a wrong answer? c3 Its message says it fixed the answer to problem 7. 3 Which commit began the alt text work? c4 It is the first commit on the alt-text branch and its message names the number-line images. 4 Which commit brought the alt text work into the main line? c7 It is the merge commit, and it has two parents, c6 and c5. 5 Which commit created the first list of changes? c8 It added CHANGELOG.md. 6 Which commit defined the word denominator? c6 Its message says it defined denominator where it first appears.

Provenance: The repository, authors, dates, and messages are made up for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative example". The terms follow the chapter section "Git".

Rules: Each question has exactly one correct commit. Clicking a branch label or the background during the quiz counts as a wrong attempt. The sim offers buttons to zoom and does not zoom with the mouse wheel.

Learner Activity:

  1. In explore mode the learner clicks each commit and reads its author, date, message, and files changed.
  2. In quiz mode the sim shows question 1 above the graph.
  3. The learner clicks the commit that answers it.
  4. If the first click is wrong, the sim says so and the learner tries once more. If the second click is also wrong, the sim reveals the commit and the Why text.
  5. After question 6 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 6 questions in the fixed order, two attempts each. Only a correct first click counts as evidence. Correct: "Correct: [commit]. [Why]". First wrong click: "Not quite. Read the commit messages again." Second wrong click: "The answer is [commit]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 6 correct on the first attempt". At 5 or more it adds "You can read a history." Below 5 it lists the questions the learner missed.

Starting State: The graph with all 8 commits visible, explore mode active, and the prompt "Click a commit to see what changed."

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's terms are repository, commit, branch, and merge. The chapter says a history records an author, a date, and a message for every change.

docs.title: GitHub Repository
docs.text:
GitHub is a website that hosts Git repositories and adds tools for people to work together. A GitHub repository is one project's page on that site, holding the files, the history, and the discussion around them. Many open resources live in GitHub repositories because the site is free for public projects, shows the history, and can publish a repository as a web page. Other hosts do the same job, and a repository can be copied between hosts because Git is open.

A repository page has parts that a reviewer learns to read:

  • The file list: the source files themselves.
  • The README: a text file shown below the file list that says what the resource is and how to use it.
  • The license file: a file, often named LICENSE, that states the license.
  • The commit history: the record of every change.
  • Issues: a place where users report problems or ask questions.
  • Pull requests: a place where people propose changes, explained a few sections ahead.

Worked example: reading a repository. A reviewer opens the repository for a practice set and answers four questions in five minutes. Is there a license file, and does it match the resource's license statement? When was the last commit, and so is the resource still maintained? Are the files in open formats such as Markdown? Do the open issues show unresolved problems? Each answer gives evidence for the open license, editable source, and accuracy metrics. Evidence from a repository, such as the date of a commit, can be checked and cited.

The MicroSim below shows an illustration of a repository page. Eight numbered markers point to the parts a reviewer reads.

docs.title: Diagram: Anatomy of a GitHub Repository Page
docs.text:
Anatomy of a GitHub Repository Page

Type: infographic sim-id: github-repository-anatomy Library: html Status: Specified Bloom Level: Remember Bloom Verb: identify Learning Objective: The learner will identify the eight parts of a repository page that a reviewer reads, from a description of each part's appearance, with at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: GitHub Repository, Version Control, Git (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: In quiz mode the learner clicks the marker that matches a visual hint. A click is correct when it matches the marker named in the Hint column of Content. Mastery is at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Hovering in explore mode is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) The README is the license. (2) The fork button changes the original repository. (3) The file list shows only the final version.

Instructional Rationale: Identifying the parts of a page is a Remember-level task, and an illustration of the page places each part where the reviewer will find it. The quiz asks the learner to go from the look of a part to its name, which is how they will navigate a real repository.

Content:

The illustration is a text-free flat drawing of a repository page in a browser frame. Under the page header is a row of five small tabs. At the upper right is a small button with a branching-line icon. At the left, above the main area, is a drop-down box. Below it is a thin strip holding a small round avatar and one short line of text, and beside the strip is a small clock icon with a number. Under the strip is a column of rows, each with a folder icon or a file icon. Below the column is a large block of text lines. In a narrow column at the right is a small scales icon beside a short line. The eight markers:

# Label Hint (describes the look, not the name) Description Tip 1 Tab row A row of five small tabs under the page header. The tabs switch between the files, the reported problems (issues), and the proposed changes (pull requests). Open the issues tab to see problems others have found. 2 Fork button A small button with a branching-line icon at the upper right. Creates your own copy of the repository, which you can change without touching the original. Fork before you revise, so the original stays as the author left it. 3 Branch selector A drop-down box at the left above the main area. Switches between lines of work, like the main line and a branch for a new feature. The main branch is the usual place to read the current version. 4 Latest commit strip A thin strip with a small round avatar and one short line of text. Shows who made the most recent change, what they said about it, and when. A last commit that is years old suggests the resource is no longer maintained. 5 Commit history link A small clock icon with a number beside it. Opens the full list of commits, with authors, dates, and messages. Use it to date your evidence: cite the commit you reviewed. 6 File list A column of rows, each with a folder icon or a file icon. Lists the source files and folders in the repository. Check the file types: Markdown or HTML suggest an editable source. 7 README A large block of text lines below the file list. Explains what the resource is, how its files fit together, and how to use it. A README is the note that the editable source metric's seventh check asks for. 8 License entry A small scales icon beside a short line in the narrow column at the right. Shows the repository's license, taken from its license file. Compare it with the license statement on the resource itself.

Provenance: The parts follow the chapter section "GitHub Repository". The illustration is synthetic, and the sim labels the page "illustrative example". The sim states that the layout of a real GitHub page can change over time and that the parts, not their positions, are what a reviewer should look for.

Rules: Each hint matches exactly one marker. The illustration contains no text, so every label comes from the table above. Markers are numbered 1 to 8 in the order of the table.

Learner Activity:

  1. In explore mode the learner hovers or clicks a marker and reads its label, description, and tip.
  2. In quiz mode the sim shows a hint.
  3. The learner clicks the marker they think the hint describes.
  4. If the first click is wrong, the sim says so and lets the learner try once more. If the second click is also wrong, the sim reveals the marker and its description.
  5. After all 8 hints the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 8 hints in a shuffled order, two attempts each. Only a correct first click counts as evidence. Correct: "Correct: [label]. [Description]". First wrong click: "Not quite. Look again at the hint: [hint]". Second wrong click: "This is [label]. [Description]". The summary shows "[n] of 8 correct on the first attempt". At 7 or more it adds "You can read a repository page." Below 7 it lists the labels of the missed parts.

Starting State: The illustration with eight numbered markers, explore mode active, and the prompt "Hover a marker to see what it is."

Chapter Anchors: The chapter lists the parts of a repository page as the file list, the README, the license file, the commit history, issues, and pull requests. The chapter says a README is the short note that explains how the pieces fit together.

docs.title: Fork
docs.text: A fork is your own copy of someone else's repository, made on the same site. The copy is independent: you can change it freely without affecting the original, and it keeps a link back to the source. Forking is the repository version of the revise and remix permissions. An open license gives you the right to change a resource, and a fork gives you the place to do it. A teacher who wants to adapt an open lesson for her class forks the repository, edits her copy, and keeps the original untouched.

docs.title: Pull Request
docs.text:
A pull request is a proposal to merge changes from one copy of a repository into another. It lets you offer a correction to the original author instead of keeping it in your fork. You make the change in your fork, open a pull request, and the maintainer reads it, comments, and either merges it or asks for changes. Pull requests are how a small fix, such as a typo or a missing alt text, travels from one teacher to every other teacher who uses the resource. They also keep the original's quality under review, because every change is read before it joins the main line.

The MicroSim below tests whether you know the order of a contribution. It gives you seven steps in a scrambled order, and you put them into the right sequence.

docs.title: Diagram: Fork and Pull Request Sequencer
docs.text:
Fork and Pull Request Sequencer

Type: microsim sim-id: fork-pull-request-sequencer Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Remember Bloom Verb: list Learning Objective: The learner will list the seven steps of contributing an improvement to an open resource in the correct order, with at least 6 of 7 steps in the correct position on the first Check.

Prerequisites: Fork, Pull Request, GitHub Repository, Git (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: The learner arranges seven steps and presses Check. A step is correct when it sits in the position given in the Position column of Content. Mastery is at least 6 of 7 steps in the correct position on the first Check. Rearranging steps before pressing Check is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) You edit the original repository directly. (2) A pull request is sent before the change is made. (3) The maintainer must accept every pull request.

Instructional Rationale: Ordering the steps of a process is a Remember-level task that checks whether the learner holds the sequence. Each step depends on the one before, so a wrong position can be explained by a dependency.

Content:

The seven steps, with their correct positions and the reason each follows its predecessor:

Position Step Why it comes here 1 Find the repository of the resource you want to improve. You cannot copy what you have not found. 2 Fork the repository to make your own copy. You change your copy, not the original. 3 Make your change in your copy and save it with a message that says what you did. A pull request needs a change to propose. 4 Open a pull request that proposes your change to the original repository. The maintainer can only review a change that has been proposed. 5 The maintainer reads your pull request and leaves comments. The review follows the proposal. 6 You answer any comments by adding more changes to your copy. You respond to what the review found. 7 The maintainer merges the pull request into the original. Merging is the last step, after the review is satisfied.

Provenance: The steps follow the chapter sections "Fork" and "Pull Request". The sim states that a maintainer may also decline a pull request, and that the sequence shows the successful path.

Rules: Each step has exactly one correct position, and the seven positions are distinct. The learner may move steps freely before pressing Check. After a Check, steps in the correct position are marked correct and the rest are marked out of place.

Learner Activity:

  1. The sim shows the seven steps in a shuffled order.
  2. The learner moves steps up or down to put them in the order they think is correct.
  3. The learner presses Check.
  4. The sim shows which steps are in the correct position and, for each out-of-place step, the reason it belongs where it does.
  5. The learner may rearrange and Check again.

Feedback: The learner may press Check as many times as they like, and only the first Check counts as evidence. After each Check the sim shows "[n] of 7 steps in the correct position". Correct steps are marked correct. For each out-of-place step the sim shows its Why text. At 6 or more on the first Check it adds "You know the order of a contribution." Below 6 it reports the count and invites another try.

Starting State: The seven steps in a shuffled order that is not the correct order, and the prompt "Put the steps in the order a contribution happens."

Chapter Anchors: The chapter says a fork is your own copy, that you make the change in your fork, and that a pull request proposes your change to the original, where the maintainer reads it and may merge it.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text:
A changelog is a file that lists the notable changes to a resource in order, usually with a date or a version number and a line for each change. A reviser can read it to see what changed without comparing files, and a reuser can decide whether to update. A changelog is also the right place to record changes for the attribution requirement from Chapter 2, which asks anyone who adapts a CC BY work to say what they changed. A common convention uses a file named CHANGELOG.md, with the newest entry first.

## 2026-09-16

- Added alt text to four images.
- Defined the word denominator where it first appears.
- Fixed the answer to problem 7.

The Markdown above shows a changelog entry: a date as a heading, then one bullet per change. Each bullet is short and says what changed, not why.

One Line, Two Jobs

Write each change in the changelog as one dated line. The same line later serves as the change note that a CC BY credit requires, so you write it once and use it twice.

docs.title: Scoring the Editable Source Metric
docs.text:
You now have what you need to score the metric. The procedure has six steps. List the files the resource offers. Open the source files in a free tool. Run the ten checks from the first section of this chapter. Count the passes and find the band. Choose the number inside the band, using the lower one when a failed check blocks revision. Record the evidence for each failed check.

The last MicroSim of the chapter is a scoring practice. It shows five resources with their ten check results, and for each one you choose the score from 0 to 10.

docs.title: Diagram: Editable Source Metric Scorer
docs.text:
Editable Source Metric Scorer

Type: microsim sim-id: editable-source-metric-scorer Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: apply Learning Objective: The learner will apply the ten editable source checks and the Chapter 3 scoring rules to choose the metric score for each of five resources, with at least 4 of 5 scores exactly correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: The Editable Source Metric, Metric Score, Scoring Descriptor, Source Format, Open File Format, Changelog (all defined in this chapter or in Chapter 3 above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each resource the learner chooses a whole-number score from 0 to 10 after seeing the ten check results. A score is correct when it equals the Correct score column in Content. Mastery is at least 4 of 5 scores correct on the first attempt. Opening the check list and the descriptor table is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Any failed check lowers the score by the same amount. (2) A resource with some editable files scores at least 5. (3) The higher number in a band is always correct.

Instructional Rationale: Applying a scoring procedure to new cases is an Apply-level task. Five resources with different mixes of passes and blocking failures make the learner use every step: count, band, then choose within the band.

Content:

The ten checks, each marked as blocking or not:

# Check Blocks revision if it fails? 1 An editable source file is offered, not only a PDF Yes 2 The source is in an open format Yes 3 The source holds all of the content Yes 4 The source can be downloaded with no login or payment Yes 5 Images have their original or vector source files No 6 Interactive parts supply their code Yes 7 A short note explains how the pieces fit together No 8 A record of changes is available No 9 The reviewer opened the source in a free tool and it displayed correctly Yes 10 Editing needs no paid software or special template Yes

The descriptor bands, applied to the share of checks passed: 0% is 0; 1% to 24% is 1 to 2; 25% to 49% is 3 to 4; 50% to 74% is 5 to 6; 75% to 89% is 7 to 8; 90% to 100% is 9 to 10. Within a two-number band, choose the lower number when any failed check blocks revision, and the higher number otherwise. A score of 10 requires every check to pass. A check that does not apply counts as passed.

The five resources:

# Resource Checks failed Checks passed Share Band Blocking failure? Correct score Why (shown as feedback) 1 Open Algebra None 10 100% 9 to 10 No 10 Every check passed, so the score is 10. 2 Watershed Basics 5 and 8 8 80% 7 to 8 No 8 Neither failed check blocks revision, so the higher number applies. 3 District Unit 3 and 7 8 80% 7 to 8 Yes, check 3 7 The source is missing part of the content, which blocks revision, so the lower number applies. 4 Handout Scans 1, 2, 3, 5, 9 5 (checks 4, 6, 7, 8, 10) 50% 5 to 6 Yes 5 Check 6 does not apply and counts as passed. Several blocking checks failed, so the lower number applies. 5 PDF-Only Report 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 8, 9 3 (checks 4, 6, 10) 30% 3 to 4 Yes 3 Check 6 does not apply and counts as passed. Blocking checks failed, so the lower number applies.

Provenance: The ten checks and the descriptor bands follow the chapter sections "The Editable Source Metric" and Chapter 3. The five resources are illustrative cases written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". Resource 2 is the chapter's worked example.

Rules: A score is the band chosen from the share passed, and then the number chosen within the band by the blocking rule. Each resource has exactly one correct score. For a band that holds a single number, that number is the score.

Learner Activity:

  1. The sim shows resource 1 with its ten check results.
  2. The learner may open the check list and the descriptor table.
  3. The learner chooses a score from 0 to 10, and the choice is committed.
  4. The sim shows the count of passes, the band, whether any failure blocks revision, and the correct score with the Why text.
  5. After resource 5 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 5 resources in the fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [score]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. [passes] checks passed, which is [share] and the [band] band. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 5 correct on the first attempt". At 4 or more it adds "You can score editable source." Below 4 it lists the Why text of each missed resource.

Starting State: Resource 1 with all ten results shown and no score chosen. The question shown is "What editable source score does this resource earn?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's worked example for Watershed Basics fails checks 5 and 8, passes 8 of 10, and scores 8, with the higher number chosen because neither failure blocks revision.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• The editable source metric asks whether others can change the resource. Ten checks decide the score, and a failed check that blocks revision pulls the score to the lower number in its band.
  • A source format is the form you edit, and a delivery format is the form you read. An open file format has a public specification, can be implemented without a fee, and opens in free software.
  • Markdown and HTML are plain-text open formats. A word processing file is a reasonable source. PDF-only distribution is a locked file.
  • Version control records every change with an author, a date, and a message. Git is the open-source tool, and a GitHub repository is a project's page on a hosting site.
  • A fork is your own copy, a pull request proposes your change to the original, and a changelog lists the changes in order.

You Can Tell Source From Cake

You can now tell an editable source from a locked file, name an open format, read a repository's history, and score the editable source metric with evidence. A resource you can change is a resource you can improve, and this chapter gave you the means to check.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Open File Formats and Version Control
docs.text: Test your understanding of the editable source metric, open file formats, Markdown, and version control with Git and GitHub with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. What is a fork of a repository?
docs.text:
1. A separate line of work inside the same repository that leaves the main line undisturbed
  2. Your own independent copy of someone else's repository, which keeps a link back to the source
  3. A proposal to merge changes from one copy of a repository into another copy, for the maintainer to review
  4. A saved snapshot of changes, with an author, a date, and a message that says what was done
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. A fork is your own independent copy of someone else's repository, made on the same site. You can change it freely without affecting the original, and it keeps a link back to the source. Forking is the repository version of the revise and remix permissions: the open license gives you the right to change a resource, and the fork gives you the place to do it. Option A describes a branch, C a pull request, and D a commit.

Concept Tested: Fork

See: Fork

docs.title: 2. Which set of tests identifies an open file format?
docs.text:
1. The specification is published, anyone can implement it without paying, and free software opens it
  2. The file is free to download, widely used, and created by a nonprofit organization
  3. The file prints well, looks the same on every device, and is saved as a PDF by a design program
  4. The file is plain text, is under one megabyte, and contains no images or any other media
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Three questions test a format: is the specification published, can anyone implement it without paying a fee or asking permission, and does free software exist that opens it? A format that passes all three stays readable when a company changes its products or closes. Price, popularity, printing quality, and file size say nothing about openness. A file can also be an open standard and still be a poor source for editing, as the PDF shows.

Concept Tested: Open File Format

See: Open File Format

docs.title: 3. Why is a resource that offers only a PDF a poor choice for a teacher who wants to revise it?
docs.text:
1. A PDF is a closed format that no free software can open, so it cannot be edited or even read at all
  2. A PDF cannot carry an open license, so revision is not permitted even if the owner agrees
  3. A PDF records how pages look, not how content is built, so a change means rebuilding the structure
  4. A PDF is too large to download without creating a login, which blocks every revision attempt
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. A PDF is an open international standard and free software opens it, so option A is wrong. The problem is structure: a PDF records the appearance of each page, so changing a sentence means copying text out of the page, losing headings and tables, and rebuilding the layout. A license can be attached to a PDF, so the right to revise may exist even though the practical means do not. Ask the author for the source file.

Concept Tested: PDF-Only Distribution

See: PDF-Only Distribution

docs.title: 4. What is the difference between a source format and a delivery format?
docs.text:
1. A source format is always an open standard that free tools can read, while a delivery format is always a closed one
  2. A source format is meant for readers who study the content, while a delivery format is meant for authors who write it
  3. A source format keeps the structure so the content can be changed, while a delivery format is for reading or printing
  4. A source format is stored on GitHub in a repository, while a delivery format is stored on a school website
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The chapter compares a source to a recipe and a delivery file to a cake. You can change an ingredient in the recipe and bake again, but you cannot take the sugar out of the cake. A source format such as Markdown, HTML, or a word processing file keeps headings, lists, and links. A delivery format such as a PDF or a scan often keeps only the appearance. Where a file is stored (D) does not decide which kind it is.

Concept Tested: Source Format

See: Source Format

docs.title: 5. Why does version control help when several teachers improve the same open resource?
docs.text:
1. It stops anyone except the original author from changing the files, so no edits can conflict
  2. It stores each person's edits in a separate copy that is never combined with the other copies
  3. It converts every file to a PDF, so that all of the changes look the same to every reader
  4. It records every change with an author, date, and message, combines edits, and can restore any earlier version
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Version control replaces a folder of confusing copies such as lesson_final2.docx with one set of files and a recorded history. A reviser can see exactly what changed, a mistake can be undone by returning to an earlier state, and several people can work at once and combine their changes. A reuser can also judge a resource's health from the date of its last change. Open resources depend on this, because anyone may revise them.

Concept Tested: Version Control

See: Version Control

docs.title: 6. A reviewer applies the ten editable source checks to a district unit. Check 3 (the source holds all of the content) and check 7 (a note explains how the pieces fit) fail, and the other eight pass. What score does the chapter's rule give?
docs.text:
1. 7, because 80 percent falls in the 7 to 8 band and the missing content blocks revision
  2. 8, because 80 percent falls in the 7 to 8 band and the higher number is always used
  3. 6, because each failed check lowers a score of 10 by two points
  4. 5, because a failed check that blocks revision caps the score at 5
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Eight of ten checks pass, a share of 80 percent, which falls in the 7 to 8 band. Check 3 blocks revision when it fails, because a reviser cannot change content that is missing from the source. When a failed check blocks revision, choose the lower number in the band, so the score is 7. The higher number (B) is correct only when no failed check blocks revision, as with the image and change-record failures in the chapter's Watershed Basics example.

Concept Tested: Editable Source Metric

See: Scoring the Editable Source Metric

docs.title: 7. Which line of Markdown shows an image whose alt text is "A river flowing through a valley"?
docs.text:
1. [A river flowing through a valley](https://example.org/images/river.png)
  2. ![A river flowing through a valley](https://example.org/images/river.png)
  3. ![https://example.org/images/river.png](A river flowing through a valley)
  4. ## A river flowing through a valley
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. An image uses the same pattern as a link, with an exclamation mark in front: square brackets hold the alt text, and parentheses hold the address. Option A has no exclamation mark, so it creates a link and not an image. Option C swaps the alt text and the address. Option D creates a level-2 heading. Alt text is the description that a screen reader speaks, so a reviser should never leave the brackets empty.

Concept Tested: Markdown

See: Markdown

docs.title: 8. A teacher finds a typo in an open lesson on GitHub and wants every teacher who uses the lesson to benefit from the fix. Which sequence should she follow?
docs.text:
1. Edit the original repository directly, then fork it to record the change
  2. Fork the repository, fix the typo in her copy, then open a pull request to the original
  3. Open a pull request first, then fork the repository and make the change
  4. Fork the repository, fix the typo, and keep it in her fork, because pull requests are only for large changes
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. She forks the repository to make her own copy, makes the change in the fork, and then opens a pull request that proposes the change to the original. The maintainer reads it, comments, and may merge it. A pull request is how a small fix, such as a typo or missing alt text, travels to every teacher who uses the resource. A pull request needs a change to propose, so it cannot come first (C).

Concept Tested: Pull Request

See: Pull Request

docs.title: 9. A reviewer opens a repository and finds a README, a LICENSE file stating CC BY 4.0, and Markdown source files. The latest commit is four years old, and several open issues report errors that nobody has answered. What does this evidence most strongly suggest?
docs.text:
1. The resource is high quality, because it uses open formats and an open license and has a README
  2. The resource has no editable source, because its commits are old and the files are therefore locked
  3. The license is invalid, because the repository is no longer active and the owner has not replied
  4. The resource has an open license and editable source but may be unmaintained, so accuracy and currency need checking
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The license file and Markdown files are good evidence for the open license and editable source metrics. A last commit that is years old suggests the resource is no longer maintained, and unanswered issues that report errors point to problems in accuracy and currency. Open formats say nothing about quality (A), and the age of the commits does not remove the source files (B) or invalidate the license (C). Evidence from a repository can be checked and cited.

Concept Tested: GitHub Repository

See: GitHub Repository

docs.title: 10. A reviewer's editable source checks fail for four different resources. Which failed check would block a reviser from changing the content and so pull the score to the lower number in its band?
docs.text:
1. The images are PNG files, and no original or vector source files are offered for them
  2. No short note explains how the pieces of the resource fit together or what each file does
  3. The source file leaves out part of the content, such as tables and equations
  4. No record of changes is available, such as a changelog or a list of past versions
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. A failed check blocks revision when a reviser cannot change the content without it. If the source omits tables or equations, those parts cannot be edited at all. A reviser can still change every word and replace any picture without the original image files (A), and a missing note (B) or change record (D) makes the work harder but does not stop it. The chapter marks checks 5, 7, and 8 as non-blocking.

Concept Tested: Editable Source Metric

See: The Editable Source Metric

docs.title: References: Open File Formats and Version Control
docs.text:
1. Open file format - Wikipedia - Defines file formats whose specifications are published so anyone can implement them without fees, with examples. Background for deciding whether a resource's source files count as open and editable.

  2. Markdown - Wikipedia - Describes the lightweight plain-text syntax, its history, and variants such as CommonMark. Shows why Markdown is this book's recommended editable source format for text.

  3. Git - Wikipedia - Explains Git's distributed model, commits, branches, and history. Background for the chapter's version control section and for reading repository history as evidence when scoring editable source.

  4. Pro Git (2nd ed.) - Scott Chacon and Ben Straub - Apress (2014) - Chacon and Straub explain Git as a series of snapshots of the whole project rather than a list of file differences. That mental model, with clear diagrams of commits and branches, makes history easy to picture.

  5. Version Control by Example - Eric Sink - Pyrenean Gold Press (2011) - Sink walks two fictional developers through parallel edits and merges, repeating the story in centralized and distributed tools. The approach helps nonprogrammers see why a shared history matters.

  6. Markdown Guide: Basic Syntax - Markdown Guide - A clear reference for headings, emphasis, lists, links, and images in Markdown, with side-by-side examples. Enough to read and edit the Markdown source of an OER and to try the chapter's exercises.

  7. CommonMark Help - CommonMark - A quick Markdown reference plus an interactive ten-minute tutorial built on the CommonMark standard. Lets teachers practice the syntax in the browser before editing a resource.

  8. Hello World - GitHub Docs - A short tutorial that creates a repository, a branch, a commit, and a pull request. Gives teachers hands-on experience with the version control steps this chapter describes.

  9. Version Control with Git - Software Carpentry - A free lesson for beginners on tracking changes, viewing history, and collaborating with Git, written for people who are not programmers. A gentle companion to the chapter's version control section.

  10. Basic HTML Syntax - MDN Web Docs - Introduces elements, tags, and attributes in HTML. Helps teachers recognize HTML as an open, editable source format and read the pages they will adapt.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Teaches teachers to score accuracy and currency by fact checking, evaluating citations, spotting outdated content and broken links, and deciding when expert review is needed. It is the first of the quality-metric chapters and relies on the rubric from the previous chapters. After this chapter you can check a resource's facts and citations, find outdated content and broken links, and record the evidence for an accuracy score.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 14 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Accuracy Metric 198 Currency Metric 11 Factual Error 6 Fact Checking 3 Source Citation 191 Primary Source 3 Secondary Source 2 Citation Quality 1 Outdated Content 8 Publication Date 2 Revision History 1 Link Rot 4 Broken Link Check 3 Expert Review 2

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 3: The Ten-Metric Rubric and Scoring

A Confident Sentence Is Not a True One

A resource can be well written, nicely designed, and wrong. This chapter teaches you to check the facts, follow each citation back to its source, and test the links, so that your first quality score rests on evidence and not on how sure the text sounds. Let's dive in and check the evidence!

The first quality metric in the ten-metric rubric asks one question: are the facts correct and up to date? It sounds simple, and it is the metric where a careless reviewer does the most damage. Readers trust a resource that sounds certain, and a text that sounds certain is not always right. A reviewer's job is to ask what each important sentence rests on.

This chapter splits the metric into its two halves. Accuracy asks whether the facts were correct when written. Currency asks whether they are still correct now. You will learn to check a sample of facts, to follow citations back to their sources, to judge whether a citation really supports a claim, to spot content that has aged, to test links, and to decide when you need an expert. The last section combines all of it into a score.

docs.title: The Accuracy Metric
docs.text:
The accuracy metric is the half of the first quality metric that asks whether the facts in a resource are correct. A fact here means any claim that can be checked against a source: a date, a number, a definition, a name, a quotation, a procedure, or a step in a calculation. Pictures make claims too, because a caption or a labeled diagram states something that can be right or wrong. Accuracy does not cover opinions or teaching choices, which other metrics score.

No reviewer can check every claim in a resource. The method is to check a sample. Pick at least 10 checkable facts, spread across the resource's sections, and favor the kinds of claims that are likeliest to be wrong or most costly if they are: numbers, dates, names, and statements about cause. For each fact record where it appears, the source you checked it against, and the result, which is match, mismatch, or not checkable. Report the sample size with the score, since "9 of 10 matched" says more than "mostly accurate".

Check each fact against a reliable source that is independent of the resource. Checking against another copy of the same text proves nothing, because copied errors spread.

Worked example: a 10-fact sample for Watershed Basics. The reviewer reads the three sections, picks ten claims that can be checked, and checks each against a reliable source. The river, the lake, and the agency are made up for this book, and the table labels the data illustrative.

# Where Claim in the resource Checked against Result 1 Section 1 A watershed is an area of land that drains to a common outlet. A national water agency's glossary Match 2 Section 1 Rain that falls on a watershed flows downhill to streams, lakes, or the sea. The agency's introduction to watersheds Match 3 Section 1 A large watershed can contain many smaller watersheds. The agency's introduction Match 4 Section 2 The Clearwater River is 410 miles long. The State Water Agency's current river data page Mismatch: the page now gives 398 miles, and the text uses an older figure 5 Section 2 The Clearwater River drains about 6,000 square miles. The State Water Agency's river data page Match 6 Section 2 The Clearwater River flows into Lake Marlow. The state atlas Match 7 Section 3 Groundwater stored in underground layers is called an aquifer. A geological survey glossary Match 8 Section 3 Wetlands can slow floodwater and filter pollutants. The agency's wetlands page Match 9 Section 3 Many rivers are fed in part by springs. The geological survey's water pages Match 10 Section 3 Paved surfaces increase runoff. The agency's runoff page Match

Nine of the ten facts match. The mismatch is a figure that was right once and has since been corrected, so it is both an accuracy finding and a currency finding. The final section of this chapter shows how that single fact affects the score.

docs.title: Factual Error
docs.text:
A factual error is a statement in a resource that is false, because it disagrees with reliable evidence about what is true. Errors come in several kinds, and naming the kind tells the reviewer what to record and the author what to fix.

Kind What it looks like Wrong fact A claim that is simply false, such as the wrong number of chambers in a human heart Wrong number or unit A correct fact with a wrong figure, such as milliliters written as liters Misattributed quote A real statement credited to the wrong person Outdated statement A claim that was true once and is no longer Unsupported claim A claim that offers no evidence, so no one can tell Misleading simplification A claim that is true as far as it goes and leaves out something that changes the meaning

An error is serious when a learner could take away a false or outdated fact, and minor when it does not mislead, as with a misspelled name. A disagreement among experts is not an error. If reliable sources differ, record the claim as contested and say so, instead of marking it wrong.

Worked example: classifying five findings.

Finding Kind Severity The text says water boils at 90 degrees Celsius at sea level. Wrong number or unit Serious A famous quotation is credited to the wrong person in a footnote. Misattributed quote Minor The text gives a river's length from an older survey. Outdated statement Serious A statistic appears with no source. Unsupported claim Not yet known, until someone checks it The text says plants get their food from the soil and never mentions sunlight. Misleading simplification Serious

The first MicroSim of the chapter trains this distinction. It shows eight short reports of errors, and for each one you choose the kind of error it describes.

docs.title: Diagram: Error Type Sorter
docs.text:
Error Type Sorter

Type: microsim sim-id: error-type-sorter Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: distinguish Learning Objective: The learner will distinguish six kinds of factual error by choosing the kind that each of eight error reports describes, with at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Factual Error, The Accuracy Metric (both defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each report the learner chooses one of six kinds. A choice is correct when it matches the Correct kind column in Content. Mastery is at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the kind definitions is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) An outdated statement is a wrong fact. (2) A claim with no source is false. (3) A simplification is never an error.

Instructional Rationale: Distinguishing kinds of error is an Analyze-level action, and the six kinds overlap in everyday speech. Eight reports that each isolate one kind make the learner attend to what exactly is wrong.

Content:

The six kinds: Wrong fact, Wrong number or unit, Misattributed quote, Outdated statement, Unsupported claim, Misleading simplification.

The eight reports:

# Report shown to the learner Correct kind Why (shown as feedback) 1 A reading says the human heart has three chambers. Wrong fact The claim is false: the human heart has four chambers. 2 A lab page tells students to measure 5 liters where its own source says 5 milliliters. Wrong number or unit The fact is right and the unit is wrong. 3 A history page credits a famous speech to the wrong speaker. Misattributed quote A real statement is credited to the wrong person. 4 A technology page tells students to use a program that was discontinued in 2019. Outdated statement The advice was sound when written and no longer works. 5 A health page says studies prove a diet works and cites nothing. Unsupported claim No evidence is offered, so no one can tell whether it is true. 6 A science page says plants get their food from the soil and never mentions sunlight. Misleading simplification It is partly true and leaves out what changes the meaning. 7 A math page says the area of a rectangle is its length plus its width. Wrong fact The formula is false: area is length times width. 8 A page quotes statistics from a recent study that is ten years old. Outdated statement The statistics were current once and are old now.

Provenance: The reports are illustrative cases written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The kinds follow the chapter section "Factual Error". The product named in report 4 is not named in the sim.

Rules: Each report has exactly one correct kind. Reports 1 and 7 are Wrong fact, and reports 4 and 8 are Outdated statement.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads one report and sees the six kinds.
  2. The learner may open the kind definitions. Opening them does not change the score.
  3. The learner chooses a kind, and the choice is committed.
  4. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text.
  5. After report 8 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 8 reports in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [kind]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. This is [kind]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 8 correct on the first attempt". At 7 or more it adds "You can name the error." Below 7 it lists the Why text of each missed report.

Starting State: The first report, the six kinds, and the definitions closed. The question shown is "What kind of error is this?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter lists six kinds of factual error: wrong fact, wrong number or unit, misattributed quote, outdated statement, unsupported claim, and misleading simplification.

docs.title: Fact Checking
docs.text:
Fact checking is the process of testing a claim by tracing it to a reliable source and comparing the two. The process has six steps:

  1. Pick the claim, and write down its exact words.
  2. Decide what would count as a reliable source for that kind of claim.
  3. Find the source, preferably the original and not a copy.
  4. Compare the claim and the source word for word and number for number.
  5. Record the result as match, mismatch, or not addressed by the source.
  6. Cite where you looked, so another reviewer can repeat the check.

The result "not addressed" matters. A source that does not mention a claim neither supports nor contradicts it, and a reviewer who counts silence as support will pass claims that were never checked.

Silence Is Not Support

A source that never mentions a claim has not confirmed it. Count "not addressed" as its own result, and never as a match.

The MicroSim below practices the comparison step. It shows a short source and eight claims, and for each claim you decide whether the source supports it, contradicts it, or does not address it.

docs.title: Diagram: Fact Check Matcher
docs.text:
Fact Check Matcher

Type: microsim sim-id: fact-check-matcher Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: judge Learning Objective: The learner will judge whether a source supports, contradicts, or does not address each of eight claims, with at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Fact Checking, Factual Error, The Accuracy Metric (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each claim the learner commits one of three verdicts. A verdict is correct when it matches the Correct verdict column in Content. Mastery is at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Rereading the source is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A claim the source does not mention is supported. (2) A claim that looks similar to the source is supported. (3) A small number difference can be ignored.

Instructional Rationale: Judging a claim against a source is an Evaluate-level action that fact checking depends on. Including claims that the source does not address, and claims that differ by one digit, teaches the learner to read the source closely and to count silence separately.

Content:

The source, shown at all times (a made-up fact sheet): "Lake Marlow Fact Sheet, State Water Agency, 2025. Lake Marlow covers 14 square kilometers. Its deepest point is 31 meters.
