The lake is fed by the Clearwater River and two smaller streams. Fishing is permitted year-round. Swimming is permitted from June to September. The lake was formed by a glacier about 12,000 years ago."

The three verdicts: Supported, Contradicted, Not addressed.

The eight claims:

# Claim shown to the learner Correct verdict Why (shown as feedback) 1 Lake Marlow covers 14 square kilometers. Supported The source states this figure. 2 The deepest point of Lake Marlow is 13 meters. Contradicted The source says 31 meters, and the claim swaps the digits. 3 The Clearwater River feeds Lake Marlow. Supported The source names it as one of the inflows. 4 Swimming is allowed all year. Contradicted The source says swimming is permitted from June to September. 5 Lake Marlow is home to rainbow trout. Not addressed The source does not name any fish species. 6 The lake was formed by a glacier. Supported The source says so. 7 Lake Marlow is the largest lake in the state. Not addressed The source gives the lake's area and does not compare it with other lakes. 8 The lake has three inflows. Supported The source lists the river and two smaller streams, which makes three.

Provenance: The lake, the agency, and the fact sheet are made up for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative example". No claim in the sim is a statement about a real place.

Rules: Each claim has exactly one correct verdict. Four claims are Supported, two are Contradicted, and two are Not addressed. A claim is Supported only when the source states it or a direct count or calculation from the source gives it.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees the source and one claim.
  2. The learner chooses Supported, Contradicted, or Not addressed, and the choice is committed.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text, and highlights the part of the source that decides it.
  4. After claim 8 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 8 claims in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [verdict]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. This is [verdict]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 8 correct on the first attempt". At 7 or more it adds "You can compare a claim with a source." Below 7 it lists the Why text of each missed claim.

Starting State: The source and claim 1 or the first claim in the shuffled order, with the three verdicts. The question shown is "Does the source support this claim?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's fact-checking steps end with the three results: match, mismatch, and not addressed by the source. The chapter says silence is not support.

docs.title: Source Citation
docs.text:
A source citation is a reference that tells the reader where a claim came from, in enough detail that the reader can find the source. Citations do three jobs. They let a reviewer check a claim. They let a learner go deeper. And they give credit to the people whose work the resource builds on. A claim with no citation asks the reader to trust the author, and a reviewer cannot score trust.

Citations appear in three common places. An inline citation sits beside the claim, as a number or a short author-and-year mark. A footnote puts the reference at the bottom of the page. A reference list collects all the references at the end. The form varies with the citation style, but a complete reference always carries the same parts: the author, the year, the title, the publisher or journal, a link or identifier, and, for web pages, the date you accessed it.

Not every sentence needs a citation. A claim needs one when it states a statistic, a date, a quotation, a finding of research, or anything a reasonable reader might doubt. Common knowledge and the author's own explanations do not.

Citations also form chains. A textbook cites a review article, the review cites a study, and the study reports the original measurement. An error can enter at any link. A reviewer who stops at the first link has checked the textbook's summary, and has not checked the evidence. The further back you trace a claim, the more you can trust the check.

Worked example: tracing one claim back. A resource says "Wetlands filter pollutants." The reviewer follows the chain.

Step Source What it says Is it the original? 1 The resource's footnote 4 Cites a textbook No 2 The textbook Says wetlands filter pollutants and cites a review No 3 The review article Summarizes several studies of wetland filtering No 4 One of those studies Reports measurements of pollutant levels before and after water passed through a wetland Yes

The claim is supported by the study at the end of the chain. A reviewer who stopped at step 2 would have found only that a textbook agreed with the resource. The next MicroSim shows the parts of a single reference. Six numbered markers point to the parts that a reviewer checks.

docs.title: Diagram: Anatomy of a Source Citation
docs.text:
Anatomy of a Source Citation

Type: infographic sim-id: citation-anatomy Library: html Status: Specified Bloom Level: Remember Bloom Verb: identify Learning Objective: The learner will identify the six parts of a complete reference from a description of each part's look, with at least 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Source Citation, Fact Checking (both defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: In quiz mode the learner clicks the marker that matches a visual hint. A click is correct when it matches the marker named in the Hint column of Content. Mastery is at least 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Hovering in explore mode is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A link alone is a complete citation. (2) The year is the date the reader accessed the page. (3) The publisher is the same as the author.

Instructional Rationale: Identifying the parts of a reference is a Remember-level task, and an illustration of one entry shows how the parts sit together. The quiz asks the learner to recognize a part from its place and look.

Content:

The illustration is a text-free flat drawing of one entry in a reference list on a printed page. The entry is made of separate bars on two lines: a short bar for a name, a small bar inside parentheses, a long bar that is drawn as slanted italic text, a medium bar, an underlined bar that looks like a link, and a small bar with a calendar icon beside it. The six markers:

# Label Hint (describes the look, not the name) Description Tip 1 Author The short bar at the start of the entry. The person or organization that created the work, and the first thing a reviewer checks for expertise. An entry with no author needs extra checking, because no one is accountable for the claim. 2 Year The small bar inside parentheses after the author. The year the work was published, which a reviewer compares with the claim's age. Compare the year with how fast the topic changes. 3 Title The long slanted bar in the middle of the first line. The name of the work, which lets a reader search for it. A title that does not match the claim is a warning sign. 4 Publisher or journal The medium bar after the title. The organization or periodical that published the work, which says something about review and reliability. A reference work from a government agency or a university press has usually been reviewed. 5 Link or identifier The underlined bar on the second line. A web address or a persistent identifier, so a reader can open the source. Test the link, and note the date you tested it. 6 Date accessed The small bar with a calendar icon at the end. The date the citing author last saw the page, which matters because web pages change. A page accessed years ago needs a fresh check.

Provenance: The six parts follow the chapter section "Source Citation". The illustration is synthetic, and the sim labels the entry "illustrative example". The sim states that citation styles order the parts differently.

Rules: Each hint matches exactly one marker. The illustration contains no text, so every label comes from the table above. Markers are numbered 1 to 6 in the order of the table.

Learner Activity:

  1. In explore mode the learner hovers or clicks a marker and reads its label, description, and tip.
  2. In quiz mode the sim shows a hint.
  3. The learner clicks the marker they think the hint describes.
  4. If the first click is wrong, the sim says so and lets the learner try once more. If the second click is also wrong, the sim reveals the marker and its description.
  5. After all 6 hints the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 6 hints in a shuffled order, two attempts each. Only a correct first click counts as evidence. Correct: "Correct: [label]. [Description]". First wrong click: "Not quite. Look again at the hint: [hint]". Second wrong click: "This is [label]. [Description]". The summary shows "[n] of 6 correct on the first attempt". At 5 or more it adds "You can read a reference." Below 5 it lists the labels of the missed parts.

Starting State: The illustration with six numbered markers, explore mode active, and the prompt "Hover a marker to see what it is."

Chapter Anchors: The chapter says a complete reference carries the author, the year, the title, the publisher or journal, a link or identifier, and for web pages the date accessed.

docs.title: Primary Source
docs.text: A primary source is original evidence from the time or the person being described: a measurement, a document, a photograph, an interview, a dataset, or a first report of research. A primary source is the closest you can get to the thing itself. A census table is a primary source for the population on the census date. A lab notebook entry is a primary source for what the experimenter measured.

docs.title: Secondary Source
docs.text:
A secondary source describes, summarizes, or interprets primary sources. Textbooks, review articles, news stories about research, and histories are secondary sources. Encyclopedias and similar reference works also summarize other sources, and some classification schemes call them tertiary. This book treats them as secondary. Secondary sources are useful, because they gather and explain. They are also one step removed, so an error in the summary can hide the original evidence. For important claims, a reviewer follows a secondary source back to a primary one.

The MicroSim below is a sorting practice. Each of ten sources supports a stated claim, and you decide whether it is a primary or a secondary source for that claim.

docs.title: Diagram: Primary or Secondary Source Sorter
docs.text:
Primary or Secondary Source Sorter

Type: microsim sim-id: source-type-sorter Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: classify Learning Objective: The learner will classify each of ten sources as a primary or a secondary source for the claim it supports, with at least 9 of 10 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Primary Source, Secondary Source, Source Citation (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each source the learner commits one of two bins. A placement is correct when it matches the Correct bin column in Content. Mastery is at least 9 of 10 correct on the first attempt. Reading the definitions is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Anything old is a primary source. (2) A website is always a secondary source. (3) A source is primary or secondary in itself, whatever the claim.

Instructional Rationale: Classifying a source is an Understand-level action, and the same document can be primary for one claim and secondary for another. Giving the claim with each source teaches the learner to ask what the source is evidence of.

Content:

The two bins: Primary source (original evidence from the time or person described) and Secondary source (describes, summarizes, or interprets primary sources).

The ten sources:

# Claim Source shown to the learner Correct bin Why (shown as feedback) 1 The town had 4,200 residents in 1990. A census table from 1990 Primary source It is the original count. 2 The town had 4,200 residents in 1990. A textbook paragraph that summarizes the 1990 census Secondary source It describes the census and is not the census. 3 The dam was built with two spillways to handle floods. A recorded interview with the engineer who designed the dam Primary source It comes from the person who made the decision. 4 The dam was built with two spillways to handle floods. A magazine article about that interview Secondary source It reports what someone else said. 5 The temperature in trial 3 was 22 degrees Celsius. The scientist's lab notebook entry for trial 3 Primary source It records the measurement when it was made. 6 Teenagers benefit from later school start times. A review article that summarizes thirty studies Secondary source It summarizes research done by others. 7 The flood water reached the second step of the library. A photograph taken at the library during the flood Primary source It is a record made at the time. 8 The flood water reached the second step of the library. A history book about the flood Secondary source It interprets records of the flood. 9 The river's peak flow was recorded on 12 April. The original data file from the river gauge Primary source It is the instrument's own record. 10 The river is the main water supply for the county. An encyclopedia entry about the river Secondary source It summarizes other sources.

Provenance: The claims and sources are illustrative cases written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The definitions follow the chapter sections "Primary Source" and "Secondary Source".

Rules: Each source has exactly one correct bin, five per bin. The bin depends on the source's relation to the stated claim.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one claim with its source and the two bins.
  2. The learner places the source in a bin, and the placement is committed.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text.
  4. After source 10 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 10 sources in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [bin]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. This is a [bin]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 10 correct on the first attempt". At 9 or more it adds "You can tell original evidence from a summary." Below 9 it lists the Why text of each missed source.

Starting State: The first source with its claim, the two bin definitions, and two empty bins. The question shown is "Is this source original evidence or a summary of it?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter says an encyclopedia is treated as a secondary source, and that a census table is a primary source for the population on its date.

docs.title: Citation Quality
docs.text:
Citation quality is how well a citation supports the claim it is attached to. A citation can exist and still be poor. Four questions test it:

  • Relevant: does the source actually address this claim?
  • Reliable: do its author and publisher have expertise, and does the work show how it knows?
  • Retrievable: can a reader find the source, through a working link or complete details?
  • Current: is the source recent enough for a claim that changes?

A citation that fails any of the four is a weaker support than it looks, and the reviewer notes which one failed.

A Citation That Exists May Not Support the Claim

A real source with a working link can still say nothing about the claim beside it, and AI agents are known to produce references that look right and are not. Open the source and read the line that supports the claim, and record that you did.

The MicroSim below is a quality check. Each of six citations is attached to the same claim, and for each one you mark which of the four questions it fails.

docs.title: Diagram: Citation Quality Checker
docs.text:
Citation Quality Checker

Type: microsim sim-id: citation-quality-checker Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: assess Learning Objective: The learner will assess six citations for the same claim by marking exactly which of four quality criteria each fails, with at least 5 of 6 judged correctly on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Citation Quality, Source Citation, Primary Source, Secondary Source (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each citation the learner marks the failed criteria, or marks none. A judgment is correct when the marked set equals the Failed criteria column in Content exactly. Mastery is at least 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Reading the criteria is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A citation with a link is always good. (2) A recent source is always reliable. (3) A source that exists supports the claim.

Instructional Rationale: Assessing a citation against explicit criteria is an Evaluate-level action. Six citations for one claim, with different mixes of failures, force the learner to apply each criterion separately.

Content:

The claim shown at all times: "Lake Marlow's deepest point is 31 meters." The four criteria: Relevant, Reliable, Retrievable, Current. A criterion is met when: the source states the depth (Relevant); the author or publisher is an agency, a reviewed publication, or a reference work with a stated method (Reliable); the link works or full details let a reader find the source (Retrievable); and the source is dated within the last five years (Current).

The six citations (all made up):

# Citation shown to the learner Failed criteria Why (shown as feedback) 1 State Water Agency. "Lake Marlow Fact Sheet." 2025. https://example.gov/lake-marlow (link works, and the sheet gives the depth) None It states the depth, comes from an agency, can be opened, and is recent. 2 A blog post titled "Why I Love Lakes," 2019, no link, which never mentions depth Relevant, Reliable, Retrievable The post does not state the depth, has no stated method, and cannot be found. 3 State Water Agency. "Lake Marlow Fact Sheet." 1998. https://example.gov/lake-marlow-1998 (link works, and the sheet gives the depth) Current The source is old for a measurement that can be resurveyed. 4 State Water Agency. "Lake Marlow Fact Sheet." 2025. https://example.gov/old-link (the link returns "page not found") Retrievable The source may be good, and the reader cannot reach it. 5 A student slide deck about lakes, 2025, no author, no link, which states the depth Reliable, Retrievable The deck states the depth, and no one is accountable for it and no one can find it. 6 State Water Agency. "Lake Marlow Survey." 2025. https://example.gov/marlow-survey (link works, and the survey reports area and shoreline length but not depth) Relevant The source is reliable and current, and it does not address depth.

Provenance: The claim and citations are made up for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The criteria follow the chapter section "Citation Quality". The five-year limit for Current is a teaching choice, and the sim labels it "illustrative threshold".

Rules: Each citation has a fixed set of failed criteria, and the empty set is valid. A citation is Current when it is dated >= 2021, because the sim's review date is 2026. The criteria are judged independently.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees the claim, the four criteria, and one citation.
  2. The learner marks each criterion that the citation fails, or marks "None fail".
  3. The learner presses Check. The sim shows the correct set and the Why text.
  4. The learner moves to the next citation, until citation 6 is done.

Feedback: 6 citations in the fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. Failed: [criteria, or none]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 6 correct on the first attempt". At 5 or more it adds "You can judge a citation." Below 5 it lists the Why text of each missed citation.

Starting State: The claim, the four criteria with their definitions, and citation 1 with no criteria marked. The question shown is "Which criteria does this citation fail?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter lists the four citation-quality questions as relevant, reliable, retrievable, and current. The chapter says a citation that exists can fail to support the claim.

docs.title: The Currency Metric
docs.text:
The currency metric is the half of the first quality metric that asks whether the content is still correct and in current use: the facts, figures, practices, software, laws, and links that were right when the resource was written but may have changed since. Accuracy asks about the day of writing, and currency asks about today. A resource can score well on one and badly on the other. A careful 2012 text with no errors on the day it was published can be full of out-of-date statements now.

Content ages at different speeds, so a reviewer matches the amount of checking to how fast the topic moves. The multiplication table does not change, while a software screenshot can change within a year.

Worked example: how fast does it age? The table groups six kinds of content by how quickly they go out of date.

Kind of content How fast it ages How often to check Basic mathematics and definitions Very slowly At each major review The sequence of historical events Slowly At each major review Statistics and survey results Moderately Every few years, or whenever new data appear Standards, curricula, and guidelines Moderately Every few years, and when a standard is revised Software screenshots, prices, and web addresses Quickly Every year or more often Laws, policies, and contact details Quickly Every year or more often

docs.title: Outdated Content
docs.text:
Outdated content is content that was correct when it was written and is no longer correct or in use. It is different from a factual error, because the author did nothing wrong at the time. The reader is harmed all the same. Several signs point to outdated content:

  • Dates in the text that are many years old, or the words "recent" and "new" with no date beside them.
  • Products, versions, or standards that have been replaced or discontinued.
  • Statistics that come from an old dataset for a quantity that changes.
  • Screenshots of an interface that has since been redesigned.
  • Links to pages that no longer exist, which later sections cover.
  • No sign of any update in years, for a topic that moves fast.

Worked example: reading a short passage for signs of aging. A reviewer on 12 October 2026 reads this made-up passage: "Our district uses Quizlette 2.0, the newest quiz tool, adopted in 2014. The county has about 52,000 people, according to the 2010 census. To sign in, click the blue Sign On button, shown in the screenshot below."

Statement Sign of aging What to check "the newest quiz tool, adopted in 2014" "Newest" with a date twelve years old Whether the tool still exists and is still the district's choice "about 52,000 people, according to the 2010 census" A figure from a dataset that changes The most recent census figure "click the blue Sign On button" in a screenshot An interface screenshot Whether the interface still looks like that

The MicroSim below practices the same judgment. It shows eight statements read on a review date, and for each one you decide whether it is current, likely outdated, or cannot be judged without checking.

docs.title: Diagram: Outdated Content Spotter
docs.text:
Outdated Content Spotter

Type: microsim sim-id: outdated-content-spotter Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: judge Learning Objective: The learner will judge whether each of eight statements read on a stated review date is current, likely outdated, or cannot be judged without checking, with at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: The Currency Metric, Outdated Content (both defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each statement the learner commits one of three bins. A placement is correct when it matches the Correct bin column in Content. Mastery is at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the signs of aging is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Anything with a date is outdated. (2) Old facts about the past are outdated. (3) A rule written long ago is still in force.

Instructional Rationale: Judging currency is an Evaluate-level action that needs a criterion, which is how fast the kind of content changes. Including timeless statements, fast-aging ones, and ones that need a check teaches the learner to match the judgment to the content.

Content:

The review date, shown at all times: 12 October 2026. The three bins: Current, Likely outdated, Cannot tell without checking.

The eight statements:

# Statement shown to the learner Correct bin Why (shown as feedback) 1 The Pythagorean theorem says a squared plus b squared equals c squared for a right triangle. Current Mathematical results do not age. 2 In 2014 the district adopted Quizlette 2.0 for all quizzes. (Quizlette was discontinued in 2019.) Likely outdated The product has been discontinued, so the advice no longer works. 3 Photosynthesis takes in carbon dioxide and releases oxygen. Current Basic science of this kind changes very slowly. 4 The county has about 52,000 people (2010 census). Likely outdated A population figure from sixteen years before the review date is old for a quantity that changes. 5 To sign in, click the blue Sign On button at the top right (screenshot from 2015). Likely outdated Interface screenshots age quickly. 6 The United States Declaration of Independence was adopted in 1776. Current A historical date does not change. 7 The state requires 180 days of instruction (the law in effect since 1999). Cannot tell without checking Laws can be amended, so the reviewer must check the current law. 8 The tallest building in the city is Harbor Tower (completed 2008). Cannot tell without checking A taller building may have been built since, so the reviewer must check.

Provenance: The statements are illustrative cases written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The product, county, law, and building are made up, and the two historical and scientific statements are common knowledge. The rules of thumb follow the chapter section "The Currency Metric".

Rules: Each statement has exactly one correct bin. Three statements are Current, three are Likely outdated, and two are Cannot tell without checking. A statement about a quantity that changes is Likely outdated when its source date is > 5 years before the review date.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees the review date and one statement.
  2. The learner places the statement in a bin, and the placement is committed.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text.
  4. After statement 8 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 8 statements in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [bin]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. This is [bin]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 8 correct on the first attempt". At 7 or more it adds "You can read a date and a topic together." Below 7 it lists the Why text of each missed statement.

Starting State: The first statement, the review date, and the three bins. The question shown is "Is this statement still current?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's passage example is read on 12 October 2026 and flags the 2014 product, the 2010 census figure, and the screenshot. The chapter's shelf-life table puts mathematics and definitions at the slow end and screenshots, prices, laws, and contact details at the fast end.

docs.title: Publication Date
docs.text:
A publication date is the date a resource was first published or last substantially updated. Three dates can appear, and they mean different things. The published date is when the resource first appeared. The updated date is when it was last changed. The accessed date is when a reader last looked at it. A reviewer wants the first two. Where to look: the page's header or footer, the front matter of a book, the file's properties, the repository's commit history, or an archive of the page.

A resource with no date is a currency concern, because no one can tell how old the facts are. An updated date alone does not prove that the content was reviewed. Some websites refresh the date automatically each time the page is served. Look for evidence that the date reflects real revision.

docs.title: Revision History
docs.text: A revision history is the record of the changes made to a resource over time, with dates. It is evidence of maintenance. For a resource hosted in a repository, the history is the list of commits from Chapter 4. For a document it may be a changelog or a note at the end. A frequent, recent revision history suggests that someone is looking after the resource. A long gap with no revisions is a signal, and for a fast-aging topic it is a warning.

docs.title: Link Rot
docs.text:
Link rot is the gradual breaking of web links over time. Sites are reorganized, domains lapse, pages are removed, and addresses change, so a link that worked when the author wrote the resource may lead nowhere years later. A resource full of citations to web pages is exposed to link rot, and the broken links make the citations impossible to check. Authors can reduce the damage by citing stable sources, by using persistent identifiers such as a DOI (a digital object identifier that points to a work wherever it moves), and by saving an archived copy of important pages.

Cite the Original and an Archive

When you rely on a web page, save an archived copy with a service such as the Internet Archive's Wayback Machine and record both addresses. If the original disappears, the archive keeps your evidence checkable.

docs.title: Broken Link Check
docs.text:
A broken link check tests every external link in a resource to see whether it still reaches the intended page. Free link-checking tools do the testing automatically, and a reviewer then looks at the failures by hand. Record the date of the test, because a link that works today may fail next month.

A link checker reports a status code, a three-digit number from the web server. The table shows the most common ones and the action each one calls for.

Result What it means What to do 200 The page loaded Confirm that it is still the cited page, then keep the link 301 The page moved permanently to a new address Update the link to the new address 403 The server refused the tool, though a person may be allowed in Open the link by hand 404 The page was not found Search for the new address, or replace the source 410 The page is gone for good Replace the source Timeout The server did not answer Try again later, and open it by hand

A page can also load with code 200 and no longer be the page that was cited, such as a site that sends every old address to its home page. A tool will report success, so a reviewer opens a sample of working links to confirm they lead where they should.

The MicroSim below practices reading link-check results. It shows eight results from a link checker, and for each one you choose the action to take.

docs.title: Diagram: Link Check Results Reader
docs.text:
Link Check Results Reader

Type: microsim sim-id: link-check-reader Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: interpret Learning Objective: The learner will interpret eight link-check results by choosing the action each calls for, with at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Link Rot, Broken Link Check, Source Citation (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each result the learner commits one of three actions. A choice is correct when it matches the Correct action column in Content. Mastery is at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the status code table is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A 200 result always means the link is good. (2) A 403 result means the page is gone. (3) A timeout means the source is permanently lost.

Instructional Rationale: Interpreting a result is an Understand-level action that connects a code to its meaning. Results that look alike but call for different actions teach the learner not to rely on the code alone.

Content:

The three actions: Keep, Fix or replace, Check by hand.

The eight results:

# Result shown to the learner Correct action Why (shown as feedback) 1 200: the page loaded, and it is the cited article. Keep The link works and reaches the cited page. 2 404: the page was not found. Fix or replace The page is missing, so find its new address or replace the source. 3 301: the page moved permanently to a new address, which shows the same article. Fix or replace Update the link to the new address. 4 403: the tool was refused, and the page opens in a browser. Check by hand The server blocks tools, so a person must confirm the page. 5 200: the page loaded, but it is a site home page and not the cited article. Fix or replace The address now leads somewhere else, so the citation no longer works. 6 410: the page is gone. Fix or replace The server says the page was removed for good. 7 Timeout: no answer after 30 seconds. Check by hand The server may be down for now, so try again later and open it by hand. 8 200: the page loaded, but it asks for a paid subscription to read. Check by hand The link works, and a reader without a subscription cannot check the claim, so a person must decide.

Provenance: The results are illustrative cases written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The status codes follow the chapter section "Broken Link Check".

Rules: Each result has exactly one correct action. One result is Keep, four are Fix or replace, and three are Check by hand.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one result and the three actions.
  2. The learner may open the status code table. Opening it does not change the score.
  3. The learner chooses an action, and the choice is committed.
  4. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text.
  5. After result 8 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 8 results in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [action]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. The action is [action]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 8 correct on the first attempt". At 7 or more it adds "You can read a link check." Below 7 it lists the Why text of each missed result.

Starting State: The first result, the three actions, and the status code table closed. The question shown is "What should the reviewer do with this link?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's status code table lists 200, 301, 403, 404, 410, and timeout, with the actions keep, update, open by hand, replace, and try again. The chapter says a page that loads with code 200 may not be the cited page.

docs.title: Expert Review
docs.text:
An expert review is a check of a resource's content by a person with deep knowledge of its subject. A reviewer cannot be an expert in everything, and for some claims an expert's judgment is the only reliable check. Ask for an expert review when the topic is outside your knowledge, when the content bears on health, safety, or law, when claims are contested, or when your sample finds two or more mismatches in ten facts.

Make the request easy to answer. Send the list of claims you could not check, with the exact words and the context, and ask a specific question about each: is this correct, and if not, what is? Record the expert's name, their qualification, the date, and the result in your evidence. An expert's confirmation counts as evidence, and a note that says only "an expert looked at it" does not.

Asking an Expert Is Part of the Method

If a claim is beyond what you know, that does not make you a weak reviewer, because careful reviewers say so and ask. You already hand a question to a colleague when it falls outside your subject. Write down the claim, the expert, and the answer, and the score rests on evidence again.

docs.title: Scoring Accuracy and Currency
docs.text:
You now have the parts for scoring the metric. The review has six steps. Note the review date. Sample and check at least 10 facts. Trace the claims that carry weight back through their citations. Test all external links. Run the ten checks below. Then count the passes, find the band, and choose the number.

A failed check is serious when a learner could take away a false or outdated fact. If a serious check fails, choose the lower number in a two-number band. Otherwise choose the higher one, as in Chapter 3.

# Check Serious if it fails? 1 A sample of at least 10 checkable facts was tested against reliable sources No 2 At least 9 of every 10 sampled facts match their sources Yes 3 No sampled error teaches a main idea falsely Yes 4 Claims that need support carry a citation No 5 Cited sources are reliable No 6 A publication or update date is shown No 7 No outdated fact, figure, or practice appears in the sample Yes 8 Cited sources are recent enough for the claims No 9 All tested links work No 10 A way to report errors is offered No

Worked example: Watershed Basics. The reviewer applies the checks to the reading from Chapter 3, and the ten-fact sample is the table from the first section of this chapter.

# Result Evidence 1 Pass Ten facts were checked in sections 1 to 3. 2 Pass Nine of ten matched. 3 Pass The one mismatch is a river length, not a main idea. 4 Pass Every statistic and date carries a citation. 5 Pass The citations are to agencies and survey pages. 6 Pass The page shows a publication date. 7 Fail The river-length figure in section 2 is outdated: the text gives 410 miles and the agency now gives 398. 8 Pass The cited agency pages were updated within the last five years. 9 Fail 2 of 14 links return "page not found" (tested 2026-10-12). 10 Pass The author's contact address is on the page.

Eight of ten checks pass, a share of 80 percent, in the 7 to 8 band. Check 7 failed, and it is a serious check, because a learner could memorize the old river length. The reviewer therefore chooses the lower number, 7, which is the score recorded on the Chapter 3 worksheet. The two broken links are a lesser gap, and the reviewer records both with the date.

The last MicroSim of the chapter is a scoring practice. It shows five resources with their ten check results, and for each one you choose the metric score.

docs.title: Diagram: Accuracy and Currency Scorer
docs.text:
Accuracy and Currency Scorer

Type: microsim sim-id: accuracy-currency-metric-scorer Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: apply Learning Objective: The learner will apply the ten accuracy and currency checks and the Chapter 3 scoring rules to choose the metric score for each of five resources, with at least 4 of 5 scores exactly correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: The Accuracy Metric, The Currency Metric, Factual Error, Outdated Content, Metric Score, Scoring Descriptor (all defined in this chapter or in Chapter 3 above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each resource the learner chooses a whole-number score from 0 to 10 after seeing the ten check results. A score is correct when it equals the Correct score column in Content. Mastery is at least 4 of 5 scores correct on the first attempt. Opening the check list and the descriptor table is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Every failed check lowers the score equally. (2) A single serious failure always puts the score in a lower band. (3) The higher number in a band is always correct.

Instructional Rationale: Applying a scoring procedure to new cases is an Apply-level task. Five resources that differ in how many checks fail and whether a serious check fails make the learner use every step: count, band, then choose within the band.

Content:

The ten checks, each marked serious or not, are those in the chapter's check table. The descriptor bands applied to the share of checks passed: 0% is 0; 1% to 24% is 1 to 2; 25% to 49% is 3 to 4; 50% to 74% is 5 to 6; 75% to 89% is 7 to 8; 90% to 100% is 9 to 10. Within a two-number band, choose the lower number when a serious check failed and the higher number otherwise. A score of 10 requires every check to pass.

The five resources:

# Resource Checks failed Checks passed Share Band Serious failure? Correct score Why (shown as feedback) 1 Open Algebra None 10 100% 9 to 10 No 10 Every check passed. 2 Watershed Basics 7 and 9 8 80% 7 to 8 Yes, check 7 7 An outdated figure is a serious failure, so the lower number applies. 3 Clinic Guide 2 9 90% 9 to 10 Yes, check 2 9 More than one in ten sampled facts did not match, which is serious, so the lower number applies. 4 Teacher Lab Notes 6, 9, and 10 7 70% 5 to 6 No 6 None of the failed checks is serious, so the higher number applies. 5 Old Handbook 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, and 8 4 (checks 1, 6, 9, 10) 40% 3 to 4 Yes 3 Several serious checks failed, so the lower number applies.

Provenance: The ten checks and the bands follow the chapter section "Scoring Accuracy and Currency" and Chapter 3. The five resources are illustrative cases written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". Resource 2 is the chapter's worked example.

Rules: A score is the band chosen from the share passed, and then the number chosen within the band by the serious-failure rule. Each resource has exactly one correct score. For a band that holds a single number, that number is the score.

Learner Activity:

  1. The sim shows resource 1 with its ten check results.
  2. The learner may open the check list and the descriptor table.
  3. The learner chooses a score from 0 to 10, and the choice is committed.
  4. The sim shows the count of passes, the band, whether a serious check failed, and the correct score with the Why text.
  5. After resource 5 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 5 resources in the fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [score]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. [passes] checks passed, which is [share] and the [band] band. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 5 correct on the first attempt". At 4 or more it adds "You can score accuracy and currency." Below 4 it lists the Why text of each missed resource.

Starting State: Resource 1 with all ten results shown and no score chosen. The question shown is "What accuracy and currency score does this resource earn?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's worked example for Watershed Basics fails checks 7 and 9, passes 8 of 10, and scores 7, with the lower number chosen because the outdated figure is a serious failure. The chapter says the ten-fact sample has nine matches.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• The accuracy metric asks whether facts were correct when written, and the currency metric asks whether they are correct now. Together they make the first quality metric.
  • Check a sample of at least 10 facts against reliable, independent sources. Fact checking records match, mismatch, or not addressed, and silence is never support. A factual error is serious when a learner could take away a false or outdated fact.
  • A source citation lets a reviewer trace a claim. A primary source is original evidence and a secondary source summarizes it. Citation quality asks whether a citation is relevant, reliable, retrievable, and current.
  • Outdated content was right once. Check the publication date and the revision history, and match the checking to how fast the topic moves.
  • Link rot breaks citations, and a broken link check finds the failures. Ask for expert review when a claim is beyond your knowledge, bears on safety, or fails your sample.

You Can Check a Claim to Its Source

You can now check a sample of facts, trace a citation back to its source, spot content that has aged, test the links, and score accuracy and currency with evidence. Every quality score from here on rests on the same habit of asking what a claim stands on.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Accuracy and Currency
docs.text: Test your understanding of fact checking, citations, outdated content, link checks, and scoring the accuracy and currency metric with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. According to the chapter, when should a reviewer ask for an expert review?
docs.text:
1. When the resource shows a publication date and a revision history that are both recent
  2. When the sampled facts all match, but the reviewer likes the writing style and the layout
  3. When the claims bear on health, safety, or law, or the sample shows two or more mismatches in ten
  4. When the resource carries an open license that allows commercial reuse and editing by anyone, anywhere
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Ask for an expert review when the topic is outside your knowledge, when the content bears on health, safety, or law, when claims are contested, or when your sample finds two or more mismatches in ten facts. A date, a revision history (A), and an open license (D) are useful evidence for other checks, and none of them calls for an expert. Liking the writing style (B) is an opinion, not evidence.

Concept Tested: Expert Review

See: Expert Review

docs.title: 2. Why does the chapter say to check each sampled fact against a source that is independent of the resource?
docs.text:
1. Independent sources are always free to read online, whereas the resource's references usually are not
  2. Checking against another copy of the same text proves nothing, because copied errors spread
  3. Only independent sources can be primary sources, and the resource's own references never can
  4. An independent source is much easier to cite correctly than the resource's own list of references
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. If a reviewer compares a claim with a copy of the same text, a copied error will match and the check proves nothing. Choose a reliable source that was produced separately, such as an agency's current data page, and compare word for word and number for number. The sample should hold at least 10 checkable facts, spread across the sections, with numbers, dates, and names favored because they are likeliest to be wrong.

Concept Tested: Accuracy Metric

See: The Accuracy Metric

docs.title: 3. Why must a reviewer record "not addressed" as its own fact-checking result instead of counting it as a match?
docs.text:
1. A source that does not mention a claim has shown that the claim is false and should be rejected
  2. A source that never mentions a claim neither supports nor contradicts it, so silence cannot count as a match
  3. Every claim that a source does not address must be removed from the resource by the reviewer
  4. A source that is silent on one claim cannot be trusted for any other claim in the resource
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. A source can support a claim, contradict it, or fail to address it. Silence is not support: a reviewer who counts it as a match will pass claims that no one actually checked. The reviewer should look for a source that does address the claim, or record the claim as not checkable and report it. Echo's reminder is that a source which never mentions a claim has not confirmed it.

Concept Tested: Fact Checking

See: Fact Checking

docs.title: 4. Which description matches a secondary source?
docs.text:
1. A review article that summarizes thirty studies done by other researchers
  2. A lab notebook entry that records a measurement when it was made
  3. A census table that gives the population count on the census date
  4. A photograph taken at the library while the flood water was rising
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. A secondary source describes, summarizes, or interprets primary sources. Textbooks, review articles, news stories about research, and histories are secondary sources, and this book treats encyclopedias the same way. The other three options are primary sources, because each is original evidence from the time or person described. Secondary sources are useful but one step removed, so for an important claim a reviewer follows them back to a primary source.

Concept Tested: Secondary Source

See: Secondary Source

docs.title: 5. An AI-generated reference lists a real author, a working link, and a reputable publisher. Why might it still be a weak citation?
docs.text:
1. A working link means the page will disappear soon, which is called link rot by reviewers
  2. A reputable publisher cannot be a reliable source for any claim, however well it is cited
  3. A real author's work is always a secondary source and so cannot support a claim
  4. The source may say nothing about the claim beside it, so it can fail the relevance test
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Citation quality asks four questions: is the source relevant, reliable, retrievable, and current? A real source with a working link can still say nothing about the claim, and AI agents are known to produce references that look right and are not. Open the source, read the line that supports the claim, and record that you did. Neither a working link (A) nor a reputable publisher (B) is a weakness.

Concept Tested: Citation Quality

See: Citation Quality

docs.title: 6. A reviewer applies the ten accuracy and currency checks to a clinic guide. Only check 2 fails, because fewer than 9 of every 10 sampled facts match, and the chapter marks that check as serious. What score does the scoring rule give?
docs.text:
1. 9, because 90 percent is in the 9 to 10 band and a serious failure selects the lower number
  2. 10, because only one check in ten failed and so the higher number in the band is always used
  3. 8, because a single serious failure always moves the score down one band
  4. 5, because more than one in ten sampled facts did not match, which halves the score
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Nine of ten checks pass, a share of 90 percent, which falls in the 9 to 10 band. A failed check is serious when a learner could take away a false or outdated fact, and check 2 is serious, so the reviewer chooses the lower number, 9. A score of 10 requires every check to pass (B). A serious failure selects a number within the band and does not move the score to another band (C).

Concept Tested: Accuracy Metric

See: Scoring Accuracy and Currency

docs.title: 7. A link checker reports a 301 result for a cited page, and the new address shows the same article. What should the reviewer do?
docs.text:
1. Keep the link unchanged, because the page still loads
  2. Replace the source, because 301 means the page is gone for good
  3. Update the link to the new address, because the page moved permanently
  4. Open the link by hand later, because 301 means the server refused the tool
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. A 301 result means the page moved permanently to a new address, so the reviewer updates the link. A 404 calls for finding the new address or replacing the source, and a 410 means the page is gone for good, so replace it. A 403 means the server refused the tool, so open the link by hand. Record the date of the test, because a link that works today may fail next month.

Concept Tested: Broken Link Check

See: Broken Link Check

docs.title: 8. A reviewer reads four statements in a lab guide on 12 October 2026. Which statement shows the strongest sign of outdated content?
docs.text:
1. Photosynthesis takes in carbon dioxide and releases oxygen as plants make food
  2. To sign in, click the blue Sign On button in the screenshot, which dates from 2015
  3. The United States Declaration of Independence was adopted in 1776 by the Continental Congress
  4. The area of a rectangle is its length times its width, measured in square units
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Content ages at different speeds, so a reviewer matches the checking to how fast the topic moves. Software screenshots, prices, and web addresses age quickly, and an interface screenshot from 2015 is likely to have been redesigned. Basic science, mathematics, and historical dates change very slowly or not at all. Outdated content was correct when written, which is why the author did nothing wrong at the time and a learner is harmed all the same.

Concept Tested: Outdated Content

See: Outdated Content

docs.title: 9. A resource states "Wetlands filter pollutants" and cites a textbook. The textbook cites a review article, and the review summarizes several studies. A reviewer stops after confirming that the textbook says the same thing. What has the reviewer actually shown?
docs.text:
1. That the claim is fully supported by primary evidence at the end of the citation chain
  2. That the claim is false, because textbooks are never reliable sources for a scientific claim
  3. That the citation chain is broken at the textbook and cannot be followed any further back
  4. That a secondary source agrees with the resource, not that the original evidence supports the claim
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Citations form chains, and an error can enter at any link. The textbook is a secondary source, and the review is another step removed. A reviewer who stops at the textbook has found only that a textbook agreed with the resource. Following the chain to the study that reported the measurements before and after water passed through a wetland gives a check that can be trusted. The further back you trace a claim, the stronger the check.

Concept Tested: Source Citation

See: Source Citation

docs.title: 10. Resource A was carefully written in 2012 and had no errors on the day it was published, but it has never been updated. Resource B was published last month and gives a wrong date for a historical event. Which analysis is correct?
docs.text:
1. Both fail on accuracy, because neither resource's facts can be trusted by a careful reader today
  2. Resource A fails on accuracy, because it is old, and Resource B fails on currency
  3. Resource A passes both halves, because it contained no errors when it was published
  4. Resource A is weak on currency though accurate when written, and Resource B fails on accuracy
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Accuracy asks whether the facts were correct when written, and currency asks whether they are still correct now. A careful 2012 text can score well on one half and badly on the other, because facts, figures, software, and links age. Resource A is a currency problem. Resource B contains a false statement from the start, so it is an accuracy problem. The two halves together make up the first quality metric.

Concept Tested: Currency Metric

See: The Currency Metric

docs.title: References: Accuracy and Currency
docs.text:
1. Fact-checking - Wikipedia - Describes how claims are checked before and after publication and the methods professional fact-checkers use. Supports this chapter's procedure for sampling and verifying the facts in a resource.

  2. Link rot - Wikipedia - Explains how links stop working over time, how common the problem is, and what can be done about it. Background for the currency checks that test a resource's links.

  3. Peer review - Wikipedia - Surveys how experts evaluate work before it is accepted or published, and the strengths and limits of the process. Informs the chapter's guidance on when a resource needs expert review.

  4. Web Literacy for Student Fact-Checkers - Mike Caulfield - Pressbooks (2017) - Caulfield's "four moves" (check for previous work, go upstream to the source, read laterally, circle back) teach students to verify a claim by leaving the page. He later condensed them into the SIFT method.

  5. Calling Bullshit: The Art of Skepticism in a Data-Driven World - Carl T. Bergstrom and Jevin D. West - Random House (2020) - Grew out of the authors' University of Washington course of the same name. Its examples of misleading statistics and charts give reviewers concrete questions to ask about any number in a resource.

  6. Civic Online Reasoning - Digital Inquiry Group - Free lessons and assessments built on lateral reading, the strategy professional fact-checkers use to judge a source. Gives teachers ready practice for checking an author's authority and a claim's support.

  7. SIFT (The Four Moves) - Hapgood - Mike Caulfield's own post explaining Stop, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, and Trace claims. A short, usable routine for tracing a citation back to its origin.

  8. Evaluating Resources - UC Berkeley Library - A library guide with questions about authority, purpose, currency, and bias for judging any source. Provides a ready checklist for the citation evaluation described in this chapter.

  9. Evaluating Sources of Information - Purdue OWL - Explains how to judge a source's author, publisher, date, and evidence. A plain companion for deciding whether a resource's citations are reliable and recent enough.

  10. Wayback Machine - Internet Archive - Lets reviewers retrieve archived copies of pages that have moved or vanished and see what a page said on an earlier date. A practical tool for the broken-link and currency checks in this chapter.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Shows how to score alignment to learning outcomes, standards, and Bloom's levels, and readability through reading level, vocabulary, plain language, and how well the text fits its audience. It continues the quality metrics by asking whether a resource teaches what it claims to teach, in words its audience can read. After this chapter you can map a resource to learning outcomes and standards, and rate its reading level and fit to its audience.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 25 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Learning Outcome 83 Alignment Metric 16 Learning Objective 26 Measurable Verb 3 Standards Alignment 15 Curriculum Map 14 Bloom's Taxonomy 3 Bloom Cognitive Levels 2 Outcome Coverage 3 Assessment Alignment 1 Content Gap 1 Scope and Sequence 10 Prerequisite Knowledge 9 Readability Metric 23 Reading Level 16 Readability Formula 3 Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level 1 Vocabulary Level 7 Defined Terms 4 Glossary 3 Plain Language 1 Jargon 1 Text Structure 6 Headings and Subheadings 3 Audience Fit 3

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 3: The Ten-Metric Rubric and Scoring

Teach What You Test, and Say It Plainly

A resource can be accurate and still miss the point: it teaches one thing and tests another, or it speaks far above its readers. This chapter gives you two checks for those problems, one for whether the parts line up and one for whether the words fit. Let's dive in and check the evidence!

Chapter 5 checked whether a resource's facts are right. Two more quality questions remain before we reach accessibility and practice. The first is alignment: does the resource teach and test what it says learners will achieve? The second is readability: can its intended readers read it? Both ask whether the resource fits the learners and the course, and both reward the same habit, which is to compare what a resource says it will do with what it actually does.

The chapter takes the metrics in turn. The alignment half introduces learning outcomes, objectives, Bloom's taxonomy, standards, and the maps that show what is taught and what is tested. The readability half covers reading level, vocabulary, plain language, and text structure. Each half ends with a scoring section built on ten checks.

docs.title: Learning Outcome
docs.text:
A learning outcome is a statement of what a learner will be able to do after finishing a course, unit, or resource. Two features matter. An outcome describes the learner and not the teacher: "students will explain" and not "the teacher will cover". And it names a capability and not a topic. "Photosynthesis" is a topic, and "Explain how plants make food from light, water, and carbon dioxide" is an outcome. A reviewer needs outcomes because alignment can only be judged against something, and a resource that states none gives the reviewer nothing to compare with.

Outcomes work at different scales. A course has a few broad outcomes, and a unit narrows them. This book's course description, for example, lists its outcomes under the six levels of Bloom's taxonomy, which a later section explains.

Worked example: from topic to outcome. Each row takes a topic that a resource might list and rewrites it as an outcome.

Topic (not an outcome) Outcome Watersheds Describe what a watershed is and name its parts. Runoff Explain how water moves over land and into streams. Paving and flooding Predict how paving a field changes the amount of runoff.

These three outcomes are the ones the resource Watershed Basics from Chapter 3 states. The rest of this section keeps using them.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
A learning objective is a narrow, specific statement of what a learner will do in one lesson, written so that someone can see whether it happened. Where an outcome describes the end of a unit, an objective describes one step toward it. A well-formed objective has three parts, which come from the educator Robert Mager's classic model:

  • Performance: what the learner will do, written with a measurable verb.
  • Condition: the situation or help the learner has, such as "given a map" or "without notes".
  • Criterion: how well the learner must do it, such as "with no more than one error".

Compare "Students will learn about runoff" with "Given a diagram of a hillside, the student will explain in two sentences where runoff flows". The second states what the learner does, under what condition, and to what standard. A teacher can assess it.

Worked example: one outcome, two objectives. The outcome is "Explain how water moves over land and into streams."

Part Objective 1 Objective 2 Performance Label the path of a raindrop Explain in writing where runoff goes Condition On a diagram of a hillside After reading section 2, without notes Criterion All four stages correct Two complete sentences

docs.title: Measurable Verb
docs.text:
A measurable verb is a verb that names something a teacher could observe a learner doing. List, describe, calculate, compare, and design are measurable, since you can watch someone do each one. Know, understand, learn, appreciate, and be familiar with are not, because no one can see them happen. A quick test is to ask, "How would I know the learner did this?" If the answer is "I couldn't tell", the verb is vague.

Swap the Vague Verb

When an outcome says "understand", ask what a learner would do to show it, and write that verb instead. "Understand the water cycle" becomes "explain the water cycle in four steps".

The first MicroSim of the chapter trains the test. It shows ten outcome statements, and for each one you decide whether its verb is measurable.

docs.title: Diagram: Outcome Verb Checker
docs.text:
Outcome Verb Checker

Type: microsim sim-id: outcome-verb-checker Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: judge Learning Objective: The learner will judge whether the verb in each of ten outcome statements is measurable, with at least 9 of 10 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Learning Outcome, Learning Objective, Measurable Verb (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each statement the learner commits one of two bins. A placement is correct when it matches the Correct bin column in Content. Mastery is at least 9 of 10 correct on the first attempt. Reading the test question is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) "Understand" is measurable because teachers use it all the time. (2) A longer statement is more measurable. (3) A measurable verb makes an outcome a good one.

Instructional Rationale: Judging a verb against the test "could I observe this?" is an Evaluate-level action. Ten statements that mix vague and measurable verbs in similar sentences make the learner apply the test to the verb itself and not to the topic.

Content:

The test, shown at all times: could a teacher watch a learner do this and tell whether it happened?

The two bins: Measurable, and Not measurable.

The ten statements:

# Statement shown to the learner Correct bin Why (shown as feedback) Better wording (for Not measurable) 1 Students will understand the water cycle. Not measurable "Understand" cannot be observed. Students will explain the water cycle in four steps. 2 Students will list the four main stages of the water cycle. Measurable A list can be seen and checked. Not needed. 3 Students will know the parts of a cell. Not measurable "Know" cannot be observed. Students will label the parts of a cell on a diagram. 4 Students will calculate the area of a rectangle from its length and width. Measurable A calculation produces a result that can be checked. Not needed. 5 Students will appreciate the importance of clean water. Not measurable "Appreciate" is a feeling that cannot be observed directly. Students will describe two ways clean water affects health. 6 Students will compare a primary source and a secondary source. Measurable A comparison can be written or spoken and then checked. Not needed. 7 Students will learn about fractions. Not measurable "Learn about" names no action. Students will add two fractions with like denominators. 8 Students will design a fair test to compare two fertilizers. Measurable A design is a product that can be reviewed. Not needed. 9 Students will be familiar with the causes of the war. Not measurable "Be familiar with" cannot be observed. Students will name three causes of the war and explain one. 10 Students will judge which of two websites is more reliable and give two reasons. Measurable The judgment and the reasons can be checked. Not needed.

Provenance: The statements are illustrative cases written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The list of measurable and vague verbs follows the chapter section "Measurable Verb".

Rules: Each statement has exactly one correct bin, five per bin. A statement is Measurable when its main verb names an observable action.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one statement and the two bins.
  2. The learner places the statement in a bin, and the placement is committed.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text.
  4. For a Not measurable statement the sim also shows the better wording.
  5. After statement 10 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 10 statements in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [bin]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. This is [bin]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 10 correct on the first attempt". At 9 or more it adds "You can spot a vague verb." Below 9 it lists the Why text of each missed statement.

Starting State: The first statement, the test question, and two empty bins. The question shown is "Could a teacher observe this?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter says know, understand, learn, appreciate, and be familiar with are not measurable, and that list, describe, calculate, compare, and design are measurable.

docs.title: Bloom's Taxonomy
docs.text: Bloom's taxonomy is a classification of the thinking that learning goals ask for, from simple recall to creating something new. Benjamin Bloom and colleagues published the first version in 1956, and Lorin Anderson and David Krathwohl revised it in 2001. This book uses the 2001 revision. The taxonomy helps with alignment because it gives reviewers a shared way to say how demanding an outcome or an activity is.

docs.title: Bloom Cognitive Levels
docs.text:
The Bloom cognitive levels are the six steps of the revised taxonomy, each of which asks more of the learner than the one before. Each level has verbs that signal it, and the table gives the level, a typical verb, and an example objective.

Level What it asks Typical verbs Example Remember Recall facts and terms list, name, define List the five parts of a lesson plan. Understand Explain ideas in your own words explain, summarize, interpret Explain why the seasons change. Apply Use knowledge in a new situation calculate, use, solve Calculate the perimeter of a garden. Analyze Break material into parts and see how they relate distinguish, differentiate, examine Differentiate a cause from an effect in a historical event. Evaluate Judge using criteria judge, critique, justify Judge which of two designs is fairer, and justify the choice. Create Put parts together into something new design, compose, construct Design an experiment to test how light affects plant growth.

The levels matter to a reviewer because an outcome and the activities that teach it should sit at the same level. If an outcome says "predict" and every activity asks only for recall, learners practice a skill that the outcome does not ask for, and they never practice the skill it does.

The second MicroSim practices the levels. It shows twelve objectives, and for each one you choose the Bloom level its verb signals.

docs.title: Diagram: Bloom Level Sorter
docs.text:
Bloom Level Sorter

Type: microsim sim-id: bloom-level-sorter Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: classify Learning Objective: The learner will classify each of twelve learning objectives under the Bloom cognitive level its verb signals, with at least 10 of 12 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Bloom's Taxonomy, Bloom Cognitive Levels, Learning Objective, Measurable Verb (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each objective the learner commits one of six levels. A choice is correct when it matches the Correct level column in Content. Mastery is at least 10 of 12 correct on the first attempt. Reading the level table is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) The level depends on the topic. (2) "Identify" and "explain" are the same level. (3) A harder-sounding verb is always a higher level.

Instructional Rationale: Classifying objectives by level is an Understand-level action that builds the skill reviewers need when they compare an outcome with its activities. Two objectives per level, each with an unambiguous verb, teach the learner to read the verb first.

Content:

The six levels: Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyze, Evaluate, Create.

The twelve objectives:

# Objective shown to the learner Correct level Why (shown as feedback) 1 List the five parts of a lesson plan. Remember "List" asks for recall. 2 Name the three main types of rock. Remember "Name" asks for recall. 3 Explain in your own words why the seasons change. Understand "Explain" asks for meaning in your own words. 4 Summarize the main idea of a news article. Understand "Summarize" asks for a restatement of meaning. 5 Calculate the perimeter of a garden from its side lengths. Apply "Calculate" uses a procedure on a new case. 6 Use a map scale to find the distance between two towns. Apply "Use" applies a rule in a new situation. 7 Distinguish a fact from an opinion in a short article. Analyze "Distinguish" separates parts and sees how they differ. 8 Differentiate a cause from an effect in a historical event. Analyze "Differentiate" separates parts and relates them. 9 Judge which of two experiment designs is fairer, and justify the choice. Evaluate "Judge" and "justify" use criteria to decide. 10 Critique a persuasive essay using a checklist of criteria. Evaluate "Critique" judges against criteria. 11 Design an experiment to test how light affects plant growth. Create "Design" produces something new. 12 Compose a short story that uses three given vocabulary words. Create "Compose" produces something new.

Provenance: The objectives are illustrative cases written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The levels and their verbs follow the chapter section "Bloom Cognitive Levels", which follows the 2001 revision of the taxonomy.

Rules: Each objective has exactly one correct level, two per level. The level is determined by the main verb.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one objective and the six levels.
  2. The learner may open the level table. Opening it does not change the score.
  3. The learner chooses a level, and the choice is committed.
  4. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text.
  5. After objective 12 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 12 objectives in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [level]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. This is [level]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 12 correct on the first attempt". At 10 or more it adds "You can read the level in a verb." Below 10 it lists the Why text of each missed objective.

Starting State: The first objective, the six levels, and the level table closed. The question shown is "Which Bloom level does this objective ask for?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter lists six levels in the order remember, understand, apply, analyze, evaluate, and create, and says this book uses the 2001 revision.

docs.title: Alignment Metric
docs.text:
The alignment metric asks whether a resource's activities, assessments, and content match its stated learning outcomes. Educators call a design with all three in agreement constructively aligned: the outcomes say what learners should be able to do, the activities give practice at doing it, and the assessments check that they can. A resource can fail the metric in several ways. It can state no outcomes. It can teach something and never test it, or test something it never taught. It can ask for recall when the outcome asks for judgment.

Alignment is a matching problem among three lists, and the reviewer's tool is a table that puts the three side by side. The worked example below builds that table for Watershed Basics, using the three outcomes from the start of this chapter.

Worked example: matching the three lists. The resource has two reading sections and a quiz. The table shows which section teaches each outcome and which quiz items check it.

Outcome Taught by Checked by Result 1. Describe what a watershed is and name its parts Section 1 Quiz items 1 to 4 Aligned 2. Explain how water moves over land and into streams Section 2 Quiz items 5 to 8 Aligned 3. Predict how paving a field changes the amount of runoff No section No quiz item Gap: neither taught nor checked

Two outcomes are covered, and the third is not. Chapter 3's evidence for this resource noted exactly that: "Outcome 3 has no activity", and quiz items map to two of the three outcomes. A reviewer who reads only the outcome list would think the resource covers prediction. The table shows that it does not.

docs.title: Standards Alignment
docs.text:
A standard is a public statement of what learners should know or be able to do at a given grade or in a given subject, written by a state, a national body, or a professional group. Standards alignment is the match between a resource and the standards it claims to meet. Resources often list standard codes, and listing is not matching. A reviewer reads the standard and checks that the resource asks learners to do what the standard asks, at the level it asks. Three results are possible. A strong match has learners doing what the standard names. A partial match touches the topic without asking for the performance. No match means that only a topic word is shared.

Standards differ from place to place. This book uses two made-up standards so that no claim here concerns a real state or country. The first is S-W1: "Explain how water moves through a watershed, including runoff, infiltration, and flow to a river or lake."

Worked example: three claims against S-W1.

Lesson activity Claims S-W1 Result Why Students sketch a hillside, draw arrows to show where runoff flows, and explain the path in two sentences. Yes Strong Learners explain how water moves, which is what the standard asks. Students read a paragraph that mentions runoff. Yes Partial The topic appears, and learners are not asked to explain anything. Students color a picture of a river. Yes No match Only the word river is shared with the standard.

A Standard Code Is a Claim, Not Evidence

A code printed beside an activity tells you what the author hopes, not what learners do. Read the standard, find the verb it asks for, and look for an activity that asks for it; if only the topic matches, mark the match partial.

The MicroSim below practices the judgment. It shows six lesson activities that each claim to meet one of two made-up standards, and for each one you rate the match.

docs.title: Diagram: Standards Claim Checker
docs.text:
Standards Claim Checker

Type: microsim sim-id: standards-claim-checker Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: assess Learning Objective: The learner will assess whether each of six lesson activities is a strong match, a partial match, or no match for the standard it claims, with at least 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Standards Alignment, Learning Outcome, Bloom Cognitive Levels (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each claim the learner commits one of three ratings. A rating is correct when it matches the Correct rating column in Content. Mastery is at least 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Reading the standards is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A shared topic is a match. (2) A listed code proves alignment. (3) A match must be exact in wording.

Instructional Rationale: Assessing a claim against a standard is an Evaluate-level action that requires reading what the standard asks learners to do. Pairing near-matches with strong matches teaches the learner to compare the verb and the content, and not only the topic.

Content:

The two made-up standards, shown at all times:

  • S-W1: Explain how water moves through a watershed, including runoff, infiltration, and flow to a river or lake.
  • S-W2: Predict how changes in land use affect runoff.

The three ratings: Strong match (learners do what the standard names), Partial match (the topic appears and the performance is missing or weaker), No match (only a topic word is shared).

The six claims:

# Lesson activity shown to the learner Standard claimed Correct rating Why (shown as feedback) 1 Students read about runoff, infiltration, and river flow, then explain the path of a raindrop in a written paragraph. S-W1 Strong match Learners explain how water moves, which is the standard's verb and content. 2 Students label the parts of a watershed diagram. S-W1 Partial match Labeling names parts and does not explain movement. 3 Students watch a video about a famous river. S-W1 No match The topic word river is shared, and no explanation is asked for. 4 Students compare runoff from a grass plot and a paved plot in a model, then predict what happens when more land is paved. S-W2 Strong match Learners predict the effect of a land-use change on runoff. 5 Students list ways people use land near rivers. S-W2 Partial match Listing land uses touches the topic and asks for no prediction. 6 Students memorize the names of five rivers. S-W2 No match Nothing in the activity concerns land use or runoff.

Provenance: The standards and activities are made up for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The three ratings follow the chapter section "Standards Alignment".

Rules: Each claim has exactly one correct rating, two per rating. The rating depends on the standard's verb and content together.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees the two standards and one claim.
  2. The learner chooses a rating, and the choice is committed.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text, and highlights the standard's verb.
  4. After claim 6 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 6 claims in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [rating]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. This is [rating]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 6 correct on the first attempt". At 5 or more it adds "You can check a standards claim." Below 5 it lists the Why text of each missed claim.
