Starting State: The two standards and claim 1 or the first claim in the shuffled order. The question shown is "How well does this activity match the standard?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's example standard S-W1 reads "Explain how water moves through a watershed, including runoff, infiltration, and flow to a river or lake." The chapter says a strong match has learners doing what the standard names.

docs.title: Curriculum Map
docs.text:
A curriculum map is a table that shows how a course's outcomes, activities, and assessments connect. Each row is an outcome. The columns show the activities that teach it and the assessment items that check it. A map makes gaps visible that a list of outcomes hides. Teachers build full maps for courses, and a reviewer builds a quick one for a resource, as in the Watershed Basics table earlier in this chapter.

Worked example: a small map for a fraction unit. The unit has three outcomes, three sections, and five quiz items.

Outcome Taught by Checked by Result F1. Name the numerator and denominator of a fraction Section 1 Items 1 and 2 Aligned F2. Compare two fractions with the same denominator Section 2 Items 3, 4, and 5 Aligned F3. Add two fractions with the same denominator Section 3 None Gap: taught but not checked

Three Lists, One Story

Outcomes, activities, and assessments are one story told three ways. Wherever the three disagree, a learner is practicing one thing and being tested on another.

docs.title: Outcome Coverage
docs.text: Outcome coverage is the share of a resource's stated outcomes that are both taught and assessed. To compute it, count the outcomes that have at least one activity and at least one assessment item, and divide by the number of outcomes. Watershed Basics covers 2 of its 3 outcomes, a coverage of 67 percent. A coverage below 100 percent means the resource makes a promise that it does not keep.

docs.title: Assessment Alignment
docs.text: Assessment alignment is the match between an assessment item and the outcome it claims to check. An item is aligned when it checks that outcome, at the level the outcome asks. An item can fail in two ways. It can check something other than the outcome, as when a quiz on rivers asks about river lengths while the outcome is to explain runoff. Or it can check the right topic at the wrong level, as when an outcome says "explain" and every item asks the learner to choose a vocabulary word. The second failure is easy to miss, because the topic matches.

docs.title: Content Gap
docs.text:
A content gap is an outcome that is not taught, not assessed, or not assessed at the level it asks. The gap may be in the teaching, in the checking, or in both, and the fix differs: add an activity, add a question, or raise the level of the question. The reverse problem is content with no outcome, such as a video that supports nothing the resource promises. That is not a gap, but it adds length and may distract, so a reviewer notes it.

The MicroSim below puts all of this together. It shows a curriculum map for a watershed unit, with four outcomes, five activities, and five quiz items. Your job is to find six problems in the map.

docs.title: Diagram: Curriculum Map Gap Finder
docs.text:
Curriculum Map Gap Finder

Type: microsim sim-id: curriculum-map-gap-finder Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: examine Learning Objective: The learner will examine a curriculum map and find all six gaps and mismatches in it, with no more than one incorrect mark.

Prerequisites: Curriculum Map, Outcome Coverage, Assessment Alignment, Content Gap, Bloom Cognitive Levels (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: The learner marks the problems they find on the map and presses Check. The learner passes when all six problems in the Content table are marked and at most one other mark is wrong. Only the first Check counts as evidence. Opening the problem types is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) An outcome with a matching topic is covered. (2) Content with no outcome is always harmless. (3) A quiz item at any level checks any outcome on its topic.

Instructional Rationale: Finding gaps in a map is an Analyze-level action, because the learner must examine each connection and decide which is missing, extra, or at the wrong level. A map with several kinds of problem teaches the learner to look in every direction.

Content:

The four outcomes, with the Bloom level of each verb:

  • O1: Describe what a watershed is. (Remember)
  • O2: Explain how water moves through a watershed. (Understand)
  • O3: Predict how paving changes runoff. (Analyze)
  • O4: Compare two ways to reduce flooding. (Analyze)

The five activities and what each supports:

  • A1: Reading, "What is a watershed?" supports O1.
  • A2: Reading, "How water moves" supports O2.
  • A3: Label a watershed diagram supports O1.
  • A4: Video of famous rivers supports no outcome.
  • A5: Group discussion on ways to reduce flooding supports O4.

The five quiz items and what each checks:

  • Q1: Choose the definition of a watershed checks O1.
  • Q2: Name the parts of a watershed checks O1.
  • Q3: Choose the word for water flowing over land checks O2, and asks only for recall.
  • Q4: Choose the term for water soaking into the ground checks O2, and asks only for recall.
  • Q5: Choose the longest river in the region checks no outcome.

The six problems to find:

# Problem Type Why it is a problem 1 O3 has no activity. Not taught No activity gives practice at predicting. 2 O3 has no quiz item. Not checked Nothing checks whether learners can predict. 3 O4 has no quiz item. Not checked The discussion is never checked. 4 A4 supports no outcome. Content with no outcome The video adds length and supports no promise. 5 Q5 checks no outcome. Item with no outcome The question tests something the resource never promised. 6 O2 is checked only at the recall level. Level mismatch O2 asks learners to explain, and both items ask only for recall.

Provenance: The outcomes, activities, and quiz items are made up for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative example". The problem types follow the chapter sections "Outcome Coverage", "Assessment Alignment", and "Content Gap".

Rules: The map has exactly six problems, one per row of the table. A mark is correct when it identifies one of the six, by the outcome, activity, or item and the problem type. The learner may mark an outcome as unchecked or untaught, an activity or item as having no outcome, and an outcome as checked at the wrong level.

Learner Activity:

  1. The sim shows the map as a grid of outcomes against activities and quiz items, with the Bloom level of each outcome.
  2. The learner clicks a cell, an activity, an item, or an outcome and chooses the problem type from a short list.
  3. The learner may remove a mark.
  4. The learner presses Check.
  5. The sim shows which of the six were found, which marks were wrong, and the Why text for each missed problem.

Feedback: One Check counts as evidence, and the learner may try again afterward. Pass: "You found all six problems with [n] wrong marks." Not yet: "You found [n] of 6. Missing: [problems with their Why text]." Wrong marks are named with the reason they are not problems. At a pass it adds "You can find the gaps in a map."

Starting State: The map with no marks and the prompt "Find six problems in this map."

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's Watershed Basics table has three outcomes with outcome 3 neither taught nor checked, and the chapter says outcome coverage is the number of taught and assessed outcomes divided by the number of outcomes. This sim's map is a larger unit with four outcomes.

docs.title: Scope and Sequence
docs.text:
Scope and sequence is the plan for what a course covers and in what order. Scope is the content included, and sequence is the order in which it arrives. Sequence matters because ideas build on each other. A section that uses a term or an idea before the resource has introduced it leaves learners guessing, and a section that is introduced and never used may not belong. A reviewer checks sequence by listing, for each section, what it introduces and what it uses, and looking for a section that uses what comes later.

Worked example: a forward reference. A resource on water has four sections.

Section Introduces Uses 1. Parts of a watershed Watershed, tributary None 2. Where rain goes Runoff Watershed 3. Flooding Flood Runoff, infiltration 4. Soaking in Infiltration Runoff

Section 3 uses infiltration, and section 4 is where it is introduced. The sequence is broken. The fix is to introduce infiltration before section 3, by moving section 4 up.

docs.title: Prerequisite Knowledge
docs.text:
Prerequisite knowledge is what a learner must already know or be able to do to use a resource. A resource should state its prerequisites, so that teachers can judge whether their learners are ready and can teach what is missing first. A good statement names concepts and skills and does not name only a grade. "Students should be able to count to 100 and tell when two groups have the same size" is more useful than "grade 1".

Worked example: prerequisites for adding fractions. The table lists three prerequisites for a unit on adding fractions, how a teacher could check each one, and where the resource addresses it.

Prerequisite How to check Where the resource addresses it Count and compare whole numbers Ask learners to order four numbers Assumed, not taught Understand a fraction as part of a whole Ask learners to shade three of four parts Section 1 Find equivalent fractions Ask learners to write two fractions equal to one half Section 4

The MicroSim below practices the sequence check. It shows the six sections of a fraction unit, with what each introduces and what each uses. For each section you decide whether the sequence works.

docs.title: Diagram: Scope and Sequence Order Checker
docs.text:
Scope and Sequence Order Checker

Type: microsim sim-id: scope-sequence-order-checker Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: examine Learning Objective: The learner will examine a six-section unit and judge for each section whether its sequence is sound, uses an idea before it is introduced, or uses an idea that is never introduced, with at least 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Scope and Sequence, Prerequisite Knowledge, Curriculum Map (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each section the learner commits one of three judgments. A judgment is correct when it matches the Correct judgment column in Content. Mastery is at least 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Reading the section list is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A term used in the section title counts as introduced. (2) Every used idea is introduced somewhere. (3) A section is fine if the idea appears later in the unit.

Instructional Rationale: Examining a sequence is an Analyze-level action, because the learner must follow what each part introduces and uses and trace the dependencies. A unit with one forward reference and one missing introduction teaches the learner that the two errors differ and need different fixes.

Content:

The three judgments: Sound, Uses an idea before it is introduced, Uses an idea that is never introduced.

The six sections, in order:

# Section Introduces Uses Correct judgment Why (shown as feedback) 1 Parts of a whole fraction, numerator, denominator none Sound It uses nothing that is not already given. 2 Comparing fractions comparing fractions numerator, denominator, equivalent fractions Uses an idea before it is introduced Equivalent fractions are introduced in section 4. 3 Adding fractions with like denominators adding like fractions numerator, denominator Sound Both terms were introduced in section 1. 4 Equivalent fractions equivalent fractions fraction Sound Fraction was introduced in section 1. 5 Adding fractions with unlike denominators common denominator equivalent fractions, adding like fractions Sound Both ideas were introduced earlier, in sections 4 and 3. 6 Fractions on a number line number line fraction, comparing fractions, mixed numbers Uses an idea that is never introduced Mixed numbers appear in no section.

Provenance: The unit is made up for this chapter, and the sim labels it "illustrative example". The judgments follow the chapter section "Scope and Sequence".

Rules: Each section has exactly one correct judgment. Four sections are Sound, one is Uses an idea before it is introduced, and one is Uses an idea that is never introduced. An idea counts as introduced only in a section numbered before the section that uses it.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees the six sections in a table with what each introduces and uses.
  2. The learner chooses a judgment for section 1, and the choice is committed.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text.
  4. The learner continues through sections 2 to 6.
  5. After section 6 the sim shows the summary, and the learner may suggest the fix for each unsound section, which the sim then compares with the Why text.

Feedback: 6 sections in the fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [judgment]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. This section is [judgment]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 6 correct on the first attempt". At 5 or more it adds "You can check a sequence." Below 5 it lists the Why text of each missed section.

Starting State: The six sections with their introduces and uses columns, and no judgments chosen. The question shown is "Is the sequence sound for section 1?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's sequence example has four sections about water with a forward reference to infiltration, and the chapter says a section that uses an idea before it is introduced is a sequence problem.

docs.title: Scoring Alignment
docs.text:
Alignment is scored with ten checks. A failed check is serious when it leaves the reviewer unable to judge alignment at all, which happens when the resource states no outcomes or states ones that cannot be observed. When a serious check fails, choose the lower number in a two-number band. Otherwise choose the higher number.

# Check Serious if it fails? 1 Learning outcomes are stated Yes 2 Each outcome uses a measurable verb Yes 3 Every outcome is taught by at least one section or activity No 4 Every outcome is checked by at least one assessment item No 5 Every activity and assessment item maps to a stated outcome No 6 The Bloom levels of activities and items match the levels of the outcomes No 7 Standards alignment is shown where a standard applies No 8 Prerequisite knowledge is stated No 9 The sections follow a sound sequence No 10 The intended course, grade, or audience is named No

A check that does not apply, such as standards alignment for a resource that claims no standard, counts as passed.

Worked example: Watershed Basics. The reviewer builds the map shown earlier in this chapter and applies the ten checks.

# Result Evidence 1 Pass The page states three outcomes. 2 Pass The verbs are describe, explain, and predict. 3 Fail Outcome 3 has no section or activity. 4 Fail Quiz items check outcomes 1 and 2, and none checks outcome 3. 5 Pass Every section and quiz item maps to an outcome. 6 Fail Outcome 3 asks learners to predict, and only the remember and understand levels appear anywhere. 7 Pass The resource claims no standard, so the check does not apply. 8 Fail No note says what students should know first. 9 Pass The two sections follow a sound order. 10 Pass The page names its audience as grade 6 to 7.

Six of ten checks pass, a share of 60 percent, in the 5 to 6 band. None of the four failures is serious, because the outcomes exist and can be observed. The reviewer therefore chooses the higher number, 6, the score on the Chapter 3 worksheet. That worksheet recorded the three main gaps. The full check also finds that no prerequisite knowledge is stated.

docs.title: Readability Metric
docs.text:
The readability metric asks whether a resource's intended readers can read it with understanding. It is the second half of this chapter's pair, and it looks at the words and the layout instead of at what the resource covers. A resource can be aligned to its outcomes and still fail the metric, because a learner who cannot read the text cannot reach the outcomes. Five things feed the metric: the reading level of the text, the difficulty of its vocabulary, how plainly it is written, how it is organized, and how well all of that fits the people who will use it.

Worked example: four readers, four barriers. A grade 6 class uses a resource, and each reader meets a different barrier that the metric is designed to catch.

Reader Barrier What the metric looks at A student who reads at grade level Sentences of 40 words and more Reading level A student who is learning English Words such as "aquifer" with no definition Vocabulary and defined terms A student who skims A wall of text with no headings Text structure A teacher choosing a reading Cannot tell who the text is for Audience fit

docs.title: Reading Level
docs.text:
A reading level is the school grade, or age, at which a typical reader can read a text with understanding. A text written at grade 6 level is one that a typical grade 6 reader can handle. Reading level can be measured with a formula, which counts features of the words and sentences, or judged by a reader who knows the audience. The two methods answer slightly different questions, so a careful reviewer uses both.

A mismatch between the reading level and the audience is a barrier either way. A text far above the audience is hard to follow and can make a reader stop. A text far below it can feel childish and can leave out the ideas that older learners need. A good fit usually falls within about one grade of the audience's level.

Worked example: three passages for a grade 6 audience. The reading levels come from a readability tool.

Passage Measured level Distance from grade 6 Fit A 6.4 0.4 grades above Good fit B 9.8 3.8 grades above Too hard C 3.1 2.9 grades below Too easy for this audience

docs.title: Readability Formula
docs.text: A readability formula is a calculation that estimates how hard a text is from features that a computer can count, usually the length of sentences and the length of words. Several are in common use, including the Flesch Reading Ease score, the Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level, the Gunning Fog index, and the SMOG index. They are quick and repeatable, which is why reviewers use them. They are also limited. A formula counts the surface of the text and cannot see how difficult the ideas are, how familiar the words are to a particular reader, or whether the passage is well organized.

docs.title: Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level
docs.text:
The Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level is a readability formula that gives a U.S. school grade. It uses three counts from a passage: the number of sentences, the number of words, and the number of syllables. Longer sentences and longer words raise the grade. For a stable result, use passages of at least 100 words, because a short sample can swing wildly. The formula is:

grade = 0.39 x (words / sentences) + 11.8 x (syllables / words) - 15.59

The first part of the formula measures sentence length, as the average number of words per sentence. The second part measures word length, as the average number of syllables per word. The last number only adjusts the result so that it lines up with school grades. You never need to work it out by hand, because free tools do the counting, but seeing the arithmetic once shows what the number is made of.

Worked example: a 120-word passage. The passage has 6 sentences, 120 words, and 168 syllables.

  1. Words per sentence: 120 divided by 6 is 20.
  2. Syllables per word: 168 divided by 120 is 1.4.
  3. Sentence part: 0.39 times 20 is 7.8.
  4. Word part: 11.8 times 1.4 is 16.52.
  5. Add the two parts: 7.8 plus 16.52 is 24.32.
  6. Subtract 15.59: 24.32 minus 15.59 is 8.73, which rounds to a grade level of 8.7.

The Tool Does the Counting

If counting syllables by hand sounds tedious, it is, and that is why tools do it. You already read other formulas by asking what they measure, and the question here is what a grade number is made of. Once you know that, you can judge when to trust it.

The formula has a blind spot that is worth naming before you rely on it.

The Formula Measures the Sentence, Not the Idea

A passage of short words and short sentences can score as easy and still be hard, if its ideas are dense or its terms are never defined. Treat the number as one piece of evidence and read the passage yourself.

The MicroSim below lets you work the formula. In explore mode you change the three counts and watch the grade move. In practice mode you compute the grade for four passages.

docs.title: Diagram: Flesch-Kincaid Calculator
docs.text:
Flesch-Kincaid Calculator

Type: microsim sim-id: flesch-kincaid-calculator Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: calculate Learning Objective: The learner will calculate the Flesch-Kincaid grade level of each of four passages from its counts of sentences, words, and syllables, to within 0.1 of the correct value, with at least 3 of 4 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Reading Level, Readability Formula, Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each passage the learner enters a grade level before the answer is shown. An answer is correct when it is within 0.1 of the Grade level column in Content. Mastery is at least 3 of 4 correct on the first attempt. Moving the explore-mode inputs is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) More syllables per word has little effect. (2) A shorter passage always gives a lower grade. (3) The grade is a score out of 10.

Instructional Rationale: Calculating with a formula is an Apply-level task. Exploration first shows how each count moves the grade, and committed calculations afterward test whether the learner can apply all three steps without help.

Content:

The formula, shown at all times: grade = 0.39 x (words / sentences) + 11.8 x (syllables / words) - 15.59.

The four passages:

# Sentences Words Syllables Words per sentence Syllables per word Grade level (to one decimal) 1 8 110 143 13.75 1.30 5.1 2 5 100 150 20.00 1.50 9.9 3 10 150 195 15.00 1.30 5.6 4 4 100 160 25.00 1.60 13.0

Provenance: The counts are illustrative cases written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The formula is the Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level as stated in the chapter section "Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level".

Rules: In explore mode the sentences input has minimum 1, maximum 30, step 1, default 6, unit sentences. The words input has minimum 50, maximum 400, step 1, default 120, unit words. The syllables input has minimum equal to the number of words, maximum equal to 3 times the number of words, step 1, default 168, unit syllables. The grade is computed with the formula, rounded to one decimal place, and shown even when it is less than 0. In practice mode the learner enters the grade to one decimal place. An answer is correct when it differs from the Grade level column by <= 0.1.

Learner Activity:

  1. In explore mode the learner changes sentences, words, and syllables and watches the two averages and the grade update.
  2. The learner should notice that adding words without adding sentences raises the grade quickly.
  3. In practice mode the sim shows passage 1 with its three counts.
  4. The learner enters the grade and presses Check.
  5. The sim shows the two averages, the grade, and the three steps of the arithmetic, then shows the next passage, until passage 4 is done.

Feedback: 4 passages in the fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: grade [grade]. [Words per sentence] words per sentence and [syllables per word] syllables per word." Incorrect: "Not quite. The grade is [grade]. Step through: [three steps]". The summary shows "[n] of 4 correct on the first attempt". At 3 or more it adds "You can work the formula." Below 3 it shows the steps for each missed passage.

Starting State: Explore mode with 6 sentences, 120 words, and 168 syllables, so the grade is 8.7. The prompt is "Change a count to see the grade move."

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states the formula as grade = 0.39 x (words / sentences) + 11.8 x (syllables / words) - 15.59, and its worked example of 6 sentences, 120 words, and 168 syllables gives a grade of 8.7. The chapter advises passages of at least 100 words.

docs.title: Vocabulary Level
docs.text:
Vocabulary level is how difficult a text's words are for its readers. The educators Isabel Beck, Margaret McKeown, and Linda Kucan describe three tiers of words that help a reviewer decide what to do. Tier 1 words are everyday words that most readers know, such as because and river. Tier 2 words are general academic words that appear across subjects, such as analyze, however, and evidence. Tier 3 words belong to one field, such as aquifer and runoff. The tiers call for different treatment: Tier 1 words need nothing, Tier 2 words are worth teaching and using consistently, and Tier 3 words must be defined where they first appear.

Worked example: sorting six words from a reading.

Word Tier What the author should do because Tier 1 Nothing river Tier 1 Nothing however Tier 2 Use it consistently, and make sure the audience knows it analyze Tier 2 Use it consistently, and teach it if learners will meet it often aquifer Tier 3 Define it where it first appears, and list it in a glossary runoff Tier 3 Define it where it first appears, and list it in a glossary

docs.title: Defined Terms
docs.text:
Defined terms are the specialized words that a resource explains in the text, and the practice of explaining each one where it first appears. The test is simple: when a reader meets a term for the first time, is its meaning in the same sentence or the next? A term defined three pages later, or never, forces the reader to guess. A good definition says what the term means in plain words, without using the term itself.

Define It Where It First Appears

Put the definition in the same sentence as the term's first use, or in the sentence right after. A reader should never have to scroll or flip pages to learn what a word means.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
A glossary is an alphabetical list of a resource's specialized terms with a definition for each. It supports defined terms in the text. A reader who forgets a term can look it up without hunting through earlier pages. A good glossary entry is short, precise, and written in terms simpler than the term itself. Many resources also link each term in the text to its glossary entry, so the definition is one click away.

The MicroSim below practices the check for defined terms. It shows a passage of eight sentences with five specialized terms, and for each term you decide whether it is defined at first use, defined later, or never defined.

docs.title: Diagram: Term Before Definition Finder
docs.text:
Term Before Definition Finder

Type: microsim sim-id: term-before-definition-finder Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: examine Learning Objective: The learner will examine a passage and judge for each of five specialized terms whether it is defined at first use, defined later, or never defined, with at least 4 of 5 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Vocabulary Level, Defined Terms, Glossary (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each term the learner commits one of three judgments. A judgment is correct when it matches the Correct judgment column in Content. Mastery is at least 4 of 5 correct on the first attempt. Rereading the passage is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A term defined anywhere in the passage is fine. (2) A word the reader probably knows needs no definition. (3) A glossary makes in-text definitions unnecessary.

Instructional Rationale: Examining a passage for the position of each definition is an Analyze-level action, because the learner must locate the first use and the definition and compare their order. Five terms with three different outcomes teach the learner to check each one separately.

Content:

The passage, shown at all times, with its sentences numbered:

  1. A watershed is an area of land where all the water drains to the same place.
  2. When rain falls, some of it becomes runoff and flows over the land.
  3. The rest soaks in by infiltration, which means water seeping into the ground.
  4. Water that collects underground fills an aquifer.
  5. Runoff is the water that flows over the ground instead of soaking in.
  6. Pavement increases runoff because water cannot seep through it.
  7. A tributary is a smaller river that flows into a larger one.
  8. Many tributaries join to form the main river.

The three judgments: Defined at first use, Defined later, Never defined.

The five terms:

# Term First used in sentence Defined in sentence Correct judgment Why (shown as feedback) 1 watershed 1 1 Defined at first use The definition is in the same sentence as the term. 2 runoff 2 5 Defined later The term is used in sentence 2, and its definition arrives in sentence 5. 3 infiltration 3 3 Defined at first use The sentence says what it means right after the term. 4 aquifer 4 none Never defined No sentence says what an aquifer is. 5 tributary 7 7 Defined at first use The definition is in the same sentence as the term.

Provenance: The passage is written for this chapter and states general facts about watersheds, and the sim labels it "illustrative example". The judgments follow the chapter section "Defined Terms".

Rules: Each term has exactly one correct judgment. A term is Defined at first use when its definition is in the same sentence as its first use or the sentence immediately after. A term is Defined later when its definition appears more than one sentence after its first use. A term is Never defined when no sentence defines it.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads the passage with its numbered sentences.
  2. The learner chooses a judgment for the first term, and the choice is committed.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text, and highlights the first use and the definition in the passage.
  4. The learner continues through the five terms.
  5. After the fifth term the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 5 terms in the fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [judgment]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. This term is [judgment]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 5 correct on the first attempt". At 4 or more it adds "You can find a missing definition." Below 4 it lists the Why text of each missed term.

Starting State: The passage and the first term, watershed, with the three judgments. The question shown is "Is this term defined where it first appears?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter says a term should be defined in the same sentence as its first use or the sentence right after, and its Watershed Basics example uses the word aquifer before it is defined.

docs.title: Plain Language
docs.text:
Plain language is writing that readers can understand the first time they read it. It does not mean simple ideas or small words only. It means choosing the clearest way to say what you mean. Its habits are easy to list: short sentences with one idea each, the active voice, common words where a common word is as accurate, the reader's own terms, and examples. Plain language is not "dumbing down", because the ideas stay the same and the clutter goes away.

The MicroSim below practices the choice. For each of six sentences you pick the best of three rewrites.

docs.title: Diagram: Plain Language Chooser
docs.text:
Plain Language Chooser

Type: microsim sim-id: plain-language-chooser Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: apply Learning Objective: The learner will apply plain-language habits to choose the best rewrite of each of six sentences from three options, with at least 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Plain Language, Reading Level, Vocabulary Level (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each sentence the learner chooses one of three rewrites. A choice is correct when it matches the Best rewrite column in Content. Mastery is at least 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Reading the habit list is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) The shortest rewrite is always the plainest. (2) Plain language drops technical accuracy. (3) Passive voice is always wrong.

Instructional Rationale: Applying plain-language habits to new sentences is an Apply-level task. Options that include a wordy rewrite, an over-trimmed rewrite, and a plain and accurate rewrite make the learner weigh clarity against meaning.

Content:

The habits, shown on request: one idea per sentence; active voice; common words where they are as accurate; keep the meaning.

The six sentences:

# Original sentence Option A Option B Option C Best rewrite Why (shown as feedback) 1 Individuals should endeavor to utilize the water conservation methodology. People should try to use ways to save water. Individuals ought to make an attempt to employ water-saving measures. Water should be saved. A A keeps the meaning in common words. B keeps the long words, and C loses who should act. 2 The experiment was conducted by the students, and the results were recorded. The students ran the experiment and recorded the results. The experiment was done by students and results were put down. Students conducted experimentation and recorded results. A A uses the active voice and plain verbs. B stays passive, and C uses stiffer words. 3 Photosynthetic organisms synthesize carbohydrates using solar radiation. Plants make sugar from sunlight. Plants and algae make sugar from sunlight. Organisms that photosynthesize synthesize sugars from light. B B is plain and keeps the meaning, since algae also photosynthesize. A leaves them out, and C repeats the specialist words. 4 In the event that precipitation occurs, the field trip will be postponed. If it rains, we will move the field trip to another day. Should precipitation take place, the field trip is postponed. If it rains, no trip. A A is plain and complete. B keeps the formal wording, and C drops the plan. 5 The aforementioned data indicates a significant increase. The data in the table above show a large increase. The data shows it went up. The aforementioned figures reveal a major rise. A A replaces the stiff words and says where the data are. B is vague, and C keeps "aforementioned". 6 Utilize the glossary for the purpose of locating unfamiliar terms. Use the glossary to find words you do not know. Utilize the glossary to locate terms. Look at the glossary. A A is plain and complete. B keeps "utilize", and C loses the purpose.

Provenance: The sentences and rewrites are written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The habits follow the chapter section "Plain Language".

Rules: Each sentence has exactly one best rewrite. Options are shown in a fixed order for each sentence. A rewrite is best when it uses plain words and keeps the meaning of the original.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one original sentence and three rewrites.
  2. The learner chooses one rewrite, and the choice is committed.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text.
  4. After sentence 6 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 6 sentences in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [option]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. The best rewrite is [option]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 6 correct on the first attempt". At 5 or more it adds "You can write plainly and keep the meaning." Below 5 it lists the Why text of each missed sentence.

Starting State: The first sentence with its three rewrites. The question shown is "Which rewrite is the plainest and keeps the meaning?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter says plain language uses short sentences with one idea each, the active voice, and common words where they are as accurate, and that it does not change the ideas.

docs.title: Jargon
docs.text:
Jargon is specialized language that a person outside a field would not know, and that the author uses without need or without explaining. Some specialized words are necessary: aquifer is the right word for an aquifer, and the fix is to define it. Jargon is the extra: an insider phrase where a common one would do, such as "utilize" for "use" or "operationalize" for "put into practice". A reviewer's test has two parts. If a common word says the same thing, ask for it. If the specialized word is necessary, ask for a definition.

Do Not Trade Accuracy for a Lower Grade

Stripping out technical terms to lower a reading score can make a resource vague or wrong. Keep the term that is needed, define it where it first appears, and cut only the words that add nothing.

docs.title: Text Structure
docs.text:
Text structure is how a resource's text is organized: its headings, paragraph length, lists, signposts, examples, and summaries. Good structure lets a reader see the shape of the content, find a section again, and skip what they already know. Structure also affects readability for learners who struggle with long blocks of text, and it is the foundation for accessibility, because screen readers use headings to navigate.

Worked example: before and after. The table contrasts two versions of the same page.

Feature Before After Headings None A heading for each of five sections Paragraphs One block of 600 words Paragraphs of three to five sentences, each with one idea Lists Steps buried in a paragraph A numbered list of four steps Signposts None A sentence that says what the section will do Ending The text stops A short summary of key points

The next MicroSim shows the parts of a readable page. Its illustration shows a page with seven features, each marked with a numbered marker.

docs.title: Diagram: Anatomy of a Readable Page
docs.text:
Anatomy of a Readable Page

Type: infographic sim-id: readable-page-anatomy Library: html Status: Specified Bloom Level: Remember Bloom Verb: identify Learning Objective: The learner will identify seven features of a readable page from a description of how each looks, with at least 6 of 7 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Text Structure, Defined Terms, Plain Language (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: In quiz mode the learner clicks the marker that matches a visual hint. A click is correct when it matches the marker named in the Hint column of Content. Mastery is at least 6 of 7 correct on the first attempt. Hovering in explore mode is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A heading is just larger text. (2) A summary repeats the whole page. (3) Examples make a page longer without helping.

Instructional Rationale: Identifying features of a page is a Remember-level task, and an illustration of a readable page shows how the features sit together on one page. The quiz asks the learner to recognize each by its look.

Content:

The illustration is a text-free flat drawing of one lesson page. At the top is a wide bar of heading text. Under it is a short block of three thin lines. Further down a single word in the block is highlighted with a small dot beside it. A box with a small lightbulb icon holds two thin lines. A short list of three lines, each with a dot at its left, follows. Next is a framed picture with a thin strip beneath it. At the bottom is a shaded box with two thin lines and a small checkmark icon. The seven markers:

# Label Hint (describes the look, not the name) Description Tip 1 Descriptive heading The wide bar of text at the top of the page. A heading that tells the reader what the section is about, in words that match its content. Write headings as short phrases that say what is inside. 2 Short paragraph A block of three thin lines under the heading. A paragraph of three to five sentences with one idea. Break a paragraph when the idea changes. 3 Defined term A single highlighted word with a small dot beside it. A specialized word whose meaning is given where it first appears. Put the definition in the same sentence. 4 Example box A box with a small lightbulb icon holding two thin lines. A concrete example that shows the idea at work. Use an example whenever an idea is abstract. 5 List A short list of three lines, each with a dot at its left. Steps or items set apart, so the reader can scan them. Use a numbered list when order matters. 6 Figure with caption A framed picture with a thin strip beneath it. A picture that supports the text, with a caption that says what to notice. Describe the figure in the caption and credit its source. 7 Summary box A shaded box at the bottom with a small checkmark icon. A short recap of the key points at the end of the section. Name the two or three ideas a reader should keep.

Provenance: The seven features follow the chapter sections "Text Structure", "Defined Terms", and "Plain Language". The illustration is synthetic, and the sim labels the page "illustrative example".

Rules: Each hint matches exactly one marker. The illustration contains no text, so every label comes from the table above. Markers are numbered 1 to 7 in the order of the table.

Learner Activity:

  1. In explore mode the learner hovers or clicks a marker and reads its label, description, and tip.
  2. In quiz mode the sim shows a hint.
  3. The learner clicks the marker they think the hint describes.
  4. If the first click is wrong, the sim says so and lets the learner try once more. If the second click is also wrong, the sim reveals the marker and its description.
  5. After all 7 hints the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 7 hints in a shuffled order, two attempts each. Only a correct first click counts as evidence. Correct: "Correct: [label]. [Description]". First wrong click: "Not quite. Look again at the hint: [hint]". Second wrong click: "This is [label]. [Description]". The summary shows "[n] of 7 correct on the first attempt". At 6 or more it adds "You can read a page's structure." Below 6 it lists the labels of the missed features.

Starting State: The illustration with seven numbered markers, explore mode active, and the prompt "Hover a marker to see what it is."

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's text-structure example lists headings, short paragraphs, lists, signposts, and a summary, and its page features include a defined term, an example box, and a figure with a caption.

docs.title: Headings and Subheadings
docs.text: Headings and subheadings are the titles that label a resource's sections, with the main heading at the top and subheadings nested beneath it. A good heading is descriptive: "How runoff reaches a river" tells the reader more than "More information". Headings should follow a hierarchy, so that a section heading contains its subheadings and no level is skipped. A page that jumps from a main heading straight to a sub-sub-heading confuses readers and breaks screen readers, which is why the accessibility chapter checks it.

docs.title: Audience Fit
docs.text: Audience fit is how well the whole of a resource matches the people who will use it: their reading level, prior knowledge, language, culture, and purpose. It is the summary question that the other readability features serve. A grade number cannot capture it. A passage at the right grade level can still be a poor fit if it assumes background the audience lacks, uses examples from an unfamiliar setting, or serves a purpose different from the audience's. A reviewer judges fit by asking a person from the audience to read a section aloud, and by noting where they stumble.

docs.title: Scoring Readability
docs.text:
Readability is scored with ten checks. A failed check is serious when it can stop the intended audience from reading the resource at all, which happens when the audience is not stated or the measured reading level is far from it. When a serious check fails, choose the lower number in a two-number band. Otherwise choose the higher number.

# Check Serious if it fails? 1 The intended audience, a grade or level, is stated Yes 2 The measured reading level of sampled passages is within one grade of the audience level Yes 3 At least three passages from different sections were sampled No 4 Technical terms are defined at first use No 5 A glossary or term list is provided No 6 Sentences are plain: mostly one idea each, in the active voice No 7 Jargon is replaced or explained No 8 Headings describe the content of their sections No 9 Paragraphs are short and focused No 10 Examples and visuals fit the audience's experience No

Worked example: Watershed Basics. The reviewer samples three passages and applies the ten checks.

# Result Evidence 1 Pass The page names its audience as grade 6 to 7. 2 Pass A readability tool gave grade 6.4, 6.9, and 7.3 for the three samples. 3 Pass The samples come from sections 1, 2, and 3. 4 Fail The word "aquifer" is used in section 3 before any definition. 5 Fail The resource has no glossary. 6 Pass The sampled sentences are mostly one idea each. 7 Pass No unexplained jargon appears in the samples. 8 Pass Every heading says what its section contains. 9 Pass Paragraphs run three to five sentences. 10 Pass The examples use local rivers that a grade 6 reader would know.

Eight of ten checks pass, a share of 80 percent, in the 7 to 8 band. Neither failed check is serious, because the audience is stated and the reading level fits it. The reviewer therefore chooses the higher number, 8, the score on the Chapter 3 worksheet.

The last MicroSim of the chapter is a scoring practice for both halves. It shows three resources scored on alignment and three scored on readability, with each one's ten check results, and for each you choose the metric score.

docs.title: Diagram: Alignment and Readability Scorer
docs.text:
Alignment and Readability Scorer

Type: microsim sim-id: alignment-readability-scorer Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: apply Learning Objective: The learner will apply the ten alignment checks and the ten readability checks, with the Chapter 3 scoring rules, to choose the metric score for each of six cases, with at least 5 of 6 scores exactly correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: The Alignment Metric, The Readability Metric, Scoring Alignment, Scoring Readability, Metric Score, Scoring Descriptor (all defined in this chapter or in Chapter 3 above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each case the learner chooses a whole-number score from 0 to 10 after seeing the ten check results. A score is correct when it equals the Correct score column in Content. Mastery is at least 5 of 6 scores correct on the first attempt. Opening the check lists and the descriptor table is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Every failed check lowers the score equally. (2) A serious failure always drops a full band. (3) The two metrics use different scoring rules.

Instructional Rationale: Applying a scoring procedure to new cases is an Apply-level task. Three cases for each metric, with different counts and different serious failures, make the learner repeat the same procedure on two sets of checks.

Content:

The two ten-check lists are those in the chapter sections "Scoring Alignment" and "Scoring Readability", each marked serious or not. The descriptor bands applied to the share of checks passed: 0% is 0; 1% to 24% is 1 to 2; 25% to 49% is 3 to 4; 50% to 74% is 5 to 6; 75% to 89% is 7 to 8; 90% to 100% is 9 to 10. Within a two-number band, choose the lower number when a serious check failed and the higher number otherwise. A score of 10 requires every check to pass. A check that does not apply counts as passed.

The six cases:

# Metric Resource Checks failed Checks passed Share Band Serious failure? Correct score Why (shown as feedback) 1 Alignment Open Algebra Unit None 10 100% 9 to 10 No 10 Every check passed. 2 Alignment Watershed Basics 3, 4, 6, 8 6 60% 5 to 6 No 6 None of the failures is serious, so the higher number applies. 3 Alignment Unit Without Outcomes 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8 3 (checks 7, 9, 10) 30% 3 to 4 Yes, checks 1 and 2 3 The unit states no outcomes, which is serious, so the lower number applies. 4 Readability Open Algebra Unit None 10 100% 9 to 10 No 10 Every check passed. 5 Readability Watershed Basics 4 and 5 8 80% 7 to 8 No 8 Neither failure is serious, so the higher number applies. 6 Readability College Text Used in Grade 7 2, 4, 5, 6, 7 5 (checks 1, 3, 8, 9, 10) 50% 5 to 6 Yes, check 2 5 The reading level is far above the audience, which is serious, so the lower number applies.

Provenance: The ten checks and the bands follow the chapter sections "Scoring Alignment" and "Scoring Readability" and Chapter 3. The six cases are illustrative cases written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". Cases 2 and 5 are the chapter's worked examples.

Rules: A score is the band chosen from the share passed, then the number chosen within the band by the serious-failure rule. Each case has exactly one correct score. For a band that holds a single number, that number is the score.

Learner Activity:

  1. The sim shows case 1 with its ten check results and the name of the metric.
  2. The learner may open the check list and the descriptor table.
  3. The learner chooses a score from 0 to 10, and the choice is committed.
  4. The sim shows the count of passes, the band, whether a serious check failed, and the correct score with the Why text.
  5. After case 6 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 6 cases in the fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [score]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. [passes] checks passed, which is [share] and the [band] band. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 6 correct on the first attempt". At 5 or more it adds "You can score both metrics." Below 5 it lists the Why text of each missed case.

Starting State: Case 1 with all ten results shown and no score chosen. The question shown is "What alignment score does this resource earn?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's worked examples score Watershed Basics 6 on alignment, with failures of checks 3, 4, 6, and 8, and 8 on readability, with failures of checks 4 and 5. The chapter says a serious failure puts the score at the lower number in the band.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• A learning outcome says what a learner will be able to do. A learning objective is one lesson's narrower, measurable step toward it, built with a measurable verb. Bloom's taxonomy and its six cognitive levels describe how demanding an outcome or an activity is.
  • The alignment metric asks whether outcomes, activities, and assessments match. Standards alignment needs more than a code, a curriculum map shows what is taught and checked, outcome coverage measures the share covered, and assessment alignment and content gaps mark where the match breaks.
  • Scope and sequence and prerequisite knowledge decide whether ideas arrive in an order a learner can follow.
  • The readability metric asks whether intended readers can read the text. Reading level can be estimated with a readability formula such as the Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level, which counts the surface of the text and not the difficulty of its ideas.
  • Vocabulary level, defined terms, a glossary, plain language, and the avoidance of jargon make a text easier to read. Text structure, with clear headings and subheadings, makes it easier to navigate, and audience fit is the overall judgment.

You Can Check the Match and the Words

You can now map a resource to its outcomes and find the gaps, rate its reading level, check its terms and structure, and score both alignment and readability with evidence. These two scores tell you whether a resource teaches what it promises in words its readers can use.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Alignment and Readability
docs.text: Test your understanding of learning outcomes, Bloom's taxonomy, alignment checks, reading level, vocabulary, and plain language with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. Which verb is measurable, meaning a teacher could observe a learner doing it?
docs.text:
1. Understand
  2. Calculate
  3. Appreciate
  4. Be familiar with
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. A measurable verb names something a teacher could watch a learner do and check afterward. List, describe, calculate, compare, and design are measurable. Know, understand, learn, appreciate, and be familiar with are not, because no one can see them happen. A quick test is to ask, "How would I know the learner did this?" If the answer is "I couldn't tell," swap in a verb such as explain or label.

Concept Tested: Measurable Verb

See: Measurable Verb

docs.title: 2. Which three parts make up a well-formed learning objective in the model the chapter uses?
docs.text:
1. Topic, activity, and assessment
  2. Outcome, standard, and sequence
  3. Audience, verb, and grade level
  4. Performance, condition, and criterion
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The model comes from the educator Robert Mager. The performance is what the learner will do, written with a measurable verb. The condition is the situation or help the learner has, such as "given a map." The criterion is how well the learner must do it, such as "with no more than one error." An objective written this way can be assessed, unlike "Students will learn about runoff."

Concept Tested: Learning Objective

See: Learning Objective

docs.title: 3. Which list shows the six levels of the revised Bloom's taxonomy in order from the simplest to the most demanding?
docs.text:
1. Remember, understand, apply, evaluate, analyze, create
  2. Understand, remember, apply, analyze, evaluate, create
  3. Remember, understand, apply, analyze, evaluate, create
  4. Remember, apply, understand, analyze, create, evaluate
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The 2001 revision by Anderson and Krathwohl orders the levels remember, understand, apply, analyze, evaluate, and create, and each level asks more of the learner than the one before. The order matters to a reviewer because an outcome and the activities that teach it should sit at the same level. If an outcome says "predict" and every activity asks only for recall, learners never practice the skill the outcome names.

Concept Tested: Bloom Cognitive Levels

See: Bloom Cognitive Levels

docs.title: 4. Why does the chapter say that a standard code printed beside an activity is not evidence of alignment?
docs.text:
1. The code states what the author hopes, so a reviewer must read the standard and check what learners do
  2. Standard codes are usually out of date by the time a resource is published and reviewed
  3. Only state standards can be matched to activities, and codes come from national bodies
  4. A code shows that the activity matches the standard, but at the Remember level only
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Listing a code is not matching. The reviewer reads the standard, finds the verb it asks for, and looks for an activity that asks learners to do that. A strong match has learners doing what the standard names, a partial match touches the topic without the performance, and no match shares only a topic word. For example, coloring a picture of a river does not meet a standard that asks learners to explain how water moves.

Concept Tested: Standards Alignment

See: Standards Alignment

docs.title: 5. An outcome says "Explain how water moves over land," but every quiz item asks learners to choose a vocabulary word. What is the problem?
docs.text:
1. The outcome uses a vague verb such as 'know', so no quiz item could check it
  2. The items check a different topic from the one that the outcome names
  3. The items check the right topic at a lower level than the outcome asks
  4. The outcome has no activity, so nothing in the resource teaches it to learners
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. An assessment item is aligned when it checks the outcome at the level the outcome asks. Here the topic matches, but "explain" asks for understanding and the items ask only for recall, so the level is wrong. This failure is easy to miss because the topic lines up. The fix is to raise the level of the questions. "Explain" is a measurable verb (A), and the problem lies in the items, not the teaching (D).

Concept Tested: Assessment Alignment

See: Assessment Alignment

docs.title: 6. Why can a passage score as easy on the Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level and still be hard to read?
docs.text:
1. The formula works only on passages of more than 1,000 words, and short samples give no result
  2. The formula measures vocabulary tiers and ignores sentence length, so it misses long sentences
  3. The formula gives a score out of 10 and not a school grade, so it cannot show reading level
  4. The formula counts sentence and word length, so it cannot see dense ideas, undefined terms, or poor organization
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The formula uses three counts: sentences, words, and syllables. It measures the surface of the text. A passage of short words and short sentences can score as easy and still be hard if its ideas are dense or its terms are never defined. Treat the number as one piece of evidence and read the passage yourself. For a stable result, use passages of at least 100 words, not 1,000.

Concept Tested: Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level

See: Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level

docs.title: 7. A passage has 5 sentences, 100 words, and 150 syllables. Using grade = 0.39 × (words ÷ sentences) + 11.8 × (syllables ÷ words) − 15.59, what is its Flesch-Kincaid grade level?
docs.text:
1. 7.8
  2. 9.9
  3. 13.0
  4. 25.5
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Words per sentence is 100 divided by 5, which is 20, and 0.39 times 20 is 7.8. Syllables per word is 150 divided by 100, which is 1.5, and 11.8 times 1.5 is 17.7. Adding gives 25.5, and subtracting 15.59 gives 9.91, which rounds to 9.9. Option A stops after the sentence part, and option D forgets the final subtraction that lines the result up with school grades.

Concept Tested: Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level

See: Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level

docs.title: 8. Which rewrite of "Utilize the glossary for the purpose of locating unfamiliar terms" is plainest while keeping the meaning?
docs.text:
1. Look at the glossary
  2. Utilize the glossary to locate terms
  3. Use of the glossary is advised for the location of unfamiliar terms
  4. Use the glossary to find words you do not know
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Plain language uses short sentences with one idea, the active voice, and common words where a common word is as accurate. Option D keeps both the action and the purpose in everyday words. Option A is short but loses the purpose, option B keeps the stiff word "utilize," and option C buries the action in a passive, noun-heavy phrase. Plain language is not dumbing down, because the ideas stay the same and the clutter goes away.

Concept Tested: Plain Language

See: Plain Language

docs.title: 9. A water unit has four sections. Section 1 introduces watershed and tributary. Section 2 introduces runoff and uses watershed. Section 3 introduces flood and uses runoff and infiltration. Section 4 introduces infiltration and uses runoff. What is the sequence problem, and how is it fixed?
docs.text:
1. Section 3 uses infiltration before section 4 introduces it, so section 4 should move up before section 3
  2. Section 2 uses watershed before it is introduced, so section 2 should come before section 1
  3. Section 4 uses runoff before it is introduced, so section 4 should come before section 2
  4. There is no problem, because every idea is introduced somewhere in the unit before the quiz
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. To check sequence, list what each section introduces and what it uses, then look for a section that uses an idea that arrives later. Section 3 uses infiltration, but section 4 is where infiltration is introduced, so learners meet the idea before they are taught it. Moving section 4 ahead of section 3 fixes it. Option D is the misconception that an idea appearing anywhere in the unit is enough.

Concept Tested: Scope and Sequence

See: Scope and Sequence

docs.title: 10. In a curriculum map for a fraction unit, the outcome "Add two fractions with the same denominator" is taught by Section 3, but no quiz item checks it. How should a reviewer classify and fix this?
docs.text:
1. A content gap in teaching, so add a new section that teaches the outcome to learners
  2. Content with no outcome, so delete Section 3 from the unit to shorten the resource
  3. A content gap in checking, so add a quiz item that checks the outcome at the level it asks
  4. A level mismatch in teaching, so raise the Bloom level of Section 3
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. A content gap is an outcome that is not taught, not assessed, or not assessed at the level it asks. The gap can lie in the teaching, in the checking, or in both, and the fix differs: add an activity, add a question, or raise the level of the question. Here the outcome is taught but never checked, so the fix is a quiz item. The reverse problem, content with no outcome, is noted but is not a gap.

Concept Tested: Content Gap

See: Content Gap

docs.title: References: Alignment and Readability
docs.text:
1. Bloom's taxonomy - Wikipedia - Describes the original and revised Bloom's taxonomies and their six cognitive levels with example verbs. Supports the chapter's method of matching a resource's activities to the level of its stated outcomes.

  2. Flesch–Kincaid readability tests - Wikipedia - Gives the formulas for the Reading Ease and Grade Level tests, their history, and their limits. Background for the reading level checks in the readability metric.

  3. Constructive alignment - Wikipedia - Explains John Biggs's principle that outcomes, teaching activities, and assessment should match one another. The idea behind this chapter's alignment metric and its outcome-to-content mapping.

  4. Teaching for Quality Learning at University (4th ed.) - John Biggs and Catherine Tang - McGraw-Hill / Open University Press (2011) - Biggs introduced constructive alignment, asking teachers to write outcomes as verbs and then design activities and assessments that require those verbs. It is the basis of this chapter's outcome-to-content mapping.

  5. Understanding by Design (2nd expanded ed.) - Grant Wiggins and Jay McTighe - ASCD (2005) - Wiggins and McTighe's backward design starts with desired results, then evidence, then activities. A reviewer can follow the same sequence to judge whether a resource's content serves its stated outcomes.

  6. Plain Language Guide Series - Digital.gov - Federal guidance on writing short sentences, active voice, and familiar words, with examples. Gives concrete criteria for judging a resource's plain-language quality and text structure.

  7. Learning Objectives - Carnegie Mellon Eberly Center - Explains how to write measurable learning objectives with action verbs and how objectives shape assessment and activities. Helps reviewers judge whether a resource's stated objectives are testable.

  8. Common Core State Standards Initiative - CCSSI - Home of the K-12 English language arts and mathematics standards. Reviewers scoring a K-12 resource use these standards as the target when checking alignment.

  9. Readability Formulas - Readability Formulas - Explains common readability formulas and offers a free online test for pasted text. Lets reviewers check a passage's reading level quickly and see how the formulas differ.

  10. Legibility, Readability, and Comprehension: Making Users Read Your Words - Nielsen Norman Group - Separates how legible the type is, how readable the words are, and how well readers understand. A reminder that a reading-level score alone does not measure comprehension.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Explains how to score accessibility against WCAG 2.1 AA, covering alt text, headings, color contrast, captions, keyboard use, screen readers, accessible math, and automated checkers. It applies the accessibility metric and builds on HTML and the rubric from earlier chapters. After this chapter you can check a resource against WCAG 2.1 AA, write useful alt text, and run an accessibility checker.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 3: The Ten-Metric Rubric and Scoring
  • Chapter 4: Open File Formats and Version Control
  • Chapter 6: Alignment and Readability

Can Every Learner Get Through It?

A resource that some learners cannot see, hear, or operate is unfinished, however well it teaches. This chapter gives you the checks that decide whether a blind learner, a deaf learner, or a learner who cannot use a mouse can get all the way through. Let's dive in and check the evidence!

Every other quality metric assumes that the learner can reach the content. The accessibility metric tests that assumption. A beautifully accurate, well-aligned, readable chapter fails a learner who cannot see its diagrams, hear its video, or reach its quiz with a keyboard. Accessibility is also where a reviewer finds the problems that authors see least, since an author who can see and hear and use a mouse rarely notices what a different learner meets.

This chapter explains what accessibility is, introduces the standard that the rubric uses, and then works through the practical checks: images, headings, color, media, keyboard use, screen readers, links, tables, language, math, and the tools that test them. The last section combines them into a score.

docs.title: Accessibility
docs.text:
Accessibility is the degree to which people with disabilities can perceive, understand, navigate, and use a resource. Disabilities include differences in vision, hearing, movement, and thinking, and they can be permanent, temporary, or situational. A learner with a broken arm, a learner in a noisy room, and a learner who is blind all benefit from a resource built so that information is available more than one way. Accessibility is a property of how the resource is designed. It is not a trait of the learner, and it is the author's responsibility to build it in.

In the United States, laws such as Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act and the Americans with Disabilities Act apply to many schools and colleges, and the technical standard that policies most often cite is the one in the next section. Your institution's policy tells you what applies to you. The practical case is stronger than the legal one, because accessible design helps every learner.

Several of these supports depend on assistive technology, the tools that people with disabilities use to read and operate a page. The most common is a screen reader, software that reads a page aloud or sends it to a braille display, which a later section covers in detail.

Worked example: five learners, five supports. The table pairs learners with the feature that lets each one use the resource.

Learner What gets in the way The feature that helps A blind learner Cannot see images or the layout Text descriptions of images, and a clear heading structure for a screen reader A deaf learner Cannot hear a video Captions A learner who cannot use a mouse Cannot point and click Keyboard navigation A learner with low vision Faint text on a pale background Strong color contrast and text that enlarges A learner with a reading disability Dense text Clear structure, short paragraphs, and alternative formats

docs.title: Accessibility Metric
docs.text: The accessibility metric is the fourth quality metric of the rubric. It asks whether learners with disabilities can use the resource, judged against WCAG 2.1 at level AA. It is scored with ten checks, listed in the scoring section at the end of this chapter, and the checks follow the topics in between.

docs.title: WCAG
docs.text:
WCAG, the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, is the international standard for accessible web content. The World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) publishes it through its Web Accessibility Initiative. WCAG is a long list of success criteria, each of which is a testable statement, such as "images have text alternatives" or "text has enough contrast". A reviewer can answer each one with pass or fail.

The criteria are grouped under four principles, often abbreviated POUR. Content must be Perceivable: users can see or hear it, through some sense. It must be Operable: users can control it, including without a mouse. It must be Understandable: users can follow what it says and how it works. And it must be Robust: it works with a range of browsers and with assistive technology, the tools that people with disabilities use to read and operate a page.

Each criterion has a conformance level. Level A is the most basic, level AA is the middle level that most policies require, and level AAA is the highest and is not required for whole sites. The standard has appeared in versions: 2.0 in 2008, 2.1 in 2018, and 2.2 in 2023.

Worked example: one criterion under each principle.

Principle The question it asks An example criterion Perceivable Can users perceive the content? Non-text content has a text alternative Operable Can users operate the controls? All functions work with a keyboard Understandable Can users follow it? The language of the page is identified Robust Does it work with assistive technology? Custom controls expose a name and role

The first MicroSim sorts requirements under the four principles. It shows twelve requirements, and for each one you choose the principle it belongs to.

docs.title: Diagram: WCAG Principles Sorter
docs.text:
WCAG Principles Sorter

Type: microsim sim-id: wcag-principles-sorter Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: classify Learning Objective: The learner will classify each of twelve accessibility requirements under the WCAG principle it belongs to (perceivable, operable, understandable, or robust), with at least 10 of 12 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Accessibility, WCAG (both defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each requirement the learner commits one of four principles. A placement is correct when it matches the Correct principle column in Content. Mastery is at least 10 of 12 correct on the first attempt. Reading the principle definitions is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Captions belong under Understandable because they explain speech. (2) Contrast is Operable because users act on the page. (3) All requirements about HTML are Robust.

Instructional Rationale: Classifying requirements under the four principles is an Understand-level action that shows the learner how the long list of criteria is organized. Three requirements per principle, each tied to a different need, teach the learner to ask which kind of barrier a requirement removes.

Content:

The four principles: Perceivable (users can sense the content), Operable (users can control it), Understandable (users can follow it), Robust (it works with assistive technology).

The twelve requirements:

# Requirement shown to the learner Correct principle Why (shown as feedback) 1 Images have text alternatives. Perceivable A user who cannot see needs another way to perceive it. 2 Video with sound has captions. Perceivable A user who cannot hear needs another way to perceive it. 3 Text has enough contrast with its background. Perceivable A user with low vision must be able to see it. 4 Every function can be used with a keyboard. Operable A user who cannot use a mouse must be able to control it. 5 Users can pause or stop moving content. Operable Users must be able to control content that moves. 6 Users can see which element has keyboard focus. Operable A keyboard user must see where they are in order to operate the page. 7 The language of the page is identified. Understandable Tools and users need to know which language the text is in. 8 Navigation is consistent from page to page. Understandable Users can follow a page when its navigation behaves as before. 9 Form errors are described in text. Understandable Users must be able to understand what went wrong and how to fix it. 10 Custom buttons expose a name and a role to assistive technology. Robust Assistive technology must be able to read and operate them. 11 Status messages can be announced without moving focus. Robust Assistive technology must be able to report them. 12 The content works with a range of browsers and assistive technologies. Robust The content must not depend on one tool.

Provenance: The principles and the requirements follow the chapter section "WCAG", and each requirement paraphrases a criterion of WCAG 2.1. The sim states that the wording is simplified and names the WCAG documents as the authority.

Rules: Each requirement has exactly one correct principle, three per principle.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one requirement and the four principles.
  2. The learner may open the principle definitions. Opening them does not change the score.
  3. The learner places the requirement under a principle, and the placement is committed.
  4. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text.
  5. After requirement 12 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 12 requirements in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [principle]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. This is [principle]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 12 correct on the first attempt". At 10 or more it adds "You can sort the WCAG requirements." Below 10 it lists the Why text of each missed requirement.

Starting State: The first requirement, the four principles, and the definitions closed. The question shown is "Which principle does this requirement serve?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter says the four principles are perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust, abbreviated POUR, and that the levels are A, AA, and AAA.

docs.title: WCAG 2.1 AA
docs.text:
WCAG 2.1 AA is version 2.1 of the guidelines at conformance level AA, which means a resource meets every level A criterion and every level AA criterion. It is the target of this book's rubric because policies at many schools and colleges cite it, and because it is demanding enough to protect the main groups of learners and practical enough for a teacher to check. Version 2.1 added criteria to 2.0 for people who use mobile devices, who have low vision, or who have cognitive differences. Version 2.2 adds further criteria to 2.1, so a resource that does well on 2.2 is in good shape for 2.1.

Worked example: six criteria and their levels. The criteria below are among those that this chapter's checks draw on.

Criterion Level What it asks Covered in this chapter under 1.1.1 Non-text Content A Images and other non-text content have text alternatives Alt Text 1.2.2 Captions (Prerecorded) A Prerecorded video with sound has captions Captions 2.1.1 Keyboard A All functions work from a keyboard Keyboard Navigation 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum) AA Text has a contrast ratio of at least 4.5 to 1, or 3 to 1 for large text Contrast Ratio 1.2.5 Audio Description (Prerecorded) AA Prerecorded video has audio description Audio Description 1.4.6 Contrast (Enhanced) AAA Text has a contrast ratio of at least 7 to 1 Not required at AA

docs.title: Alt Text
docs.text:
Alt text is a short text description attached to an image, so that a person who cannot see the image still gets what it is for. It is stored in the image's alt attribute in HTML, and a screen reader reads it aloud. Good alt text answers the question "what does this image do here?" and not "what does this image look like?". A photo of a river in a lesson about meanders needs alt text that mentions the bends. The same photo used as a mood image needs none.

Four habits make alt text useful. Say what matters in the context, in a sentence or two. Do not begin with "image of" or "picture of", because the screen reader already announces that it is an image. Do not repeat a caption that sits right beside the image. And never leave a filename or a single word such as "photo".

Describe the Purpose, Not the Picture

Ask what the image is doing in this sentence, and write alt text that does the same job for a reader who cannot see it. If the lesson is about river bends, the alt text should mention the bends.

Worked example: three alt texts for one photo. The photo shows a school garden's rain barrel under a roof downspout, in a lesson on reducing runoff.

Alt text Verdict Why "photo" Poor One word that says nothing. "A rain barrel at the end of a roof downspout holds runoff from the school roof" Good It names the object and the point it makes in the lesson. "Image of a picture of the school garden taken on a sunny day with flowers, a bench, and the principal's car in the background" Poor It starts with "image of" and lists details that do not serve the lesson.

docs.title: Decorative Image
docs.text: A decorative image is an image that adds appearance only and carries no information, such as a border line or a mood photo beside a heading. A screen reader should skip it, and the way to say so in HTML is an empty alt attribute, alt="". An image with no alt attribute at all is a different case, because many screen readers then read out the file name. When an image looks decorative but a learner might wonder what it is, the safer choice is a short description.

docs.title: Complex Image Description
docs.text:
A complex image description is a longer text that conveys the content of an image that is too detailed for a sentence, such as a chart, a map, or a labeled diagram. The pattern has two parts. A short alt text names the image and what it shows, and a longer description or a data table nearby gives the full content. For a bar chart of monthly rainfall, the short alt text says "Bar chart of monthly rainfall" and a table below lists every month and its value. The long description should let a reader who never sees the image answer the same questions a sighted reader could.

The next two MicroSims practice images. The first sorts nine images into three types, and the second judges nine alt texts for one photo.

docs.title: Diagram: Image Type Sorter
docs.text:
Image Type Sorter

Type: microsim sim-id: image-type-sorter Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: classify Learning Objective: The learner will classify each of nine images as informative, decorative, or complex, with at least 8 of 9 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Alt Text, Decorative Image, Complex Image Description (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each image the learner commits one of three bins. A placement is correct when it matches the Correct bin column in Content. Mastery is at least 8 of 9 correct on the first attempt. Reading the definitions is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Every image needs a long description. (2) A logo needs no alt text. (3) A decorative image should have alt text that says "decoration".

Instructional Rationale: Classifying an image by its role is an Understand-level action that decides what kind of text it needs. Three images per type, each in a different setting, teach the learner to ask what the image does and not what it shows.

Content:

The three bins: Informative (needs short alt text), Decorative (needs empty alt text), Complex (needs short alt text and a long description or data table).

The nine images:
