# Image shown to the learner (described in words) Correct bin Why (shown as feedback) 1 A photo of a river with sharp bends, used to show how a river meanders. Informative It carries information the lesson uses, and a sentence can convey it. 2 A thin decorative line between two sections. Decorative It adds no information. 3 A bar chart of monthly rainfall with twelve bars. Complex The values need a table or a long description. 4 A school logo in the page header that links to the home page. Informative Its alt text should state where the link goes. 5 A stock photo of smiling students beside a heading, adding mood only. Decorative It carries no information. 6 A labeled diagram of the water cycle with six labels and arrows. Complex The parts and the order of the arrows need a longer description. 7 A screenshot showing which button to click in a software tool. Informative It shows where to click, and a sentence can say so. 8 A map of a river and its tributaries with several labeled towns. Complex The places and their relations need a longer description. 9 A small lightbulb icon beside the word "Tip" that the text already states. Decorative The adjacent text carries the meaning.

Provenance: The images are described in words for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The bins follow the chapter sections "Alt Text", "Decorative Image", and "Complex Image Description".

Rules: Each image has exactly one correct bin, three per bin.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees a description of one image and the three bins.
  2. The learner places the image in a bin, and the placement is committed.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct, the Why text, and the kind of text the image needs.
  4. After image 9 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 9 images in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [bin]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. This is [bin]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 9 correct on the first attempt". At 8 or more it adds "You can tell which images need which text." Below 8 it lists the Why text of each missed image.

Starting State: The first image description and the three bins. The question shown is "What does this image need?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter says a decorative image takes an empty alt attribute, a complex image takes short alt text plus a longer description or table, and an informative image takes a short alt text.

docs.title: Diagram: Alt Text Evaluator
docs.text:
Alt Text Evaluator

Type: microsim sim-id: alt-text-evaluator Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: judge Learning Objective: The learner will judge whether each of nine alt texts for one photo is useful or needs work, with at least 8 of 9 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Alt Text, Decorative Image (both defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each alt text the learner commits one of two bins. A placement is correct when it matches the Correct bin column in Content. Mastery is at least 8 of 9 correct on the first attempt. Reading the four habits is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Longer alt text is always better. (2) "Image of" helps the reader. (3) Empty alt text is safe for any image.

Instructional Rationale: Judging alt text against stated habits is an Evaluate-level action. Nine alternatives for one photo isolate the differences that matter, so the learner learns what separates a useful description from a poor one.

Content:

The photo, described in words and shown at all times: a school garden's rain barrel under a roof downspout, used in a lesson on reducing runoff.

The four habits, shown on request: say what matters in the context; do not begin with "image of"; do not repeat an adjacent caption; never use a filename or a single word.

The nine alt texts:

# Alt text shown to the learner Correct bin Why (shown as feedback) 1 image1.png Needs work A filename says nothing about the image. 2 photo Needs work One word that says nothing. 3 A rain barrel under a roof downspout collects water from the roof Useful It names the object and what it does. 4 Image of a photograph of a barrel Needs work It begins with "image of" and does not say what matters. 5 A rain barrel in a school garden collects roof runoff, one way to keep water from flowing onto pavement Useful It connects the object to the lesson. 6 A rain barrel at the end of a roof downspout Useful It is short and names what is shown and where. 7 A picture of the school garden taken by Ms. Lee on a sunny day with many flowers, a bench, and the principal's car in the background Needs work It is long and lists details that do not serve the lesson. 8 (empty alt text) Needs work The photo carries information the lesson uses, so it is not decorative. 9 Rain barrel connected to a downspout, holding runoff from the school roof Useful It is plain and says what the picture shows and why it matters.

Provenance: The photo and the alt texts are written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The habits follow the chapter section "Alt Text".

Rules: Each alt text has exactly one correct bin. Four are Useful and five Need work. A screen reader reads alt text aloud and announces that the element is an image, so the sim treats "image of" as redundant.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees the photo description, the four habits on request, and one alt text.
  2. The learner places the alt text in a bin, and the placement is committed.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text.
  4. After alt text 9 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 9 alt texts in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [bin]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. This is [bin]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 9 correct on the first attempt". At 8 or more it adds "You can judge alt text." Below 8 it lists the Why text of each missed alt text.

Starting State: The photo description and alt text 1 or the first in the shuffled order. The question shown is "Is this alt text useful?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's worked example of three alt texts for the rain barrel photo agrees with this sim: "photo" needs work and the rain barrel at the end of a roof downspout is useful.

docs.title: Heading Structure
docs.text:
Heading structure is the order and nesting of a page's headings. A page should have one main heading, with subheadings nested beneath it in order, and no level skipped: an h2 contains h3 headings, and an h3 never sits directly under an h1. Real headings, made with heading tags and not bold text, matter because assistive technology builds a map of the page from them, and a screen reader user can jump from heading to heading to skim a page the way a sighted reader scans one.

A reviewer checks three things. Are the headings real heading tags? Is the order logical, with no skipped level? And does each heading describe its section, as Chapter 6 asked? The accessibility check adds the first two to the readability check from that chapter.

The MicroSim below practices the check. It shows two outlines of ten heading lines in all, and for each line you decide whether it is fine or has one of three defects.

docs.title: Diagram: Heading Outline Checker
docs.text:
Heading Outline Checker

Type: microsim sim-id: heading-outline-checker Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: examine Learning Objective: The learner will examine ten heading lines from two page outlines and mark each as fine or as having a skipped level, a second main heading, or a vague heading, with at least 9 of 10 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Heading Structure (defined in this chapter above this block) and Headings and Subheadings (defined in Chapter 6).

Evidence of Mastery: For each heading line the learner commits one of four options. A choice is correct when it matches the Correct option column in Content. Mastery is at least 9 of 10 correct on the first attempt. Reading the defect definitions is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A heading level is chosen for how large it looks. (2) A page may have several main headings. (3) A short heading is a good heading.

Instructional Rationale: Examining an outline is an Analyze-level action, because the learner must compare each line with the line before it and with the page's structure. Ten lines with three different defects teach the learner to look for each defect separately.

Content:

The four options: Fine, Skipped level, Second main heading, Vague heading.

The two outlines (each line shows the heading level and text):

Outline Line Level Text Correct option Why (shown as feedback) A A1 h1 Watershed Basics Fine The one main heading names the page. A A2 h2 What a watershed is Fine It sits directly under the main heading and says what follows. A A3 h4 Parts of a watershed Skipped level It jumps from h2 to h4 and skips h3. A A4 h2 How water moves Fine It returns to the section level and says what follows. A A5 h3 Runoff Fine It sits directly under an h2 and names its topic. B B1 h1 Rivers Fine The one main heading names the page. B B2 h2 Where rivers start Fine It sits directly under the main heading and says what follows. B B3 h1 River safety Second main heading A page should have one main heading, and this line starts a second. B B4 h2 Stuff Vague heading The word does not tell the reader what the section holds. B B5 h3 Cold water Fine It sits under an h2 and says what follows.

Provenance: The outlines are made up for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The defects follow the chapter section "Heading Structure".

Rules: Each line has exactly one correct option. Seven lines are Fine, and the three defects each occur once. A line is a Skipped level when its level is more than one deeper than the previous line's level.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees outline A as an indented list with levels shown.
  2. The learner chooses an option for each line, and the choice is committed.
  3. The sim shows whether each choice was correct and the Why text.
  4. The learner repeats for outline B.
  5. After line B5 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 10 lines in outline order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [option]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. This line is [option]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 10 correct on the first attempt". At 9 or more it adds "You can read a page's outline." Below 9 it lists the Why text of each missed line.

Starting State: Outline A with no choices made. The question shown is "Is this heading fine?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter says a page should have one main heading with subheadings nested in order and no skipped level, and that headings should describe their sections.

docs.title: Color Contrast
docs.text: Color contrast is the difference in brightness between text, or another meaningful element, and the background behind it. Strong contrast makes text easy to read for everyone and essential for people with low vision, for aging eyes, and for anyone reading in bright light. Weak contrast, such as pale gray text on white, is one of the most common accessibility failures. The requirement covers text, the parts of controls that identify them, and the lines and shapes that carry meaning in a chart. It does not cover a logo or a purely decorative element.

docs.title: Contrast Ratio
docs.text:
A contrast ratio is a number that measures color contrast, from 1 to 1 for no difference to 21 to 1 for black on white. WCAG 2.1 AA sets three minimums. Normal text needs a ratio of at least 4.5 to 1. Large text, which means text of at least 18 points, or at least 14 points if bold, needs at least 3 to 1. And the parts of controls and graphics that convey meaning need at least 3 to 1.

The ratio comes from the relative luminance of the two colors, a number from 0 for black to 1 for white that measures how bright a color appears to the eye. The formula is:

contrast ratio = (L1 + 0.05) / (L2 + 0.05)

Here L1 is the relative luminance of the lighter color and L2 is that of the darker one. You never compute luminance by hand, because free tools do it, but the formula shows why black on white scores the maximum: white has a luminance of 1, black has 0, and the ratio is (1 + 0.05) divided by (0 + 0.05), which is 21.

Worked example: a difference you cannot see. Two grays on a white background look almost the same. A tool gives #767676 on white a ratio of 4.54 to 1, which passes the 4.5 minimum for normal text. It gives the slightly lighter #777777 on white a ratio of 4.48 to 1, which fails. The tests use the unrounded ratio, so 4.499 fails even though a tool may display it as 4.50. A pass or fail can hinge on a difference no one can see, and that is why reviewers measure instead of judging by eye.

docs.title: Color Independence
docs.text:
Color independence means that color is never the only way a resource conveys information. A chart that marks the winner in green and the loser in red, with no other cue, fails a learner who is color blind and a learner who prints the page in gray. The fix is a second cue: a label, a pattern, a shape, an icon, or underlined text. Links inside a paragraph are a common case. A link marked only by a slightly different color needs an underline or another cue.

The MicroSim below practices contrast. In explore mode you enter two colors and read the ratio, and in practice mode you decide whether nine color pairs pass for normal text, for large text only, or not at all.

docs.title: Diagram: Contrast Ratio Checker
docs.text:
Contrast Ratio Checker

Type: microsim sim-id: contrast-ratio-checker Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: use Learning Objective: The learner will use the contrast ratio and the 4.5 and 3 minimums to decide whether each of nine color pairs passes for normal text, passes for large text only, or fails, with at least 8 of 9 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Color Contrast, Contrast Ratio, Color Independence (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each pair the learner commits one of three verdicts after seeing the colors and before the ratio is shown. A verdict is correct when it matches the Correct verdict column in Content. Mastery is at least 8 of 9 correct on the first attempt. Using the explore mode is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) If two colors look different, they pass. (2) Rounding 4.499 up to 4.5 makes it pass. (3) Large text needs the same ratio as normal text.

Instructional Rationale: Using a numeric threshold on measured values is an Apply-level action. Predicting from sight first, and then seeing the measured ratio, shows the learner that sight is unreliable near the threshold, which is the reason the check exists.

Content:

The thresholds, shown at all times: normal text needs a ratio >= 4.5; large text (18 points or larger, or 14 points or larger if bold) needs a ratio >= 3.0. The three verdicts: Passes for normal text (ratio >= 4.5), Passes for large text only (ratio >= 3.0 and < 4.5), Fails (ratio < 3.0).

The nine pairs, with each ratio computed from relative luminance as the chapter states:

# Text color Background color Ratio Correct verdict Why (shown as feedback) 1 #000000 #FFFFFF 21.00 Passes for normal text The largest possible ratio. 2 #757575 #FFFFFF 4.61 Passes for normal text The ratio is at least 4.5. 3 #949494 #FFFFFF 3.03 Passes for large text only The ratio is at least 3.0 and less than 4.5. 4 #FFFFFF #1A5FB4 6.29 Passes for normal text White text on a deep blue has a high ratio. 5 #FFFFFF #FF8C00 2.33 Fails White on orange is less than 3.0, so no text size passes. 6 #FF0000 #FFFFFF 4.00 Passes for large text only Red on white is at least 3.0 and less than 4.5. 7 #767676 #F0F0F0 3.99 Passes for large text only The same gray that passes on white is less than 4.5 on a light gray background. 8 #DDDDDD #FFFFFF 1.36 Fails Pale gray on white has almost no contrast. 9 #FFFFFF #2E7D32 5.13 Passes for normal text White on a dark green has a ratio of at least 4.5.

Provenance: The ratios are computed from the WCAG definition of relative luminance and are shown to two decimals. The color pairs are illustrative cases written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The thresholds follow the chapter section "Contrast Ratio".

Rules: The ratio is (L1 + 0.05) / (L2 + 0.05) with L1 the luminance of the lighter color and L2 that of the darker. Tests use the unrounded ratio. Each pair has exactly one correct verdict. In explore mode the learner enters a text color and a background color as hex codes, and the sim shows the ratio to two decimals and the three verdicts for normal text, for large text, and for graphics. Four pairs are Passes for normal text, three are Passes for large text only, and two are Fails.

Learner Activity:

  1. In explore mode the learner enters two colors and reads the ratio and the verdicts.
  2. In practice mode the sim shows pair 1 as a sample of text on its background, without the ratio.
  3. The learner chooses a verdict, and the choice is committed.
  4. The sim shows the ratio, whether the verdict was correct, and the Why text.
  5. After pair 9 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 9 pairs in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [verdict]. The ratio is [ratio]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. The ratio is [ratio], so this is [verdict]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 9 correct on the first attempt". At 8 or more it adds "You can read a contrast ratio." Below 8 it lists the Why text of each missed pair.

Starting State: Explore mode with black text on a white background and a ratio of 21.00. The prompt is "Enter two colors to see the ratio."

Chapter Anchors: The chapter says normal text needs a ratio of at least 4.5 to 1, large text at least 3 to 1, black on white is 21 to 1, #767676 on white is 4.54 to 1, and #777777 on white is 4.48 to 1.

docs.title: Captions
docs.text: Captions are a text version of the speech and important sounds in a video, shown in time with the video. They serve learners who are deaf or hard of hearing, and they also help learners who watch with the sound off, learners who are still learning the language, and anyone in a noisy room. Good captions include who is speaking when that is not obvious, and sounds that matter, such as "[a door slams]". Automatic captions are a start. A reviewer checks them for errors, because a wrong word in a technical term can change the meaning.

docs.title: Transcript
docs.text: A transcript is a text version of the audio and, when there is video, of the important visual information too, given as a separate document. A transcript serves learners who prefer to read, learners who use a braille display, and anyone who wants to search for a quotation. It does not replace captions for video, since captions are timed and a transcript is not, and the two work well together.

docs.title: Audio Description
docs.text:
Audio description is spoken narration of the important visual information in a video that the soundtrack does not already give: actions, scene changes, on-screen text, and charts. It serves learners who are blind or have low vision. A video in which an instructor says "as you can see here" and points to a chart, with no description of the chart, leaves a blind learner out. The simplest fix is to say what the chart shows. At level AA, prerecorded video with sound needs captions and audio description.

The MicroSim below matches eight situations to the alternative each one calls for.

docs.title: Diagram: Media Alternative Matcher
docs.text:
Media Alternative Matcher

Type: microsim sim-id: media-alternative-matcher Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: classify Learning Objective: The learner will classify each of eight situations by the media alternative it calls for (captions, transcript, or audio description), with at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Captions, Transcript, Audio Description (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each situation the learner commits one of three alternatives. A choice is correct when it matches the Correct alternative column in Content. Mastery is at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the definitions is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A transcript replaces captions. (2) Audio description is only for blind learners watching films. (3) Captions help only deaf learners.

Instructional Rationale: Classifying a need by its alternative is an Understand-level action. Eight situations that vary the learner and the barrier teach the learner to ask what is missing: the sound, the sight, or a readable text.

Content:

The three alternatives: Captions (timed text of speech and sounds), Transcript (a separate text document of the audio and the key visual information), Audio description (narration of important visual information).

The eight situations:

# Situation shown to the learner Correct alternative Why (shown as feedback) 1 A deaf learner watches a lecture video. Captions The learner needs the speech as timed text. 2 A blind learner watches a science demonstration in which the steps appear only on screen. Audio description The visual steps are not in the audio. 3 A learner wants to search a podcast for a quotation. Transcript Text can be searched, and audio alone cannot. 4 A learner watches a video in a noisy cafeteria with the sound off. Captions Timed text lets the learner follow without sound. 5 A learner who is deaf and blind reads a video's content on a braille display. Transcript A text document can be read in braille. 6 A video shows a chart that the narrator never describes. Audio description The chart is visual information that the audio leaves out. 7 A learner with a reading difference prefers to read at their own pace instead of watching. Transcript A document lets the learner set the pace. 8 A learner still learning the language wants to follow the words on screen as they are spoken. Captions Timed text matches the speech as it is said.

Provenance: The situations are illustrative cases written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The definitions follow the chapter sections "Captions", "Transcript", and "Audio Description".

Rules: Each situation has exactly one correct alternative. Three situations call for Captions, three for Transcript, and two for Audio description.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one situation and the three alternatives.
  2. The learner chooses an alternative, and the choice is committed.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text.
  4. After situation 8 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 8 situations in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [alternative]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. This calls for [alternative]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 8 correct on the first attempt". At 7 or more it adds "You can match the need to the alternative." Below 7 it lists the Why text of each missed situation.

Starting State: The first situation and the three alternatives. The question shown is "What does this learner need?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter says captions are timed text, a transcript is a separate text document, and audio description narrates visual information the audio omits.

docs.title: Keyboard Navigation
docs.text:
Keyboard navigation is the ability to use every function of a resource with a keyboard alone. Many learners cannot use a mouse, including learners with motor disabilities, learners who use a screen reader, and learners who use a device that sends keyboard signals. The Tab key moves from one control to the next, Shift and Tab together move back, and Enter or Space activates a control. A resource passes when every link, button, and quiz can be reached and used this way, the focus is visible as an outline or highlight, the order of focus follows the order of the page, and the keyboard never gets stuck in one place.

Put the Mouse Aside for Two Minutes

Open the page, set the mouse out of reach, and press Tab through the whole thing. If you lose track of where you are, or you cannot reach a control, you have found a keyboard failure.

docs.title: Screen Reader
docs.text:
A screen reader is software that reads a page aloud, or sends it to a braille display, for people who cannot see the screen. Examples include NVDA, which is free for Windows, VoiceOver, which is built into Apple devices, and JAWS, a commercial program. A screen reader does not read the page as it looks. It reads the page's underlying structure: headings, links, buttons, image descriptions, and table cells. A user typically moves through a page by jumping from heading to heading or by pulling up a list of all the links, so structure and good text are everything.

A reviewer who has never heard a screen reader read a page learns a great deal from five minutes of listening. Missing alt text becomes a file name read aloud, a link that says only "click here" is useless in a list of links, and a heading structure that looked fine shows its gaps.

Worked example: what four snippets sound like. The table gives each snippet of HTML and what a screen reader typically says. Wording varies between programs.

What the page contains What a screen reader typically says What it tells the reviewer A heading that reads "How water moves" "Heading level 2, How water moves" Real headings are announced with their level An image with alt text "A river meandering through a valley" "Image, A river meandering through a valley" The alt text does its job An image with no alt attribute "Image, river.png" The file name is read, which is useless An image with an empty alt attribute Nothing The image is skipped, which is correct only for a decorative image

Listen Once and You Will Hear It Forever

The first time you hear a screen reader read a page aloud it can feel fast and strange, and that is normal for every new listener. You already skim a page by its headings, and a screen reader user does the same by ear. Five minutes with one will change how you write alt text.

The MicroSim below practices the connection. It shows six snippets, and for each one you choose what a screen reader typically says.

docs.title: Diagram: Screen Reader Announcement Matcher
docs.text:
Screen Reader Announcement Matcher

Type: microsim sim-id: screen-reader-announcement-matcher Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: infer Learning Objective: The learner will infer what a screen reader typically announces for each of six snippets of page markup, with at least 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Screen Reader, Alt Text, Decorative Image, Heading Structure (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each snippet the learner commits one of three announcements before the answer is shown. A choice is correct when it matches the Correct announcement column in Content. Mastery is at least 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Reading the worked-example table is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A screen reader describes what an image looks like by itself. (2) An image with no alt attribute is skipped. (3) A heading is read as ordinary text.

Instructional Rationale: Inferring the announcement from the markup is an Understand-level action that connects what an author writes to what a listener hears. Six snippets that differ in one detail each teach the learner to read markup as a listener would.

Content:

The sim states that announcements are typical and simplified, and that wording differs between screen readers.

The six snippets:

# Snippet shown to the learner Option A Option B Option C Correct Why (shown as feedback) 1 A heading "How water moves" at level 2 Heading level 2, How water moves How water moves Link, How water moves A A heading is announced with its level. 2 An image with alt text "A river meandering through a valley" Image, river dot png Image, A river meandering through a valley Nothing B The alt text is read as the image's description. 3 An image with no alt attribute and the file name river.png Image, river dot png Image, a river Nothing A Without alt text, the file name is often read. 4 An image with an empty alt attribute Image, no description Image, decorative Nothing C An empty alt attribute tells the reader to skip the image. 5 A link whose text is "click here" Link, click here Link, goes to the runoff page Button, click here A The reader announces only the link text, which says nothing about the destination. 6 A button that contains only an image with no alt text, file name close.png Button, close dot png Button, close Nothing A The file name becomes the button's name, which is useless.

Provenance: The snippets are illustrative cases written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The announcements are typical and simplified, and the sim states that they vary between programs.

Rules: Each snippet has exactly one correct option, in the position shown in the Correct column.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one snippet and three options.
  2. The learner chooses an option, and the choice is committed.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text.
  4. After snippet 6 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 6 snippets in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [announcement]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. A screen reader typically says: [announcement]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 6 correct on the first attempt". At 5 or more it adds "You can hear the markup." Below 5 it lists the Why text of each missed snippet.

Starting State: The first snippet and its three options. The question shown is "What does a screen reader typically say?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's worked example lists four snippets and what a screen reader typically says: a heading with its level, an image with alt text, an image with no alt attribute read as its file name, and an image with empty alt text skipped.

docs.title: Link Text
docs.text: Link text is the visible words of a link. Good link text says where the link goes, such as "Chapter 5: Accuracy and Currency" or "the state water agency's river data". Screen reader users often pull up a list of all the links on a page, and a list that reads "click here, click here, read more" is useless. A link inside a sentence should still make sense out of context. Avoid raw web addresses as link text, and avoid the same text for links that go to different places.

docs.title: Table Accessibility
docs.text: Table accessibility is the practice of building tables so that a screen reader can read the cells in relation to their headings. A data table has a header row, and sometimes a header column, marked as headers in HTML with the th tag, so that a reader hearing a cell also hears its column heading. A table needs a short caption or title, and a simple structure without merged cells where possible. Tables are for data. Using a table to lay out a page confuses screen readers, so layout should be done another way.

docs.title: Document Language
docs.text: Document language is the human language of the page's text, set in HTML with the lang attribute on the page, such as lang="en" for English. A screen reader uses it to choose the right pronunciation, and a translation tool uses it to know what to translate. When a passage in another language appears, such as a Spanish quotation, it can carry its own language setting.

docs.title: Accessible Math
docs.text: Accessible math is the practice of writing equations so that a screen reader can read them and a learner can enlarge them. A picture of an equation is not accessible, because it cannot be read aloud or resized without blurring. Better choices are MathML, a web standard for math notation, or LaTeX rendered by a web library that exposes the equation to assistive technology. If an image is unavoidable, give it alt text that states the equation in words. Writing the equation in words beside it is a good habit as well.

docs.title: ARIA Labels
docs.text: ARIA labels are attributes from a web standard called WAI-ARIA that add a name or description to an element when the page's ordinary HTML does not provide one. A button that shows only an icon can carry aria-label="Close" so that a screen reader announces "Close". The first rule of ARIA is to use ordinary HTML elements first, because a real button already has a name and a role. ARIA used wrongly can make a page worse than no ARIA at all, so add it only where ordinary HTML falls short.

docs.title: Universal Design for Learning
docs.text:
Universal Design for Learning (UDL) is a framework for designing learning so that it works for the widest range of learners from the start, instead of adding fixes later. CAST, an education nonprofit, developed it around three principles: give learners multiple ways to engage with the material, multiple ways to take it in, and multiple ways to show what they know. A resource that offers a text version, a captioned video, and an interactive simulation of the same idea follows UDL. Accessibility removes barriers for learners with disabilities, and UDL plans for variety among all learners, so the two support each other.

A Ramp Helps More Than the Wheelchair

A curb cut built for wheelchairs also helps strollers, carts, and tired travelers. Captions, clear headings, and strong contrast work the same way, and they help learners you never planned for.

docs.title: Accessibility Checker
docs.text:
An accessibility checker is a tool that scans a page or a document and reports accessibility problems automatically. Free examples include WAVE, axe, and the accessibility audit built into the Chrome browser's Lighthouse tool. Checkers find real problems quickly, such as images with no alt attribute, text with weak contrast, and form fields with no label. They cannot judge everything. A tool can tell that alt text exists and cannot tell whether it is useful, and it cannot tell whether a heading describes its section. Use a checker to find the problems it can see, then check the rest by hand.

A Clean Report Is Not a Pass

A checker can pass a page whose alt text says "photo" on every image, because the text exists. Run the tool, then do the human checks it cannot do: read the alt text, listen with a screen reader, and tab through the page.

The next MicroSim is an illustration of a page that follows the checks in this chapter. Its eight numbered markers point to the features that a reviewer looks for.

docs.title: Diagram: Anatomy of an Accessible Page
docs.text:
Anatomy of an Accessible Page

Type: infographic sim-id: accessibility-page-anatomy Library: html Status: Specified Bloom Level: Remember Bloom Verb: identify Learning Objective: The learner will identify eight accessibility features on an illustrated page from a description of how each looks, with at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Alt Text, Captions, Transcript, Link Text, Table Accessibility, Keyboard Navigation, Color Independence, Heading Structure (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: In quiz mode the learner clicks the marker that matches a visual hint. A click is correct when it matches the marker named in the Hint column of Content. Mastery is at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Hovering in explore mode is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A video player with a caption button is captioned. (2) The focus ring is a design flaw. (3) A chart is accessible if its colors are bright.

Instructional Rationale: Identifying features on an illustrated page is a Remember-level task that anchors each check to something the learner can look for. The quiz asks the learner to go from the look of a feature to its name.

Content:

The illustration is a text-free flat drawing of a lesson page. At the top is a wide bar of heading text. Below it is a picture with a small tag icon at one corner. A video frame follows, with a strip of thin text lines along its bottom edge and a small badge at the lower right. Under the video is an underlined bar with a small document icon. In the paragraph below, one underlined phrase is set apart. A grid with a shaded top row and a shaded left column follows. A button has a thick outline around it. At the bottom is a bar chart whose bars differ by pattern as well as by shading. The eight markers:

# Label Hint (describes the look, not the name) Description Tip 1 Descriptive heading The wide bar of text at the top of the page. A real heading that names the page, the start of a logical heading structure. Use one main heading and nest the others in order. 2 Image with alt text A picture with a small tag icon at one corner. An image whose purpose is described in its alt text. Describe the purpose, not just the look. 3 Captioned video A video frame with a strip of thin text lines along its bottom edge. A video whose speech appears as timed captions. Check automatic captions for errors. 4 Transcript link An underlined bar with a small document icon beneath the video. A link to a text version of the video's audio and key visuals. Place it right next to the video. 5 Descriptive link One underlined phrase set apart inside a paragraph. A link whose words say where it goes. Avoid "click here". 6 Table with headers A grid with a shaded top row and a shaded left column. A data table whose header cells are marked, so a screen reader pairs each cell with its headings. Give the table a short caption. 7 Visible focus A button with a thick outline around it. The outline shows which control a keyboard user is on. Never remove the focus outline without a replacement. 8 Chart with patterns A bar chart whose bars differ by pattern as well as shading. A chart that does not depend on color alone to tell its bars apart. Add labels or patterns to any chart that uses color to carry meaning.

Provenance: The features follow the chapter sections on alt text, captions, transcripts, link text, table accessibility, keyboard navigation, color independence, and heading structure. The illustration is synthetic, and the sim labels the page "illustrative example".

Rules: Each hint matches exactly one marker. The illustration contains no text, so every label comes from the table above. Markers are numbered 1 to 8 in the order of the table.

Learner Activity:

  1. In explore mode the learner hovers or clicks a marker and reads its label, description, and tip.
  2. In quiz mode the sim shows a hint.
  3. The learner clicks the marker they think the hint describes.
  4. If the first click is wrong, the sim says so and lets the learner try once more. If the second click is also wrong, the sim reveals the marker and its description.
  5. After all 8 hints the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 8 hints in a shuffled order, two attempts each. Only a correct first click counts as evidence. Correct: "Correct: [label]. [Description]". First wrong click: "Not quite. Look again at the hint: [hint]". Second wrong click: "This is [label]. [Description]". The summary shows "[n] of 8 correct on the first attempt". At 7 or more it adds "You can spot an accessible page." Below 7 it lists the labels of the missed features.

Starting State: The illustration with eight numbered markers, explore mode active, and the prompt "Hover a marker to see what it is."

Chapter Anchors: The chapter lists these features as checks: headings in order, alt text, captions, a transcript, descriptive link text, table headers, visible keyboard focus, and color independence.

docs.title: Scoring Accessibility
docs.text:
Accessibility is scored with ten checks. A failed check is serious when it keeps a group of learners out of the content altogether: images with no alt text, text that cannot be read for lack of contrast, video with no captions, or controls that a keyboard cannot reach. When a serious check fails, choose the lower number in a two-number band. Otherwise choose the higher number.

# Check Serious if it fails? 1 Every meaningful image has alt text Yes 2 Alt text is useful, not a filename or a single word No 3 Decorative images are marked to be skipped No 4 Headings are real headings, in order, with no skipped level No 5 Text and background colors meet the contrast minimums Yes 6 Color is not the only way information is shown No 7 Video has captions Yes 8 Audio and video also have transcripts or audio description where needed No 9 Every function works with a keyboard alone Yes 10 The page language is set, links have descriptive text, and tables have header cells No

A check that does not apply, such as captions for a resource with no video, counts as passed. A check that was not tested counts as failed until it is tested.

Worked example: Watershed Basics. The reviewer applies the checks to the reading from Chapter 3.

# Result Evidence 1 Fail 4 of 5 images have alt text, so one meaningful image has none. 2 Fail Two of the four alt texts are one word long, "photo". 3 Pass The reading has no decorative images, so the check does not apply and counts as passed. 4 Fail One heading jumps from level 2 to level 4. 5 Fail Color contrast was not tested, so the check counts as failed until it is. 6 Pass The chart uses labels as well as color. 7 Fail The video has no captions. 8 Pass The video's visuals are all described in its narration, so no audio description is needed. 9 Pass The quiz and every link work with the keyboard. 10 Pass The page language is set, links are descriptive, and the data table has header cells.

Five of ten checks pass, a share of 50 percent, in the 5 to 6 band. Checks 1, 5, and 7 are serious failures. The reviewer therefore chooses the lower number, 5, the score on the Chapter 3 worksheet. That worksheet recorded the image, video, heading, and contrast findings. The full check also records the one-word alt text.

The last MicroSim of the chapter is a scoring practice. It shows five resources with their ten check results, and for each one you choose the metric score.

docs.title: Diagram: Accessibility Metric Scorer
docs.text:
Accessibility Metric Scorer

Type: microsim sim-id: accessibility-metric-scorer Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: apply Learning Objective: The learner will apply the ten accessibility checks and the Chapter 3 scoring rules to choose the metric score for each of five resources, with at least 4 of 5 scores exactly correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Accessibility Metric, WCAG 2.1 AA, Metric Score, Scoring Descriptor (all defined in this chapter or in Chapter 3 above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each resource the learner chooses a whole-number score from 0 to 10 after seeing the ten check results. A score is correct when it equals the Correct score column in Content. Mastery is at least 4 of 5 scores correct on the first attempt. Opening the check list and the descriptor table is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Every failed check lowers the score equally. (2) A clean automated checker report earns a 10. (3) A check not tested can be skipped.

Instructional Rationale: Applying a scoring procedure to new cases is an Apply-level task. Five resources that differ in how many checks fail and whether a serious check fails make the learner use every step: count, band, then choose within the band.

Content:

The ten checks, each marked serious or not, are those in the chapter's check table. The descriptor bands applied to the share of checks passed: 0% is 0; 1% to 24% is 1 to 2; 25% to 49% is 3 to 4; 50% to 74% is 5 to 6; 75% to 89% is 7 to 8; 90% to 100% is 9 to 10. Within a two-number band, choose the lower number when a serious check failed and the higher number otherwise. A score of 10 requires every check to pass. A check that does not apply counts as passed, and a check that was not tested counts as failed.

The five resources:

# Resource Checks failed Checks passed Share Band Serious failure? Correct score Why (shown as feedback) 1 Open Algebra None 10 100% 9 to 10 No 10 Every check passed. 2 Watershed Basics 1, 2, 4, 5, 7 5 50% 5 to 6 Yes, checks 1, 5, and 7 5 Missing alt text, untested contrast, and uncaptioned video are serious, so the lower number applies. 3 Science Lab Page 6 and 10 8 80% 7 to 8 No 8 Neither failed check is serious, so the higher number applies. 4 Lecture Video Series 7, 8, and 10 7 70% 5 to 6 Yes, check 7 5 Videos with no captions are a serious failure, so the lower number applies. 5 Scanned Worksheets 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, and 10 2 (checks 7 and 9) 20% 1 to 2 Yes, checks 1 and 5 1 Scans have no alt text and weak contrast, and the failures are serious, so the lower number applies.

Provenance: The ten checks and the bands follow the chapter section "Scoring Accessibility" and Chapter 3. The five resources are illustrative cases written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". Resource 2 is the chapter's worked example.

Rules: A score is the band chosen from the share passed, and then the number chosen within the band by the serious-failure rule. Each resource has exactly one correct score. For a band that holds a single number, that number is the score.

Learner Activity:

  1. The sim shows resource 1 with its ten check results.
  2. The learner may open the check list and the descriptor table.
  3. The learner chooses a score from 0 to 10, and the choice is committed.
  4. The sim shows the count of passes, the band, whether a serious check failed, and the correct score with the Why text.
  5. After resource 5 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 5 resources in the fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [score]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. [passes] checks passed, which is [share] and the [band] band. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 5 correct on the first attempt". At 4 or more it adds "You can score accessibility." Below 4 it lists the Why text of each missed resource.

Starting State: Resource 1 with all ten results shown and no score chosen. The question shown is "What accessibility score does this resource earn?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's worked example for Watershed Basics fails checks 1, 2, 4, 5, and 7, passes 5 of 10, and scores 5, with the lower number chosen because checks 1, 5, and 7 are serious failures.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Accessibility means learners with disabilities can use a resource. The accessibility metric is scored against WCAG at level AA, which means WCAG 2.1 AA, organized under four principles: perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust.
  • Images need alt text that serves their purpose. A decorative image takes empty alt text, and a complex image description adds a longer text or a table. Heading structure must be real and in order.
  • Color contrast is measured by a contrast ratio, with minimums of 4.5 to 1 for normal text and 3 to 1 for large text. Color independence means color is never the only cue.
  • Captions, a transcript, and audio description open media to learners who cannot hear or see it. Keyboard navigation and a screen reader test whether a page can be operated without a mouse or a screen.
  • Link text, table accessibility, document language, accessible math, and ARIA labels handle the details. Universal Design for Learning plans for variety, and an accessibility checker finds only part of the problems, so the human checks remain.

You Can Check Who Gets Left Out

You can now check a resource against WCAG 2.1 AA, write useful alt text, measure a contrast ratio, test a page with a keyboard, and score accessibility with evidence. Every learner who can get through a resource is a learner your score helped to count.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Accessibility
docs.text: Test your understanding of WCAG 2.1 AA, alt text, contrast, media alternatives, keyboard use, screen readers, and accessibility checkers with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. What are the four principles of WCAG, often abbreviated POUR?
docs.text:
1. Perceivable, organized, usable, and reliable
  2. Photographic, operable, universal, and readable
  3. Practical, open, understandable, and responsive across devices
  4. Perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines group their testable success criteria under four principles. Content must be perceivable, so users can sense it through sight or hearing or touch. It must be operable, including without a mouse. It must be understandable, so users can follow what it says and how it works. And it must be robust, so it works with browsers and assistive technology. Each criterion carries a level of A, AA, or AAA.

Concept Tested: WCAG

See: WCAG

docs.title: 2. What does conformance to WCAG 2.1 AA require?
docs.text:
1. Meeting every level A criterion and every level AA criterion
  2. Meeting only the level AA criteria and none of the level A criteria
  3. Meeting every level A, level AA, and level AAA criterion
  4. Passing an automated accessibility checker with no errors
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. WCAG 2.1 AA is version 2.1 at conformance level AA, which means a resource meets every level A criterion and every level AA criterion. This book targets it because many school and college policies cite it, and because it protects the main groups of learners while staying practical for a teacher to check. Level AAA is the highest level and is not required for whole sites, and a clean checker report (D) is not the same as conformance.

Concept Tested: WCAG 2.1 AA

See: WCAG 2.1 AA

docs.title: 3. How should a decorative image, such as a thin border line, be marked in HTML so that a screen reader skips it?
docs.text:
1. Leave out the alt attribute entirely so that the reader skips the image altogether
  2. Give it alt text that says "decoration" so that readers know it is not content
  3. Use its file name as the alt text so that the image is still identified
  4. Give it an empty alt attribute, written as alt="", so that the reader skips it
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. A decorative image adds appearance only, so a screen reader should skip it, and an empty alt attribute tells the reader to do that. An image with no alt attribute at all is a different case, because many screen readers then read out the file name, which is useless. Alt text that says "decoration" (B) makes the reader announce something that carries no information. When a learner might wonder what the image is, write a short description instead.

Concept Tested: Decorative Image

See: Decorative Image

docs.title: 4. Why should alt text describe what an image does in its context instead of only how it looks?
docs.text:
1. Screen readers cannot announce descriptions that are longer than one word, so short text is always required
  2. A reader who cannot see the image needs text that does the same job the image does for a sighted reader
  3. Alt text is shown only on printed copies of a page, where the appearance of an image does not matter
  4. Describing the appearance would repeat the page's heading and so add nothing for the reader
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Good alt text answers "what does this image do here?" A photo of a river in a lesson about meanders needs alt text that mentions the bends, while the same photo used only for mood needs none. Say what matters in a sentence or two, do not begin with "image of," do not repeat an adjacent caption, and never leave a file name or a single word such as "photo."

Concept Tested: Alt Text

See: Alt Text

docs.title: 5. Which media alternative narrates the important visual information in a video that the soundtrack does not already give?
docs.text:
1. Captions
  2. Keyboard navigation
  3. Color independence
  4. Audio description
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Audio description is spoken narration of actions, scene changes, on-screen text, and charts. It serves learners who are blind or have low vision, and it fills the gap when an instructor says "as you can see here" and points to a chart that is never described. Captions (A) are timed text of speech and important sounds for learners who cannot hear. At level AA, prerecorded video with sound needs captions and audio description.

Concept Tested: Audio Description

See: Audio Description

docs.title: 6. A page contains an image with no alt attribute, and the image file is named river.png. What does a screen reader typically say?
docs.text:
1. "Image, river dot png," reading the file name aloud to the listener
  2. Nothing, because the image is skipped and the reader moves on to the next element
  3. "Image, a river," describing the picture to the listener in words
  4. "Image, decorative," announcing that the image carries no meaning
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. A screen reader reads the page's underlying structure and does not look at the picture, so without alt text it often falls back on the file name. That is useless to the listener. An empty alt attribute is what makes a reader skip an image (B), and no screen reader describes a photo by itself (C). Wording varies between programs, so listen to a page for five minutes before you score.

Concept Tested: Screen Reader

See: Screen Reader

docs.title: 7. A reviewer measures four text-and-background pairs. Which one passes for normal-size body text under WCAG 2.1 AA?
docs.text:
1. Gray on white with a contrast ratio of 4.61 to 1
  2. Gray on white with a contrast ratio of 3.03 to 1
  3. White on orange with a contrast ratio of 2.33 to 1
  4. Pale gray on white with a contrast ratio of 1.36 to 1
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Normal text needs a contrast ratio of at least 4.5 to 1. A ratio of 3.03 to 1 (B) meets only the 3 to 1 minimum for large text, which means at least 18 points, or 14 points if bold. The other two pairs fail for every size. Pass or fail can hinge on a difference no one can see, so reviewers measure with a tool instead of judging by eye.

Concept Tested: Contrast Ratio

See: Contrast Ratio

docs.title: 8. A reviewer applies the ten accessibility checks to a lecture video series. Check 7 (captions), check 8 (transcripts or audio description), and check 10 (page language, link text, table headers) fail, and the other seven pass. What score does the chapter's rule give?
docs.text:
1. 6, because 70 percent falls in the 5 to 6 band and the higher number applies
  2. 7, because seven checks passed, so the score equals the number of passes
  3. 5, because 70 percent falls in the 5 to 6 band and uncaptioned video is a serious failure
  4. 3, because three checks failed, so the score equals the number of failures
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Seven of ten checks pass, a share of 70 percent, which falls in the 5 to 6 band. A failed check is serious when it keeps a group of learners out of the content altogether, and video with no captions is one of the named examples. When a serious check fails, choose the lower number in the band, so the score is 5. The higher number (A) applies only when no serious check fails.

Concept Tested: Accessibility Metric

See: Scoring Accessibility

docs.title: 9. An automated checker reports zero errors for a page, but every image on the page has the alt text "photo." Which analysis is correct?
docs.text:
1. The page passes the accessibility metric, because the tool reports no errors on any of its images
  2. The checker is faulty, because any good checker would flag one-word alt text as a failure
  3. The checker confirms alt text exists but cannot judge whether it is useful, so the page still fails that check
  4. Alt text is no longer required once an automated checker reports no errors for the page
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. A checker finds real problems quickly, such as images with no alt attribute, weak contrast, and unlabeled form fields. It cannot tell whether alt text is useful, and it cannot tell whether a heading describes its section. A clean report is therefore not a pass. Run the tool, then do the human checks: read the alt text, listen with a screen reader, and tab through the page.

Concept Tested: Accessibility Checker

See: Accessibility Checker

docs.title: 10. A chart marks the winning team in green and the losing team in red and offers no other cue. Which learners does this exclude, and what is the fix?
docs.text:
1. Only learners who use a screen reader, so add alt text to the chart and nothing else
  2. Learners who are color blind or print in gray, so add a second cue such as a label, pattern, or icon
  3. Only learners who are deaf or hard of hearing, so add captions to the chart
  4. No one, because red and green contrast strongly, so no change is needed to the chart
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Color independence means color is never the only way a resource conveys information. A learner who is color blind cannot tell the two colors apart, and a learner who prints in gray loses the distinction. Strong contrast between two colors does not help when the difference is in hue (D). The same rule applies to links in a paragraph, which need an underline or another cue beyond a slightly different color.

Concept Tested: Color Independence

See: Color Independence

docs.title: References: Accessibility
docs.text:
1. Web Content Accessibility Guidelines - Wikipedia - Explains the WCAG versions, their four principles, and the A, AA, and AAA conformance levels. The standard behind this book's accessibility metric, which targets WCAG 2.1 AA.

  2. Web accessibility - Wikipedia - Surveys barriers that disabilities create on the web, the laws that require access, and common solutions. Background for why alt text, headings, captions, and keyboard use matter to learners.

  3. Screen reader - Wikipedia - Describes how screen readers turn on-screen content into speech or braille and what they need from a page's structure. Helps reviewers understand why headings and alt text are scored.

  4. A Web for Everyone: Designing Accessible User Experiences - Sarah Horton and Whitney Quesenbery - Rosenfeld Media (2014) - The authors frame accessibility around people rather than checklists, using personas such as a person with low vision or a person using speech input to show why each guideline exists.

  5. Universal Design for Learning: Theory and Practice - Anne Meyer, David H. Rose, and David Gordon - CAST Professional Publishing (2014) - The authors argue for designing for learner variability from the start, with multiple means of representation such as captions and text alternatives. Explains why accessibility features help every learner.

  6. WCAG 2 Overview - W3C Web Accessibility Initiative - The W3C's overview of the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines covering versions 2.0, 2.1, and 2.2, with links to the full standard and quick references. The official starting point for the accessibility metric.

  7. Alternative Text - WebAIM - Explains when and how to write alt text for informative, decorative, functional, and complex images, with examples. Directly supports the chapter's section on images.

  8. Contrast Checker - WebAIM - A free tool that takes a foreground and background color and reports the contrast ratio against the WCAG AA and AAA thresholds. Lets reviewers measure color contrast instead of guessing.

  9. Keyboard Accessibility - WebAIM - Explains how people use a page without a mouse, including tab order, visible focus, and skip links. Gives a simple procedure for the chapter's keyboard test.

  10. WAVE Web Accessibility Evaluation Tools - WebAIM - A free tool that marks errors and alerts directly on a web page. Shows which accessibility problems automated checks can find and which still need a human reviewer.

  11. The 6th "R" of Intelligent Textbooks - Dan McCreary, Intelligent Textbooks - Extends David Wiley's 5Rs of open content (retain, reuse, revise, remix, redistribute) with a sixth right, regenerate, for rebuilding a textbook from its learning graph and course description. The rights to revise and remix are what let someone other than the author fix a missing alt text or caption.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Covers the practice metric: worked examples, formative assessment, quizzes, question quality, immediate feedback, retrieval practice, and interactive simulations that let learners try and check their understanding. It completes the quality metrics by asking whether learners can practice and get feedback. After this chapter you can judge quizzes and worked examples, and decide when an interactive simulation would help a learner more than text.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 18 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Worked Example 2 Practice Metric 28 Formative Assessment 21 Self-Check Question 4 Quiz 16 Multiple-Choice Question 9 Question Bank 1 Answer Key 4 Feedback Message 3 Immediate Feedback 2 Distractor Quality 1 Question Difficulty 1 Retrieval Practice 2 Spaced Practice 1 Interactive Simulation 4 MicroSim 3 Practice Problem 2 Worked Solution 1

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 3: The Ten-Metric Rubric and Scoring
  • Chapter 4: Open File Formats and Version Control
  • Chapter 6: Alignment and Readability

Reading Is Not the Same as Learning

A resource can be accurate, aligned, readable, and accessible and still leave learners with nothing to do. This chapter shows you how to check whether learners can try something, find out how they did, and improve. Let's dive in and check the evidence!

The last quality metric asks the question that decides whether a resource teaches or only informs: can learners practice, and do they find out how they did? People rarely learn a skill by reading about it. They learn by trying, being told what went wrong, and trying again. A resource that offers a thousand words and no way to check understanding leaves that work to chance.

This chapter covers the parts of practice that a reviewer inspects: the examples that show a solution, the questions that let learners try, the feedback that follows, the research-backed habits that make practice work, and the interactive simulations that go beyond a quiz. It ends with the scoring section for the metric.

docs.title: The Practice Metric
docs.text:
The practice metric is the fifth quality metric of the rubric, and it asks whether learners can practice and get feedback. Practice means a task that makes the learner use the idea: answer a question, solve a problem, run an experiment. Feedback means information that tells the learner how the attempt went and how to improve. Both are needed. Practice with no feedback leaves a learner repeating a mistake, and feedback with no practice has nothing to respond to. The metric is scored with ten checks, listed in the scoring section at the end of this chapter.

Worked example: three resources, one question. The table gives three resources on the same topic and what each offers a learner.

Resource What the learner can do Practice and feedback A reading with no questions Read None A reading with a quiz that shows only a score Read and answer Practice, with weak feedback A reading with a quiz that explains each answer and a simulation Read, answer, and experiment Practice and useful feedback

docs.title: Formative Assessment
docs.text:
Formative assessment is assessment that happens during learning, to help the learner and the teacher see what is understood and what is not, and that is used to adjust what comes next. It is assessment for learning. It contrasts with summative assessment, which comes at the end of a unit and judges what was learned, such as a final exam. Formative assessment is low stakes: it often carries no grade, it is repeatable, and its purpose is information. Reviews of the research by Paul Black and Dylan Wiliam found that regular formative assessment with good feedback can produce substantial learning gains. Quizzes, self-checks, and short problems in a chapter are the usual formative tools in an open resource.

Worked example: formative or summative? The table sorts four activities by their purpose.

Activity Kind Why A three-question ungraded check at the end of a lesson, with answers shown at once Formative It helps learners see what they understand now A final exam that sets the course grade Summative It judges what was learned at the end A draft essay returned with comments and no grade Formative It guides the next draft A certificate exam that decides pass or fail Summative It decides an outcome

The first MicroSim sorts ten activities into the two kinds.

docs.title: Diagram: Formative or Summative Sorter
docs.text:
Formative or Summative Sorter

Type: microsim sim-id: formative-summative-sorter Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: classify Learning Objective: The learner will classify each of ten assessment activities as formative or summative by its purpose, with at least 9 of 10 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: The Practice Metric, Formative Assessment (both defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each activity the learner commits one of two bins. A placement is correct when it matches the Correct bin column in Content. Mastery is at least 9 of 10 correct on the first attempt. Reading the definitions is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A quiz is always formative. (2) Formative assessment never involves a grade. (3) Summative assessment is more important than formative assessment.

Instructional Rationale: Classifying by purpose is an Understand-level action. Ten activities in which the format is the same but the purpose differs teach the learner to ask what the result is used for.

Content:

The two bins: Formative (used during learning to guide the next step) and Summative (used at the end to judge what was learned).

The ten activities:

# Activity shown to the learner Correct bin Why (shown as feedback) 1 A three-question ungraded check at the end of a lesson, with answers shown at once. Formative It helps learners see what they know now. 2 A final exam that sets the course grade. Summative It judges what was learned at the end. 3 A teacher asks learners to hold up cards with their answer to a question in the middle of a lesson. Formative It tells the teacher what to do next. 4 A state test given at the end of the school year. Summative It judges what was learned over the year. 5 A draft essay returned with comments and no grade. Formative It guides the next draft. 6 A unit test that counts toward the report card. Summative It judges what was learned in the unit. 7 A self-check quiz in a chapter that lets learners retry. Formative It supports practice and can be repeated. 8 A capstone project graded against a rubric at the end of a program. Summative It judges final achievement. 9 An exit ticket that asks learners to name one thing they are still unsure about. Formative It shows what to teach next. 10 A certificate exam that decides whether a learner passes. Summative It decides an outcome.

Provenance: The activities are illustrative cases written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The definitions follow the chapter section "Formative Assessment".

Rules: Each activity has exactly one correct bin, five per bin. The bin depends on how the result is used.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one activity and the two bins.
  2. The learner places the activity in a bin, and the placement is committed.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text.
  4. After activity 10 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 10 activities in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [bin]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. This is [bin]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 10 correct on the first attempt". At 9 or more it adds "You can tell assessment for learning from assessment of learning." Below 9 it lists the Why text of each missed activity.

Starting State: The first activity and two empty bins. The question shown is "Is this used during learning or at the end?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter says formative assessment guides learning and is low stakes, and summative assessment judges what was learned at the end.

docs.title: Self-Check Question
docs.text: A self-check question is a question placed in a resource for learners to answer for themselves, with the answer or feedback available at once. It carries no grade and no one else sees the result. Self-checks give learners a way to test their own understanding as they read, and they give a reviewer evidence that the resource includes practice. A good self-check follows directly after the idea it tests, so that the learner can still correct a misunderstanding.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
A quiz is a short set of questions that checks understanding of a topic. In an open resource it is usually a formative tool: low stakes, repeatable, and answered on the page. A good quiz covers the stated outcomes, mixes levels from simple recall to application, and gives feedback on every item. A quiz is a reviewer's evidence at three of the ten checks: that practice exists, that feedback follows, and that the practice matches the outcomes from Chapter 6.

Worked example: reading a quiz. A reviewer opens the eight-question quiz that ends Watershed Basics and notes what it offers.

Question What the reviewer sees What it shows Items 1 to 4 Multiple choice on the definition and parts of a watershed Practice for outcome 1 Items 5 to 8 Multiple choice on how water moves Practice for outcome 2 Feedback Six of the eight items explain the answer, and two say only "correct" or "incorrect" Feedback is partly in place Levels Every item asks for recall of a term or a fact Only the remember level is practiced

docs.title: Multiple-Choice Question
docs.text:
A multiple-choice question is a question that offers several answers and asks the learner to choose one. It has three parts: the stem, which is the question or the incomplete statement; the key, which is the correct option; and the distractors, which are the wrong options. Multiple-choice questions are easy for a computer to score and fast for learners to answer, which is why most open resources use them. They test recognition more easily than they test the ability to produce an answer, so a good quiz also includes other kinds.

Writing a good multiple-choice question takes care. A reviewer watches for seven common flaws:

  • An ambiguous stem that can be read two ways.
  • An implausible distractor that no one would choose.
  • The correct answer being noticeably longer than the others.
  • An option such as "all of the above".
  • A stem written in the negative, such as "which is NOT".
  • A grammatical clue that points to the key, such as "a" or "an" before the options.
  • A pattern in the position of the keys across the quiz.

The MicroSim below practices the check. It shows eight questions, and for each one you name the flaw, or decide that it has none.

docs.title: Diagram: Multiple-Choice Flaw Finder
docs.text:
Multiple-Choice Flaw Finder

Type: microsim sim-id: mcq-flaw-finder Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: distinguish Learning Objective: The learner will distinguish the flaw in each of eight multiple-choice questions from six named flaws and a no-flaw option, with at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Multiple-Choice Question, Quiz, Formative Assessment (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each question the learner chooses one of seven options. A choice is correct when it matches the Correct option column in Content. Mastery is at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Opening the flaw list is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A tricky question is a good question. (2) "All of the above" makes a question more thorough. (3) A question with silly wrong answers is easy to write well.

Instructional Rationale: Distinguishing flaws is an Analyze-level action, because the learner must look at the stem and each option and relate them. Eight questions that each isolate one flaw, and two that have none, teach the learner to name the specific problem and to recognize a sound question.

Content:

The seven options: Ambiguous stem, Implausible distractor, Giveaway (the key is longest), All of the above, Negative stem, Grammatical clue, No flaw.

The eight questions:

# Question shown to the learner Correct option Why (shown as feedback) 1 Which of these is a river? A. The Clearwater River. B. A purple banana. C. The number seven. D. Tuesday. Implausible distractor Three of the options are silly, so the learner can answer without knowing anything. 2 Which is NOT a cause of runoff increasing? A. More pavement. B. Heavy rain. C. More trees. D. Bare soil. Negative stem A negative stem makes learners reverse their thinking and causes errors that do not reflect understanding. 3 Water is important. Which is correct? A. Water moves. B. Water is wet. C. Water is blue. D. Water is clear. Ambiguous stem The stem does not say what is being asked. 4 Which describes infiltration? A. Runoff. B. Evaporation. C. The process in which water soaks into the soil, moves downward, and is stored in underground layers. D. Freezing. Giveaway (the key is longest) The key is far longer and more detailed than the others. 5 Which cause increased runoff? A. Paving. B. Bare soil. C. Heavy rain. D. All of the above. All of the above A learner who knows two options are right can guess the third, and the question stops testing each option. 6 A watershed is an A. area that drains to a common outlet. B. river. C. lake. D. ocean. Grammatical clue The word "an" only fits the option that begins with a vowel, which is the key. 7 A field is paved. Compared with grass, what happens to runoff? A. It increases because water cannot soak in. B. It decreases because pavement holds water. C. It stays the same because rain is unchanged. D. It disappears because pavement dries fast. No flaw The stem is clear, and the distractors are plausible misconceptions. 8 Which describes infiltration? A. Water soaking into the ground. B. Water flowing over the ground. C. Water turning to vapor. D. Water freezing. No flaw The stem is clear, and each distractor is a real process that learners may confuse.

Provenance: The questions are written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The flaws follow the chapter section "Multiple-Choice Question". The Clearwater River is made up.

Rules: Each question has exactly one correct option. Six questions have one flaw each, and two have none. Flaws are named as in the chapter's list, with the seventh flaw, a pattern in key positions, not shown because it needs a whole quiz.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads one question and sees the seven options.
  2. The learner may open the flaw list. Opening it does not change the score.
  3. The learner chooses an option, and the choice is committed.
  4. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text.
  5. After question 8 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 8 questions in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [option]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. This is [option]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 8 correct on the first attempt". At 7 or more it adds "You can find the flaw in a question." Below 7 it lists the Why text of each missed question.

Starting State: The first question and the seven options, with the flaw list closed. The question shown is "What is wrong with this question, if anything?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter lists seven flaws: an ambiguous stem, an implausible distractor, a longest key, an "all of the above" option, a negative stem, a grammatical clue, and a pattern in key positions.

docs.title: Question Bank
docs.text: A question bank is a collection of questions, usually tagged by topic, outcome, and difficulty, from which quizzes are drawn. A bank lets an author build a different quiz for each learner or each attempt, so that a learner who retries does not see the same items in the same order. A question bank is also a reusable component, since a teacher who adopts the resource can draw a new quiz from it. The size of the bank matters less than its coverage: every outcome should have several items.

docs.title: Answer Key
docs.text: An answer key is the list of correct answers for a set of questions, with an explanation where the reason is not obvious. Learners use it to check their work, and teachers use it to grade. For practice problems, a bare list of final answers helps little, so a good key shows the method as well, which a later section calls a worked solution. Publishing an answer key under an open license is a gift to other teachers, though some authors keep a separate version for instructors only.

docs.title: Feedback Message
docs.text:
A feedback message is the text a learner sees after answering a question. It is the part of practice that does the teaching. A weak message says only "correct" or "incorrect". A strong one confirms or corrects the answer, says why, and, when the answer was wrong, names the likely misunderstanding and points to what to review. A message should also speak to the learner's attempt without blame.

Worked example: one wrong answer, three messages. A learner chooses "water flowing over the ground" for the question "Which describes infiltration?"

Message What it does Verdict "Wrong." Says the answer failed and says nothing else Weak "Incorrect. The answer is A." Gives the answer and no reason Weak "Not quite. Water flowing over the ground is runoff. Infiltration is water soaking into the ground, so the answer is A." Corrects, explains, and names the mix-up Strong

Name the Mix-Up in the Message

When you write feedback for a wrong answer, name the mistake the learner probably made and say what the chosen answer actually describes. "That is runoff, and infiltration is the opposite" teaches more than "try again".

docs.title: Immediate Feedback
docs.text:
Immediate feedback is feedback that appears right after the learner answers, while the attempt is still fresh. Feedback that comes a week later, with a grade, helps far less, because the learner has forgotten why they chose what they chose. Online resources are well placed to give immediate feedback automatically, which is a strength that print cannot match. A reviewer checks that the feedback is immediate, and that it is shown for every item.

The next MicroSim practices the judgment of feedback quality. It shows eight messages for the same wrong answer, and for each one you decide whether it is helpful.

docs.title: Diagram: Feedback Message Rater
docs.text:
Feedback Message Rater

Type: microsim sim-id: feedback-message-rater Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: judge Learning Objective: The learner will judge whether each of eight feedback messages for the same wrong answer is helpful or not helpful, with at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Feedback Message, Immediate Feedback, Multiple-Choice Question (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each message the learner commits one of two bins. A placement is correct when it matches the Correct bin column in Content. Mastery is at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the criteria is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Encouraging words are feedback. (2) Giving the answer is enough. (3) A longer message is always better.
