Instructional Rationale: Judging a message against criteria is an Evaluate-level action. Eight messages for one wrong answer hold the situation constant, so the learner sees what separates feedback that teaches from feedback that only grades.

Content:

The situation, shown at all times: the question is "Which describes infiltration?" with options A. Water soaking into the ground; B. Water flowing over the ground; C. Water turning to vapor; D. Water freezing. The learner chose B.

The criteria, shown on request: a helpful message says the answer was wrong, explains why, and points toward the right idea or the next step, without blaming the learner.

The two bins: Helpful and Not helpful.

The eight messages:

# Message shown to the learner Correct bin Why (shown as feedback) 1 "Wrong." Not helpful It says nothing about why. 2 "Incorrect. The answer is A." Not helpful It gives the answer and no explanation. 3 "Not quite. Water flowing over the ground is runoff. Infiltration is water soaking into the ground, so the answer is A. Reread section 2 if the two terms are mixed up." Helpful It corrects, explains, and points to what to review. 4 "Good try!" Not helpful It does not say whether the answer was right. 5 "You chose B, which describes runoff. Infiltration is the opposite: water going into the ground, which is A." Helpful It names the mix-up and explains the difference. 6 "Check your notes." Not helpful It is vague and does not explain the error. 7 "That is a common mix-up. Runoff stays on top of the ground, and infiltration goes down into it. Try the next question with that in mind." Helpful It explains the difference and points forward without blame. 8 "You are wrong because you did not read the question carefully." Not helpful It blames the learner and does not explain the content.

Provenance: The question and messages are written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The criteria follow the chapter sections "Feedback Message" and "Immediate Feedback".

Rules: Each message has exactly one correct bin. Three messages are Helpful and five are Not helpful.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees the question, the wrong answer, and one message.
  2. The learner places the message in a bin, and the placement is committed.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text.
  4. After message 8 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 8 messages in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [bin]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. This is [bin]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 8 correct on the first attempt". At 7 or more it adds "You can tell feedback that teaches." Below 7 it lists the Why text of each missed message.

Starting State: The question, the learner's wrong answer, and the first message. The question shown is "Would this message help the learner?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's worked example of three messages for the same wrong answer treats "Wrong." and "Incorrect. The answer is A." as weak and the explanation of runoff versus infiltration as strong.

docs.title: Distractor Quality
docs.text: Distractor quality is how well the wrong options of a multiple-choice question do their job. A good distractor is plausible: a learner who has not understood the idea would be tempted by it, because it reflects a real misconception. A poor distractor is silly, or obviously wrong, or so close to the key that no one could call it wrong. Good distractors make a question measure understanding, and they give feedback its material, since each wrong option points to a specific mistake. Some research suggests that three well-written options can work as well as four or five, so a quality check looks at the options' quality and not at their number.

docs.title: Question Difficulty
docs.text:
Question difficulty is how hard a question is for the learners it serves. A simple measure is the difficulty index: the share of learners who answer correctly. A question that nearly everyone gets right, or that nearly no one gets right, tells you little about differences among learners. A quiz should include a range, from items that check basic understanding to items that need application, so that every learner finds some success and some challenge. Difficulty should come from the idea, and not from a confusing stem.

The parts of a quiz question are now all defined, so the next MicroSim puts them on one page. Its illustration is a single quiz card, and its seven numbered markers point to the parts a reviewer checks.

docs.title: Diagram: Anatomy of a Quiz Question
docs.text:
Anatomy of a Quiz Question

Type: infographic sim-id: quiz-question-anatomy Library: html Status: Specified Bloom Level: Remember Bloom Verb: identify Learning Objective: The learner will identify the seven parts of an interactive quiz question from a description of how each looks, with at least 6 of 7 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Multiple-Choice Question, Distractor Quality, Feedback Message, Question Difficulty, Question Bank (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: In quiz mode the learner clicks the marker that matches a visual hint. A click is correct when it matches the marker named in the Hint column of Content. Mastery is at least 6 of 7 correct on the first attempt. Hovering in explore mode is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) The distractors are decoration. (2) Feedback appears only for wrong answers. (3) The difficulty tag is a score.

Instructional Rationale: Identifying the parts of a question is a Remember-level task, and an illustration of one quiz card gives each part a place. The quiz asks the learner to recognize a part by its look, which is how they will spot it in a real quiz.

Content:

The illustration is a text-free flat drawing of one quiz card. At the top is a block of three thin lines. Below it are four rows, each with a round selector, and one row carries a check icon. Under the rows is a panel with a speech-bubble icon holding two thin lines. In the upper right corner are two small tags, one with a target icon and one with a gauge icon. At the lower left is a small button with a circular arrow icon. The seven markers:

# Label Hint (describes the look, not the name) Description Tip 1 Stem The block of three thin lines at the top of the card. The question or incomplete statement that the learner answers. Make the stem clear enough that a learner who knows the answer can give it without reading the options. 2 Key The option row with a check icon. The one correct answer. Make sure only one option can be defended as correct. 3 Distractors The three option rows without a check icon. The wrong options, written to reflect likely misconceptions. Give each distractor a reason a learner might choose it. 4 Feedback message The panel with a speech-bubble icon under the options. The text shown after an answer, which explains why. Write feedback for every option, not only for the key. 5 Outcome tag The small tag with a target icon at the upper right. Links the question to the learning outcome it checks. Use the tag to confirm that every outcome has questions. 6 Difficulty tag The small tag with a gauge icon at the upper right. Marks how hard the question is expected to be. Mix easy, medium, and hard questions across a quiz. 7 Retry control The small button with a circular arrow at the lower left. Lets the learner try again, or draw a fresh question from the bank. Allow retries, because practice needs repetition.

Provenance: The parts follow the chapter sections on multiple-choice questions, feedback, distractor quality, question difficulty, and the question bank. The illustration is synthetic, and the sim labels the card "illustrative example".

Rules: Each hint matches exactly one marker. The illustration contains no text, so every label comes from the table above. Markers are numbered 1 to 7 in the order of the table. Marker 3 covers all three distractor rows as one marker.

Learner Activity:

  1. In explore mode the learner hovers or clicks a marker and reads its label, description, and tip.
  2. In quiz mode the sim shows a hint.
  3. The learner clicks the marker they think the hint describes.
  4. If the first click is wrong, the sim says so and lets the learner try once more. If the second click is also wrong, the sim reveals the marker and its description.
  5. After all 7 hints the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 7 hints in a shuffled order, two attempts each. Only a correct first click counts as evidence. Correct: "Correct: [label]. [Description]". First wrong click: "Not quite. Look again at the hint: [hint]". Second wrong click: "This is [label]. [Description]". The summary shows "[n] of 7 correct on the first attempt". At 6 or more it adds "You can read a quiz question." Below 6 it lists the labels of the missed parts.

Starting State: The illustration with seven numbered markers, explore mode active, and the prompt "Hover a marker to see what it is."

Chapter Anchors: The chapter says a multiple-choice question has a stem, a key, and distractors, that a feedback message explains why, and that questions can be tagged by outcome and difficulty in a question bank.

docs.title: Retrieval Practice
docs.text:
Retrieval practice is practice in which the learner tries to recall something from memory, without looking at the source. Answering a question, writing down what you remember of a chapter, and using flash cards are all retrieval practice. Decades of research on what psychologists call the testing effect find that retrieving information strengthens memory more than reading it again. The effort of recalling is part of what makes the learning last. Retrieval works best when feedback follows, so the learner can fix what they got wrong.

Trying to Remember Is the Learning

A quiz is not only a way to measure what you know, because the act of recalling makes the knowledge stronger. Rereading feels easier and teaches less.

docs.title: Spaced Practice
docs.text:
Spaced practice is practice spread over time, with gaps between sessions, as opposed to massed practice, which crams the same work into one sitting. The spacing effect is among the most reliable findings in the study of learning: material practiced over several days is remembered longer than the same time spent in one session. A resource supports spacing when later chapters or quizzes revisit earlier material. A reviewer looks for review questions that return to older ideas.

The MicroSim below sorts six study plans on two questions at once. For each plan you decide what the learner does and when they do it.

docs.title: Diagram: Study Plan Classifier
docs.text:
Study Plan Classifier

Type: microsim sim-id: study-plan-classifier Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: classify Learning Objective: The learner will classify each of six study plans by what the learner does (retrieval practice or rereading) and by when (spaced or massed), with at least 10 of 12 judgments correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Retrieval Practice, Spaced Practice, Formative Assessment (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each plan the learner makes two judgments, one about the activity and one about the timing. A judgment is correct when it matches the Content table. Mastery is at least 10 of 12 judgments correct on the first attempt. Reading the definitions is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Rereading counts as retrieval practice. (2) Highlighting is a form of testing. (3) Any practice done over several days is spaced practice.

Instructional Rationale: Classifying a plan on two features is an Understand-level action that separates the two ideas learners often merge. Six plans that cross the two features teach the learner that retrieval and spacing are independent.

Content:

The two judgments for each plan: Activity (Retrieval practice, where the learner tries to recall without looking, or Rereading, where the learner looks at material again) and Timing (Spaced, with gaps of a day or more between sessions, or Massed, all in one sitting or the night before).

The six plans:

# Plan shown to the learner Activity Timing Why (shown as feedback) 1 Read the chapter three times the night before the test. Rereading Massed The learner looks at the text again, and does it all at once. 2 Close the book and write down everything you remember, then check. Do it the day after reading and again a week later. Retrieval practice Spaced The learner recalls without looking, with gaps between sessions. 3 Highlight the chapter on Monday and reread the highlights on Tuesday and Friday. Rereading Spaced The learner looks at material again, with gaps between sessions. 4 Make flash cards and quiz yourself on all of them for three hours the evening before the exam. Retrieval practice Massed The learner recalls without looking, all in one sitting. 5 Take a five-question quiz at the start of each class on last week's material. Retrieval practice Spaced The learner recalls without looking, a week later and each week. 6 Copy your notes neatly the weekend before the test. Rereading Massed Copying is a form of looking again, done in one stretch.

Provenance: The plans are illustrative cases written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The definitions follow the chapter sections "Retrieval Practice" and "Spaced Practice".

Rules: Each plan has exactly one correct activity and one correct timing, so the sim holds 12 judgments. Three plans are Retrieval practice and three are Rereading. Three are Spaced and three are Massed.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one plan and two questions.
  2. The learner chooses the activity and the timing, and both choices are committed together.
  3. The sim shows whether each was correct and the Why text.
  4. After plan 6 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 6 plans in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [activity], [timing]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. This plan is [activity] and [timing]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 12 judgments correct on the first attempt". At 10 or more it adds "You can tell recall from rereading and spacing from cramming." Below 10 it lists the Why text of each missed plan.

Starting State: The first plan and the two questions, "What does the learner do?" and "When?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter defines retrieval practice as recalling without looking and spaced practice as gaps between sessions, and says rereading is not retrieval.

docs.title: Worked Example
docs.text: A worked example is a problem shown with every step of its solution explained, so that a learner can study the method before trying one alone. Research on the worked example effect, associated with the psychologist John Sweller and colleagues, finds that learners who are new to a topic often learn more from studying worked examples than from solving the same problems unaided, because solving a problem from scratch uses up attention that they need to see the method. The best worked examples show each step and the reason for it, and they use a problem close to what the learner will meet. As the learner gains skill, the examples can fade: later ones leave out steps for the learner to fill in.

docs.title: Practice Problem
docs.text: A practice problem is a task that makes the learner use an idea, such as a calculation, a classification, or a short explanation. Good practice problems match the outcomes, begin close to the worked example and then vary, rise in difficulty, and come with an answer key. A resource with a worked example and no practice problem shows the method and never lets the learner try it. A resource with problems and no worked example leaves new learners to guess.

docs.title: Worked Solution
docs.text:
A worked solution is the full step-by-step solution to a practice problem, shown after the learner has tried it. It resembles a worked example, and the difference is timing and purpose. A worked example comes before practice, as a model. A worked solution comes after an attempt, so the learner can compare their method with a correct one and find where they went wrong. The table sets the three side by side.

Item When it appears What it shows Worked example Before the learner tries A model of the method Answer key After the learner tries Only the final answers Worked solution After the learner tries Every step to the answer

The MicroSim below shows a faded worked example. Three problems on the same type of question move from a fully worked solution, to one with steps left blank, to one the learner does alone.

docs.title: Diagram: Faded Worked Example Stepper
docs.text:
Faded Worked Example Stepper

Type: microsim sim-id: faded-worked-example-stepper Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: solve Learning Objective: The learner will solve the area of an L-shaped region by subtracting a cut-out rectangle from the outer rectangle, correctly on both of the last two problems on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Worked Example, Practice Problem, Worked Solution (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: The learner studies problem 1, completes the missing steps of problem 2, and solves problem 3 alone. Problems 2 and 3 count as evidence. A problem is correct when every entered value matches the Content table. Mastery is both problems correct on the first attempt. Studying problem 1 is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) The area of an L-shape is the sum of its side lengths. (2) The cut-out is added to the area. (3) The answer needs no unit.

Instructional Rationale: Solving a problem of a taught type is an Apply-level action. A faded sequence moves the learner from studying a model to supplying steps to solving alone, which matches how worked examples are meant to be used with beginners.

Content:

The method, shown in problem 1: find the area of the outer rectangle, find the area of the cut-out rectangle, subtract the second from the first, and write the answer in square meters. The area of a rectangle is its width times its height.

The three problems (all made up):

Problem Outer rectangle (width x height) Cut-out corner (width x height) Step 1: outer area Step 2: cut-out area Step 3: subtract Step 4: answer with unit How it is presented 1 10 m x 8 m 4 m x 3 m 80 12 80 - 12 = 68 68 square meters All four steps shown with reasons 2 12 m x 9 m 5 m x 4 m 108 20 108 - 20 = 88 88 square meters Steps 1 and 2 shown; the learner supplies steps 3 and 4 3 15 m x 6 m 7 m x 2 m 90 14 90 - 14 = 76 76 square meters Only the problem is shown; the learner supplies all four steps

Provenance: The problems are made up for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The method follows the chapter section "Worked Example".

Rules: Each entered number must equal the table value. The unit "square meters" must be present in the answer. The learner may not skip a step. For problem 3 the learner enters steps 1 to 4 in order.

Learner Activity:

  1. The sim shows problem 1 with all four steps and the reason for each. The learner reads it and presses Next.
  2. The sim shows problem 2 with steps 1 and 2 filled in. The learner enters step 3 and step 4 and presses Check.
  3. The sim shows whether each entry was correct and the full solution.
  4. The sim shows problem 3 with only the problem. The learner enters steps 1 to 4 and presses Check.
  5. The sim shows whether each entry was correct and the full solution, then the summary.

Feedback: One attempt for each of problems 2 and 3 counts as evidence. For a correct step: "Correct: [value]." For an incorrect step: "Not quite. [Step reason]. The value is [value]." Typical errors get a targeted message: adding the cut-out instead of subtracting it ("The corner is missing from the region, so subtract it"), and omitting the unit ("Write the unit: square meters"). The summary shows "[n] of 2 problems correct on the first attempt". At 2 it adds "You can solve an L-shaped area." Below 2 it shows the full solution of each missed problem.

Starting State: Problem 1 with all four steps shown and the prompt "Study how each step follows from the one before."

Chapter Anchors: The chapter says a worked example shows every step with its reason, that worked examples can fade, and that a worked solution comes after the learner's attempt. The three problems use the same method.

docs.title: Interactive Simulation
docs.text:
An interactive simulation is a model of a system that the learner can change and watch respond. The learner moves a slider, picks a value, or presses a button, and the simulation shows what happens. A simulation suits ideas where the interesting part is how one quantity affects another, such as how the length of a pendulum changes its swing, or how paving changes runoff. It can also serve as practice, by asking the learner to predict a result and then run the model to check. A simulation is a strong form of practice with feedback, because the feedback is the system's own response.

Simulations are not always the right tool. For a fixed fact or a definition, a sentence is faster and clearer. A simulation also has to meet the checks of other chapters: it must be accessible, with keyboard controls and text alternatives, and it must be portable, running in a browser with no login.

docs.title: MicroSim
docs.text:
A MicroSim is a small interactive simulation that teaches one idea, runs in a web browser, and embeds in a page. In this book a MicroSim lives in its own folder, with a web page that can be embedded by iframe and a page of lesson notes, and it is built with open web tools, such as the p5.js library for drawing and interaction. MicroSims are meant to be reused: another teacher can embed the same simulation in a different course. That makes a MicroSim both a piece of practice and a reusable component, which connects this chapter to the modularity and portability metrics later in the book.

You Do Not Have to Build It to Review It

Judging a simulation takes no programming, because you can try it, press the keys, and check whether it explains itself. You already review other things you cannot make yourself. Ask what the learner does, and whether the simulation tells them how they did.

The MicroSim below practices the decision. For each of eight learning goals you decide whether a simulation would help more than plain text.

docs.title: Diagram: Simulation Fit Judge
docs.text:
Simulation Fit Judge

Type: microsim sim-id: simulation-fit-judge Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: judge Learning Objective: The learner will judge whether a simulation or plain text serves each of eight learning goals better, with at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Interactive Simulation, MicroSim, Practice Problem (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each goal the learner commits one of two bins. A placement is correct when it matches the Correct bin column in Content. Mastery is at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the rule of thumb is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A simulation is always better than text. (2) A simulation is only for science. (3) Interactive means a game.

Instructional Rationale: Judging the fit of a tool to a goal is an Evaluate-level action that a reviewer needs when deciding whether a resource lacks interactivity or is padded with it. Eight goals that split evenly teach the learner to apply one test to each.

Content:

The rule of thumb, shown at all times: a simulation helps when the learner needs to change a quantity and see an effect, or to practice a procedure with immediate feedback. Plain text suffices for fixed facts and definitions.

The two bins: A simulation would help more, and Text or a table is enough.

The eight goals:

# Learning goal shown to the learner Correct bin Why (shown as feedback) 1 See how changing a pendulum's length changes how fast it swings. A simulation would help more The learner changes a quantity and sees an effect. 2 Memorize the names of the planets. Text or a table is enough It is a fixed list, and flash cards fit better than a simulation. 3 Understand how paving changes runoff by changing the share of paved land. A simulation would help more The learner varies a quantity and watches runoff change. 4 Read the definition of a watershed. Text or a table is enough A definition is a fixed statement. 5 Explore how a savings rate changes the growth of savings over thirty years. A simulation would help more The learner varies a rate and sees the long-run effect. 6 Learn the dates of five historical events. Text or a table is enough They are fixed facts. 7 Practice balancing a chemical equation with immediate checking. A simulation would help more The learner practices a procedure and gets feedback at once. 8 Find out who wrote a famous poem. Text or a table is enough It is a single fact.

Provenance: The goals are illustrative cases written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The rule of thumb follows the chapter sections "Interactive Simulation" and "MicroSim".

Rules: Each goal has exactly one correct bin, four per bin.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one goal and the two bins.
  2. The learner places the goal in a bin, and the placement is committed.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text.
  4. After goal 8 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 8 goals in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [bin]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. [bin]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 8 correct on the first attempt". At 7 or more it adds "You can tell when interactivity earns its place." Below 7 it lists the Why text of each missed goal.

Starting State: The first goal and the two bins. The question shown is "Would a simulation teach this better than text?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter says a simulation suits ideas where the learner varies a quantity and sees an effect, or practices a procedure with feedback, and that plain text is better for a fixed fact or a definition.

docs.title: Scoring Practice and Feedback
docs.text:
Practice is scored with ten checks. A failed check is serious when the resource offers no practice with feedback at all, which is check 1. When check 1 fails, the checks that depend on practice existing, which are checks 2 to 5, 9, and 10, count as failed. When a serious check fails, choose the lower number in a two-number band. Otherwise choose the higher number.

# Check Serious if it fails? 1 The resource offers practice questions or tasks with feedback on at least some items Yes 2 Every practice item gives feedback after the learner responds No 3 Feedback explains why an answer is right or wrong, and not only "correct" or "incorrect" No 4 An answer key or worked solutions are available No 5 Multiple-choice distractors are plausible and reflect likely misconceptions No 6 Items vary in difficulty and in Bloom level, not only recall No 7 At least one worked example shows a full solution step by step No 8 At least one interactive element lets learners act and see results No 9 Practice is spread across the resource and revisits earlier material No 10 Learners can retry items without penalty No

A Score Is Not Feedback

A quiz that ends with "You got 5 of 8" has told the learner how they did and nothing about why. Open each item and look for a message that explains the answer, because the total can hide that the feedback is missing.

Worked example: Watershed Basics. The reviewer applies the checks to the reading from Chapter 3.

# Result Evidence 1 Pass The resource has an eight-question quiz with feedback. 2 Fail Six of the eight items give feedback, and two say only "correct" or "incorrect". 3 Pass The six messages explain the answer. 4 Pass An answer key follows the quiz. 5 Pass The reviewer read all eight items, and the distractors are plausible misconceptions. 6 Fail All eight items ask for recall of a term or a fact. 7 Fail The resource has no worked example. 8 Fail The resource has no simulation or other interactive element. 9 Pass Quiz items 5 to 8 revisit terms from section 1. 10 Pass Learners can retry the quiz as often as they like.

Six of ten checks pass, a share of 60 percent, in the 5 to 6 band. The check that would be serious, check 1, passed, so the reviewer chooses the higher number, 6, the score on the Chapter 3 worksheet. That worksheet recorded the partial feedback, the missing worked example, and the missing simulation. The full check also records the recall-only items.

The last MicroSim of the chapter is a scoring practice. It shows five resources with their ten check results, and for each one you choose the metric score.

docs.title: Diagram: Practice Metric Scorer
docs.text:
Practice Metric Scorer

Type: microsim sim-id: practice-metric-scorer Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: apply Learning Objective: The learner will apply the ten practice checks and the Chapter 3 scoring rules to choose the metric score for each of five resources, with at least 4 of 5 scores exactly correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: The Practice Metric, Metric Score, Scoring Descriptor (all defined in this chapter or in Chapter 3 above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each resource the learner chooses a whole-number score from 0 to 10 after seeing the ten check results. A score is correct when it equals the Correct score column in Content. Mastery is at least 4 of 5 scores correct on the first attempt. Opening the check list and the descriptor table is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Having a quiz earns a high score. (2) Every failed check lowers the score equally. (3) A resource with no practice can still pass the feedback checks.

Instructional Rationale: Applying a scoring procedure to new cases is an Apply-level task. Five resources, including one with no practice at all, make the learner use every step and the rule that dependent checks fail when check 1 fails.

Content:

The ten checks, each marked serious or not, are those in the chapter's check table. The descriptor bands applied to the share of checks passed: 0% is 0; 1% to 24% is 1 to 2; 25% to 49% is 3 to 4; 50% to 74% is 5 to 6; 75% to 89% is 7 to 8; 90% to 100% is 9 to 10. Within a two-number band, choose the lower number when a serious check failed and the higher number otherwise. A score of 10 requires every check to pass. When check 1 fails, checks 2, 3, 4, 5, 9, and 10 count as failed.

The five resources:

# Resource Checks failed Checks passed Share Band Serious failure? Correct score Why (shown as feedback) 1 Open Algebra None 10 100% 9 to 10 No 10 Every check passed. 2 Watershed Basics 2, 6, 7, 8 6 60% 5 to 6 No 6 None of the failures is serious, so the higher number applies. 3 Reading Only Unit 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10 1 (check 7) 10% 1 to 2 Yes, check 1 1 The unit has no practice, which is serious, and its one worked example is the only check that passes. 4 Quiz Only Unit 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 4 (checks 1, 2, 4, 10) 40% 3 to 4 No 4 None of the failures is serious, so the higher number applies. 5 Simulation Lab 4 and 9 8 80% 7 to 8 No 8 Neither failed check is serious, so the higher number applies.

Provenance: The ten checks and the bands follow the chapter section "Scoring Practice and Feedback" and Chapter 3. The five resources are illustrative cases written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". Resource 2 is the chapter's worked example.

Rules: A score is the band chosen from the share passed, and then the number chosen within the band by the serious-failure rule. Each resource has exactly one correct score. For a band that holds a single number, that number is the score.

Learner Activity:

  1. The sim shows resource 1 with its ten check results.
  2. The learner may open the check list and the descriptor table.
  3. The learner chooses a score from 0 to 10, and the choice is committed.
  4. The sim shows the count of passes, the band, whether a serious check failed, and the correct score with the Why text.
  5. After resource 5 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 5 resources in the fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [score]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. [passes] checks passed, which is [share] and the [band] band. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 5 correct on the first attempt". At 4 or more it adds "You can score practice and feedback." Below 4 it lists the Why text of each missed resource.

Starting State: Resource 1 with all ten results shown and no score chosen. The question shown is "What practice score does this resource earn?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's worked example for Watershed Basics fails checks 2, 6, 7, and 8, passes 6 of 10, and scores 6, with the higher number chosen because no serious check failed. The chapter says that when check 1 fails, checks 2 to 5, 9, and 10 count as failed.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• The practice metric asks whether learners can practice and learn how they did. Formative assessment supports learning during instruction, and a self-check question or a quiz is its usual form.
  • A multiple-choice question has a stem, a key, and distractors. Distractor quality and question difficulty decide whether it measures understanding, and a question bank and an answer key make a set of questions reusable.
  • A feedback message should explain, and immediate feedback helps most. Retrieval practice and spaced practice are two habits that make practice last.
  • A worked example models the method before the learner tries, a practice problem lets them try, and a worked solution shows the steps afterward.
  • An interactive simulation suits ideas where a learner varies a quantity and sees an effect, and a MicroSim is a small, reusable simulation that teaches one idea.

You Can Judge Practice and Feedback

You can now judge a quiz question, rate a feedback message, spot a missing worked example, decide when a simulation earns its place, and score practice with feedback with evidence. With this chapter, all five quality metrics are in your hands.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Practice and Feedback
docs.text: Test your understanding of formative assessment, quiz design, feedback messages, retrieval and spaced practice, worked examples, and simulations with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. What are the three parts of a multiple-choice question?
docs.text:
1. The stem, the key, and the distractors
  2. The prompt, the rubric, and the answer key
  3. The stem, the feedback message, and the question bank
  4. The key, the outcome tag, and the retry control
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The stem is the question or incomplete statement, the key is the correct option, and the distractors are the wrong options. Multiple-choice questions are easy for a computer to score and fast to answer, but they test recognition more easily than the ability to produce an answer, so a good quiz includes other kinds too. A feedback message, a tag, and a retry control are useful extras and not parts of the question itself.

Concept Tested: Multiple-Choice Question

See: Multiple-Choice Question

docs.title: 2. Which term names practice in which the learner tries to recall something from memory without looking at the source?
docs.text:
1. Spaced practice
  2. Massed practice
  3. Retrieval practice
  4. Summative assessment
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Retrieval practice includes answering a question, writing down what you remember of a chapter, and using flash cards. Research on the testing effect finds that retrieving information strengthens memory more than rereading it, and it works best when feedback follows. Spaced practice (A) and massed practice (B) describe when practice happens, not what the learner does, so a plan can be retrieval and spaced at once.

Concept Tested: Retrieval Practice

See: Retrieval Practice

docs.title: 3. How does a worked solution differ from a worked example?
docs.text:
1. A worked example gives only final answers, while a worked solution gives every step of the method
  2. A worked example comes before the learner tries, as a model, while a worked solution comes after an attempt
  3. A worked example is written for teachers, while a worked solution is written for learners
  4. A worked example appears after the attempt, while a worked solution appears before it
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Both show a full step-by-step solution, and the difference is timing and purpose. A worked example comes before practice as a model of the method. A worked solution comes after the learner's attempt, so the learner can find where their own method went wrong. An answer key, by contrast, shows only the final answers (A). Option D reverses the order.

Concept Tested: Worked Solution

See: Worked Solution

docs.title: 4. Which pair correctly contrasts formative and summative assessment?
docs.text:
1. Formative assessment is always graded, while summative assessment is never graded at all
  2. Formative assessment comes at the end of a unit, while summative assessment happens during learning
  3. Formative assessment guides learning as it happens, while summative assessment judges what was learned at the end
  4. Formative assessment uses only multiple-choice items, while summative assessment uses only essays
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Formative assessment is assessment for learning: it is low stakes, often ungraded, repeatable, and used to adjust what comes next. Summative assessment, such as a final exam or a certificate exam, judges what was learned at the end. The same format can serve either purpose, so the question to ask is what the result is used for. A quiz in an open resource is usually a formative tool.

Concept Tested: Formative Assessment

See: Formative Assessment

docs.title: 5. Why does the chapter say that a quiz ending with "You got 5 of 8" has not given the learner useful feedback?
docs.text:
1. A score always arrives too late to affect what the learner does next, however soon it is shown to them
  2. Quizzes should never show scores to learners, because scores discourage them from trying again
  3. Feedback must always be delivered in person by a teacher, because software cannot explain
  4. A score says how the learner did but not why, so nothing explains or corrects a misunderstanding
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. A feedback message is the part of practice that does the teaching. A strong message confirms or corrects the answer, says why, and, when the answer was wrong, names the likely misunderstanding and points to what to review. A total can hide that explanations are missing, so a reviewer opens each item and looks for a message. Online resources can show this feedback immediately and automatically, which print cannot match.

Concept Tested: Feedback Message

See: Feedback Message

docs.title: 6. Why do worked examples often help learners who are new to a topic more than solving the same problems unaided?
docs.text:
1. Beginners learn more from guessing before they see any solution, because errors are memorable
  2. Solving from scratch uses attention that a beginner needs to see the method, so studying a full solution helps
  3. Worked examples remove the need for any practice problems, because the method is already shown
  4. Worked examples let learners skip feedback because the steps are already shown to them
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Research on the worked example effect, associated with John Sweller and colleagues, finds that novices often learn more from studying worked examples because problem solving from scratch takes the attention they need to see the method. The best examples show each step and the reason for it. As skill grows, examples can fade, leaving steps for the learner to fill in. Practice problems are still needed, because a worked example never lets the learner try the method.

Concept Tested: Worked Example

See: Worked Example

docs.title: 7. A learner answers "Which describes infiltration?" with "Water flowing over the ground." Which feedback message best follows the chapter's guidance?
docs.text:
1. "Not quite. That is runoff, which flows over the ground. Infiltration is water soaking in, so review the two."
  2. "Wrong. Try again, and this time read the question and all four options more carefully before you answer."
  3. "Incorrect. The answer is the first option, so mark it as correct and move on to the next question when you are ready."
  4. "Good try! Keep going, because you are doing well and the next question is easier than this one was."
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. A strong message corrects the answer, explains why, names the likely mix-up, and points to what to review, without blaming the learner. Option A says that the chosen answer describes runoff and defines infiltration as its opposite. "Wrong" (B) and the bare answer (C) say what failed or what is right without a reason. "Good try" (D) does not even say whether the answer was correct, which makes it unhelpful.

Concept Tested: Feedback Message

See: Feedback Message

docs.title: 8. A student closes the book and quizzes themself with flash cards on Monday, again on Thursday, and again the following Monday. How should this plan be classified?
docs.text:
1. Retrieval practice, spaced across several days
  2. Rereading, spaced over several days with gaps between the sessions
  3. Retrieval practice, massed into one long sitting
  4. Rereading, massed into one sitting the night before
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Quizzing with the book closed is retrieval practice, because the learner tries to recall without looking. The gaps of several days between sessions make the practice spaced, and the spacing effect is among the most reliable findings in the study of learning. Retrieval and spacing are independent ideas: a plan can have one without the other. Cramming flash cards for three hours the evening before an exam would be retrieval that is massed (C).

Concept Tested: Spaced Practice

See: Spaced Practice

docs.title: 9. A reviewer reads this question: "Which caused increased runoff? A. Paving. B. Bare soil. C. Heavy rain. D. All of the above." What is the main flaw?
docs.text:
1. The stem is written in the negative, which makes learners reverse their thinking before answering
  2. The key is noticeably longer than the other options, which gives the answer away
  3. A grammatical clue before the options points to the key, so learners can guess it
  4. "All of the above" lets a learner who knows two options are right guess the third without testing it
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The chapter lists seven common flaws in multiple-choice questions: an ambiguous stem, an implausible distractor, a longer key, an "all of the above" option, a negative stem, a grammatical clue, and a pattern in key positions. This question has none of the others. Each option is short, the stem is positive, and no article points to an answer. A learner who recognizes two correct options can guess the third without knowing anything about it.

Concept Tested: Multiple-Choice Question

See: Multiple-Choice Question

docs.title: 10. A reviewer finds that a unit has no practice questions at all, only one worked example. How does the chapter's scoring rule treat the other practice checks, and what is the effect on the score?
docs.text:
1. Checks 2 to 5, 9, and 10 count as passed because they do not apply, so the score stays high
  2. Checks 2 to 5, 9, and 10 are skipped, and only check 7, the worked example, is scored
  3. Checks 2 to 5, 9, and 10 count as failed because check 1 fails, and the serious failure selects the lower number
  4. Checks 2 to 5, 9, and 10 count as failed, but the higher number applies because the worked example passes
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Check 1 asks whether the resource offers practice with feedback on at least some items, and it is the one serious check. When it fails, the checks that depend on practice existing, which are 2 to 5, 9, and 10, count as failed. In the chapter's Reading Only Unit only the worked example passes, a share of 10 percent, and the serious failure selects the lower number, so the score is 1. Practice with no feedback, or feedback with no practice, is not enough.

Concept Tested: Practice Metric

See: Scoring Practice and Feedback

docs.title: References: Practice and Feedback
docs.text:
1. Formative assessment - Wikipedia - Describes assessment used during learning to guide teaching and give feedback, as opposed to grading at the end. Background for judging whether a resource's questions help learners improve.

  2. Testing effect - Wikipedia - Summarizes research showing that retrieving information from memory strengthens it more than rereading. Supports the chapter's sections on quizzes and retrieval practice.

  3. Worked-example effect - Wikipedia - Explains how studying fully worked solutions helps novices learn faster than solving problems alone, within cognitive load theory. Background for scoring whether a resource includes worked examples.

  4. Make It Stick: The Science of Successful Learning - Peter C. Brown, Henry L. Roediger III, and Mark A. McDaniel - Harvard University Press (2014) - Turns laboratory research on retrieval practice, spacing, and interleaving into stories of real learners, arguing that effortful recall beats rereading. A clear base for judging a resource's practice design.

  5. Embedded Formative Assessment (2nd ed.) - Dylan Wiliam - Solution Tree Press (2018) - Wiliam's five key strategies (clarify intentions, elicit evidence, give feedback that moves learners forward, activate peers, activate ownership) give reviewers a practical test of whether questions and feedback do formative work.

  6. RetrievalPractice.org - Pooja K. Agarwal - Cognitive scientist Pooja Agarwal's free guides, strategies, and research summaries on retrieval practice and spacing. Gives teachers ready examples of the practice this chapter asks reviewers to look for.

  7. The Learning Scientists - The Learning Scientists - Cognitive psychologists explain six research-based study strategies, including spaced practice and retrieval practice, with downloadable materials. Useful for judging whether a resource lets learners use them.

  8. Formative vs Summative Assessment - Carnegie Mellon Eberly Center - Contrasts assessment that guides learning with assessment that measures it, with examples of each. Helps reviewers decide whether a resource's quizzes give feedback or only a grade.

  9. PhET Interactive Simulations - University of Colorado Boulder - Free, research-based simulations in science and mathematics that let learners change variables and see results. A model of the interactive simulations the chapter says earn their place.

  10. Creating Exams - Carnegie Mellon Eberly Center - Guidance on designing exams and writing different question types, with tips for tying items to learning objectives. Supports the chapter's criteria for judging question quality.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Shows how to score the open license, modularity, and metadata metrics, including standalone components, Dublin Core records, controlled vocabularies, and machine-readable metadata that help others find and reuse a resource. It starts the reusability metrics, which score how easily others can find and reuse a resource. After this chapter you can judge whether a resource is split into standalone components and whether its metadata lets others find it.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 23 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Open License Metric 2 License Clarity 1 Modularity Metric 21 Modular Content 20 Standalone Component 15 Component Granularity 1 Cross-Reference Dependence 1 Embeddable Component 8 Metadata Metric 98 Metadata Record 97 Dublin Core 92 Title Field 14 Author Field 14 Subject Field 17 Grade Level Field 15 License Field 15 Description Field 14 Keywords 3 Controlled Vocabulary 1 LRMI 1 Schema.org Markup 3 Machine-Readable Metadata 2 Metadata Completeness 13

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 2: Open Licenses and Attribution
  • Chapter 3: The Ten-Metric Rubric and Scoring
  • Chapter 4: Open File Formats and Version Control

You Cannot Reuse What You Cannot Find

The reusability metrics ask whether another teacher can find a resource, know what it is, and lift out the part they need. This chapter covers three of them: whether the license is clear, whether the parts stand alone, and whether the description lets a search find it. Let's dive in and check the evidence!

The first five metrics of the rubric asked how well a resource teaches. The last five ask how easily others can reuse it, and the first three of those fill this chapter. A resource may be superb and still go unused, because no one can tell what license it has, because its best part is tangled into the rest, or because nothing records its subject, so a search never turns it up.

The order of the chapter follows a reuser's path. A teacher first needs to know what she may do, which is the open license metric. She then needs to take out only the part she wants, which is modularity. And before any of that, she must find the resource, which is the metadata metric and the largest part of the chapter.

docs.title: The Open License Metric
docs.text:
The open license metric is the sixth metric of the rubric. It asks whether a clear open license is stated on every component of the resource and whether attribution is complete. Chapter 2 taught you to read a license and to credit one, and this metric turns that skill into a score. It is scored with ten checks. The checks below are the book's list, and they replace the preview list in the Chapter 3 worked example. The score for Watershed Basics comes out the same.

A failed check is serious when it leaves a reuser unsure of their rights to some part of the resource. When a serious check fails, the score cannot go above the band's lower number, and a score of 10 requires every check to pass.

# Check Serious if it fails? 1 A license is named on the main page Yes 2 The license version is stated No 3 A link to the license text is given No 4 The owner is named No 5 The scope of the license is stated No 6 The license appears on every page or component No 7 Machine-readable license marking is present No 8 Every third-party item is identified and carries its own notice Yes 9 Credit lines for reused material are complete No 10 The license is an open license that permits revision and redistribution Yes

Worked example: Watershed Basics. Nine of the ten checks pass. Check 8 fails, because two of the three third-party images carry their own notice and the third has none. That gap is serious, since a reuser cannot tell whether the third image may be copied. The share is 90 percent, in the 9 to 10 band, and a failed check means the score is 9.

docs.title: License Clarity
docs.text: License clarity is how plainly a resource tells a reuser what the license is and what it covers. A clear statement names one specific license, gives its version, links to it, says what it covers, and gives the same answer everywhere the resource appears. A resource is unclear when the page says "CC BY" and the file says "some rights reserved", when a license covers the text and says nothing about the images, or when a resource says "free to use" and names no license. Unclear licensing is a risk for the reuser, because the safe assumption is that no permission was granted.

docs.title: Modular Content
docs.text:
Modular content is content built from separate, self-contained pieces that can be used alone or together, in the way a set of building blocks can be assembled in different shapes. A modular resource divides its material into sections, quizzes, simulations, figures, and glossaries that each have a clear purpose. Modularity helps learners, because short focused pieces are easier to study and review. It helps teachers more, because a teacher can take the one module she needs and leave the rest. It helps authors, since one module can be revised without touching the others.

Worked example: one chapter, two designs. A chapter on watersheds can be built in two ways.

Feature Woven design Modular design Structure One long page that mixes explanation, a quiz, and a simulation Separate pieces: a reading, a quiz, and a simulation Taking out the quiz Copy it from the middle of the page and repair the links Link or embed the quiz's own page Revising the simulation Edit the whole page and risk breaking the reading Edit the simulation's folder Reuse by another teacher Take everything or nothing Take any piece

Modularity is a matter of degree. At one end is a single page that mixes everything together. A step up is a page with clear sections, a step further has each part in its own file, and at the far end each part is packaged with its own license and metadata. Each step makes a part easier to take out and reuse, and a reviewer notes how far along the line a resource has gone.

docs.title: Standalone Component
docs.text:
A standalone component is a piece of a resource that works on its own, without the rest of the resource around it. The test is to lift it out. Copy the piece to a new place and ask whether it still makes sense and still works. A reading that begins "as we saw in the last section" fails. A quiz that refers to "the diagram above" fails. A simulation that needs a script from a sibling folder fails. A component passes when everything it needs travels with it, and when a reader who has never seen the rest can use it.

Worked example: the lift test on Watershed Basics. The reviewer tries to lift out each of three parts.

Part What happens when it is lifted out Result The reading It begins with a definition and uses only terms it defines Standalone The quiz It asks about "the river in section 2", which is not in the quiz page Not standalone The images Each has its own file, caption, and alt text Standalone

Lift It Out Before You Score It

Copy one component into an empty file and read it cold. Whatever confuses you in that empty file will confuse the next teacher who reuses it.

The first MicroSim of the chapter practices the lift test. It shows eight components, and for each one you decide whether it stands alone.

docs.title: Diagram: Standalone Lift Test
docs.text:
Standalone Lift Test

Type: microsim sim-id: standalone-lift-test Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: judge Learning Objective: The learner will judge whether each of eight components stands alone or depends on the rest of its resource, with at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Modular Content, Standalone Component (both defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each component the learner commits one of two bins. A placement is correct when it matches the Correct bin column in Content. Mastery is at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the lift test is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A component is standalone if it has its own file. (2) A short component is always standalone. (3) A reference to another section is harmless.

Instructional Rationale: Judging whether a component stands alone is an Evaluate-level action that applies a stated test. Eight components that differ in one detail each teach the learner to look for hidden dependencies.

Content:

The lift test, shown at all times: copy the component to a new place, and check that it makes sense without the rest, and that everything it needs comes with it.

The two bins: Stands alone, and Depends on the rest.

The eight components:

# Component shown to the learner Correct bin Why (shown as feedback) 1 A reading that opens with a definition and uses only terms it defines. Stands alone It needs nothing from other sections. 2 A quiz whose questions say "refer to the diagram in section 2". Depends on the rest The diagram is not part of the quiz. 3 A simulation in its own folder with its own page, instructions, and script. Stands alone Everything it needs travels with it. 4 A figure with its own caption and alt text but a caption that begins "as discussed above". Depends on the rest The caption refers to text that is not there. 5 A glossary page that defines each term in full. Stands alone Each definition is complete. 6 A section that begins "now that you have finished section 3, turn to section 4". Depends on the rest It assumes the reader came from section 3. 7 A worked example that restates the problem, the method, and the answer. Stands alone It holds everything needed to follow it. 8 A simulation page that loads a script from a different chapter's folder. Depends on the rest It breaks when moved without that folder.

Provenance: The components are illustrative cases written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The test follows the chapter section "Standalone Component".

Rules: Each component has exactly one correct bin, four per bin.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one component and the two bins.
  2. The learner places the component in a bin, and the placement is committed.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text.
  4. After component 8 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 8 components in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [bin]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. This [bin]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 8 correct on the first attempt". At 7 or more it adds "You can run the lift test." Below 7 it lists the Why text of each missed component.

Starting State: The first component, the lift test, and two empty bins. The question shown is "Would this still work if you copied it somewhere new?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's worked example lifts out the reading, the quiz, and the images from Watershed Basics, and finds that the quiz is not standalone because it refers to the river in section 2.

docs.title: Component Granularity
docs.text: Component granularity is the size of a component: how much one piece contains. A component can be too big, such as a whole textbook when someone needs one idea. It can be too small, such as a single sentence, which is not worth finding or reusing. A useful size is usually one idea or one learning objective with its explanation, an example, and a check question. The right grain also depends on the reuser: a teacher planning a lesson wants a section, and a department building a course wants a unit.

docs.title: Cross-Reference Dependence
docs.text: Cross-reference dependence is the way a component relies on other parts of its resource through words like "as shown above" or "see section 4". Each such phrase is a thread that breaks when the component moves. The fix is to restate the idea in one sentence, or to link to the other piece by its own address, so that the reference works wherever the component lands. A reviewer searches a component for phrases such as "above", "below", "earlier", "next section", and "the figure", and checks each one.

docs.title: Embeddable Component
docs.text:
An embeddable component is a component that can be placed inside another page, either by a link or by an iframe, an HTML element that displays one web page inside another. Embedding lets a teacher put your simulation in her course page without copying it, and any improvements you make later reach her page too. For a component to embed, it needs its own web address, it must open with no login, and it must be built so the other site's page does not break it.

An iframe is a short piece of HTML. Before the example, here is what its parts mean. The src attribute holds the address of the page to display. The width and height attributes set its size. The title attribute gives the frame a name that a screen reader announces, which the accessibility chapter requires.

<iframe src="https://example.org/sims/runoff/main.html"
        width="100%" height="500"
        title="Runoff simulation"></iframe>

Worked example: testing an embed. A reviewer wants to know whether the runoff simulation can be embedded. She follows four steps.

  1. She opens the simulation's address in a private browser window and confirms that it loads with no login.
  2. She pastes the iframe above into a blank test page and opens that page.
  3. She checks that the simulation appears, responds to the controls, and fits within the frame.
  4. She repeats the test on a second platform, such as a course management system, and records what happened.

The MicroSim below checks your reading of iframe snippets. It shows six snippets of embed code, and for each one you decide whether it is fine or what needs fixing.

docs.title: Diagram: Iframe Snippet Reviewer
docs.text:
Iframe Snippet Reviewer

Type: microsim sim-id: iframe-snippet-reviewer Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: critique Learning Objective: The learner will critique six iframe snippets by naming the problem in each or judging it fine, with at least 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Embeddable Component, Standalone Component (both defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each snippet the learner chooses one of four verdicts. A choice is correct when it matches the Correct verdict column in Content. Mastery is at least 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Reading the attribute list is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A relative address works anywhere. (2) A fixed width is harmless. (3) The title attribute is optional.

Instructional Rationale: Critiquing a snippet against a short list of requirements is an Evaluate-level action that a reviewer performs when testing portability. Six snippets, each with at most one defect, isolate the requirements.

Content:

The requirements, shown on request: the address must be complete and public; the frame must fit any page; the frame must have a title; the page must open with no login.

The four verdicts: Fine, Fix the address, Make the width flexible, Add a title.

The six snippets (all with example addresses):

# Snippet shown to the learner Correct verdict Why (shown as feedback) 1 iframe with src "https://example.org/sims/runoff/main.html", width "100%", height "500", title "Runoff simulation" Fine It has a complete address, a flexible width, and a title. 2 iframe with src "main.html", width "100%", height "500", title "Runoff simulation" Fix the address A relative address points to a file that exists only beside the original page. 3 iframe with src "https://example.org/sims/runoff/main.html", width "1200", height "500", title "Runoff simulation" Make the width flexible A fixed width of 1200 overflows a narrow page. 4 iframe with src "https://example.org/sims/runoff/main.html", width "100%", height "500" and no title Add a title A screen reader cannot name the frame. 5 iframe with src "https://example.org/sims/pendulum/main.html", width "100%", height "450", title "Pendulum simulation" Fine It has a complete address, a flexible width, and a title. 6 iframe with src "file:///Users/teacher/sims/runoff/main.html", width "100%", height "500", title "Runoff simulation" Fix the address The address points to a file on one person's computer, which no one else can open.

Provenance: The snippets are illustrative cases written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The requirements follow the chapter section "Embeddable Component". The addresses use the reserved example.org domain.

Rules: Each snippet has exactly one correct verdict. Two snippets are Fine, two are Fix the address, one is Make the width flexible, and one is Add a title.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one snippet and the four verdicts.
  2. The learner may open the requirements. Opening them does not change the score.
  3. The learner chooses a verdict, and the choice is committed.
  4. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text.
  5. After snippet 6 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 6 snippets in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [verdict]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. The verdict is [verdict]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 6 correct on the first attempt". At 5 or more it adds "You can read embed code." Below 5 it lists the Why text of each missed snippet.

Starting State: The first snippet and the four verdicts. The question shown is "What, if anything, needs fixing?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's iframe example uses the attributes src, width, height, and title, and says a relative address, a fixed width, and a missing title are problems.

docs.title: The Modularity Metric
docs.text:
The modularity metric is the seventh metric of the rubric. It asks whether each section, quiz, or simulation stands alone and can be embedded elsewhere. It is scored with ten checks. A failed check is serious when it means the resource cannot be taken apart at all, which is checks 1 and 2. When a serious check fails, choose the lower number in a two-number band. Otherwise choose the higher number.

# Check Serious if it fails? 1 The resource is divided into identifiable components Yes 2 Each component has its own page, file, or address Yes 3 Each component can be understood without reading the rest No 4 Each component states the prior knowledge it assumes No 5 Components are of useful size, one idea or objective each No 6 Each component carries its own license statement and credits No 7 Each component carries its own metadata No 8 Interactive components embed without edits No 9 Components keep working when moved, with no broken relative links No 10 Each component is named so that a reuser can tell what it is No

Worked example: Watershed Basics. The reviewer applies the checks to the reading from Chapter 3.

# Result Evidence 1 Pass The page has a reading, a quiz, and images, each identifiable. 2 Fail All parts sit in one HTML page, and the quiz has no address of its own. 3 Pass The reading stands alone, and the images each have a caption. 4 Fail No part states what students should know first. 5 Pass The reading is one idea of about 2,400 words. 6 Pass The footer on the page covers all of its parts. 7 Fail No component has its own metadata. 8 Fail The quiz cannot be embedded by itself. 9 Fail The quiz script uses a relative path that breaks when the quiz is moved. 10 Pass Each part has a clear heading or title.

Five of ten checks pass, a share of 50 percent, in the 5 to 6 band. Check 2 failed and is serious, so the reviewer chooses the lower number, 5, the score on the Chapter 3 worksheet. That worksheet recorded the main finding, that the quiz cannot be opened apart from the reading.

docs.title: The Metadata Metric
docs.text:
The metadata metric is the eighth metric of the rubric. It asks whether a resource records its title, author, subject, grade level, license, and description in a standard form, so that others can find it and tell what it is. Metadata means data about a resource: it describes the resource and is not part of its content. A library catalog card is metadata about a book. A teacher searching for a resource sees metadata first, and a resource whose metadata is missing may as well not exist, since nothing leads a searcher to it.

Worked example: three records, one search. A teacher searches a repository for "watershed grade 6 reading open license". The repository matches the words in each resource's metadata.

Resource Its metadata Does the search find it? A Title "Watershed Basics", subject "Earth science", grade "6 to 7", license "CC BY 4.0", a clear description Yes, and it ranks high B Title "Reading 4" and nothing else No: no field mentions a watershed C Title "Watershed Basics" and an author, with no subject, grade, or license Possibly, but the teacher cannot tell the grade or whether she may reuse it

Metadata Is for People and for Machines

A person reads a description to decide whether a resource fits, and a search engine reads the same fields to decide whether to show it. A record that serves only one of them wastes the effort.

docs.title: Metadata Record
docs.text:
A metadata record is the structured set of fields that describes one resource, with a name and a value for each field. A record is like a catalog card: it has the same slots for every resource, so records can be compared, searched, and sorted. Fields hold short values, such as a title or a license, and a few hold a sentence or two, such as a description. A record can live inside the resource, as tags in a web page, or beside it, as a separate file.

Worked example: before and after. The first column shows what Watershed Basics records today, and the second shows a complete record. The field names follow Dublin Core, which the next section explains. The date and address are made up.

Field Today Complete record Title Watershed Basics Watershed Basics Creator Maria Lopez Lopez, Maria Subject Missing Watersheds; Water cycle; Earth science Description Missing A short reading and eight-question quiz that explain what a watershed is and how water moves through one, for grades 6 and 7. Education level Missing Grades 6 to 7 Rights Missing CC BY 4.0, https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ Date Shown on the page only 2025-03-14 Language Missing en Identifier Missing https://example.org/watershed-basics Type Missing Text; InteractiveResource

docs.title: Dublin Core
docs.text:
Dublin Core is a standard vocabulary for describing resources, maintained by the Dublin Core Metadata Initiative and published as an international standard. Its core is a set of 15 elements, simple enough that anyone can fill them in, and it is used by library catalogs, repositories, and web publishers. The elements fall into four groups. Some describe the content: title, subject, description, type, and coverage. Some describe who is responsible: creator, contributor, publisher, and rights. Some describe the particular copy: date, format, identifier, and language. And two describe relations to other resources: source and relation. Dublin Core has also grown a larger set of terms, which includes useful ones for education such as audience and education level.

Element What it records Title The name of the resource Creator The person or organization mainly responsible Subject The topic, given as terms or phrases Description A summary of the content Publisher The organization that makes it available Contributor Others who contributed Date A date in the resource's life, such as when it was created Type The kind of resource, such as text or interactive resource Format The file format or medium Identifier An unambiguous reference, such as a web address Source A resource from which this one is derived Language The language of the content Relation A related resource Coverage A place or time the content covers Rights The license or rights statement

This book's six core fields map onto Dublin Core as the table shows. Dublin Core has no core element for grade level, so the record uses the education level term.

This book's field Dublin Core element or term Title Title Author Creator Subject Subject Grade level Education level License Rights Description Description

The MicroSim below practices the mapping. It shows ten pieces of information about a resource, and for each one you choose the Dublin Core element that holds it.

docs.title: Diagram: Dublin Core Matcher
docs.text:
Dublin Core Matcher

Type: microsim sim-id: dublin-core-matcher Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: classify Learning Objective: The learner will classify each of ten pieces of information about a resource under the Dublin Core element that holds it, with at least 9 of 10 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: The Metadata Metric, Metadata Record, Dublin Core (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each piece of information the learner commits one of eleven elements. A choice is correct when it matches the Correct element column in Content. Mastery is at least 9 of 10 correct on the first attempt. Reading the element table is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) The author's name belongs in Contributor. (2) The license belongs in Description. (3) The format of a file is its type.

Instructional Rationale: Classifying information by field is an Understand-level action that a reviewer performs when reading or writing a record. Ten distinct fields teach the learner what each element is for.

Content:

The eleven elements offered: Title, Creator, Subject, Description, Date, Type, Format, Identifier, Source, Language, Rights.

The ten pieces of information:

# Information shown to the learner Correct element Why (shown as feedback) 1 Maria Lopez Creator The person mainly responsible for the resource. 2 https://example.org/watershed-basics Identifier An unambiguous reference to the resource. 3 en Language The language of the content. 4 2025-03-14 Date A date in the resource's life. 5 CC BY 4.0 with a link to the license Rights The license is the rights statement. 6 A short reading and quiz that explain what a watershed is. Description A summary of the content. 7 Watersheds; Water cycle Subject The topics of the resource. 8 InteractiveResource Type The kind of resource. 9 text/html Format The file format or medium. 10 Adapted from an earlier lesson plan Source A resource from which this one is derived.

Provenance: The pieces of information are illustrative cases written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The element definitions follow the chapter section "Dublin Core".

Rules: Each piece of information has exactly one correct element, and the ten correct elements are all different.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one piece of information and the eleven elements.
  2. The learner may open the element table. Opening it does not change the score.
  3. The learner chooses an element, and the choice is committed.
  4. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text.
  5. After item 10 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 10 items in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [element]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. This belongs in [element]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 10 correct on the first attempt". At 9 or more it adds "You can file information in a record." Below 9 it lists the Why text of each missed item.

Starting State: The first item, the eleven elements, and the element table closed. The question shown is "Which Dublin Core element holds this?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter says Dublin Core has 15 core elements, that the rubric's author field is Creator and its license field is Rights, and that grade level uses the education level term.

docs.title: Title Field
docs.text:
The title field records the name of the resource. It is the first thing a searcher sees, so a good title is specific, descriptive, and unique. It tells the searcher the topic and, when it helps, the kind of resource. A title like "Lesson 3" or "Chapter 4" says nothing outside its original context. Titles should also stay stable, because other pages link to a resource by its title and repositories index it that way.

Worked example: three titles for one resource.

Title Verdict Why Lesson 3 Poor It names no topic, and many resources share it. Water Weak It names a topic that is too broad to find the resource. Watershed Basics: A Grade 6 Reading and Quiz Good It names the topic, the audience, and the kind of resource.

Keep a resource's title stable once it is published, since links and repository entries use it. If a revised edition appears, change the version or the date in the record and keep the title, so readers can tell the editions apart and still find both. Avoid file names in place of titles, such as "final_v2", and avoid unusual characters that some systems cannot display.

docs.title: Author Field
docs.text:
The author field records who created the resource, and it is what lets others credit it, as Chapter 2 required. Record the person or the organization responsible, and use a consistent form, such as family name, then given name. Where a resource has several creators, list each. When someone adapts a resource, the record names the original creator and the person who adapted it separately, so that credit travels with the work. An organization can be an author, such as a district or a university department.

Worked example: who goes in the field?

Situation What to record One teacher wrote the resource The teacher's name Two teachers wrote it together Both names, in the order the authors prefer A teacher adapted another author's CC BY lesson The original author as creator, and the adapter as contributor A district office produced it The district office as the creator

Consistency helps credit travel. "Lopez, Maria", "M. Lopez", and "Maria Lopez" look like three different people to a search tool. Many repositories also accept a persistent personal identifier, such as an ORCID iD, a number that belongs to one person for life and ties their works together, though teachers need not have one. Record the author the way the creator wishes to be credited, which may be a pen name or an organization.

docs.title: Subject Field
docs.text:
The subject field records what the resource is about, as one or more terms. It is the field searchers rely on most, after the title. Good subject terms are specific enough to separate the resource from others and come from a shared list where one exists, so that "runoff" and "run-off" do not fragment the results. A resource may have several subjects, such as a topic and a field: "Watersheds" and "Earth science".

Worked example: subject terms for Watershed Basics.

Terms Verdict Why Science Too broad Thousands of resources share it. Watersheds; Water cycle; Earth science Good The terms are specific and standard. stuff about rivers Poor It is vague and not a standard term.

Subject terms and keywords differ. Subject terms describe what the resource is about, often from a shared list, and keywords are the extra words a searcher might type. Two to five subject terms usually serve a resource, enough to place it in its field without padding the list. The ERIC Thesaurus, maintained for education research, is one shared list that education repositories use.

docs.title: Grade Level Field
docs.text:
The grade level field records the learners a resource is written for, as a grade, a range of grades, an age range, or a level such as college. It is not the same as reading level. Grade level says who the resource is for, and reading level says how hard its text is. A searcher uses grade level to filter, so a consistent scheme matters: "6-7" in one record and "middle school" in another will not group together. Use one scheme across all your records.

Worked example: three schemes.

Scheme Example value When it fits Grade range Grades 6 to 7 Resources for U.S. schools Age range Ages 11 to 13 Resources used across countries Level Introductory college Higher education

A resource can serve more than one level, and a record can say so with a range such as grades 6 to 8. Countries label grades differently, so a resource meant for international use should add an age range beside the grade. Grade level also differs from difficulty: a challenging resource for grade 6 and a gentle one for grade 9 may both be correctly labeled. Chapter 6's audience fit asks whether the level matches the text.

docs.title: License Field
docs.text:
