The license field records the resource's license in the metadata, apart from the statement on the page. A good entry names the license and links to its text, so that software can read it. The field must agree with the statement on the page, and a record that says CC BY next to a page that says CC BY-NC invites a dispute. For a resource with parts under different licenses, the field names the license of the resource as a whole and each component carries its own.

Worked example: three entries.

Entry Verdict Why Free Poor It names no license. CC BY Weak It names the license and gives no version or link. CC BY 4.0, https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ Good It names the license, the version, and the text.

Repeat the license in the same words wherever it appears, so that a search tool and a person read the same thing. If you change the license when you adapt a resource, update the field at the same time, because an old value left behind is the most common cause of mismatched records.

docs.title: Description Field
docs.text:
The description field records a short summary of what the resource is, what it covers, and who it is for. It is the field a human reads when deciding whether to open the resource, and search engines also match on its words. A good description runs one to three sentences, uses the words a teacher would type to look for it, and says what the resource contains, such as a reading, a quiz, or a simulation. It is not an advertisement and not a copy of the first paragraph.

Worked example: three descriptions.

Description Verdict Why An amazing resource everyone will love! Poor It says nothing about the content. Watershed. Weak It gives a topic and nothing else. A short reading and eight-question quiz that explain what a watershed is and how water moves through one, for grades 6 and 7. Good It names the content, the topic, and the audience.

Search tools often show only the start of a description in their results, so put the most important words first: the topic, the kind of resource, and the audience. Mention what is included, such as a quiz or a simulation, because a teacher choosing among resources wants to know. Avoid claims that the metadata cannot back up, like "complete" or "best".

Write the Description for the Searcher

Imagine the words a busy teacher would type to find your resource, and make sure those words appear in the description. A searcher who types "grade 6 watershed quiz" should land on a description that says exactly that.

The next MicroSim judges field entries. It shows ten entries for the six fields, and for each one you decide whether it is good or needs work.

docs.title: Diagram: Metadata Entry Judge
docs.text:
Metadata Entry Judge

Type: microsim sim-id: metadata-entry-judge Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: judge Learning Objective: The learner will judge whether each of ten metadata field entries is good or needs work, with at least 9 of 10 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Title Field, Author Field, Subject Field, Grade Level Field, License Field, Description Field (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each entry the learner commits one of two bins. A placement is correct when it matches the Correct bin column in Content. Mastery is at least 9 of 10 correct on the first attempt. Reading the field guidance is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Any filled field is a good field. (2) A short entry is always weak. (3) A license field only needs the license's short name.

Instructional Rationale: Judging an entry against what its field is for is an Evaluate-level action that a reviewer performs when scoring metadata. Ten entries across six fields, half good and half weak, teach the learner what each field needs.

Content:

The two bins: Good, and Needs work.

The ten entries:

# Field Entry shown to the learner Correct bin Why (shown as feedback) 1 Title Lesson 3 Needs work It names no topic and many resources share it. 2 Title Watershed Basics: A Grade 6 Reading and Quiz Good It names the topic, audience, and kind of resource. 3 Author Lopez, Maria Good It names the person in a consistent form. 4 Author the teacher Needs work It names no one, so no one can be credited. 5 Subject Watersheds; Water cycle; Earth science Good The terms are specific and standard. 6 Subject Science Needs work It is too broad to separate the resource from others. 7 Grade level Grades 6 to 7 Good It states the audience in one consistent scheme. 8 License CC BY Needs work It gives no version and no link. 9 License CC BY 4.0, https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ Good It names the license, version, and text. 10 Description An amazing resource everyone will love! Needs work It says nothing about the content.

Provenance: The entries are illustrative cases written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The guidance follows the chapter sections for each field.

Rules: Each entry has exactly one correct bin, five per bin.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one field name and entry and the two bins.
  2. The learner places the entry in a bin, and the placement is committed.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text.
  4. After entry 10 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 10 entries in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [bin]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. This entry is [bin]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 10 correct on the first attempt". At 9 or more it adds "You can judge a metadata entry." Below 9 it lists the Why text of each missed entry.

Starting State: The first entry with its field name and the two bins. The question shown is "Does this entry do its field's job?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's worked examples of titles, subjects, licenses, and descriptions give the same verdicts: Lesson 3 is poor, Science is too broad, CC BY alone is weak, and the amazing-resource description is poor.

docs.title: Keywords
docs.text: Keywords are words or short phrases that a searcher might use to find a resource, recorded freely, with no fixed list. They supplement the subject field by adding the everyday and alternative terms that a person might type. A resource about runoff might carry the keywords "runoff", "stormwater", and "flooding". Keywords are easy to add and easy to get wrong in two ways: too few leaves the resource hard to find, and too many unrelated ones, a practice called keyword stuffing, makes it appear in searches where it does not belong.

docs.title: Controlled Vocabulary
docs.text: A controlled vocabulary is a fixed list of approved terms that everyone describing resources agrees to use, so that the same idea always carries the same label. Where free keywords scatter the same idea across "runoff", "run-off", and "surface water flow", a controlled vocabulary gathers them under one term. The trade-off is effort: an author must learn the list, and a term the list lacks cannot be recorded. Many repositories use one for subjects and for grade levels, and a reviewer notes whether a resource's terms come from a shared list.

docs.title: LRMI
docs.text: LRMI, the Learning Resource Metadata Initiative, is a specification that adds educational properties to web metadata. Where Dublin Core describes any resource, LRMI describes what matters in education: the type of learning resource, the educational level, the age range, the educational use, and the standards a resource is aligned to. LRMI is maintained by the Dublin Core Metadata Initiative, and its properties are part of Schema.org, the vocabulary described next. Four of its properties show the idea. The property learningResourceType says whether a resource is a lesson, a quiz, or a simulation. The property typicalAgeRange gives the ages it suits. The property educationalAlignment links it to a standard. And timeRequired says how long it takes.

docs.title: Schema.org Markup
docs.text:
Schema.org markup is a shared vocabulary that web pages use to tell search engines what they contain. Search engines read it to understand a page, and a resource marked up with it can be recognized as a learning resource, with its author, license, and level. The usual form is JSON-LD, a block of structured data placed in the page's head. Before the example, here is what its parts do. The @type line says what kind of thing the page describes. The other lines give property names, such as name and license, with their values.

<script type="application/ld+json">
{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "LearningResource",
  "name": "Watershed Basics",
  "author": { "@type": "Person", "name": "Maria Lopez" },
  "description": "A short reading and eight-question quiz that explain what a watershed is and how water moves through one, for grades 6 and 7.",
  "license": "https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/",
  "educationalLevel": "Grades 6 to 7",
  "learningResourceType": "reading",
  "inLanguage": "en"
}
</script>

It Looks Like Code, and You Can Read It

A block of JSON-LD can look intimidating, and it is only a list of names and values. You already read a form with labels and answers, and the left side of each line is the label. If you can read the record in the table earlier in this chapter, you can read this.

docs.title: Machine-Readable Metadata
docs.text: Machine-readable metadata is metadata in a form that software can read and process, as opposed to text that only a person reads. A description written in a paragraph on a web page is for people. The same facts in a JSON-LD block, in tags in the page's head, or in a separate metadata file are for machines. Machine-readable metadata lets a repository harvest records automatically and a search engine filter by license or grade. In this book's convention, a MicroSim's folder can hold a metadata file beside its web page. A reviewer checks that a machine-readable copy exists and that it matches what the page says.

docs.title: Metadata Completeness
docs.text:
Metadata completeness is how many of a resource's expected metadata fields are filled in with valid values. It is a simple measure: count the fields that are filled and valid, divide by the number of fields expected, and multiply by 100. With the six core fields, a record that has four filled fields has a completeness of about 67 percent. Completeness shows what is missing and says nothing of whether what is there is good. A field filled with "TBD" is present and useless, and a value that does not match the resource is worse than a blank, because it misleads.

Worked example: the completeness of two records. The expected fields are the six core fields.

Field Watershed Basics today Watershed Basics, complete record Title Filled Filled Author Filled Filled Subject Empty Filled Grade level Empty Filled License Empty Filled Description Empty Filled Fields filled 2 of 6 6 of 6 Completeness 33% 100%

A Wrong Value Is Worse Than a Blank

Filling a field with "TBD", a guess, or the wrong license makes a record look complete and sends searchers to the wrong place. Leave a field empty until you know the value, and then count it as missing.

The MicroSim below puts the arithmetic into practice. It shows four records, and for each one you compute the completeness.

docs.title: Diagram: Metadata Completeness Calculator
docs.text:
Metadata Completeness Calculator

Type: microsim sim-id: metadata-completeness-calculator Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: calculate Learning Objective: The learner will calculate the metadata completeness of each of four records over the six core fields, treating invalid values as empty, with at least 3 of 4 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Metadata Record, Metadata Completeness, Title Field, Author Field, Subject Field, Grade Level Field, License Field, Description Field (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each record the learner enters the completeness as a whole-number percent, rounded to the nearest whole number. An answer is correct when it equals the Completeness column in Content. Mastery is at least 3 of 4 correct on the first attempt. Reading the formula is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A filled field always counts. (2) Completeness measures quality. (3) A field filled with a placeholder is a partial credit.

Instructional Rationale: Calculating a percentage from a count is an Apply-level action, and requiring the learner to judge which values are valid first links the arithmetic to the judgment of entries. Four records with different mixes of empty and invalid fields make both steps necessary.

Content:

The formula, shown at all times: completeness = fields filled with a valid value, divided by 6, times 100, rounded to a whole number. A value is invalid when it is a placeholder like "TBD" or "unknown", or when it does not match the resource.

The four records, each over the fields Title, Author, Subject, Grade level, License, Description:

# Record Field values Valid fields Completeness 1 Watershed Basics today Title and Author filled; the other four empty 2 33% 2 Draft Record Title, Author, Subject, Grade level filled; License "TBD"; Description empty 4 67% 3 Mismatched Record Title, Author, Subject, Grade level, Description filled; License says CC BY but the page says CC BY-NC 5 83% 4 Complete Record All six fields filled with valid values 6 100%

Provenance: The records are illustrative cases written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The formula follows the chapter section "Metadata Completeness".

Rules: Completeness is (valid fields / 6) x 100, rounded to the nearest whole number. In record 3 the license value does not match the page, so it counts as invalid, which gives 5 valid fields. Each record has exactly one correct answer.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees a record with its six fields and their values.
  2. The learner marks each field as valid or not valid, and counts the valid fields.
  3. The learner enters the completeness percent and presses Check.
  4. The sim shows the valid fields, the arithmetic, and the correct percent.
  5. After record 4 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 4 records in the fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [percent]. [n] of 6 fields are valid." Incorrect: "Not quite. [n] of 6 fields are valid, which is [percent]. [Why a field was invalid, if one was]". The summary shows "[n] of 4 correct on the first attempt". At 3 or more it adds "You can measure completeness." Below 3 it shows the arithmetic for each missed record.

Starting State: Record 1 with its six fields shown and no answer entered. The question shown is "What is this record's completeness?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter says completeness is valid fields divided by fields expected, times 100, that Watershed Basics today has 2 of 6 fields and 33 percent, and that a placeholder or a mismatched value counts as not valid.

The last illustration of the metadata half shows a record as a card. It has eight numbered markers, one for each part of a good record.

docs.title: Diagram: Anatomy of a Metadata Record
docs.text:
Anatomy of a Metadata Record

Type: infographic sim-id: metadata-record-anatomy Library: html Status: Specified Bloom Level: Remember Bloom Verb: identify Learning Objective: The learner will identify the eight parts of a metadata record from a description of how each looks, with at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Metadata Record, Dublin Core, Keywords, Machine-Readable Metadata, and the six core field sections (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: In quiz mode the learner clicks the marker that matches a visual hint. A click is correct when it matches the marker named in the Hint column of Content. Mastery is at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Hovering in explore mode is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) The description repeats the title. (2) The identifier is the file name. (3) Keywords and subject are the same field.

Instructional Rationale: Identifying the parts of a record is a Remember-level task, and an illustration of a card gives each field a place. The quiz asks the learner to recognize a field by its look, which is how they will read a real record.

Content:

The illustration is a text-free flat drawing of a catalog record card. At the top is a wide bar for a title. Below it, in a column, are seven rows. The first holds a short bar and a small person icon. The second holds a short bar and a small tag icon. The third holds a block of three thin lines. The fourth holds a short bar and a small graduation-cap icon. The fifth holds a short bar and a small scales icon. The sixth holds a row of three small rounded tags. The seventh holds a short bar with a small calendar icon and a long underlined bar. The eight markers:

# Label Hint (describes the look, not the name) Description Tip 1 Title The wide bar at the top of the card. The name of the resource, the first thing a searcher sees. Make it specific and unique. 2 Creator The row with a short bar and a small person icon. The person or organization responsible, the basis for credit. Use one consistent name form. 3 Subject The row with a short bar and a small tag icon. The topic, as specific terms from a shared list where possible. Use more than one specific term. 4 Description The block of three thin lines. A short summary of what the resource is and who it is for. Use the words a searcher would type. 5 Education level The row with a short bar and a small graduation-cap icon. The learners the resource is written for. Use one scheme across all records. 6 Rights The row with a short bar and a small scales icon. The license, with its version and a link. It must match the statement on the page. 7 Keywords The row of three small rounded tags. Free words a searcher might use, in addition to the subject. Add everyday terms, and avoid stuffing. 8 Date and identifier The row with a small calendar icon and a long underlined bar. When the resource was made or updated, and its permanent address. Use an address that will not change.

Provenance: The parts follow the chapter sections "Metadata Record", "Dublin Core", "The Six Core Fields", and "Keywords". The illustration is synthetic, and the sim labels the card "illustrative example".

Rules: Each hint matches exactly one marker. The illustration contains no text, so every label comes from the table above. Markers are numbered 1 to 8 in the order of the table.

Learner Activity:

  1. In explore mode the learner hovers or clicks a marker and reads its label, description, and tip.
  2. In quiz mode the sim shows a hint.
  3. The learner clicks the marker they think the hint describes.
  4. If the first click is wrong, the sim says so and lets the learner try once more. If the second click is also wrong, the sim reveals the marker and its description.
  5. After all 8 hints the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 8 hints in a shuffled order, two attempts each. Only a correct first click counts as evidence. Correct: "Correct: [label]. [Description]". First wrong click: "Not quite. Look again at the hint: [hint]". Second wrong click: "This is [label]. [Description]". The summary shows "[n] of 8 correct on the first attempt". At 7 or more it adds "You can read a metadata record." Below 7 it lists the labels of the missed parts.

Starting State: The illustration with eight numbered markers, explore mode active, and the prompt "Hover a marker to see what it is."

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's complete record for Watershed Basics has the fields title, creator, subject, description, education level, rights, date, language, identifier, and type, and its six core fields are title, author, subject, grade level, license, and description.

docs.title: Scoring the Three Reusability Metrics
docs.text:
The open license and modularity checks appear earlier in this chapter. The metadata metric has its own ten checks, and a failed check is serious when the resource cannot be identified at all, which is the case when the title or the author is missing. When a serious check fails, choose the lower number in a two-number band. Otherwise choose the higher number.

# Check Serious if it fails? 1 A title is recorded Yes 2 An author or creator is recorded Yes 3 A subject is recorded No 4 A grade level or audience is recorded No 5 The license is recorded in the metadata, and matches the page No 6 A description is recorded No 7 Keywords or controlled subject terms are included No 8 A date and a permanent address are recorded No 9 The metadata is in a machine-readable form No 10 The record is complete and accurate, with no placeholders No

Worked example: Watershed Basics. The reviewer applies the checks to the reading from Chapter 3.

# Result Evidence 1 Pass The title is in the page's head. 2 Pass The author is named in a tag in the page's head. 3 Fail No subject is recorded. 4 Fail No grade level is recorded in the metadata. 5 Fail The file properties carry no license. 6 Fail No description is recorded. 7 Fail No keywords are recorded. 8 Pass A publication date and the page address are present. 9 Pass The title and author are in tags in the page's head that software can read. 10 Fail Four of six core fields are empty, so the record is not complete.

Four of ten checks pass, a share of 40 percent, in the 3 to 4 band. Neither serious check failed, because the title and the author are present, so the reviewer chooses the higher number, 4, the score on the Chapter 3 worksheet. Completeness is 2 of 6 core fields, or 33 percent, and the metric's checks reach further than the six fields.

The last MicroSim of the chapter is a scoring practice for all three metrics. It shows nine cases, three for each metric, and for each one you choose the metric score.

docs.title: Diagram: Reusability Metrics Scorer
docs.text:
Reusability Metrics Scorer

Type: microsim sim-id: reusability-metrics-scorer Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: apply Learning Objective: The learner will apply the ten open license checks, the ten modularity checks, and the ten metadata checks, with the Chapter 3 scoring rules, to choose the metric score for each of nine cases, with at least 8 of 9 scores exactly correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: The Open License Metric, The Modularity Metric, The Metadata Metric, Metric Score, Scoring Descriptor (all defined in this chapter or in Chapter 3 above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each case the learner chooses a whole-number score from 0 to 10 after seeing the ten check results. A score is correct when it equals the Correct score column in Content. Mastery is at least 8 of 9 scores correct on the first attempt. Opening the check lists and the descriptor table is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) The three metrics use different scoring rules. (2) A serious failure always drops a full band. (3) Full completeness of the six fields earns a 10.

Instructional Rationale: Applying a scoring procedure to new cases is an Apply-level task. Nine cases across three check lists make the learner run the same procedure on different lists, with different serious checks.

Content:

The three ten-check lists are those in the chapter sections "The Open License Metric", "The Modularity Metric", and "Scoring the Three Reusability Metrics", each marked serious or not. The descriptor bands applied to the share of checks passed: 0% is 0; 1% to 24% is 1 to 2; 25% to 49% is 3 to 4; 50% to 74% is 5 to 6; 75% to 89% is 7 to 8; 90% to 100% is 9 to 10. Within a two-number band, choose the lower number when a serious check failed and the higher number otherwise. A score of 10 requires every check to pass.

The nine cases:

# Metric Resource Checks failed Checks passed Share Band Serious failure? Correct score Why (shown as feedback) 1 Open license Open Algebra None 10 100% 9 to 10 No 10 Every check passed. 2 Open license Watershed Basics 8 9 90% 9 to 10 Yes, check 8 9 A failed check means the score is 9, and the failure is serious. 3 Open license Mixed Rights Packet 2, 3, 6, 8, 9 5 (checks 1, 4, 5, 7, 10) 50% 5 to 6 Yes, check 8 5 A serious failure puts the score at the lower number. 4 Modularity Open Algebra None 10 100% 9 to 10 No 10 Every check passed. 5 Modularity Watershed Basics 2, 4, 7, 8, 9 5 50% 5 to 6 Yes, check 2 5 Components with no address of their own is serious, so the lower number applies. 6 Modularity Single Long Page 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 9, 10 3 (checks 4, 6, 7) 30% 3 to 4 Yes, checks 1 and 2 3 The page cannot be taken apart, which is serious, so the lower number applies. 7 Metadata Open Algebra None 10 100% 9 to 10 No 10 Every check passed. 8 Metadata Watershed Basics 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 10 4 40% 3 to 4 No 4 The title and author are present, so no serious check failed and the higher number applies. 9 Metadata Untitled Files 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9, 10 1 (check 8) 10% 1 to 2 Yes, checks 1 and 2 1 The files have no title or author, which is serious, so the lower number applies.

Provenance: The ten-check lists and the bands follow this chapter and Chapter 3. The nine cases are illustrative cases written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". Cases 2, 5, and 8 are the chapter's worked examples.

Rules: A score is the band chosen from the share passed, and then the number chosen within the band by the serious-failure rule. A band of 9 to 10 gives 10 only when every check passes. Each case has exactly one correct score.

Learner Activity:

  1. The sim shows case 1 with its ten check results and the name of the metric.
  2. The learner may open the check list and the descriptor table.
  3. The learner chooses a score from 0 to 10, and the choice is committed.
  4. The sim shows the count of passes, the band, whether a serious check failed, and the correct score with the Why text.
  5. After case 9 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 9 cases in the fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [score]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. [passes] checks passed, which is [share] and the [band] band. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 9 correct on the first attempt". At 8 or more it adds "You can score all three reusability metrics." Below 8 it lists the Why text of each missed case.

Starting State: Case 1 with all ten results shown and no score chosen. The question shown is "What open license score does this resource earn?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's worked examples score Watershed Basics 9 on open license, 5 on modularity, and 4 on metadata, each with the failed checks named in the chapter.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• The open license metric asks for a clear open license on every component. License clarity means one specific license, a version, a link, and a scope, stated the same way everywhere.
  • Modular content is built from separate pieces. A standalone component passes the lift test, cross-reference dependence breaks it, component granularity sets the useful size, and an embeddable component can sit inside another page. The modularity metric scores all of this.
  • The metadata metric asks whether the resource can be found and identified. A metadata record holds the fields, Dublin Core names them, and the six core fields are the title field, author field, subject field, grade level field, license field, and description field.
  • Keywords and a controlled vocabulary help search. LRMI and Schema.org markup carry educational metadata in a form search engines read, and machine-readable metadata lets software do the reading.
  • Metadata completeness counts valid fields. It does not measure quality, and a wrong value is worse than a blank.

You Can Check Whether It Can Be Found and Reused

You can now score a resource's license, test whether its parts stand alone, read and write a metadata record, and score all three reusability metrics with evidence. A resource that can be found, understood, and lifted out is a resource that other teachers can actually use.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Modularity and Metadata
docs.text: Test your understanding of license clarity, standalone components, Dublin Core, the six core metadata fields, and metadata completeness with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. What does a reviewer do in the lift test for a standalone component?
docs.text:
1. Counts how many pages the component spans in the original resource and compares it with the other components
  2. Copies the component to a new place and checks that it still works there with everything it needs
  3. Asks the author whether the component was intended to stand alone, and accepts the answer
  4. Runs an automated accessibility checker on the component and records the number of errors
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. A standalone component works on its own, without the rest of the resource around it. The test is to lift it out: copy the piece into an empty file and read it cold. A reading that begins "as we saw in the last section" fails, a quiz that refers to "the diagram above" fails, and a simulation that needs a script from a sibling folder fails. A component passes when everything it needs travels with it.

Concept Tested: Standalone Component

See: Standalone Component

docs.title: 2. In Dublin Core, which element holds a resource's license or rights statement?
docs.text:
1. Source
  2. Relation
  3. Description
  4. Rights
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Dublin Core is a standard vocabulary of 15 core elements. The Rights element records the license or rights statement, which is why this book's license field maps to it. Author maps to Creator, and grade level uses the education level term because Dublin Core has no core element for it. Source (A) records a resource from which this one is derived, and Relation (B) records a related resource.

Concept Tested: Dublin Core

See: Dublin Core

docs.title: 3. Why does the chapter say that a wrong value in a metadata field is worse than a blank field?
docs.text:
1. Blank fields are scored as valid, while wrong values are scored as invalid
  2. A blank field lets a search tool fill in the correct value automatically
  3. A wrong value makes a record look complete and sends searchers to the wrong place
  4. A wrong value always makes the resource fail the open license metric
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Metadata completeness counts fields filled with valid values. A placeholder such as "TBD", a guess, or a license that does not match the page counts as invalid, so the record looks complete when it is not. It also misleads: a record that says CC BY next to a page that says CC BY-NC invites a dispute. Leave a field empty until you know the value, and then count it as missing.

Concept Tested: Metadata Completeness

See: Metadata Completeness

docs.title: 4. How do subject terms differ from keywords in a metadata record?
docs.text:
1. Subject terms are written for machines to read, while keywords are written only for people
  2. Subject terms describe what the resource is about, often from a shared list, while keywords are free extra words
  3. Subject terms are free text with no rules at all, while keywords must come from a fixed list
  4. Subject terms record the grade level of the resource, while keywords record only its topic
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Subject terms describe the topic, ideally from a shared list such as the ERIC Thesaurus, and two to five usually serve a resource. Keywords supplement them with everyday and alternative terms, such as "stormwater" beside "runoff." Too few keywords make a resource hard to find, and too many unrelated ones, called keyword stuffing, make it appear in searches where it does not belong. A controlled vocabulary gathers variants under one term.

Concept Tested: Keywords

See: Keywords

docs.title: 5. Why do phrases such as "as shown above" and "see section 4" reduce a component's modularity?
docs.text:
1. Each phrase is a thread that breaks when the component is moved to a new place
  2. Each phrase makes the component too long to embed in another page
  3. The Dublin Core standard does not allow such phrases in a resource
  4. Each phrase prevents the component from carrying its own license
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Cross-reference dependence is the way a component relies on other parts of its resource. When the component moves, "above" points at nothing. The fix is to restate the idea in one sentence, or to link to the other piece by its own address, so the reference works wherever the component lands. A reviewer searches for words such as "above," "below," "earlier," "next section," and "the figure" and checks each one.

Concept Tested: Cross-Reference Dependence

See: Cross-Reference Dependence

docs.title: 6. A teacher embeds a simulation with an iframe whose src is just main.html. What is wrong, and what is the fix?
docs.text:
1. The width is fixed at a number of pixels, so it should be changed to 100 percent
  2. The frame has no title, so a title attribute should be added for screen reader users
  3. The simulation needs a login, so the iframe should be removed from the course page
  4. A relative address works only beside the original page, so use a complete public address
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. For a component to embed, it needs its own complete address, it must open with no login, and the frame must fit any page. A relative address such as main.html works only where that file sits next to the page. Replace it with a full address such as https://example.org/sims/runoff/main.html. The snippet gives no information about the width (A), the title (B), or a login (C), so the address is the clear defect.

Concept Tested: Embeddable Component

See: Embeddable Component

docs.title: 7. A metadata record has valid Title, Author, Subject, and Grade level fields, a License value of "TBD," and an empty Description. Using the six core fields, what is its metadata completeness?
docs.text:
1. 67 percent
  2. 83 percent
  3. 100 percent
  4. 50 percent
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Completeness is the number of fields filled with a valid value, divided by the number of fields expected, times 100. Only four fields are valid, because a placeholder such as "TBD" counts as invalid and the Description is empty. Four divided by six is about 0.67, so completeness is 67 percent. Counting the "TBD" field as valid would give 83 percent (B). Completeness shows what is missing and says nothing about whether what is there is good.

Concept Tested: Metadata Completeness

See: Metadata Completeness

docs.title: 8. A reviewer applies the ten modularity checks to a single long page. Checks 1 and 2 fail, which are serious, and so do checks 3, 5, 8, 9, and 10. Only checks 4, 6, and 7 pass. What score does the chapter's rule give?
docs.text:
1. 4, because 30 percent falls in the 3 to 4 band and the higher number in the band applies
  2. 5, because three checks passed and two serious checks failed, so the score is 5
  3. 3, because 30 percent falls in the 3 to 4 band and failing checks 1 and 2 is serious
  4. 1, because the page cannot be taken apart at all, so no points are earned
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Three of ten checks pass, a share of 30 percent, in the 3 to 4 band. Checks 1 and 2 are serious because failing them means the resource cannot be taken apart at all. When a serious check fails, choose the lower number in a two-number band, so the score is 3. The higher number (A) applies only when no serious check fails. The score depends on the share of checks passed and not on how many serious checks failed.

Concept Tested: Modularity Metric

See: The Modularity Metric

docs.title: 9. A teacher searches for "grade 6 watershed quiz." Record A has a clear title, subject terms, grades 6 to 7, a license, and a description of a reading and eight-question quiz. Record B has only the title "Reading 4." Record C has the title "Watershed Basics" and an author, with nothing else. Which analysis is best?
docs.text:
1. All three records are found equally, because a title alone is enough for a search to match
  2. A is found and understood, B cannot be found, and C may be found but its grade and license are unknown
  3. Record C ranks highest, because naming an author helps a search engine more than any other field of the record
  4. Record B is found, because a unique title such as "Reading 4" always matches any search
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. A search matches the words in a resource's metadata. Record A has fields that mention the topic, grade, and contents, so it is found and a teacher can tell what it is. Record B has no field that mentions a watershed. Record C may match on its title, but without a grade level or license the teacher cannot tell whether it fits or whether she may reuse it. A resource whose metadata is missing may as well not exist.

Concept Tested: Metadata Metric

See: The Metadata Metric

docs.title: 10. A reviewer finds that a page footer says CC BY-NC, while the license field in the metadata says CC BY. Which analysis is best?
docs.text:
1. The record and the page disagree, so the license is unclear and must be confirmed and made to match
  2. The page always wins automatically, so the metadata can stay as it is and be ignored
  3. There is no problem, because both are Creative Commons licenses and both allow reuse
  4. The more permissive license is the valid one, so CC BY applies to the whole resource
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The license field must agree with the statement on the page, and a mismatch invites a dispute. Unclear licensing is a risk for the reuser, because the safe assumption is that no permission was granted. Both licenses are Creative Commons licenses, but they grant different permissions, since NC bars commercial use (C). The reviewer should trace the work to its owner, confirm the license, and fix both places, and a mismatched value counts as invalid.

Concept Tested: License Field

See: License Field

docs.title: References: Modularity and Metadata
docs.text:
1. Dublin Core - Wikipedia - Describes the fifteen-element Dublin Core metadata set, its history, and its use in libraries and repositories. The basis of the metadata record taught in this chapter.

  2. Metadata - Wikipedia - Surveys kinds of metadata, standards, and uses, from library catalogs to web pages. Background for scoring whether a resource carries complete, useful metadata.

  3. Learning object - Wikipedia - Explains the learning object idea of small, self-contained, reusable units of instruction and the standards built around it. Supports the chapter's modularity metric.

  4. The Instructional Use of Learning Objects - David A. Wiley (ed.) - Agency for Instructional Technology and AECT (2002) - Wiley's writing on learning objects popularized the LEGO-block metaphor for small reusable pieces and argued that pieces do not combine at random. That is why a module must stand alone yet fit its neighbors.

  5. Metadata - Jeffrey Pomerantz - MIT Press (2015) - No single signature analogy stands out for this topic, so this is the short introduction most praised for making metadata clear to non-specialists. It explains standards, schemas, and uses in plain language.

  6. Metadata Basics - Dublin Core Metadata Initiative - The DCMI introduction to metadata and the Dublin Core style, listing the fifteen core elements such as title, creator, subject, and description. The primary reference for the chapter's core fields.

  7. DCMI Metadata Terms - Dublin Core Metadata Initiative - The official definitions of every Dublin Core term. Lets reviewers check exactly what a field such as rights, format, or audience is meant to record.

  8. LearningResource - Schema.org - The Schema.org type for educational materials, with properties such as educational level, learning resource type, and what the resource teaches. Shows how machine-readable metadata describes an OER.

  9. Learning Resource Metadata Initiative (LRMI) - Dublin Core Metadata Initiative - Describes the vocabulary, maintained by DCMI, that adds educational properties such as alignment to standards and typical age range to resource descriptions. Supports scoring education-specific metadata.

  10. Introduction to Metadata - Getty Research Institute - A free online edition of the Getty's guide to metadata types, standards, and crosswalks, with examples from cultural collections. Gives deeper background for writing consistent records.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Explains how to score portability: browser compatibility, no-login access, iframe embedding, LMS import, Common Cartridge, and the platform lock-in that stops a resource from moving. It finishes the reusability metrics and builds on the components and metadata of the previous chapter. After this chapter you can test whether a resource runs in a browser without a login, embeds in another page, and moves between platforms.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 12 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Portability Metric 15 Browser Compatibility 2 No-Login Access 3 Iframe Embedding 2 Link Sharing 1 Export Format 5 LMS Import 3 Common Cartridge 1 LTI Integration 1 Responsive Layout 1 Offline Access 1 Platform Lock-In 1

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 3: The Ten-Metric Rubric and Scoring
  • Chapter 4: Open File Formats and Version Control
  • Chapter 9: Modularity and Metadata

Can It Travel?

A resource that is open, well made, and easy to find still fails a teacher if it will not open on her laptop, asks her for an account, or breaks inside her course page. This chapter gives you the tests that tell you whether a resource can travel. Let's dive in and check the evidence!

Chapter 9 asked whether a reuser can find a resource and lift out the part she needs. This chapter asks the last reusability question: once she has it, will it work where she wants to use it? A resource that runs only in one company's system, needs a login, or falls apart on a phone is not portable, however good its license. The tenth and last metric of the rubric measures that, and it finishes the ten-metric rubric.

docs.title: The Portability Metric
docs.text:
The portability metric is the tenth metric of the rubric. It asks whether a resource runs in a browser with no login and can be shared or embedded elsewhere. A portable resource goes with the reuser to wherever she teaches: a course page, a learning management system, a phone, a classroom with a weak internet connection. The metric is scored with ten checks, listed at the end of this chapter. The sections between them take each idea in turn.

Worked example: five questions a reuser asks. A teacher who finds an open simulation asks five questions before she commits to it, and each one is a portability check.

The question What it tests Will it open on my computer and my students' devices? Browser compatibility and responsive layout Do my students need an account? No-login access Can I put it on my course page? Iframe embedding and link sharing Can I take a copy, or bring it into my LMS? Export format and LMS import Will I be stuck if the host disappears? Platform lock-in and offline access

docs.title: Browser Compatibility
docs.text: Browser compatibility is a resource's ability to work correctly in the main web browsers, such as Chrome, Firefox, Safari, and Edge, and in recent versions of each. Resources built from open web standards, which means plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, usually work everywhere. Resources that depend on browser plug-ins do not. Adobe Flash is the cautionary example: it powered many educational animations and was discontinued at the end of 2020, and the content that depended on it stopped working. A reviewer opens a resource in at least three browsers and notes any that fail.

docs.title: No-Login Access
docs.text: No-login access means a learner or teacher can open and use a resource without creating an account or signing in. A login is a barrier in three ways. It stops a resource from embedding in someone else's page, because the frame would show a sign-in form. It blocks sharing by link, since the person who receives the link cannot open it. And it adds a privacy burden, because an account holds personal data. Some content, such as an answer key for teachers, may reasonably need a login. A resource that claims to be open should offer its learner-facing content without one.

docs.title: Iframe Embedding
docs.text: Iframe embedding is the placing of a resource inside another page, as Chapter 9 introduced. A component may pass the test on its own and still fail on a particular platform, for three common reasons. The server may tell browsers not to show the page inside a frame, which some sites do for security. The page may be served over an insecure connection, which a secure page's browser refuses to mix in. Or the platform may strip the frame out of the pages its users write. So a reviewer tests the embed on more than one platform, and records which worked.

docs.title: Link Sharing
docs.text: Link sharing is the ability to send a person a web address that opens the resource, or a specific part of it, directly. A good link is permanent, goes straight to the content, and works for the person who receives it. Links fail when the address changes with every visit, when it opens a home page instead of the component, or when the link only works for someone already signed in. For a resource made of components, each component should have its own address, as the modularity metric asked.

docs.title: Export Format
docs.text: An export format is a form in which a resource or a copy of it can be downloaded and kept, ideally in an open format from Chapter 4, such as HTML, Markdown, or a standard package. Export is the exit door. A resource that can be exported can be backed up, moved to a new host, and worked on offline. A resource whose only copy lives inside a web service, with no download, is exactly as portable as the service is permanent.

docs.title: LMS Import
docs.text: LMS import is the ability to bring a resource into a learning management system, the software that schools use to run courses, such as Canvas, Moodle, Blackboard, or Brightspace. A teacher can bring an OER into an LMS in four ways: she can link to it, embed it, upload its files, or import it as a package. The more of these a resource supports, the more teachers can use it where they already work. A reviewer tests at least the link and the embed in a real LMS, or a test site, and notes what happened.

docs.title: Common Cartridge
docs.text: Common Cartridge is a standard from 1EdTech, the education technology standards group, for packaging course content so that it can be imported into different learning management systems. A cartridge is a single compressed file that holds the content together with a manifest, a list that says what is inside and how it is organized. A unit exported as a Common Cartridge from one LMS can be imported into another, which is why it is the common exchange form for course material. Not every resource offers one, but those that do travel farther.

docs.title: LTI Integration
docs.text: LTI integration uses Learning Tools Interoperability, a 1EdTech standard that lets an external tool open inside an LMS and exchange information with it, such as sending a learner's score back to the gradebook. An LTI tool looks like part of the course and runs on another company's server. It is more powerful than a link and more demanding, because it passes information about learners from one system to another, which raises the privacy questions of Chapter 13. For the portability metric, LTI counts as a plus where a resource claims an LMS integration, and not as a requirement.

docs.title: Reaching Every Learner and Every Setting
Responsive Layout
docs.text: A responsive layout is a page design that adapts to the size of the screen, so that the same page is readable on a phone, a tablet, and a large monitor. A page with a fixed width forces a phone user to scroll sideways and pinch, and a resource inside an iframe on a narrow page overflows. Responsive pages use flexible widths and text that wraps. A reviewer tests by narrowing the browser window to the width of a phone and checking that nothing is cut off or overlaps.

docs.title: Offline Access
docs.text: Offline access is the ability to use a resource without an internet connection, by downloading it or saving it first. It matters for classrooms and homes with unreliable connections, for field trips, and for learners who pay for data. A single web page with its files can often be saved and opened from a folder, as long as it does not load code or images from elsewhere on the web. A resource that offers a download, or that works from a saved folder, gains here.

docs.title: Platform Lock-In
docs.text:
Platform lock-in is the dependence of a resource on one platform in a way that makes leaving costly or impossible. Signs include content stored only in a vendor's proprietary format, no export, features that exist only inside the vendor's system, and accounts that would be lost on leaving. Lock-in is a risk to the author and to every reuser, because the resource lives only as long as the platform's business model. The test is simple: could you move the resource to another host in an afternoon, with nothing lost?

A Free Platform Can Still Be a Cage

A resource can be free to read and open-licensed and still live only inside one vendor's system, with no export and no copy. Look for a way out before you rely on it, and score the metric on whether you could actually leave.

The first MicroSim of the chapter sorts barriers. It shows ten problems that a reuser might meet, and for each one you name the portability idea it breaks.

docs.title: Diagram: Portability Barrier Sorter
docs.text:
Portability Barrier Sorter

Type: microsim sim-id: portability-barrier-sorter Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: classify Learning Objective: The learner will classify each of ten reuse problems by the portability idea it breaks, with at least 9 of 10 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: The Portability Metric and the ten portability sections of this chapter (all defined above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each problem the learner commits one of ten ideas. A choice is correct when it matches the Correct idea column in Content. Mastery is at least 9 of 10 correct on the first attempt. Reading the idea list is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A login problem and a lock-in problem are the same. (2) A link that fails is an embedding problem. (3) Offline access means no internet is ever needed.

Instructional Rationale: Classifying a problem by the idea it breaks is an Understand-level action that connects a symptom to a check. Ten problems, one per idea, teach the learner to name what is actually wrong.

Content:

The ten ideas: Browser compatibility, No-login access, Iframe embedding, Link sharing, Export format, LMS import, LTI integration, Responsive layout, Offline access, Platform lock-in.

The ten problems:

# Problem shown to the learner Correct idea Why (shown as feedback) 1 The page works in one browser and shows an error in the others. Browser compatibility The page does not work across the main browsers. 2 Visitors must create an account before they can see the first page. No-login access An account is a barrier to use. 3 A teacher's course page shows a blank frame where the simulation should be. Iframe embedding The page cannot be shown inside another page. 4 The address changes every time the page is opened, so a saved link fails. Link sharing There is no stable address to send. 5 The only download is a file that opens in one company's program. Export format There is no open copy to keep. 6 A teacher cannot bring the unit into her LMS as a package. LMS import The resource offers no way to import it. 7 A quiz tool opened from the LMS cannot send scores back to the gradebook. LTI integration The tool and the LMS do not exchange information. 8 On a phone the text is tiny and the right half of the page is cut off. Responsive layout The page does not adapt to the screen width. 9 A field trip has no internet, and the resource offers no download. Offline access The resource cannot be used without a connection. 10 The author's content exists only inside one company's service, with no export. Platform lock-in Leaving the platform would lose the content.

Provenance: The problems are illustrative cases written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The ideas follow the chapter sections on each concept.

Rules: Each problem has exactly one correct idea, and the ten ideas are all different.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one problem and the ten ideas.
  2. The learner may open the idea list. Opening it does not change the score.
  3. The learner chooses an idea, and the choice is committed.
  4. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text.
  5. After problem 10 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 10 problems in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [idea]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. This breaks [idea]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 10 correct on the first attempt". At 9 or more it adds "You can name what stops a resource from traveling." Below 9 it lists the Why text of each missed problem.

Starting State: The first problem and the ten ideas. The question shown is "Which portability idea does this break?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's ten ideas are browser compatibility, no-login access, iframe embedding, link sharing, export format, LMS import, LTI integration, responsive layout, offline access, and platform lock-in.

The second MicroSim practices diagnosis. It shows six reports from embed tests, and for each one you name the cause.

docs.title: Diagram: Embed Failure Diagnoser
docs.text:
Embed Failure Diagnoser

Type: microsim sim-id: embed-failure-diagnoser Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: differentiate Learning Objective: The learner will differentiate six causes of an embedding result by choosing the cause that each of six test reports describes, with at least 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Iframe Embedding, No-Login Access, Responsive Layout, Embeddable Component (defined in Chapter 9) (all defined above this block or in Chapter 9).

Evidence of Mastery: For each report the learner commits one of six causes. A choice is correct when it matches the Correct cause column in Content. Mastery is at least 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Reading the cause list is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A blank frame always means the file is missing. (2) If the page works on its own, it will embed. (3) A sign-in form in the frame is a platform error.

Instructional Rationale: Differentiating among causes is an Analyze-level action, because the learner must read the evidence in a report and decide which cause fits it. Six reports that look alike on the surface teach the learner to read the details.

Content:

The six causes: Frame blocked by the host, Insecure address in a secure page, Needs a login, Script path broken, Layout not responsive, Works.

The six reports:

# Test report shown to the learner Correct cause Why (shown as feedback) 1 The frame stays blank, and the browser's message says the page refused to be displayed in a frame. Frame blocked by the host The server told browsers not to show the page inside a frame. 2 The frame is blank on a secure page, and the simulation's address begins with http and not https. Insecure address in a secure page A browser refuses to mix an insecure frame into a secure page. 3 The frame shows a sign-in form. Needs a login The resource requires an account, so it cannot embed for visitors. 4 The page loads, the buttons do nothing, and the browser's message says a script file was not found. Script path broken The page loads a script by a path that does not exist at the new location. 5 The frame shows the simulation, and every control responds. Works The embed passed. 6 The simulation appears, and on a phone the right side is cut off. Layout not responsive The page has a fixed width and does not adapt to the frame.

Provenance: The reports are illustrative cases written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The causes follow the chapter sections "Iframe Embedding", "No-Login Access", and "Responsive Layout".

Rules: Each report has exactly one correct cause, and the six causes are all different.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads one test report and sees the six causes.
  2. The learner chooses a cause, and the choice is committed.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text.
  4. After report 6 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 6 reports in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [cause]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. The cause is [cause]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 6 correct on the first attempt". At 5 or more it adds "You can read an embed test." Below 5 it lists the Why text of each missed report.

Starting State: The first report and the six causes. The question shown is "What explains this result?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter says an embed can fail because the host blocks frames, because an insecure address is shown in a secure page, because a login is required, or because the layout is fixed, and the sim adds a broken script path.

The third MicroSim is a decision exercise. For each of six teacher needs you choose how best to bring an open resource into a learning management system.

docs.title: Diagram: LMS Integration Chooser
docs.text:
LMS Integration Chooser

Type: microsim sim-id: lms-integration-chooser Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: apply Learning Objective: The learner will apply the differences among a link, an embed, a Common Cartridge import, and an LTI tool to choose the best way to bring a resource into an LMS for each of six teacher needs, with at least 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: LMS Import, Common Cartridge, LTI Integration, Iframe Embedding, Link Sharing (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each need the learner commits one of four methods. A choice is correct when it matches the Correct method column in Content. Mastery is at least 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Reading the method list is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) An embed copies the resource into the LMS. (2) A Common Cartridge only works inside one LMS. (3) LTI is just a fancy link.

Instructional Rationale: Choosing a method for a need is an Apply-level action. Six needs that map to four methods teach the learner what each method does and does not give a teacher.

Content:

The four methods: Link (students open the resource at its own address), Embed (the resource appears on the course page through a frame), Common Cartridge import (a whole unit is copied into the LMS as a package), LTI tool (an external tool opens inside the LMS and can send results back).

The six needs:

# Teacher need shown to the learner Correct method Why (shown as feedback) 1 "I want students to open one reading in a new tab." Link A link opens the resource at its own address. 2 "I want a simulation to appear on my course page." Embed A frame shows the simulation inside the page. 3 "I want to copy a whole unit, with pages, quizzes, and files, into my course." Common Cartridge import A package carries the whole unit into the LMS. 4 "I want an external quiz tool to send each student's score to the LMS gradebook." LTI tool LTI lets the tool exchange information with the LMS. 5 "I want colleagues in another school, with a different LMS, to receive the same unit." Common Cartridge import A cartridge is the common exchange form between LMSs. 6 "I want students to read chapter 4 of an open textbook." Link A link to the chapter is enough.

Provenance: The needs are illustrative cases written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The methods follow the chapter sections "LMS Import", "Common Cartridge", "LTI Integration", "Iframe Embedding", and "Link Sharing".

Rules: Each need has exactly one correct method. Two needs call for a Link, one for an Embed, two for a Common Cartridge import, and one for an LTI tool.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one need and the four methods.
  2. The learner may open the method descriptions. Opening them does not change the score.
  3. The learner chooses a method, and the choice is committed.
  4. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text.
  5. After need 6 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 6 needs in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [method]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. The best method is [method]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 6 correct on the first attempt". At 5 or more it adds "You can choose how to bring a resource into an LMS." Below 5 it lists the Why text of each missed need.

Starting State: The first need and the four methods. The question shown is "Which method fits this need?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter says a teacher can bring an OER into an LMS by link, embed, file upload, or package import, that a Common Cartridge is a single package that moves between LMSs, and that LTI lets an external tool exchange information with an LMS.

docs.title: Scoring Portability
docs.text:
Portability is scored with ten checks. A failed check is serious when it stops a reuser from using the resource at all in a common setting, which covers a resource that does not open in the main browsers, one that needs a login, and one that cannot be embedded. When a serious check fails, choose the lower number in a two-number band. Otherwise choose the higher number.

# Check Serious if it fails? 1 The resource opens without errors in at least three current browsers Yes 2 No login or account is needed to view the learner-facing content Yes 3 The resource, and each component, has a permanent address that can be shared No 4 It embeds by iframe on test platforms without changes Yes 5 The layout adapts to a phone-width screen No 6 A downloadable copy in an open format is offered No 7 It can be brought into an LMS by link, embed, or package No 8 Where an LMS integration is claimed, it works No 9 The resource can be used offline from a saved copy No 10 Nothing is lost by moving it to another host, so there is no lock-in No

A check that does not apply, such as the LMS integration check for a resource that claims none, counts as passed.

Worked example: Watershed Basics. The reviewer applies the checks to the reading from Chapter 3.

# Result Evidence 1 Pass The page opens without errors in three browsers. 2 Pass No login is needed. 3 Pass Each section has its own address. 4 Fail The iframe embed works on 2 of 3 test platforms. On the third the quiz script fails, for the broken relative path that the Chapter 9 modularity review found. 5 Pass The layout adapts to a phone-width screen. 6 Pass HTML and Markdown downloads are offered. 7 Pass The reading links into an LMS and embeds on two platforms. 8 Pass The resource claims no LMS integration, so the check does not apply. 9 Fail The page loads its fonts and a quiz library from other sites, so a saved copy loses its styling and the quiz stops working without an internet connection. 10 Pass Nothing is tied to one vendor, and the files move with no loss.

Eight of ten checks pass, a share of 80 percent, in the 7 to 8 band. Check 4 failed and is serious, so the reviewer chooses the lower number, 7, the score on the Chapter 3 worksheet. That worksheet recorded the embed result. The full check also finds the offline gap.

Test in a Private Window

Open the resource in a private or incognito browser window, which carries none of your sign-ins or saved settings. If it opens there with no login, you have seen what a stranger will see.

The last MicroSim of the chapter is a scoring practice. It shows five resources with their ten check results, and for each one you choose the metric score.

docs.title: Diagram: Portability Metric Scorer
docs.text:
Portability Metric Scorer

Type: microsim sim-id: portability-metric-scorer Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: apply Learning Objective: The learner will apply the ten portability checks and the Chapter 3 scoring rules to choose the metric score for each of five resources, with at least 4 of 5 scores exactly correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: The Portability Metric, Metric Score, Scoring Descriptor (all defined in this chapter or in Chapter 3 above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each resource the learner chooses a whole-number score from 0 to 10 after seeing the ten check results. A score is correct when it equals the Correct score column in Content. Mastery is at least 4 of 5 scores correct on the first attempt. Opening the check list and the descriptor table is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Every failed check lowers the score equally. (2) A free platform is automatically portable. (3) A check that does not apply counts as failed.

Instructional Rationale: Applying a scoring procedure to new cases is an Apply-level task. Five resources that differ in how many checks fail and whether a serious check fails make the learner use every step: count, band, then choose within the band.

Content:

The ten checks, each marked serious or not, are those in the chapter's check table. The descriptor bands applied to the share of checks passed: 0% is 0; 1% to 24% is 1 to 2; 25% to 49% is 3 to 4; 50% to 74% is 5 to 6; 75% to 89% is 7 to 8; 90% to 100% is 9 to 10. Within a two-number band, choose the lower number when a serious check failed and the higher number otherwise. A score of 10 requires every check to pass. A check that does not apply counts as passed.

The five resources:

# Resource Checks failed Checks passed Share Band Serious failure? Correct score Why (shown as feedback) 1 Open Algebra None 10 100% 9 to 10 No 10 Every check passed. 2 Watershed Basics 4 and 9 8 80% 7 to 8 Yes, check 4 7 Failing to embed on one platform is serious, so the lower number applies. 3 Login-Only Course 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 9, 10 3 (checks 1, 5, 8) 30% 3 to 4 Yes, checks 2 and 4 3 A required login and no embedding are serious, so the lower number applies. 4 Desktop-Only Page 1 and 5 8 80% 7 to 8 Yes, check 1 7 A page that does not open in the main browsers is serious, so the lower number applies. 5 Vendor Platform Module 4, 6, 7, and 10 6 (checks 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 9) 60% 5 to 6 Yes, check 4 5 The module cannot embed, which is serious, so the lower number applies.

Provenance: The ten checks and the bands follow the chapter section "Scoring Portability" and Chapter 3. The five resources are illustrative cases written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". Resource 2 is the chapter's worked example.

Rules: A score is the band chosen from the share passed, and then the number chosen within the band by the serious-failure rule. Each resource has exactly one correct score. For a band that holds a single number, that number is the score.

Learner Activity:

  1. The sim shows resource 1 with its ten check results.
  2. The learner may open the check list and the descriptor table.
  3. The learner chooses a score from 0 to 10, and the choice is committed.
  4. The sim shows the count of passes, the band, whether a serious check failed, and the correct score with the Why text.
  5. After resource 5 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 5 resources in the fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [score]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. [passes] checks passed, which is [share] and the [band] band. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 5 correct on the first attempt". At 4 or more it adds "You can score portability." Below 4 it lists the Why text of each missed resource.

Starting State: Resource 1 with all ten results shown and no score chosen. The question shown is "What portability score does this resource earn?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's worked example for Watershed Basics fails checks 4 and 9, passes 8 of 10, and scores 7, with the lower number chosen because the embed failure is serious.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• The portability metric asks whether a resource runs in a browser with no login and can be shared or embedded elsewhere. It completes the ten-metric rubric.
  • A portable resource has browser compatibility, offers no-login access, supports iframe embedding and link sharing, and adapts through a responsive layout.
  • An export format is the exit door. LMS import, a Common Cartridge package, and LTI integration bring a resource into the systems schools use.
  • Offline access keeps a resource usable without a connection, and platform lock-in is the dependence on one platform that makes leaving costly.

All Ten Metrics Are in Your Hands

You can now test whether a resource opens in the main browsers, needs a login, embeds in another page, and moves between platforms, and you can score portability with evidence. With this chapter you have met all ten metrics, and the rest of the book puts them to work.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Portability and Reuse Across Platforms
docs.text: Test your understanding of browser compatibility, no-login access, embedding, LMS import, Common Cartridge, and platform lock-in with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. What is a responsive layout?
docs.text:
1. A page design that adapts to the screen size, so one page reads well on phone, tablet, and monitor
  2. A page that responds to each quiz answer with a feedback message that explains the answer
  3. A page that loads faster when the learner is signed in to the learning platform
  4. A page that saves a copy of itself automatically so that it can be used offline when needed
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. A responsive layout uses flexible widths and text that wraps. A page with a fixed width forces a phone user to scroll sideways and pinch, and a resource inside an iframe on a narrow page overflows. A reviewer tests by narrowing the browser window to the width of a phone and checking that nothing is cut off or overlaps. Feedback messages (B) belong to the practice metric, and offline copies (D) belong to offline access.

Concept Tested: Responsive Layout

See: Responsive Layout

docs.title: 2. Which standard lets an external tool open inside a learning management system and exchange information with it, such as sending a learner's score back to the gradebook?
docs.text:
1. Common Cartridge
  2. LTI integration
  3. Iframe embedding
  4. Link sharing
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Learning Tools Interoperability, from the standards group 1EdTech, makes an external tool look like part of the course while it runs on another company's server. It is more powerful than a link and more demanding, because it passes information about learners between systems, which raises the privacy questions of Chapter 13. Common Cartridge (A) packages content for import, and an iframe (C) or a link (D) only displays or opens a page.

Concept Tested: LTI Integration

See: LTI Integration

docs.title: 3. Why is a required login a barrier to a resource's portability?
docs.text:
1. It always makes the resource cost money, because every account requires a paid subscription
  2. It makes the resource unreadable on phones, because login pages never adapt to small screens or to tablets
  3. It prevents the resource from carrying an open license, because licenses cannot cover accounts
  4. It stops embedding because the frame shows a sign-in form, blocks link sharing, and adds a privacy burden
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. A login breaks portability in three ways. A frame on someone else's page would show a sign-in form instead of the resource. A person who receives a link cannot open it. And an account holds personal data, which adds a privacy burden. Some content, such as a teacher's answer key, may reasonably need a login, but a resource that claims to be open should offer its learner-facing content without one.

Concept Tested: No-Login Access

See: No-Login Access

docs.title: 4. Why does the chapter say that a resource whose only copy lives inside a web service is "exactly as portable as the service is permanent"?
docs.text:
1. Web services always delete content after one year, so every hosted resource disappears
  2. Open licenses expire when a resource is hosted on a web service that charges a fee
  3. Without an export, a reuser cannot back up or move the resource, so it lasts only as long as the service
  4. Creative Commons requires every resource to offer an export format in order to be licensed
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. An export format is the exit door. A resource that can be downloaded in an open format, such as HTML, Markdown, or a standard package, can be backed up, moved to a new host, and used offline. A resource with no download depends entirely on the service that holds it. The risk is practical and not legal: licenses do not expire when a resource is hosted (B), and no license requires an export (D).

Concept Tested: Export Format

See: Export Format

docs.title: 5. Why are resources built from plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript usually more portable than resources that rely on browser plug-ins?
docs.text:
1. Plug-ins cannot display text or images, so pages that are built with them are always blank for readers
  2. Open web standards work in the main browsers, while a plug-in like Flash can be discontinued and stop working
  3. Plain HTML always downloads faster than any plug-in, so pages built from it load more quickly for readers
  4. Browsers require the learner to install a plug-in before they open any page at all
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Browser compatibility means working correctly in the main browsers, such as Chrome, Firefox, Safari, and Edge, and in recent versions of each. Resources built on open web standards usually work everywhere. Adobe Flash powered many educational animations, and when it was discontinued, the content that depended on it stopped working. A reviewer opens a resource in at least three browsers and notes any that fail.

Concept Tested: Browser Compatibility

See: Browser Compatibility

docs.title: 6. A teacher wants to copy a whole unit, with its pages, quizzes, and files, into her course, and she also wants a colleague who uses a different learning management system to receive the same unit. Which method fits best?
docs.text:
1. A link to each page of the unit
  2. An iframe embed of the unit's home page
  3. A Common Cartridge import
  4. An LTI tool
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. A Common Cartridge is a single compressed file that holds the content together with a manifest, a list of what is inside and how it is organized. It can be imported into different learning management systems, which is why it is the common exchange form for course material. Links (A) and embeds (B) leave the content at its original address, and an LTI tool (D) runs an external tool inside the course rather than copying a unit into it.

Concept Tested: LMS Import

See: Common Cartridge

docs.title: 7. A teacher places an iframe for an open simulation on a secure (https) course page. The frame stays blank, and the simulation's address begins with http. What is the most likely cause?
docs.text:
1. A browser refuses to mix an insecure frame into a secure page, so the address must use https
  2. The simulation's server tells browsers not to show the page inside a frame
  3. The simulation requires a login, so the frame shows a sign-in form instead
  4. The simulation uses a fixed layout that is cut off on a narrow phone screen
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Iframe embedding can fail on a particular platform for several reasons. The server may tell browsers not to show the page in a frame, the page may be served over an insecure connection that a secure page's browser refuses to mix in, or the platform may strip frames out of what its users write. A login would show a sign-in form (C), not a blank frame, and a fixed layout (D) would show the simulation cut off. Test on more than one platform.

Concept Tested: Iframe Embedding

See: Iframe Embedding

docs.title: 8. A reviewer applies the ten portability checks to a page that does not open in the main browsers. Checks 1 and 5 fail, and the other eight pass. What score does the chapter's rule give?
docs.text:
1. 8, because 80 percent falls in the 7 to 8 band and the higher number in the band applies
  2. 6, because two checks failed and each failed check subtracts two points from 10
  3. 7, because 80 percent falls in the 7 to 8 band and failing the browser check is serious
  4. 5, because failing the browser check caps the score at 5 whatever else passes
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Eight of ten checks pass, a share of 80 percent, which falls in the 7 to 8 band. A failed check is serious when it stops a reuser from using the resource at all in a common setting, and not opening in the main browsers, needing a login, and being unable to embed all qualify. When a serious check fails, choose the lower number in the band, so the score is 7. The higher number (A) applies only when no serious check fails.

Concept Tested: Portability Metric

See: Scoring Portability

docs.title: 9. A reviewer saves a resource's page to a folder and opens it without an internet connection. The styling is lost and the quiz stops working, because the page loads fonts and a quiz library from other websites. Which portability check does this reveal as failing?
docs.text:
1. Check 2, because a login is needed to view the content
  2. Check 5, because the layout does not adapt to a phone-width screen
  3. Check 6, because no downloadable copy in an open format is offered with the page
  4. Check 9, because the resource cannot be used offline from a saved copy
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Offline access is the ability to use a resource without an internet connection. A single web page with its files can often be saved and opened from a folder, as long as it does not load code or images from elsewhere on the web. Here the saved copy depends on outside fonts and a library, so it breaks. The page itself can be downloaded, so check 6 is not the failing check, and nothing in the description involves a login or a phone.

Concept Tested: Offline Access

See: Offline Access

docs.title: 10. An author builds a lesson on a free platform. The lesson is openly licensed and free to read, but its interactive parts exist only inside the vendor's system, and the platform offers no export. Which analysis is correct?
docs.text:
1. The resource is fully portable, because it is free to read and openly licensed
  2. The license grants permissions, but the content is locked in, so portability should score poorly
  3. The resource is portable, because learners do not need to pay anything to use it
  4. Lock-in is a risk only for the author and does not affect people who reuse the resource
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Platform lock-in is dependence on one platform in a way that makes leaving costly or impossible. Signs include content in a vendor's proprietary format, no export, features that exist only in the vendor's system, and accounts that would be lost on leaving.
