Instructional Rationale: Classifying a task by whether it needs steps and tools is an Understand-level action that guides the learner's choice of tool. Four tasks per bin teach the learner to look for steps, tools, and files.

Content:

The two bins: Assistant (one reply from the model is enough) and Agent (the task needs several steps, tools, or files).

The eight tasks:

# Task shown to the learner Correct bin Why (shown as feedback) 1 Explain what a watershed is in two sentences. Assistant One reply can do it. 2 Read every file in this folder, run a link checker on each page, and fill in the rubric worksheet. Agent It needs files, a tool, and many steps. 3 Suggest a better title for this lesson. Assistant One reply can do it. 4 Open the resource, measure the reading level of three passages with a tool, and report the grade levels. Agent It needs a tool and a sequence of steps. 5 Rewrite this paragraph in plain language. Assistant One reply can do it. 6 Check all 14 links, record which return errors, and save the list to a file. Agent It needs a tool, a record of results, and a file. 7 What does CC BY-SA allow? Assistant One reply can do it. 8 Score each of 30 resources against the rubric and save a report for each. Agent It needs files, many steps, and repeated work.

Provenance: The tasks are illustrative cases written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The definitions follow the chapter sections "AI Assistant" and "AI Agent".

Rules: Each task has exactly one correct bin, four per bin.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one task and the two bins.
  2. The learner places the task in a bin, and the placement is committed.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text.
  4. After task 8 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 8 tasks in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [bin]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. This needs [bin]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 8 correct on the first attempt". At 7 or more it adds "You can tell a reply from a job." Below 7 it lists the Why text of each missed task.

Starting State: The first task and two empty bins. The question shown is "Is one reply enough, or does this need steps and tools?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter says an assistant answers and waits, and an agent plans, acts, observes, and acts again, using tools and files.

docs.title: Agent Skill
docs.text: An agent skill is a packaged set of instructions, and sometimes helper scripts and reference files, that an agent loads when a task matches it. A skill lets someone write down a procedure once and reuse it. A typical skill is a folder containing a text file of instructions, with a short description at the top that tells the agent when the skill applies. A skill for this book's rubric could hold the ten metrics, the checks, the descriptor bands, and the rules for evidence, so that any agent with the skill scores resources in the same way. The skill is the durable form of a rubric prompt, and it is what a teacher can share with colleagues.

docs.title: Tool Use
docs.text:
Tool use is an agent's ability to call external programs and read what they return. A tool can be a link checker, a readability calculator, an accessibility checker, a search engine, or a program that counts the images in a page. The agent decides when a tool is needed, calls it with the right input, and reads the result. Tool use matters for evaluation because language models are weak at exact work. Counting the images that lack alt text, adding a column of numbers, and measuring a contrast ratio are tasks that a model can get wrong while sounding sure, and a tool does them the same way every time.

A useful rule divides the work. Give exact tasks to tools: counting, measuring, testing, and comparing. Give judgment tasks to the model: is the alt text useful, does the heading describe the section, does the feedback explain the answer. Keep real-world tasks for a person: confirming that a fact is true against a source, or testing an embed on a platform you can only reach by hand. The division reduces errors, and it tells you which parts of an agent's report to trust most.

Worked example: counting images three ways. Three methods answer the question "How many of the images lack alt text?" for a page with five images.

Method Typical result Reliability Ask a model to read the page and count "Two images lack alt text" (the true number is one) Low: models miscount, and may skip small items Run an accessibility checker "One image has no alt attribute" High for presence, and it says nothing of quality Open the page source and count by hand "One image has no alt attribute, and two of the others have one-word alt text" High, and slow

The agent's best choice is the tool for the count and the model for the quality judgment. Reviewers commonly give agents four kinds of tool: a link checker, a readability calculator, an accessibility checker, and a validator for metadata files. Record which tool and which version produced each result, because tools disagree and update, and a result is evidence only if someone can say how it was obtained. Tools also raise false alarms and miss real problems, so treat a tool's report as a strong clue and not as a verdict. The MicroSim below practices that division. It shows ten checks, and for each one you decide who should do it.

docs.title: Diagram: Tool or Model Sorter
docs.text:
Tool or Model Sorter

Type: microsim sim-id: tool-vs-model-sorter Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: judge Learning Objective: The learner will judge whether each of ten rubric checks should be done by a tool, by the model, or by a person, with at least 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Tool Use, AI Agent, Large Language Model (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each check the learner commits one of three bins. A placement is correct when it matches the Correct bin column in Content. Mastery is at least 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt. Reading the division rule is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A model can count and measure reliably. (2) A tool can judge whether alt text is useful. (3) A model can confirm facts without a source.

Instructional Rationale: Judging who should do a check is an Evaluate-level action that applies the division rule. Ten checks drawn from the rubric, with four for tools, four for the model, and two for a person, teach the learner to match the task to the right worker.

Content:

The division rule, shown at all times: tools do exact tasks like counting, measuring, testing, and comparing; the model does judgment tasks on text; a person does tasks that need a real source or a real-world test.

The three bins: Tool, Model, Person.

The ten checks:

# Check shown to the learner Correct bin Why (shown as feedback) 1 Count the images that have no alt attribute. Tool Counting is exact work. 2 Measure the reading level of three passages. Tool A readability formula is a calculation. 3 Test whether each link returns an error. Tool Testing a link is a repeatable test. 4 Judge whether a piece of alt text is useful. Model It is a judgment about text, and a person should spot-check it. 5 Decide whether a heading describes its section. Model It is a judgment about text. 6 Decide whether a quiz feedback message explains why. Model It is a judgment about text. 7 Test whether the resource embeds on a particular LMS. Person It needs a real test on a real platform. 8 Compare the license on the page with the license in the metadata. Tool A comparison of two values is exact. 9 Decide whether a learning outcome uses a measurable verb. Model It is a judgment about text. 10 Confirm that a statistic in the resource matches its cited source. Person It needs the real source, and a person must open it.

Provenance: The checks are drawn from Chapters 5 to 10, and the sim labels the sorting "illustrative". The division rule follows the chapter section "Tool Use".

Rules: Each check has exactly one correct bin. Four checks are Tool, four are Model, and two are Person.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one check and the three bins.
  2. The learner places the check in a bin, and the placement is committed.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text.
  4. After check 10 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 10 checks in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [bin]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. This is for a [bin]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 10 correct on the first attempt". At 8 or more it adds "You can divide the work well." Below 8 it lists the Why text of each missed check.

Starting State: The first check, the division rule, and three empty bins. The question shown is "Who should do this check?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter says exact tasks go to tools, judgment tasks go to the model, and real-world tasks stay with a person.

docs.title: File Access
docs.text:
File access is the ability of an agent to read, and sometimes write, files on a computer or in a folder. It lets an agent open a resource's source files, read a rubric from a file, and save a report. It also creates risk, because an agent with broad access can read files it should not and change ones it should leave alone. The sound principle is least access: give the agent only the folder it needs, make it read-only unless it must write, and keep anything private out of reach. A reviewer's folder for an evaluation should hold the resource and the rubric, and nothing else.

Worked example: what to allow.

Folder or file Should the agent have access? Why The resource's source files Yes, read-only The agent must read them to score the resource The rubric prompt and the check lists Yes, read-only They hold the instructions A reports folder Yes, read and write The agent saves its report there Student grade files or records No They hold private data The original resource folder, when editing is not needed Read-only A mistake should not damage the original

Give an Agent Only the Folder It Needs

An agent can open any file you let it reach, and an error can overwrite one. Point it at a folder that holds the resource and the rubric, make the resource read-only, and keep student records out of reach altogether.

docs.title: Document Ingestion
docs.text:
Document ingestion is the process of turning a resource into text that an agent can read, together with the structure that carries meaning. A model reads text, not files. A web page must be turned into its words, headings, image descriptions, and links. A document must be turned into text with its headings and tables. A video must be turned into a transcript first. What the agent receives decides what it can check: if the ingestion strips out the alt text, the agent cannot judge the alt text, and it may report that none exists. Images need special care. A model that reads only text sees an image's alt attribute and nothing of its pixels. Some models can look at pictures directly, which can help check whether alt text matches the image, and their description is the model's reading and not a fact. An agent should be told what it received, so that "the image has no alt text" and "the agent could not see the image" are never confused.

Formats ingest very differently, and Chapter 4's lesson about editable sources returns here. Markdown and HTML hold their structure in the text itself, so they ingest cleanly and keep headings, lists, links, and alt text. A word processing file ingests well. A PDF made from a document often ingests with damage, because the file records where words sit on a page and not how the document is built, so columns, headings, and tables can come out scrambled. A scan of a printed page is a picture, and it needs optical character recognition, software that reads text from an image, before an agent can use it. A video or an image needs a transcript or a description.

Worked example: three ways to ingest the same resource. Watershed Basics exists as HTML, as a PDF, and as a scan of a printed copy.

Source What the agent receives What the agent can check The HTML page All text, headings, image alt text, link addresses, and the footer license Nearly every check The PDF Text in a possibly scrambled order, with no alt text and uncertain headings Reading level and some facts, and not accessibility or structure The scan A picture of the page, with no text until it is processed Nothing until text is extracted, and then only text

The MicroSim below practices the judgment. It shows eight kinds of source, and for each one you decide how well it ingests.

docs.title: Diagram: Ingestion Path Judge
docs.text:
Ingestion Path Judge

Type: microsim sim-id: ingestion-path-judge Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: judge Learning Objective: The learner will judge whether each of eight kinds of source ingests well, ingests with loss, or needs extra work first, with at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Document Ingestion, File Access, Open File Format (defined in Chapter 4) (all defined in this chapter above this block or in Chapter 4).

Evidence of Mastery: For each source the learner commits one of three bins. A placement is correct when it matches the Correct bin column in Content. Mastery is at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the definitions is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A PDF ingests as well as the document it came from. (2) A picture of text is text. (3) A video can be read directly.

Instructional Rationale: Judging how well a source ingests is an Evaluate-level action that applies what the learner knows about editable formats to the work of an agent. Eight sources across three bins teach the learner to ask where the structure lives.

Content:

The three bins: Ingests well (text and structure come through), Ingests with loss (text comes through, and structure or order may be damaged), and Needs extra work first (the source must be converted before an agent can read it).

The eight sources:

# Source shown to the learner Correct bin Why (shown as feedback) 1 A Markdown file Ingests well Its structure is in the text. 2 An HTML page Ingests well Headings, links, and alt text are in the markup. 3 A word processing document Ingests well Text and headings extract cleanly, with only small formatting loss. 4 A PDF made from a word processor Ingests with loss The text comes through, and the reading order, headings, and tables may be scrambled. 5 A scanned PDF that is a picture of each page Needs extra work first It must be run through text recognition before there is any text. 6 A slide deck Ingests with loss The text in boxes comes through, and the order and any images are uncertain. 7 A video lecture Needs extra work first It must be turned into a transcript first. 8 An image of a chart Needs extra work first The values must be described or extracted first.

Provenance: The sources are illustrative cases written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The judgments follow the chapter section "Document Ingestion".

Rules: Each source has exactly one correct bin. Three sources are Ingests well, two are Ingests with loss, and three are Needs extra work first.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one source and the three bins.
  2. The learner places the source in a bin, and the placement is committed.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text.
  4. After source 8 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 8 sources in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [bin]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. This [bin]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 8 correct on the first attempt". At 7 or more it adds "You know which sources an agent can read." Below 7 it lists the Why text of each missed source.

Starting State: The first source and the three bins. The question shown is "How well will this source ingest?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter says Markdown and HTML ingest cleanly, a PDF made from a document often ingests with damage, and a scan or a video needs conversion first.

docs.title: Structured Output
docs.text:
Structured output is an answer in a fixed, predictable form, with named fields and defined values, that a person or a program can read without guessing. A free-form answer is a paragraph of prose, and every response is shaped differently. A structured answer has the same fields every time: for each metric, the score, the checks that passed and failed, and the evidence. Structure makes answers comparable across resources, checkable by a script, and easy to load into a worksheet or a spreadsheet. It also forces completeness: a field that is missing is visible.

Worked example: the same review, free-form and structured.

Form Looks like What a reviewer can do with it Free-form "The resource has good accessibility overall, though some images could use better descriptions and I did not notice captions." Read it, and little else: no number, no checks, no evidence to verify Structured Metric: Accessibility. Score: 5. Checks passed: 5 of 10. Evidence: "4 of 5 images have alt text; the video has no captions." Check each field, compare with a human score, and load it into a worksheet

A schema describes the shape an answer must take: which fields exist, what type each holds, which values are allowed, and which are required. The table gives a schema for one metric's result.

Field Type Allowed values Required? metric text One of the ten metric names Yes checks list of objects Each with a number from 1 to 10, a result, and evidence Yes result text pass, fail, or not checkable Yes passes whole number 0 to 10 Yes band text One of the six descriptor bands Yes score whole number 0 to 10 Yes checks_not_verified list of numbers Check numbers from 1 to 10 Yes

A program can test every answer against the schema, reject an answer that fails, and ask the agent to try again. Validation catches errors of form and cannot tell whether the content is true, so it is the first filter and never the last. A program can also check the rubric's own arithmetic: it can recount the passes in the checks list and recompute the band, and flag a report whose score does not follow from its own table.

docs.title: JSON Output
docs.text:
JSON output is structured output written in JSON, a plain-text format that computers read easily and people can read too. JSON, short for JavaScript Object Notation, writes information as pairs of a name and a value, separated by colons and wrapped in braces. Names are in double quotes, text values are in double quotes, numbers have no quotes, and a list goes in square brackets. A comma separates each pair. Because the rules are strict, a program can tell at once whether a piece of JSON is valid, and a reviewer can too. Before the example, here is what its parts mean: metric names the metric, checks is a list with one entry per check, and each entry has a number, a result, and the evidence. The example is shortened to two of the ten checks.

{
  "metric": "Open license",
  "checks": [
    {"number": 1, "result": "pass", "evidence": "Footer of page 1 names CC BY 4.0"},
    {"number": 8, "result": "fail", "evidence": "Third-party image 3 on page 4 has no notice"}
  ],
  "passes": 9,
  "band": "9 to 10",
  "score": 9,
  "checks_not_verified": []
}

A reviewer reads JSON by its labels. The score is 9 in the 9 to 10 band, check 8 failed with a stated reason, and no checks were left unverified. The MicroSim below practices spotting defects. It shows six snippets, and for each one you decide whether the JSON is valid and meets the required form, or what is wrong.

docs.title: Diagram: JSON Output Checker
docs.text:
JSON Output Checker

Type: microsim sim-id: json-output-checker Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: assess Learning Objective: The learner will assess whether each of six JSON snippets is valid and meets the required form, or name its defect, with at least 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Structured Output, JSON Output (both defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each snippet the learner commits one of four verdicts. A verdict is correct when it matches the Correct verdict column in Content. Mastery is at least 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Reading the required form is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Single quotes are acceptable in JSON. (2) A number may be written as a word. (3) A missing field is harmless.

Instructional Rationale: Assessing a snippet against a required form is an Evaluate-level action that a reviewer performs on every agent response. Six snippets with one defect each, and one valid snippet, teach the learner the four kinds of problem.

Content:

The required form, shown at all times: a JSON object with the keys metric (text), score (a whole number from 0 to 10), and evidence (text). All three keys must be present.

The four verdicts: Valid, Not valid JSON, Wrong value, Missing field.

The six snippets (all made up):

# Snippet shown to the learner Correct verdict Why (shown as feedback) 1 {"metric": "Readability", "score": 8, "evidence": "Grade 6.4, 6.9, and 7.3 for an audience of grade 6 to 7"} Valid It is valid JSON with all three keys and a score in range. 2 {"metric": "Readability", "score": 8 "evidence": "Grade 6.4, 6.9, and 7.3"} Not valid JSON A comma is missing between score and evidence. 3 {"metric": "Readability", "score": "eight", "evidence": "Grade 6.4, 6.9, and 7.3"} Wrong value The score is text, and it must be a whole number. 4 {"metric": "Readability", "score": 11, "evidence": "Grade 6.4, 6.9, and 7.3"} Wrong value The score is greater than 10, outside the scale of 0 to 10. 5 {"metric": "Readability", "score": 8} Missing field The evidence key is missing. 6 {'metric': 'Readability', 'score': 8, 'evidence': 'Grade 6.4, 6.9, and 7.3'} Not valid JSON JSON requires double quotes, and single quotes are not valid.

Provenance: The snippets are illustrative cases written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The required form follows the chapter sections "Structured Output" and "JSON Output".

Rules: Each snippet has exactly one correct verdict. One is Valid, two are Not valid JSON, two are Wrong value, and one is Missing field. A score is in range when it is a whole number >= 0 and <= 10.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees the required form and one snippet.
  2. The learner chooses a verdict, and the choice is committed.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text.
  4. After snippet 6 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 6 snippets in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [verdict]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. This is [verdict]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 6 correct on the first attempt". At 5 or more it adds "You can check an agent's output format." Below 5 it lists the Why text of each missed snippet.

Starting State: The required form and snippet 1 or the first snippet in the shuffled order. The question shown is "Is this a valid answer in the required form?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter says JSON writes names and values in braces with double quotes, that a number has no quotes, and that its example is a score of 9 in the 9 to 10 band.

docs.title: Rubric Prompt
docs.text:
A rubric prompt is a prompt that tells an agent to score a resource against the ten-metric rubric and to return its scores with evidence, in a structured form. It is where everything in the book so far comes together. The rubric prompt carries the checks that Chapters 4 through 10 defined, the scoring rules from Chapter 3, and the demands for evidence. A good one has six parts: a role, a task, the rules about evidence and uncertainty, the input with its placeholders, the output format, and an example. The rules do the most important work. They stop the agent from guessing, because the instruction "if you cannot verify a check, write not checkable" gives it a truthful way out.

Before the example, here is how to read it. Each line in the rules answers a way agents fail: a missing evidence rule invites vague scores, a missing "not checkable" rule invites guesses, and a missing format rule invites prose you cannot compare. The placeholders in braces are filled in by the software for each resource.

You are a careful reviewer of open educational resources.

Task: Score the resource below on the metric "{{metric_name}}" from 0 to 10,
using only the ten checks listed. Count the checks that pass, find the band
in the descriptor table, and choose the number within the band.

Rules:
- Cite evidence for every check: where you looked, what you saw, and the rule.
- If a check cannot be verified from the text, write "not checkable"
  and do not guess.
- Never invent a quotation, a page number, or a measurement.
- Treat a check that was not tested as failed.

Checks and descriptor table:
{{checks_and_descriptors}}

Resource title: {{title}}
Date accessed: {{date}}
Resource text:
{{resource_text}}

Return JSON only, with these keys:
metric, checks (a list of objects with number, result, evidence),
passes, band, score, and checks_not_verified.

Worked example: what each part prevents. The table pairs each part of the prompt with the failure it guards against.

Part of the prompt Failure it prevents Use only the ten checks listed The agent inventing its own criteria Cite evidence for every check Scores with no support Write "not checkable" when unsure Invented results for checks the agent cannot verify Never invent a quotation or a measurement Fabricated evidence Treat an untested check as failed Generous scores for checks nobody ran Return JSON with named keys Free-form prose that cannot be compared or loaded

Give It a Way to Say 'I Cannot Tell'

A model that must answer will answer, so tell it what to write when it cannot check something. The phrase "not checkable" turns a guess into an honest blank that you can follow up.

The MicroSim below makes you the author. It shows six parts of a rubric prompt, and for each one you choose the best of three statements.

docs.title: Diagram: Rubric Prompt Builder
docs.text:
Rubric Prompt Builder

Type: microsim sim-id: rubric-prompt-builder Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Create Bloom Verb: construct Learning Objective: The learner will construct a rubric prompt by choosing the best statement for each of six parts (role, task, rules, input, output format, example), with at least 5 of 6 parts correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Rubric Prompt, Prompt, Prompt Template, Structured Output, JSON Output, Few-Shot Example, Role Prompting (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of six parts the learner chooses one of three statements. A choice is correct when it is the statement marked Best in Content. Mastery is at least 5 of 6 parts correct on the first attempt. Reading the part definitions is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A confident role is enough to make the model careful. (2) A short task is a clear task. (3) The model can use what it remembers of a resource.

Instructional Rationale: Assembling a prompt from parts is a Create-level action in a guided form. Offering a best statement, a vague statement, and a risky statement for each part makes the learner weigh clarity, completeness, and safety, and the finished prompt is a template the learner can reuse.

Content:

The six parts, each with three statements (shown in a shuffled order). The statement marked Best is the correct choice.

Part Statement Mark Why (shown as feedback) Role "You are a careful reviewer of open educational resources who checks every claim against the text." Best It sets a standard of care and ties it to the text. Role "You are the world's greatest genius." Vague It claims ability and sets no standard of care. Role "You are the author of this resource." Risky An author is biased toward the resource. Task "Score the resource on each of the ten metrics, using only the checks listed below." Best It names the action and limits the criteria. Task "Tell me if the resource is good." Vague It names no criteria and no scale. Task "Give an overall grade out of 100 with no detail." Risky It hides the metric scores that the rubric needs. Rules "Cite evidence for every check. If a check cannot be verified from the text, write 'not checkable'." Best It demands evidence and gives a truthful way out. Rules "Be generous and round scores up." Vague It tells the model to bias the scores. Rules "If you find no evidence, make up plausible evidence." Risky It tells the model to fabricate. Input "Resource text: {{resource_text}}. Date accessed: {{date}}." Best It supplies the text and the date, with placeholders. Input "The resource is something about water." Vague It gives no material to check. Input "Use whatever you remember about this resource." Risky It relies on memory and not on the text. Output format "Return JSON with one object per metric, with the keys metric, score (a whole number from 0 to 10), evidence, and checks_not_verified." Best It fixes the form and the allowed values. Output format "Write a paragraph about the resource." Vague It cannot be compared or checked. Output format "Return whatever format you like." Vague It leaves the form open. Example A sample object for the metric Open license with a score of 9 and evidence naming the footer and the image without a notice Best It shows the form and the level of detail. Example "Example: Score: great!" Vague It shows no form and no evidence. Example "Example: Open license: 10, all good." Risky It shows a score with no evidence, which teaches the wrong habit.

Provenance: The statements are written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The parts and the failures they prevent follow the chapter section "Rubric Prompt".

Rules: Each part has exactly one Best statement. The sim shows the learner's chosen statements assembled into a prompt as they are chosen, and states that the assembled prompt is a study example.

Learner Activity:

  1. The sim shows the part Role with its three statements.
  2. The learner chooses one statement, and the choice is committed.
  3. The sim shows whether it was the best, the Why text, and adds the chosen statement to the growing prompt.
  4. The learner continues through the parts Task, Rules, Input, Output format, and Example.
  5. After the sixth part the sim shows the assembled prompt and the summary.

Feedback: 6 parts in the fixed order, one attempt each. Best: "Best choice. [Why]". Not best: "Not the best. The best statement is [statement]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 6 parts correct on the first attempt". At 5 or more it adds "You can write a rubric prompt." Below 5 it lists the Why text of each missed part.

Starting State: The Role part with three statements and an empty prompt. The question shown is "Which statement belongs in a rubric prompt?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's rubric prompt has a role, a task, rules (evidence and not checkable), an input with placeholders, an output format in JSON, and says an example shows the form.

docs.title: Agent Scoring
docs.text:
Agent scoring is the process in which an agent applies the rubric prompt to a resource and returns scores with evidence. The agent ingests the resource, runs the tools for the exact checks, judges the checks that need judgment, assigns a score to each metric, and writes the result in the required form. The output is a draft. It is a fast first pass that a person must check, because an agent can be wrong in ways that look right: a check marked as passed that was never run, a quotation that is not in the resource, a score that does not match the checks it lists.

Worked example: an agent's draft on accessibility, and how to check it. The agent returned the following claims for Watershed Basics. This is an illustrative draft, and it contains errors that a reviewer should catch.

Agent claim How a reviewer checks it What the reviewer finds "4 of 5 images have alt text." Count the images and their alt attributes Correct "The video has captions." Play the video and look for a caption control False: the video has no captions "Headings are in order." Run a heading outline tool False: one heading skips from level 2 to level 4 "Contrast ratio tested: 5.2 to 1." Ask which tool produced the number, and run it Invented: the agent ran no contrast tool "Score: 6." Count the passes in the agent's own table and apply the bands Does not match: its table shows five passes, and the bands give 5, with a serious failure

Three of the five claims fail a check, one of them an invented measurement. A reviewer who accepted the draft would have scored the resource too high. This is the reason Chapter 14 exists, and it is why the agent's report must always carry evidence that a person can test.

Agents suit some metrics better than others. Metrics built on exact checks, such as editable source, metadata, portability, and the link and reading-level parts of accuracy and readability, are good candidates for a first pass by an agent with tools. Metrics that rest on judgment about content, such as whether facts are true, whether activities match outcomes, and whether feedback teaches, are where an agent is most likely to be confidently wrong, so a person should check them closely.

Kind of metric Examples Agent first pass Human check Exact checks Editable source, metadata, portability, links, reading level Good with tools Spot-check Judgment on text Accessibility quality, alignment, practice quality Useful draft Check all of it Needs a source or a real test Factual accuracy, embedding on a platform Weak Always

docs.title: Agent Evaluation Report
docs.text:
An agent evaluation report is the document an agent produces from a scoring run. It should contain, for each of the ten metrics, the score, the checks with their results, and the evidence for each; the subtotals, the total, and the band; a list of checks the agent could not verify; a short recommendation; and a note on its limits. It should also record how it was made: the agent and model used, the date of the run, and the version of the prompt. A report without a record of its own origin cannot be repeated or compared with a later one.

The MicroSim below shows the parts of a report as an illustration. Eight numbered markers point to the parts that a reviewer looks for.

docs.title: Diagram: Anatomy of an Agent Evaluation Report
docs.text:
Anatomy of an Agent Evaluation Report

Type: infographic sim-id: agent-report-anatomy Library: html Status: Specified Bloom Level: Remember Bloom Verb: identify Learning Objective: The learner will identify the eight parts of an agent evaluation report from a description of how each looks, with at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Agent Scoring, Agent Evaluation Report, Structured Output (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: In quiz mode the learner clicks the marker that matches a visual hint. A click is correct when it matches the marker named in the Hint column of Content. Mastery is at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Hovering in explore mode is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A report without a not-checkable list is complete. (2) The run record is optional. (3) The recommendation replaces the evidence.

Instructional Rationale: Identifying the parts of a report is a Remember-level task, and an illustration of one page gives each part a place. The quiz asks the learner to recognize a part by its look, which is how they will audit a real report.

Content:

The illustration is a text-free flat drawing of an evaluation report page. At the top is a wide bar with a small robot icon and a small calendar icon. Below it is a table of ten rows. Each row has a short bar for a metric name, a small numbered square, and a long bar with a small link icon. Some rows also carry a small flag icon at the right. At the bottom left is a box with three rows. At the bottom center is a wider box with a small thumbs-up icon. At the bottom right is a box with a small question-mark icon. In a thin strip along the very bottom is a small clock icon and a short tag. The eight markers:

# Label Hint (describes the look, not the name) Description Tip 1 Report header The wide bar at the top with a robot icon and a calendar icon. Names the resource, the agent, and the date of the run. Check that the date matches the version of the resource you reviewed. 2 Metric score The small numbered square in each table row. The whole-number score from 0 to 10 for one metric. Count the passes in the evidence and see whether the score follows. 3 Evidence The long bar with a small link icon in each row. The checks, results, and quotations that support the score. Verify at least one piece of evidence in each metric yourself. 4 Not-checkable flag A small flag icon at the right of some rows. Marks a check the agent could not verify from the text. Follow up on every flag, and do not treat a flag as a pass. 5 Totals box The box with three rows at the bottom left. The quality subtotal, the reusability subtotal, and the total. Recompute the sums from the ten scores. 6 Recommendation The wider box with a thumbs-up icon at the bottom center. The agent's adopt, revise, or reject advice, with reasons. Apply the adoption threshold yourself before accepting it. 7 Limitations The box with a question-mark icon at the bottom right. What the agent could not see or test, and what it assumed. Treat each limitation as a check for a person to do. 8 Run record The thin strip with a clock icon and a short tag along the bottom. Records the model, the date, and the prompt version. Keep it, since a later run cannot be compared without it.

Provenance: The parts follow the chapter section "Agent Evaluation Report". The illustration is synthetic, and the sim labels the report "illustrative example".

Rules: Each hint matches exactly one marker. The illustration contains no text, so every label comes from the table above. Markers are numbered 1 to 8 in the order of the table.

Learner Activity:

  1. In explore mode the learner hovers or clicks a marker and reads its label, description, and tip.
  2. In quiz mode the sim shows a hint.
  3. The learner clicks the marker they think the hint describes.
  4. If the first click is wrong, the sim says so and lets the learner try once more. If the second click is also wrong, the sim reveals the marker and its description.
  5. After all 8 hints the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 8 hints in a shuffled order, two attempts each. Only a correct first click counts as evidence. Correct: "Correct: [label]. [Description]". First wrong click: "Not quite. Look again at the hint: [hint]". Second wrong click: "This is [label]. [Description]". The summary shows "[n] of 8 correct on the first attempt". At 7 or more it adds "You can audit an agent's report." Below 7 it lists the labels of the missed parts.

Starting State: The illustration with eight numbered markers, explore mode active, and the prompt "Hover a marker to see what it is."

Chapter Anchors: The chapter says a report contains the ten scores with checks and evidence, the subtotals and band, a list of checks not verified, a recommendation, limitations, and a record of the agent, the date, and the prompt version.

docs.title: Batch Evaluation
docs.text: Batch evaluation is the running of the same rubric prompt over many resources, one after another, so that a department can score a whole collection. An agent can work through a folder of resources while a reviewer does something else. The speed brings two cautions. Errors repeat: a flaw in the prompt appears in every report, so a prompt should be tested on a few resources before it is run on hundreds. And no one will read every report, so the work needs a sampling plan. A person checks a sample of the reports, and checks every resource whose total lies near a decision boundary, where a few points of error would change the decision. Chapter 13 covers the cost of a batch.

docs.title: Agent Workflow
docs.text:
An agent workflow is the designed sequence of steps that an agent and its human partner follow to produce a trustworthy evaluation. A workflow fixes the order, the tools, and the points at which a person checks the agent. It is the agent's version of the review workflow from Chapter 11. A good workflow ends with a person, so that no score reaches a decision without a human check. People belong at three points. At the start, a person chooses the resource and the version of the rubric, so that the agent works on the right thing. In the middle, a person checks the evidence and compares with a manual score. At the end, a person makes the adoption decision, since the rubric informs the decision and does not take it.

Step Who What happens 1 Reviewer Supplies the resource and the rubric prompt 2 Agent Ingests the resource into text and structure 3 Agent and tools Runs the exact checks with tools 4 Agent Scores each metric with evidence 5 Agent Checks its own output format and evidence 6 Agent Compiles the evaluation report 7 Reviewer Checks the evidence and compares with a human score 8 Reviewer Records the decisions and updates the prompt if needed

The last MicroSim of the agent half asks you to put those eight steps in order.

docs.title: Diagram: Agent Workflow Sequencer
docs.text:
Agent Workflow Sequencer

Type: microsim sim-id: agent-workflow-sequencer Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Remember Bloom Verb: list Learning Objective: The learner will list the eight steps of an agent evaluation workflow in the correct order, with at least 7 of 8 steps in the correct position on the first Check.

Prerequisites: Agent Workflow, Agent Scoring, Document Ingestion, Tool Use (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: The learner arranges eight steps and presses Check. A step is correct when it sits in the position given in the Content table. Mastery is at least 7 of 8 steps in the correct position on the first Check. Rearranging steps before pressing Check is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) The agent scores before it ingests the resource. (2) A person checks the report before it exists. (3) The agent runs tools after it has scored.

Instructional Rationale: Ordering the steps of a workflow is a Remember-level task that checks whether the learner holds the sequence. Each step depends on the one before it, so a wrong position can be explained by a dependency.

Content:

The eight steps, with their positions and the reason each follows its predecessor:

Position Step Why it comes here 1 The reviewer supplies the resource and the rubric prompt. The agent needs a task and material. 2 The agent ingests the resource into text and structure. The agent cannot check what it cannot read. 3 The agent runs the exact checks with tools. The tool results are evidence for the scores. 4 The agent scores each metric with evidence. Scoring needs the ingested text and the tool results. 5 The agent checks its own output format and evidence. The check needs scores to examine. 6 The agent compiles the evaluation report. The report gathers the checked scores. 7 The reviewer checks the evidence and compares with a human score. A person can only check a report that exists. 8 The reviewer records the decisions and updates the prompt if needed. The prompt is improved from what the check found.

Provenance: The steps follow the chapter section "Agent Workflow".

Rules: Each step has exactly one correct position, and the eight positions are distinct. The learner may move steps freely before pressing Check. After a Check, steps in the correct position are marked correct and the rest are marked out of place.

Learner Activity:

  1. The sim shows the eight steps in a shuffled order.
  2. The learner moves steps up or down to put them in the order they think is correct.
  3. The learner presses Check.
  4. The sim shows which steps are in the correct position and, for each out-of-place step, the reason it belongs where it does.
  5. The learner may rearrange and Check again.

Feedback: The learner may press Check as many times as they like, and only the first Check counts as evidence. After each Check the sim shows "[n] of 8 steps in the correct position". For each out-of-place step the sim shows its Why text. At 7 or more on the first Check it adds "You know how an agent review runs." Below 7 it reports the count and invites another try.

Starting State: The eight steps in a shuffled order that is not the correct order, and the prompt "Put the steps in the order an agent review runs."

Chapter Anchors: The chapter lists eight workflow steps that begin with the reviewer supplying the resource and prompt and end with the reviewer recording decisions and updating the prompt.

docs.title: Prompt Iteration
docs.text:
Prompt iteration is the practice of improving a prompt in cycles: write it, run it, compare the results with what you know is right, and change it. A first rubric prompt is almost never the best one. The method is to test it on resources you have already scored by hand, such as Watershed Basics, whose ten scores you know. Run the prompt, compare the agent's scores with the human scores, look at where they differ, and change the prompt to fix the cause. Change one thing at a time, so that you know which change made the difference. Keep each version, with a note of what changed, using the version control habits of Chapter 4, so that you can go back.

A Prompt Is Just Careful Writing

A prompt can look like programming, and it is plain writing with a purpose. You already write clear instructions for students and colleagues, and each time a prompt misfires you learn which sentence was unclear. Run it on a resource you know and fix what you see.

Worked example: three rounds of iteration. A reviewer tests a rubric prompt on Watershed Basics, whose human accessibility score is 5.

Round What the agent returned What the reviewer changed 1 Score 8. No evidence for two checks, and "captions present" with no quote Added the rule "cite evidence for every check" 2 Score 7. The caption claim now has a quote that is not in the resource Added "Never invent a quotation" and "write not checkable if you cannot verify" 3 Score 6. Two checks marked not checkable, with the rest supported by evidence Left the prompt, and decided to run the contrast check with a tool

The scores moved from 8 to 6 as the prompt forced evidence, and the agent still did not match the human score of 5. The gap is a finding, and Chapter 14 shows how to measure it and what to do about it.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• An AI assistant replies to a request, and a large language model produces its text by predicting likely next pieces, in tokens, within a context window. It does not look facts up, and it can sound sure when it is wrong.
  • A prompt is the only way to steer a model, and it has up to six parts. A system prompt sets standing rules, role prompting sets a standard of care, a few-shot example shows the form, and a prompt template makes a review repeatable.
  • An AI agent adds tools, files, and a loop. Tool use hands exact tasks to tools, file access should be as narrow as possible, and an agent skill packages a procedure for reuse.
  • Document ingestion decides what an agent can see, and open, structured formats ingest best. Structured output, often JSON output, makes answers comparable and checkable.
  • A rubric prompt makes an agent apply the ten metrics and return evidence, with "not checkable" as an honest answer. Agent scoring produces a draft in an agent evaluation report, batch evaluation repeats it at scale, and an agent workflow ends with a person.
  • Prompt iteration improves the prompt against resources you have already scored by hand.

You Can Brief an Agent Like a Reviewer

You can now explain what an assistant, a model, and an agent are, write a prompt with its six parts, and build a rubric prompt that demands evidence and allows "not checkable". The agent's first pass is a draft, and the next two chapters show you how to guard it and how to check it.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: AI Agents, Prompts, and Rubric Scoring
docs.text: Test your understanding of language models, prompts, agents, tool use, structured output, and rubric prompts with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. Which description best fits an AI assistant?
docs.text:
1. A program that works toward a goal over many steps, using tools and files, until the task is finished
  2. A program that you talk to in ordinary language and that answers in ordinary language, powered by a large language model
  3. A database of verified facts that a teacher searches by keyword to find a source
  4. A scoring tool that applies a rubric to a resource without needing any written request
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. An AI assistant is a computer program you talk to in ordinary language and that answers in ordinary language, powered by a large language model. Teachers use assistants to draft quiz questions, rewrite a paragraph at a lower reading level, and explain an idea in a new way. Option A describes an agent, which adds tools, files, and a loop. An assistant is fluent, so its answers sound authoritative whether they are right or wrong.

Concept Tested: AI Assistant

See: AI Assistant

docs.title: 2. Which list names the parts of a good prompt?
docs.text:
1. Title, author, subject, grade level, license, and description
  2. Stem, key, distractors, feedback, tag, and retry control
  3. Observe, decide, act, and observe the result
  4. Role, task, input, rules, output format, and example
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. A prompt is the text you give a model to tell it what to do, and a good one has up to six parts. The role says who the model should act as, the task says what to do, and the input is the material to work on. The rules say what to do and what not to do, including what to write when unsure. The output format shapes the answer, and an example shows a good answer. Option A lists metadata fields.

Concept Tested: Prompt

See: Prompt

docs.title: 3. Why can an AI assistant write a confident review of a resource it has never seen?
docs.text:
1. It stores a copy of every web page it has seen and checks the copy against the resource
  2. It runs a built-in accessibility checker on any resource name that it is given by a user
  3. Every open educational resource is part of its training data, so it has already read them all
  4. A language model predicts likely text and does not look facts up, so it answers without the resource
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. A large language model generates text one piece at a time by predicting what is likely to come next. It does not consult a database, it knows only what it was trained on and what you give it, and it will write an answer even when it cannot do what you asked. A request such as "Score this resource for accessibility" with nothing attached gets an invented number. Supply the text, name the checks, and demand evidence.

Concept Tested: Large Language Model

See: Large Language Model

docs.title: 4. How does an AI agent differ from an AI assistant?
docs.text:
1. An agent is a larger language model, while an assistant is a smaller one of the same kind, sold at a lower price
  2. An assistant answers and waits, while an agent plans, uses tools, observes results, and acts again until done
  3. An assistant can use tools and files freely, while an agent can only reply in plain text
  4. An agent works only on resources that a human reviewer has already scored by hand first
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. An agent is a system built around a language model that works toward a goal over several steps. The model supplies judgment and language, the tools supply measurements, and the loop lets the agent keep going. An agent asked to check links lists them, tests each with a tool, reads the results, and writes a report. Agents have more ways to go wrong because each step can inherit the error of the one before, so a person stays in the loop.

Concept Tested: AI Agent

See: AI Agent

docs.title: 5. Why should exact tasks, such as counting the images that lack alt text, be given to a tool and not to the model?
docs.text:
1. Language models are weak at exact work and can miscount while sounding sure, whereas a tool is repeatable
  2. Tools can judge whether alt text is useful, and language models cannot judge text at all
  3. Language models are not allowed to read HTML, so they cannot see which images lack alt text
  4. Tools are always free to use, and language models are always too expensive to run on a resource
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The chapter divides the work three ways. Tools do exact tasks, such as counting, measuring, testing, and comparing. The model does judgment tasks on text, such as whether alt text is useful or a heading describes its section. A person keeps real-world tasks, such as confirming a fact against its source. In the chapter's example, a model counted two images without alt text when the true number was one.

Concept Tested: Tool Use

See: Tool Use

docs.title: 6. A reviewer wants an agent to score a 6,000-word resource using a 900-word prompt and expects a 1,200-word answer. Using the rule that tokens equal words divided by 0.75, rounded up, will the request fit in a window of 8,000 tokens?
docs.text:
1. Yes, because the resource alone is only 6,000 words, which is less than the window
  2. Yes, because the expected answer does not count against the window of the model
  3. No, because it needs about 10,800 tokens, so she needs a larger window or a shorter request
  4. No, because it needs about 8,100 tokens, since words and tokens are the same thing in plain English
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Everything the model uses must fit in the window: the instructions, the resource, the conversation, and the answer it writes. The total is 6,000 + 900 + 1,200 = 8,100 words, and dividing by 0.75 gives 10,800 tokens, which is more than 8,000. The three remedies are a larger window, shorter instructions, or splitting the resource, though splitting can miss checks that span the whole resource, such as whether an outcome is ever taught.

Concept Tested: Context Window

See: Context Window

docs.title: 7. The required form for an agent's answer is a JSON object with a text metric, a whole-number score from 0 to 10, and text evidence. An agent returns {"metric": "Readability", "score": "eight", "evidence": "Grade 6.4"}. What is the defect?
docs.text:
1. It is not valid JSON, because a comma is missing between two pairs
  2. A field is missing, because the answer has no evidence key
  3. A value is wrong, because the score is text and must be a whole number
  4. There is no defect, because the answer is valid and meets the required form
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The snippet is valid JSON: every name and text value is in double quotes, commas separate the pairs, and all three keys are present. The defect is the value of score. A number has no quotes, and "eight" is text, so it does not meet the schema that calls for a whole number from 0 to 10. A program can test every answer against the schema and ask the agent to try again. Validation catches errors of form and cannot tell whether the content is true.

Concept Tested: JSON Output

See: JSON Output

docs.title: 8. A department wants an agent to check the accessibility of a resource that exists as an HTML page, a PDF made from a word processor, and a scan of a printed copy. Which source should it give the agent first, and why?
docs.text:
1. The PDF, because a PDF preserves every heading and image description exactly
  2. The scan, because a scan is the original and so is the most reliable source
  3. Any of the three, because an agent receives the same information from each
  4. The HTML page, because its headings, links, and alt text stay in the markup
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Document ingestion decides what an agent can check, because a model reads text and not files. Markdown and HTML hold their structure in the text, so they ingest cleanly. A PDF often ingests with damage: reading order, headings, and tables can come out scrambled, and alt text is lost. A scan is a picture that needs text recognition first. If ingestion strips out the alt text, the agent may report that none exists.

Concept Tested: Document Ingestion

See: Document Ingestion

docs.title: 9. An agent's draft says "Contrast ratio tested: 5.2 to 1." The agent was given no contrast tool, and the reviewer finds no record of a test. What is the best analysis?
docs.text:
1. The measurement is likely accurate, because language models compute contrast reliably
  2. The claim is acceptable, because 5.2 is above the 4.5 minimum for normal text
  3. The measurement is invented and has no evidence, so the reviewer should reject it and run a contrast tool
  4. The measurement is a harmless rounding difference that can safely be ignored by the reviewer
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Agent scoring produces a draft that a person must check, because an agent can be wrong in ways that look right: a check marked as passed that was never run, a quotation that is not in the resource, or a measurement from a tool it never called. The reviewer's test is to ask which tool produced the number and to run it. A measurement without a source is not evidence, whatever value it reports.

Concept Tested: Agent Scoring

See: Agent Scoring

docs.title: 10. A reviewer tests a rubric prompt on Watershed Basics, whose human accessibility score is 5. In three rounds the agent's score moves from 8 to 7 to 6 as rules are added that demand evidence and allow "not checkable." What does this pattern show?
docs.text:
1. Forcing evidence moved the agent toward the human score, but a gap remains that should be measured
  2. The prompt is now perfect, because the score went down in every round of testing
  3. The agent must be right, because the human score cannot be trusted to be accurate
  4. The prompt should be abandoned, because it never matched the human score exactly
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Prompt iteration improves a prompt in cycles: write it, run it on a resource you have already scored by hand, compare, and change one thing at a time. The rules that required evidence and honest blanks pulled the score down, but the agent still reads 6 against the human 5. A gap that remains is a finding. Chapter 14 shows how to measure it, and the human score is the reference, not the agent's.

Concept Tested: Prompt Iteration

See: Prompt Iteration

docs.title: References: AI Agents, Prompts, and Rubric Scoring
docs.text:
1. Large language model - Wikipedia - Explains how large language models are trained, how they use tokens and context, and what they can and cannot do. Background for the chapter's sections on models and the context window.

  2. Prompt engineering - Wikipedia - Surveys techniques such as few-shot examples and chain-of-thought prompting for steering a model's output. Supports the chapter's guidance on writing prompts and prompt templates.

  3. Intelligent agent - Wikipedia - Defines an agent as a system that perceives its environment and acts toward goals, with common agent types. The foundation for the chapter's distinction between an assistant and an agent.

  4. Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach (4th ed.) - Stuart Russell and Peter Norvig - Pearson (2020) - Russell and Norvig organize the whole field around the rational agent and describe tasks with PEAS: performance measure, environment, actuators, and sensors. This gives a precise vocabulary for what an agent is.

  5. Hands-On Large Language Models - Jay Alammar and Maarten Grootendorst - O'Reilly (2024) - Alammar, known for his illustrated explainers, uses diagrams to show how language models handle tokens, context, and prompts without heavy mathematics. A readable base for the chapter's model and prompt concepts.

  6. Building Effective AI Agents - Anthropic - Separates workflows from agents and describes patterns such as prompt chaining, routing, and evaluator-optimizer. Helps teachers understand the agent workflow this chapter uses for rubric scoring.

  7. Prompt Engineering Overview - Claude Platform Docs - Official guidance on writing clear prompts, giving examples, and iterating with tests. Supports the chapter's section on prompt iteration, where a rubric prompt is refined after checking the agent's first results.

  8. Agent Skills Overview - Claude Platform Docs - Explains skills as packaged instructions and resources that an agent loads when relevant. Shows the format behind the reusable evaluator skills this book teaches readers to build.

  9. Prompt Engineering Guide - DAIR.AI - A free catalog of prompting techniques with examples, including zero-shot, few-shot, and chain-of-thought prompts. A handy reference while building a rubric prompt.

  10. Transformers, the Tech Behind LLMs - 3Blue1Brown - A visual explanation of how a language model turns text into predictions, with animated diagrams. Builds intuition for why a model can sound sure and still be wrong.

docs.title: Automated Checks, Cost, and Student Privacy
Summary
docs.text: Covers multi-agent review, keeping a human in the loop, automated link, accessibility, license, and readability checks, AI cost, and protecting student data under FERPA. It extends AI-agent scoring with the automated checks teachers can run and the limits they must respect. After this chapter you can choose which checks to automate, keep a human in the loop, estimate agent cost, and protect student data.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 9 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Multi-Agent Review 22 Human in the Loop 160 Automated Link Checker 1 Automated Accessibility Scan 1 Automated License Detection 1 Automated Readability Scan 1 AI Cost 1 Student Data Privacy 27 FERPA 1

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 2: Open Licenses and Attribution
  • Chapter 5: Accuracy and Currency
  • Chapter 6: Alignment and Readability
  • Chapter 7: Accessibility
  • Chapter 11: Manual Evaluation and Adoption Decisions
  • Chapter 12: AI Agents, Prompts, and Rubric Scoring

Automate the Counting, Keep the Judgment

An agent can run a hundred checks while you drink your coffee, and it can also make a hundred confident mistakes. This chapter shows you what to automate, where a person must stay, what it costs, and how to keep student information out of harm's way. Let's dive in and check the evidence!

Chapter 12 gave you an agent that can read a resource and return scores. Before you let it loose on a collection, four questions deserve answers. Which checks are safe to automate, and which can fool you? Where does a person have to stay in the process? What will a large run cost? And what information must never go into an AI service at all? This chapter answers them, in that order, and the answers shape how the rest of the book uses agents.

docs.title: Human in the Loop
docs.text:
Human in the loop is a way of working in which a person reviews, approves, or corrects an automated system's output at the points where errors matter. It does not mean that a person redoes the work. It means that the machine's draft passes through a person before it becomes a decision. The idea fits this book's whole method: an agent produces a fast first pass with evidence, and a human checks the evidence, settles disagreements, and makes the adoption decision.

There are three reasons to keep a person in the loop. Agents make confident mistakes, as Chapter 12 showed, and Chapter 14 teaches you to find them. Accountability cannot be delegated: when a district adopts a resource, a person answers for the choice, and "the agent said so" is not an answer. And some checks depend on knowledge or context that an agent lacks, such as what a particular class needs. The cost is time, so the practical question is where a person's attention buys the most.

A useful way to spend that attention is to match the level of checking to the risk. A report that follows the rules, carries tool logs, and shows exact evidence needs only a spot check. A report whose claims rest on the agent's own memory needs every claim checked. A report that breaks the rubric's own rules, for example a total that does not equal the sum of its scores, goes back for another run.

Worked example: three levels of oversight. The table compares three ways of using the same agent on the same collection.

Approach What happens Likely outcome No oversight The agent's totals go straight into the adoption list A resource with an invented caption claim is adopted, and a blind learner meets a video with no captions Check everything A person redoes every score by hand The review is accurate, and the agent saved no time Risk-matched oversight Rule-breaking reports go back, claims with no source are checked in full, and well-evidenced reports are spot-checked Errors are caught where they occur, and most of the agent's time saving remains

The Answer Still Belongs to a Person

An agent can supply scores and evidence, and it cannot take responsibility for the decision. Plan the loop so that a named person looks at each report before it is used.

The first MicroSim of the chapter practices matching the check to the risk. It shows eight features of agent reports, and for each one you choose how much checking it needs.

docs.title: Diagram: Human Check Planner
docs.text:
Human Check Planner

Type: microsim sim-id: human-check-planner Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: apply Learning Objective: The learner will apply risk-matched oversight to choose send back, check every claim, or spot-check for each of eight features of agent reports, with at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Human in the Loop, and the sections on agent scoring and agent evaluation reports in Chapter 12 (all defined in this chapter above this block or in Chapter 12).

Evidence of Mastery: For each feature the learner commits one of three responses. A response is correct when it matches the Correct response column in Content. Mastery is at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the oversight levels is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A report with numbers is trustworthy. (2) A person must redo every score. (3) A rule-breaking report can be fixed by hand.

Instructional Rationale: Choosing a response from a risk rule is an Apply-level action. Eight report features that map to three responses teach the learner to read a report for the signs that need attention.

Content:

The three responses: Send back (the report breaks a rule of the rubric or the prompt, so the agent must run again), Check every claim (the report may follow the rules, but its claims rest on the agent's own word), and Spot-check (the report follows the rules and shows exact evidence, so a person verifies a sample).

The eight features:

# Feature of an agent report shown to the learner Correct response Why (shown as feedback) 1 The total is 71, and the ten metric scores add up to 68. Send back The arithmetic is wrong, and the report breaks its own rule. 2 The decision is Adopt for a resource with a total of 76 and one metric at 4. Send back The decision breaks the adoption rule, which needs every metric at 5 or more. 3 An alignment score of 7 with no evidence quoted. Send back The prompt required evidence for every score. 4 A factual accuracy score of 9 that rests on the agent's own knowledge, with no sources. Check every claim No source is cited, so each claim must be checked. 5 A statement that all links work, with no link-checker log attached. Check every claim The claim may be invented, and the test must be run again. 6 An open license score of 9, with footer evidence on 6 of 6 pages and a tool log. Spot-check The evidence is exact and checkable, so a sample is enough. 7 A reading level from a tool, with the grade numbers shown. Spot-check The numbers are in the tool log, and a person can recompute one. 8 An editable source score of 10, with a file list and all ten check results. Spot-check The evidence is complete and verifiable.

Provenance: The features are illustrative cases written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The responses follow the chapter section "Human in the Loop".

Rules: Each feature has exactly one correct response. Three features are Send back, two are Check every claim, and three are Spot-check.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one feature and the three responses.
  2. The learner may open the oversight levels. Opening them does not change the score.
  3. The learner chooses a response, and the choice is committed.
  4. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text.
  5. After feature 8 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 8 features in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [response]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. The response is [response]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 8 correct on the first attempt". At 7 or more it adds "You can match the check to the risk." Below 7 it lists the Why text of each missed feature.

Starting State: The first feature and the three responses. The question shown is "How much checking does this report need?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter says rule-breaking reports go back, claims with no source are checked in full, and well-evidenced reports are spot-checked.

docs.title: Multi-Agent Review
docs.text:
Multi-agent review is the use of two or more agents, or several runs of one agent with different prompts or models, to score the same resource independently, so that their results can be compared. It copies the logic of the two-reviewer method from Chapter 11. Where the agents agree, a person can look less closely, and where they disagree, a person looks first. The spread between scores is a cheap signal. It points to the metrics where the evidence is unclear or where an agent has gone astray.

Multi-agent review has a limit that a reviewer must remember. Agreement among agents is not truth. Agents built on similar models can share the same blind spots, so three agents can all be wrong in the same way. Agreement with no evidence behind it is especially suspect. A sensible rule flags any metric where the scores spread by more than 3 points, flags any agreement where an agent has quoted no evidence, and leaves the rest for a spot check.

Worked example: three agents score six metrics. The table shows the scores and the action each row calls for.

Metric Agent 1 Agent 2 Agent 3 Spread Evidence Action Readability 8 8 7 1 Quoted by all three Accept for a spot check Accessibility 5 9 6 4 Quoted by all three Flag: the spread exceeds 3 Open license 9 9 9 0 None quoted by any agent Check anyway: agreement without evidence Metadata 4 4 3 1 Quoted by all three Accept for a spot check

The next MicroSim practices the triage. It shows six metrics scored by three agents, and for each row you choose the action.

docs.title: Diagram: Multi-Agent Triage
docs.text:
Multi-Agent Triage

Type: microsim sim-id: multi-agent-triage Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: examine Learning Objective: The learner will examine the scores and evidence of three agents for each of six metrics and choose accept, flag, or check anyway, with at least 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Multi-Agent Review, Human in the Loop, Inter-Rater Agreement (defined in Chapter 3) (all defined in this chapter above this block or in Chapter 3).

Evidence of Mastery: For each row the learner commits one of three actions. An action is correct when it matches the Correct action column in Content. Mastery is at least 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Reading the triage rule is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Agreement among agents proves a score is right. (2) Only disagreement needs a person. (3) The average of three scores is the right score.

Instructional Rationale: Triaging results from several agents is an Analyze-level action, because the learner must examine each row's spread and evidence together. Rows that agree with no evidence teach the learner that agreement alone proves little.

Content:

The triage rule, shown at all times: the spread is the highest score minus the lowest. If the spread is > 3, Flag. Otherwise, if any agent quoted no evidence, Check anyway. Otherwise, Accept for a spot check.

The three actions: Accept for a spot check, Flag, Check anyway.

The six rows (all made up, for Watershed Basics):

# Metric Agent 1 Agent 2 Agent 3 Evidence quoted Correct action Why (shown as feedback) 1 Readability 8 8 7 All three agents Accept for a spot check The spread is 1, and all three quoted evidence. 2 Accessibility 5 9 6 All three agents Flag The spread is 4, which is > 3. 3 Open license 9 9 9 No agent Check anyway The agents agree and none quoted any evidence. 4 Metadata 4 4 3 All three agents Accept for a spot check The spread is 1, and all three quoted evidence. 5 Portability 7 3 7 All three agents Flag The spread is 4, which is > 3. 6 Alignment 6 6 6 Agent 1 only Check anyway The agents agree and two of them quoted no evidence.

Provenance: The rows are illustrative cases written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The rule follows the chapter section "Multi-Agent Review" and the agreement rule of Chapter 3.

Rules: Each row has exactly one correct action, two per action. The spread is computed as the highest minus the lowest of the three scores.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one row with the three scores and the evidence note.
  2. The learner chooses an action, and the choice is committed.
  3. The sim shows the spread, whether the choice was correct, and the Why text.
  4. After row 6 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 6 rows in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [action]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. The action is [action]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 6 correct on the first attempt". At 5 or more it adds "You can triage several agents." Below 5 it lists the Why text of each missed row.

Starting State: The first row and the three actions. The question shown is "What should a person do with this row?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter says a spread of more than 3 is flagged, agreement with no evidence is checked anyway, and agreement among agents is not truth.

docs.title: Automated Checks
docs.text: Four kinds of check are worth automating, because each one is exact and repeatable, and each can be run by a free tool that an agent can call. They map onto metrics you have already learned. Each one finds a certain kind of problem and misses another, and a reviewer needs to know both.

docs.title: Automated Link Checker
docs.text: An automated link checker is a tool that tests every link in a resource and reports which ones fail, as Chapter 5 described. It is the model automated check: exact, fast, and repeatable. It finds links that return errors or move. It cannot tell whether a working link still leads to the cited content, and it may be refused by sites that block tools. The report supports the accuracy and currency metric, and a person opens a sample of working links to confirm they reach the right page.

docs.title: Automated Accessibility Scan
docs.text: An automated accessibility scan is a tool that examines a page for the machine-detectable parts of WCAG, as Chapter 7 described. It finds images with no alt attribute, text with weak contrast, missing form labels, and some heading problems. It cannot judge whether alt text is useful, whether captions are accurate, or whether a page makes sense to a screen reader user. A clean scan is a starting point and never a pass, and the accessibility metric still needs the human checks.

docs.title: Automated License Detection
docs.text: Automated license detection is the use of a tool to find license statements in a resource and read their names, versions, and links, and to compare them with the license recorded in the metadata. It catches a missing license, a license that differs between the page and the metadata, and an unrecognized or custom license text. It cannot tell whether the statement is true, so a work copied from someone else with a license label added still passes, and it can miss a license that appears only in an image. The check supports the open license metric.

docs.title: Automated Readability Scan
docs.text:
An automated readability scan computes a reading level for sampled passages, using a formula such as the Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level from Chapter 6. It gives a repeatable number quickly and can run over every section. It measures the surface of the text and cannot see whether the words are defined or the ideas are dense. Use it for a first screen, and read the passages that surprise you.

The table sums up what each scan is good for and where it stops.

Automated check Finds Cannot find Link checker Links that return errors or have moved A working link that leads to the wrong content Accessibility scan Missing alt attributes, weak contrast, missing labels Whether alt text is useful, or captions are accurate License detection Missing, mismatched, or unrecognized license statements Whether the license claim is true Readability scan A reading level for each passage Undefined terms, dense ideas, audience fit

The MicroSim below practices the match. It shows eight problems, and for each one you choose the automated check that would find it, or decide that no scan can.

docs.title: Diagram: Automated Check Matcher
docs.text:
Automated Check Matcher

Type: microsim sim-id: automated-check-matcher Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: classify Learning Objective: The learner will classify each of eight problems by the automated check that finds it, or as one that no scan finds, with at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Automated Link Checker, Automated Accessibility Scan, Automated License Detection, Automated Readability Scan (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each problem the learner commits one of five options. A choice is correct when it matches the Correct option column in Content. Mastery is at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the table of what each scan finds is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A clean accessibility scan means the page is accessible. (2) A license tool can tell whether a license claim is true. (3) A link checker can tell whether the cited content is right.

Instructional Rationale: Classifying a problem by the check that finds it is an Understand-level action that teaches the limits of each scan. Two problems that no scan finds teach the learner that automation leaves gaps.

Content:

The five options: Link checker, Accessibility scan, License detection, Readability scan, No scan finds it.

The eight problems:

# Problem shown to the learner Correct option Why (shown as feedback) 1 A link in the reference list returns "page not found". Link checker A link checker tests exactly this. 2 An image has no alt attribute at all. Accessibility scan A scan detects a missing alt attribute. 3 The footer says CC BY-NC, and the metadata says CC BY.
