License detection License detection compares the two statements. 4 A passage measures at grade 11 for a grade 6 audience. Readability scan A readability scan computes the grade level. 5 The alt text says only "photo". No scan finds it A scan sees that alt text exists and cannot judge whether it is useful. 6 White text on a pale yellow background has a contrast ratio of 1.4 to 1. Accessibility scan A scan computes contrast ratios. 7 A statistic in the text is ten years out of date. No scan finds it Only a person with a current source can tell. 8 No license statement appears anywhere in the resource. License detection License detection reports that no license was found.

Provenance: The problems are illustrative cases written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The matches follow the chapter section "Automated Checks".

Rules: Each problem has exactly one correct option. One is Link checker, two are Accessibility scan, two are License detection, one is Readability scan, and two are No scan finds it.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one problem and the five options.
  2. The learner may open the table of what each scan finds. Opening it does not change the score.
  3. The learner chooses an option, and the choice is committed.
  4. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text.
  5. After problem 8 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 8 problems in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [option]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. The answer is [option]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 8 correct on the first attempt". At 7 or more it adds "You know what each scan can and cannot see." Below 7 it lists the Why text of each missed problem.

Starting State: The first problem and the five options. The question shown is "Which automated check would find this?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's table lists what the link checker, accessibility scan, license detection, and readability scan each find and cannot find.

docs.title: AI Cost
docs.text:
AI cost is the money a service charges for the language model's work. Most services bill by the token, with one price for the tokens you send and a higher price for the tokens the model writes. Prices vary widely between models and change often, so a reviewer should look up current prices and never rely on a figure in a book. The arithmetic is stable, and it takes one formula:

cost of one run = (input tokens x input price + output tokens x output price) / 1,000,000

The prices are per million tokens, so the division by 1,000,000 turns a price per million into a price for the tokens you used. The total for a batch is the cost of one run, times the number of resources, times the number of runs on each. A multi-agent review that uses three agents multiplies the cost by three, and a retry after an invalid answer adds another run.

Worked example: the cost of a batch. The prices are illustrative, at $2.00 per million input tokens and $8.00 per million output tokens. A run reads 6,000 input tokens and writes 1,000 output tokens.

Step Calculation Result Input cost 6,000 x 2.00 / 1,000,000 $0.012 Output cost 1,000 x 8.00 / 1,000,000 $0.008 One run 0.012 + 0.008 $0.02 500 resources, one run each 500 x 0.02 $10.00 500 resources, three agents 3 x 10.00 $30.00

Cost can be reduced without cutting quality. Give exact checks to free tools, which cost nothing per token. Shorten the instructions and send only the parts of the resource that a check needs. Use a smaller, cheaper model for first screens and a larger one for judgment. Test the prompt on three resources before running it on three hundred, so a flaw costs three runs and not three hundred.

Run a Pilot Before You Run the Batch

Score three resources, read the reports, and multiply the cost by the size of the collection. A pilot tells you the price and shows whether the prompt works before you commit to the whole batch.

The MicroSim below practices the arithmetic. It shows five scenarios, and for each one you compute the total cost.

docs.title: Diagram: AI Cost Calculator
docs.text:
AI Cost Calculator

Type: microsim sim-id: ai-cost-calculator Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: calculate Learning Objective: The learner will calculate the total cost of each of five scenarios from tokens, prices, resources, and runs, to the nearest cent, with at least 4 of 5 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: AI Cost, Token, Context Window (defined in Chapter 12), Batch Evaluation (defined in Chapter 12) (all defined in this chapter above this block or in Chapter 12).

Evidence of Mastery: For each scenario the learner enters the total cost in dollars before the answer is shown. An answer is correct when it equals the Total cost column in Content to the nearest cent. Mastery is at least 4 of 5 correct on the first attempt. Using the explore mode is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Input and output tokens cost the same. (2) A multi-agent review costs the same as one agent. (3) Prices in a book stay current.

Instructional Rationale: Calculating a cost from a formula is an Apply-level action. Five scenarios that change one quantity at a time teach the learner which quantity drives the total.

Content:

The formula, shown at all times: cost of one run = (input tokens x input price + output tokens x output price) / 1,000,000, with prices in dollars per million tokens. Total cost = cost of one run x resources x runs per resource.

The five scenarios (all prices are illustrative and labeled so):

# Input tokens Output tokens Input price Output price Resources Runs each Cost of one run Total cost Why (shown as feedback) 1 6,000 1,000 $2.00 $8.00 1 1 $0.02 $0.02 (12,000 + 8,000) / 1,000,000 = 0.02. 2 6,000 1,000 $2.00 $8.00 500 1 $0.02 $10.00 500 runs at $0.02 each. 3 6,000 1,000 $2.00 $8.00 500 3 $0.02 $30.00 Three agents triple the runs. 4 60,000 2,000 $2.00 $8.00 1 1 $0.136 $0.14 (120,000 + 16,000) / 1,000,000 = 0.136, which rounds to 0.14. 5 6,000 1,000 $10.00 $30.00 500 1 $0.09 $45.00 A model with higher prices costs $0.09 a run, and 500 runs cost $45.00.

Provenance: The scenarios and prices are illustrative cases written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative prices, not a price list". Real prices vary by model and change.

Rules: The cost of one run is (input tokens x input price + output tokens x output price) / 1,000,000. The total is that cost x resources x runs, rounded to the nearest cent. In explore mode each input token count has minimum 1,000, maximum 200,000, step 1,000, default 6,000, unit tokens. Each output token count has minimum 500, maximum 10,000, step 500, default 1,000, unit tokens. Each price has minimum 0.10, maximum 50.00, step 0.10, unit dollars per million tokens. Resources have minimum 1, maximum 1,000, step 1, default 500. Runs have minimum 1, maximum 5, step 1, default 1.

Learner Activity:

  1. In explore mode the learner changes the inputs and watches the cost of one run and the total.
  2. The learner should notice that the number of runs multiplies the total in the same way as the number of resources.
  3. In practice mode the sim shows scenario 1 with its numbers.
  4. The learner enters the total cost in dollars and presses Check.
  5. The sim shows the arithmetic and the correct total, then the next scenario, until scenario 5 is done.

Feedback: 5 scenarios in the fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: $[total]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. One run costs $[run], so the total is $[total]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 5 correct on the first attempt". At 4 or more it adds "You can price a batch." Below 4 it shows the arithmetic for each missed scenario.

Starting State: Explore mode with 6,000 input tokens, 1,000 output tokens, $2.00 and $8.00 prices, 500 resources, and 1 run, giving a total of $10.00. The prompt is "Change a number to see the cost move."

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's worked example uses illustrative prices of $2.00 and $8.00 per million tokens, 6,000 input tokens and 1,000 output tokens, and arrives at $0.02 per run, $10.00 for 500 resources, and $30.00 for three agents.

docs.title: Student Data Privacy
docs.text:
Student data privacy is the protection of information about students from being collected, shared, or used in ways they and their families have not agreed to. Student data includes names, identification numbers, grades, test results, written work, photographs, attendance, and health and disability information, and anything that could identify a student when combined with other details. The duty to protect it applies to every tool you use, and AI services need particular care because text sent to a service leaves your control. The service may store it, a company's staff may read it, and some services use submitted text to improve their models.

For the work in this book, the rule is simple. An AI agent that reviews a resource needs only the resource, which is published or ready to publish and holds no student data. Keep student information out of the folder, the prompt, and the reports. The A/B tests in Chapters 16 and 17 do involve student data, and they need consent, anonymizing, and an approved way to handle the data. A teacher who is unsure should ask the school's privacy officer or technology office before sending anything.

Worked example: sorting what may go to an AI service. The table sorts six items.

Item May it be sent to an AI service? Why The published text of an open textbook chapter Yes It is public and holds no student data A rubric prompt template Yes It holds no student data A class's quiz scores with student names Not as it is Names make the scores personal data, so anonymize or get approval first A spreadsheet of grades with student ID numbers No It is identifiable and sensitive A student's photograph No It identifies a person An email thread with a parent about a student No It is private and identifies a student

Once It Is Sent, You Cannot Pull It Back

Text pasted into an AI service has left your computer, and a deletion request may not undo it. Keep student names, grades, and records out of every prompt, and if you are not sure an item is safe, ask before you send it.

The MicroSim below practices the sort. It shows ten items, and for each one you decide whether it is safe to send, needs approval or anonymizing first, or must not be sent.

docs.title: Diagram: Student Data Sorter
docs.text:
Student Data Sorter

Type: microsim sim-id: student-data-sorter Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: judge Learning Objective: The learner will judge whether each of ten items is safe to send to an AI service, needs approval or anonymizing first, or must not be sent, with at least 9 of 10 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Student Data Privacy, FERPA, AI Assistant (defined in Chapter 12) (all defined in this chapter above this block or in Chapter 12).

Evidence of Mastery: For each item the learner commits one of three bins. A placement is correct when it matches the Correct bin column in Content. Mastery is at least 9 of 10 correct on the first attempt. Reading the definitions is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Removing names always makes data anonymous. (2) A small class cannot be identified from its scores. (3) Anything a teacher already holds is safe to send.

Instructional Rationale: Judging whether an item may be sent is an Evaluate-level action that applies a privacy rule. Ten items that include re-identifiable ones teach the learner that anonymizing takes more than deleting names.

Content:

The three bins: Safe to send (public material with no student data), Needs approval or anonymizing first (could identify students, or is sensitive), and Do not send (clearly identifies a student or is private).

The ten items:

# Item shown to the learner Correct bin Why (shown as feedback) 1 The published text of an open textbook chapter. Safe to send It is public and holds no student data. 2 A rubric prompt template with placeholders. Safe to send It holds no student data. 3 A class's quiz scores listed with student names. Needs approval or anonymizing first The names make the scores personal data. 4 A spreadsheet of grades with student ID numbers. Do not send It is identifiable and sensitive. 5 A photograph of a student. Do not send It identifies a person. 6 Quiz results with names replaced by codes, from a class of four students. Needs approval or anonymizing first In a very small group, the scores may still identify students. 7 A teacher's own lesson plan with no student information. Safe to send It holds no student data. 8 An email thread with a parent about a student's progress. Do not send It is private and identifies a student. 9 A public district policy document. Safe to send It is public and holds no student data. 10 Unsigned survey comments from a class of 120 students. Needs approval or anonymizing first Comments can reveal who wrote them, so check them before sending.

Provenance: The items are illustrative cases written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The sim states that it is a study aid and not legal advice, and that a school's own policy decides.

Rules: Each item has exactly one correct bin. Four items are Safe to send, three are Needs approval or anonymizing first, and three are Do not send.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one item and the three bins.
  2. The learner places the item in a bin, and the placement is committed.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text.
  4. After item 10 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 10 items in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [bin]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. This is [bin]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 10 correct on the first attempt". At 9 or more it adds "You can keep student data out of an AI service." Below 9 it lists the Why text of each missed item.

Starting State: The first item and the three bins. The question shown is "May this go to an AI service?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's worked example sorts a public textbook chapter and a rubric prompt as safe, class scores with names as needing anonymizing first, and a grade spreadsheet, a photograph, and a parent email as not to be sent.

docs.title: FERPA
docs.text: FERPA, the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act, is a United States federal law of 1974 that protects the privacy of student education records. It applies to schools and colleges that receive funds from the U.S. Department of Education. It gives parents the right to see their children's education records and to ask for corrections, and those rights pass to the student at age 18 or on entering a college. It generally requires written consent before a school discloses personally identifiable information from a student's education record, with exceptions, such as sharing with school officials who have a legitimate educational interest. Sending identifiable student records to an AI company is a disclosure that FERPA may restrict. Other laws also apply in other places or to other data, and this book does not give legal advice, so ask your school's privacy officer which rules cover you.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Human in the loop means a named person reviews the agent's output where errors matter, and matches the level of checking to the risk. The decision stays with a person.
  • Multi-agent review compares independent runs, and a spread of more than 3 points flags a metric. Agreement among agents is not truth, and agreement with no evidence needs a check.
  • An automated link checker, accessibility scan, license detection, and readability scan each do an exact job well and miss a kind of problem, so a clean scan is never a pass.
  • AI cost is tokens times price, times resources, times runs. Give exact checks to free tools, and run a pilot before a batch.
  • Student data privacy means keeping student information out of every prompt and report. FERPA is the U.S. law that protects student education records, and your school's policy decides what you may send.

You Can Automate With Care

You can now choose which checks to automate, keep a person in the loop, triage several agents, price a batch, and keep student data out of harm's way. The agent can do the counting, and you keep the judgment and the responsibility.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Automated Checks, Cost, and Student Privacy
docs.text: Test your understanding of human oversight, multi-agent review, automated checks, AI cost, and student data privacy with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. What does FERPA protect?
docs.text:
1. The copyright of teachers' lesson plans
  2. The accessibility of web content for learners with disabilities
  3. The licensing terms of open textbooks
  4. The privacy of student education records in the United States
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. FERPA, the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act of 1974, is a U.S. federal law that protects the privacy of student education records. It applies to schools and colleges that receive funds from the U.S. Department of Education, and it generally requires written consent before a school discloses personally identifiable information from a record. Sending identifiable student records to an AI company is a disclosure that FERPA may restrict. Ask your school's privacy officer which rules cover you.

Concept Tested: FERPA

See: FERPA

docs.title: 2. In multi-agent review, what spread between the highest and lowest agent scores flags a metric for a person to examine first?
docs.text:
1. More than 1 point
  2. More than 3 points
  3. More than 5 points
  4. Any spread at all
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Multi-agent review has two or more agents, or several runs with different prompts or models, score the same resource independently. It copies the two-reviewer method of Chapter 11, so it uses the same rule: a metric is flagged when the scores differ by more than 3 points. The spread is a cheap signal that points to metrics where the evidence is unclear or an agent has gone astray. Agreement within 3 points still needs a check if no evidence was quoted.

Concept Tested: Multi-Agent Review

See: Multi-Agent Review

docs.title: 3. Why does the chapter recommend matching the level of checking to the risk instead of redoing every score by hand?
docs.text:
1. Risk-matched oversight catches errors where they occur and keeps most of the agent's time saving
  2. Agents are always accurate on low-risk metrics, so no one needs to read their reports at all
  3. A person is not responsible for decisions that an agent's report supports, because the agent made them
  4. Reports with exact evidence should be accepted without any human check, because the evidence is exact
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Human in the loop means a person reviews the agent's output where errors matter. The cost is time, so the practical question is where attention buys the most. A report that follows the rules, carries tool logs, and shows exact evidence needs a spot check, a report built on the agent's memory needs every claim checked, and a report that breaks the rubric's rules goes back. Accountability cannot be delegated, so a person always answers for the decision.

Concept Tested: Human in the Loop

See: Human in the Loop

docs.title: 4. Why is a clean automated accessibility scan a starting point and not a pass?
docs.text:
1. Automated scans are never accurate about missing alt attributes, so every image must be checked by hand
  2. A scan can examine only the first page of a resource, so most pages are never checked
  3. A scan checks only the color of text and nothing else, so most problems are never found
  4. A scan finds machine-detectable problems but cannot judge whether alt text is useful or captions are accurate
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. An automated scan finds images with no alt attribute, text with weak contrast, missing form labels, and some heading problems. Those are real findings, and they are quick to get. It cannot judge quality: alt text that says "photo" exists, so the scan passes it. The accessibility metric still needs the human checks, which means reading the alt text, listening with a screen reader, and tabbing through the page.

Concept Tested: Automated Accessibility Scan

See: Automated Accessibility Scan

docs.title: 5. Which approach does the chapter recommend for reducing AI cost without cutting quality?
docs.text:
1. Run every resource three times and keep the cheapest result, whatever the quality of the answer
  2. Skip the human check on every report that comes from a larger model, to save the reviewer's time
  3. Use the largest and most expensive model for every check, so that no check needs to be repeated
  4. Give exact checks to free tools, send only what a check needs, use a cheaper model first, and pilot
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Cost is tokens times price, times resources, times runs, so each lever matters. Free tools cost nothing per token, shorter instructions and trimmed inputs cut the tokens, and a smaller model suffices for a first screen. A pilot of three resources shows the price and whether the prompt works, so a flaw costs three runs and not three hundred. Prices change often, so look up current ones and never rely on a figure in a book.

Concept Tested: AI Cost

See: AI Cost

docs.title: 6. A run reads 6,000 input tokens and writes 1,000 output tokens, at $2.00 per million input tokens and $8.00 per million output tokens. What does a batch of 500 resources cost if three agents each score every resource once?
docs.text:
1. $30.00
  2. $10.00
  3. $90.00
  4. $0.06
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. One run costs (6,000 × 2.00 + 1,000 × 8.00) ÷ 1,000,000, which is 0.012 + 0.008, or $0.02. Five hundred resources at one run each cost $10.00, and three agents triple the number of runs, so the batch costs $30.00. Option B forgets the extra agents, and option D is the cost of one resource scored by three agents. The prices here are illustrative, and a retry after an invalid answer adds another run.

Concept Tested: AI Cost

See: AI Cost

docs.title: 7. A teacher wants an agent to review a published open textbook chapter. She also has a spreadsheet of her class's quiz scores listed with student names. What should she send?
docs.text:
1. Only the published chapter, because the scores with names need approval or anonymizing first
  2. Both files, because anything a teacher already holds is safe to send to an AI service
  3. Neither file, because every file is private once it is on a teacher's computer and cannot leave it
  4. Only the spreadsheet, because the chapter is already public and so needs no review by the agent
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. An agent that reviews a resource needs only the resource, which is published or ready to publish and holds no student data. Names make quiz scores personal data, so the spreadsheet needs anonymizing or approval first, and even coded scores from a very small class may still identify students. Text pasted into an AI service leaves your control, and a deletion request may not undo it. If unsure, ask the school's privacy officer or technology office.

Concept Tested: Student Data Privacy

See: Student Data Privacy

docs.title: 8. A page footer says CC BY-NC, while the license recorded in the page's metadata says CC BY. Which automated check would find this mismatch?
docs.text:
1. An automated link checker
  2. An automated readability scan
  3. Automated license detection
  4. An automated accessibility scan
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Automated license detection finds license statements in a resource, reads their names, versions, and links, and compares them with the license recorded in the metadata. It catches a missing license, a mismatch between page and metadata, and an unrecognized license text. It cannot tell whether the statement is true: a work copied from someone else with a license label added still passes. The check supports the open license metric.

Concept Tested: Automated License Detection

See: Automated License Detection

docs.title: 9. Three agents score two metrics. For accessibility they give 5, 9, and 6, and all three quote evidence. For open license they all give 9, and none quotes any evidence. Which analysis is correct?
docs.text:
1. Accessibility needs a check, but open license can be accepted because all three agents agree on it
  2. Both metrics should be accepted, using the average of the three scores for each metric
  3. Accessibility is flagged by its spread of 4, and open license needs a check because agreement alone proves little
  4. Open license is flagged because the agents agree, and accessibility can be accepted because its evidence was quoted
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The spread for accessibility is 9 minus 5, which is 4, and that is more than 3, so the metric is flagged. For open license the spread is 0, but no agent quoted evidence. Agreement among agents is not truth, because agents built on similar models can share the same blind spots. Agreement with no evidence is especially suspect, so a person checks it anyway. The average of three scores is not the right score.

Concept Tested: Multi-Agent Review

See: Multi-Agent Review

docs.title: 10. An agent's report recommends Adopt for a resource with a total of 76, but one metric scores 4. Which analysis is correct?
docs.text:
1. Adopt is correct, because the total is at least 75 and that is what the rule requires
  2. The decision breaks the adoption rule, which needs every metric at 5 or more, so the report goes back
  3. The report needs only a spot check, because its numbers look exact and complete
  4. A person should check every claim, because the report has no evidence for its decision
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The Adopt rule has two parts: a total of at least 75 and every metric at least 5. The report meets the first and fails the second, so its own decision breaks the rubric's rule. A report that breaks the rules goes back to the agent for another run, which is the highest level of oversight, ahead of checking every claim or spot-checking. The details of the report do not make it trustworthy, since the error lies in the logic and not in a missing source.

Concept Tested: Human in the Loop

See: Human in the Loop

docs.title: References: Automated Checks, Cost, and Student Privacy
docs.text:
1. Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act - Wikipedia - Explains the U.S. law that protects the privacy of student education records and when schools may disclose them. The legal basis for the chapter's student data privacy guidance.

  2. Human-in-the-loop - Wikipedia - Describes systems in which a person reviews or corrects an automated process. Background for the chapter's rule that a human checks the agent's evidence before any score is accepted.

  3. Multi-agent system - Wikipedia - Surveys systems where several agents work together or check one another. Supports the chapter's multi-agent review, in which one agent's findings are triaged against another's.

  4. Privacy in Context: Technology, Policy, and the Integrity of Social Life - Helen Nissenbaum - Stanford Law Books (2010) - Nissenbaum's contextual integrity judges a flow of information by whether it matches the norms of the setting where it was shared. It offers a test for whether student work may be sent to an AI service.

  5. Co-Intelligence: Living and Working with AI - Ethan Mollick - Portfolio (2024) - Mollick's practical rules, including always being the human in the loop, and his centaur and cyborg modes of working with AI frame this chapter's balance between automation and human judgment.

  6. Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA) - U.S. Department of Education - The Student Privacy Policy Office's official FERPA page, with guidance for schools and teachers on education records and disclosure. The primary source for the chapter's privacy rules.

  7. Common Sense Privacy Program - Common Sense Media - Evaluates the privacy policies of educational apps and tools and rates them. Helps teachers check an AI service's data practices before sending it any student material.

  8. Web Accessibility Evaluation Tools List - W3C Web Accessibility Initiative - A filterable directory of accessibility checkers by purpose, platform, price, and standard. Helps readers choose the automated accessibility checks this chapter recommends.

  9. Pricing - Claude Platform Docs - Lists per-token prices and discounts for batch processing and prompt caching. Gives the numbers needed for the chapter's exercise on estimating the cost of scoring a batch of resources.

  10. AI Risk Management Framework - NIST - A voluntary framework for governing, mapping, measuring, and managing the risks of AI systems. Supports decisions about which checks to automate and which need human oversight.

docs.title: Checking and Calibrating AI Agent Output
Summary
docs.text: Teaches teachers to catch hallucinations, invented citations, license misreadings, and overconfident scores, and to measure agreement with human reviewers using simple statistics. It is the chapter that makes AI scoring trustworthy, and it relies on the prompts and checks from the previous two chapters. After this chapter you can catch common agent errors, log your findings, and measure how closely an agent agrees with human reviewers.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 2: Open Licenses and Attribution
  • Chapter 3: The Ten-Metric Rubric and Scoring
  • Chapter 5: Accuracy and Currency
  • Chapter 11: Manual Evaluation and Adoption Decisions
  • Chapter 12: AI Agents, Prompts, and Rubric Scoring
  • Chapter 13: Automated Checks, Cost, and Student Privacy

Trust, But Check the Evidence

This is the chapter I have been waiting for, because it turns an agent's confident first pass into something you can rely on. You will learn the mistakes agents make, how to catch each one, and how to measure how closely an agent agrees with careful human reviewers. Let's dive in and check the evidence!

An agent's report looks finished. It has ten scores, a table of evidence, a total, and a recommendation, all in a tidy form. The earlier chapters warned that this polish can hide errors, and this chapter shows you what the errors look like and how to find them. It has two parts. The first part is about checking: the kinds of mistake an agent makes, the steps that catch each one, and the habit of accepting, correcting, or rejecting every claim. The second part is about measuring: the simple statistics that tell you, across many resources, how closely an agent agrees with human reviewers, and whether it is safe to use as a first pass.

docs.title: Hallucination
docs.text:
A hallucination is a statement by a language model that is fluent and confident and not true: a fact it made up, a quotation that does not appear in the source, a feature of the resource that is not there, or a reference to something that does not exist. Chapter 12 explained why this happens. A model writes what is likely to come next, and a plausible continuation is not always a true one. In a review the danger is sharper than usual, because the agent is asked to report what it found in a resource, and a hallucination is a report of something it did not find.

Hallucinations take four common forms in an evaluation report:

  • An invented feature: the report says the video has captions, and it has none.
  • An invented quotation: the report quotes a sentence as evidence, and the sentence is not in the resource.
  • An invented measurement: the report gives a contrast ratio or a reading level, and no tool produced it.
  • An invented source: the report cites a paper or a page that does not exist, which the next section treats separately.

The defense is the rule that every claim must carry evidence a person can find. A quotation can be searched for in the resource. A measurement can be traced to a tool log. A claim with neither is a claim to reject.

Worked example: four hallucinations in one draft. An agent's draft for Watershed Basics contains four invented claims. The table shows each one and how a reviewer finds it.

Kind What the agent wrote How the reviewer found it Invented feature "The video has English captions." Played the video, and found no caption control Invented quotation Evidence: "Alt text: A detailed map of the river and nearby towns" Searched the page for the sentence, and found different alt text: "A map showing the river and its tributaries" Invented measurement "Contrast ratio tested: 5.2 to 1" Asked for the tool log, and found that no tool had run Invented count "All 14 links work" Ran a link checker, and found that 2 links fail

The Smoothest Sentence May Be the Invented One

A hallucination does not look different from a true statement, because the model writes both in the same confident voice. Search for every quotation, trace every number to a tool, and treat any claim you cannot find as false until you do.

The first MicroSim of the chapter trains the search for invented quotations. It shows a short excerpt of a resource and eight quotations that an agent offered as evidence, and for each one you decide whether it is exact, altered, or not in the text.

docs.title: Diagram: Quote Verifier
docs.text:
Quote Verifier

Type: microsim sim-id: quote-verifier Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: judge Learning Objective: The learner will judge whether each of eight quotations offered by an agent is an exact quote, an altered quote, or not in the text, with at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Hallucination, Evidence for a Score (defined in Chapter 3), Agent Evaluation Report (defined in Chapter 12) (all defined in this chapter above this block or in earlier chapters).

Evidence of Mastery: For each quotation the learner commits one of three verdicts. A verdict is correct when it matches the Correct verdict column in Content. Mastery is at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Rereading the excerpt is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A quotation that sounds right is exact. (2) A small change to a quotation does not matter. (3) A quotation that is plausible must be somewhere in the text.

Instructional Rationale: Judging a quotation against its source is an Evaluate-level action that every review of an agent's evidence needs. Altered quotations, which differ in one detail, teach the learner to compare word for word, and invented ones teach the learner to search the whole text.

Content:

The excerpt, shown at all times (made up): "Watershed Basics by Maria Lopez. Licensed under CC BY 4.0. A watershed is an area of land where all the water drains to the same place. Section 2: The Clearwater River drains about 6,000 square miles and flows into Lake Marlow. Figure 1: A map of the Clearwater watershed. Alt text: A map showing the river and its tributaries. Quiz: Question 1 asks the learner to choose the definition of a watershed."

The three verdicts: Exact quote, Altered quote, Not in the text.

The eight quotations:

# Quotation offered by the agent Correct verdict Why (shown as feedback) 1 "Licensed under CC BY 4.0" Exact quote The words appear exactly. 2 "A watershed is an area of land where all the water drains to the same place." Exact quote The sentence appears exactly. 3 "The Clearwater River drains about 6,000 square miles and flows into the sea." Altered quote The excerpt says it flows into Lake Marlow, so "the sea" is a change. 4 "Captions are available in English and Spanish." Not in the text Nothing in the excerpt mentions captions. 5 "Figure 1: A map of the Clearwater watershed." Exact quote The caption appears exactly. 6 "Alt text: A detailed map of the river, its tributaries, and nearby towns." Altered quote The excerpt says "A map showing the river and its tributaries", so details were added. 7 "Licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0" Altered quote The excerpt says CC BY, so the license was changed. 8 "An answer key is included for all quiz questions." Not in the text Nothing in the excerpt mentions an answer key.

Provenance: The excerpt and quotations are made up for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The verdicts follow the chapter section "Hallucination".

Rules: Each quotation has exactly one correct verdict. Three are Exact quote, three are Altered quote, and two are Not in the text. A quotation is exact only when it matches the excerpt word for word.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees the excerpt and one quotation.
  2. The learner chooses a verdict, and the choice is committed.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text, and highlights the matching or conflicting part of the excerpt.
  4. After quotation 8 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 8 quotations in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [verdict]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. This is [verdict]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 8 correct on the first attempt". At 7 or more it adds "You can check an agent's quotations." Below 7 it lists the Why text of each missed quotation.

Starting State: The excerpt and quotation 1 or the first quotation in the shuffled order. The question shown is "Does this quotation appear in the text?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter lists four forms of hallucination: an invented feature, quotation, measurement, and source. The chapter's worked example includes an altered alt text for a map.

docs.title: Invented Citation
docs.text:
An invented citation is a reference to a source that does not exist, or that exists and does not say what the agent claims. Agents produce these readily, because a citation has a predictable shape, with authors, a title, a journal, a year, and pages, and a model can write that shape without any real source behind it. The result looks scholarly. It is also useless, because no one can find the paper, and it is misleading, because it lends a claim an authority it has not earned.

Two kinds of invented citation need different checks. A nonexistent source is one that cannot be found at all: the journal, the article, or the author is made up. A misattributed source exists and does not support the claim: a real paper on urban runoff cited for a claim about wetlands. A reviewer needs four checks to tell them apart. Search for the exact title. Check that the journal exists and has the issue cited. Resolve the identifier or the link. And open the source and read the passage that is supposed to support the claim.

An identifier helps. A DOI (digital object identifier) is a permanent code that should lead to the article's page, so a DOI that leads nowhere, or leads to a different article, is a strong sign of an invented or misattributed citation. A missing identifier is a weaker sign, since many real sources, such as a school's own pages, have none. The best defense sits in the prompt: tell the agent to cite only sources that appear in the resource or that you supplied, and to write "no source found" in place of supplying one from memory.

Worked example: three citations from an agent's report. The table shows the checks and the verdicts.

Citation What the checks found Verdict State Water Agency, "Lake Marlow Fact Sheet", 2025, with a link The link opens a fact sheet that gives the lake's depth, which supports the claim Real and supports the claim Lopez, M. (2024), "Rivers of the Plain", Journal of Water Education, 12(3), 44 to 59 No journal by that name appears in any index, and no article has that title Invented Okafor, S. (2022), "Runoff and Land Use", Earth Science Review The article exists and studies urban runoff, and it does not mention wetlands Real and does not support the claim

The MicroSim below practices the checks. It shows six citations, each with the result of a lookup, and for each one you decide what the lookup shows.

docs.title: Diagram: Citation Existence Checker
docs.text:
Citation Existence Checker

Type: microsim sim-id: citation-existence-checker Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: examine Learning Objective: The learner will examine the lookup result for each of six citations and decide whether the source exists and supports the claim, exists and does not support it, or does not exist, with at least 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Invented Citation, Hallucination, Citation Quality (defined in Chapter 5) (all defined in this chapter above this block or in Chapter 5).

Evidence of Mastery: For each citation the learner commits one of three verdicts. A verdict is correct when it matches the Correct verdict column in Content. Mastery is at least 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Reading the four checks is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A citation that looks complete is real. (2) A source that exists supports the claim. (3) A working link means the claim is supported.

Instructional Rationale: Examining a lookup result against a claim is an Analyze-level action, because the learner must relate what was found to what the agent claimed. Six citations that mix real, misattributed, and invented ones teach the learner to ask two questions each time: does it exist, and does it say that.

Content:

The three verdicts: Exists and supports the claim, Exists but does not support the claim, Does not exist.

The six citations (all made up), each with the claim the agent attached to it and the result of a lookup:

# Agent's claim and citation Lookup result shown to the learner Correct verdict Why (shown as feedback) 1 Claim: the deepest point of Lake Marlow is 31 meters. Citation: State Water Agency, "Lake Marlow Fact Sheet", 2025, https://example.gov/lake-marlow The page loads and gives the lake's area and its deepest point of 31 meters. Exists and supports the claim The source is real and states the figure. 2 Claim: rivers on plains meander more. Citation: Lopez, M. (2024), "Rivers of the Plain", Journal of Water Education, 12(3), 44 to 59. No journal named Journal of Water Education appears in any index, and no article has this title. Does not exist Neither the journal nor the article can be found. 3 Claim: wetlands filter pollutants. Citation: Okafor, S. (2022), "Runoff and Land Use", Earth Science Review. The article exists and studies urban runoff, and it does not discuss wetlands. Exists but does not support the claim The source is real and says nothing about the claim. 4 Claim: the reading is licensed CC BY 4.0. Citation: https://example.org/watershed-basics The page loads, and its footer says CC BY 4.0. Exists and supports the claim The source is real and states the license. 5 Claim: soil infiltration varies with grain size. Citation: Reyes, D. (2021), "Soil Infiltration Rates", Geology Quarterly, 5(2), 10 to 19. The journal exists, and volume 5 issue 2 has no article with this title or author. Does not exist The journal is real and the article is not in the issue cited. 6 Claim: aquifers store groundwater. Citation: National Water Atlas (2019), entry on aquifers. The atlas exists, and its aquifer entry says aquifers store groundwater. Exists and supports the claim The source is real and states the claim.

Provenance: The claims, citations, and lookup results are made up for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The checks follow the chapter section "Invented Citation".

Rules: Each citation has exactly one correct verdict. Three are Exists and supports the claim, one is Exists but does not support the claim, and two are Does not exist.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees the claim, the citation, and the lookup result.
  2. The learner chooses a verdict, and the choice is committed.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text.
  4. After citation 6 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 6 citations in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [verdict]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. The verdict is [verdict]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 6 correct on the first attempt". At 5 or more it adds "You can tell a real citation from an invented one." Below 5 it lists the Why text of each missed citation.

Starting State: The first citation with its claim and lookup result. The question shown is "Does this source exist, and does it support the claim?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter says an invented citation is either nonexistent or misattributed, and lists four checks: search the title, check the journal and issue, resolve the identifier, and read the supporting passage.

docs.title: License Misreading
docs.text:
A license misreading is an agent's wrong statement about what a resource's license says or what it allows. Agents misread licenses in a handful of predictable ways. They treat a page's single license as covering every item on it, when the images carry other rights. They confuse neighboring licenses, so CC BY-NC reads as CC BY. They ignore a restriction, such as ND, when summarizing what a reuser may do. They read the license of the site's template and not of the content. And they conclude that a public page is free to copy because it is on the web. Because a misreading can send a teacher into a legal problem, a reviewer checks every license claim against the statement itself, the way Chapter 2 taught.

The prompt can lower the risk. Ask the agent to quote the license statement word for word, to name each item the statement covers, and to write "not stated" for any item the statement does not mention. A report that quotes the statement can be checked in seconds, and a report that paraphrases it cannot.

Worked example: five misreadings. The page states: "Text: CC BY-SA 4.0. Images: © their owners, used with permission, except where marked CC BY."

What the agent said What the page says The misreading "Everything on the page is CC BY-SA 4.0." The license covers the text, and the images are separate Treating one license as covering all items "The license is CC BY-NC-SA." The text is CC BY-SA, with no NC element Confusing neighboring licenses "The images may be reused freely with credit." The images are © their owners unless marked Ignoring a restriction "The page is public, so it can be copied." A public page is still protected by copyright, and the license sets the permissions Equating public with free "Adaptations may be shared under any license." CC BY-SA requires adaptations to carry CC BY-SA Missing the ShareAlike condition

The next MicroSim practices the check. It shows one page statement and eight license claims that an agent made about it, and for each one you decide whether the agent read it correctly.

docs.title: Diagram: License Misreading Checker
docs.text:
License Misreading Checker

Type: microsim sim-id: license-misreading-checker Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: judge Learning Objective: The learner will judge whether each of eight agent claims about a page's license is correct or a misreading, with at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: License Misreading, Hallucination, and the license sections of Chapter 2 (all defined in this chapter above this block or in Chapter 2).

Evidence of Mastery: For each claim the learner commits one of two bins. A placement is correct when it matches the Correct bin column in Content. Mastery is at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Rereading the statement is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) One license on a page covers every item. (2) A public page may be copied. (3) CC BY-SA and CC BY-NC-SA are the same.

Instructional Rationale: Judging a license claim against a statement applies the Chapter 2 skill to an agent's output. Eight claims that fail in the five ways named in the chapter teach the learner to check each claim against the exact words.

Content:

The page statement, shown at all times (made up): "Text: CC BY-SA 4.0. Images: © their owners, used with permission, except where marked CC BY."

The two bins: Correct reading, and Misreading.

The eight claims:

# Claim made by the agent Correct bin Why (shown as feedback) 1 The text is licensed CC BY-SA 4.0. Correct reading It matches the statement. 2 Everything on the page is CC BY-SA 4.0. Misreading The images carry other rights. 3 Adaptations of the text must be shared under CC BY-SA. Correct reading ShareAlike requires it. 4 The images may be reused freely with credit. Misreading The images are © their owners unless marked CC BY. 5 The license allows commercial use of the text. Correct reading CC BY-SA has no NonCommercial element. 6 The license is CC BY-NC-SA. Misreading The statement names CC BY-SA, with no NC element. 7 The images marked CC BY may be reused with credit. Correct reading CC BY allows reuse with credit. 8 Because the page is public, it can be copied without a license. Misreading A public page is still protected, and the license sets the permissions.

Provenance: The statement and claims are made up for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The license rules follow Chapter 2.

Rules: Each claim has exactly one correct bin, four per bin.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees the page statement and one claim.
  2. The learner places the claim in a bin, and the placement is committed.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text.
  4. After claim 8 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 8 claims in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [bin]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. This is a [bin]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 8 correct on the first attempt". At 7 or more it adds "You can check an agent's license reading." Below 7 it lists the Why text of each missed claim.

Starting State: The page statement and claim 1 or the first claim in the shuffled order. The question shown is "Did the agent read the license correctly?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter lists five license misreadings: treating one license as covering all items, confusing neighboring licenses, ignoring a restriction, equating public with free, and missing ShareAlike.

docs.title: Overconfident Score
docs.text:
An overconfident score is a score that is higher or more certain than its evidence supports. It is the quietest error, because nothing in the report is invented. The agent simply gives a 9 for a metric it did not fully check, or a 10 where a careful reviewer would find a gap. Signs include a high score with no quoted evidence, a pass on a check that needs a tool when no tool log is attached, an empty list of checks not verified when some checks could not have been verified from the text, and round scores of 9 and 10 across many metrics.

The rubric's own rules offer the remedy, and Chapter 12's prompt built it in. A check that was not tested counts as failed. A check that cannot be verified is marked "not checkable", and it is listed. A score of 10 requires every check to pass. When a report follows those rules, a high score is earned and shows its evidence. When it does not, a reviewer lowers the score to what the evidence supports.

Worked example: a 9 that should be a 5. The agent gave accessibility a 9. The human reviewer scored it 5.

What the agent reported What the evidence supports "Images have alt text" with no count The count is 4 of 5, and 2 of the 4 are one word "Video is accessible" with no quote The video has no captions, which is a serious failure "Contrast is fine" with no tool log The contrast was never tested, so the check counts as failed Checks not verified: an empty list Several checks were never verified Score: 9 Five checks pass, which gives a score of 5

A quick test works on any report: recompute the band from the agent's own checks. The agent lists its ten checks, the number that pass is divided by ten, and the share sets the band by the rule of Chapter 3. If 6 of 10 checks pass, the share is 60 percent, which is the Adequate band of 5 to 6, and a reported 8 is overconfident by at least two points. The test needs no outside source, only the report itself, and it catches a mismatch between the agent's evidence and its own score.

docs.title: Score Inflation
docs.text:
Score inflation is a systematic tendency of an agent to score higher than careful human reviewers, across many metrics and many resources. It differs from a single overconfident score, since inflation is a pattern. An agent that is a little generous on every metric produces totals that are too high, which can lift a resource across the adoption threshold that a human would not cross. It shows up as a positive average difference between agent and human scores, which the section on mean absolute difference later calls the bias. The fix is a stricter prompt, the "untested counts as failed" rule, and calibration against human scores, as the second half of the chapter explains.

The MicroSim below practices the detection. It shows six metric results from agents, and for each one you decide whether the score is plausible or overconfident.

docs.title: Diagram: Overconfident Score Detector
docs.text:
Overconfident Score Detector

Type: microsim sim-id: overconfident-score-detector Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: examine Learning Objective: The learner will examine the score, evidence, tool log, and unverified list of each of six agent results and decide whether the score is plausible or overconfident, with at least 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Overconfident Score, Score Inflation, Agent Scoring (defined in Chapter 12) (all defined in this chapter above this block or in Chapter 12).

Evidence of Mastery: For each result the learner commits one of two bins. A placement is correct when it matches the Correct bin column in Content. Mastery is at least 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Reading the rule is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A high score is always suspect. (2) A detailed paragraph is evidence. (3) An empty unverified list means everything was verified.

Instructional Rationale: Examining a result for the match between score and evidence is an Analyze-level action. Results with high scores and strong evidence teach the learner that a high score is not itself a warning, and results with weak evidence teach them what is.

Content:

The rule, shown at all times: a result is Overconfident when its score is >= 9 and at least one of these holds: no specific evidence is quoted; a check that needs a tool was marked passed with no tool log; or the unverified list is empty although some checks cannot be verified from the text. Otherwise it is Plausible.

The two bins: Plausible, and Overconfident.

The six results (all made up, for Watershed Basics):

# Metric and score What the result shows Correct bin Why (shown as feedback) 1 Open license, 9 Evidence names the footer on 6 of 6 pages and an image with no notice. A license scan log is attached. The unverified list is empty. Plausible The score has exact evidence and a tool log. 2 Accessibility, 9 Evidence says "looks accessible". No tool log. The unverified list is empty. Overconfident The score has no specific evidence, and the contrast and caption checks were never run. 3 Readability, 8 A readability tool log with three grade levels is attached. The unverified list is empty. Plausible The score is < 9, and it rests on a tool log. 4 Portability, 10 Evidence says "works everywhere". No test log. Overconfident A 10 with no test evidence cannot be earned. 5 Accuracy and currency, 6 Evidence quotes 10 facts checked with 2 mismatches. The unverified list names the link checks. Plausible The score is < 9, and the report lists what it could not verify. 6 Editable source, 9 The evidence lists the source files and all ten check results. The unverified list is empty. Plausible The score has exact evidence and a complete check list.

Provenance: The results are illustrative cases written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The rule follows the chapter section "Overconfident Score".

Rules: Each result has exactly one correct bin. Two results are Overconfident and four are Plausible.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one result and the rule.
  2. The learner places the result in a bin, and the placement is committed.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text.
  4. After result 6 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 6 results in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [bin]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. This is [bin]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 6 correct on the first attempt". At 5 or more it adds "You can spot a score that outruns its evidence." Below 5 it lists the Why text of each missed result.

Starting State: The first result and the rule. The question shown is "Does the evidence support this score?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter says an overconfident score is higher than its evidence supports, and that a check not tested counts as failed and a score of 10 requires every check to pass.

docs.title: Agent Error Type
docs.text:
An agent error type is a category of mistake that an agent makes, used to organize what a reviewer finds. Naming the type tells the reviewer how to catch it and tells the prompt writer how to fix it. This book uses four types, which match the errors a reviewer meets most often.

Type What it looks like How to catch it Factual error A wrong claim about the resource, such as a feature that is absent or a count that is off Open the resource and check the claim License error A wrong reading of the resource's license, or a missed or mismatched license Compare the claim with the statement itself Citation error A reference that does not exist or does not support its claim Look up the source and read the passage Scoring error A score that does not follow from the agent's own checks, or arithmetic that does not add up Recount the passes, recompute the band, and re-add the total

Each type also points to a fix in the prompt, which is why the type is worth naming. The log of a calibration run, described later in this chapter, shows which type is most common, and that tells the prompt writer where to spend effort.

Type Typical fix in the prompt Factual error Require a quotation or a location for every claim, and a tool log for every measurement License error Require the license statement quoted word for word, and "not stated" for anything it does not mention Citation error Allow only sources found in the resource or supplied by the reviewer Scoring error Ask for the list of checks with a pass or fail on each, and have a spreadsheet or script add the total

A fifth case is useful to name: a claim by the agent that turns out to be correct is not an error. Reviewers who see only mistakes become suspicious of everything, and an accurate record of what the agent got right is as useful as a list of what it got wrong.

The next MicroSim practices the naming. It shows ten findings from reviews of agent reports, and for each one you choose its type or decide that it is not an error.

docs.title: Diagram: Agent Error Type Sorter
docs.text:
Agent Error Type Sorter

Type: microsim sim-id: agent-error-type-sorter Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: differentiate Learning Objective: The learner will differentiate four agent error types and the no-error case by sorting each of ten findings, with at least 9 of 10 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Agent Error Type, Hallucination, Invented Citation, License Misreading, Overconfident Score (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each finding the learner commits one of five bins. A placement is correct when it matches the Correct bin column in Content. Mastery is at least 9 of 10 correct on the first attempt. Reading the type table is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A wrong score is always a scoring error. (2) A hallucinated feature is a citation error. (3) Every finding is an error.

Instructional Rationale: Differentiating among categories is an Analyze-level action. Ten findings that include two no-error cases and look alike on the surface teach the learner to name the specific kind of failure.

Content:

The five bins: Factual error, License error, Citation error, Scoring error, Not an error.

The ten findings:

# Finding shown to the learner Correct bin Why (shown as feedback) 1 The agent says the video has captions, and it has none. Factual error It is a wrong claim about the resource. 2 The agent says the footer license is CC BY-NC, and it is CC BY. License error It misreads the license. 3 The agent cites a paper that does not exist. Citation error The reference is invented. 4 The agent's table lists five passes and it reports a score of 8, where the bands give 5 or 6. Scoring error The score does not follow from its own checks. 5 The agent says 4 of 5 images have alt text, and the true count is 4 of 5. Not an error The claim is correct. 6 The agent attributes the lake depth to a fact sheet that gives a different figure. Citation error The source does not support the claim. 7 The agent reports a total of 71, and the ten scores add to 68. Scoring error The arithmetic is wrong. 8 The agent says the resource has no license, and a footer states CC BY 4.0. License error It misses a license that is there. 9 The agent says the reading states three outcomes, and it states three. Not an error The claim is correct. 10 The agent says the quiz has 12 questions, and it has 8. Factual error It is a wrong claim about the resource.

Provenance: The findings are illustrative cases written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The types follow the chapter section "Agent Error Type".

Rules: Each finding has exactly one correct bin, two per bin.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one finding and the five bins.
  2. The learner may open the type table. Opening it does not change the score.
  3. The learner places the finding in a bin, and the placement is committed.
  4. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text.
  5. After finding 10 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 10 findings in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [bin]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. This is [bin]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 10 correct on the first attempt". At 9 or more it adds "You can name an agent's mistake." Below 9 it lists the Why text of each missed finding.

Starting State: The first finding and the five bins. The question shown is "What type of error is this, if any?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter lists four error types: factual, license, citation, and scoring, and names a fifth case, a correct claim, as not an error.

The poster below pulls the error types together on one picture. It shows an agent's report with five places where a reviewer checks first, and each marker names the check and the error it catches.

docs.title: Diagram: Agent Report Checkpoints
docs.text:
Agent Report Checkpoints

Type: infographic sim-id: agent-report-checkpoints Library: html Status: Specified Bloom Level: Remember Bloom Verb: identify Learning Objective: The learner will identify the five places in an agent's report where a reviewer checks for errors, and the error each place catches, with at least 4 of 5 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Hallucination, Invented Citation, License Misreading, Overconfident Score, Agent Error Type (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: In quiz mode the learner clicks the marker that matches a visual hint. A click is correct when it matches the marker named in the Hint column of Content. Mastery is at least 4 of 5 correct on the first attempt. Hovering in explore mode is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A report needs checking only at its score. (2) One check catches every kind of error. (3) A report with a tool log needs no checking.

Instructional Rationale: Identifying where each error type hides is a Remember-level task, and a picture of one report with five marked places gives each check a location. The quiz asks the learner to recognize a place by its look.

Content:

The illustration is a text-free flat drawing of a one-page report. The top of the page has a row of ten small boxes with a bar chart icon above them. Below it is a block of three thin lines, the first with a magnifying glass icon at its left. Below that is a line with a small book icon and a chain-link icon. Next is a line with a circled copyright symbol. Next is a large box holding one big digit, with a small empty tray beside it. At the bottom is a line of ten small boxes joined by plus signs and ending in an equals sign and a wider box. The five markers:

# Label Hint (describes the look, not the name) Description Tip 1 Quoted evidence The block of three thin lines with a magnifying glass icon at its left. A quotation or fact that the agent says it found in the resource. It can hide a hallucination. Search the resource for the exact words. 2 Citation The line with a small book icon and a chain-link icon. A reference that the agent offers as support. It can hide an invented citation. Look up the source and read the supporting passage. 3 License claim The line with a circled copyright symbol. What the agent says the license is and allows. It can hide a license misreading. Compare the claim with the license statement on the page. 4 Score and tool log The large box holding one big digit, with a small empty tray beside it. A score and the tool log behind it. An empty tray beside a high score can mean an overconfident score. Ask for the tool log, and lower any score the evidence does not support. 5 Total The bottom line of ten small boxes joined by plus signs. The ten scores and their sum. A wrong sum is a scoring error. Add the ten scores yourself.

Provenance: The five checkpoints follow the chapter sections "Hallucination", "Invented Citation", "License Misreading", "Overconfident Score", and "Agent Error Type". The illustration is synthetic, and the sim labels the report "illustrative example".

Rules: Each hint matches exactly one marker. The illustration contains no text, so every label comes from the table above. Markers are numbered 1 to 5 in the order of the table, from the middle of the page to its bottom.

Learner Activity:

  1. In explore mode the learner hovers or clicks a marker and reads its label, description, and tip.
  2. In quiz mode the sim shows a hint.
  3. The learner clicks the marker they think the hint describes.
  4. If the first click is wrong, the sim says so and lets the learner try once more. If the second click is also wrong, the sim reveals the marker and its description.
  5. After all 5 hints the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 5 hints in a shuffled order, two attempts each. Only a correct first click counts as evidence. Correct: "Correct: [label]. [Description]". First wrong click: "Not quite. Look again at the hint: [hint]". Second wrong click: "This is [label]. [Description]". The summary shows "[n] of 5 correct on the first attempt". At 4 or more it adds "You know where to look in an agent's report." Below 4 it lists the labels of the missed checkpoints.

Starting State: The illustration with five numbered markers, explore mode active, and the prompt "Hover a marker to see what it checks."

Chapter Anchors: The chapter names four error types and the checks that catch them. The poster places a check for each one on the page of a report: quotations, citations, license claims, scores, and the total.

docs.title: Verification Step
docs.text:
A verification step is a defined action a person takes to confirm or refute one claim in an agent's report. A step names the claim, the way to test it, and what result would confirm it. Verification steps get stronger as they move away from the agent's own words. The weakest is to ask the agent whether it is sure, which proves nothing. Better is to recompute arithmetic from the table. Better still is to run a tool and read its log. The strongest is to open the actual source, such as the resource's page or a cited paper, and see for yourself. The ladder ranks the common steps by how much each one proves.

Step What it proves Strength Ask the agent whether it is sure Nothing, since the same model answers again Weakest Recompute the arithmetic from the report's own table The totals follow from the scores Weak Run a tool and read its log A measurement is real and can be repeated Strong Open the resource and find the quoted text The evidence exists where the agent says Strong Open the cited source and read the passage The source exists and supports the claim Strongest

A good verification step has four parts. State the claim in its exact words. Say how to test it, such as the tool to run or the page to open. Record what you found, with a date. And mark the result: confirmed, or not confirmed.

Worked example: three verification steps.

Claim How to test it Result recorded "4 of 5 images have alt text" Open the page source and count the images and their alt attributes Confirmed: 4 of 5 "The total is 65" Add the ten scores in the table Confirmed: 65 "The footer states CC BY 4.0 on all six pages" Open each page and read the footer Not confirmed: the footer is missing on page 4

docs.title: Spot Check
docs.text: A spot check is the verification of a sample of an agent's claims and not all of them. It saves effort where the agent's work is well evidenced and the risk is low. A good sample is not random alone. It includes at least one claim from each metric, every claim that carries a lot of weight, such as one that decides a band or a floor, and a few chosen at random. If the sample turns up an error, widen it: an error in a sample suggests more errors outside it. Record which claims were checked, so that the report says what was and was not verified.

docs.title: Source Verification
docs.text:
Source verification is the verification of a claim by going to the original source and not to the agent's summary of it. It is the strongest verification step. For a license claim, the original source is the license statement on the page. For a fact, it is the cited reference, opened and read. For a measurement, it is the tool's own log. Source verification is the antidote to invented citations and hallucinated quotations, because an invented source cannot be opened. It takes longer than a spot check, so a reviewer reserves it for the claims that decide the outcome.

Check the Claims That Decide the Outcome First

If you only have time to verify five claims, verify the ones that would change the band or the decision, such as the lowest metric and any score that sits at the edge of a band. A mistake there costs the most.

docs.title: Second-Agent Cross-Check
docs.text:
A second-agent cross-check is the use of a second agent to review the first agent's report, looking for unsupported claims, missing evidence, and arithmetic that does not add up. The second agent gets the resource, the first agent's report, and a prompt that asks for faults, not for a fresh score. It is a cheap first filter. It catches many errors that a person would otherwise find by hand, such as a quotation that is not in the text, and it can run on every report.

It has the limit that Chapter 13 noted. A second agent built on the same kind of model can share the first one's blind spots, so it may miss the same errors, and it may also raise false alarms that waste a person's time. A cross-check narrows the list of things to verify and does not replace verification.

Worked example: a cross-check on five known errors. A reviewer planted five known errors in a draft report and asked a second agent to find faults.

Result Count Real errors the second agent flagged 3 of 5 Real errors the second agent missed 2 of 5 Flags that were false alarms 1

The cross-check found 60 percent of the real errors and raised one false alarm. A person would still need to check the other two errors and the alarm, and the cross-check cut the list down.

docs.title: Agent Disagreement
docs.text: Agent disagreement is a difference in the scores or findings of two agents, or of an agent and a human, on the same metric. It is information. A disagreement shows where the evidence is unclear, where an agent may have erred, or where a check in the rubric is ambiguous. Handle it the way Chapter 11 handled disagreement between human reviewers: ask for the evidence on each side, repeat the check, and decide by what the evidence supports. The agent's score does not win because it came from a machine, and it does not lose for the same reason. A disagreement that traces to an unclear check is also a finding about the rubric, and it belongs in the notes for the rubric's owner. The next section gives the three outcomes that a disagreement, or any other checked claim, can end in.

docs.title: Accept, Correct, or Reject
docs.text:
Accept, correct, or reject names the three outcomes of checking one claim from an agent's report. A claim is accepted when verification shows it is true as stated. It is corrected when it is right in substance and a detail is wrong, as when a count is off by one: the reviewer fixes the detail and notes the change. It is rejected when it is false, invented, or impossible to verify. A rejected claim is removed, and the score is recomputed without it, treating any check that rested on it as failed or not checkable.

Worked example: six claims triaged. The table shows what verification found and the decision.

Agent claim What verification found Decision "4 of 5 images have alt text" The count is exactly 4 of 5 Accept "Reading level is grade 6.9" The tool reports 7.1 Correct to 7.1 "The footer states CC BY 4.0 on all six pages" The footer is on five of the six pages Correct to five pages "The video has captions" The video has none Reject "Contrast tested at 5.2 to 1" No tool was run Reject "Citation: Reyes (2021)" No such article exists Reject

Two rules cover the hard cases. A claim that cannot be verified in the time available is not accepted: mark it "not verified", and treat the check that rests on it as failed or not checkable, as the rubric says. And a rejection changes the score, so recompute the score from the checks that remain.

Worked example: rescoring after four rejections. The agent gave Accessibility a 9 and reported 9 of its 10 checks as passed. Verification rejected four claims: the captions, the contrast test, the heading order, and alt text on every image. Each rejected claim turns a passed check into a failed one.

Step Value Checks the agent reported as passed 9 of 10 Checks whose claims were rejected 4 Checks that still pass 5 of 10 Share of the check met 50 percent, the Adequate band of 5 to 6 Serious failure present Yes, the video has no captions Corrected score 5, the lower number

The corrected score of 5 matches the human reviewers' score for Accessibility, and the log records the four rejections as the reason for the change.

docs.title: Findings Log
docs.text: A findings log is the record of every agent claim a reviewer checked and what was decided. Its columns are the agent's finding, the decision (accepted, corrected, or rejected), and the reason, as in the findings log of this book's sample rubric worksheet. The log serves three purposes. It makes the review auditable: anyone can see what was checked. It feeds the measurement in the next sections, since the share of rejected claims is the agent's error rate. And it feeds prompt refinement, because the rejected claims show which instructions the prompt needs.

docs.title: Agent Error Rate
docs.text:
The agent error rate is the share of the agent's checked claims that were corrected or rejected. To compute it, count the claims verified and the number that were not accepted as stated, and divide. If a reviewer verified 40 claims and 6 were corrected or rejected, the error rate is 6 divided by 40, which is 15 percent. A breakdown by error type is more useful than the total, since it shows where the agent fails: perhaps two citation errors, one license error, two overconfident scores, and one miscount. The rate is only as honest as the sample behind it. A rate from claims chosen because they looked suspicious overstates the agent's errors, and a rate from only the easy claims understates them.

The MicroSim below practices the three decisions. It shows eight claims with what verification found, and for each one you decide.

docs.title: Diagram: Claim Triage Judge
docs.text:
Claim Triage Judge

Type: microsim sim-id: claim-triage-judge Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: judge Learning Objective: The learner will judge whether each of eight verified agent claims should be accepted, corrected, or rejected, with at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Accept Correct or Reject, Verification Step, Spot Check, Source Verification, Findings Log (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each claim the learner commits one of three decisions. A decision is correct when it matches the Correct decision column in Content. Mastery is at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the decision definitions is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A claim that is almost right is rejected. (2) A claim that cannot be verified is accepted. (3) A corrected claim needs no note.

Instructional Rationale: Judging what to do with a verified claim is an Evaluate-level action that reviewers repeat dozens of times in a review. Eight claims split across the three decisions teach the learner the dividing lines.

Content:

The three decisions: Accept (verified as stated), Correct (right in substance with one detail wrong, so fix the detail and log it), Reject (false, invented, or unverifiable, so remove it and rescore without it).

The eight claims (all made up, for Watershed Basics):

# Agent claim What verification found Correct decision Why (shown as feedback) 1 "4 of 5 images have alt text." The count is exactly 4 of 5. Accept It is true as stated. 2 "Reading level is grade 6.9." The tool reports 7.1. Correct The claim is right in substance and the number is wrong. 3 "Citation: Reyes (2021), Soil Infiltration Rates." No such article exists. Reject The reference is invented. 4 "The footer states CC BY 4.0 on 6 of 6 pages." The footer is on 5 of 6 pages. Correct The license is right and the page count is wrong. 5 "The video has captions." The video has no captions. Reject The claim is false. 6 "Heading order is correct." One heading skips from level 2 to level 4. Reject The claim is false, and the defect is recorded as a new finding. 7 "Contrast tested at 5.2 to 1." No tool was run. Reject The measurement is invented. 8 "The author is named as Maria Lopez." The page names Maria Lopez. Accept It is true as stated.

Provenance: The claims are illustrative cases written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The decisions follow the chapter section "Accept, Correct, or Reject".

Rules: Each claim has exactly one correct decision. Two are Accept, two are Correct, and four are Reject.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one claim with what verification found, and the three decisions.
  2. The learner chooses a decision, and the choice is committed.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text.
  4. After claim 8 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 8 claims in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [decision]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. The decision is [decision]. [Why]".
