License statement repair is the completion of missing or partial license statements. It adds the license to every page or component and to the file properties, and it adds a credit line for each third-party item in the title, author, source, and license form of Chapter 2. An agent can draft the lines from information you provide.

The mistake to expect is an agent that fills a gap by assigning a license to something it does not own. An agent must never choose a license for someone else's work or guess the owner's terms. If the terms of a third-party item cannot be found, replace the item. For Watershed Basics, one of the three third-party images has no notice. The repair finds its source and records the notice, or replaces the image if the source cannot be found.

docs.title: Chapter Splitting
docs.text:
Chapter splitting is the division of a long page or file into modules that each cover one idea or objective and stand alone. Chapter 9 gave the checks: each module has its own address, its own title, its own license, and its own metadata, and it makes no reference to "the section above". An agent can propose the split points, copy the license and metadata into each module, and rewrite cross-references so that they work.

The mistake to expect is a module that still depends on another, such as a quiz that says "use the diagram from the reading". The check is to open each module alone and read it as a stranger would. For Watershed Basics, the quiz is inseparable from the reading. The split makes two modules, each with its own address and metadata, and changes the quiz script's relative path to a complete address so that the quiz can be embedded alone. Modularity rises from 5 to 8.

docs.title: PDF-to-Markdown Conversion
docs.text:
PDF-to-Markdown conversion is the change of a resource from a PDF, which is hard to edit, into Markdown, which is plain text that anyone can revise. It raises the editable source metric of Chapter 4, and it helps portability. A conversion tool or an agent extracts the text and rebuilds the structure.

PDFs store where things sit on a page and not what they mean, so conversion makes predictable errors. The table lists the common ones and the check for each.

Error What goes wrong The check Column order Two columns are read across the page, mixing their lines Read a paragraph from each column in the output Flattened table A table becomes a run of separate lines Compare each table with the original Lost heading A large heading becomes plain text List the headings in the output Garbled equation A formula turns into scrambled symbols Compare each formula with the original Lost image A picture is dropped, with no note Count the pictures before and after Split word A word hyphenated at a line end stays broken Search for stray hyphens inside words

The poster below places each error on a picture of a converted page.

docs.title: Diagram: PDF Conversion Error Poster
docs.text:
PDF Conversion Error Poster

Type: infographic sim-id: pdf-conversion-error-poster Library: html Status: Specified Bloom Level: Remember Bloom Verb: identify Learning Objective: The learner will identify the six common errors of a PDF-to-Markdown conversion from a description of how each looks, with at least 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: PDF-to-Markdown Conversion (defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: In quiz mode the learner clicks the marker that matches a visual hint. A click is correct when it matches the marker named in the Hint column of Content. Mastery is at least 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Hovering in explore mode is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A conversion that opens without an error is correct. (2) A tool converts every element equally well. (3) Only text can be lost.

Instructional Rationale: Identifying conversion errors is a Remember-level task, and a picture of a converted page with the errors marked gives each one a place and a look. The quiz asks the learner to recognize an error by its appearance.

Content:

The illustration is a text-free flat drawing of a converted page. The page has a large heading bar at the top. Below it are two columns of thin lines, with lines from the left column running into lines from the right column. Under the columns is a grid of cells whose lines have collapsed into one stack. To the right is a row of scrambled small symbols where a formula should be. Below that is an empty frame with a dashed outline where a picture should be. At the bottom is a thin line with a short hyphen inside one word. The six markers:

# Label Hint (describes the look, not the name) Description Tip 1 Lost heading The large bar at the top that has shrunk to the same weight as plain lines. A heading that has become plain text. List the headings in the output and compare with the original. 2 Column order The two columns whose lines run into each other. Lines from two columns are mixed together. Read one paragraph from each column in the output. 3 Flattened table The grid of cells whose lines have collapsed into one stack. A table whose rows and columns are lost. Compare each table with the original. 4 Garbled equation The row of scrambled small symbols. A formula that no longer reads correctly. Compare each formula with the original. 5 Lost image The empty frame with a dashed outline. A picture that is missing, with no note. Count the pictures before and after. 6 Split word The thin line with a short hyphen inside one word. A word broken at a line end that stayed broken. Search for stray hyphens inside words.

Provenance: The six errors follow the chapter section "PDF-to-Markdown Conversion". The illustration is synthetic, and the sim labels the page "illustrative example".

Rules: Each hint matches exactly one marker. The illustration contains no text, so every label comes from the table above. Markers are numbered 1 to 6 from the top of the page to its bottom.

Learner Activity:

  1. In explore mode the learner hovers or clicks a marker and reads its label, description, and tip.
  2. In quiz mode the sim shows a hint.
  3. The learner clicks the marker they think the hint describes.
  4. If the first click is wrong, the sim says so and lets the learner try once more. If the second click is also wrong, the sim reveals the marker and its description.
  5. After all 6 hints the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 6 hints in a shuffled order, two attempts each. Only a correct first click counts as evidence. Correct: "Correct: [label]. [Description]". First wrong click: "Not quite. Look again at the hint: [hint]". Second wrong click: "This is [label]. [Description]". The summary shows "[n] of 6 correct on the first attempt". At 5 or more it adds "You can spot a conversion error." Below 5 it lists the labels of the missed errors.

Starting State: The illustration with six numbered markers, explore mode active, and the prompt "Hover a marker to see what went wrong."

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's table of conversion errors lists the same six errors, in a different order, with a check for each.

docs.title: Practice Question Generation
docs.text:
Practice question generation is the use of an agent to draft questions, answer keys, wrong choices, and explanations at a chosen cognitive level for a stated learning outcome. Chapter 8 taught that practice needs feedback, so the explanation matters as much as the question.

The mistakes to expect are a wrong answer key, two correct choices, a stem that gives the answer away, and questions that stay at the remember level. The check is to answer every question yourself without looking at the key, to confirm that each wrong choice is plausible and wrong, and to confirm that each explanation says why. For Watershed Basics, 6 of 8 quiz questions have explanations. The plan asks the agent to draft the two missing explanations, and a person to verify them.

docs.title: MicroSim Building
docs.text:
MicroSim building is the use of an agent to build a small interactive simulation from a written specification. A good specification states the learning objective, the evidence that proves learning, the complete content, the rules, and the feedback. The agent builds from it, and a person tests the result.

The mistakes to expect are wrong science, a control that does nothing, a simulation that works on one page and fails when embedded elsewhere, and a missing keyboard path. The check is to use every control, check each number against a hand calculation, tab through the page with the keyboard, and embed the simulation on each platform you care about. For Watershed Basics, the plan adds a short simulation, "Where does the rain go?", in which a slider changes ground cover. Its script is blocked on one of the three platforms, and the re-score below finds the cost.

docs.title: The Fixes Together
docs.text:
The table summarizes the thirteen fixes. Each row names the metric the fix mainly raises, the mistake to expect, and the human check.

Fix Mainly raises A typical agent mistake The human check AI alt text generation Accessibility Generic text or invented details Look at each image beside its draft Caption generation Accessibility Mis-heard technical terms Watch the video while reading the captions Heading repair Accessibility Renamed or merged sections Compare the outline before and after Reading level rewrite Readability Lost precision or meaning Run the readability tool and the meaning checks Glossary generation Readability A definition that differs from the resource's use Compare with the resource and a trusted source Link repair Accuracy and currency An invented address Open every new link Content update Accuracy and currency A figure from memory Open the source and confirm the figure Metadata generation Metadata A guessed author or license Verify each field against the page License statement repair Open license A license assigned to someone else's work Find the owner's terms or replace the item Chapter splitting Modularity A module that still depends on another Open each module alone PDF-to-Markdown conversion Editable source Lost tables, headings, or pictures Compare the output with the PDF Practice question generation Practice with feedback A wrong key or a leading stem Answer each question without the key MicroSim building Practice with feedback Wrong science or a failed embed Use every control and embed it on each platform

The MicroSim below practices the link between fix and metric. It gives each fix, and you name the metric that it mainly raises.

docs.title: Diagram: Fix and Metric Matcher
docs.text:
Fix and Metric Matcher

Type: microsim sim-id: fix-metric-matcher Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: classify Learning Objective: The learner will classify each of thirteen fixes under the rubric metric it mainly raises, with at least 11 of 13 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: All thirteen fixes of the chapter section "The Fix Toolkit", and the ten metrics of Chapter 3 (all defined in this chapter above this block or in earlier chapters).

Evidence of Mastery: For each fix the learner commits one of eight metrics. A placement is correct when it matches the Correct metric column in Content. Mastery is at least 11 of 13 correct on the first attempt. Reading the fix summary table is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Every fix raises the accessibility metric. (2) One fix raises only one metric and never affects another. (3) Practice questions raise the readability metric.

Instructional Rationale: Classifying fixes by the metric they mainly raise is an Understand-level action that lets the learner choose a fix from a low score. Thirteen fixes spread over eight metrics teach the learner which fix belongs to which gap.

Content:

The eight metric bins: Accessibility, Readability, Accuracy and currency, Open license, Modularity, Metadata, Editable source, Practice with feedback.

The thirteen fixes:

# Fix Correct metric Why (shown as feedback) 1 AI alt text generation Accessibility Alt text is a WCAG text alternative. 2 Caption generation Accessibility Captions serve learners who cannot hear the video. 3 Heading repair Accessibility A clean outline serves screen reader users. 4 Reading level rewrite Readability It moves the text toward the audience's grade. 5 Glossary generation Readability It defines terms the audience may not know. 6 Link repair Accuracy and currency A working link is part of a current resource. 7 Content update Accuracy and currency It replaces an outdated fact. 8 Metadata generation Metadata It fills the record's descriptive fields. 9 License statement repair Open license It completes the license and credit statements. 10 Chapter splitting Modularity It makes modules that stand alone. 11 PDF-to-Markdown conversion Editable source It turns a locked file into one that anyone can revise. 12 Practice question generation Practice with feedback It adds questions with answers and explanations. 13 MicroSim building Practice with feedback It adds an interactive activity with feedback.

Provenance: The pairs follow the chapter section "The Fix Toolkit" and the metric definitions of Chapters 4 through 10. The sim notes that a fix can affect more than one metric and that each pair shows the main metric.

Rules: Each fix has exactly one correct metric. Accessibility holds three fixes. Readability, Accuracy and currency, and Practice with feedback hold two each. Open license, Modularity, Metadata, and Editable source hold one each.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one fix and the eight metric bins.
  2. The learner may open the fix summary table. Opening it does not change the score.
  3. The learner places the fix in a bin, and the placement is committed.
  4. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text.
  5. After fix 13 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 13 fixes in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [metric]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. This fix mainly raises [metric]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 13 correct on the first attempt". At 11 or more it adds "You can pick the fix for a low metric." Below 11 it lists the Why text of each missed fix.

Starting State: The first fix in the shuffled order and the eight bins. The question shown is "Which metric does this fix mainly raise?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's table of thirteen fixes names the same metric for each fix.

docs.title: Controlling the Changes
docs.text: An agent can make dozens of changes in minutes, and that speed is the danger. A change that nobody reviews can be wrong, and a change that nobody records cannot be explained later. Two practices keep the work under control: a person reviews every change, and every change goes in a log.

docs.title: Human Review of Changes
docs.text:
Human review of changes is the step in which a named person examines each change an agent made before it is kept. Nothing goes live on the agent's say-so. The agent's own summary of what it changed is not enough, because an agent can leave a change out of its summary. Use a difference view that shows every change, and decide on each one: accept, correct, or reject, as Chapter 14 taught.

Match the depth of review to the risk. High-risk changes get a full check against the source: facts, numbers, quotations, citations, captions, license statements, and anything that touches meaning. Low-risk changes, such as heading levels and formatting, get a spot check by the sampling rule of Chapter 14.

Worked example: reviewing 15 text changes to Watershed Basics.

Change type Changes Review depth Accepted Corrected Rejected Alt text 3 Full 2 1 0 Caption file 1 Full, the whole video watched 0 1 0 Heading level 1 Spot check 1 0 0 Metadata fields 5 Full 4 1 0 Link replacements 2 Full 1 0 1 Figure update 1 Full 1 0 0 Quiz explanations 2 Full 1 1 0 Total 15 10 4 1

Five of the 15 changes, or 33 percent, needed a correction or a rejection. That is the agent error rate of Chapter 14, and it is the best argument for the review: one change in three would have gone live with a defect.

docs.title: Change Log Entry
docs.text:
A change log entry is the record of one change to a resource. It answers seven questions: when the change was made, where in the resource, what changed, why, who or what made it, who reviewed it, and what was decided. The log serves four readers. A reuser needs it, since CC BY asks you to indicate that you changed the work. A future reviewer needs it, to know what has already been fixed. The re-score uses it, to tie each change to the check it was meant to fix. And the version history of Chapter 4 reads best when each saved version has one clear log entry.

Worked example: three entries for Watershed Basics.

When Where What changed Why Made by Reviewed by Decision 2026-10-24 Section 2, paragraph 1 "410 miles" became "398 miles", with the State Water Agency page cited Accuracy: outdated figure Agent, from a supplied source Reviewer A Accepted 2026-10-24 Image 3 Alt text "map" became "Map showing the river and its two tributaries" Accessibility: one-word alt text Agent, corrected because the draft said three tributaries Reviewer A Corrected 2026-10-24 Link 9 A broken address was replaced by an archived copy of the same page Accuracy: broken link Person, because the agent's suggested address did not exist Reviewer A Agent suggestion rejected

The MicroSim below practices reading a log. It shows seven entries, each missing one of the seven answers, and you name what is missing.

docs.title: Diagram: Change Log Gap Finder
docs.text:
Change Log Gap Finder

Type: microsim sim-id: change-log-gap-finder Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: examine Learning Objective: The learner will examine seven change log entries and name the one field that is missing from each, with at least 6 of 7 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Change Log Entry, Human Review of Changes, Accept Correct or Reject (all defined in this chapter above this block or in Chapter 14).

Evidence of Mastery: For each entry the learner commits the missing field from a list of seven. A choice is correct when it matches the Missing field column in Content. Mastery is at least 6 of 7 correct on the first attempt. Reading the field list is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A log needs only what changed. (2) Naming the reviewer is optional. (3) The reason for a change can be guessed later.

Instructional Rationale: Examining an entry for a missing part is an Analyze-level action. Seven entries that each lack a different field teach the learner what each field contributes.

Content:

The seven fields: When, Where, What changed, Why, Made by, Reviewed by, Decision.

The seven entries (all made up for Watershed Basics). A dash marks the missing field:

# When Where What changed Why Made by Reviewed by Decision Missing field Why it matters (shown as feedback) 1 - Section 2, paragraph 1 "410 miles" became "398 miles" Outdated figure Agent Reviewer A Accepted When Without a date, no one can tell which version was scored. 2 2026-10-24 - "410 miles" became "398 miles" Outdated figure Agent Reviewer A Accepted Where A reuser cannot find the change. 3 2026-10-24 Image 3 - One-word alt text Agent Reviewer A Corrected What changed A reuser must be able to indicate what was changed. 4 2026-10-24 Link 9 Address replaced - Person Reviewer A Accepted Why The change cannot be tied to the check it fixes. 5 2026-10-24 Heading 4 Level 4 became level 3 Skipped heading level - Reviewer A Accepted Made by The log cannot show how often agents are right. 6 2026-10-24 Question 3 Explanation added No explanation Agent - Accepted Reviewed by Nothing shows that a person checked the change. 7 2026-10-24 Section 3 Sentence shortened Reading level Agent Reviewer A - Decision No one can tell whether the change was kept.

Provenance: The entries are illustrative examples written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The seven fields follow the chapter section "Change Log Entry".

Rules: Each entry lacks exactly one field, and each of the seven fields is missing from exactly one entry.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one entry as a row with one empty cell.
  2. The learner chooses which of the seven fields is missing, and the choice is committed.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text.
  4. After entry 7 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 7 entries in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [field]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. The missing field is [field]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 7 correct on the first attempt". At 6 or more it adds "You can read a change log." Below 6 it lists the Why text of each missed entry.

Starting State: The first entry in the shuffled order and the list of seven fields. The question shown is "Which field is missing?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter lists seven questions that a log entry answers, and gives three complete entries for the running example.

docs.title: Re-Scoring
docs.text:
Re-scoring is scoring the improved resource again, on all ten metrics, with the same rubric, the same evidence rules, and the same prompt and tools as the first scoring. Two choices matter most.

The first choice is to score all ten metrics and not only the ones you worked on. Fixes have side effects. A simulation added to raise Practice can lower Portability if its script is blocked somewhere. A split can break a link. A rewrite can drop a fact. Only a full re-score finds these, and only a full re-score gives the true total and decision.

The second choice is who scores. An agent that edited a resource tends to score it generously, and a reviewer who approved the changes is anchored on them. Use a fresh agent session with the same calibrated prompt, so that the two scorings are comparable, and have a person verify every metric whose score changed and sample the rest, as Chapter 14 taught. Changing the scoring prompt between the two scorings would make the comparison meaningless.

The steps are short:

  1. Freeze the improved version and save it in the version history.
  2. Run the same checks and the same scoring prompt on it.
  3. Verify every changed score against its evidence, and sample the unchanged ones.
  4. Record the evidence for each score in the same form as before.
  5. Put the old and new scores side by side.

Worked example: the re-score of Watershed Basics.

Metric Before After Change Evidence for the new score Accuracy and currency 7 9 +2 14 of 14 links work, tested 2026-10-24, and the river length cites the agency page Alignment 6 6 0 Unchanged: the quiz still maps to 2 of 3 outcomes Readability 8 8 0 Unchanged Accessibility 5 8 +3 5 of 5 images have descriptive alt text, the video has captions, heading order is correct, and contrast was tested Practice with feedback 6 8 +2 8 of 8 questions have explanations, and there is a worked example and a simulation Open license 9 9 0 Unchanged Modularity 5 8 +3 The reading and the quiz are separate modules, each with its own address Metadata 4 8 +4 All six core fields are present, plus keywords Editable source 8 8 0 Unchanged Portability 7 6 -1 The new simulation's script is blocked on one of the three platforms Total 65 78 +13

The decision rule of Chapter 11 gives Adopt, since 78 is at least 75 and the lowest metric is 6. The surprise is the last row. The simulation that raised Practice also cost a point of Portability, and no one planned for that. The plan forecast 79, and the re-score found 78 because the full re-score caught a side effect that a targeted check would have missed.

docs.title: Score Gain
docs.text:
Score gain is the difference between the total after an improvement and the total before it. A positive gain means the resource now passes more of the rubric's checks. Report three numbers: the gain in the total, the gain on each metric, and the gap between the projected gain in the plan and the actual gain. For Watershed Basics the total rose from 65 to 78, a gain of +13 against a projection of +14, a shortfall of 1.

Divide the gain by the human hours to see where the effort paid off. The table compares the plan with the result.

Fix Hours Projected gain Actual gain Actual gain per hour Metadata 0.5 +4 +4 8.0 Accessibility 2.0 +3 +3 1.5 Modularity 1.5 +3 +3 2.0 Practice, with the simulation 2.5 +2 +1 0.4 Accuracy 1.0 +2 +2 2.0 Total 7.5 +14 +13 1.7

The Practice row shows +1 because the +2 on Practice is offset by the -1 on Portability. The whole set returned about 1.7 points per hour, and the cheapest fix, Metadata, returned 8. This is the evidence for the lowest-metric-first rule, and it is also a lesson in pricing: the simulation took the longest and returned the least.

Two warnings keep a score gain honest. First, a small change may be noise. Chapter 14 showed that an unstable metric can move a point or two from run to run, so trust the evidence about which checks changed and not the number alone. Second, a score gain is not a learning gain. It says that the resource meets more of the rubric's checks. It does not say that students learn more. Better metadata may help teachers find the resource and teach students nothing. Whether the improved version helps students is a question to settle with students, and Chapters 16 and 17 show how to design and analyze such a test.

The MicroSim below puts the numbers in your hands. It gives the before and after scores of all ten metrics, and you work out the total, the gain, and the side effect.

docs.title: Diagram: Re-Scoring Ledger
docs.text:
Re-Scoring Ledger

Type: microsim sim-id: rescoring-ledger Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: calculate Learning Objective: The learner will calculate the total after, the score gain, the shortfall against the projection, and the gain per hour from a before and after table, and name the metric that fell and the resulting decision, with at least 5 of 6 answers correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Re-Scoring, Score Gain, Improvement Plan, Lowest Metric First (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: The learner answers six questions. An answer is correct when it matches the Correct answer column in Content. Numeric answers are correct when they match to the precision stated in the table. Mastery is at least 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Reading the decision rule is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Only the metrics you worked on can change. (2) A higher total always means every metric improved. (3) The projected gain is the real gain.

Instructional Rationale: Calculating a gain from a table is an Apply-level action. A table in which one metric falls teaches the learner that the total can rise while a metric gets worse, and that only a full re-score shows it.

Content:

The decision rule, shown at all times: Adopt when the total >= 75 and every metric >= 5. Revise when the total >= 50 and the resource is not Adopt. Reject when the total < 50.

The data (made up for Watershed Basics), shown at all times:

Metric Before After Accuracy and currency 7 9 Alignment 6 6 Readability 8 8 Accessibility 5 8 Practice with feedback 6 8 Open license 9 9 Modularity 5 8 Metadata 4 8 Editable source 8 8 Portability 7 6 Total 65 78

The plan projected a gain of +14 and took 7.5 hours.

The six questions:

# Question Answer type Correct answer Why (shown as feedback) 1 What is the total after the improvements? Whole number 78 9 + 6 + 8 + 8 + 8 + 9 + 8 + 8 + 8 + 6 = 78. 2 What is the score gain? Whole number with a sign +13 78 minus 65 is 13. 3 Which metric went down? Choice among the ten metrics Portability It fell from 7 to 6. 4 What is the decision after the improvements? Choice among Adopt, Revise, Reject Adopt The total is 78 >= 75 and the lowest metric is 6 >= 5. 5 By how many points did the actual gain fall short of the projected gain? Whole number 1 The projection was +14 and the gain was +13. 6 What is the gain per hour, rounded to one decimal place? Number 1.7 13 divided by 7.5 is about 1.7.

Provenance: The scores come from the chapter's re-scoring example and are labeled "illustrative examples". The decision rule follows Chapter 11 and is labeled "provisional adoption rule".

Rules: Total = sum of the ten scores. Gain = total after minus total before. The shortfall = projected gain minus actual gain. Gain per hour = gain divided by hours, rounded to one decimal place.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees the data table and the first question.
  2. The learner enters or chooses an answer, and the answer is committed.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text.
  4. After question 6 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 6 questions in the order of the table, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [answer]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. The answer is [answer]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 6 correct on the first attempt". At 5 or more it adds "You can read a re-score." Below 5 it lists the Why text of each missed question.

Starting State: The data table and question 1.

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's re-scoring table and its score gain table use the same numbers as this sim.

docs.title: Improvement Challenge
docs.text:
An improvement challenge is a structured exercise in which you take one real resource, improve it on a stated set of metrics with the help of agents, review and log every change, re-score it, and report the gain. It is the working form of everything in this chapter. This book's capstone project is an improvement challenge on a resource from your own subject, and it asks for more than a score: it asks you to improve at least two quality and two reusability metrics, to test the change with students, and to publish the result under a CC BY license.

The challenge has eight deliverables.

Step What you deliver 1. Baseline The ten scores with evidence, the total, and the decision 2. License check The license, whether it permits a derivative work, and your obligations 3. Plan The fixes in lowest-metric-first order, with hours and projected gain 4. Fixes The changes made with agents, and the prompts used 5. Review An accept, correct, or reject decision for every change 6. Change log One entry for each change 7. Re-score All ten metrics, scored the same way as the baseline 8. Report The gain, any side effect, the hours, and the decision after

An improvement challenge succeeds when it meets four tests. It raises at least two quality metrics and at least two reusability metrics. Every change was reviewed and logged. No metric fell without a stated reason, and the report names any that did. And the report states the decision before and after. Watershed Basics meets all four: it raised three quality metrics (Accessibility, Practice with feedback, and Accuracy and currency) and two reusability metrics (Modularity and Metadata). It also reports honestly that Portability fell by one point and why.

A Side Effect Is a Finding, Not a Failure

When the re-score shows a metric that fell, you have learned something real about your fix. Write it in the report and plan the next round around it.

The first MicroSim of the challenge lets you plan under a budget. It gives eight fixes with their hours and expected gains, and you build the plan.

docs.title: Diagram: Improvement Planner
docs.text:
Improvement Planner

Type: microsim sim-id: improvement-planner Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: prioritize Learning Objective: The learner will prioritize eight candidate fixes for a resource under a 5.0 hour budget and commit a plan that includes the lowest-metric fix, stays within the budget, reaches the Adopt decision, and gains at least 11 points.

Prerequisites: Improvement Plan, Lowest Metric First, Score Gain, Re-Scoring (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: The learner commits a plan. The plan is correct when it meets all four conditions in Rules. Mastery is a correct plan on the first commit. Selecting and deselecting fixes before committing is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) The plan should use the whole budget. (2) Fixes with the biggest gain per fix are always best. (3) A plan that reaches 75 is always an Adopt.

Instructional Rationale: Choosing among competing fixes under a budget is an Evaluate-level action. Eight fixes with different costs, and a decision rule with a floor, teach the learner to weigh gain, cost, and the floor together.

Content:

The baseline (made up for Watershed Basics), shown at all times:

Metric Score Accuracy and currency 7 Alignment 6 Readability 8 Accessibility 5 Practice with feedback 6 Open license 9 Modularity 5 Metadata 4 Editable source 8 Portability 7 Total 65

The eight fixes:

Id Fix Metric raised Gain Hours A Metadata generation Metadata +4 0.5 B Accessibility repair Accessibility +3 2.0 C Chapter splitting Modularity +3 1.5 D Link repair and content update Accuracy and currency +2 1.0 E Explanations, a worked example, and a simulation Practice with feedback +2 2.5 F Reading level rewrite of the one section above the audience Readability +1 1.0 G A new question for the third learning outcome Alignment +2 1.5 H Source files for the images Editable source +1 2.0

The decision rule, shown at all times: Adopt when the total >= 75 and every metric >= 5. Revise when the total >= 50 and the resource is not Adopt. Reject when the total < 50.

The four plans that meet every condition:

Plan Fixes Hours Total after Gain 1 A, B, C, D 5.0 77 +12 2 A, B, C, F 5.0 76 +11 3 A, B, D, G 5.0 76 +11 4 A, C, D, G 4.5 76 +11

Provenance: The scores and fixes come from the chapter's running example and are labeled "illustrative examples". The sim ignores side effects, and it says so, because the chapter's re-score shows that real results can differ.

Rules: The budget is 5.0 hours. The gains are independent and add. A plan is correct when all four hold: it includes fix A, the lowest metric's fix; its hours are <= 5.0; its decision is Adopt; and its gain is >= 11. The sim shows the live total, hours, gain, and decision as fixes are selected. It lets the learner select fixes beyond the budget and marks such a plan over budget.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees the baseline, the eight fixes, and the budget.
  2. The learner selects and deselects fixes and watches the live total, hours, gain, and decision.
  3. The learner presses Commit.
  4. The sim states which of the four conditions the plan meets, and shows the four plans that meet all four.

Feedback: One commit counts as evidence. Correct: "Your plan meets all four conditions: [total], [gain], [hours]." Incorrect: "Your plan misses: [conditions that fail]." In both cases the sim then lists the four plans. The summary shows "Correct plan on the first commit" or "Not yet". When correct it adds "You can plan under a budget."

Starting State: The baseline, the eight fixes unselected, the live total of 65, hours of 0.0, and the decision Revise.

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's plan for Watershed Basics uses fixes A through E on a larger budget of 7.5 hours. The sim shows that a smaller budget reaches Adopt with fewer fixes.

The poster below sums up the workflow of the whole chapter in six steps. Hover over a step to see its rules, then use the quiz mode to test yourself.

docs.title: Diagram: Improvement Workflow Poster
docs.text:
Improvement Workflow Poster

Type: infographic sim-id: improvement-workflow-poster Library: html Status: Specified Bloom Level: Remember Bloom Verb: identify Learning Objective: The learner will identify which of the six workflow steps matches each of six descriptions, with at least 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Derivative Work, Improvement Plan, Lowest Metric First, Human Review of Changes, Change Log Entry, Re-Scoring (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: In quiz mode the learner clicks the poster zone that matches each description. A click is correct when the zone's id equals the Correct zone column in Content. Mastery is at least 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Hovering a zone in explore mode is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Re-scoring covers only the metrics you changed. (2) Logging can wait until the end. (3) The license check is needed only when publishing.

Instructional Rationale: Remembering the order and purpose of the six steps is a Remember-level task, and a poster with six panels in order lets the learner hold the whole workflow at once. The quiz asks for the step by its purpose.

Content:

The poster is a flat illustration of six equal panels in two rows of three, read left to right and top to bottom. Each panel shows one simple pictogram and a step number, and the printed text is limited to the six step numbers. The first panel shows an open padlock above a document. The second shows a row of bars with the shortest bar highlighted. The third shows a hand holding a wand over a document. The fourth shows a magnifying glass over two stacked pages with a check mark. The fifth shows a notebook with ruled lines. The sixth shows two sets of ten bars side by side. All other words come from the explore and quiz data. The six zones:

Zone id Label Summary Facts shown on hover or click step-1-license 1. Check the license Confirm you may make and share a derivative work. Read the license first. NoDerivatives and a missing license stop the work. Note the credit and the statement of changes that the license requires. step-2-plan 2. Plan lowest first Write the fixes in order, with hours and projected gain. Start with the lowest metric. Set a budget. Write the projected gain so you can compare it later. step-3-fix 3. Fix with an agent Let the agent draft each fix. Give the agent the context. Expect the known mistake for each fix. Keep the original meaning. step-4-review 4. Review every change A person checks each change against the source. Use a difference view. Accept, correct, or reject each change. Check high-risk changes in full. step-5-log 5. Log each change Record when, where, what, why, who, reviewer, and decision. One entry per change. The log supports the statement of changes and the re-score. step-6-rescore 6. Re-score all ten Score the improved version the same way as the first. Use the same prompt. Verify the changed scores. Report the gain and any metric that fell.

The six quiz questions, in this order:

# Question Correct zone Why (shown as feedback) 1 Which step stops the work if the original is NoDerivatives? step-1-license The license decides whether a changed version may be shared. 2 Which step sets a budget and projected gain? step-2-plan The plan holds the hours and the forecast. 3 Which step catches a figure the agent invented? step-4-review A person checks each change against the source. 4 Which step finds that a new simulation lowered portability? step-6-rescore Only scoring all ten metrics shows a side effect. 5 Which step records who reviewed each change? step-5-log The log holds the reviewer and the decision. 6 Which step drafts alt text and metadata? step-3-fix The agent drafts the fixes.

Provenance: The six steps follow the chapter sections "Improvement Plan", "Derivative Work", "The Fix Toolkit", "Human Review of Changes", "Change Log Entry", and "Re-Scoring". The illustration is synthetic, and it carries no statistics.

Rules: Each question has exactly one correct zone. Zones are distinct regions of the poster, so a click belongs to at most one zone. Because the poster prints only step numbers, the sim shows the zone labels on hover.

Learner Activity:

  1. In explore mode the learner hovers or clicks a panel and reads its summary and facts.
  2. In quiz mode the sim shows question 1 above the poster.
  3. The learner clicks the panel they think matches.
  4. The sim shows the Why text and moves to the next question, until question 6 is done.

Feedback: 6 questions in the fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [label]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. The answer is [label]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 6 correct on the first attempt". At 5 or more it adds "You know the improvement workflow." Below 5 it lists the Why text of each missed question.

Starting State: The poster with no zone selected, explore mode active, and the prompt "Hover a panel to learn about the step."

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's eight deliverables of the improvement challenge include these six steps. The poster leaves out the baseline and the report, which bracket the workflow.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• An improvement plan lists the fixes in order, with hours and the projected gain for each. Lowest metric first is the rule for the order, because a low metric blocks adoption and is often the cheapest to raise.
  • Improving a resource creates a derivative work. Read the license before the first edit, and credit the author and indicate your changes. A NoDerivatives or missing license stops the work.
  • Preserving original meaning means changing the form and not the claims. Watch for a changed quantity, a changed strength, a dropped qualifier, an added claim, and a dropped item.
  • Thirteen fixes cover most gaps: AI alt text generation, caption generation, heading repair, reading level rewrite, glossary generation, link repair, content update, metadata generation, license statement repair, chapter splitting, PDF-to-Markdown conversion, practice question generation, and MicroSim building. Each has a known agent mistake and a human check.
  • Human review of changes examines every change in a difference view and decides accept, correct, or reject, with the most care for facts, numbers, captions, and licenses.
  • A change log entry records when, where, what, why, who made it, who reviewed it, and the decision.
  • Re-scoring scores all ten metrics with the same rubric and prompt, because fixes have side effects. A fresh scorer and a human check keep it honest.
  • Score gain is the new total minus the old total. Compare it with the projection, divide it by the hours, and remember that a score gain is not a learning gain.
  • An improvement challenge raises at least two quality and two reusability metrics, reviews and logs every change, and reports the gain and any side effect.

You Can Turn a Score Into a Better Resource

You can now plan an improvement, check what the license allows, fix a resource with an agent, review and log each change, and prove the gain with a full re-score. The next chapters ask the harder question of whether students learn more from the improved version.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Improving a Resource with AI Agents
docs.text: Test your understanding of improvement plans, derivative works, the fix toolkit, human review, change logs, and re-scoring with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. Which list gives the five parts of a useful improvement plan?
docs.text:
1. Title, author, subject, grade level, license, description, and keywords
  2. The baseline, the gaps, the fixes, the order and the budget, and the target
  3. Role, task, input, rules, output format, and a worked example
  4. Stem, key, distractors, feedback message, outcome tag, difficulty tag, and retry control
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. An improvement plan is the bridge between the scores and the work. The baseline holds the ten scores, the total, and the decision before any change. The gaps are the failed checks that hold each low score down, the fixes are one task per gap, the order and budget say what comes first and how many human hours each needs, and the target names the score and decision the plan aims for. Write it before the work and compare it with the result afterward.

Concept Tested: Improvement Plan

See: Improvement Plan

docs.title: 2. What does the lowest-metric-first rule say?
docs.text:
1. Start with the metric whose fix costs the most hours, because it will be the hardest to finish
  2. Start with the highest-scoring metric to build momentum, because it needs the fewest changes
  3. Start the plan with the lowest-scoring metric, because a metric under 5 blocks adoption and is often cheap
  4. Start with whichever metric the agent finds easiest to improve, whatever its current score
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Three reasons support the rule. The adoption rule sets a floor, so a metric under 5 blocks adoption however high the total is. The lowest scores often have the cheapest large gains, since a record with two of six fields filled can reach six in minutes. And a total hides the weakest metric. The exception is a lowest-metric fix that is expensive or needs the author's decision, in which case do cheaper fixes first and flag it.

Concept Tested: Lowest Metric First

See: Lowest Metric First

docs.title: 3. Why should a reviewer read a resource's license before an agent makes the first edit?
docs.text:
1. Agents are unable to edit any resource that carries an open license of any kind, so the license must be removed first
  2. An edited version is a derivative work, and a NoDerivatives or missing license does not allow sharing it
  3. The license decides which agent and which model to use, since each model has its own license
  4. The license determines the reading level of the improved version, so it limits the rewrite
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. A derivative work is a new work based on an existing one, such as a translation, an adaptation, a remix, or an improved edition. An open license is the owner's advance permission with conditions. CC BY allows an improved version with credit, a link, and a note of changes, while CC BY-ND allows changes only for private use, and a resource with no license needs the owner's permission. Check this first, before any effort goes in.

Concept Tested: Derivative Work

See: Derivative Work

docs.title: 4. Why does the chapter require a re-score of all ten metrics and not only the ones that were fixed?
docs.text:
1. The rubric states that every metric must be re-scored once a year, whether or not it changed
  2. Fixes have side effects, such as a simulation lowering portability, and only a full re-score finds them
  3. Metrics that were not fixed always improve as a side effect, so they must all be confirmed
  4. Agents refuse to score fewer than ten metrics, so a partial re-score cannot be run
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. A simulation added to raise Practice can lower Portability if its script is blocked on a platform, a split can break a link, and a rewrite can drop a fact. Only a full re-score gives the true total and the true decision. Use the same rubric, evidence rules, and calibrated prompt as the first scoring, and use a fresh scorer, since an agent that edited a resource tends to score it generously. A person verifies every changed score.

Concept Tested: Re-Scoring

See: Re-Scoring

docs.title: 5. An agent rewrites "Most rain soaks into the ground" as "Rain soaks into the ground." Which kind of meaning change is this?
docs.text:
1. A dropped qualifier
  2. A changed strength
  3. A changed quantity
  4. An added claim
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Preserving original meaning means an improvement changes the form of a resource and not what it says. The word "most" limits the claim to a share of the rain, and dropping it makes the claim cover all rain. The five quiet changes are a changed quantity, a changed strength, a dropped qualifier, an added claim, and a dropped item. Compare before and after in a difference view, and ask the agent to list every claim it changed, added, or removed.

Concept Tested: Preserving Original Meaning

See: Preserving Original Meaning

docs.title: 6. A teacher plans to improve a CC BY-NC resource and post the improved version for free for other teachers. What must she do?
docs.text:
1. Nothing, because an open license requires nothing in return from the person who adapts the work
  2. Ask the owner for permission first, because NonCommercial forbids any change
  3. Release the new version under CC BY so that others may also sell it and change it freely
  4. Credit the author, link to the license, say that she changed the work, and keep the use noncommercial
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. CC BY-NC allows an improved version to be published without commercial use. The conditions are the same as for CC BY: credit the author, link to the license, and say that the work was changed. NonCommercial limits selling or commercial gain, and it does not forbid changes, so permission is not needed (B). Releasing the version under CC BY (C) would let others sell it, which the original forbids. Sharing free with other teachers is allowed.

Concept Tested: Derivative Work

See: Derivative Work

docs.title: 7. In the chapter's re-score of Watershed Basics, Practice rose from 6 to 8 and Portability fell from 7 to 6, and the total rose by 13 against a projected 14. Which analysis is correct?
docs.text:
1. A gain of 13 shows that every metric improved, so no individual metric needs a closer look
  2. The projection was exact to within a point, so no side effect occurred in any of the ten metrics
  3. Portability fell because the agent edited the portability checks while it was re-scoring the resource
  4. The new simulation raised Practice but is blocked on one platform, a side effect only a full re-score catches
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The simulation that earned the Practice gain cost a point of Portability because its script is blocked on one of the three test platforms. The plan forecast 79 and the re-score found 78. A total can rise while one metric gets worse, which is why a report names any metric that fell and the reason. The Practice fix returned a net gain of 1, because its +2 was offset by the −1 on Portability.

Concept Tested: Re-Scoring

See: Re-Scoring

docs.title: 8. The chapter's gain-per-hour table shows Metadata returning 8.0 points per hour and Practice with its simulation returning 0.4. Which conclusion do the figures support?
docs.text:
1. Cheap fixes to the lowest metric return the most per hour, and the slowest fix returned the least
  2. The simulation was the best investment of time, because it took the longest to build
  3. Accessibility fixes are not worth doing, because they take 2.0 hours for only 3 points
  4. Gain per hour is nearly identical across all fixes, so the order in which the work is done does not matter
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Metadata took half an hour and returned +4, which is 8.0 points per hour. The Practice fix took 2.5 hours and returned a net +1, which is 0.4 per hour. The whole set returned about 1.7 points per hour. The figures argue for starting with the lowest metric. Two warnings apply: a small change may be noise, and a score gain is not a learning gain, since it shows that the resource meets more checks and not that students learn more.

Concept Tested: Score Gain

See: Score Gain

docs.title: 9. An agent's summary says it changed 12 items, but a reviewer's difference view shows 15 changes. What is the best judgment?
docs.text:
1. Rely on the difference view and review every change, because an agent's summary can omit a change
  2. Trust the agent's summary, because the agent made the changes and so knows what it did
  3. Reject all of the agent's changes without reading them, since the summary is unreliable
  4. Ignore the three extra changes, because they were probably low risk and can safely be checked later on
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Human review of changes means a named person examines each change before it is kept, using a difference view that shows every change, and decides accept, correct, or reject. The agent's own summary is not enough. Match the depth of review to risk: facts, numbers, quotations, citations, captions, license statements, and anything touching meaning get a full check, while heading levels and formatting get a spot check. In the chapter's example, one change in three needed a correction or a rejection.

Concept Tested: Human Review of Changes

See: Human Review of Changes

docs.title: 10. A resource totals 65, with Metadata at 4 and Accessibility and Modularity at 5. You have 5.0 hours. The candidate fixes are: A, Metadata (+4, 0.5 hours); B, Accessibility (+3, 2.0 hours); C, Modularity (+3, 1.5 hours); D, Accuracy (+2, 1.0 hour); E, Practice (+2, 2.5 hours); and H, Editable source (+1, 2.0 hours). Which plan best meets the chapter's guidance and earns the Adopt decision?
docs.text:
1. B, C, and E, which raise the most metrics that sit at 5 or 6 but leave metadata at 4
  2. A, E, and H, which use exactly 5.0 hours but reach a total of only 72, below the Adopt bar
  3. A, B, C, and D, which start with the lowest metric, use 5.0 hours, and reach a total of 77
  4. A, B, C, D, and E, which raise the most points but use 7.5 hours, over the budget
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The plan starts with the lowest metric. Fixes A, B, C, and D take 0.5 + 2.0 + 1.5 + 1.0 = 5.0 hours and add 4 + 3 + 3 + 2 = 12 points, for a total of 77. Every metric then sits at 6 or above, so the Adopt rule is met. Option A leaves Metadata at 4 and runs to 6.0 hours. Option B reaches only 72. Option D needs 7.5 hours, over the budget.

Concept Tested: Improvement Plan

See: Improvement Plan

docs.title: References: Improving a Resource with AI Agents
docs.text:
1. Derivative work - Wikipedia - Explains how a work based on another is treated in copyright law. Background for the chapter's check of what a license allows before an agent changes a resource.

  2. Readability - Wikipedia - Surveys what makes text easy to read, the formulas used to measure it, and their limits. Supports the chapter's reading-level fixes and the re-scoring that checks them.

  3. Continual improvement process - Wikipedia - Describes ongoing, incremental improvement cycles such as plan, do, check, act. Frames the chapter's improvement plan and its re-scoring after each round of changes.

  4. Refactoring: Improving the Design of Existing Code (2nd ed.) - Martin Fowler - Addison-Wesley (2018) - Fowler's discipline of making many small changes that preserve behavior, checking after each one, is the model for having an agent change one thing at a time and re-score.

  5. Style: Lessons in Clarity and Grace - Joseph M. Williams and Joseph Bizup - Pearson - Williams's principle of making characters the subjects and actions the verbs gives a concrete method for rewriting dense prose. Useful for judging and directing an agent's reading-level edits.

  6. Alt Decision Tree - W3C Web Accessibility Initiative - A decision tree for choosing the right alt attribute for each kind of image. Lets a reviewer judge whether an agent's alt text suits the image's purpose.

  7. Pull Requests - GitHub Docs - GitHub's documentation on proposing, reviewing, and merging changes. The standard way to let a person inspect every change an agent made before accepting it.

  8. Best Practices for Claude Code - Anthropic - Guidance for directing an AI coding agent, including giving it a check to verify its own work. The same practice applies when an agent edits an OER.

  9. Marking Your Work with a CC License - CC Public Wiki - Shows how to place a license notice on a work. This is the step needed when a revised version is published.

  10. git-diff Documentation - Git - Reference for showing exactly what changed between two versions of a file. Lets a reviewer see every line an agent altered before approving the change.

docs.title: Designing an A/B Test with Students
Summary
docs.text: Explains how to compare an original and an improved resource with students, covering hypotheses, control and treatment groups, before-and-after comparison, pre-tests and post-tests, sampling, consent, and student privacy. It tests whether the improvements help students, and relies on the improvement work in the previous chapter. After this chapter you can write a hypothesis, set up control and treatment groups, and plan a student test that respects consent and privacy.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 17 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score A/B Test 99 Control Group 19 Treatment Group 19 Original Version 1 Improved Version 2 Before-and-After Comparison 1 Test Hypothesis 29 Outcome Measure 28 Pre-Test 2 Post-Test 2 Learning Gain 1 Random Assignment 8 Sample Size 4 Confounding Variable 1 Sampling Bias 2 Informed Consent 26 Student Privacy in Testing 25

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Foundations of Open Educational Resources
  • Chapter 8: Practice and Feedback
  • Chapter 13: Automated Checks, Cost, and Student Privacy
  • Chapter 15: Improving a Resource with AI Agents

Does the Better Score Mean Better Learning?

The last chapter raised a resource's score, and a score is only a reviewer's judgment. In this chapter you will plan a fair test with real students to find out whether the improved version helps them learn. Let's dive in and check the evidence!

Chapter 15 ended with a warning: a score gain is not a learning gain. The rubric measures the properties of a resource, such as whether it has alt text or a clear license. It cannot tell you whether a student who uses the resource learns more. Only students can tell you that, and a fair test is how you ask them.

This chapter is about designing the test, which is where most of the quality of a test is decided. A well-designed test on 24 students can teach you something real. A badly designed test on 240 students teaches you nothing, however carefully the numbers are added up afterward. The next chapter covers the data and the analysis. The running example is the test of Watershed Basics: the original, which scored 65, against the improved version, which scored 78.

docs.title: A/B Test
docs.text:
An A/B test is a comparison of two versions of something, A and B, in which different people use each version at the same time and the results are compared. The idea comes from product design, where companies show two versions of a page to different visitors and count which one works better. In education the same idea compares an original resource with an improved one, using student learning as the result. The formal research cousin of the A/B test is the randomized controlled trial. In this book the test is manual: you set it up, run it, and tally it yourself, with no special software.

An A/B test answers a different question from the rubric. The rubric asks, "Does this resource have the properties that make a resource good?" The A/B test asks, "Do students who use this version learn more than students who use that one?" The two questions can have different answers. A resource can gain 13 rubric points from better metadata, which no student ever sees, and teach no better. The test is how you find out.

The method has eight steps.

  1. State a hypothesis that predicts what the improved version will do.
  2. Freeze both versions so that they do not change during the test.
  3. Choose the outcome measure, and a pre-test and a post-test.
  4. Get consent and plan how student data will be protected.
  5. Assign students to the two versions by chance.
  6. Run both groups under the same conditions.
  7. Collect the data with care for privacy.
  8. Compare the groups, which is the subject of Chapter 17.

Steps 1 through 5 are design, and they fill this chapter. A test can show that, for these students and these conditions, one version did better. It cannot prove that the improved version works for all students everywhere, and a good report says so.

docs.title: Original Version
docs.text: The original version is the resource exactly as it was before the improvements. For the test it must be frozen: the same files, saved in the version history of Chapter 4 under a label such as v1, and the same one that received the baseline score. If the original is quietly fixed during the test, the control group no longer uses what you said it did. Keep it available at its own address so that every student assigned to it reaches the same thing.

docs.title: Improved Version
docs.text:
The improved version is the resource after the improvement plan, frozen in the same way and labeled, for example, v1.1. Its change log from Chapter 15 is the list of differences between the two versions, and it should be written down before the test. Watershed Basics v1.1 differs from v1 in five ways: richer metadata, fuller alt text with captions, a separated quiz, explanations with a worked example and a simulation, and corrected facts and links.

Because five fixes arrive together, a test of these two versions can tell you whether the bundle helps students. It cannot say which fix did the work. If you need to know that, test one fix at a time, which takes more students and more time. Both versions carry CC BY 4.0, so you may give both to students and share both afterward.

Original version Improved version Label v1 v1.1 Rubric total 65 78 Decision Revise Adopt What changed Nothing Five fixes from the change log License CC BY 4.0 CC BY 4.0

docs.title: Control Group
docs.text:
The control group is the group of students who use the original version. It is the yardstick for the test. Without it you could say how well students did with the improved version, and you could not say how well they would have done without the improvement. The control group answers the question, "Compared with what?"

A control group is not a group that receives no teaching. It is a group that receives the ordinary teaching with the original resource, which is a fully acceptable lesson. That matters for fairness. No student should be given a version that you believe will harm their learning, and a control group that uses the original is not harmed. Many teachers also offer the improved version to the control group after the test ends, so that every student benefits from the work.

For the comparison to mean anything, the control group must differ from the treatment group in one way only: the version. The same teacher, the same instructions, the same time allowed, the same outcome measure, and the same week. The rest of this chapter is largely about protecting that one-difference rule.

docs.title: Treatment Group
docs.text:
The treatment group is the group of students who use the improved version. The word treatment comes from medicine, where it names the thing being tested. Here the treatment is the set of improvements. The group should be about the same size as the control group, because equal groups give the most information from a given number of students.

The treatment group gets nothing extra beyond the improved resource. It gets no longer time, no additional help from the teacher, and no review session, since any of those would be a second difference between the groups. In the Watershed Basics pilot, a class of 24 students is split into a control group of 12 and a treatment group of 12.

Control group Treatment group Students 12 12 Version Original, v1 Improved, v1.1 Teacher The same teacher The same teacher Time allowed The same two class periods The same two class periods Instructions The same script The same script Pre-test and post-test The same The same

docs.title: Test Hypothesis
docs.text:
A test hypothesis is a prediction, written down before the test, about what the improved version will do for students compared with the original. It turns a hope, such as "the new version is better", into a statement that data can support or fail to support. Writing it first protects you from the common trap of looking at the results and then deciding what you were trying to show.

A good hypothesis has five properties.

  • Specific: it names the students, the versions, and the measure.
  • Measurable: the measure is something you can count or score.
  • Directional: it says which version should do better.
  • Sized: it says how large a difference would matter.
  • Falsifiable: some result would show it to be wrong.

The hypothesis for the Watershed Basics pilot is: "Grade 6 students who use the improved version will have a mean learning gain at least 5 percentage points larger than students who use the original." The size, 5 points, is a teaching choice that marks the smallest difference a teacher would care about. The statement that the two versions do not differ is the null hypothesis, and Chapter 17 shows how data are weighed against it.

Weak hypothesis Why it is weak Strong hypothesis The improved version is better. "Better" has no measure Students on the improved version will score higher on the post-test Students will like it. No comparison and no measure More students will rate the improved version 4 or 5 on a 5-point scale Every student will learn more. Cannot be shown for every student The mean gain will be larger in the treatment group

The MicroSim below practices the skill. It shows eight statements, and for each one you decide whether it can be tested as written.

docs.title: Diagram: Hypothesis Sharpener
docs.text:
Hypothesis Sharpener

Type: microsim sim-id: hypothesis-sharpener Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: judge Learning Objective: The learner will judge whether each of eight statements is a testable hypothesis for a student A/B test or is not testable as written, with at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Test Hypothesis, A/B Test, Original Version, Improved Version (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each statement the learner commits one of two bins. A placement is correct when it matches the Correct bin column in Content. Mastery is at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the five properties is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A hypothesis only needs to state what you hope. (2) A statement about the rubric score is a statement about students. (3) A hypothesis can claim that every student will benefit.

Instructional Rationale: Judging a hypothesis against the five properties is an Evaluate-level action that every test design needs. Four testable and four untestable statements, each failing in a different way, teach the learner to look for the measure, the comparison, and the claim of every.

Content:

The two bins: Testable as written, and Not testable as written.

The five properties, available on demand: specific, measurable, directional, sized, falsifiable.

The eight statements (all made up, for the Watershed Basics pilot):

# Statement Correct bin Why (shown as feedback) 1 Students will like the improved version. Not testable as written It has no comparison and no measure of liking. 2 Grade 6 students who use the improved version will score at least 5 points higher on the 20-question post-test than students who use the original. Testable as written It names the students, the measure, the direction, and the size. 3 The improved version is better. Not testable as written "Better" has no measure. 4 A larger share of students will finish the improved version's quiz than the original's, measured by the count of completed quizzes. Testable as written The measure is a count, and the direction is stated. 5 The improved version will raise the rubric score. Not testable as written The rubric score is set by reviewers, so the statement does not test an effect on students. 6 Students who use the improved version will have a larger learning gain, post-test minus pre-test, than students who use the original. Testable as written Learning gain is defined, and the direction is stated. 7 Every student will learn more from the improved version. Not testable as written A claim about every student cannot be shown. 8 Students who use the improved version will spend less time on the task and score the same or higher on the post-test. Testable as written Time on task and post-test score are both measures, and the direction is stated.

Provenance: The statements are illustrative examples written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The five properties follow the chapter section "Test Hypothesis".

Rules: Each statement has exactly one correct bin, four per bin.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one statement and the two bins, and may open the five properties. Opening them does not change the score.
  2. The learner places the statement in a bin, and the placement is committed.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text.
  4. After statement 8 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 8 statements in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [bin]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. This is [bin]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 8 correct on the first attempt". At 7 or more it adds "You can tell a testable hypothesis from a hope." Below 7 it lists the Why text of each missed statement.

Starting State: The first statement in the shuffled order and the two bins. The question shown is "Can this be tested as written?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter lists five properties of a good hypothesis, shows a table of weak and strong hypotheses, and states the hypothesis for the Watershed Basics pilot.

docs.title: Outcome Measure
docs.text:
An outcome measure is the thing you measure to decide which version did better. It is the answer to the question, "What would I see in the students if the improved version worked?" For a test of learning, the main outcome measure is a score on a test of the skills the resource teaches. Others, such as how many students finish and how long they take, add detail, and Chapter 17 uses them.

Choose one primary outcome in advance, and name it in the hypothesis. A test that measures twenty things and then reports whichever came out well is a test that has found noise.

A good outcome measure has five properties.

Property What it means In the Watershed Basics pilot Aligned It measures the learning outcomes the resource targets, as in Chapter 6 The test covers all three outcomes Fair to both versions It is not built from one version's own quiz A separate 20-question test, not the resource's quiz Reliable It has enough questions to give a steady score 20 questions Right difficulty Not so easy that everyone scores high, nor so hard that everyone scores low Trial questions were tried before the test Scored the same way The same key and, if possible, a scorer who does not know the group An answer key, with names hidden

The second property deserves attention. The improved version of Watershed Basics has extra explanations and a worked example. If the post-test were the resource's own quiz, the treatment group would have practiced exactly the questions on the test. That would measure rehearsal and not learning.

docs.title: Pre-Test
docs.text: A pre-test is a test given before students use the resource, to find out what they already know. It does two jobs. It shows whether the two groups started at the same level, and it provides the starting score from which learning is measured. Without it, a group that scores higher at the end may simply have known more at the start. Use a pre-test that covers the same outcomes as the post-test, and tell students that it is for learning about the resource and not for a grade.

docs.title: Post-Test
docs.text: A post-test is a test given after students use the resource, to find out what they learned. It should cover the same outcomes as the pre-test, and it should be given under the same conditions to both groups, at the same time after the lesson. A test given the same day shows immediate learning. A test given a week later shows what students kept. The choice belongs in the plan, and the same choice applies to both groups. Using the same questions on the pre-test and the post-test can inflate scores through memory, so many tests use two equivalent forms of the same length.

docs.title: Learning Gain
docs.text:
Learning gain is the amount a student's score rose from the pre-test to the post-test. The simplest form is the raw gain: the post-test score minus the pre-test score, in percentage points. A student who scores 40 and then 70 has a raw gain of 30 points.

Raw gain has a weakness. A student who starts at 90 can gain at most 10 points, while a student who starts at 20 can gain 80. The normalized gain fixes this by comparing the gain to the room available:

normalized gain = (post - pre) / (100 - pre)

The student who goes from 40 to 70 has a normalized gain of 30 divided by 60, which is 0.50. A student who goes from 90 to 95 has a raw gain of only 5 points, and a normalized gain of 5 divided by 10, which is also 0.50. Both students closed half of the gap that was open to them. When the pre-test is 100, the normalized gain is undefined, since there was no room to gain.

The MicroSim below practices both forms.

docs.title: Diagram: Learning Gain Calculator
docs.text:
Learning Gain Calculator

Type: microsim sim-id: learning-gain-calculator Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: calculate Learning Objective: The learner will calculate the raw gain and the normalized gain for six students from their pre-test and post-test scores, with at least 5 of 6 cases fully correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Pre-Test, Post-Test, Learning Gain (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each case the learner enters the raw gain and the normalized gain. A case is fully correct when both match the Content table. Normalized gain is rounded to two decimal places, and the learner enters Undefined when the pre-test is 100. Mastery is at least 5 of 6 cases fully correct on the first attempt. Reading the formulas is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A larger raw gain always means more learning. (2) A negative gain cannot happen. (3) The normalized gain is always defined.

Instructional Rationale: Calculating a gain from two scores is an Apply-level action. Cases with different starting points, a loss, and a perfect pre-test show why the normalized gain exists and where it fails.

Content:

The formulas, shown at all times: raw gain = post - pre. Normalized gain = (post - pre) / (100 - pre). The normalized gain is undefined when pre = 100.

The six cases (all made up, scores out of 100):

# Pre-test Post-test Raw gain Normalized gain Why (shown as feedback) 1 40 70 30 0.50 30 divided by 60 is 0.50. 2 60 80 20 0.50 20 divided by 40 is 0.50. 3 20 50 30 0.38 30 divided by 80 is 0.375, which rounds to 0.38. 4 90 95 5 0.50 5 divided by 10 is 0.50, the same share of the room as case 1. 5 80 70 -10 -0.50 The score fell, so both gains are negative. 6 100 100 0 Undefined There was no room to gain.

Provenance: The scores are illustrative examples written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The normalized gain follows the chapter section "Learning Gain".

Rules: Raw gain is an integer and may be negative. Normalized gain is rounded to two decimal places with 0.375 rounded to 0.38. A case is fully correct only when both entries match.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one pre-test and post-test pair and the formulas.
  2. The learner enters the raw gain and the normalized gain, and presses Check.
  3. The sim shows which entries were correct and the Why text.
  4. After case 6 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 6 cases in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: raw gain [raw], normalized gain [normalized]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. The raw gain is [raw] and the normalized gain is [normalized]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 6 correct on the first attempt". At 5 or more it adds "You can calculate a learning gain." Below 5 it lists the Why text of each missed case.

Starting State: The first case in the shuffled order, the formulas, and empty fields.

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's worked examples are cases 1 and 4, which both give a normalized gain of 0.50.

docs.title: Before-and-After Comparison
docs.text:
A before-and-after comparison looks at one group's scores before and after using a single version. It has no second group. A teacher gives a pre-test, teaches the improved lesson, gives a post-test, and sees a gain of 18 points. It is tempting to call this evidence that the lesson works.

It is weak evidence, because anything that happened between the two tests can explain the gain: the students were also learning in other classes, they had seen the test questions before, and they simply got older. Without a control group you cannot separate the effect of the lesson from the effect of time. A before-and-after comparison is useful when no second group is possible, and a report should name that limit. The A/B test is stronger because both groups have the same time, the same other classes, and the same test, so those effects cancel when you compare the groups' gains.

docs.title: Random Assignment
docs.text:
Random assignment is the use of chance to decide which version each student receives. Flip a coin, draw a slip, or sort a column of random numbers: the point is that neither the teacher nor the student chooses. Chance matters because students differ in ways you cannot see and cannot measure, such as motivation, home support, and sleep. Chance spreads those differences across the two groups, so that on average the groups are alike before the lesson begins.

The alternatives are worse. If students pick their version, the keenest ones may pick the new one. If the teacher picks, the choice may favor the students the teacher expects to succeed. If the two classes in different periods get different versions, the periods differ in many ways.

The simplest method uses a spreadsheet. List the student codes in a column, put a random number from the RAND function beside each, sort by the random column, and give the top half the improved version. A better method for small classes is blocked random assignment. Give the pre-test first, sort the students by their scores, pair up neighbors, and flip a coin within each pair to decide who gets which version. Each pair then contributes one student to each group, which keeps the groups close in starting level.

Random assignment balances the groups on average, and a small class can still be unlucky. Take the class of 24 students in the pilot, with made-up pre-test scores that range from 22 to 78 and average 51.9. The table compares three ways of forming two groups of 12. The simulated figures come from 20,000 random assignments of this class, computed for this chapter.

Method How groups are formed Gap between the groups' pre-test averages Students choose The 12 highest scorers choose the improved version 23.8 points, built in Simple random assignment Each student is placed by chance Median about 4 points; 95 percent of splits within 12 points; 42 percent of splits more than 5 points apart Blocked random assignment Pairs matched on the pre-test, coin flip within each pair Median about 0.6 points; 95 percent of splits within 1.6 points; the largest gap 2.6 points

Choice builds a large imbalance into the test before the lesson starts. Simple random assignment usually gives a small gap and sometimes gives a large one. Blocked assignment keeps the gap small every time, and it needs the pre-test scores before assigning. Whichever method you use, record the pre-test averages of the two groups, and compare gains and not only post-test scores.

Pre-Test, Pair, Then Flip

When a class is small, give the pre-test first, sort the scores, pair neighbors, and flip a coin inside each pair. It takes ten minutes and keeps luck from stacking the groups.
