The MicroSim below lets you see the difference for yourself by forming the groups again and again.

docs.title: Diagram: Group Assignment Lab
docs.text:
Group Assignment Lab

Type: microsim sim-id: group-assignment-lab Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: compare Learning Objective: The learner will compare how three assignment methods balance two groups of 12 students on their pre-test averages, and answer 4 of 4 questions about the methods, with at least 3 of 4 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Random Assignment, Pre-Test, Control Group, Treatment Group (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: The learner answers four questions after running the methods. An answer is correct when it matches the Correct answer column in Content. Mastery is at least 3 of 4 correct on the first attempt. Running the methods is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Random assignment always gives equal groups. (2) Letting students choose is fair because it respects their preferences. (3) Blocked assignment can be done before the pre-test.

Instructional Rationale: Comparing methods on the same class is an Analyze-level action. Running each method many times shows that random assignment works on average, varies from run to run, and is improved by blocking.

Content:

The class: 24 students with these made-up pre-test scores, out of 100: 22, 28, 31, 35, 38, 41, 43, 45, 47, 48, 50, 52, 53, 55, 57, 58, 60, 62, 64, 66, 68, 70, 74, 78. The average of all 24 is 51.875.

The three methods:

Method What the sim does Students choose The 12 highest scores form the improved group and the 12 lowest form the original group. Every press gives the same result. Simple random assignment Each press forms two groups of 12 by a fresh random shuffle of the 24 students. Blocked random assignment The sim sorts the scores, pairs neighbors (22 with 28, 31 with 35, and so on up to 74 with 78), and decides by a fresh coin flip within each pair which student goes to each group.

For every press the sim shows the two group averages and the absolute difference between them, and keeps a running list of the differences for each method.

Facts shown after at least 20 presses of a method, from 20,000 simulated assignments of this class:

Method Difference between group averages Students choose 23.75 points: group averages of 63.75 and 40.0 Simple random assignment Median 4.25; 95 percent of splits are <= 11.9; 42 percent of splits are > 5 Blocked random assignment Median 0.58; 95 percent of splits are <= 1.6; the largest is 2.6

The four questions:

# Question Choices Correct answer Why (shown as feedback) 1 Which method builds the largest imbalance into the groups? Students choose; Simple random assignment; Blocked random assignment Students choose The 12 highest scorers form one group, so the averages differ by 23.75. 2 Does simple random assignment guarantee equal pre-test averages? Yes; No No Some splits differ by more than 5 points. 3 What must you know before you can use blocked random assignment? The post-test scores; Each student's pre-test score; The teacher's preference Each student's pre-test score The scores are needed to sort and pair the students. 4 Which method gave the smallest typical difference? Students choose; Simple random assignment; Blocked random assignment Blocked random assignment Its median difference is 0.58.

Provenance: The scores are made up for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The simulated figures were computed for this class from 20,000 random assignments with a fixed seed, and the sim labels them "simulation results for this class".

Rules: The group sizes are always 12 and 12. A press never changes the class. The facts appear only after at least 20 presses of the method, so that the learner sees the spread before reading the summary.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner picks a method and presses Form groups at least 20 times for each random method.
  2. After each press the learner sees the two averages and their difference.
  3. The learner presses Quiz and answers the four questions.
  4. After question 4 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 4 questions in the order of the table, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [answer]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. The answer is [answer]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 4 correct on the first attempt". At 3 or more it adds "You can compare ways to form groups." Below 3 it lists the Why text of each missed question.

Starting State: The class table, the Students choose method selected, and no presses yet.

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's table of three methods uses the same class and the same figures as this sim.

docs.title: Sample Size
docs.text:
Sample size is the number of students in the test. A larger sample gives a steadier answer, because chance fluctuations in who is in each group average out. A small sample gives a noisy one: a few unusually strong or weak students can swing the result.

The practical rule is that the smaller the difference you hope to find, the more students you need. The table gives rough guidance for comparing the averages of two groups under the usual research standards. The sizes are rules of thumb, and a real study should confirm them with a statistician. Chapter 17 defines large, medium, and small differences more exactly.

Students in each group What the test can tell you 5 to 10 A pilot only: it checks the procedure and the measure About 25 A large difference, and it may miss a medium one About 65 A medium difference About 400 A small difference

The Watershed Basics test is a pilot with 12 students in each group. That is enough to find out whether the test runs smoothly, whether the post-test is too easy or too hard, and how widely scores vary. It is not enough to prove that the improved version works. A pilot's purpose is to decide whether a larger test is worth running, and to say honestly that its own result is suggestive and not conclusive.

docs.title: Confounding Variable
docs.text:
A confounding variable is a factor other than the version that differs between the groups and could explain the result. If the treatment group did better and also had a different teacher, you cannot tell whether the improved version or the teacher made the difference. The two are tangled together, or confounded.

The cure is the one-difference rule from the section on the control group: arrange everything except the version to be the same, and let random assignment handle what you cannot arrange. The table lists the usual confounders and the defense against each.

Confounder How it misleads The defense Different teachers One teacher's enthusiasm lifts one group One teacher for both groups Different times of day Students are more alert at one time Both groups at the same time Extra help One group gets a review or hints The same script and help for both Different tests The versions are measured in different ways The same test and key for both Student choice Motivated students choose one version Random assignment

Ask What Else Is Different

Before you trust any difference between groups, list everything that was different besides the version. If the list is not empty, one of those things may be the real cause.

The MicroSim below practices the hunt. It describes eight test setups, and for each one you decide whether a confounder is present and name it.

docs.title: Diagram: Confounder Finder
docs.text:
Confounder Finder

Type: microsim sim-id: confounder-finder Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: examine Learning Objective: The learner will examine eight test setups and decide whether a confounding variable is present and, if so, name its source, with at least 7 of 8 setups fully correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Confounding Variable, Control Group, Treatment Group, Random Assignment (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each setup the learner chooses Confounder present or No confounder, and when a confounder is present picks its source from the list. A setup is fully correct when the choice and the source both match the Content table. Mastery is at least 7 of 8 setups fully correct on the first attempt. Reading the confounder table is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A large sample removes a confounder. (2) Random assignment is unnecessary when the groups look alike. (3) A confounder always makes the improved version look better.

Instructional Rationale: Examining a setup for a second difference between groups is an Analyze-level action. Setups that differ in one way each, and two with no confounder, teach the learner to name the difference and to know when to stop looking.

Content:

The two choices: Confounder present, No confounder. The sources: Teacher, Time of day, Extra help, Different tests, Student choice, Different period of the year.

The eight setups (all made up):

# Setup Correct choice Source Why (shown as feedback) 1 The morning section uses the original, and the afternoon section uses the improved version. Confounder present Time of day Alertness and the students in each section differ, so the version is not the only difference. 2 One teacher teaches both groups with the same script in the same week, students are assigned by random number, and both groups take the same test. No confounder None The groups differ only in version. 3 The treatment group also gets a 10-minute review before the post-test. Confounder present Extra help The review is a second difference. 4 The control group is tested in September and the treatment group in March. Confounder present Different period of the year Students learn more in the intervening months. 5 Students choose which version to use. Confounder present Student choice Motivated students may choose the new version. 6 The improved version is taught by a teacher who is excited about it, and the original by a teacher who is not. Confounder present Teacher The teacher's attitude is a second difference. 7 The treatment group takes the resource's own quiz as the post-test, and the control group takes a separate test. Confounder present Different tests The groups are measured differently. 8 Both groups use their version for the same time, in the same room, with the same instructions, and a coin flip assigns each student. No confounder None The groups differ only in version.

Provenance: The setups are illustrative examples written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The sources follow the chapter section "Confounding Variable".

Rules: Each setup has exactly one correct choice. Six have a confounder and two do not. Each of the six sources appears once.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one setup.
  2. The learner chooses Confounder present or No confounder. If a confounder is present, the learner also picks the source.
  3. The sim shows whether the choice and the source were correct, and the Why text.
  4. After setup 8 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 8 setups in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [choice], [source]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. The answer is [choice], [source]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 8 correct on the first attempt". At 7 or more it adds "You can find what else is different." Below 7 it lists the Why text of each missed setup.

Starting State: The first setup in the shuffled order and the two choices. The question shown is "Is anything besides the version different between the groups?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's table of confounders lists teacher, time of day, extra help, different tests, and student choice. The sim adds a different period of the year.

docs.title: Sampling Bias
docs.text:
Sampling bias is a distortion that arises when the students in the test are not like the students you want to learn about, or when the students who finish are not like the ones who started. The result is true for the group that was tested and misleading about everyone else.

Four forms are common.

  • Volunteer bias: only students who volunteer or return a form take part, and volunteers tend to be more motivated.
  • Convenience sampling: you test the class that is easiest to reach and then speak as if it represented all students.
  • Attrition: students drop out unevenly, so the scores that remain come from the students who stayed.
  • Exclusion: some students cannot take part, for instance because the online version needs a device that they do not have.

Exclusion is also an equity problem. If students who use assistive technology, or who lack a home computer, cannot use one of the versions, the test measures only the students that the version suits. Chapter 17 comes back to this under equity.

The defenses are practical. Invite every student in the class, and do not select. Record how many were invited, how many agreed, and how many finished each group. Offer both versions in forms that every student can use. And report who took part, so that readers can decide how far the result applies to their students.

The MicroSim below practices naming the bias.

docs.title: Diagram: Sampling Bias Spotter
docs.text:
Sampling Bias Spotter

Type: microsim sim-id: sampling-bias-spotter Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: differentiate Learning Objective: The learner will differentiate volunteer bias, convenience sampling, attrition, exclusion, and no concern by sorting each of six recruitment scenarios, with at least 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Sampling Bias, Sample Size, Treatment Group, Control Group (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each scenario the learner commits one of five bins. A placement is correct when it matches the Correct bin column in Content. Mastery is at least 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Reading the four forms is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Bias only occurs when the researcher is dishonest. (2) A volunteer is as good as a randomly chosen student. (3) Dropping students who did not finish is harmless.

Instructional Rationale: Differentiating the forms of sampling bias is an Analyze-level action. Scenarios that each fail in one way, and two that are sound, teach the learner to ask who is missing and why.

Content:

The five bins: Volunteer bias, Convenience sampling, Attrition, Exclusion, No concern.

The six scenarios (all made up):

# Scenario Correct bin Why (shown as feedback) 1 A note is sent home, and only students who return a signed form take part. Volunteer bias Students who return forms tend to be more motivated. 2 Only the teacher's honors class is tested, and the results are reported for all Grade 6 students. Convenience sampling One easy-to-reach class does not represent the grade. 3 Nine students in the treatment group leave the test because the simulation would not load on their devices, and their scores are dropped. Attrition The students who remain are the ones whose devices worked. 4 The improved version needs a laptop, so students without laptops are left out. Exclusion The test cannot speak for students who could not use it. 5 Every student in the grade is invited, 24 of 25 in each section take part, and the reasons for the missing students are recorded. No concern Nearly everyone is included and the gaps are recorded. 6 Three schools of different sizes are invited, and every student with consent takes part. No concern Participation does not depend on motivation or access.

Provenance: The scenarios are illustrative examples written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The four forms follow the chapter section "Sampling Bias".

Rules: Each scenario has exactly one correct bin. Four scenarios have one of the four forms each, and two have no concern.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one scenario and the five bins, and may open the four forms. Opening them does not change the score.
  2. The learner places the scenario in a bin, and the placement is committed.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text.
  4. After scenario 6 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 6 scenarios in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [bin]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. This is [bin]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 6 correct on the first attempt". At 5 or more it adds "You can spot who is missing from a test." Below 5 it lists the Why text of each missed scenario.

Starting State: The first scenario in the shuffled order and the five bins. The question shown is "Who is missing, and why?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter lists four forms of sampling bias: volunteer bias, convenience sampling, attrition, and exclusion. The sim adds two cases with no concern.

docs.title: The Design on One Page
docs.text: The poster below pulls the whole design onto one picture. It follows the students from the pool, through random assignment, into the two groups, through the same tests, to the comparison.

docs.title: Diagram: A/B Test Anatomy
docs.text:
A/B Test Anatomy

Type: infographic sim-id: ab-test-anatomy Library: html Status: Specified Bloom Level: Remember Bloom Verb: identify Learning Objective: The learner will identify the six parts of an A/B test design from a description of how each looks, with at least 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: A/B Test, Control Group, Treatment Group, Random Assignment, Pre-Test, Post-Test, Outcome Measure (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: In quiz mode the learner clicks the marker that matches a visual hint. A click is correct when it matches the marker named in the Hint column of Content. Mastery is at least 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Hovering in explore mode is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) The two groups are formed by choice. (2) Only the post-test is needed. (3) The control group gets no lesson.

Instructional Rationale: Identifying the parts of a design is a Remember-level task, and a picture of the whole flow from pool to comparison gives each part a place. The quiz asks the learner to recognize a part by its look.

Content:

The illustration is a text-free flat drawing read from left to right. At the left is a circle of 24 identical small figures. An arrow leaves the circle and passes through a pair of dice. Beyond the dice the figures split into two equal clusters, an upper cluster of 12 holding a page with one dot and a lower cluster of 12 holding a page with two dots. Each cluster has a pencil-and-paper icon before it and another after it. At the right is a balance scale with a cluster on each pan. The six markers:

# Label Hint (describes the look, not the name) Description Tip 1 Student pool The circle of identical figures at the left. The students invited to take part. Invite every student in the class, and record who agrees. 2 Random assignment The pair of dice on the arrow. Chance decides who gets which version. Sort by the pre-test, pair neighbors, and flip a coin inside each pair. 3 Control group The upper cluster holding the page with one dot. The students who use the original version. Treat them exactly like the other group in every way but the version. 4 Treatment group The lower cluster holding the page with two dots. The students who use the improved version. Give them nothing extra beyond the improved version. 5 Pre-test and post-test The pencil-and-paper icons before and after each cluster. The same tests, given to both groups. Use equivalent forms and the same conditions for both groups. 6 Comparison The balance scale at the right. The two groups' learning gains are compared. Compare the gains and not only the post-test scores.

Provenance: The six parts follow the chapter sections "A/B Test", "Random Assignment", "Control Group", "Treatment Group", "Pre-Test", "Post-Test", and "Outcome Measure". The illustration is synthetic, and the sim labels it "illustrative example".

Rules: Each hint matches exactly one marker. The illustration contains no text, so every label comes from the table above. Markers are numbered 1 to 6 in the order of the table, from left to right.

Learner Activity:

  1. In explore mode the learner hovers or clicks a marker and reads its label, description, and tip.
  2. In quiz mode the sim shows a hint.
  3. The learner clicks the marker they think the hint describes.
  4. If the first click is wrong, the sim says so and lets the learner try once more. If the second click is also wrong, the sim reveals the marker and its description.
  5. After all 6 hints the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 6 hints in a shuffled order, two attempts each. Only a correct first click counts as evidence. Correct: "Correct: [label]. [Description]". First wrong click: "Not quite. Look again at the hint: [hint]". Second wrong click: "This is [label]. [Description]". The summary shows "[n] of 6 correct on the first attempt". At 5 or more it adds "You can read the design of an A/B test." Below 5 it lists the labels of the missed parts.

Starting State: The illustration with six numbered markers, explore mode active, and the prompt "Hover a marker to see a part of the design."

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's eight-step method and its sections on groups, assignment, and tests describe the same six parts.

docs.title: Informed Consent
docs.text:
Informed consent is a person's agreement to take part in a test, given freely after they understand what taking part involves. Students in a test are not just data. They are children and young people whose time, learning, and information are being used, and they and their families have a right to decide. For students under 18, a parent or guardian gives permission, and the student gives assent, which is agreement in words that the student can understand.

Valid consent has these parts.

Part What the letter says Purpose Why the test is being done, in plain words What students do Which version, which tests, how long What data is collected Which scores and which information, and no more than needed Risks and benefits What could go wrong, and what may be gained, without promises Voluntary Taking part is a choice, and saying no has no penalty Right to withdraw A student may stop at any time without penalty Confidentiality Who sees the data, and how it is kept Keeping and sharing How long the data is kept, and whether results are shared Contact A person to ask, with a way to reach them

Three practical rules follow. Consent comes before any data is collected, and not after. Declining must cost the student nothing: no grade penalty, no loss of access, and an equally good alternative activity during the test. And the test needs approval from the school or district before it starts. Rules differ between schools, districts, and countries, and some require review by an ethics board for research with students. This book does not give legal advice, so ask your administrator or privacy officer what applies to you.

Consent Comes Before the First Score

Do not run the pre-test and send the form afterward. Anything collected before consent is data you may not be allowed to use. Get the answer first.

The MicroSim below practices reading a consent letter. It shows eight sentences from drafts, and for each one you decide whether it belongs in a good letter.

docs.title: Diagram: Consent Letter Checker
docs.text:
Consent Letter Checker

Type: microsim sim-id: consent-letter-checker Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: judge Learning Objective: The learner will judge whether each of eight sentences from draft consent letters is acceptable or a problem, with at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Informed Consent, Sampling Bias (both defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each sentence the learner commits one of two bins. A placement is correct when it matches the Correct bin column in Content. Mastery is at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the consent parts is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A promise of a better grade encourages participation. (2) Participation can be required if the activity is part of class. (3) More data is always better.

Instructional Rationale: Judging a sentence against the parts of valid consent is an Evaluate-level action. Sentences that pressure, over-collect, or over-share, mixed with sound ones, teach the learner what a letter must and must not say.

Content:

The two bins: Acceptable, and Problem.

The eight sentences (all made up, for the Watershed Basics pilot):

# Sentence from a draft letter Correct bin Why (shown as feedback) 1 Your child will use one of two versions of a lesson on watersheds, and a computer will choose which version by chance. Acceptable It states what students do and that assignment is random. 2 Taking part will raise your child's science grade. Problem It promises a benefit that the test cannot promise, and it ties participation to the grade. 3 Taking part is voluntary. Your child may stop at any time, and nothing will happen to their grade. Acceptable It states that participation is voluntary and withdrawal is free. 4 All students must take part, and those who decline will lose participation points. Problem It forces participation and penalizes refusal. 5 We will collect your child's name, birthdate, home address, and phone number with every test. Problem It collects personal information that the test does not need. 6 Scores are stored under a code number. Names are kept in a separate locked file that only the teacher can open, and the file will be deleted on 2027-06-30. Acceptable It states how data is protected and when it is deleted. 7 Results may be shared with any company that wants them. Problem It allows unlimited sharing of student information. 8 Questions about the test may be sent to the teacher at the school office or to the district research contact. Acceptable It gives a way to reach a person.

Provenance: The sentences are illustrative examples written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The consent parts follow the chapter section "Informed Consent". The sim adds the note "check your school's rules".

Rules: Each sentence has exactly one correct bin, four per bin.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one sentence and the two bins, and may open the table of consent parts. Opening it does not change the score.
  2. The learner places the sentence in a bin, and the placement is committed.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text.
  4. After sentence 8 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 8 sentences in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [bin]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. This is [bin]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 8 correct on the first attempt". At 7 or more it adds "You can read a consent letter critically." Below 7 it lists the Why text of each missed sentence.

Starting State: The first sentence in the shuffled order and the two bins. The question shown is "Does this sentence belong in a good consent letter?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's table of consent parts and its three practical rules are the basis of the sentences.

docs.title: Student Privacy in Testing
docs.text:
Student privacy in testing is the set of practices that keep information about students safe while a test is run and afterward. Chapter 13 explained that the work of reviewing resources needs no student data, and that an A/B test does. This is where the rules for that data are set.

Six practices cover most of the risk.

  1. Collect only what the question needs. To compare gains you need a version label, a pre-test score, a post-test score, and a grade level. You do not need a name, a birthdate, or a home address in the data.
  2. Use a code in place of a name. Give each student a code such as S01. Keep a key that links codes to names in a separate, locked file, and give the data file only the codes.
  3. Store data in an approved place. Use storage that the school or district approves, with access limited to the people who need it.
  4. Keep it only as long as needed. Set a deletion date before the test, state it in the consent letter, and delete the data and the key on that date.
  5. Report in groups. Publish averages, and do not publish an individual's score. Many agencies hide results for groups smaller than a set size, such as 10, so follow your district's rule.
  6. Keep identifiable data away from AI agents. Do not paste student names, scores tied to names, or free-text answers that name a student into an agent unless the school has approved that agent for that use. Use codes, and remove names from written answers first.

Laws add to these practices. In the United States, FERPA covers student education records, as Chapter 13 explained, and the law known as COPPA can apply to online tools that collect personal information from children under 13. The laws differ by place and by tool, so check with your school's privacy officer before you collect anything.

Stage What is held Where Who sees it Collect Code, version, pre-test, post-test The approved school system The teacher Store The data file, and the key in a separate file Two locked locations The teacher and the data owner Analyze Codes and scores only The teacher's computer, or an approved tool The teacher Report Group averages, with small groups hidden The published report The public Delete Nothing remains The date stated in the letter No one

The MicroSim below practices the first two practices. It shows ten possible data items, and for each one you decide whether to collect it, replace it with a code, or not collect it.

docs.title: Diagram: Privacy Data Sorter
docs.text:
Privacy Data Sorter

Type: microsim sim-id: privacy-data-sorter Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: apply Learning Objective: The learner will apply the data-minimization practices to ten possible data items by sorting each into Collect, Replace with a code, or Do not collect, with at least 9 of 10 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Student Privacy in Testing, Informed Consent, Pre-Test, Post-Test (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each item the learner commits one of three bins. A placement is correct when it matches the Correct bin column in Content. Mastery is at least 9 of 10 correct on the first attempt. Reading the six practices is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) More data makes a better test. (2) Replacing a name with a code makes the key unnecessary to protect. (3) A birthdate is needed to know a student's grade level.

Instructional Rationale: Sorting data items by what the question needs is an Apply-level use of data minimization. Ten items that cover the scores, the identifiers, and the contact details teach the learner to ask whether each item answers the research question.

Content:

The three bins: Collect (keep it in the data file), Replace with a code (keep it only in the separate key file), Do not collect.

The ten items (all for the Watershed Basics pilot):

# Data item Correct bin Why (shown as feedback) 1 Pre-test score Collect The gain cannot be computed without it. 2 Post-test score Collect The gain cannot be computed without it. 3 Which version the student used Collect The comparison depends on it. 4 Grade level Collect It describes the sample without identifying a student. 5 Student name Replace with a code The name belongs only in the separate key file. 6 School student ID number Replace with a code The ID identifies the student, so only a code goes in the data. 7 Email address Do not collect The test does not need it. 8 Home address Do not collect The test does not need it. 9 Birthdate Do not collect Grade level answers the question without it. 10 Photograph of the student working Do not collect It identifies the student and the test does not need it.

Provenance: The items are illustrative examples written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The practices follow the chapter section "Student Privacy in Testing". The sim adds the note "your school's rules decide".

Rules: Each item has exactly one correct bin. Four items are Collect, two are Replace with a code, and four are Do not collect.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one item and the three bins, and may open the six practices. Opening them does not change the score.
  2. The learner places the item in a bin, and the placement is committed.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text.
  4. After item 10 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 10 items in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [bin]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. This item belongs in [bin]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 10 correct on the first attempt". At 9 or more it adds "You can collect only what the test needs." Below 9 it lists the Why text of each missed item.

Starting State: The first item in the shuffled order and the three bins. The question shown is "Does the test need this item, and in what form?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's first two practices are to collect only what the question needs and to use a code in place of a name. The sim applies both.

docs.title: Reviewing a Test Plan
docs.text: The last MicroSim puts the whole chapter together. It shows a draft plan for a test, one section at a time, and for each section you decide whether it is sound or has a flaw.

docs.title: Diagram: Test Plan Reviewer
docs.text:
Test Plan Reviewer

Type: microsim sim-id: test-plan-reviewer Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: critique Learning Objective: The learner will critique the eight sections of a draft test plan, deciding for each whether it is sound or flawed, with at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Test Hypothesis, Control Group, Treatment Group, Random Assignment, Outcome Measure, Sample Size, Confounding Variable, Informed Consent, Student Privacy in Testing (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each section the learner commits Sound or Flawed. A verdict is correct when it matches the Correct verdict column in Content. When the verdict is Flawed, the learner also names the flaw from the list, and the name is checked in the feedback. Mastery is at least 7 of 8 verdicts correct on the first attempt. Reading the chapter summary is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A plan is sound if it has all the section headings. (2) A small test can prove that a version works. (3) A note sent home after the test counts as consent.

Instructional Rationale: Critiquing a plan section by section is an Evaluate-level action that brings the chapter's concepts together. Four flawed and four sound sections teach the learner to find the weak point and to leave a sound section alone.

Content:

The two verdicts: Sound, Flawed. The flaws: Vague hypothesis, Confounded groups, Overclaim from a small sample, Consent after the test, Privacy gap.

The eight sections of the draft plan (all made up, for a Watershed Basics pilot):

# Section Text of the draft Correct verdict Flaw Why (shown as feedback) 1 Hypothesis The improved version will be better. Flawed Vague hypothesis "Better" has no measure, size, or direction. 2 Groups The control group is the third-period class using the original. The treatment group is the fifth-period class using the improved version. Flawed Confounded groups The periods differ in students, time of day, and more. 3 Assignment Students are paired by pre-test score, and a random number decides which student in each pair gets the improved version. Sound None It is blocked random assignment. 4 Outcome measure Both groups take a 20-question test written for the three learning outcomes, with the same key, before and after the lesson. Sound None The measure is aligned, the same for both, and scored alike. 5 Sample size and claim All 24 students in one class take part, and the result will be reported as proof that the improved version works for all Grade 6 students. Flawed Overclaim from a small sample A pilot of 24 students cannot prove an effect for all students. 6 Consent Students take part as a class activity, and a note will be sent home afterward. Flawed Consent after the test Consent must come before any data is collected. 7 Privacy Scores are stored under code numbers, the key is kept in a separate locked file, and no names are sent to any AI agent. Sound None It follows the minimization, code, and agent practices. 8 Timeline The pre-test is in week 1, the lesson is in weeks 2 and 3, and the post-test is in week 4, on the same days for both groups. Sound None The conditions are the same for both groups.

Provenance: The sections are illustrative examples written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The flaws follow the chapter sections on the hypothesis, the groups, the sample, consent, and privacy.

Rules: Each section has exactly one correct verdict. Four are Flawed and four are Sound. The flaw named for each Flawed section is unique.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one section of the plan.
  2. The learner chooses Sound or Flawed. If Flawed, the learner also names the flaw.
  3. The sim shows whether the verdict was correct, the flaw, and the Why text.
  4. After section 8 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 8 sections in the order of the table, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [verdict]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. This section is [verdict]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 8 correct on the first attempt". At 7 or more it adds "You can review a test plan." Below 7 it lists the Why text of each missed section.

Starting State: Section 1 of the draft plan and the two verdicts. The question shown is "Is this section ready to use?"

Chapter Anchors: The sections correspond to the chapter's hypothesis, groups, assignment, outcome measure, sample size, consent, privacy, and the timeline of the eight-step method.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• An A/B test compares two versions, with different students using each at the same time. It answers a question the rubric cannot: whether students learn more from the improved version.
  • Freeze the original version and the improved version before the test. The change log lists the differences, and a bundle of fixes tests only the bundle.
  • The control group uses the original and the treatment group uses the improved version. They must differ in the version and in nothing else.
  • A test hypothesis is written first, and it is specific, measurable, directional, sized, and falsifiable.
  • An outcome measure is chosen in advance, aligned to the outcomes, fair to both versions, and scored alike. A pre-test and a post-test give the learning gain, and the normalized gain accounts for the room to improve. A before-and-after comparison without a second group cannot separate the lesson from the passage of time.
  • Random assignment spreads unseen differences across the groups. It balances groups on average, so small classes should use blocked assignment, which needs the pre-test first.
  • Sample size limits what a test can show. A pilot of 12 students per group checks the procedure and does not prove an effect.
  • A confounding variable is a second difference between the groups, and sampling bias is a distortion in who takes part. Defend against both with the one-difference rule, random assignment, and a record of who participated.
  • Informed consent comes before any data, is voluntary and free of penalty, and needs school or district approval. Student privacy in testing means collecting only what is needed, using codes, storing and deleting data safely, reporting in groups, and keeping identifiable data away from agents.

You Can Design a Fair Test

You can now write a testable hypothesis, form two comparable groups, choose fair measures, and plan consent and privacy for a student test. The next chapter turns to the data and shows how to tell whether the improved version helped.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Designing an A/B Test with Students
docs.text: Test your understanding of control and treatment groups, hypotheses, learning gain, random assignment, confounders, sampling bias, consent, and student privacy in testing with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. In an A/B test of an original resource and an improved resource, what is the control group?
docs.text:
1. The students who use the original version and receive ordinary teaching with it
  2. The students who receive no lesson at all while the others use the improved version
  3. The students who use the improved version of the resource and are tested the same way
  4. The students who choose their own version of the resource after seeing both of them
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The control group is the yardstick for the test. It answers the question "Compared with what?" It is not a group that receives no teaching: it gets the ordinary lesson with the original resource, which is a fully acceptable lesson, so no student is harmed. Many teachers offer the improved version to the control group after the test ends. The control group must differ from the treatment group in the version and in nothing else.

Concept Tested: Control Group

See: Control Group

docs.title: 2. Which formula gives a student's normalized learning gain?
docs.text:
1. The gain divided by the room available: (post − pre) ÷ (100 − pre)
  2. The raw difference between the two scores: post − pre
  3. The gain divided by the starting score: (post − pre) ÷ pre
  4. The ratio of the final score to the starting score on the same test: post ÷ pre
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The normalized gain compares the gain with the room available to gain. A student who goes from 40 to 70 has a gain of 30 out of a possible 60, which is 0.50. A student who goes from 90 to 95 gains only 5 points but also closes half the available gap, 5 out of 10. The raw gain, post minus pre (B), cannot compare these students fairly. When the pre-test score is 100, the normalized gain is undefined.

Concept Tested: Learning Gain

See: Learning Gain

docs.title: 3. Why does an A/B test use a control group instead of only comparing one group's scores before and after the lesson?
docs.text:
1. A single group cannot take both a pre-test and a post-test on the same set of questions in the same school week
  2. Anything that happened between the tests can explain the gain, and a control group shares that time
  3. A control group makes the sample size larger, which makes every result more reliable
  4. A report is never allowed to include a before-and-after result from a single group
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. A gain of 18 points after a lesson is weak evidence on its own, because students were also learning in other classes, may have seen the test questions before, and simply got older. Without a second group you cannot separate the effect of the lesson from the effect of time. In an A/B test those effects cancel when you compare the two groups' gains. A before-and-after comparison is acceptable when no second group is possible, if the report names the limit.

Concept Tested: Before-and-After Comparison

See: Before-and-After Comparison

docs.title: 4. Why does the chapter prefer assigning students to versions by chance instead of letting them choose?
docs.text:
1. Chance always produces two groups with exactly equal pre-test averages, however small the class
  2. Letting students choose is against the law in most schools and so cannot be used in a test
  3. Chance increases the number of students who can take part in the test at the same time
  4. Chance spreads unseen differences, such as motivation, across the groups, while choice clusters keen students
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Students differ in ways you cannot see or measure, such as motivation, home support, and sleep. Random assignment spreads those differences across the groups so that, on average, the groups are alike before the lesson. It balances groups only on average, so a small class can still be unlucky, and the chapter recommends pairing students by pre-test score and flipping a coin inside each pair. When the 12 highest scorers chose the improved version, the group averages differed by 23.75 points.

Concept Tested: Random Assignment

See: Random Assignment

docs.title: 5. A student scores 40 on the pre-test and 70 on the post-test. What are the raw gain and the normalized gain?
docs.text:
1. 30 points and 0.30
  2. 70 points and 0.70
  3. 30 points and 0.50
  4. 30 points and 0.75
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The raw gain is the post-test score minus the pre-test score, which is 70 minus 40, or 30 percentage points. The normalized gain divides that by the room available, which is 100 minus 40, or 60. Thirty divided by 60 is 0.50, so the student closed half of the gap that was open. Option A divides by 100, which ignores the starting score. Compare gains, and not only post-test scores, because the groups may not start at the same level.

Concept Tested: Learning Gain

See: Learning Gain

docs.title: 6. Which statement is a testable hypothesis for the Watershed Basics pilot?
docs.text:
1. The improved version is better than the original version for the students who use it in class
  2. Students will like the improved version more than they like the original version of the lesson
  3. Every student will learn more from the improved version than from the original version of the lesson
  4. Grade 6 students on the improved version will have a larger mean learning gain than those on the original
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. A good hypothesis is specific, measurable, directional, sized, and falsifiable. Option D names the students and the measure and states the direction, and the chapter's own version adds a size of at least 5 percentage points. "Better" (A) has no measure. "Like" (B) has no comparison or measure. A claim about every student (C) cannot be shown, because some result would have to show it wrong. Write the hypothesis before the test, not after the results.

Concept Tested: Test Hypothesis

See: Test Hypothesis

docs.title: 7. For the pilot, which set of items should the teacher keep in the data file?
docs.text:
1. The student's name, birthdate, home address, and scores, so each student can be contacted
  2. The version label, pre-test score, post-test score, and grade level, with a code in place of the name
  3. The scores, the email addresses, and a photograph of each student working on the lesson
  4. The scores and the school student ID number, so that each score can be traced back
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Collect only what the question needs. To compare gains you need the version, the pre-test, the post-test, and a grade level, which describes the sample without identifying anyone. Give each student a code such as S01, and keep the key that links codes to names in a separate, locked file. Names, ID numbers, birthdates, addresses, emails, and photographs are not needed, and each adds risk. Keep identifiable data away from AI agents too.

Concept Tested: Student Privacy in Testing

See: Student Privacy in Testing

docs.title: 8. In a test, the morning section uses the original version and the afternoon section uses the improved version, and the afternoon group scores higher. Which analysis is best?
docs.text:
1. The improved version is proven better, because its group scored higher than the other group
  2. The sample is too large to trust, because larger samples contain more unusual students
  3. Time of day and the students in each section also differ, so the version cannot be separated from them
  4. The result is valid, because the same teacher taught both sections and so removed every other difference
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. A confounding variable is a factor other than the version that differs between the groups and could explain the result. Alertness changes through the day, and the two sections differ in other ways, so the version is tangled with them. The cure is the one-difference rule: arrange everything but the version to be the same, and let random assignment handle what you cannot arrange. A single teacher (D) removes one confounder and leaves the others in place.

Concept Tested: Confounding Variable

See: Confounding Variable

docs.title: 9. Nine students in the treatment group leave the test because the simulation would not load on their devices, and their scores are dropped. What problem does this show?
docs.text:
1. Volunteer bias, because the students chose to leave the test of their own accord
  2. Convenience sampling, because the class was easy for the teacher to reach and test
  3. Attrition, because the students who remain are those whose devices worked, so the result is biased
  4. No concern, because the remaining students still took the test and their scores count
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Sampling bias is a distortion when the students in the test are not like the students you want to learn about, or when the students who finish are not like those who started. Attrition is uneven dropout, so the scores that remain come from students who stayed. Record how many were invited, how many agreed, and how many finished each group, and report who took part. Offer both versions in forms that every student can use.

Concept Tested: Sampling Bias

See: Sampling Bias

docs.title: 10. A draft test plan says, "Students take part as a class activity, and a note will be sent home afterward." What is the best judgment?
docs.text:
1. It is sound, because a class activity does not need consent from the parents or the students
  2. It is flawed, because consent must come before any data is collected, and declining must cost nothing
  3. It is sound if the note is sent within a week, because the test is a normal class activity
  4. It is flawed only because the note is too short to explain the test to the parents
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Informed consent is agreement given freely after a person understands what taking part involves. For students under 18, a parent or guardian gives permission and the student gives assent. Consent comes before any data is collected, and anything collected earlier may not be usable. Declining must cost nothing, with an equally good alternative activity. The test also needs approval from the school or district before it starts.

Concept Tested: Informed Consent

See: Informed Consent

docs.title: References: Designing an A/B Test with Students
docs.text:
1. A/B testing - Wikipedia - Defines A/B testing, how users are split between versions, and how results are compared. The core idea behind comparing an original resource with its improved version.

  2. Randomized controlled trial - Wikipedia - Explains random assignment to treatment and control groups and why it supports causal claims. Background for the chapter's sections on random assignment and control and treatment groups.

  3. Informed consent - Wikipedia - Describes what people must be told and agree to before taking part in research, and the special rules for minors. Supports the chapter's guidance on consent and student privacy.

  4. Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments: A Practical Guide to A/B Testing - Ron Kohavi, Diane Tang, and Ya Xu - Cambridge University Press (2020) - Drawing on years of running experiments at large technology companies, the authors explain Twyman's law and sample ratio mismatch as checks that catch broken experiments before anyone trusts the result.

  5. Experimental and Quasi-Experimental Designs for Generalized Causal Inference - William R. Shadish, Thomas D. Cook, and Donald T. Campbell - Houghton Mifflin (2002) - Extends Campbell and Stanley's 1963 list of threats to validity, such as history, maturation, and selection. That list remains the standard vocabulary for why two groups differ for reasons other than the treatment.

  6. Sample Size Calculator - Evan Miller - A free calculator that estimates how many participants a two-group test needs for a chosen effect and confidence. Supports the chapter's sample size planning.

  7. How Not To Run an A/B Test - Evan Miller - Explains why checking results repeatedly and stopping when they look good inflates false positives. A caution for anyone running a small test with students.

  8. Identifying and Implementing Educational Practices Supported by Rigorous Evidence - Institute of Education Sciences - A user-friendly guide to what counts as strong evidence in education, with emphasis on randomized studies. Helps teachers judge what their own small test can and cannot show.

  9. What Works Clearinghouse Handbooks - Institute of Education Sciences - The standards the WWC uses to rate study designs, covering random assignment, attrition, and baseline equivalence. A benchmark for a well-planned classroom comparison.

  10. Protection of Human Subjects (45 CFR Part 46) - eCFR - The federal regulations, known as the Common Rule, for research with human subjects, including informed-consent requirements. Context for the chapter's consent planning and when review boards are involved.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Shows how to collect and anonymize data, compare group means, read effect size, combine surveys with qualitative feedback, check rubric scores against outcomes, and consider equity. It follows the A/B test design chapter and closes the loop between rubric scores and learning outcomes. After this chapter you can collect and anonymize data, compare two groups, read an effect size, and check whether rubric scores predict learning.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 13 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Data Collection 23 Anonymized Data 1 Mean Score 11 Difference of Means 10 Effect Size 5 Student Survey 8 Completion Rate 1 Time on Task 1 Qualitative Feedback 5 Results Summary 4 Rubric-Outcome Correlation 1 Pilot Test 1 Equity Consideration 1

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 3: The Ten-Metric Rubric and Scoring
  • Chapter 7: Accessibility
  • Chapter 14: Checking and Calibrating AI Agent Output
  • Chapter 16: Designing an A/B Test with Students

Now Let the Data Speak

The test is run and the scores are in. This chapter shows you how to look after the data, compare the two groups fairly, and say what the numbers do and do not show. Let's dive in and check the evidence!

The last chapter designed a test, and this chapter reads its results. The test is the Watershed Basics pilot: one class of 24 students, split by blocked random assignment into a control group of 12 who used the original version and a treatment group of 12 who used the improved version. Everyone took the same 20-question pre-test and post-test. The hypothesis, written in advance, was that the treatment group's mean learning gain would be at least 5 percentage points larger.

The analysis is deliberately simple. It needs a calculator or a spreadsheet and a few ideas: what to collect, how to compare averages, how big a difference is, what students say, and how far to trust a small test. At the end, the results close a loop. They show whether the rubric scores of Chapters 3 through 10 predict what students learn, which is how the automated scoring in this book is checked against reality.

docs.title: Data Collection
docs.text:
Data collection is the careful gathering of the measurements the test needs, in the same way for both groups. Chapter 16 chose the measures. This step gets them into a table where they can be trusted. A plan covers four things: what is collected, when, by whom, and where it is kept.

For the pilot, the schedule follows the design.

Week What happens Data collected 1 Pre-test, then assignment Pre-test score for each student 2 and 3 Students use their assigned version Completion of the quiz and minutes on task, logged by the platform 4 Post-test and survey Post-test score, survey ratings, and written comments

Everything goes into one spreadsheet with one row per student. The table gives the columns, which together are the data dictionary.

Column Meaning Code The student's code, such as S07, and nothing else that identifies them Version C for the original, T for the improved version Pre-test Score from 0 to 100 Post-test Score from 0 to 100 Gain Post-test minus pre-test, computed by formula Completed quiz Yes or No Minutes on task Whole minutes Survey items 1 to 3 Ratings from 1 to 5 Comment Written text with names removed

Four habits protect the quality of the data. Use the same procedure, script, and timing for both groups. Keep a short log of anything unusual, such as a fire drill during the post-test or a device that failed. Check the table for errors before analyzing it: missing values, scores outside 0 to 100, repeated codes, and labels typed two ways. And keep a backup in an approved location. A calculation on a mistyped table gives a confident wrong answer.

The MicroSim below practices the check. It shows a table of ten rows with five planted errors, and you find them.

docs.title: Diagram: Data Quality Detective
docs.text:
Data Quality Detective

Type: microsim sim-id: data-quality-detective Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: examine Learning Objective: The learner will examine a ten-row test data table and identify the five rows with errors and the kind of error in each, with at least 4 of 5 error rows named correctly on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Data Collection, Pre-Test, Post-Test, Learning Gain (all defined in this chapter above this block or in Chapter 16).

Evidence of Mastery: The learner marks each row Clean or Error, and for each Error row picks the kind of error. An error row is correct when both the marking and the kind match the Content table. Clean rows marked Error count against the learner. Mastery is at least 4 of the 5 error rows correct and no more than 1 clean row marked as an error, on the first attempt. Reading the error kinds is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A table that opens without a warning is correct. (2) A score of 120 belongs to a high-performing student. (3) A blank cell can be treated as zero.

Instructional Rationale: Examining a data table for errors is an Analyze-level action that comes before any calculation. A table with five different kinds of error and five clean rows teaches the learner to check each column against its meaning.

Content:

The data dictionary, shown at all times: Code (unique), Version (C or T), Pre-test (0 to 100), Post-test (0 to 100).

The five kinds of error: Missing value, Out of range, Repeated code, Inconsistent label, Wrong unit.

The ten rows (all made up):

Row Code Version Pre-test Post-test Correct marking Kind of error Why (shown as feedback) 1 S01 T 28 59 Clean None The values are in range and the label is valid. 2 S02 C 22 42 Clean None The values are in range and the label is valid. 3 S03 T 31 (blank) Error Missing value The post-test is blank, and a blank must not be treated as zero. 4 S04 C 35 50 Clean None The values are in range and the label is valid. 5 S05 T 41 120 Error Out of range A score of 120 is outside 0 to 100. 6 S06 C 0.38 46 Error Wrong unit The pre-test is a fraction and the column holds percentages. 7 S07 Treatment 43 76 Error Inconsistent label The column uses C and T, and this row uses a word. 8 S08 C 45 64 Clean None The values are in range and the label is valid. 9 S08 T 47 70 Error Repeated code Code S08 appears twice, so two students share a code. 10 S10 C 48 66 Clean None The values are in range and the label is valid.

Provenance: The rows are illustrative examples written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The error kinds follow the chapter section "Data Collection".

Rules: Exactly five rows are errors and five are clean. Each of the five kinds of error appears once.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees the table and the data dictionary.
  2. The learner marks each row Clean or Error, and for each Error row picks the kind of error.
  3. The learner presses Check.
  4. The sim shows which markings were correct, the kind of each error, and the Why text.

Feedback: One check, after all ten rows are marked. Correct: "Correct: row [n], [kind]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. Row [n] is [marking], [kind]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 5 error rows correct, [m] clean rows marked as errors". When mastery is met it adds "You can check a table before you use it." Otherwise it lists the Why text of each missed row.

Starting State: The table with all rows unmarked, and the data dictionary.

Chapter Anchors: The chapter says to check for missing values, scores outside 0 to 100, repeated codes, and labels typed two ways. The sim adds a wrong-unit error.

docs.title: Anonymized Data
docs.text:
Anonymized data is data from which every link to a particular person has been removed, so that no one, including the teacher, can tell whose scores they are. It differs from coded data. Coded data replaces names with codes and keeps a key somewhere, so the link can be rebuilt. Anonymizing happens when the key is destroyed on the deletion date promised in the consent letter, and when nothing else in the table points to a person.

Codes alone are not always enough. In a class of 24, a column that records gender, class period, and the teacher's name can single out a student, and a written comment such as "the girl who sits by the window" can name one. The steps are to drop columns the analysis does not need, to generalize others (grade level, not birthdate), to hide results for any group under the size your district sets, and to remove identifying detail from comments. A good test is to ask whether someone who knows the class could pick out a single student from what you plan to share. If yes, remove more.

The MicroSim below practices the test. It describes eight tables or notes, and for each you decide whether it is safe to share.

docs.title: Diagram: Re-identification Risk Checker
docs.text:
Re-identification Risk Checker

Type: microsim sim-id: reidentification-risk-checker Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: judge Learning Objective: The learner will judge whether each of eight data items from a class test is safe to share or a re-identification risk, with at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Anonymized Data, Student Privacy in Testing (defined in this chapter above this block or in Chapter 16).

Evidence of Mastery: For each item the learner commits one of two bins. A placement is correct when it matches the Correct bin column in Content. Mastery is at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the four steps is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Replacing names with codes makes data anonymous. (2) A group average is always safe. (3) A quotation is harmless if the name is removed.

Instructional Rationale: Judging whether data can point to a person is an Evaluate-level action. Items that look harmless but identify a student in a class of 24 teach the learner to ask who could pick out a student.

Content:

The two bins: Safe to share, Re-identification risk.

The eight items (all made up, for the Watershed Basics pilot of 24 students in one class):

# Item Correct bin Why (shown as feedback) 1 A table with the columns code, version, pre-test, and post-test. Safe to share It holds codes and scores only. 2 A table with code, version, pre-test, post-test, class period, teacher name, and gender. Re-identification risk In a class of 24 these columns can single out a student. 3 A table with student name, version, pre-test, and post-test. Re-identification risk The names identify each student. 4 Comments with names removed and details about seat and appearance removed. Safe to share Nothing in them points to one student. 5 A comment that reads "The girl who sits by the window said the video was too fast." Re-identification risk The detail points to one student. 6 The average gain for the control group and the average gain for the treatment group. Safe to share Each average covers 12 students. 7 The average gain for the 3 students who use captions. Re-identification risk A group of 3 is below the size most districts allow to be reported. 8 A file of codes and scores after the key file has been deleted on the stated date. Safe to share No link to a person remains.

Provenance: The items are illustrative examples written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The sim adds the note "your school's rules decide the smallest group you may report".

Rules: Each item has exactly one correct bin, four per bin.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one item and the two bins.
  2. The learner places the item in a bin, and the placement is committed.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text.
  4. After item 8 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 8 items in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [bin]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. This is [bin]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 8 correct on the first attempt". At 7 or more it adds "You can tell safe data from risky data." Below 7 it lists the Why text of each missed item.

Starting State: The first item in the shuffled order and the two bins. The question shown is "Could someone who knows the class pick out a student?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter says that codes alone are not always enough and lists the steps of dropping columns, generalizing, hiding small groups, and cleaning comments.

docs.title: Mean Score
docs.text:
A mean score is the average of a set of scores: add them all and divide by how many there are. It is the most common way to summarize a group with one number. For the pilot, the number to summarize is each student's learning gain, the post-test minus the pre-test.

The control group's 12 gains add to 180, so their mean gain is 180 divided by 12, which is 15.0 points. The treatment group's 12 gains add to 264, so their mean gain is 264 divided by 12, which is 22.0 points.

A mean hides how scores are spread out, so report the spread too. The standard deviation is the typical distance of a score from the mean: the larger it is, the more the scores vary. The median is the middle score when they are sorted, and it is a useful check against one very high or very low score. The table gives all three for the pilot.

Control group Treatment group Students 12 12 Mean pre-test score 51.5 52.25 Mean post-test score 66.5 74.25 Mean gain 15.0 22.0 Median gain 17.5 21.5 Standard deviation of the gains 6.0 7.4

The two groups began almost level, with mean pre-test scores of 51.5 and 52.25, which is what blocked random assignment was meant to do.

docs.title: Difference of Means
docs.text:
The difference of means is the mean of the treatment group minus the mean of the control group. It is the single number that answers the hypothesis: how much more did students gain with the improved version?

For the pilot, the difference of mean gains is 22.0 minus 15.0, which is +7.0 points. The hypothesis set a bar of at least 5 points, and 7.0 is above it, so in this pilot the result supports the hypothesis. Compare gains and not post-test means alone. The post-test means differ by 7.75 points, but the groups started 0.75 points apart, and the gain removes that head start.

A difference of means has to be read with care, especially in a small test. With 12 students per group, a few unusually strong or weak students can move an average. The gains of the two groups overlap: the control group's run from 3 to 22 and the treatment group's from 9 to 33. The difference is a real finding about these 24 students, and it may partly be luck. The effect size, next, puts the difference in context, and the pilot section later in the chapter says what to do about the uncertainty.

The MicroSim below puts the data in your hands. It gives the twelve gains for each group, and you calculate the means, the medians, and the difference.

docs.title: Diagram: Mean and Difference Calculator
docs.text:
Mean and Difference Calculator

Type: microsim sim-id: mean-difference-calculator Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: calculate Learning Objective: The learner will calculate the mean gain of each group, the difference of means, and the median gain of each group from a table of 24 gains, and decide whether the difference meets the 5-point threshold, with at least 5 of 6 answers correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Mean Score, Difference of Means, Learning Gain (defined in this chapter above this block or in Chapter 16).

Evidence of Mastery: The learner answers six questions. An answer is correct when it matches the Correct answer column in Content. Numeric answers are correct to one decimal place. Mastery is at least 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Sorting the gains or using a calculator inside the sim is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) The mean and the median are the same number. (2) A positive difference always meets the hypothesis. (3) The mean of post-test scores can replace the mean of gains.

Instructional Rationale: Calculating means and a difference from raw data is an Apply-level action that the learner will repeat on a real test. Twelve values per group are few enough to calculate by hand and enough to need a method.

Content:

The data, shown at all times (learning gains in percentage points, made up for the Watershed Basics pilot):

Group The twelve gains, in the order of student code Control (original version) 20, 15, 8, 19, 18, 17, 21, 10, 18, 9, 3, 22 Treatment (improved version) 31, 11, 20, 33, 23, 26, 18, 28, 9, 18, 27, 20

The hypothesis, shown at all times: the treatment group's mean gain will be at least 5 percentage points larger than the control group's.

The six questions:

# Question Answer type Correct answer Why (shown as feedback) 1 What is the mean gain of the control group? Number to one decimal place 15.0 The gains add to 180, and 180 divided by 12 is 15.0. 2 What is the mean gain of the treatment group? Number to one decimal place 22.0 The gains add to 264, and 264 divided by 12 is 22.0. 3 What is the difference of means, treatment minus control? Number with a sign +7.0 22.0 minus 15.0 is 7.0. 4 Does the difference meet the hypothesis? Yes or No Yes 7.0 >= 5. 5 What is the median gain of the control group? Number to one decimal place 17.5 Sorted, the sixth and seventh gains are 17 and 18, and their middle is 17.5. 6 What is the median gain of the treatment group? Number to one decimal place 21.5 Sorted, the sixth and seventh gains are 20 and 23, and their middle is 21.5.

Provenance: The gains are illustrative examples made up for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The calculations follow the chapter sections "Mean Score" and "Difference of Means".

Rules: The mean is the sum divided by 12. The median of twelve values is the mean of the sixth and seventh values after sorting. The difference is treatment minus control.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees the data and the first question.
  2. The learner enters an answer, and the answer is committed.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text.
  4. After question 6 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 6 questions in the order of the table, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [answer]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. The answer is [answer]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 6 correct on the first attempt". At 5 or more it adds "You can compare two groups." Below 5 it lists the Why text of each missed question.

Starting State: The data table, the hypothesis, and question 1.

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's table of group statistics and its difference of means use the same gains.

docs.title: Effect Size
docs.text:
An effect size is a measure of how big a difference is, in units that do not depend on the test, so that studies can be compared. The most widely used is Cohen's d:

d = (mean of treatment - mean of control) / pooled standard deviation

The pooled standard deviation combines the spread of the two groups: for equal sizes it is the square root of the average of the two squared standard deviations. In the pilot, 6.05 squared is about 36.5 and 7.45 squared is about 55.5. They average 46.0, whose square root is 6.78. So d is 7.0 divided by 6.78, about 1.03.

By convention, a d of 0.2 is called small, 0.5 medium, and 0.8 large. These are rules of thumb, and what counts as important depends on the cost of the change and the setting. By the convention 1.03 is large, but a small pilot gives a noisy estimate, and impressive estimates from small tests tend to shrink when repeated with more students.

A Big Number From a Small Test Deserves a Second Look

Twelve students per group can produce a lovely effect size by luck. Treat a pilot's result as a reason to test again, and do not treat it as the final answer.

The MicroSim below lets you see how the difference and the spread combine into an effect size.

docs.title: Diagram: Effect Size Explorer
docs.text:
Effect Size Explorer

Type: microsim sim-id: effect-size-explorer Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: calculate Learning Objective: The learner will calculate Cohen's d from a difference of means and a pooled standard deviation for six cases and name its conventional size, with at least 5 of 6 cases fully correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Effect Size, Difference of Means, Mean Score (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each case the learner enters d to two decimal places and chooses a size label. A case is fully correct when both match the Content table. Mastery is at least 5 of 6 cases fully correct on the first attempt. Moving the two sliders in free play is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A bigger difference of means always means a bigger effect size. (2) An effect size of 0.2 is worthless. (3) The same difference means the same thing whatever the spread.

Instructional Rationale: Calculating d from a difference and a spread is an Apply-level action. Cases that hold the difference fixed while the spread changes teach the learner that the spread is part of the answer.

Content:

The formula, shown at all times: d = difference of means / pooled standard deviation.

The size labels, shown at all times: d < 0.2 is Less than small. 0.2 <= d < 0.5 is Small. 0.5 <= d < 0.8 is Medium. d >= 0.8 is Large. These are conventional rules of thumb, labeled "rule of thumb" in the sim.

The six cases (all made up, in test-score points):

# Difference of means Pooled standard deviation d Size label Why (shown as feedback) 1 7.0 6.8 1.03 Large 7.0 divided by 6.8 is about 1.03, the Watershed Basics pilot. 2 5.0 10.0 0.50 Medium 5.0 divided by 10.0 is 0.50. 3 2.0 10.0 0.20 Small 2.0 divided by 10.0 is 0.20. 4 8.0 10.0 0.80 Large 8.0 divided by 10.0 is 0.80. 5 3.0 15.0 0.20 Small A 3-point difference is small when scores vary by 15. 6 1.0 10.0 0.10 Less than small 1.0 divided by 10.0 is 0.10.

Free play: two sliders set the difference of means from 0 to 15 and the pooled standard deviation from 3 to 15, and the sim shows d and its label. Free play is labeled "not scored".

Provenance: The cases are illustrative examples written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The size labels are Cohen's conventions and are marked "rule of thumb".

Rules: d is rounded to two decimal places. A case is fully correct only when d and the label both match.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one case with its difference and spread.
  2. The learner enters d and chooses a size label, and presses Check.
  3. The sim shows which entries were correct and the Why text.
  4. After case 6 the sim shows the summary and opens free play.

Feedback: 6 cases in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: d is [d], which is [label]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. d is [d], which is [label]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 6 correct on the first attempt". At 5 or more it adds "You can read an effect size." Below 5 it lists the Why text of each missed case.

Starting State: The first case in the shuffled order, the formula, and the size labels.

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's worked calculation gives d = 1.03 for the pilot, and the sim's case 1 is the same calculation.

docs.title: Student Survey
docs.text:
A student survey is a short set of questions that asks students what they thought of the lesson. The test scores say what students learned. The survey says what they experienced: whether they could follow it, whether they met barriers, and whether they would want more. The two kinds of evidence answer different questions, and a version can do well on one and not on the other.

Good survey questions follow five rules.

  • Same for both groups: the same wording and scale, so ratings can be compared.
  • Neutral: a question must not hint at the answer. "Did you enjoy the great new simulation?" pushes students to say yes.
  • One idea each: "The lesson was clear and the quiz was fair" asks two things, and a student who thinks one is true and the other false cannot answer.
  • Specific: "The lesson was good" says nothing about what to fix.
  • Anonymous: answers are tied to a code and not a name, so students can be honest.

A common format is a rating from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree). The pilot's survey had three such questions, and all 24 students answered. The table gives the mean rating in each group.

Survey question Control mean Treatment mean The lesson helped me understand what a watershed is. 3.5 4.3 I could read or hear every part of the lesson without help. 3.3 4.4 I would like more lessons like this one. 3.4 4.3

The treatment group rated all three questions about one point higher, and the largest gap is on the accessibility question, which fits the added captions and image descriptions. Read ratings with care. They report opinion and not learning, and students given something new may rate it higher partly because it is new. They are a useful companion to the scores and a poor substitute for them.

The MicroSim below practices writing questions. It shows eight draft questions, and for each one you decide whether it is good or has a problem.

docs.title: Diagram: Survey Question Reviewer
docs.text:
Survey Question Reviewer

Type: microsim sim-id: survey-question-reviewer Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: critique Learning Objective: The learner will critique eight draft survey questions as good or problematic and name the problem in each problematic question, with at least 7 of 8 verdicts correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Student Survey (defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each question the learner commits Good or Problem, and for a Problem picks its kind from Leading, Double-barreled, or Vague. A verdict is correct when it matches the Correct verdict column in Content, and the kind is checked in the feedback. Mastery is at least 7 of 8 verdicts correct on the first attempt. Reading the five rules is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A longer question gets a better answer. (2) A positive question is a neutral question. (3) Asking two things at once saves time.
