Instructional Rationale: Critiquing a question against the survey rules is an Evaluate-level action. Questions that fail in different ways, and four sound ones, teach the learner to read each question as a student would.

Content:

The two verdicts: Good, Problem. The kinds of problem: Leading, Double-barreled, Vague.

The eight draft questions (all made up):

# Draft question Correct verdict Kind of problem Why (shown as feedback) 1 The lesson helped me understand what a watershed is. (1 to 5, disagree to agree) Good None It is neutral, specific, and about one idea. 2 Did you enjoy the great new simulation? Problem Leading The word "great" pushes students toward yes. 3 The lesson was clear and the quiz was fair. Problem Double-barreled It asks two things at once. 4 The lesson was good. Problem Vague It does not say what to fix. 5 I could read or hear every part of the lesson without help. (1 to 5, disagree to agree) Good None It is neutral and specific, and it asks about access. 6 Which parts of the lesson, if any, were hard to use? (open answer) Good None It is neutral and invites specific answers. 7 Don't you agree that the explanations were helpful? Problem Leading It asks the student to agree. 8 I would like more lessons like this one. (1 to 5, disagree to agree) Good None It is neutral and about one idea.

Provenance: The questions are illustrative examples written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The rules follow the chapter section "Student Survey".

Rules: Each question has exactly one correct verdict, four per verdict. The four problems are two Leading, one Double-barreled, and one Vague.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one draft question.
  2. The learner chooses Good or Problem. For a Problem the learner also picks its kind.
  3. The sim shows whether the verdict was correct, the kind of problem, and the Why text.
  4. After question 8 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 8 questions in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [verdict]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. This question is [verdict]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 8 correct on the first attempt". At 7 or more it adds "You can write fair survey questions." Below 7 it lists the Why text of each missed question.

Starting State: The first question in the shuffled order and the two verdicts. The question shown is "Would this question get an honest answer?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter lists five rules for survey questions, and its examples of a leading question, a double-barreled question, and a vague question appear in the sim.

docs.title: Completion Rate
docs.text:
The completion rate is the share of students who finished an activity out of those who started it. Divide the number who finished by the number who started and write the answer as a percentage. In the pilot, 10 of the 12 control students finished the quiz, a rate of 83 percent, and all 12 treatment students did, a rate of 100 percent.

A low completion rate is a signal to look for the reason. Here the two control students who did not finish could not make the original quiz load on the school's tablets. That is the portability failure that Chapter 10 found: the quiz script failed on one platform. It is a barrier and not a lack of interest. Because the post-test was separate from the resource's quiz, those two students still took it, and their gains stayed in the analysis.

docs.title: Time on Task
docs.text:
Time on task is the number of minutes a student spends working on the activity. A platform log or a teacher's timer records it. The pilot's mean was 38 minutes for the control group and 47 for the treatment group, a difference of 9 minutes.

Read the number with care, because more time is not automatically better or worse. The improved version contains a worked example and a simulation, so 9 more minutes is about what they would add. If a change cut time on task and left the gain unchanged, that would suggest a more efficient resource. If it cut time and the gain fell, students may have lost interest. Always read time on task together with the learning gain.

docs.title: Qualitative Feedback
docs.text:
Qualitative feedback is what students say in their own words: written comments, answers to open questions, or short interviews. It tells you the why behind the numbers. A rating tells you a student was unhappy. A comment tells you that the quiz would not open on a tablet.

To use comments, code them. Read all the comments, list the themes that recur, and count how many comments mention each. Have two people code independently and compare, as with the human raters of Chapter 14, and resolve differences by discussion. Remove names and identifying detail before you quote anyone. The table gives the themes of the pilot's comments from the 24 students, counted by the number of students who raised each one.

Theme Control (of 12) Treatment (of 12) Unfamiliar words, such as "aquifer" 4 1 The quiz would not load 2 0 Wanted a worked example or more practice 5 1 The simulation helped me see it 0 7 Captions or image descriptions helped 0 4 The quiz explanations helped 1 6

The themes agree with the numbers: the control group's comments cluster around problems the plan fixed, and the treatment group's around the features it added. Comments hint at causes without proving them.

Quote the Comment That Surprised You

Counts show the pattern, and one well-chosen comment makes it real for a reader. Pick a comment that explains a number, and take out anything that could identify the student.

The MicroSim below practices coding. It shows ten comments, and for each one you choose the theme it belongs to.

docs.title: Diagram: Feedback Theme Coder
docs.text:
Feedback Theme Coder

Type: microsim sim-id: feedback-theme-coder Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: classify Learning Objective: The learner will classify each of ten student comments under one of seven themes, with at least 9 of 10 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Qualitative Feedback, Student Survey (both defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each comment the learner commits one of seven themes. A placement is correct when it matches the Correct theme column in Content. Mastery is at least 9 of 10 correct on the first attempt. Reading the theme list is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Comments are too subjective to code. (2) A comment can belong to only one study. (3) The most vivid comment is the most common theme.

Instructional Rationale: Classifying comments under themes is an Understand-level action that turns words into counts. Ten comments over seven themes teach the learner to read for the main point of each.

The seven themes: Unfamiliar words, Technical problem, Wanted more practice, Simulation helped, Captions or descriptions helped, Explanations helped, Other.

The ten comments (all made up, names removed):

Technical problem It describes a failure to load. 3 The slider that changes the ground cover showed me where the rain goes. Simulation helped It credits the simulation. 4 I could follow the video because of the captions. Captions or descriptions helped It credits the captions. 5 I wanted more questions to practice before the test. Wanted more practice It asks for more practice. 6 When I got a question wrong, the explanation told me why. Provenance: The comments are illustrative examples written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The themes follow the chapter section "Qualitative Feedback".

Rules: Each comment has exactly one correct theme. Unfamiliar words, Technical problem, and Wanted more practice have two comments each. Simulation helped, Captions or descriptions helped, Explanations helped, and Other have one each.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one comment and the seven themes.
  2. The learner places the comment under a theme, and the placement is committed.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text.
  4. After comment 10 the sim shows the summary with the count for each theme.

Feedback: 10 comments in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [theme]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. This comment is [theme]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 10 correct on the first attempt" and the counts per theme. At 9 or more it adds "You can turn comments into counts." Below 9 it lists the Why text of each missed comment.

Starting State: The first comment in the shuffled order and the seven themes. The question shown is "What is this student mainly saying?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's table of themes for the pilot uses the same six named themes.

docs.title: Results Summary
docs.text:
A results summary is a short written account of what the test showed. It is the document a colleague, a principal, or an adopter will read, so it has to be clear, honest, and complete in one or two pages. A good summary has seven parts.

Part What it says Question What the test set out to find out, and the hypothesis Design The two versions, the groups, the assignment, and the measures Participants How many students, from where, and how many finished Results The means, the difference, and the other measures Effect size How big the difference is, with the convention noted Limitations The small sample, the bundle of fixes, and anything unusual Decision What follows, such as adopt, revise, or run a larger test

For the pilot, the Results part would read: "The treatment group's mean gain was 22.0 points and the control group's was 15.0, a difference of 7.0, above the 5-point threshold in the hypothesis. The effect size was 1.03." The Limitations part would say that this was one class of 24 students, that five fixes were tested as a bundle, and that a pilot's effect size often shrinks in a larger test. The Decision would be to run a larger test.

The poster below shows the seven parts on a picture of a one-page summary.

docs.title: Diagram: Results Summary Anatomy
docs.text:
Results Summary Anatomy

Type: infographic sim-id: results-summary-anatomy Library: html Status: Specified Bloom Level: Remember Bloom Verb: identify Learning Objective: The learner will identify the seven parts of a results summary from a description of how each looks, with at least 6 of 7 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Results Summary, Effect Size, Difference of Means (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: In quiz mode the learner clicks the marker that matches a visual hint. A click is correct when it matches the marker named in the Hint column of Content. Mastery is at least 6 of 7 correct on the first attempt. Hovering in explore mode is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A results summary lists only the good news. (2) The limitations belong in a footnote. (3) The decision is separate from the results.

Instructional Rationale: Identifying the parts of a report is a Remember-level task, and a picture of a one-page summary with its parts marked gives each a place. The quiz asks the learner to recognize a part by its look.

Content:

The illustration is a text-free flat drawing of a one-page report. At the top is a banner with a question-mark icon. Below it is a small drawing of two groups of figures joined by an arrow. Next is a grid of 24 small dots. Next is a pair of bars of different heights. Beside the bars is a ruler with one marker on it. Below is a triangle with an exclamation mark. At the bottom is a signpost with two arrows. The seven markers:

# Label Hint (describes the look, not the name) Description Tip 1 Question The banner with the question-mark icon. What the test set out to find out, and the hypothesis. State the hypothesis as it was written before the test. 2 Design The two groups of figures joined by an arrow. The versions, the groups, and the measures. Name the one difference between the groups. 3 Participants The grid of 24 small dots. How many students took part and finished. Report how many were invited, agreed, and finished. 4 Results The pair of bars of different heights. The means and the difference. Report the gain and not only the post-test. 5 Effect size The ruler with one marker on it. How big the difference is. Say which convention you used. 6 Limitations The triangle with an exclamation mark. What the test cannot show. Name the small sample and the bundle of fixes. 7 Decision The signpost with two arrows. What follows from the results. Tie the decision to the hypothesis.

Provenance: The seven parts follow the chapter section "Results Summary". The illustration is synthetic, and the sim labels it "illustrative example".

Rules: Each hint matches exactly one marker. The illustration contains no text, so every label comes from the table above. Markers are numbered 1 to 7 from the top of the page to its bottom.

Learner Activity:

  1. In explore mode the learner hovers or clicks a marker and reads its label, description, and tip.
  2. In quiz mode the sim shows a hint.
  3. The learner clicks the marker they think the hint describes.
  4. If the first click is wrong, the sim says so and lets the learner try once more. If the second click is also wrong, the sim reveals the marker and its description.
  5. After all 7 hints the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 7 hints in a shuffled order, two attempts each. Only a correct first click counts as evidence. Correct: "Correct: [label]. [Description]". First wrong click: "Not quite. Look again at the hint: [hint]". Second wrong click: "This is [label]. [Description]". The summary shows "[n] of 7 correct on the first attempt". At 6 or more it adds "You can read a results summary." Below 6 it lists the labels of the missed parts.

Starting State: The illustration with seven numbered markers, explore mode active, and the prompt "Hover a marker to see a part of the summary."

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's table of seven parts lists the same parts in the same order.

The MicroSim below tests the most important habit of a results summary: claiming no more than the data allow. It shows eight statements about the pilot, and for each one you decide whether the data support it.

docs.title: Diagram: Claim and Data Judge
docs.text:
Claim and Data Judge

Type: microsim sim-id: claim-data-judge Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: judge Learning Objective: The learner will judge whether each of eight statements about the pilot is supported by the data, is an overclaim, or is not shown by this test, with at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Results Summary, Difference of Means, Effect Size, Completion Rate (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each statement the learner commits one of three bins. A placement is correct when it matches the Correct bin column in Content. Mastery is at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the pilot's facts is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A large effect size proves the improved version works everywhere. (2) A test of a bundle shows which fix worked. (3) A test with 24 students can report on subgroups.

Instructional Rationale: Judging a claim against the data is an Evaluate-level action that every results summary needs. Statements that are supported, overreach, or go beyond what was measured teach the learner to tie each claim to a number.

Content:

The three bins: Supported by the data, Overclaim, Not shown by this test. An Overclaim says more than the data allow, usually by generalizing past the students or the conditions tested. A statement that is Not shown by this test concerns something that the test did not measure or could not separate.

The pilot facts, available on demand: 24 students in one class, 12 per group. Mean gains 15.0 (control) and 22.0 (treatment), difference 7.0, effect size 1.03. The hypothesis threshold was 5. Quiz completion was 10 of 12 (control) and 12 of 12 (treatment). Five fixes were tested as a bundle. No subgroup results were collected, and the largest subgroup had 3 students.

The eight statements (all about the made-up Watershed Basics pilot):

# Statement Correct bin Why (shown as feedback) 1 The treatment group's mean learning gain was 7.0 points larger than the control group's. Supported by the data It restates the difference of means. 2 The improved version works for all Grade 6 students. Overclaim The test used 24 students in one class. 3 The result met the 5-point threshold set in the hypothesis. Supported by the data 7.0 >= 5. 4 The simulation caused the larger gain. Not shown by this test Five fixes were tested together, so the test cannot say which one mattered. 5 The effect size was 1.03, which is large by the usual convention. Supported by the data It restates the calculation and the convention. 6 More students finished the quiz with the improved version: 12 of 12 against 10 of 12. Supported by the data It restates the completion counts. 7 Students who use captions benefited most from the improved version. Not shown by this test No subgroup results were collected, and the subgroup had 3 students. 8 A higher rubric score always means more learning. Overclaim One pilot cannot show an "always".

Provenance: The facts and statements are illustrative examples written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples".

Rules: Each statement has exactly one correct bin. Four statements are Supported by the data, two are Overclaim, and two are Not shown by this test.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one statement and the three bins, and may open the pilot facts. Opening them does not change the score.
  2. The learner places the statement in a bin, and the placement is committed.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text.
  4. After statement 8 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 8 statements in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [bin]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. This is [bin]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 8 correct on the first attempt". At 7 or more it adds "You can tie a claim to the data." Below 7 it lists the Why text of each missed statement.

Starting State: The first statement in the shuffled order and the three bins. The question shown is "Does the data support this?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's Limitations part names the small sample, the bundle of fixes, and the lack of subgroup data, and its results come from the same pilot.

docs.title: Rubric-Outcome Correlation
docs.text:
The rubric-outcome correlation is the strength of the relationship between resources' rubric scores and how much students learn from them. This check closes the loop of the whole book. If resources with higher rubric scores tend to produce larger gains, the rubric measures something that matters. If not, the rubric and the automated scores built on it need rethinking.

Compute it across several resources, each tested in a pilot like this one. Because pilots use different tests, compare the normalized gain of Chapter 16. The table pairs seven resources' rubric totals with their mean normalized gains. Two are the original and improved Watershed Basics, taken from the pilot, and five are made-up pilots of resources from earlier chapters.

Resource Rubric total Mean normalized gain Thin Material 37 0.12 Open Unit With Errors 65 0.22 Locked Chemistry E-book 65 0.28 Watershed Basics, original 65 0.33 Watershed Basics, improved 78 0.50 One Gap 85 0.46 Open Algebra 90 0.55

The Pearson correlation of these seven pairs, which is the same statistic as in Chapter 14, is about 0.93. A value close to 1 means that higher totals go with higher gains. The squared value, 0.87, says that a straight line through the totals accounts for about 87 percent of the differences among these seven gains.

Read the result with care. Seven resources are few, so a correlation from them can swing widely. Different teachers taught different classes, and a correlation does not show that raising a rubric score causes more learning. Look also at the three resources that share a total of 65: their gains are 0.22, 0.28, and 0.33. Equal totals do not guarantee equal learning, and the lowest gain belongs to the resource with an Accuracy score of 3, which supports reading the lowest metric before the total. A serious check of the rubric needs 20 or more resources.

The MicroSim below lets you explore the scatter plot of these seven resources.

docs.title: Diagram: Rubric-Outcome Scatter
docs.text:
Rubric-Outcome Scatter

Type: chart sim-id: rubric-outcome-scatter Library: Chart.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: examine Learning Objective: The learner will examine a scatter plot of rubric totals against mean normalized gains for seven resources and answer five questions about the correlation and its limits, with at least 4 of 5 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Rubric-Outcome Correlation, Learning Gain, Score Correlation (defined in this chapter above this block, in Chapter 16, or in Chapter 14).

Evidence of Mastery: The learner answers five questions about the plot. An answer is correct when it matches the Correct answer column in Content. Mastery is at least 4 of 5 correct on the first attempt. Hovering over points and toggling a point off are exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A correlation near 1 shows that raising the rubric score causes learning. (2) Resources with the same rubric total have the same gain. (3) Seven points are enough to settle the question.

Instructional Rationale: Examining a scatter plot against a number is an Analyze-level action that links a picture to a statistic. Points that share a total but differ in gain, and a toggle that removes a point, teach the learner what a correlation can and cannot say.

Content:

The plot, with the rubric total on the horizontal axis and the mean normalized gain on the vertical axis, shows the seven points:

Resource Rubric total Mean normalized gain Thin Material 37 0.12 Open Unit With Errors 65 0.22 Locked Chemistry E-book 65 0.28 Watershed Basics, original 65 0.33 Watershed Basics, improved 78 0.50 One Gap 85 0.46 Open Algebra 90 0.55

The correlation is shown as r and updates when a point is toggled off. With all seven points r is 0.93. With Thin Material toggled off r is 0.92.

The five questions:

# Question Choices Correct answer Why (shown as feedback) 1 What is the correlation r for all seven points? 0.43; 0.93; 1.00 0.93 The plot's statistic is 0.93. 2 Which resource has the lowest gain among the three with a total of 65? Open Unit With Errors; Locked Chemistry E-book; Watershed Basics, original Open Unit With Errors Its gain of 0.22 is the lowest of the three. 3 Does r = 0.93 show that raising a rubric score causes more learning? Yes; No No A correlation does not show cause. 4 With Thin Material toggled off, is r still > 0.9? Yes; No Yes r is 0.92. 5 Are seven resources enough to settle whether the rubric predicts learning? Yes; No No Seven points can swing widely, and 20 or more are needed.

Provenance: The two Watershed Basics values come from the chapter's pilot. The other five values are illustrative examples made up for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The correlation is the Pearson correlation of the seven pairs as displayed.

Rules: r is rounded to two decimal places. Toggling a point off recomputes r from the remaining points. The sim labels the plot "illustrative data".

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner hovers over points to see the resource names and values.
  2. The learner may toggle any point off and see r change. Toggling is not scored.
  3. The learner presses Quiz and answers the five questions.
  4. After question 5 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 5 questions in the order of the table, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [answer]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. The answer is [answer]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 5 correct on the first attempt". At 4 or more it adds "You can read a scatter plot and its limits." Below 4 it lists the Why text of each missed question.

Starting State: The scatter plot with all seven points shown, r displayed as 0.93, and the Quiz button.

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's table of seven resources and its correlation of 0.93 are the data and the statistic of this sim.

docs.title: Pilot Test
docs.text:
A pilot test is a small first run of a test, done to check the procedure and to learn what a larger test would need. The Watershed Basics test was a pilot: one class, 24 students. A pilot is not a weak version of the real test. It has its own jobs:

  • Check the procedure. Did the assignment, the timing, and the data collection work? The pilot found that the original's quiz failed to load for two students.
  • Check the measures. Was the post-test too easy? Three students reached 95 to 98, so the test had little room above them, and harder questions would measure the strongest students better.
  • Estimate the spread and the effect. These guide the size of the larger test.

The estimate leads to a planning rule. Under the usual research standards, the students needed in each group is about 16 divided by d squared, where d is the effect size you want to detect. The rule is an approximation that a statistician should confirm for a real study, and it gives the figures of the Chapter 16 table.

Effect size to detect Students per group 0.8, large 25 0.5, medium 64 0.4 100 0.2, small 400

Do not plan on the pilot's own effect size. Its d of 1.03 would suggest 16 students per group (16 divided by 1.06 is about 15.1, rounded up), which is too optimistic, since pilot estimates tend to be inflated. A safer habit is to plan for about half the pilot's effect, close to 0.5, which calls for about 64 students per group.

The MicroSim below practices the planning rule.

docs.title: Diagram: Pilot Sample Planner
docs.text:
Pilot Sample Planner

Type: microsim sim-id: pilot-sample-planner Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: calculate Learning Objective: The learner will calculate the number of students needed in each group for six effect sizes by the rule of 16 divided by d squared, rounded up, with at least 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Pilot Test, Effect Size, and Sample Size (defined in this chapter above this block or in Chapter 16).

Evidence of Mastery: For each effect size the learner enters the students needed per group. An answer is correct when it matches the Content table. Mastery is at least 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Reading the rule is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A larger effect needs a larger sample. (2) The pilot's effect size is the right one to plan on. (3) Rounding down is acceptable.

Instructional Rationale: Calculating a sample size from an effect size is an Apply-level action. Six effect sizes show that the number grows quickly as the effect shrinks, and the pilot's own value shows why it is a poor planning value.

Content:

The rule, shown at all times: students per group = 16 / d squared, rounded up to a whole number. The rule is labeled "rule of thumb for comparing two group means under the usual research standards".

The six cases:

# Effect size d Students per group Why (shown as feedback) 1 0.80 25 16 divided by 0.64 is 25. 2 0.50 64 16 divided by 0.25 is 64. 3 0.40 100 16 divided by 0.16 is 100. 4 0.20 400 16 divided by 0.04 is 400. 5 0.60 45 16 divided by 0.36 is about 44.4, which rounds up to 45. 6 1.03 16 16 divided by 1.0609 is about 15.1, which rounds up to 16. The sim adds: "Do not plan on a pilot's own effect size."

Provenance: The rule of thumb is labeled as an approximation that a statistician should confirm. The cases are illustrative examples, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". Case 6 is the pilot's effect size.

Rules: The answer is the smallest whole number >= 16 divided by d squared.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one effect size and the rule.
  2. The learner enters the students per group, and the answer is committed.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text.
  4. After case 6 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 6 cases in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [answer] students per group. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. The answer is [answer]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 6 correct on the first attempt". At 5 or more it adds "You can size a larger test." Below 5 it lists the Why text of each missed case.

Starting State: The first case in the shuffled order, the rule, and an empty field.

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's table of effect sizes and group sizes contains cases 1, 2, 3, and 4, and the chapter's planning advice discusses case 6.

docs.title: Equity Consideration
docs.text:
An equity consideration is a check that a resource, and the test of it, work fairly for all the students who might use them. A result that says a version helps "students" on average can hide the fact that it helps some and leaves others out. Equity here includes students who use assistive technology, students learning English, and students without a home device or a fast connection.

Build the check into the test. Confirm before the test that every student can use both versions: captions, readable text, devices that load the content. Include a survey question about barriers, such as the second question in the pilot. Record what the teacher observes. And report with care. Chapter 16 and the section on anonymized data explain why results for groups of fewer than about ten students should not be published. In the pilot, 2 students used captions and 3 were learning English. Those groups are too small to report, so their experience comes from comments and observation and not from subgroup averages.

The pilot found equity differences of a different kind. The original version had no captions and an inaccessible quiz script, and both are barriers for some students. The improvement removed them. A fair summary says so, and it also says that the test could not measure how much those students benefited.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Data collection uses one procedure for both groups and a data dictionary with one row per student. Check the table for missing, out-of-range, repeated, and mislabeled values before analyzing.
  • Anonymized data has no link to a person. Codes are not enough in a small class, so drop columns, generalize, hide small groups, and clean comments.
  • A mean score summarizes a group, and the difference of means answers the hypothesis. Compare gains, report the spread, and remember that a small test can mislead.
  • An effect size puts a difference on a common ruler. Cohen's d is the difference divided by the pooled standard deviation, with 0.2, 0.5, and 0.8 as conventional markers. Small pilots tend to overstate it.
  • A student survey needs neutral, specific, one-idea questions. Completion rate and time on task are read with the learning gain. Qualitative feedback is coded into themes and counted.
  • A results summary has seven parts and claims no more than the data allow.
  • The rubric-outcome correlation checks whether rubric scores predict learning, using normalized gains across many resources. It shows association and not cause, and it needs far more than seven resources.
  • A pilot test checks the procedure and the measures and estimates the size of a larger test. Plan on a smaller effect than the pilot found.
  • An equity consideration checks that both versions work for every student and reports small groups with care.

You Can Read the Evidence

You can now collect and protect test data, compare two groups, size an effect, weigh what students say, and check whether the rubric predicts learning. Next comes the work of packaging and publishing an improved resource, and of training the reviewers who will keep the loop going.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Analyzing A/B Test Results
docs.text: Test your understanding of data collection, anonymized data, means, effect size, surveys, results summaries, pilot tests, and equity with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. What does Cohen's d measure?
docs.text:
1. The probability that the two groups differ by chance alone, given the sample
  2. The share of students who finished the activity out of those who started it
  3. The average of the two groups' post-test scores, taken together as one number
  4. How large a difference is, as the difference of means over the pooled standard deviation
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. An effect size measures the size of a difference in units that do not depend on the test, so that studies can be compared. Cohen's d divides the difference of means by the pooled standard deviation, which combines the spread of the two groups. In the Watershed Basics pilot, a difference of 7.0 points and a pooled standard deviation of about 6.78 give a d of about 1.03. Chance is a different question, and d does not answer it.

Concept Tested: Effect Size

See: Effect Size

docs.title: 2. How is a completion rate calculated?
docs.text:
1. The number of students who started divided by the number who were invited, as a percentage
  2. The minutes of work divided by the intended length of the quiz, as a percentage
  3. The number of students who finished divided by the number who started, as a percentage
  4. The post-test mean divided by the pre-test mean, as a percentage of the class
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. In the pilot, 10 of the 12 control students finished the quiz, a rate of 83 percent, and all 12 treatment students did, a rate of 100 percent. A low rate is a signal to look for the reason. The two control students who did not finish could not make the original quiz load on the school's tablets, which is a barrier and not a lack of interest. The post-test was separate from the quiz, so those students stayed in the analysis.

Concept Tested: Completion Rate

See: Completion Rate

docs.title: 3. How does anonymized data differ from coded data?
docs.text:
1. Coded data keeps a key that can rebuild the link to a person, while anonymized data has no such link
  2. Anonymized data replaces names with codes, while coded data removes them completely from every table in the study
  3. Coded data can never be shared with anyone outside the research team or school
  4. Anonymized data still contains names but hides the scores of each individual student
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Coded data replaces names with codes and keeps a key somewhere, so the link can be rebuilt. Data becomes anonymized when the key is destroyed on the deletion date promised in the consent letter and nothing else in the table points to a person. Codes alone are not always enough: in a class of 24, columns for gender, period, and teacher can single out a student. Ask whether someone who knows the class could pick out one student.

Concept Tested: Anonymized Data

See: Anonymized Data

docs.title: 4. Why does the chapter compare the groups' mean gains and not only their post-test means?
docs.text:
1. Post-test means cannot be expressed in percentage points, so they cannot be compared
  2. Gains are always easier to compute than post-test means, so they save time
  3. Post-test means can never be negative, so they hide a loss in learning
  4. The groups may not start at the same level, and the gain removes any head start
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. In the pilot, the post-test means differ by 7.75 points, but the groups began 0.75 points apart, so the gain removes that head start. The difference of means, treatment minus control, is the single number that answers the hypothesis. Here it is 22.0 minus 15.0, or +7.0 points, above the 5-point bar. In a small test a few unusually strong or weak students can move an average, so the difference may partly be luck.

Concept Tested: Difference of Means

See: Difference of Means

docs.title: 5. A test finds a difference of means of 5.0 points and a pooled standard deviation of 10.0 points. What are Cohen's d and its conventional size?
docs.text:
1. 0.20, small
  2. 0.50, medium
  3. 2.00, large
  4. 0.80, large
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Cohen's d is the difference of means divided by the pooled standard deviation, so 5.0 divided by 10.0 is 0.50. By convention, 0.2 is small, 0.5 is medium, and 0.8 is large. These are rules of thumb, and what matters in practice depends on the cost of the change and the setting. The same 5-point difference would be a larger effect if the scores varied less, which is why the spread is part of the answer.

Concept Tested: Effect Size

See: Effect Size

docs.title: 6. Five control students gained 10, 12, 15, 18, and 20 points. Five treatment students gained 16, 18, 22, 26, and 28 points. What is the difference of means, treatment minus control?
docs.text:
1. +5.0
  2. +6.0
  3. +7.0
  4. +22.0
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The control gains add to 75, so their mean is 75 divided by 5, which is 15.0. The treatment gains add to 110, so their mean is 110 divided by 5, which is 22.0. The difference of means is 22.0 minus 15.0, which is +7.0 points. Option D is the treatment mean alone. A mean hides how scores are spread out, so also report the standard deviation and the median.

Concept Tested: Mean Score

See: Mean Score

docs.title: 7. A pilot finds an effect size of 1.03. A teacher uses the rule of 16 divided by d squared and plans a larger test with 16 students per group. What is wrong with this plan?
docs.text:
1. Pilot effect sizes tend to be inflated, so plan on about half, which calls for about 64 students per group
  2. The rule works only when d is larger than 1.5, so it cannot be used for this pilot or for any other
  3. The pilot's effect size is too small to use for planning, so a larger one is needed from some other study
  4. The rule produces too many students when d is large, so the number must be cut to fit the budget
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Impressive estimates from small tests tend to shrink when repeated with more students, so a pilot's own effect size is too optimistic to plan on. A safer habit is to plan for about half of it, close to 0.5, and 16 divided by 0.25 gives 64 students per group. For comparison, detecting a small effect of 0.2 needs about 400 per group. The rule is an approximation, and a statistician should confirm the numbers for a real study.

Concept Tested: Pilot Test

See: Pilot Test

docs.title: 8. Three resources each have a rubric total of 65, and their mean normalized gains are 0.22, 0.28, and 0.33. The resource with the lowest gain has an Accuracy score of 3. What does this show?
docs.text:
1. The rubric has no relationship with learning, because equal totals gave different gains
  2. Equal totals do not guarantee equal learning, and the pattern supports reading the lowest metric first
  3. Rubric totals cause learning gains, because higher totals went with higher gains
  4. The correlation between totals and gains must be exactly 1 for the rubric to be valid
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Across the seven resources in the chapter's table, the correlation between totals and gains is about 0.93, so higher totals go with higher gains. A correlation does not show cause (C), and it can swing widely with only seven points, so a serious check needs 20 or more resources. The three equal totals with different gains show that a total hides the weakest metric, which is the lesson the chapters on the rubric kept repeating.

Concept Tested: Rubric-Outcome Correlation

See: Rubric-Outcome Correlation

docs.title: 9. A draft results summary for the pilot says, "The simulation caused the larger gain." The pilot tested five fixes together as a bundle. What is the best judgment of this claim?
docs.text:
1. It is supported, because the simulation was the biggest change made to the resource
  2. It is supported, because the effect size was large enough to show which fix mattered
  3. It is supported, because the treatment group's gain was larger than the control group's gain in the pilot
  4. It is not shown by this test, because the fixes arrived together and one cannot be singled out
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. A test of two versions with five fixes tests the bundle. It can say whether the bundle helped students, and it cannot say which fix did the work. To learn that, test one fix at a time, which takes more students and more time. A results summary claims no more than the data allow, so its Limitations part names the small sample, the bundle of fixes, and anything unusual. A large pilot effect size is a reason to test again.

Concept Tested: Results Summary

See: Results Summary

docs.title: 10. A teacher wants to build an equity check into the next test of the improved resource. Which plan best follows the chapter?
docs.text:
1. Report separate averages for the 2 students who used captions and the 3 students learning English
  2. Confirm before the test that all students can use both versions, ask about barriers, and use comments for tiny groups
  3. Assume both versions work for everyone, because students were assigned by chance to each version
  4. Leave out students who use assistive technology so that the two groups stay more similar
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. An equity consideration is a check that the resource, and the test of it, work fairly for all students, including those who use assistive technology, are learning English, or lack a home device or a fast connection. Build the check in before the test, ask about barriers in the survey, and record observations. Groups smaller than about ten students should not be reported as averages, because they can identify students. Excluding students (D) is an equity failure.

Concept Tested: Equity Consideration

See: Equity Consideration

docs.title: References: Analyzing A/B Test Results
docs.text:
1. Effect size - Wikipedia - Explains effect sizes such as Cohen's d, how they are computed, and how to interpret them. Supports the chapter's section on reading the size of a difference, not only whether it exists.

  2. Student's t-test - Wikipedia - Describes the t-test for comparing two group means, its assumptions, and how to read the result. Background for the chapter's comparison of mean scores between groups.

  3. Pearson correlation coefficient - Wikipedia - Defines the correlation coefficient and how to interpret its sign and size. Supports the chapter's check of whether rubric scores track learning outcomes.

  4. Statistical Power Analysis for the Behavioral Sciences (2nd ed.) - Jacob Cohen - Lawrence Erlbaum Associates (1988) - Cohen introduced the standardized difference d and offered 0.2, 0.5, and 0.8 as rough small, medium, and large conventions. He also showed how to plan sample size for them. The source of this chapter's effect size convention.

  5. Understanding the New Statistics: Effect Sizes, Confidence Intervals, and Meta-Analysis - Geoff Cumming - Routledge (2012) - Cumming's estimation approach asks how big the effect is and how uncertain, instead of only whether p is below .05. His "dance of the p values" shows how much results vary between samples.

  6. Using Effect Size—or Why the P Value Is Not Enough - Journal of Graduate Medical Education - Sullivan and Feinn explain why a significant p value says little about how large or useful a difference is. A short, readable argument for reporting effect size.

  7. Interpreting Cohen's d - R Psychologist (Kristoffer Magnusson) - An interactive visualization showing how two overlapping distributions change as Cohen's d grows. Helps teachers picture what a small or medium effect looks like.

  8. Online Statistics Education - Rice University and partners - A free introductory statistics text covering means, t-tests, correlation, and confidence intervals with simulations. Enough background for the basic two-group comparisons in this chapter.

  9. Writing Survey Questions - Pew Research Center - Practical guidance on wording survey questions and answer choices to avoid bias and confusion. Supports the chapter's design of a student survey.

  10. UDL Guidelines - CAST - The Universal Design for Learning guidelines describe how to give learners varied ways to engage, understand, and show what they know. A lens for the chapter's equity consideration.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Shows how to package components, build a library, publish improved OER with MkDocs and GitHub Pages, share through a clearinghouse, track reuse, and report impact. It covers what happens after improvement and testing, and builds on the components, metadata, and results from earlier chapters. After this chapter you can package a reusable component, publish it openly, and track how others reuse it.

docs.text:

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Foundations of Open Educational Resources
  • Chapter 2: Open Licenses and Attribution
  • Chapter 4: Open File Formats and Version Control
  • Chapter 5: Accuracy and Currency
  • Chapter 6: Alignment and Readability
  • Chapter 8: Practice and Feedback
  • Chapter 9: Modularity and Metadata
  • Chapter 10: Portability and Reuse Across Platforms
  • Chapter 15: Improving a Resource with AI Agents
  • Chapter 17: Analyzing A/B Test Results

An Improved Resource Is Only Useful When Others Can Use It

You improved a resource and tested it with students. Now you will package it so other teachers can reuse it, publish it so they can find it, and keep it healthy once it is out. Let's dive in and check the evidence!

A resource that sits on your computer helps one class. The point of an open educational resource is that it can help many, and that only happens if others can find it, understand what they may do with it, and use it without rebuilding it. This chapter covers the work after the improvement and the test: packaging the parts, publishing the whole, and learning what happened next.

The example is the improved Watershed Basics v1.1. After the test of Chapter 17 the teacher decides to release it, so the chapter follows that release from a folder of files to a public site and a report on its use.

docs.title: Reusable Component
docs.text:
A reusable component is a part of a resource that a stranger can lift out and use in a different course without asking for help. Chapter 9 gave the tests: the part stands alone, it embeds without edits, and it carries its own license and metadata. This chapter adds the work of making components available to others.

After the splitting of Chapter 15, Watershed Basics v1.1 has three components.

Component What it is Stands alone because watershed-reading The reading with its images and captions It defines its terms and refers to nothing outside itself watershed-quiz The 8-question quiz with explanations It repeats what it needs and loads its own script watershed-sim The "Where does the rain go?" simulation It has its own page and instructions

docs.title: Component Packaging
docs.text:
Component packaging is the gathering of everything a component needs into one folder that can be copied, downloaded, or embedded as a unit. A package contains the content, a short README that says what the component is and how to use it, a license file, a metadata file, and any images or scripts. All links inside the package should be complete addresses or point to files inside the package, so that nothing breaks when the folder moves, which was the portability problem of Chapter 10.

A package is easiest to understand as a folder with a fixed shape. The listing below shows the quiz package, with the purpose of each file in the table that follows it.

watershed-quiz/
  index.html
  quiz.js
  README.md
  LICENSE.txt
  metadata.json
  img/
File Purpose index.html The quiz page itself quiz.js The script the page needs, kept inside the folder README.md What the component is, how to embed it, and how to credit it LICENSE.txt The license text or a link to it metadata.json The metadata record of Chapter 9 in a form a program can read img/ The images the page uses

docs.title: Component Licensing
docs.text:
Component licensing is the practice of giving each component its own license statement and credit lines, so that a component keeps its terms when it travels alone. A reuser who copies only the quiz must still see that it is CC BY 4.0, who wrote it, and what it adapted. The statement appears in three places: the visible footer of the page, the license file, and the metadata record.

Licenses can interact inside a component. If the quiz includes an image under CC BY-SA, the component as a whole must be shared in a way that satisfies that condition, as Chapter 2 taught. List every third-party item with its title, author, source, and license, and check that the licenses are compatible with the one you choose.

docs.title: Component Discoverability
docs.text:
Component discoverability is how easily the people who need a component can find it. A component that no one can find is not reused. Discoverability comes from a clear descriptive name, a complete metadata record with subject, grade level, and keywords, a short description in plain words, and a place where it is listed: an index page of your own site and a catalog that others search. A name like watershed-quiz tells a visitor what the component is, and a name like final-v2 tells them nothing. A description of one or two sentences that begins with what the component does, such as "An 8-question quiz on how water drains from land", lets a search match it to a teacher's need.

The MicroSim below practices the checks of this section. It shows seven packages, and for each one you decide whether it is ready to publish.

docs.title: Diagram: Component Package Inspector
docs.text:
Component Package Inspector

Type: microsim sim-id: component-package-inspector Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: judge Learning Objective: The learner will judge whether each of seven component packages is ready to publish and name the gap in each package that is not, with at least 6 of 7 verdicts correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Reusable Component, Component Packaging, Component Licensing, Component Discoverability (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each package the learner commits Ready or Not ready, and for a Not ready package picks the gap from five. A verdict is correct when it matches the Correct verdict column in Content, and the gap is checked in the feedback. Mastery is at least 6 of 7 verdicts correct on the first attempt. Reading the package table is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A package with a page and images is complete. (2) The license can be added when someone asks. (3) A package that works on the author's computer works everywhere.

Instructional Rationale: Judging a package against the checks is an Evaluate-level action that precedes every release. Packages that each lack one thing, and two that lack nothing, teach the learner to inspect a package item by item.

Content:

The two verdicts: Ready, Not ready. The five gaps: No license, No metadata, No README, Link outside the folder, Not standalone.

The seven packages (all made up, for Watershed Basics v1.1):

# Package Files and notes Correct verdict Gap Why (shown as feedback) 1 watershed-reading index.html, README.md, LICENSE.txt, metadata.json, img/ with complete image addresses Ready None It has every file and its links work from anywhere. 2 watershed-quiz index.html, README.md, LICENSE.txt, metadata.json, and a script loaded from ../shared/quiz.js Not ready Link outside the folder The script lives outside the folder and will not travel with it. 3 watershed-sim index.html, sim.js, README.md, metadata.json, and no license file or statement Not ready No license A reuser cannot tell what they may do. 4 watershed-glossary index.html, README.md, LICENSE.txt, and no metadata file Not ready No metadata The component cannot be found or described by a catalog. 5 watershed-map map.png, LICENSE.txt, metadata.json, and no README or page Not ready No README Nothing explains what the map is or how to credit it. 6 watershed-unit index.html, README.md, LICENSE.txt, metadata.json, and a page that says "use the quiz in watershed-quiz" Not ready Not standalone It depends on another component. 7 watershed-video index.html, captions.vtt, transcript.md, README.md, LICENSE.txt, metadata.json Ready None It has every file, including captions and a transcript.

Provenance: The packages are illustrative examples written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The gaps follow the chapter sections on packaging, licensing, and discoverability.

Rules: Each package has exactly one correct verdict. Two are Ready and five are Not ready, one for each gap.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one package as a file listing with notes.
  2. The learner chooses Ready or Not ready. If Not ready, the learner also picks the gap.
  3. The sim shows whether the verdict was correct, the gap, and the Why text.
  4. After package 7 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 7 packages in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [verdict]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. This package is [verdict]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 7 correct on the first attempt". At 6 or more it adds "You can inspect a package." Below 6 it lists the Why text of each missed package.

Starting State: The first package in the shuffled order and the two verdicts. The question shown is "Could a stranger use this package as it is?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's file table lists the README, the license file, and the metadata file, and it says links must stay inside the package.

docs.title: Component Library
docs.text:
A component library is an organized collection of reusable components, with an index that lets a visitor see what is there and pick what they need. A library turns a pile of packages into something a teacher can browse. It works best with consistent names, one folder per component, a catalog page, and a release version for the library as a whole.

The catalog is a table with one row per component. The Watershed Basics library lists its three components and a glossary.

Component Description Grade License Version watershed-reading A short reading that explains what a watershed is 6 and 7 CC BY 4.0 1.1 watershed-quiz An 8-question quiz with explanations 6 and 7 CC BY 4.0 1.1 watershed-sim A simulation of rain and ground cover 6 and 7 CC BY 4.0 1.1 watershed-glossary Eleven terms with definitions 6 and 7 CC BY 4.0 1.1

A library also makes upkeep easier, since one maintenance plan and one feedback channel serve every component.

docs.title: Learning Graph
docs.text:
A learning graph is a map of the concepts of a subject in which each concept is linked to the concepts it depends on. It answers the question, "What must a learner know before this?" A learning graph helps reuse because a teacher can place a component in a sequence by checking what it assumes and what it teaches, and an author can order a textbook so that nothing is used before it is explained.

This book has a learning graph of its own, with 351 concepts joined by 586 dependencies. Its longest chain of prerequisites is 24 concepts deep, and it ends at the concept of Rubric-Outcome Correlation from Chapter 17.

docs.title: Concept Dependency
docs.text:
A concept dependency is a link that says one concept needs another first. If a learner cannot understand Re-Scoring without understanding an Improvement Plan, then Re-Scoring depends on Improvement Plan. In this book's graph, each link points from the concept to the concept it depends on, so the arrow reads "needs".

Concept Depends on (examples from this book's graph) Score Gain Re-Scoring Re-Scoring Improvement Plan, Agent Scoring, Total Score Improvement Plan Total Score, Accept Correct or Reject Impact Reporting Reuse Tracking, Usage Analytics, Results Summary

A valid graph has no loops. If A needs B and B needs A, neither can be learned first. Checking for loops, and for concepts used before their prerequisites, is how a graph earns trust.

Read an Arrow as the Word Needs

When an arrow runs from Score Gain to Re-Scoring, it says Score Gain needs Re-Scoring. Learn the concept at the arrow's tip first.

docs.title: Chapter Structure
docs.text: A chapter structure is the division of a textbook's concepts into chapters in an order that respects the dependencies: every concept's prerequisites must appear in the same chapter or an earlier one. A structure that breaks this rule forces the reader to use a term before it is defined. Suppose Chapter 4 needed Re-Scoring, which this book teaches in Chapter 15: the reader would meet the term eleven chapters early. The fix is to move the concept later or to move its prerequisites earlier. A short script can test every dependency against the chapter order, and for this book it checked all 586 dependencies of the 351 concepts and found none placed before a prerequisite.

docs.title: Intelligent Textbook
docs.text:
An intelligent textbook is a textbook built as a website from a learning graph, chapters in dependency order, a glossary, quizzes, and interactive simulations called MicroSims. The learning graph gives it a map of its own contents, and the MicroSims let readers practice. This book is one: its chapters follow the learning graph, its terms are defined before they are used, and its practice activities are specified as MicroSims. The improved Watershed Basics library can be published inside such a book or on its own.

The MicroSim below makes the dependency idea concrete. It shows a piece of this book's graph, and you explore it.

docs.title: Diagram: Learning Graph Explorer
docs.text:
Learning Graph Explorer

Type: graph-model sim-id: learning-graph-explorer Library: vis-network Status: Specified Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: examine Learning Objective: The learner will examine an excerpt of a learning graph and answer five questions about direct and indirect prerequisites and a valid study order, with at least 4 of 5 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Learning Graph, Concept Dependency, Chapter Structure, Intelligent Textbook (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: The learner answers five questions about the graph. An answer is correct when it matches the Correct answer column in Content. Mastery is at least 4 of 5 correct on the first attempt. Clicking nodes to highlight prerequisites is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) An arrow points from a prerequisite to the concept that needs it. (2) Only direct prerequisites matter. (3) Any order that lists all the concepts is a valid study order.

Instructional Rationale: Examining a graph for direct and indirect dependencies is an Analyze-level action. A small graph whose arrows read "needs" lets the learner trace a chain and test a study order.

Content:

The graph is an excerpt of this book's learning graph with ten concepts and ten dependencies. Each dependency is written as concept, then the concept it needs:

Concept Needs Intelligent Textbook Chapter Structure Intelligent Textbook MicroSim Intelligent Textbook Learning Graph Intelligent Textbook Glossary Chapter Structure Learning Graph Chapter Structure Modular Content Learning Graph Learning Outcome Learning Graph Prerequisite Knowledge Glossary Defined Terms Prerequisite Knowledge Scope and Sequence

The reading of an arrow: it points from a concept to the concept it needs.

The five questions:

# Question Choices Correct answer Why (shown as feedback) 1 Which concept needs the most other concepts directly? Learning Graph; Chapter Structure; Intelligent Textbook Intelligent Textbook It needs four concepts directly. 2 Which two concepts does Learning Graph need directly? Learning Outcome and Prerequisite Knowledge; Glossary and MicroSim; Modular Content and Defined Terms Learning Outcome and Prerequisite Knowledge Those are its two outgoing arrows. 3 Does Chapter Structure need Glossary, directly or through a chain? Yes; No No No chain leads from Chapter Structure to Glossary. 4 Which concept is the deepest prerequisite of Learning Graph? Learning Outcome; Prerequisite Knowledge; Scope and Sequence Scope and Sequence Learning Graph needs Prerequisite Knowledge, which needs Scope and Sequence. 5 Which study order respects every dependency? Scope and Sequence, Prerequisite Knowledge, Learning Outcome, Learning Graph; Learning Graph, Learning Outcome, Prerequisite Knowledge, Scope and Sequence; Prerequisite Knowledge, Scope and Sequence, Learning Outcome, Learning Graph Scope and Sequence, Prerequisite Knowledge, Learning Outcome, Learning Graph Each concept comes after everything it needs.

Provenance: The ten concepts and ten dependencies are an excerpt of this book's learning graph, with some of the concepts' other dependencies left out. The sim labels the graph "excerpt of this book's learning graph".

Rules: Each question has exactly one correct answer. Arrows are directed from a concept to the concept it needs. The graph has no loops.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner explores the graph and may click a node to highlight everything that node needs, directly or through a chain. Clicking is not scored.
  2. The learner presses Quiz and answers the five questions.
  3. After question 5 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 5 questions in the order of the table, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [answer]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. The answer is [answer]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 5 correct on the first attempt". At 4 or more it adds "You can read a learning graph." Below 4 it lists the Why text of each missed question.

Starting State: The graph with no node selected and the Quiz button.

Chapter Anchors: The chapter says each link points from a concept to the concept it depends on, and that a valid structure puts every prerequisite in the same chapter or an earlier one.

docs.title: Publishing OER
docs.text:
Publishing OER is the act of making a resource openly available: placed at a stable public address, under an open license, with complete metadata, so that anyone can find it, use it, copy it, and adapt it within the license. Publishing is different from posting a file. A file on a shared drive may be visible and still not be open, because no one knows the license and no one can find it.

Publishing has eight steps, in this order.

  1. Confirm the license. Check that the license of the original allows you to publish the improved version, as Chapter 15 taught.
  2. Finish the metadata for the resource and for each component.
  3. Freeze the tested version. Save it, label it, and write its release notes.
  4. Package each component with its README, license, and metadata.
  5. Build the site from the source files.
  6. Deploy the site to a host that serves it publicly.
  7. Open the feedback channel and publish the maintenance plan, so that readers know where to send problems and what to expect.
  8. List the resource in a clearinghouse and tell colleagues.

Several of these terms are defined in the sections that follow. The first page of a published resource should carry the title, the license with a link, a way to cite it, the version, a link to the source files, and a way to contact the author. A reuser who finds only the page needs all of these without hunting.

docs.title: Static Site Generator
docs.text: A static site generator is a program that turns plain source files, usually Markdown and a few settings, into a folder of finished web pages. The pages are fixed files, not built on demand, so they are fast, cheap to host, and easy to copy. That fits open resources well: the source is plain text that anyone can edit and keep in version control, as Chapter 4 explained, and the built pages work on almost any web host. Well-known generators include MkDocs, Jekyll, and Hugo. The flow is short: you write Markdown pages, the generator applies a theme and a menu from a settings file, and it writes HTML, CSS, and script files that any web server can send as they are. There is no database and no program running on the server, which is why the result is cheap to host and hard to break.

docs.title: MkDocs
docs.text:
MkDocs is a static site generator written in Python and designed for documentation and textbooks. It reads Markdown files and a settings file called mkdocs.yml, which holds the site title, the menu, and the theme, and it writes a complete website. This book is built with MkDocs using the Material theme. Two commands cover most of the work.

Command What it does mkdocs build --strict Builds the site and stops with an error on a broken link or a page missing from the menu mkdocs gh-deploy Builds the site and pushes the finished pages to a branch that GitHub Pages serves

The strict option matters because a published resource with a broken internal link fails the accuracy and portability checks that the rubric applies to everyone else's resources.

docs.title: GitHub Pages
docs.text:
GitHub Pages is a free hosting service of GitHub that serves a static site straight from a repository. After the site is deployed, it appears at an address of the form https://username.github.io/repository/, so the Watershed Basics library might sit at a site such as https://example.github.io/watershed-basics/. The repository that holds the source is public too, which lets anyone read, copy, and propose changes to the files, as Chapter 4's version control allows. GitHub Pages has usage limits and terms that change, so check them for your case.

The two commands in the table are all it takes to publish an update. The first line checks the build, and the second sends it live.

mkdocs build --strict
mkdocs gh-deploy

Run the Strict Build Before Every Deploy

A strict build catches the broken link before your readers do. Make it a habit to run it first, and deploy only when it passes.

docs.title: OER Clearinghouse
docs.text:
An OER clearinghouse is a catalog that lists open resources from many sources and links to each, so that teachers can search in one place. Two well-known examples are OER Commons and MERLOT, and each has its own submission rules and review process. A listing makes a resource more discoverable, and it does not move the resource: your repository stays the source of truth, and the listing points to it. Good metadata is what makes a listing useful, since the catalog searches the subject, grade level, and description you supply.

The poster below shows the path from source files to a reader and to a listing.

docs.title: Diagram: Publishing Pipeline
docs.text:
Publishing Pipeline

Type: infographic sim-id: publishing-pipeline-poster Library: html Status: Specified Bloom Level: Remember Bloom Verb: identify Learning Objective: The learner will identify the six parts of the publishing pipeline from a description of how each looks, with at least 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Publishing OER, Static Site Generator, MkDocs, GitHub Pages, OER Clearinghouse (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: In quiz mode the learner clicks the marker that matches a visual hint. A click is correct when it matches the marker named in the Hint column of Content. Mastery is at least 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Hovering in explore mode is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) The source files and the built site are the same thing. (2) A clearinghouse stores the resource. (3) Deploying and building are the same step.

Instructional Rationale: Identifying the parts of a pipeline is a Remember-level task, and a left-to-right picture of the whole path gives each part a place. The quiz asks the learner to recognize a part by its look.

Content:

The illustration is a text-free flat drawing read from left to right. At the left is a folder of plain text pages. An arrow leads to a gear. Another arrow leads from the gear to a folder of web pages with a frame around each. Next is a box with a branching line inside it. Beyond it is a globe on a stand. Above the globe, a separate card in a filing drawer points down to the globe with a thin line. The six markers:

# Label Hint (describes the look, not the name) Description Tip 1 Source files The folder of plain text pages at the left. The Markdown pages and settings that you write and edit. Keep the source in version control. 2 Build The gear between the two folders. A static site generator, like MkDocs, turns the source into web pages. Run the strict build first. 3 Built site The folder of web pages with a frame around each. The finished pages that a browser can show. Do not edit these by hand. 4 Repository The box with the branching line inside it. The public home of the files, with their history. Make the repository public and add the license. 5 Hosting The globe on a stand. A hosting service like GitHub Pages serves the built site at a public address. Share the stable address. 6 Clearinghouse listing The card in the filing drawer with a thin line to the globe. A catalog entry that points to the published site. The listing links to your site, and your site stays the source.

Provenance: The six parts follow the chapter sections "Publishing OER", "Static Site Generator", "MkDocs", "GitHub Pages", and "OER Clearinghouse". The illustration is synthetic, and the sim labels it "illustrative example".

Rules: Each hint matches exactly one marker. The illustration contains no text, so every label comes from the table above. Markers are numbered 1 to 6 from left to right.

Learner Activity:

  1. In explore mode the learner hovers or clicks a marker and reads its label, description, and tip.
  2. In quiz mode the sim shows a hint.
  3. The learner clicks the marker they think the hint describes.
  4. If the first click is wrong, the sim says so and lets the learner try once more. If the second click is also wrong, the sim reveals the marker and its description.
  5. After all 6 hints the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 6 hints in a shuffled order, two attempts each. Only a correct first click counts as evidence. Correct: "Correct: [label]. [Description]". First wrong click: "Not quite. Look again at the hint: [hint]". Second wrong click: "This is [label]. [Description]". The summary shows "[n] of 6 correct on the first attempt". At 5 or more it adds "You can follow the path to publication." Below 5 it lists the labels of the missed parts.

Starting State: The illustration with six numbered markers, explore mode active, and the prompt "Hover a marker to see a part of the pipeline."

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's eight publishing steps and its sections on the generator, MkDocs, GitHub Pages, and the clearinghouse describe these six parts.

docs.title: Release Notes
docs.text:
Release notes are a short, readable summary of what changed in each released version. They tell reusers whether to update and what to expect. Group the changes under four headings: Added, Changed, Fixed, and Removed. The change log of Chapter 4 and the change log entries of Chapter 15 are the raw material: the release notes are the condensed version for readers who will not read every entry.

Number each release so that people can refer to it. Watershed Basics v1.1 follows v1, and a later correction might be v1.1.1.

The MicroSim below practices the grouping. It shows ten changes, and for each one you choose the heading.

docs.title: Diagram: Release Note Sorter
docs.text:
Release Note Sorter

Type: microsim sim-id: release-note-sorter Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: classify Learning Objective: The learner will classify each of ten changes under Added, Changed, Fixed, or Removed, with at least 9 of 10 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Release Notes (defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each change the learner commits one of four headings. A placement is correct when it matches the Correct heading column in Content. Mastery is at least 9 of 10 correct on the first attempt. Reading the four headings is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Every edit is a fix. (2) A change that improves a feature is an addition. (3) Removing outdated content is not worth mentioning.

Instructional Rationale: Classifying changes under headings is an Understand-level action that turns a log into readable notes. Ten changes spread over four headings teach the learner the dividing lines.

Content:

The four headings and their meanings: Added (something new), Changed (something that existed now works or reads differently), Fixed (an error or a defect was corrected), Removed (something was taken out).

The ten changes (all made up, for Watershed Basics v1.1):

# Change Correct heading Why (shown as feedback) 1 Added captions to the lesson video. Added Captions are new. 2 Added a simulation of rain and ground cover. Added The simulation is new. 3 Updated the river length from 410 to 398 miles. Changed An existing fact now reads differently. 4 Replaced two broken links. Fixed The links were defects. 5 Split the quiz into its own component. Changed An existing part is organized differently. 6 Corrected the heading that skipped from level 2 to level 4. Fixed The heading order was a defect. 7 Removed the outdated 2019 rainfall chart. Removed Something was taken out. 8 Added a glossary entry for "aquifer". Added The entry is new. 9 Corrected the quiz script path so the quiz loads on tablets. Fixed The path was a defect. 10 Rewrote the introduction at a lower reading level. Changed An existing paragraph now reads differently.

Provenance: The changes are illustrative examples written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The headings follow the chapter section "Release Notes".

Rules: Each change has exactly one correct heading. Added, Changed, and Fixed hold three changes each, and Removed holds one.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one change and the four headings.
  2. The learner places the change under a heading, and the placement is committed.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text.
  4. After change 10 the sim shows the summary and the finished release notes.

Feedback: 10 changes in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [heading]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. This change is [heading]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 10 correct on the first attempt". At 9 or more it adds "You can write release notes." Below 9 it lists the Why text of each missed change.

Starting State: The first change in the shuffled order and the four headings. The question shown is "Under which heading does this change belong?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter names the four headings Added, Changed, Fixed, and Removed, and its example release is Watershed Basics v1.1.

docs.title: Maintenance Plan
docs.text:
A maintenance plan is a written commitment about how a published resource will be kept in good condition: who is responsible, what is checked, how often, and when the resource will be retired. Without one, a resource drifts out of date, and a reuser cannot tell whether it is still safe to trust. The outdated content and broken links of Chapter 5 are exactly the problems a plan prevents.

Task How often Owner Run the link checker Every three months The author Check facts that can change, such as figures and dates Once a year The author Run the accessibility scan Once a year and after any large change The author Review open issues and decide what goes in the next release Every release The author Decide whether to retire the resource and post a notice Once a year The author

Retiring is part of maintaining. A resource that nobody can keep accurate is better marked as archived, with a note on its first page, than left to mislead.

docs.title: Issue Tracking
docs.text:
Issue tracking is the practice of recording every reported problem or request in one list, with a status, so that none is lost and each is decided. GitHub provides this with Issues, attached to the repository. Each issue has a title, a description, a label such as bug, content error, accessibility, or request, and a status of open or closed. The list tells you what to fix, what to schedule, and what to decline, and the closed issues form a record of how the resource improved.

The MicroSim below practices the decision. It shows eight reports, and for each one you decide what to do.

docs.title: Diagram: Issue Triage Sorter
docs.text:
Issue Triage Sorter

Type: microsim sim-id: issue-triage-sorter Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: prioritize Learning Objective: The learner will prioritize eight incoming reports by sorting each into Fix in the next patch, Schedule for a later release, Answer and close, or Decline politely, with at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Issue Tracking, Maintenance Plan, Release Notes, Accept Correct or Reject (all defined in this chapter above this block or in Chapter 14).

Evidence of Mastery: For each report the learner commits one of four decisions. A placement is correct when it matches the Correct decision column in Content. Mastery is at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the four decisions is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Every request must be done. (2) A reader can ask the author to remove a required credit. (3) A question needs a code change.

Instructional Rationale: Prioritizing incoming reports is an Evaluate-level action that maintainers repeat. Reports that range from an urgent defect to a request that conflicts with the license teach the learner to match the response to the kind of report.

Content:

The four decisions and their meanings: Fix in the next patch (a defect that harms accuracy, access, or function, to be verified and corrected soon), Schedule for a later release (a worthwhile improvement), Answer and close (a question that the documentation or license already answers), Decline politely (a request that conflicts with the license, the purpose, or the evidence).

The eight reports (all made up, for Watershed Basics v1.1):

# Report Correct decision Why (shown as feedback) 1 The quiz does not load on my school's tablets. Fix in the next patch It stops learners from using the quiz. 2 Section 2 says the river is 398 miles but my atlas says 392. Fix in the next patch An accuracy report should be verified at the source and corrected if right. 3 Can I use this in my paid online course? Answer and close CC BY 4.0 allows it with credit. 4 Please add a Spanish version. Schedule for a later release It is a worthwhile improvement and a larger piece of work. 5 Please remove the credit line; it looks cluttered. Decline politely The license requires credit. 6 The captions say "a quiver" where the video says "aquifer". Fix in the next patch A caption error changes meaning. 7 How do I embed the simulation in my learning platform? Answer and close The README explains embedding. 8 Please add a section on desert watersheds. Schedule for a later release It is a worthwhile addition for a later release.

Provenance: The reports are illustrative examples written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The decisions follow the chapter sections "Issue Tracking" and "Maintenance Plan".

Rules: Each report has exactly one correct decision. Three are Fix in the next patch, two are Schedule for a later release, two are Answer and close, and one is Decline politely.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one report and the four decisions.
