  2. The learner places the report under a decision, and the placement is committed.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text.
  4. After report 8 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 8 reports in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [decision]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. The decision is [decision]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 8 correct on the first attempt". At 7 or more it adds "You can triage reports." Below 7 it lists the Why text of each missed report.

Starting State: The first report in the shuffled order and the four decisions. The question shown is "What should the maintainer do with this report?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter says an issue list tells the maintainer what to fix, what to schedule, and what to decline. The sim adds a category for questions that the documentation already answers.

docs.title: Feedback Channel
docs.text:
A feedback channel is the way readers tell you about problems and ideas. Provide at least one that is easy to find, put the link on every page, and say what response to expect. Good options are the repository's issue tracker for people who use GitHub, and a plain email address or a short form for those who do not. Offer more than one, since a channel that needs an account excludes teachers who have none. Ask only for what you need, never for student information, and say how long you take to reply. A channel that is promised and then ignored is worse than none.

Never Ask for Student Information in a Feedback Form

A teacher or a student may mention a name or a score in a message. Tell people not to, and delete any that arrive.

docs.title: Community Contribution
docs.text:
A community contribution is a change that someone else proposes to your resource. On GitHub this is a pull request: the contributor copies the repository, makes a change, and asks you to adopt it. Contributions are one of the great benefits of open resources, since readers fix errors, translate, and adapt for new settings. They also carry risk, so apply the same review as your own agent's changes. Check that the change keeps the meaning or is a labeled correction, that it carries a compatible license, that third-party material is credited, and that it does not collect personal data. A short contribution guide on your site, saying that contributors agree to share under the same license, keeps the exchange clear. Credit contributors in the release notes.

The MicroSim below practices the review. It shows eight proposed contributions, and for each one you decide what to do.

docs.title: Diagram: Contribution Checker
docs.text:
Contribution Checker

Type: microsim sim-id: contribution-checker Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: judge Learning Objective: The learner will judge whether each of eight proposed contributions should be accepted, sent back for changes, or declined, with at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Community Contribution, Preserving Original Meaning, Human Review of Changes, Component Licensing (defined in this chapter above this block or in Chapter 15).

Evidence of Mastery: For each contribution the learner commits one of three decisions. A decision is correct when it matches the Correct decision column in Content. Mastery is at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the review checks is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Any free contribution should be accepted. (2) A contribution that is almost right is declined. (3) A contributor can keep all rights in a change to an open resource.

Instructional Rationale: Judging a contribution against the review checks is an Evaluate-level action. Contributions that are sound, need a fix, or cannot be accepted teach the learner to check meaning, license, credit, and privacy.

Content:

The three decisions: Accept, Ask for changes first, Decline.

The review checks, available on demand: the meaning is kept or the change is a labeled correction; the license is compatible; third-party material is credited; no personal data is collected.

The eight contributions (all made up, for Watershed Basics v1.1):

# Proposed contribution Correct decision Why (shown as feedback) 1 Fixes a typo in section 3. Accept It is a small correction that keeps the meaning. 2 Adds a Spanish translation, credits the original, uses CC BY 4.0, and includes a note from a bilingual teacher who checked it. Accept The meaning is checked and the license and credit are right. 3 Replaces a figure with an image copied from a website, with no license information. Ask for changes first The contributor must show the license or use another image. 4 Changes "about 6,000" to "more than 6,000" with no source. Ask for changes first It changes the meaning, so it needs a source. 5 Adds tracking code that sends each student's name to an outside service. Decline It collects personal student data. 6 Rewrites the quiz and removes all the explanations to make it shorter. Decline It removes a feature the test found helpful. 7 Offers a change that the contributor says is "all rights reserved". Decline It is not compatible with the resource's open license. 8 Adds alt text to two images that had none, checked against the images. Accept It improves access and keeps the meaning.

Provenance: The contributions are illustrative examples written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The checks follow the chapter section "Community Contribution" and Chapter 15.

Rules: Each contribution has exactly one correct decision. Three are Accept, two are Ask for changes first, and three are Decline.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one contribution and the three decisions, and may open the review checks. Opening them does not change the score.
  2. The learner places the contribution under a decision, and the placement is committed.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text.
  4. After contribution 8 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 8 contributions in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [decision]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. The decision is [decision]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 8 correct on the first attempt". At 7 or more it adds "You can review a contribution." Below 7 it lists the Why text of each missed contribution.

Starting State: The first contribution in the shuffled order and the three decisions. The question shown is "Should this be adopted?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter lists four review checks for a contribution: meaning, license, credit, and personal data.

The MicroSim below ties the publishing steps together. It gives eight steps in a scrambled order, and you put them in sequence.

docs.title: Diagram: Publishing Steps Sorter
docs.text:
Publishing Steps Sorter

Type: microsim sim-id: publishing-steps-sorter Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: apply Learning Objective: The learner will apply the publishing workflow by placing eight steps in the correct order, with at least 7 of 8 steps in the correct position on the first commit.

Prerequisites: Publishing OER, Component Packaging, Static Site Generator, GitHub Pages, OER Clearinghouse, Release Notes, Maintenance Plan, Feedback Channel (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: The learner arranges the eight steps and commits the order once. A step is correct when it is in its position in the Content table. Mastery is at least 7 of 8 steps in the correct position on the first commit. Rearranging before the commit is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Listing in a clearinghouse comes first because it brings visitors. (2) The license check can wait until the site is built. (3) The feedback channel can open after the announcement.

Instructional Rationale: Ordering the steps of a workflow is an Apply-level action that tests whether the learner understands why each step comes where it does. Dependencies between steps, like license before building and feedback before announcing, make the order matter.

Content:

The eight steps in their correct order:

Position Step Why it comes here (shown as feedback) 1 Confirm that the license allows publishing the improved version Nothing else matters if the license forbids it. 2 Finish the metadata for the resource and each component The build and the listing use it. 3 Freeze the tested version, tag it, and write its release notes The released version must not change after testing. 4 Package each component Packages are built from the frozen version. 5 Build the site with the static site generator The build uses the packages and the metadata. 6 Deploy the site to the host Only a built site can be deployed. 7 Open the feedback channel and publish the maintenance plan Readers need a way to report problems before they arrive. 8 List the resource in a clearinghouse and announce it Announce only when everything else is ready.

Provenance: The order follows the chapter section "Publishing OER". The steps are labeled "recommended order" in the sim.

Rules: The sim presents the eight steps in a shuffled order and the learner arranges them. Each position has exactly one correct step.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees the eight steps in a scrambled order.
  2. The learner drags the steps into the order they think is right, and may rearrange them freely.
  3. The learner presses Commit.
  4. The sim marks each step correct or misplaced, and shows the Why text for the misplaced ones.

Feedback: One commit counts as evidence. The sim shows "[n] of 8 steps in the correct position". At 7 or more it adds "You can plan a release." Below 7 it lists the correct order with the Why text of each misplaced step.

Starting State: The eight steps in a shuffled order and the Commit button.

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's eight numbered publishing steps are the order used in this sim.

docs.title: Reuse Tracking
docs.text:
Reuse tracking is the effort to learn who is using your resource, and how. An open license lets people reuse without asking or telling you, so you will see only part of the picture. Several signals help, and they differ in strength.

  • Strong: a course page that links to your component and credits you, a copy (a fork) of your repository with changes, and a message from a teacher who describes using it.
  • Weak: downloads, page views, and a star on your repository show interest and not use.
  • Not evidence: your own visits, and automated crawlers that load pages without a reader.

Search for the title of your resource and the text of your attribution line, since a reuser who followed the license will have written them. Keep a simple table of reuses you learn about, with the date, who, and how. Respect privacy: track the reuse of the resource, not the identity of students.

The MicroSim below practices judging signals.

docs.title: Diagram: Reuse Evidence Sorter
docs.text:
Reuse Evidence Sorter

Type: microsim sim-id: reuse-evidence-sorter Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: assess Learning Objective: The learner will assess eight signals as strong evidence of reuse, weak evidence, or not evidence of reuse, with at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Reuse Tracking, Derivative Work, Component Licensing (defined in this chapter above this block or in Chapter 15).

Evidence of Mastery: For each signal the learner commits one of three bins. A placement is correct when it matches the Correct bin column in Content. Mastery is at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the three strengths is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Page views measure reuse. (2) A star on a repository is a use. (3) All visits come from readers.

Instructional Rationale: Assessing the strength of evidence is an Evaluate-level action. Signals that show use, interest, and nothing at all teach the learner not to count every number as impact.

Content:

The three bins: Strong evidence of reuse, Weak evidence, Not evidence of reuse.

The eight signals (all made up, for Watershed Basics v1.1):

# Signal Correct bin Why (shown as feedback) 1 A teacher's course page embeds your simulation and credits you. Strong evidence of reuse Someone is using it and has credited it. 2 Someone copied your repository and changed the quiz. Strong evidence of reuse A copy with changes is an adaptation. 3 An email says, "I used your reading with my class and added two questions." Strong evidence of reuse A user describes using and adapting it. 4 The clearinghouse listing shows 300 downloads. Weak evidence A download shows interest and not use. 5 The site had 1,200 page views last month. Weak evidence A view shows a visit and not reuse. 6 Three people starred your repository. Weak evidence A star shows interest. 7 Your own computer opened the site 40 times while you tested it. Not evidence of reuse The visits are yours. 8 Traffic spiked when automated crawlers scanned the site. Not evidence of reuse No reader was involved.

Provenance: The signals are illustrative examples written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The strengths follow the chapter section "Reuse Tracking".

Rules: Each signal has exactly one correct bin. Three signals are Strong evidence of reuse, three are Weak evidence, and two are Not evidence of reuse.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one signal and the three bins.
  2. The learner places the signal in a bin, and the placement is committed.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text.
  4. After signal 8 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 8 signals in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [bin]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. This is [bin]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 8 correct on the first attempt". At 7 or more it adds "You can weigh signs of reuse." Below 7 it lists the Why text of each missed signal.

Starting State: The first signal in the shuffled order and the three bins. The question shown is "Does this show that someone reused the resource?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter lists strong signals, weak signals, and non-evidence.

docs.title: Usage Analytics
docs.text:
Usage analytics are counts of how a site is used: visits, pages viewed, where visitors come from, and which components are opened most. They show reach and patterns, and they help plan: a component that no one opens may need to be easier to find. Choose a tool that records counts and not individuals, and tell visitors what you collect. For a site used by students, do not collect personal data, as Chapter 16 advised.

Analytics also mislead easily. A page view is not a reader, a reader is not a learner, and a drop in visits in the school holidays reflects the calendar and not the quality of the resource. Always read the counts alongside the calendar and next to the learning evidence of Chapter 17.

The chart below shows six months of page views for the three components, with each month's total. Use it to practice reading analytics with care.

docs.title: Diagram: Usage Analytics Reader
docs.text:
Usage Analytics Reader

Type: chart sim-id: usage-analytics-reader Library: Chart.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: examine Learning Objective: The learner will examine a chart of monthly page views for three components and answer five questions about totals, trends, and what the counts do and do not show, with at least 4 of 5 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Usage Analytics, Reuse Tracking (defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: The learner answers five questions about the chart. An answer is correct when it matches the Correct answer column in Content. Mastery is at least 4 of 5 correct on the first attempt. Hovering over bars and toggling a component are exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Page views show that students learned. (2) A drop in views means the resource got worse. (3) The most viewed component is the best one.

Instructional Rationale: Examining a chart with a calendar effect is an Analyze-level action. A chart with a holiday dip and one dominant component teaches the learner to separate the pattern from its causes.

Content:

The data, shown as a grouped bar chart with months on the horizontal axis and page views on the vertical axis (made up, for the Watershed Basics components over six school months):

Month Reading Quiz Simulation Month total September 180 120 60 360 October 420 300 210 930 November 380 290 270 940 December 150 100 90 340 January 90 60 40 190 February 310 240 190 740 Six-month total 1,530 1,110 860 3,500

The five questions:

# Question Choices Correct answer Why (shown as feedback) 1 Which component had the most page views over the six months? Reading; Quiz; Simulation Reading It had 1,530 views. 2 Which month had the highest total? October; November; February November Its total is 940. 3 What most likely explains the low December and January totals? The resource got worse; The school calendar; A broken link The school calendar Holidays reduce visits for every component. 4 Do these page views show that students learned? Yes; No No A view is not a reader, and a reader is not a learner. 5 What share of all views went to the simulation, to the nearest percent? 25 percent; 33 percent; 45 percent 25 percent 860 divided by 3,500 is about 24.6 percent, which rounds to 25.

Provenance: The page views are illustrative examples made up for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative data".

Rules: Month totals and the six-month totals are the sums of the values shown. Percentages are rounded to the nearest whole percent.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner hovers over bars to see exact values, and may toggle a component on or off. Toggling is not scored.
  2. The learner presses Quiz and answers the five questions.
  3. After question 5 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 5 questions in the order of the table, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [answer]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. The answer is [answer]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 5 correct on the first attempt". At 4 or more it adds "You can read analytics with care." Below 4 it lists the Why text of each missed question.

Starting State: The chart with all three components shown and the Quiz button.

Chapter Anchors: The chapter says a page view is not a reader, a reader is not a learner, and holiday drops reflect the calendar.

docs.title: Impact Reporting
docs.text:
Impact reporting is the honest account, to the people who care, of what a published resource has done. It draws on four kinds of evidence from this book: the reach from usage analytics, the reuse from reuse tracking, the learning from the A/B test of Chapters 16 and 17, and the experience from surveys, comments, and the issue list. A good report keeps the kinds apart, says how strong each is, and does not claim learning on the strength of page views.

A short report has the same bones as the results summary of Chapter 17: a question, the evidence, the limits, and the decision. For Watershed Basics v1.1 it might say that the library was viewed about 3,500 times in six months, was reused by at least three teachers, produced a learning gain of 22.0 points against 15.0 for the original in a pilot of 24 students, and received 11 issues, of which 7 were fixed. The report would add that the pilot was small, that page views do not measure learning, and that a larger test is planned.

The MicroSim below practices the key skill, which is matching each question to the evidence that can answer it.

docs.title: Diagram: Impact Evidence Matcher
docs.text:
Impact Evidence Matcher

Type: microsim sim-id: impact-evidence-matcher Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: classify Learning Objective: The learner will classify each of eight impact questions under the source of evidence that can answer it, with at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Impact Reporting, Usage Analytics, Reuse Tracking, Issue Tracking, Feedback Channel (all defined in this chapter above this block), and the A/B test of Chapter 16.

Evidence of Mastery: For each question the learner commits one of five sources. A placement is correct when it matches the Correct source column in Content. Mastery is at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the source descriptions is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Page views can answer a question about learning. (2) One source answers every question. (3) The issue list only records complaints.

Instructional Rationale: Matching a question to its evidence source is an Understand-level action that stops a report from answering a question with the wrong data. Eight questions across five sources teach the learner what each source can and cannot say.

Content:

The five sources: Usage analytics, Reuse tracking, A/B test, Survey and feedback, Issue tracker.

The eight questions (all about Watershed Basics v1.1):

# Question Correct source Why (shown as feedback) 1 How many people visited the quiz page last month? Usage analytics Visits are counted by analytics. 2 Did another teacher adapt the simulation for their class? Reuse tracking Adaptation is a sign of reuse. 3 Did students who used the improved version learn more? A/B test Only a comparison of groups can answer it. 4 What do students say about the captions? Survey and feedback It asks for opinions in students' own words. 5 How many accuracy errors were reported and fixed this year? Issue tracker Reports and their status are recorded there. 6 Which component is opened most? Usage analytics Page views by component come from analytics. 7 Which other course sites link to the reading? Reuse tracking Links with credit are a sign of reuse. 8 By how much did mean learning gain differ between the versions? A/B test The difference of means comes from the test.

Provenance: The questions are illustrative examples written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The sources follow the chapter sections "Usage Analytics", "Reuse Tracking", "Issue Tracking", and "Impact Reporting" and Chapters 16 and 17.

Rules: Each question has exactly one correct source. Usage analytics, Reuse tracking, and A/B test hold two questions each. Survey and feedback and Issue tracker hold one each.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one question and the five sources, and may open the source descriptions. Opening them does not change the score.
  2. The learner places the question under a source, and the placement is committed.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text.
  4. After question 8 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 8 questions in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [source]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. This question is answered by [source]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 8 correct on the first attempt". At 7 or more it adds "You can match a question to its evidence." Below 7 it lists the Why text of each missed question.

Starting State: The first question in the shuffled order and the five sources. The question shown is "Which source can answer this?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter names four kinds of evidence for an impact report: reach, reuse, learning, and experience.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• A reusable component stands alone, embeds without edits, and carries its own license and metadata. Component packaging gathers its content, README, license file, and metadata in one folder with links that stay inside it.
  • Component licensing keeps each component's terms with it, and component discoverability depends on a clear name, complete metadata, and a listing. A component library organizes components with a catalog.
  • A learning graph links each concept to the concepts it needs, and a concept dependency reads as "needs". A chapter structure puts every prerequisite in the same chapter or an earlier one, and an intelligent textbook is built on that structure.
  • Publishing OER puts a resource at a stable public address under an open license with complete metadata. Confirm the license, finish the metadata, freeze the tested version, package, build, deploy, open the feedback channel, then list and announce.
  • A static site generator such as MkDocs turns Markdown into pages, and GitHub Pages hosts them. Run mkdocs build --strict before mkdocs gh-deploy. An OER clearinghouse lists your resource and points to your site.
  • Release notes group changes as added, changed, fixed, and removed. A maintenance plan says who checks what and when. Issue tracking records each report and decision, a feedback channel invites reports, and a community contribution gets the same review as any change.
  • Reuse tracking weighs strong signals above weak ones, and usage analytics show reach and not learning. Impact reporting keeps reach, reuse, learning, and experience apart and claims no more than the evidence shows.

You Can Share What You Built

You can now package a component, publish it with MkDocs and GitHub Pages, keep it healthy, and report honestly on what it does. The last chapter turns to the people: how to train and certify the reviewers who keep the whole loop running.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Reusable Components and Publishing OER
docs.text: Test your understanding of packaging, learning graphs, publishing with MkDocs and GitHub Pages, maintenance, reuse tracking, and impact reporting with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. Besides its content and any images or scripts, which files does a packaged reusable component contain?
docs.text:
1. A README, a license file, and a metadata file
  2. A grade book, a rubric, and an answer key
  3. A change log, a class roster, and a consent letter
  4. A build script, a database, and a login page
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Component packaging gathers everything a component needs into one folder that can be copied, downloaded, or embedded as a unit. The README says what the component is, how to embed it, and how to credit it. The license file states the terms, and the metadata file holds the record from Chapter 9 in a form a program can read. All links inside the package should be complete addresses or point to files inside it.

Concept Tested: Component Packaging

See: Component Packaging

docs.title: 2. What does the command mkdocs build --strict do?
docs.text:
1. It builds the site and pushes the finished pages to the branch that GitHub Pages serves
  2. It deploys the site without building it first, so broken links go unnoticed
  3. It builds the site and stops with an error on a broken link or a page missing from the menu
  4. It deletes every page that is not listed in the menu, which removes unlinked files
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. MkDocs is a static site generator that reads Markdown files and a settings file called mkdocs.yml and writes a complete website. The strict option turns a broken internal link into an error, which matters because a published resource with a broken link would fail the accuracy and portability checks the rubric applies to everyone else's resources. Option A describes mkdocs gh-deploy. Run the strict build first and deploy only when it passes.

Concept Tested: MkDocs

See: MkDocs

docs.title: 3. In this book's learning graph, an arrow runs from Score Gain to Re-Scoring. How should the arrow be read?
docs.text:
1. Re-Scoring needs Score Gain, so Score Gain should be learned first
  2. Score Gain needs Re-Scoring, so Re-Scoring should be learned first
  3. Score Gain and Re-Scoring are two names for the same concept
  4. Score Gain is optional, and Re-Scoring is required
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. A concept dependency is a link saying one concept needs another first, and in this book's graph each arrow points from the concept to the concept it depends on, so the arrow reads "needs." Learn the concept at the arrow's tip first. A valid graph has no loops: if A needs B and B needs A, neither could be learned first. A chapter structure then puts every prerequisite in the same chapter or an earlier one.

Concept Tested: Concept Dependency

See: Concept Dependency

docs.title: 4. Why does a listing in an OER clearinghouse not replace the resource's own repository and site?
docs.text:
1. Clearinghouses reject resources that carry open licenses, so a listing is not possible
  2. A listing stores a frozen copy of the resource that can never be updated later
  3. Clearinghouses require every visitor to log in before they can view a listing
  4. A listing only points to the resource, so the repository and site stay the source of truth
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. An OER clearinghouse, such as OER Commons or MERLOT, is a catalog that lists open resources from many sources and links to each so that teachers can search in one place. A listing makes a resource more discoverable and does not move it. The catalog searches the subject, grade level, and description you supply, so good metadata is what makes a listing useful. List the resource last, once everything else is ready.

Concept Tested: OER Clearinghouse

See: OER Clearinghouse

docs.title: 5. For one release of Watershed Basics, the author removes an outdated 2019 rainfall chart, adds a glossary entry for "aquifer," corrects a quiz script path so the quiz loads on tablets, and updates the river length from 410 to 398 miles. Under which headings do these four changes go, in that order?
docs.text:
1. Added, Removed, Changed, Fixed
  2. Removed, Changed, Added, Fixed
  3. Removed, Added, Fixed, Changed
  4. Changed, Added, Fixed, Removed
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Release notes group changes under four headings. Added covers something new, such as the glossary entry. Changed covers something that existed and now reads differently, such as the updated river length. Fixed covers a corrected defect, such as the broken script path. Removed covers something taken out, such as the outdated chart. The change log entries are the raw material, and the release notes are the condensed version for readers who will not read every entry.

Concept Tested: Release Notes

See: Release Notes

docs.title: 6. A reader writes, "Please remove the credit line; it looks cluttered." How should the maintainer respond?
docs.text:
1. Fix it in the next patch, because a cluttered page counts as a defect
  2. Schedule it for a later release, together with other requests about the page design
  3. Decline politely, because the license requires credit to be given to the creator
  4. Answer and close by pointing to the README, which already explains the credit line
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Issue tracking records every report with a status so that each is decided. A request that conflicts with the license, the purpose, or the evidence is declined politely. CC BY 4.0 requires credit to the creator, so the maintainer cannot remove the line. Defects that harm accuracy, access, or function are fixed soon, worthwhile improvements are scheduled, and questions the documentation already answers are answered and closed.

Concept Tested: Issue Tracking

See: Issue Tracking

docs.title: 7. A contributor proposes changing "about 6,000 square miles" to "more than 6,000 square miles" and gives no source. What should the maintainer do?
docs.text:
1. Accept it, because it is a very small change that most readers will not notice
  2. Decline it permanently, because contributors may not change figures
  3. Accept it and thank the contributor in the release notes for the careful correction
  4. Ask for changes first, because the edit alters the meaning and needs a source
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. A community contribution gets the same review as the author's own changes. The review checks that the meaning is kept or the change is a labeled correction, that the license is compatible, that third-party material is credited, and that no personal data is collected. Changing "about" to "more than" is a changed quantity, so it needs a source before it is accepted. Decline is for contributions that cannot be fixed, such as one that collects student names.

Concept Tested: Community Contribution

See: Community Contribution

docs.title: 8. Page views for all three components of a resource fall sharply in December and January. Which analysis is best?
docs.text:
1. The pattern fits the school calendar, since holidays cut visits to every component
  2. The drop shows that students stopped learning from the resource over the holidays
  3. The drop shows that the simulation is the weakest component, because it fell the furthest
  4. The drop proves that a link is broken on every page of the library, so all readers are blocked
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Usage analytics show reach and patterns, and they mislead easily. A page view is not a reader, a reader is not a learner, and a dip in the holidays reflects the calendar. All three components fell together, so a flaw in one component is unlikely to explain it. Always read the counts alongside the calendar and next to the learning evidence from the A/B test, and choose a tool that records counts and not individuals.

Concept Tested: Usage Analytics

See: Usage Analytics

docs.title: 9. An author's report lists 300 downloads from a clearinghouse, 1,200 page views, three repository stars, and one teacher's course page that embeds the simulation and credits the author. Which analysis of the reuse evidence is correct?
docs.text:
1. All four signals are equally strong evidence of reuse, because each involves a reader
  2. Only the embedded course page is strong evidence of reuse; downloads, views, and stars show interest
  3. The downloads are the strongest evidence, because they are the largest number
  4. None of the four signals is evidence of reuse, because every one of them can be faked
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Strong signals show someone using the resource: a course page that links to or embeds a component and credits you, a copy of your repository with changes, and a message from a teacher describing use. Downloads, page views, and stars are weak evidence, because they show interest and not use. Your own visits and automated crawlers are not evidence at all. Search for your title and your attribution line, since a reuser who followed the license will have written them.

Concept Tested: Reuse Tracking

See: Reuse Tracking

docs.title: 10. A draft impact report says, "The library had 3,500 page views in six months, so students learned more from it." What is the best judgment of this sentence?
docs.text:
1. It is sound, because page views indicate learning and 3,500 views is a large number for a small resource
  2. It is sound, because a count of 3,500 views is large enough to show that students learned from it
  3. It is flawed only because it should give the number of downloads in place of the views
  4. It claims learning from page views, but views show reach, and learning evidence comes from the A/B test
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Impact reporting draws on four kinds of evidence: reach from usage analytics, reuse from reuse tracking, learning from the A/B test of Chapters 16 and 17, and experience from surveys, comments, and the issue list. A good report keeps the kinds apart, says how strong each is, and claims no more than the evidence shows. For Watershed Basics, the learning claim rests on a 22.0 versus 15.0 gain in a pilot of 24 students, with its limits stated.

Concept Tested: Impact Reporting

See: Impact Reporting

docs.title: References: Reusable Components and Publishing OER
docs.text:
1. MkDocs - Wikipedia - Describes MkDocs, a static site generator that builds documentation websites from Markdown files and a single configuration file. The tool behind the chapter's publishing workflow.

  2. Directed acyclic graph - Wikipedia - Explains directed graphs with no cycles and their uses, including ordering tasks by dependency. Background for the learning graph, which orders concepts by what must be learned first.

  3. Concept map - Wikipedia - Describes concept maps, which link labeled ideas to show how they relate, and their use in teaching. A close relative of the learning graph introduced in this chapter.

  4. The Pragmatic Programmer: Your Journey to Mastery (20th Anniversary ed.) - David Thomas and Andrew Hunt - Addison-Wesley (2019) - Hunt and Thomas coined DRY, Don't Repeat Yourself: every piece of knowledge should have one authoritative representation. For OER, one quiz or MicroSim embedded in many pages is the same idea.

  5. Learning, Creating, and Using Knowledge: Concept Maps as Facilitative Tools in Schools and Corporations (2nd ed.) - Joseph D. Novak - Routledge (2010) - Novak developed concept maps at Cornell in the 1970s. He shows how a labeled map of concepts and links reveals what a learner must know first, the idea behind this book's learning graph.

  6. Material for MkDocs: Getting Started - Material for MkDocs - Official instructions for installing and configuring the Material theme used by this book. Supports the chapter's steps for building a textbook site.

  7. Creating a GitHub Pages Site - GitHub Docs - Step-by-step instructions for publishing a site from a repository for free. Supports the chapter's walkthrough of publishing an improved OER.

  8. Building Intelligent Textbooks - Dan McCreary - A guide to building interactive textbooks with AI skills, covering learning graphs, MicroSims, and publishing. Background for the components and learning graph discussed in this chapter.

  9. Semantic Versioning 2.0.0 - semver.org - A simple scheme for numbering releases so users can tell a small fix from a breaking change. Useful for keeping a component library's versions clear.

  10. Zenodo - CERN - An open repository that gives uploaded files a DOI and reports views and downloads. One way to publish an OER permanently and begin tracking its reuse.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Describes how to run a teacher training workshop, set certificate requirements, review submissions, train local reviewers, and finish with a capstone project that improves a real OER. It is the capstone chapter and draws on nearly every earlier chapter. After this chapter you can run a teacher training workshop, set certificate requirements, review submissions, and complete a capstone that improves a real OER.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 16 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Teacher Training Workshop 20 Workshop Agenda 5 Facilitator Guide 3 Calibration Exercise 4 Peer Review 1 Certificate 6 Certificate Requirements 3 Certificate Submission 2 Submission Review 1 Exit Survey 2 Training Evaluation 1 Local Reviewer Role 2 Train-the-Trainer 1 Training Kit 1 Capstone Project 1 Professional Development 1

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 3: The Ten-Metric Rubric and Scoring
  • Chapter 11: Manual Evaluation and Adoption Decisions
  • Chapter 12: AI Agents, Prompts, and Rubric Scoring
  • Chapter 14: Checking and Calibrating AI Agent Output
  • Chapter 15: Improving a Resource with AI Agents
  • Chapter 16: Designing an A/B Test with Students
  • Chapter 17: Analyzing A/B Test Results
  • Chapter 18: Reusable Components and Publishing OER

From Learner to Teacher of Others

You can now evaluate a resource, check an agent, improve the resource, test the change, and publish it. This last chapter is about passing those skills to colleagues and recognizing the people who have them. Let's dive in and check the evidence!

A skill that only one teacher has helps one classroom. This chapter is about spreading it: running a workshop that teaches colleagues to evaluate and improve open educational resources with AI agents, setting a fair standard for a certificate, reviewing what people submit, and growing a group of local reviewers who keep the work going. It closes with the capstone project, which uses every skill in the book on a resource of your own.

The chapter builds on the sample materials in the book's workshop section: the Sample One-Day Workshop Schedule, the Sample Rubric Worksheet, and the Grant-Period Timeline. The chapter explains the reasons behind them.

docs.title: Teacher Training Workshop
docs.text:
A teacher training workshop is a planned session in which teachers learn a skill by practicing it on their own material. This book's workshop teaches teachers to evaluate OER for quality and reusability with AI agents and then to use the agents to improve one resource they already teach with. It is designed for about 20 teachers and fits in one day. Teachers arrive with a resource from their own subject, a laptop, and access to an agent tool, and they leave with an improved, openly licensed component and a checklist for earning a certificate.

Preparation decides much of the outcome. Before the day, each teacher chooses a resource they already use, checks that its license allows an improved version, and tests the agent tool. The facilitator prepares a sample resource with consensus scores, tests the prompts, and seats teachers in pairs, since pairs can compare scores and swap work. By the end of the day a teacher should be able to do four things: score a resource on all ten metrics with an agent, find an invented citation or a misread license in an agent's report, raise a metric with an agent and re-score it, and say what a reviewer needs to see to certify the work.

Three ideas shape the design. Teachers learn by doing, so most of the day is practice on a real resource and not lecture. The order of the skills follows the order of the book: score a resource, check the agent, improve the resource, then review each other's work. And the day ends with something real, a published component, because a workshop that ends with notes is forgotten faster than one that ends with a finished product.

docs.title: Workshop Agenda
docs.text:
A workshop agenda is the schedule of a workshop: each session, its length, and what participants take away. A good agenda puts the sessions in an order where each one prepares the next. The sample one-day agenda runs from 8:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m.

Time Session What teachers leave with 8:30 to 9:00 Check-in and setup A working agent session 9:00 to 9:45 Why quality and reusability matter: the 10 metrics A rubric card 9:45 to 10:45 Calibration: score a sample by hand, then with the agent Hand and agent scores, with gaps explained 10:45 to 11:00 Break 11:00 to 12:00 Checking the agent: invented citations, misread licenses, overconfident scores A verified evaluation of the sample 12:00 to 12:45 Lunch 12:45 to 2:15 Improvement challenge: raise one component's score with agents An improved component and its new score 2:15 to 2:30 Break 2:30 to 3:15 Peer review and publishing A published, openly licensed component 3:15 to 3:30 Next steps: certificate requirements and the exit survey A certificate checklist

The order matters. Setup comes first because nothing works without a running agent. The rubric comes before calibration, because teachers cannot score what they have not learned. Calibration comes before checking the agent, because you need your own scores to judge the agent's. Checking comes before improving, because Chapter 14 showed that an unchecked agent should not be trusted to change anything. Peer review and publishing come last because they need a finished component.

The MicroSim below practices the sequence. It gives seven sessions in a scrambled order, and you put them in the right one.

docs.title: Diagram: Workshop Agenda Sorter
docs.text:
Workshop Agenda Sorter

Type: microsim sim-id: workshop-agenda-sorter Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: apply Learning Objective: The learner will apply the logic of the workshop agenda by placing seven sessions in the correct order and naming what each session depends on, with at least 6 of 7 sessions in the correct position on the first commit.

Prerequisites: Teacher Training Workshop, Workshop Agenda, and the calibration and improvement chapters (Chapters 14 and 15).

Evidence of Mastery: The learner arranges the seven sessions and commits the order once. A session is correct when it is in its position in the Content table. Mastery is at least 6 of 7 sessions in the correct position on the first commit. Rearranging before the commit is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) The order of sessions is a matter of taste. (2) Improving a resource can come before checking the agent. (3) Peer review can come before the improvement.

Instructional Rationale: Ordering sessions by what each one needs is an Apply-level action that tests why the sequence works. Each session depends on a product of an earlier one, so a wrong order shows a missing prerequisite.

Content:

The seven sessions in their correct order:

Position Session Depends on (shown as feedback) 1 Check-in and setup Nothing, and it gives every teacher a working agent session. 2 Why quality and reusability matter: the 10 metrics The agent session is ready, and the metrics are needed to score. 3 Calibration The metrics, to score a sample by hand and with the agent. 4 Checking the agent The hand and agent scores from calibration. 5 Improvement challenge A verified evaluation, so the agent's output can be trusted. 6 Peer review and publishing A finished component to swap and re-score. 7 Next steps: certificate requirements and the exit survey Everything that came before.

Provenance: The order follows the sample one-day schedule in the book's workshop section. The sim leaves out the breaks and lunch, and says so.

Rules: The sim presents the seven sessions in a shuffled order. Each position has exactly one correct session.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees the seven sessions in a scrambled order.
  2. The learner drags the sessions into the order they think is right, and may rearrange them freely.
  3. The learner presses Commit.
  4. The sim marks each session correct or misplaced, and shows what each misplaced session depends on.

Feedback: One commit counts as evidence. The sim shows "[n] of 7 sessions in the correct position". At 6 or more it adds "You can plan a workshop day." Below 6 it lists the correct order with the dependency of each misplaced session.

Starting State: The seven sessions in a shuffled order and the Commit button.

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's agenda table and its explanation of why the order matters are the basis of this sim.

docs.title: Facilitator Guide
docs.text:
A facilitator guide is the document that tells the person running a workshop exactly what to do in each session. A facilitator who wrote the workshop can run it from memory. A colleague who did not write it needs a guide. For each session the guide gives the time, the goal, the materials, the steps, the key points to say, the questions to ask, the common problems, and the answers to any exercise.

The most useful part of a guide is the list of common problems with their fixes, because that is where an unprepared facilitator loses time. The MicroSim below practices handling them. It describes six problems from a workshop day, and for each one you choose the best response.

docs.title: Diagram: Workshop Problem Solver
docs.text:
Workshop Problem Solver

Type: microsim sim-id: workshop-problem-solver Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: recommend Learning Objective: The learner will recommend the best response to each of six problems that arise during a workshop day, with at least 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Facilitator Guide, Workshop Agenda, Teacher Training Workshop (all defined in this chapter above this block), and the privacy and licensing chapters (Chapters 2 and 13).

Evidence of Mastery: For each problem the learner chooses one of three responses. A choice is correct when it matches the Best response column in Content. Mastery is at least 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Reading the guide excerpt is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) The schedule must be kept at any cost. (2) A real resource from a teacher can be pasted into any tool. (3) A participant's licensing question can wait until after the workshop.

Instructional Rationale: Recommending a response to a live problem is an Evaluate-level action. Problems that involve time, tools, privacy, and licensing teach the learner what a facilitator guide must anticipate.

Content:

The six problems (all made up), each with three responses:

# Problem Responses Best response Why (shown as feedback) 1 Three teachers cannot log in to the agent tool at 8:45. A: Pause the whole room until all three are fixed. B: Pair each of the three with a neighbor who is logged in, and fix the logins during the first break. C: Tell them to try again at home. B Pairing keeps the room moving and the fix happens in parallel. 2 A teacher wants to paste a class roster with student names into the agent to score a quiz. A: Allow it, since the teacher owns the data. B: Stop it, remind the room that student data stays out of prompts, and use the sample quiz. C: Ask the teacher to remove only the last names. B Student information stays out of the prompt, as Chapter 13 taught. 3 The calibration session runs 20 minutes over. A: Cut the checking-the-agent session in half. B: Shorten the break and move one calibration comparison to a take-home task. C: Skip lunch. B It protects the sessions that depend on each other without cutting a core skill. 4 A teacher's resource turns out to have no license. A: Improve it anyway and publish it as CC BY. B: Switch that teacher to the sample resource for the improvement challenge, and have them ask the owner for permission later. C: Tell them to add a CC BY license themselves. B Without a license, only the owner can allow an improved version. 5 Two teachers and the agent disagree by 5 points on Accessibility. A: Average the three scores. B: Ask each to show their evidence and decide which one the evidence supports. C: Use the agent's score because it is faster. B Disagreements are settled by the evidence, as Chapters 11 and 14 taught. 6 A participant says the agent's score is obviously wrong but cannot say why. A: Ask them to find the check that the agent passed and that they believe fails, and test it. B: Agree and move on. C: Tell them the agent is usually right. A Turning a hunch into a specific check is how the finding gets verified.

Provenance: The problems are illustrative examples written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The responses follow Chapters 11, 13, 14, and 15.

Rules: Each problem has exactly one best response. The sim shuffles the order of the three responses for each problem, so that the letter shown does not give away the answer.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one problem and its three responses.
  2. The learner chooses a response, and the choice is committed.
  3. The sim shows whether it was best and the Why text.
  4. After problem 6 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 6 problems in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [response]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. The best response is [response]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 6 correct on the first attempt". At 5 or more it adds "You can handle a workshop day." Below 5 it lists the Why text of each missed problem.

Starting State: The first problem in the shuffled order and its three responses. The question shown is "What is the best response?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter says a facilitator guide includes the common problems with their fixes.

docs.title: Calibration Exercise
docs.text:
A calibration exercise is the workshop session in which each teacher scores a sample resource by hand, runs the agent on the same resource, and compares the two sets of scores. It is the teaching version of the calibration of Chapter 14. The facilitator keeps a set of consensus scores for the sample, agreed in advance by careful reviewers. Teachers compare their own scores with the agent's and with the consensus, and the worksheet asks them to list every metric on which their score and the agent's differ by more than 3 points and to explain which score they trust.

That flagging threshold of 3 is the one from Chapter 11, which suits a conversation between a person and an agent who have both read the evidence. A facilitator who wants a closer look can also compute the measures of Chapter 14 for the whole group: the agreement rate at a threshold of 1, the mean absolute difference, and the bias.

Worked example: one teacher and the agent on Watershed Basics. The teacher scored the sample, and the agent's scores follow.

Metric Teacher Agent Difference (agent minus teacher) Accuracy and currency 7 9 +2 Alignment 6 6 0 Readability 8 8 0 Accessibility 5 9 +4 Practice with feedback 6 6 0 Open license 9 10 +1 Modularity 5 5 0 Metadata 4 5 +1 Editable source 8 8 0 Portability 7 7 0 Total 65 73 +8

One metric differs by more than 3: Accessibility, where the agent gave 9 and the teacher gave 5. The teacher traces it to the evidence. The agent reported that contrast was fine but attached no tool log, and the video has no captions. The teacher trusts the 5 and writes the reason on the worksheet. The group measures also show a pattern: the agent agrees within 1 point on 8 of the 10 metrics, a rate of 80 percent, and its bias is +0.8, a mild generosity.

The Gap Is the Lesson

Do not hurry past the metrics where you and the agent disagree. Explaining one disagreement from the evidence teaches more than agreeing on nine.

The MicroSim below puts the exercise in your hands. It gives the table above, and you read it.

docs.title: Diagram: Calibration Exercise Reviewer
docs.text:
Calibration Exercise Reviewer

Type: microsim sim-id: calibration-exercise-reviewer Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: calculate Learning Objective: The learner will calculate the totals, the flagged metrics, the agreement rate, and the bias from a teacher and agent score table, and judge whether the agent meets the first-pass standard, with at least 5 of 6 answers correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Calibration Exercise, and the agreement measures of Chapter 14 (Agreement Rate, Bias, Mean Absolute Difference).

Evidence of Mastery: The learner answers six questions. An answer is correct when it matches the Correct answer column in Content. Mastery is at least 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Reading the standard is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Only the total matters. (2) A flag means the agent is wrong. (3) An agent that agrees on most metrics can be trusted as a first pass.

Instructional Rationale: Calculating the comparison measures from a score table is an Apply-level action that joins the workshop exercise to the measures of Chapter 14. A table with one flagged metric and a mild bias shows that an agent can pass one test and fail another.

Content:

The data, shown at all times (made up, for the Watershed Basics sample):

Metric Teacher Agent Accuracy and currency 7 9 Alignment 6 6 Readability 8 8 Accessibility 5 9 Practice with feedback 6 6 Open license 9 10 Modularity 5 5 Metadata 4 5 Editable source 8 8 Portability 7 7

The flag rule, shown at all times: flag a metric when the absolute difference is > 3. The adoption rule: Adopt when the total >= 75 and every metric >= 5; Revise when the total >= 50 and the resource is not Adopt; Reject when the total < 50. The illustrative first-pass standard: agreement rate at a threshold of 1 >= 80 percent, absolute bias <= 0.5, mean absolute difference <= 1.0, and the adoption decision matches the teacher's.

The six questions:

# Question Answer type Correct answer Why (shown as feedback) 1 What are the two totals? Two whole numbers 65 and 73 The teacher's scores add to 65 and the agent's to 73. 2 Which metric is flagged by the rule > 3? Choice among the ten metrics Accessibility The difference is 4. 3 What is the agreement rate at a threshold of 1? Percent 80 percent Eight of ten metrics differ by 1 or less. 4 What is the bias, agent minus teacher, per metric? Number with a sign +0.8 The differences add to +8, and 8 divided by 10 is 0.8. 5 What is the agent's adoption decision? Choice among Adopt, Revise, Reject Revise The total 73 is < 75. 6 Does the agent meet the first-pass standard? Yes or No No The bias of 0.8 is > 0.5.

Provenance: The scores are illustrative examples made up for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The flag rule follows the worksheet and Chapter 11, and the standard follows Chapter 14 and is labeled "illustrative standard".

Rules: Total = sum of the ten scores. Difference = agent minus teacher. Agreement rate = metrics with an absolute difference <= 1 divided by 10. Bias = sum of the differences divided by 10.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees the data table and the first question.
  2. The learner enters or chooses an answer, and the answer is committed.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text.
  4. After question 6 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 6 questions in the order of the table, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [answer]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. The answer is [answer]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 6 correct on the first attempt". At 5 or more it adds "You can read a calibration exercise." Below 5 it lists the Why text of each missed question.

Starting State: The data table, the rules, and question 1.

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's worked example uses the same scores and the same measures.

docs.title: Peer Review
docs.text:
Peer review is the practice in which teachers examine each other's work. In the workshop, participants swap their improved components, re-score them with the same rubric, and compare the new scores with the author's. A second reviewer catches what the author is too close to see, and reading someone else's work shows the reader new ways to solve the same problem.

Peer review works only when the feedback is useful. Three rules help. Tie every comment to evidence in the resource and to a check in the rubric. Say what to do, not only what is wrong. And review the work and not the person.

The MicroSim below practices the skill. It shows eight pieces of feedback, and for each one you decide whether it is useful.

docs.title: Diagram: Peer Feedback Judge
docs.text:
Peer Feedback Judge

Type: microsim sim-id: peer-feedback-judge Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: judge Learning Objective: The learner will judge whether each of eight peer review comments is useful or not useful, with at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Peer Review, Evidence for a Score (defined in this chapter above this block or in Chapter 3).

Evidence of Mastery: For each comment the learner commits one of two bins. A placement is correct when it matches the Correct bin column in Content. Mastery is at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the three rules is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Praise is useful feedback. (2) A harsh comment is an honest one. (3) A comment needs no evidence if the reviewer is experienced.

Instructional Rationale: Judging feedback against the three rules is an Evaluate-level action that improves the comments the learner writes. Pairs of comments about the same flaw, one useful and one not, teach the learner what the difference looks like.

Content:

The two bins: Useful, and Not useful.

The eight comments (all made up, about an improved Watershed Basics component):

# Comment Correct bin Why (shown as feedback) 1 Image 3 has the alt text "map". Describe what the map shows: the river and its two tributaries. Useful It cites the evidence and says what to do. 2 The accessibility is bad. Not useful It has no evidence and no action. 3 The quiz explanations are clear, and question 4 says why the wrong choices are wrong. Useful It names specific strengths that the author should keep. 4 Nice work! Not useful It says nothing that the author can use. 5 The license footer is missing on page 3, so check 6 of the open-license metric fails. Add the footer. Useful It ties the comment to a rubric check and an action. 6 Whoever wrote this clearly does not understand watersheds. Not useful It attacks the person and gives no evidence. 7 The reading level is grade 9 in section 3 and the audience is grade 6 to 7. Shorten the sentences there. Useful It cites a measurement and says what to do. 8 I would have done it differently. Not useful It gives no reason and no direction.

Provenance: The comments are illustrative examples written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The three rules follow the chapter section "Peer Review".

Rules: Each comment has exactly one correct bin, four per bin.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one comment and the two bins.
  2. The learner places the comment in a bin, and the placement is committed.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text.
  4. After comment 8 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 8 comments in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [bin]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. This comment is [bin]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 8 correct on the first attempt". At 7 or more it adds "You can give useful peer feedback." Below 7 it lists the Why text of each missed comment.

Starting State: The first comment in the shuffled order and the two bins. The question shown is "Could the author act on this?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter gives three rules for peer review: tie comments to evidence, say what to do, and review the work and not the person.

docs.title: Certificate
docs.text:
A certificate is a record, issued by a program, that a person has done defined work to a defined standard. In this book it is the Certificate of OER Quality Evaluation Using AI Agents. Earning it shows that a teacher attended the training, calibrated against an agent, evaluated a real resource with evidence, checked the agent's output, and improved and published a component that gained on four metrics.

A certificate is only as good as the standard behind it. It is not a legal license, an accreditation by a government body, or a promise that every later evaluation by the holder will be correct. Its value comes from design. The requirements are public, so anyone can check what the certificate means. The decision rests on evidence in the submission and not on effort or attendance alone. The reviewers are calibrated against each other, so a certificate from one reviewer means what it means from another. And there is a path for a near miss, so that a teacher who falls short on one requirement can fix it and try again.

A certificate is also a record, so keep one. For each decision the program stores the date, the reviewer, the outcome, and the reasons, and it publishes the list of certified teachers only with their consent. If a teacher later disputes a decision, the record shows what the reviewer saw. If a requirement changes, the record shows which standard applied to whom.

docs.title: Certificate Requirements
docs.text:
The certificate requirements are the conditions a teacher must meet to earn the certificate. The sample worksheet sets five, and the table says what evidence shows each one.

# Requirement Evidence Checked by 1 Attend the full training day The attendance record The program 2 Complete the calibration exercise, and explain every metric where the teacher's score and the agent's differ by more than 3 points The worksheet's calibration table The reviewer 3 Submit an evaluation of one resource from the teacher's own subject, scored on all 10 metrics, with evidence for each score and a note on every agent finding accepted, corrected, or rejected The worksheet and the findings log The reviewer 4 Publish one improved component under a CC BY license, with metadata, that gains on at least two quality and two reusability metrics The published component, its change log, and the re-score The reviewer 5 Submit both within 30 days of the workshop The date stamps The program

docs.title: Certificate Submission
docs.text:
A certificate submission is the package of evidence a teacher sends to earn the certificate. It contains the worksheet with the baseline scores and evidence, the agent's scores beside them, and the calibration explanation; the findings log; a link to the published improved component, with its metadata and license; the change log; and the re-score of all ten metrics with the gains.

The 30-day clock starts at the workshop. For a training day on February 20, 2027, the sample timeline sets the deadline at March 22, 2027. Submit early enough to leave time for a revision, since a reviewer may ask for one.

docs.title: Submission Review
docs.text:
A submission review is the examination of a certificate submission against the requirements by a reviewer who did not take part in the work. It has five steps.

  1. Check completeness. Compare the package with the requirements list.
  2. Check the published component. Open its address and confirm the license, the metadata, and the change log.
  3. Verify the gains. Re-check a sample of the claimed gains, beginning with the largest, using the verification steps of Chapter 14. A claim of "alt text added" is checked by looking at the images.
  4. Read the findings log. A log in which every agent finding was accepted, with no reasons, suggests the agent's output was not checked.
  5. Decide. The decisions are Certify, Revise and resubmit with the specific gaps named, or Not eligible when a requirement cannot be met by revision, such as missing the training day.

Borderline cases go to a second reviewer. The decisions and reasons are recorded, so that the standard stays steady.

Start With the Biggest Claimed Gain

If a metric's score jumped by four points, check that one first. A large gain with thin evidence is the most likely place for a mistake.

The MicroSim below practices the review. It shows eight submissions, and for each one you decide the outcome.

docs.title: Diagram: Certificate Submission Reviewer
docs.text:
Certificate Submission Reviewer

Type: microsim sim-id: certificate-submission-reviewer Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: judge Learning Objective: The learner will judge whether each of eight certificate submissions should be certified, revised and resubmitted, or declared not eligible, with at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Certificate, Certificate Requirements, Certificate Submission, Submission Review (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each submission the learner commits one of three outcomes. An outcome is correct when it matches the Correct outcome column in Content. Mastery is at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the five requirements is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Attendance and effort earn the certificate. (2) A submission with one gap is declined for good. (3) A claimed gain needs no checking.

Instructional Rationale: Judging a submission against the requirements is an Evaluate-level action. Submissions that meet all requirements, miss one that can be fixed, or miss one that cannot teach the learner to apply the standard evenly.

Content:

The three outcomes: Certify, Revise and resubmit, Not eligible.

The five requirements, available on demand: attend the full day; complete the calibration exercise and explain each flagged metric; submit an evaluation on all 10 metrics with evidence and a note on every agent finding; publish an improved component under CC BY with metadata that gains on at least two quality and two reusability metrics; submit within 30 days.

The eight submissions (all made up):

# Submission Correct outcome Why (shown as feedback) 1 Complete worksheet with evidence for all 10 metrics and a findings log of 5 entries (3 accepted, 1 corrected, 1 rejected). The component is published under CC BY with metadata. Gains: Accessibility +3 and Practice +2 on quality, Modularity +3 and Metadata +4 on reusability. Submitted on day 28. Certify It meets every requirement. 2 Gains on two quality metrics and one reusability metric. Everything else is complete. Revise and resubmit It needs a gain on a second reusability metric. 3 The improved component is published under CC BY-NC. Everything else is complete. Revise and resubmit The requirement is a CC BY license. 4 The findings log lists 6 agent findings, all marked accepted with no reasons. Revise and resubmit There is no sign that the agent's output was checked. 5 Evidence is missing for 4 of the 10 scores. Revise and resubmit Each score needs evidence. 6 The re-score claims that all five images now have alt text, and the published component shows two images with none. Revise and resubmit The claimed gain is not supported by the component. 7 The teacher did not attend the training day and watched a recording. Not eligible Attendance cannot be made up by revision. 8 Complete worksheet; the two flagged metrics are explained; gains on three quality and three reusability metrics; CC BY with metadata; submitted on day 21. Certify It meets every requirement.

Provenance: The submissions are illustrative examples written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The requirements follow the sample rubric worksheet in the book's workshop section.

Rules: Each submission has exactly one correct outcome. Two are Certify, five are Revise and resubmit, and one is Not eligible.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one submission and the three outcomes, and may open the five requirements. Opening them does not change the score.
  2. The learner chooses an outcome, and the choice is committed.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text.
  4. After submission 8 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 8 submissions in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [outcome]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. The outcome is [outcome]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 8 correct on the first attempt". At 7 or more it adds "You can review a submission fairly." Below 7 it lists the Why text of each missed submission.

Starting State: The first submission in the shuffled order and the three outcomes. The question shown is "What should the reviewer decide?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's table of five requirements and its five review steps are the basis of this sim.

docs.title: Exit Survey
docs.text:
An exit survey is a short survey given at the end of a workshop, while the experience is fresh. It has two jobs: to learn how participants experienced the day, and to take a quick reading of what they feel able to do. Keep it to a few minutes. Apply the rules of Chapter 17: neutral wording, one idea per question, a rating scale, one open question, and anonymity so people answer honestly.

Item Type The day gave me skills I can use with my own resources. Rating from 1 to 5 I am confident that I can score a resource with an agent. Rating from 1 to 5 I am confident that I can check an agent's output. Rating from 1 to 5 Which session was the most useful? Choice from the agenda What should change for the next workshop? Open answer

docs.title: Training Evaluation
docs.text:
A training evaluation is the assessment of whether a training worked. The widely used model of Donald Kirkpatrick asks four questions: how participants reacted, what they learned, whether their behavior changed afterward, and what results followed. The exit survey measures only the first. Judging a program needs evidence at every level, and the later levels take more time to collect.

Level The question Illustrative evidence for a workshop of 20 teachers Reaction Did participants find the day useful? 19 of 20 returned the exit survey, and 18 rated the day 4 or 5 Learning Did they gain the skills? 17 of 20 earned the certificate, and their calibration scores differed from the consensus by 1.1 points on average Behavior Do they use the skills afterward? 12 of the 17 certified teachers scored another resource within three months Results Did it change outcomes? 20 improved components were published, and 9 were reused by another teacher within three months

These numbers are made up to show the form. Real evaluation faces the cautions of Chapters 16 and 17: without a comparison group a change may have other causes, and counts of reuse are weaker than evidence of learning.

The MicroSim below practices placing evidence at the right level.

docs.title: Diagram: Training Evaluation Matcher
docs.text:
Training Evaluation Matcher

Type: microsim sim-id: training-evaluation-matcher Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: classify Learning Objective: The learner will classify each of eight pieces of evidence under Reaction, Learning, Behavior, or Results, with at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Exit Survey, Training Evaluation (both defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each item the learner commits one of four levels. A placement is correct when it matches the Correct level column in Content. Mastery is at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the four levels is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) An exit survey shows that the training worked. (2) A certificate count shows changed behavior. (3) Reuse by others is a measure of satisfaction.

Instructional Rationale: Classifying evidence by level is an Understand-level action that shows how far each piece of evidence reaches. Two items per level teach the learner to see what an exit survey cannot show.

Content:

The four levels and their meanings: Reaction (how participants felt about the training), Learning (what they learned), Behavior (what they do differently afterward), Results (what changed because of it).

The eight items (all made up):

# Evidence Correct level Why (shown as feedback) 1 18 of 19 respondents rated the day 4 or 5. Reaction It records how participants felt. 2 Participants wrote that the pace was too fast. Reaction It is an opinion about the training. 3 Teachers' calibration scores differed from the consensus by 1.1 points on average. Learning It measures a skill gained. 4 17 of 20 teachers earned the certificate. Learning It shows the skills were demonstrated. 5 12 of 17 certified teachers scored another resource within three months. Behavior It shows use of the skill afterward. 6 Teachers kept a findings log on their own reviews. Behavior It shows a practice carried over. 7 20 improved components were published. Results They are products of the training. 8 9 components were reused by another teacher within three months. Results Reuse is an outcome beyond the participants.

Provenance: The items are illustrative examples written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The four levels follow the model of Donald Kirkpatrick, as described in the chapter section "Training Evaluation".

Rules: Each item has exactly one correct level, two per level.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one item and the four levels.
  2. The learner places the item under a level, and the placement is committed.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text.
  4. After item 8 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 8 items in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [level]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. This is [level]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 8 correct on the first attempt". At 7 or more it adds "You can place evidence at the right level." Below 7 it lists the Why text of each missed item.

Starting State: The first item in the shuffled order and the four levels. The question shown is "What does this evidence show?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's table of four levels gives two examples of evidence for each level.

docs.title: Local Reviewer Role
docs.text:
A local reviewer role is a position, held by a trained and certified teacher, in which they act as the first reviewer of resources for their school or district. Colleagues bring a resource, and the local reviewer scores it with the rubric and an agent, verifies the agent's claims, keeps a findings log, and tells the colleague which metric to fix first.

The role has limits. A local reviewer reads a license statement and flags problems, and does not rule on what is legally safe: that is a question for the school's counsel or privacy officer. A local reviewer never sends student information to an agent. A local reviewer advises on an adoption, and the decision goes through the school's own process. And a local reviewer does not certify other teachers, which belongs to the program's reviewers. To stay accurate, a local reviewer repeats a calibration exercise on a reference set at least once a year and compares the result with the first-pass standard of Chapter 14.

The MicroSim below practices the boundary of the role.

docs.title: Diagram: Local Reviewer Scope Sorter
docs.text:
Local Reviewer Scope Sorter

Type: microsim sim-id: local-reviewer-scope-sorter Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: judge Learning Objective: The learner will judge whether each of eight tasks belongs to the local reviewer role or must be referred to someone else, with at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Local Reviewer Role, Certificate, Submission Review (all defined in this chapter above this block), and the privacy section of Chapter 13.

Evidence of Mastery: For each task the learner commits one of two bins. A placement is correct when it matches the Correct bin column in Content. Mastery is at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the role description is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A certified teacher can rule on what is legal. (2) A local reviewer approves adoptions alone. (3) Certifying others is part of the role.

Instructional Rationale: Judging the boundary of a role is an Evaluate-level action that protects both the reviewer and the colleagues who rely on them. Tasks that look similar to in-role tasks but fall outside teach the learner where to refer.

Content:

The two bins: In the role, and Refer or do not do.

The eight tasks (all made up):

# Task Correct bin Why (shown as feedback) 1 Score a colleague's quiz with the rubric and an agent, and verify the agent's claims. In the role It is the core of the role. 2 Keep a findings log for each review. In the role The log is part of the method. 3 Tell a colleague which metric to fix first. In the role It applies the lowest-metric-first rule. 4 Decide that a resource's license is legally safe to publish. Refer or do not do Legal questions go to the school's counsel or privacy officer. 5 Send a class roster with student names to the agent. Refer or do not do Student information stays out of prompts. 6 Approve a district-wide adoption on their own. Refer or do not do Adoption follows the school's own process. 7 Repeat the calibration exercise on a reference set once a year. In the role It keeps the reviewer accurate. 8 Certify another teacher. Refer or do not do Certification belongs to the program's reviewers.

Provenance: The tasks are illustrative examples written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The scope follows the chapter section "Local Reviewer Role" and Chapters 11, 13, and 14.

Rules: Each task has exactly one correct bin, four per bin.

Learner Activity:
