  1. The learner sees one task and the two bins.
  2. The learner places the task in a bin, and the placement is committed.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text.
  4. After task 8 the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 8 tasks in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [bin]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. This task is [bin]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 8 correct on the first attempt". At 7 or more it adds "You know where the role ends." Below 7 it lists the Why text of each missed task.

Starting State: The first task in the shuffled order and the two bins. The question shown is "Is this part of the local reviewer's job?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter lists four limits of the role: no legal rulings, no student information in prompts, no solo adoption decisions, and no certifying of others.

docs.title: Train-the-Trainer
docs.text:
Train-the-trainer is a model in which people who have learned a skill are trained to teach it to others. It lets a program grow without relying on its original founders. A certified teacher joins as a co-facilitator at a workshop, then leads one with a more experienced facilitator watching, and then leads on their own, using the training kit and the facilitator guide.

The arithmetic is encouraging. If 17 teachers earn the certificate and each trains 10 colleagues, the next round reaches 170 teachers. The risk is that quality thins as the skill passes along. Three habits protect it: trainers use the same kit and the same reference set, a new trainer is observed on the first session, and trainers repeat the calibration exercise so that their scores stay close to the consensus.

Teaching It Is the Best Way to Learn It

If you feel unsure about leading a workshop, co-facilitate one first. Explaining the rubric to a colleague will show you exactly which parts you understand best.

docs.title: Training Kit
docs.text:
A training kit is the bundle of materials that lets someone run the workshop without the original team. It is itself an open educational resource, so it should be packaged, licensed, and published by the methods of Chapter 18: under CC BY, with metadata, a version number, and release notes.

Item What it is for Agenda The one-page schedule of the day Facilitator guide Step-by-step directions, key points, and fixes for common problems Slides Visual support for the short talks Rubric worksheet The form teachers fill in during the day Sample resource with consensus scores The material for the calibration exercise Agent prompts and setup notes The prompts of Chapter 12 and instructions for getting an agent running Certificate checklist and submission template What to submit and how it is reviewed Exit survey and follow-up survey The instruments for the training evaluation

The poster below shows the kit as a box of eight items.

docs.title: Diagram: Training Kit Contents
docs.text:
Training Kit Contents

Type: infographic sim-id: training-kit-poster Library: html Status: Specified Bloom Level: Remember Bloom Verb: identify Learning Objective: The learner will identify the eight items of the training kit from a description of how each looks, with at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Training Kit, Facilitator Guide, Workshop Agenda, Exit Survey, Certificate Submission (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: In quiz mode the learner clicks the marker that matches a visual hint. A click is correct when it matches the marker named in the Hint column of Content. Mastery is at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Hovering in explore mode is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A kit is only slides. (2) The kit needs no license. (3) The sample resource can be any resource.

Instructional Rationale: Identifying the items of a kit is a Remember-level task, and a picture of an open box with its contents gives each item a place. The quiz asks the learner to recognize an item by its look.

Content:

The illustration is a text-free flat drawing of an open box seen from above, with eight items inside. One is a sheet with a grid of eight rows and two columns. One is a thick booklet with a bookmark ribbon. One is a short stack of rectangles with a play-button shape on the top one. One is a printed form with boxes and a pencil. One is a document with a ribbon and a row of ten small squares. One is a speech bubble containing short lines and a gear. One is a clipboard with a check mark. One is a card with five stars and a blank line. The eight markers:

# Label Hint (describes the look, not the name) Description Tip 1 Agenda The sheet with a grid of eight rows and two columns. The one-page schedule of the day. Show the time and what teachers leave with. 2 Facilitator guide The thick booklet with a bookmark ribbon. Step-by-step directions and fixes for common problems. Include the answers to every exercise. 3 Slides The short stack of rectangles with a play-button shape. Visual support for the short talks. Keep talks short and practice long. 4 Rubric worksheet The printed form with boxes and a pencil. The form teachers fill in during the day. Use the ten metrics and the evidence column. 5 Sample resource The document with a ribbon and a row of ten small squares. The material for the calibration exercise, with consensus scores. Agree the consensus scores before the day. 6 Agent prompts The speech bubble with short lines and a gear. The prompts and setup notes for the agent. Test the prompts before the day. 7 Certificate checklist The clipboard with a check mark. What to submit and how it is reviewed. Show the 30-day deadline. 8 Surveys The card with five stars and a blank line. The exit survey and the follow-up survey. Keep them short and anonymous.

Provenance: The eight items follow the chapter section "Training Kit". The illustration is synthetic, and the sim labels it "illustrative example".

Rules: Each hint matches exactly one marker. The illustration contains no text, so every label comes from the table above. Markers are numbered 1 to 8 in the order of the table.

Learner Activity:

  1. In explore mode the learner hovers or clicks a marker and reads its label, description, and tip.
  2. In quiz mode the sim shows a hint.
  3. The learner clicks the marker they think the hint describes.
  4. If the first click is wrong, the sim says so and lets the learner try once more. If the second click is also wrong, the sim reveals the marker and its description.
  5. After all 8 hints the sim shows the summary.

Feedback: 8 hints in a shuffled order, two attempts each. Only a correct first click counts as evidence. Correct: "Correct: [label]. [Description]". First wrong click: "Not quite. Look again at the hint: [hint]". Second wrong click: "This is [label]. [Description]". The summary shows "[n] of 8 correct on the first attempt". At 7 or more it adds "You know what goes in the kit." Below 7 it lists the labels of the missed items.

Starting State: The illustration with eight numbered markers, explore mode active, and the prompt "Hover an item to see what it is for."

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's table of eight kit items lists the same items.

docs.title: Capstone Project
docs.text:
The capstone project is the culminating work of the book: you evaluate one open educational resource from your own subject, use AI agents to improve it on at least two quality and two reusability metrics, test the change with students, and publish the result under a CC BY license. It uses every skill in the book on a resource that matters to you. The table maps its steps to the chapters.

Step What you do Chapters 1. Choose and check Pick a resource, and confirm its license allows an improved version 1, 2, 15 2. Evaluate Score it on all ten metrics with evidence, using the rubric and an agent 3 to 11 3. Check the agent Verify its claims, log your findings, and compare with your own scores 12 to 14 4. Improve Plan lowest-metric-first, fix with agents, review and log every change, and re-score 15 5. Test Design and run an A/B test with consent and privacy, and write the results summary 16 and 17 6. Publish Package the components, publish under CC BY, and set up feedback and maintenance 18 7. Share Report what you found, and offer to train a colleague 19

A capstone succeeds when it meets four tests: it improves at least two quality and two reusability metrics with evidence, it includes a test with students that follows the consent and privacy rules, it is published under CC BY with metadata, and its report states the gain, the limits of the test, and any side effect honestly.

The poster below lays the roadmap out as six panels. Hover over a panel to see what it asks of you.

docs.title: Diagram: Capstone Roadmap
docs.text:
Capstone Roadmap

Type: infographic sim-id: capstone-roadmap-poster Library: html Status: Specified Bloom Level: Remember Bloom Verb: identify Learning Objective: The learner will identify which of the six capstone stages matches each of six descriptions, with at least 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Capstone Project, Improvement Challenge, A/B Test, Publishing OER, Certificate Submission (defined in this chapter above this block or in Chapters 15, 16, and 18).

Evidence of Mastery: In quiz mode the learner clicks the poster zone that matches each description. A click is correct when the zone's id equals the Correct zone column in Content. Mastery is at least 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Hovering a zone in explore mode is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) The capstone ends with the improved resource. (2) Testing with students is optional. (3) Sharing means only posting a link.

Instructional Rationale: Remembering the stages of the capstone and what each asks is a Remember-level task, and a poster with six panels in order lets the learner hold the whole project at once. The quiz asks for the stage by its purpose.

Content:

The poster is a flat illustration of six equal panels in two rows of three, read left to right and top to bottom. Each panel shows one simple pictogram and a stage number, and the printed text is limited to the six stage numbers. The first panel shows a magnifying glass over a page with ten bars. The second shows a robot head with a check mark. The third shows a wrench over a page. The fourth shows two groups of figures joined by an arrow. The fifth shows a globe with a branching line. The sixth shows a speech bubble between two figures. All other words come from the explore and quiz data. The six zones:

Zone id Label Summary Facts shown on hover or click stage-1-evaluate 1. Evaluate Score your resource on all ten metrics with evidence. Use the rubric and an agent. Record evidence for each score. Check the license first. stage-2-check 2. Check the agent Verify the agent's claims and log your findings. Look for invented citations, misread licenses, and overconfident scores. Accept, correct, or reject each claim. stage-3-improve 3. Improve Raise at least two quality and two reusability metrics. Plan lowest first. Review and log every change. Re-score all ten metrics. stage-4-test 4. Test with students Compare the original and improved versions. State a hypothesis. Assign by chance. Get consent and protect privacy. Report the effect size and the limits. stage-5-publish 5. Publish Release the improved resource under CC BY. Package the components. Include metadata. Build and deploy. Open a feedback channel. stage-6-share 6. Share Report what you found and help others. Write the results summary. Track reuse. Offer to train a colleague.

The six quiz questions, in this order:

# Question Correct zone Why (shown as feedback) 1 Which stage asks you to compare an original and an improved version with students? stage-4-test The test is the stage with groups and consent. 2 Which stage checks for invented citations and misread licenses? stage-2-check Verifying the agent's claims is stage 2. 3 Which stage ends with the resource at a public address under CC BY? stage-5-publish Publishing releases the resource. 4 Which stage plans fixes lowest metric first? stage-3-improve The plan and the re-score belong to stage 3. 5 Which stage begins with scoring all ten metrics? stage-1-evaluate The baseline comes first. 6 Which stage includes offering to train a colleague? stage-6-share Sharing includes teaching others.

Provenance: The six stages follow the chapter section "Capstone Project" and the course description's capstone. The illustration is synthetic, and it carries no statistics.

Rules: Each question has exactly one correct zone. Zones are distinct regions of the poster, so a click belongs to at most one zone. Because the poster prints only stage numbers, the sim shows the zone labels on hover.

Learner Activity:

  1. In explore mode the learner hovers or clicks a panel and reads its summary and facts.
  2. In quiz mode the sim shows question 1 above the poster.
  3. The learner clicks the panel they think matches.
  4. The sim shows the Why text and moves to the next question, until question 6 is done.

Feedback: 6 questions in the fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [label]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. The answer is [label]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 6 correct on the first attempt". At 5 or more it adds "You know the road to the capstone." Below 5 it lists the Why text of each missed question.

Starting State: The poster with no zone selected, explore mode active, and the prompt "Hover a panel to learn about the stage."

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's table of seven capstone steps groups into these six stages, with the last step combining the report and the offer to train.

docs.title: Professional Development
docs.text:
Professional development is the continuing learning that teachers do to improve their practice. A workshop and a capstone project are good examples: they are hands-on, they use the teacher's own material, and they end in a product that others can use. Whether they count toward required hours or credits depends on your school or district, so ask before you promise anything.

The most useful professional development is a cycle and not an event. A teacher learns a skill, practices it on real work, applies it in class, shares the result, and helps the next teacher learn. That cycle is also the loop of this whole book. You evaluate a resource, check the agent that helped, improve the resource, test the change with students, publish the result, and train others. Each pass produces evidence that feeds the next one. The rubric-outcome correlation of Chapter 17 shows whether the rubric still predicts learning, the calibration of Chapter 14 shows whether the agent still agrees with careful people, and the reuse tracking of Chapter 18 shows whether the work travels. Each check makes the next evaluation more trustworthy.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• A teacher training workshop teaches by practice on the teacher's own resource, and its workshop agenda puts each session after the one it depends on. A facilitator guide lets someone else run it and lists the common problems with their fixes.
  • The calibration exercise compares a teacher's scores with the agent's and the consensus, and asks for an evidence-based explanation of every large gap. Peer review needs comments that cite evidence, say what to do, and review the work and not the person.
  • The certificate is only as good as its standard. The certificate requirements are public and evidence-based, a certificate submission gathers the evidence, and a submission review verifies the gains, reads the findings log, and decides to certify, to ask for revision, or to find the teacher not eligible.
  • An exit survey measures reaction. A training evaluation also looks for evidence of learning, behavior, and results.
  • A local reviewer role scores resources, verifies agents, and advises colleagues, and it refers legal, privacy, adoption, and certification questions to others. Train-the-trainer spreads the skill while guarding quality, and a training kit is an open resource packaged like any other.
  • The capstone project applies every skill in the book to one real resource. Professional development is a cycle of learning, practicing, applying, and sharing, and the cycle of this book makes each pass more trustworthy than the last.

You Finished the Whole Loop

You can now evaluate an open resource, check the agent that helped, improve the resource, test it with students, publish it, and teach others to do the same. Pick one resource you use this week, and start the loop.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Training Teachers and Certifying Reviewers
docs.text: Test your understanding of workshop design, calibration exercises, certificate review, training evaluation, the local reviewer role, and the capstone project with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. Within how many days of the workshop must a teacher submit the certificate evidence?
docs.text:
1. 7 days
  2. 14 days
  3. 30 days
  4. 90 days
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The fifth certificate requirement is to submit both the evaluation and the improved component within 30 days of the workshop. For a training day on February 20, 2027, the sample timeline sets the deadline at March 22, 2027. A teacher should submit early enough to leave time for a revision, because a reviewer may ask for one. The other four requirements cover attendance, the calibration exercise, the evaluation with evidence, and a published CC BY component.

Concept Tested: Certificate Requirements

See: Certificate Requirements

docs.title: 2. Which list gives the four levels of the Kirkpatrick model that the chapter uses to evaluate a training?
docs.text:
1. Reaction, learning, behavior, and results
  2. Reach, reuse, learning, and experience
  3. Attendance, completion, certificate, and publication
  4. Plan, do, check, and act
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. A training evaluation asks how participants reacted, what they learned, whether their behavior changed afterward, and what results followed. An exit survey measures only the first level. Judging a program needs evidence at every level, and the later levels take more time to collect. Option B lists the four kinds of evidence used in an impact report in Chapter 18, which is a related but different framework.

Concept Tested: Training Evaluation

See: Training Evaluation

docs.title: 3. Why does the sample workshop agenda place the session on checking the agent before the improvement challenge?
docs.text:
1. Teachers need a lunch break between the two sessions, and the agenda gives one there
  2. Chapter 14 showed that an unchecked agent should not be trusted to change anything
  3. The improvement challenge uses fewer tools than the checking session does, so it can come second
  4. The certificate checklist forbids any other order of these two sessions in a workshop
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Each session depends on a product of an earlier one. Setup comes first because nothing works without a running agent. The rubric precedes calibration, calibration precedes checking because you need your own scores to judge the agent's, and checking precedes improving. Peer review and publishing come last because they need a finished component. A good agenda puts the sessions in an order where each one prepares the next.

Concept Tested: Workshop Agenda

See: Workshop Agenda

docs.title: 4. What does a facilitator guide give a colleague who did not write the workshop?
docs.text:
1. Only the slides for the short talks, with no notes for the facilitator to follow
  2. The participants' certificates, ready to be signed and handed out at the end of the day
  3. A list of the teachers who attended, with their names and the resource each one brought
  4. For each session, the time, goal, materials, steps, key points, common problems with fixes, and answers
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. A facilitator who wrote the workshop can run it from memory, and a colleague who did not needs a guide. The most useful part is the list of common problems with fixes, because that is where an unprepared facilitator loses time. For example, if a teacher wants to paste a class roster into the agent, the guide tells the facilitator to stop it and use the sample quiz, since student data stays out of prompts.

Concept Tested: Facilitator Guide

See: Facilitator Guide

docs.title: 5. In the calibration exercise, a teacher scores Accessibility 5 and the agent scores it 9. What should the teacher do?
docs.text:
1. Flag it, because 4 is more than 3, then trace it to the evidence and record which score is trusted
  2. Average the two scores to 7 and move on, since the difference is only one band
  3. Accept the agent's score, because the agent works faster than a teacher can
  4. Ignore the difference, because it is within the agreement threshold and so needs no further comment
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The worksheet asks teachers to list every metric on which their score and the agent's differ by more than 3 points and to explain which score they trust. Here the agent said contrast was fine with no tool log, and the video has no captions, so the teacher trusts the 5. Averaging (B) hides the disagreement, and a gap of 4 exceeds the threshold of 3 (D). Explaining one disagreement from the evidence teaches more than agreeing on nine.

Concept Tested: Calibration Exercise

See: Calibration Exercise

docs.title: 6. A certificate submission is complete and published under CC BY, with gains on two quality metrics and on only one reusability metric. What should the reviewer decide?
docs.text:
1. Certify, because most of the requirements are met and the evidence is complete
  2. Not eligible, because a requirement is unmet and the submission cannot be repaired
  3. Certify, with a note asking for a later improvement on the missing reusability gain
  4. Revise and resubmit, because a gain on a second reusability metric is still needed
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The fourth requirement is a published CC BY component that gains on at least two quality and two reusability metrics. A submission with one gap that can be fixed is returned with the specific gap named, so the teacher can revise and resubmit. Not eligible is for a requirement that revision cannot meet, such as missing the training day. Effort and attendance alone do not earn the certificate, and the decision rests on evidence in the submission.

Concept Tested: Submission Review

See: Submission Review

docs.title: 7. A submission's findings log lists six agent findings, all marked "accepted," with no reasons given. What does the pattern suggest?
docs.text:
1. The agent made no errors, so the submission can be certified at once
  2. The findings log is optional and can be skipped when the agent's report looks clean
  3. The teacher checked the agent especially well and recorded only the final decisions
  4. There is no sign that the agent's output was checked, so the reviewer should ask for verification
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. A log in which every agent finding was accepted without reasons suggests that nobody tested the claims. The third requirement asks for a note on every agent finding accepted, corrected, or rejected, and the review step is to read the findings log. Agents make confident mistakes, as Chapter 14 showed, so a clean record with no reasons is a warning. The reviewer asks for the verification and does not certify on trust.

Concept Tested: Certificate Submission

See: Certificate Submission

docs.title: 8. A workshop reports that 18 of 19 respondents rated the day 4 or 5 and that 17 of 20 teachers earned the certificate. Which analysis is best?
docs.text:
1. Both figures show results, which is the top level of the model, since both are counts
  2. The ratings show reaction and the certificates show learning, but not that behavior or results changed
  3. Both figures show that behavior changed after the workshop, since teachers are using the skills
  4. Both figures show reaction only, since both come from the participants themselves
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. An exit survey measures how participants felt about the day, which is reaction. A certificate shows that skills were demonstrated, which is learning. Behavior needs evidence such as teachers scoring another resource within three months, and results need evidence such as published components being reused by others. Real evaluation also faces the cautions of Chapters 16 and 17: without a comparison group a change may have other causes.

Concept Tested: Exit Survey

See: Exit Survey

docs.title: 9. A certified teacher is asked to decide that a resource's license is legally safe to publish across the district. What is the best judgment?
docs.text:
1. It is outside the local reviewer's role, because legal questions go to the school's counsel
  2. It is inside the role, because the teacher can read licenses and flag problems
  3. It is inside the role, because the teacher holds the certificate and has been trained for the role
  4. It is inside the role if the agent agrees with the teacher's reading of the license
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. A local reviewer reads a license statement and flags problems, and does not rule on what is legally safe. The role has four limits: no legal rulings, no student information in prompts, no adoption decision made alone, and no certifying of other teachers. Inside the role are scoring with the rubric and an agent, verifying the agent's claims, keeping a findings log, and telling a colleague which metric to fix first. The reviewer repeats a calibration exercise at least once a year.

Concept Tested: Local Reviewer Role

See: Local Reviewer Role

docs.title: 10. A teacher is planning a capstone project. Which plan best meets the capstone's four tests?
docs.text:
1. Improve one metric of a resource that the teacher likes, publish it online under a license, and share a link without any report
  2. Evaluate a resource and improve it, skip the student test because testing is optional, publish it, and announce the gain
  3. Evaluate a resource, check the agent, improve two quality and two reusability metrics, test with students, publish under CC BY, and report honestly
  4. Improve four metrics, test with a few students without asking permission, publish under CC BY-NC, and share the link as the report
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The capstone uses every skill in the book on one resource from your own subject. It succeeds when it improves at least two quality and two reusability metrics with evidence, includes a test with students that follows the consent and privacy rules, is published under CC BY with metadata, and reports the gain, the limits of the test, and any side effect honestly. Testing with students is required, and the capstone ends with sharing what was found, including an offer to train a colleague.

Concept Tested: Capstone Project

See: Capstone Project

docs.title: References: Training Teachers and Certifying Reviewers
docs.text:
1. Professional certification - Wikipedia - Explains how certifications are awarded after training and assessment, and what makes them credible. Background for the chapter's certificate requirements and submission review.

  2. Capstone course - Wikipedia - Describes capstone experiences in which learners apply what they learned to a substantial project. Supports the chapter's capstone project for improving a real OER.

  3. Community of practice - Wikipedia - Explains groups of people who learn together by sharing a practice. Frames how local reviewers and trained colleagues keep improving as a network.

  4. Situated Learning: Legitimate Peripheral Participation - Jean Lave and Etienne Wenger - Cambridge University Press (1991) - Introduced legitimate peripheral participation: newcomers become skilled by doing real tasks at the edge of a community's work while experts guide them. The model behind the local reviewer role.

  5. Evaluating Professional Development - Thomas R. Guskey - Corwin Press (2000) - Guskey's five levels (participants' reactions, learning, organization support, use of new knowledge, and student outcomes) test whether a workshop changed practice, not only whether people enjoyed it.

  6. CC Training Center - Creative Commons - Offers courses on copyright and open licensing, including the ten-week CC Certificate and a newer badge-based pathway. A working example of a certificate for open licensing skills.

  7. Quality Matters - Quality Matters - A nonprofit that trains peer reviewers and certifies courses against a published rubric. A mature model for training and certifying reviewers, like the local reviewer role in this chapter.

  8. Open Education Leadership Program - SPARC - A cohort program that prepares academic leaders to advance open education on their campuses. Shows one way to structure professional development in OER.

  9. Introduction to Communities of Practice - Wenger-Trayner - Etienne Wenger-Trayner's short introduction to what communities of practice are and how they support learning. Background for building a network of local reviewers.

  10. Open Badges - 1EdTech - The standard for verifiable digital credentials that can carry evidence of what the earner did. A model for a certificate that links to a learner's reviewed work.

docs.title: Character Sheet: Echo the Loon
docs.text: The canonical identity document for Echo, the pedagogical mascot for the OER Evaluator textbook. Every pose prompt and every piece of AI-generated content involving this character must re-anchor to the description below. It is the source of truth for visual and voice consistency.

docs.title: Identity
docs.text:
• Name: Echo
  • Species: Loon
  • Subject: Evaluating and improving open educational resources (OER)
  • Catchphrase: "Let's dive in and check the evidence!"
  • Pronouns: Echo has no gender. Write "Echo" or they/them.

docs.title: Visual Description
docs.text:
• Body color: Glossy near-black head and neck with a white belly and a black back covered in a white checkered pattern, as on a common loon. Hex #1a1a2e for the black.
  • Accent color: Indigo, hex #3949ab, with a burnt-orange accent, hex #b45309. These match the book's indigo and orange theme.
  • Clothing / accessories: A small indigo scarf, and a magnifying glass with an orange handle held in one wing. Echo also has the loon's red eye.
  • Expression: Calm, sharp-eyed, and friendly, with a small closed-beak smile.
  • Size proportion: Small and compact, suitable for icon-sized display at about 90 pixels.
  • Art style: Flat cartoon illustration, modern vector, clean lines.

docs.title: Personality
docs.text:
• Patient: Echo never rushes a reviewer or a learner.
  • Sharp-eyed: Echo notices the detail others skip, such as a missing license or a broken link.
  • Encouraging: Echo treats mistakes as part of the process and celebrates progress.
  • Gently skeptical: Echo checks before trusting, especially an AI agent's confident answer.

docs.title: Voice
docs.text:
• Short, calm sentences that name the specific thing to check.
  • Asks "What is the evidence?" before accepting a claim, and models checking the work.
  • Uses water words sparingly and only when they fit: dive in, below the surface, ripples, calling across the lake. Never more than one per admonition.
  • Signature phrases: "Let's dive in and check the evidence!", "Look below the surface.", "Credit it, share it, pass it on."

docs.title: Pose Set
docs.text:
Pose Filename Use Neutral neutral.png General-purpose / sidebars Welcome welcome.png Chapter openings Thinking thinking.png Key concepts Tip tip.png Hints and helpful guidance Warning warning.png Common mistakes / pitfalls, such as AI agent errors Encouraging encouraging.png Difficult content / struggle Celebration celebration.png End of chapter / achievements

See image-prompts.md for the full text of each pose prompt. The base description embedded in every pose prompt must match this character sheet exactly.

docs.title: Why This Mascot
docs.text: A loon dives beneath the surface to see what is really there, which is what this book asks teachers to do when they check evidence and verify what an AI agent reports. A loon's call carries across a whole lake, which fits the idea of sharing and reusing OER, and the name Echo says the same thing. The loon is also Minnesota's state bird, which ties the book to the Minneapolis workshop it supports.

docs.title: Learning Graph for OER Evaluator
docs.text:
This section contains the learning graph for this textbook. A learning graph is a graph of concepts used in this textbook. Each concept is represented by a node in a network graph. Concepts are connected by directed edges that indicate what concepts each node depends on before that concept is understood by the student.

A learning graph is the foundational data structure for intelligent textbooks that can recommend learning paths. A learning graph is like a roadmap of concepts to help students arrive at their learning goals.

At the left of the learning graph are prerequisite or foundational concepts. They have no outbound edges. They only have inbound edges for other concepts that depend on understanding these foundational prerequisite concepts. At the far right we have the most advanced concepts in the course. To master these concepts you must understand all the concepts that they point to.

Here are other files used by the learning graph.

docs.title: Course Description
docs.text: We use the Course Description as the source document for the concepts that are included in this course. The course description uses the 2001 Bloom taxonomy to order learning objectives.

docs.title: List of Concepts
docs.text: We use generative AI to convert the course description into a Concept List. Each concept is in the form of a short Title Case label with most labels under 32 characters long.

docs.title: Concept Dependency List
docs.text: We next use generative AI to create a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). DAGs do not have cycles where concepts depend on themselves. We provide the DAG in two formats. One is a CSV file and the other format is a JSON file that uses the vis-network JavaScript library format. The vis-network format uses nodes, edges and metadata elements with edges containing from and to properties. This makes it easy for you to view and edit the learning graph using an editor built with the vis-network tools.

docs.title: Course Description Quality Assessment
docs.text:
This report rates the overall quality of the course description for the purpose of generating a learning graph.

  • Course description fields and content depth analysis
  • Validates course description has sufficient depth for generating 300-600 concepts
  • Compares course description against similar courses
  • Identifies content gaps and strengths
  • Suggests areas of improvement View the Course Description Quality Assessment

docs.title: Learning Graph Quality Validation
docs.text:
This report gives you an overall assessment of the quality of the learning graph. It uses graph algorithms to look for specific quality patterns in the graph.

  • Graph structure validation - all concepts are connected
  • DAG validation (no cycles detected)
  • Foundational concepts: 6 entry points
  • Indegree distribution analysis
  • Longest dependency chains
  • Connectivity: percent of nodes connected to the main cluster

View the Learning Graph Quality Validation

docs.title: Concept Taxonomy
docs.text:
In order to see patterns in the learning graph, it is useful to assign colors to each concept based on the concept type. We use generative AI to create about a dozen categories for our concepts and then place each concept into a single primary classifier.

  • A concept classifier taxonomy with approximately 12 categories (+/- 1 or 2)
  • Category organization - foundational elements first, course capstone project ideas last
  • Balanced categories (3.5% - 15% each)
  • All categories under 30% threshold
  • Pedagogical flow recommendations
  • Clear 3-5 letter abbreviations for use in CSV file
  • A Miscellaneous (MOSC) category is sometimes added View the Concept Taxonomy

docs.title: Taxonomy Distribution
docs.text:
This reports shows how many concepts fit into each category of the taxonomy. Our goal is a somewhat balanced taxonomy where each category holds an equal number of concepts. We also don't want any category to contain over 30% of our concepts.

  • Statistical breakdown
  • Detailed concept listing by category
  • Visual distribution table
  • Balance verification

View the Taxonomy Distribution Report

docs.title: Course Description Assessment
docs.text: Skill: Course Description Analyzer, version 0.05 Assessed file: Course Description

docs.title: Overall Score: 98/100
docs.text: Quality rating: Excellent. Ready for learning graph generation.

docs.title: Detailed Scoring Breakdown
docs.text: Element Points earned Points possible Notes Title 5 5 Clear and descriptive Target Audience 4 5 Specific roles named, but the range from K-12 teachers to librarians is broad Prerequisites 5 5 Stated as "None", with a note on helpful experience Main Topics Covered 9 10 Comprehensive, but 18 topics is above the ideal 5 to 10 Topics Excluded 5 5 Six clear boundaries Learning Outcomes Header 5 5 "After completing this course, students will be able to:" Remember Level 10 10 Six specific outcomes Understand Level 10 10 Six specific outcomes Apply Level 10 10 Six specific outcomes Analyze Level 10 10 Six specific outcomes Evaluate Level 10 10 Six specific outcomes Create Level 10 10 Six outcomes plus a capstone project Descriptive Context 5 5 Three paragraphs on why and how Total 98 100

docs.title: Gap Analysis
docs.text:
• Target Audience (4 of 5): four roles are named (K-12 teachers, college instructors, instructional designers, librarians and OER coordinators). The reading level and examples may need to favor one group. This slightly weakens the audience signal the learning graph uses to set concept depth.
  • Main Topics (9 of 10): the 18 topics are all relevant, but several overlap, such as the two metric topics and the two A/B testing topics. Overlap can produce duplicate concepts in the graph.

Two gaps are not scored by the rubric but matter for the book:

  • The 10 metrics have no scoring scale yet. The description names them and gives 10 points each, but does not say what earns a 10, a 5, or a 0. Chapters and the AI-agent prompts will need this.
  • The metrics are a proposal. They were drafted for the MNOP Pathfinder grant proposal, not taken from a published standard. The author should confirm or revise them.

docs.title: Improvement Suggestions
docs.text:
1. Define the scoring scale for each metric, with a short description of a 10, a 5, and a 0. This is the highest-value addition, because most chapters and sims depend on it.
  2. Merge overlapping topics if the learning graph comes out with duplicate concepts. For example, combine "Manual A/B testing" and "Analyzing A/B test results".
  3. Pick a primary audience for examples, for instance K-12 teachers, and note that the other roles can follow the same method.
  4. Cite external standards where the rubric borrows from them: the 5R permissions, WCAG 2.1 AA, Dublin Core, and Creative Commons licenses.

docs.title: Concept Generation Readiness
docs.text:
Estimated concepts: about 220 to 280.

  • The 18 topics, at roughly 10 to 15 learnable concepts each, give about 180 to 270.
  • The 10 metrics each suggest several concepts of their own, such as the evidence a score needs, common failure cases, and fixes.
  • The Bloom's outcomes add process concepts, such as calibration, agreement, and error types.
  • This is an estimate. The learning-graph generator may find fewer after removing duplicates.

The description should support the 200-concept goal. If the generator falls short, the first place to add detail is the metric scoring scales.

docs.text: The score is at least 85, so the course description is ready to proceed with learning graph generation. Run the learning-graph-generator skill next.

docs.title: OER Evaluator Instructor's Guide
docs.text: Welcome to the instructor's guide for OER Evaluator: Evaluating and Improving Open Educational Resources with AI Agents. This guide explains every feature of the textbook, how to use it in a course or workshop, and how to make your own customized copy. No technical background is assumed. Every technical term is defined before it is used.

docs.title: What Is an Intelligent Textbook?
docs.text: An intelligent textbook is a digital textbook that goes beyond static text and images. It adds interactive simulations, self-check quizzes, a searchable glossary, and a structured map of how concepts depend on each other. The goal is a richer experience than a printed book can give.

docs.title: The Five Levels of Intelligent Textbooks
docs.text:
Intelligent textbooks fall into five levels, based on how interactive and adaptive they are:

Level Name Description Example Features Level 1 Static Digital A PDF or basic web version of a print textbook Text and images only Level 2 Interactive Adds simulations, quizzes, and searchable glossaries MicroSims, self-check quizzes, concept search Level 3 Adaptive Adjusts content to student performance Personalized learning paths Level 4 AI-Assisted Includes an AI tutor that answers student questions Chatbot integration, automated feedback Level 5 Fully Adaptive AI Learns from student interactions and optimizes itself Real-time content generation

This textbook is a Level 2 Interactive Intelligent Textbook. It has 51 MicroSims, a quiz for every chapter, a glossary, a FAQ, and a learning graph. It does not track individual students or adapt to them.

docs.title: What Makes This Textbook Different
docs.text:
• A repeatable method. The book teaches one 10-metric rubric (five quality metrics and five reusability metrics, 10 points each) and applies it by hand, then with AI agents.
  • Evidence over opinion. Every chapter asks learners to name the evidence behind a score. The skill matters most when checking an AI agent's confident answer.
  • Improvement, not just judgment. Later chapters use AI agents to raise a resource's score, then test whether the change helped with a manual A/B test with students.
  • Interactive MicroSims. Learners manipulate small models in the browser with no software to install.
  • A learning graph. A visual map of all 351 concepts and their prerequisites.
  • A mascot. Echo the Loon, a friendly guide who appears in the student chapters.
  • Free and open. The book is licensed CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, so you may copy and adapt it for non-commercial teaching.

docs.title: Who Should Use This Book
docs.text:
The target audience is teachers (K-12 and college), instructional designers, librarians, and OER coordinators who select, adapt, or create open educational resources. There are no prerequisites. Readers should be comfortable with a web browser and a word processor. Experience with an AI chat assistant helps but is not required, because the book teaches the AI-agent skills it uses.

The Course Description lists the learning outcomes, organized by the six levels of the 2001 Bloom taxonomy, and the topics the book deliberately does not cover.

docs.title: Chapter Structure
docs.text:
The book has 19 chapters in a deliberate sequence. Each chapter builds on earlier ones, so learners should work through them in order.

Chapters Topic Area 1 Foundations: what OER are, the 5R permissions, adopt/adapt/create 2 Open licenses and attribution 3 The 10-metric rubric and scoring 4 Open file formats and version control 5-8 Quality metrics: accuracy and currency, alignment and readability, accessibility, practice and feedback 9-10 Reusability metrics: modularity and metadata, portability and reuse 11 Manual evaluation and adoption decisions 12-14 AI agents: prompts and rubric scoring, automated checks, cost and privacy, checking and calibrating agent output 15 Improving a resource with AI agents 16-17 Designing and analyzing an A/B test with students 18 Reusable components and publishing OER 19 Training teachers and certifying reviewers

The List of Chapters shows every chapter with its summary.

docs.title: What Each Chapter Contains
docs.text:
1. Front matter. Metadata at the top of the file (title, description, version). Students do not see it. Search engines and the site builder do.
  2. Summary. A short overview of what the chapter covers.
  3. Concepts covered. The specific concepts from the learning graph that the chapter addresses.
  4. Prerequisites. Links to earlier chapters.
  5. Main content. The core material, with tables, worked examples, and embedded MicroSims.
  6. Mascot admonitions. Short callout boxes from Echo (see Meet Echo below).
  7. Key takeaways. A numbered summary of the most important ideas.
  8. Quiz and references. Separate pages linked under each chapter in the left navigation.

docs.title: Suggested Classroom Use
docs.text:
• Before class. Assign the chapter as reading. The MicroSims keep independent reading active.
  • During class. Project a MicroSim and ask learners to predict what happens when you move a slider, then test the prediction.
  • After class. Assign the chapter quiz as a self-check, then have learners apply the rubric to a real resource.
  • Pacing. Plan roughly two to three class periods (90 to 135 minutes) per chapter. Chapters with more MicroSims take longer. For a short course, see the formats below.

docs.title: Course Formats
docs.text:
Format Suggested Path One-day workshop Chapters 1-3, 11, 15 and a hands-on scoring practice. See the workshop materials and the Sample One-Day Schedule. Manual-evaluation unit Chapters 1-11 with the Sample Rubric Worksheet AI-agent unit Chapters 12-15 after learners can score by hand Research or capstone project Chapters 16-17, designing and analyzing an A/B test Reviewer training Chapter 19, built on the earlier chapters

Teach the manual rubric first

Learners who score by hand before using an AI agent can tell when the agent is wrong. Chapter 14 depends on that skill.

docs.title: What Is a MicroSim?
docs.text: A MicroSim (micro-simulation) is a small interactive model that runs in a web browser. Learners change one or more variables with sliders, buttons, or drag-and-drop and see the result immediately. No software installation is needed. MicroSims work in any modern browser (Chrome, Firefox, Safari, Edge) on a computer, tablet, or phone.

docs.title: How MicroSims Are Embedded
docs.text:
MicroSims appear in the chapter text as rectangular interactive areas. They are embedded with an iframe, a web feature that shows one web page inside another. You do not need to understand iframes. The MicroSim loads automatically when a learner opens the page.

The book has 51 MicroSims. Browse them all on the MicroSims list. A few examples:

MicroSim What It Teaches Creative Commons License Switches How each license element changes what you may do Total Score Calculator How ten metric scores combine into one 100-point total Weak and Strong Prompt Why specific prompts produce better agent scoring Inter-Rater Agreement Explorer How to measure whether two reviewers agree Five Confounders What can spoil an A/B test

docs.title: Tips for Using MicroSims in Class
docs.text:
1. Project them. Ask learners to call out a prediction before you change a control.
  2. Let learners explore. After a demonstration, give them five to ten minutes to experiment on their own devices.
  3. Reset and retry. Encourage learners to reset a MicroSim and try a different scenario.
  4. Return to the text. Each MicroSim sits near the concept it illustrates. After exploring, have learners re-read the surrounding text.
  5. Internet required. MicroSims load from the website. For offline use, build the site locally (see "Customizing Your Own Textbook" below).

docs.title: Embedding a MicroSim in Your Own Page
docs.text:
You can add any MicroSim to a Google Site, a WordPress blog, a learning management system (LMS) such as Canvas or Schoology, or a plain HTML file. Paste one line of HTML:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/oer-evaluator/sims/YOUR-MICROSIM-NAME/main.html"
    width="100%" height="450px"
    scrolling="no">
</iframe>

Replace YOUR-MICROSIM-NAME with the folder name of any MicroSim, for example cc-license-switches. Some LMS platforms block iframes. If yours does, link to the MicroSim page instead.

docs.title: MicroSim Specifications
docs.text: Each MicroSim has its own lesson page with a description, the learning objective, the controls, and lesson-plan ideas. Use these pages for planning and to see the teaching intent behind each simulation.

docs.title: Using the Glossary
docs.text:
The glossary is an alphabetical list of the book's 351 key terms, each with a short, precise definition. Learners reach it from the Glossary link in the left navigation or from the search bar at the top of any page. The browser's find command (Ctrl+F or Cmd+F) finds a term on the glossary page.

Ways to use it in class:

  • Vocabulary preview. Before a chapter, have learners look up its key terms.
  • Definition matching. Run a warm-up where learners match definitions to terms.
  • Student-written definitions. Learners write their own definitions after reading, then compare them with the glossary.
  • Quick quizzes. Use terms for flash cards or short formative checks.

docs.title: Using the FAQ
docs.text:
The FAQ (Frequently Asked Questions) holds 100 questions that learners and reviewers commonly ask about evaluating OER, grouped by topic. Answers are written at the same reading level as the chapters.

  • Discussion starters. Pick two or three questions, have learners discuss, then reveal the answer.
  • Homework support. Point learners to the FAQ for questions outside class.
  • Extension reading. The FAQ covers angles that the chapter text skips.
  • Test review. Learners can use it as a study guide.

docs.title: Using the Quizzes
docs.text:
Every chapter has a quiz page with ten multiple-choice questions, 190 in all. Open the Quiz link under a chapter in the left navigation. Learners click a question to reveal the answer and explanation after trying it.

Quizzes are not graded automatically. They are formative self-checks, not summative tests.

  • Exit tickets. Have learners take the quiz at the end of a session.
  • Pre-reading check. Assign it before the chapter to see what learners already know.
  • Post-reading review. Use it to find concepts that need re-teaching.
  • Pair discussion. Learners discuss each question before revealing the answer.
  • Question bank. Reuse the questions in your own assessments. The license permits it, with attribution and under the same license.

docs.title: Bloom's Taxonomy Levels
docs.text:
Each quiz question is tagged with a Bloom's Taxonomy level. Bloom's Taxonomy classifies thinking skills from simple to complex:

Level Name What It Means Example Verbs L1 Remember Recall facts and definitions Define, list, name L2 Understand Explain concepts in your own words Explain, describe, compare L3 Apply Use concepts to solve problems Calculate, demonstrate, solve L4 Analyze Break down and examine relationships Differentiate, organize L5 Evaluate Make judgments based on criteria Assess, justify, critique L6 Create Produce original work Design, construct, propose

The quizzes target mostly levels L1 to L4. Rubric scoring practice, agent-output checks, and the A/B test design in the later chapters reach L5 and L6.

docs.title: Using the References
docs.text: Each chapter has an Annotated References page with about ten sources for further reading. Each entry gives the title, a link, and a note on why the source is useful. Wikipedia articles come first for stability and access, followed by authoritative books and papers.

docs.title: A Note About Link Rot
docs.text:
Link rot happens when a web link stops working because the page moved or was deleted. Wikipedia links are stable, but some others may age. If a link is broken:

  1. Search for the article title on the source's website.
  2. Look for an archived copy in the Wayback Machine.
  3. Report it as a GitHub Issue (see "Feedback" below).

A good exercise

Checking whether a link still works is itself an OER evaluation skill (accuracy and currency, Chapter 5). Ask learners to audit a reference page.

docs.title: What Is a Learning Graph?
docs.text:
A learning graph is a map showing how the concepts in a textbook depend on each other. It is a DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph): a diagram of nodes joined by one-way arrows, with no loops. An arrow from concept A to concept B means "understand A before B."

This book's graph has 351 concepts in 14 categories. Open the Learning Graph section of the left navigation to explore it and to see the quality reports.

docs.title: How Teachers Can Use the Learning Graph
docs.text:
• Prerequisite checking. Before teaching a concept, confirm that learners have covered what it depends on.
  • Remediation. When a learner struggles, trace back through the prerequisites to find the gap.
  • Curriculum mapping. Compare the graph with your syllabus to find coverage gaps.
  • Enrichment. Advanced learners can follow the graph forward to concepts beyond the current chapter.

docs.text: Report What It Tells You Course Description Assessment How complete the course description is Concept Enumeration The full list of 351 concepts Graph Quality Analysis Whether the graph is a valid DAG and how well connected it is Concept Taxonomy The 14 concept categories Taxonomy Distribution Report How concepts spread across categories Book Metrics Chapters, words, MicroSims, quizzes, and other totals Chapter Metrics The same measures chapter by chapter Glossary Quality Report, FAQ Quality Report, Quiz Generation Report Quality checks on the supporting content

docs.title: Echo the Loon: The Pedagogical Agent
docs.text:
A pedagogical agent is a character who appears in a textbook to guide learners. Research on the persona effect suggests that such characters improve engagement and learners' perception of the material.

This book's agent is Echo the Loon, who carries a magnifying glass and asks, "What is the evidence?" Echo's catchphrase is "Let's dive in and check the evidence!" See Meet Echo for the full character sheet.

Echo appears as colored callout boxes (called admonitions) in student chapters. There are seven types:

Type Purpose Where It Appears Welcome Introduces the chapter Chapter opening Thinking Highlights a key insight Occasionally Tip Shares practical advice As the material warrants Warning Alerts to a common mistake As the material warrants Encourage Supports learners on harder concepts Where learners may struggle Celebration Marks progress Chapter ending Neutral General note Rarely

Echo is used sparingly and never twice in a row. This instructor-facing guide does not use Echo.

Tips for teachers:

  • Read Echo's tips aloud. They are written in a calm, conversational voice.
  • Use "thinking" boxes as discussion prompts. They mark the most important insights.
  • Point frustrated learners to "encourage" boxes.

The Mascot Rendering Test page shows all seven styles.

docs.title: Reporting Issues and Suggestions
docs.text:
This book is an open-source project on GitHub, a website where projects are built collaboratively. You do not need to program to report a problem.

A GitHub Issue works like a support ticket. Each issue has a number and can be discussed by the author and the community.

  1. Go to the GitHub repository.
  2. Click the Issues tab.
  3. Click the green New issue button.
  4. Give a clear title, such as "Broken link in Chapter 5 references".
  5. In the description, say which page has the problem, what you expected, what you saw, and your browser and device if relevant.
  6. Click Submit new issue.

A free GitHub account is required. If you prefer not to make one, use the Contact page.

Welcome feedback includes typos and factual errors, broken links, MicroSim bugs, content suggestions, and accessibility problems.

docs.title: What Is a Creative Commons License?
docs.text: A license is a legal document that says what others may do with a work. A Creative Commons (CC) license is a standard, plain-language license used for educational and creative content. This is the same kind of license that the book teaches learners to read.

docs.title: This Textbook's License
docs.text:
The book uses CC BY-NC-SA 4.0:

Code Full Name What It Means CC Creative Commons A standard open license BY Attribution You must credit the author NC NonCommercial You may not use the material to make money SA ShareAlike If you modify it, you must share it under the same license 4.0 Version 4.0 The current version of the license

docs.title: What You Can Do
docs.text:
• Copy the book or single chapters for your learners.
  • Share the link with colleagues, learners, or parents.
  • Print chapters for classroom use.
  • Modify the content: add examples, remove sections, reorder chapters.
  • Translate it into other languages.
  • Build a derivative version based on this one.

docs.title: What You Cannot Do
docs.text:
• Sell the book or charge learners for access.
  • Remove attribution. You must credit the original author, Dan McCreary.
  • Use a different license. A modified version must stay CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.
  • Claim it as your own work.

Check the NonCommercial line before a paid workshop

"NonCommercial" has gray areas, and Chapter 2 covers them. If you charge a fee for a workshop that uses this book, read the license and the NonCommercial chapter material first, or ask the author.

See the Creative Commons License page for the full legal text.

docs.title: Customizing Your Own Textbook
docs.text: You can make your own customized copy. This section explains how, step by step.

docs.title: Key Technical Terms
docs.text:
• Repository (repo). A folder on GitHub that holds all of a project's files.
  • Git. A tool that tracks changes to files and who made them.
  • Clone. A complete copy of a repository on your own computer.
  • Fork. A complete copy of a repository in your own GitHub account.
  • MkDocs. The software that turns the book's Markdown files into a website.
  • Markdown. A simple text format. **bold** makes bold, # Heading makes a heading, and - makes a bullet point.
  • mkdocs.yml. The main settings file for the site. It controls the title, navigation, colors, and enabled features.

docs.title: Step 1: Create a GitHub Account
docs.text: If you do not have one, create a free account at github.com.

docs.title: Step 2: Fork or Clone the Repository
docs.text:
Option A: Fork (easier, stays on GitHub)

  1. Go to the repository.
  2. Click Fork in the upper right.
  3. You now have a copy in your own account that you can edit.

Option B: Clone (more control, works on your computer)

  1. Install Git from git-scm.com.
  2. Open a terminal (Command Prompt on Windows, Terminal on Mac).
  3. Run:
git clone https://github.com/dmccreary/oer-evaluator.git

docs.title: Step 3: Make Changes
docs.text: All content lives in the docs/ folder as Markdown (.md) files. Edit them with any text editor.

docs.title: Change the Title and Description
docs.text:
Edit these lines in mkdocs.yml:

site_name: "Your Custom Textbook Title"
site_description: "Your description here"
site_author: "Your Name"

docs.title: Change the Colors
docs.text:
Find the palette section in mkdocs.yml:

theme:
  palette:
    primary: indigo    # try blue, red, purple, teal, green, and others
    accent: orange     # the accent color

docs.title: Change the Logo
docs.text:
Replace the logo file under docs/img/ with your own PNG image, about 128 by 128 pixels.

Keep the license notice

If you share your customized version, keep the CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 notice and credit the original author.

docs.title: Step 4: Preview Your Changes
docs.text:
1. Install Python (3.8 or newer) from python.org.

  2. Install MkDocs and the Material theme:

    pip install mkdocs mkdocs-material

  3. In the project folder, start the preview server:

    cd oer-evaluator
mkdocs serve

  4. Open http://127.0.0.1:8000/oer-evaluator/ in your browser.

The preview refreshes each time you save a file.

docs.title: Step 5: Publish Your Version
docs.text:
To publish as a free website with GitHub Pages:

mkdocs gh-deploy

This publishes to https://YOUR-USERNAME.github.io/oer-evaluator/ in about one to two minutes.

docs.title: What Is Web Analytics?
docs.text: Web analytics measures how visitors use a website: which pages they visit, how long they stay, and where they come from. For a textbook, it shows which chapters are read and which MicroSims are used.

docs.title: Google Analytics
docs.text:
This book uses Google Analytics, a free Google service. The author's property is already set up. If you make your own copy, create your own so that your learners' visits are not mixed in with the author's.

  1. Go to analytics.google.com and sign in.
  2. Create a property (Google's word for a tracked website).
  3. Google gives you a Measurement ID that looks like G-XXXXXXXXXX.

  4. Put it in mkdocs.yml:

    extra:
  analytics:
    provider: google
    property: G-YOUR-MEASUREMENT-ID

  5. Rebuild and deploy. Data appears within 24 to 48 hours.

What you can learn: most and least visited chapters, time on page, phone versus computer use, and where visitors are located.

docs.title: xAPI Monitoring (Advanced)
docs.text:
xAPI (Experience API) is a standard for recording detailed learning activity, such as "the learner answered question 3 correctly." An LRS (Learning Record Store) is the database that holds those records.

Student privacy laws apply

Before collecting data that can identify individual learners, know the rules that apply to you:

  • FERPA (Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act), a U.S. law that protects student education records.
  • COPPA (Children's Online Privacy Protection Act), a U.S. law with extra limits for children under 13.
  • State laws. Many U.S. states add their own student privacy rules.
  • GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation), a European Union law that applies if any learner is in the EU.

The Google Analytics setup above is anonymous by default: it counts page views, not individual people. That is the safest choice. If you want per-learner tracking, talk to your school or district data privacy officer first.

docs.title: How the Quality Score Is Computed
docs.text:
The score is computed by script from mechanical checks only. It does not measure whether a question is ambiguous, and a human read of the questions is still the best check of that.

Component Points How it is scored Format, links, and anchors 20 All 190 questions pass the format check, and every See: link points to an existing heading Answer balance 15 Full points when each letter is correct 2 or 3 times in the chapter Bloom's distribution 25 Reduced by the number of questions that are off the chapter type's target mix Concept coverage 20 Distinct concepts tested, relative to the smaller of 10 and the chapter's concept count Explanation length 10 Share of explanations between 50 and 110 words Distractor length balance 10 Reduced when the correct option is both the longest and 25 percent or more above the average distractor

docs.title: Distractor Length Review
docs.text:
The first drafts made the correct option the longest in 148 of 190 questions, and in 130 of them the correct option was at least 25 percent longer than the average distractor. That is a cue that a test-wise student can use without knowing the content, and Chapter 8 of this book teaches reviewers to flag it. Five passes of revision lengthened the distractors, shortened over-long correct options, and rotated which option is longest.

After revision, the correct option is the longest in 81 of 190 questions, the correct option is at least 25 percent longer than the average distractor in 1 questions, and the correct option averages 1.06 times the length of the average distractor. The correct option is the longest in no more than 5 of 10 questions in any chapter.

docs.title: Explanation Quality
docs.text: Explanations run from 59 to 91 words and average 79 words. Every question has an explanation that confirms the correct option, a Concept Tested label that matches a concept in the chapter's own table, and a See link to a heading in the chapter. Many explanations also say why a distractor is wrong.

docs.title: Recommendations
docs.text:
1. Read the quizzes as a student would. The checks above are mechanical. An author's read for ambiguity and for a second defensible answer is the check that matters most, and it has not been done.
  2. Consider a second quiz for long chapters. Chapters 2, 3, 6, 7, 9, 12, 14, 15, and 18 list 22 or more concepts, and ten questions test fewer than half of them. A bank of 15 to 20 questions per chapter would test more, and the question bank would let a site draw a different ten each time.
  3. Review the Evaluate and Create questions. Only 9 of 190 questions are at those levels, because the target mix for chapters 4 to 13 allows none. The course description lists Evaluate and Create outcomes, and a multiple-choice question tests them only in part. Pair these quizzes with the improvement challenge and the capstone.
  4. Add difficulty data after use. The difficulty field in quiz-bank.json is derived from the Bloom level. After students take the quizzes, replace it with the share of students who answered correctly.
  5. Keep the quizzes in step with the chapters. The Concept Tested labels and See links depend on the chapter headings, so re-check them, and run mkdocs build --strict, after a chapter is edited.

docs.title: Infographic Poster Ideas
docs.text:
This page lists ideas for infographic posters for OER Evaluator. The book has two poster-style MicroSims but no overlay infographic posters yet. I read the outlines of all 19 chapters and their worked-example tables, and looked for places where a reader has to hold a comparison or a multi-part idea in mind from prose. Each idea below turns one of those into a single picture that can be understood at a glance and then explored.

Each poster is meant to be wrapped by an interactive overlay, so a reader can hover or click for detail and take a short quiz. Two overlay types are used:

  • Grid: two to six large rectangular zones, side by side. Best for comparisons. Printed zone headings can be part of the artwork.
  • Callout: five to fifteen numbered markers on one illustration. Best for anatomy and process. The artwork should contain no text, because the overlay supplies every label.

Many chapters already have a MicroSim that practices the same idea by sorting or matching. A poster does a different job: it is the reference picture a reader comes back to. Where an idea overlaps a MicroSim, the entry says so, and the poster's quiz mode can reuse that MicroSim's items. Chapter 2 has no entry because the Six Creative Commons Licenses Poster already covers its main comparison, and Chapter 11 has none because its decision rule is covered by poster 4.

Tips that apply to every poster:

  • One idea per poster, and the title states it. A reader should get the point in about ten seconds. Everything else belongs in the overlay.
  • Use a wide landscape canvas, such as 1200 by 700 pixels, which suits the side-navigation layout of this book.
  • Copy rules and numbers from the chapter. Do not round, recompute, or reword them. Where the chapter marks an example as illustrative, the poster must say so too.
  • Choose the production route by how exact the content must be. Image models garble text and numbers. Draw anything with exact values, such as radar charts, bell curves, and tables of counts, in code (SVG, Chart.js, or Plotly) and export it as the poster image. Use a generated illustration only when it carries no text, and let the overlay add the labels.
  • Build the poster to pass the rubric it teaches. Reviewers will score each poster as a component. Give it alt text and a long description in its lesson page, text contrast of at least 4.5 to 1, and a meaning that never depends on color alone (add an icon, shape, or word). Keep the editable source (the SVG or the image prompt plus data.json), a metadata.json record, and an iframe-ready main.html.
  • Use the same two colors for the same two ideas in every poster. Pick one for quality metrics and one for reusability metrics, and keep them. Pair every traffic-light color with an icon.
  • Keep Echo the Loon off the artwork. Echo belongs in the mascot admonition on the lesson page, where the placement rules in CONTENT-GENERATION-GUIDE.md apply.
  • Avoid brand logos and real interface screenshots. They age quickly and raise trademark questions. Draw generic stand-ins.
