        height="789px"
        width="100%"
        scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Teachers over-trust a clean scan, and "the scan passed" does not mean "the resource is accessible". This poster pairs what each tool finds with what it misses, taken from the Chapter 13 table. Every tool is drawn with a beam of light that lights some items and leaves others dark. The "cannot find" half has the same visual weight as the "finds" half, shaded and dotted. A footer reminds the reader to keep a human in the loop.

This MicroSim is a grid overlay: the poster is a drawing made for this book (SVG), and each zone is a clickable rectangle over it.

Zone What it shows Link checker Finds: links that return errors; links that have moved. Cannot find: a working link that leads to the wrong content. Accessibility scan Finds: missing alt attributes; weak contrast; missing labels. Cannot find: whether alt text is useful; whether captions are accurate. License detection Finds: missing license statements; mismatched license statements; unrecognized license statements. Cannot find: whether the license claim is true. Readability scan Finds: a reading level for each passage. Cannot find: undefined terms; dense ideas; audience fit.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
• Explore and Quiz Me buttons: switch modes. Quiz Me starts a new run.
  • The zones: hover over a zone or press it to read its summary and facts in the panel below the poster.
  • Quiz questions: read the question, then press the zone that answers it. A wrong press lets you try again.
  • Try Again: repeats the quiz after the last question.

docs.title: Good to Know
docs.text:
Quiz mode scores each question as you answer it. The MicroSim does not store your answers. The poster prints its own headings, so the sim adds no labels on top of it.

  • The poster keeps the chapter's wording and shows only the checks the book already uses.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can state what each of four automated checks can find and what it cannot, and explain why a clean scan is not a finished review. (Bloom level: Analyze.)

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Adult learners: teachers (K-12 and college), instructional designers, librarians, and OER coordinators.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 5-10 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Automated checks and the human in the loop from Chapter 13.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (3 min). Press each tool. What is the one thing it cannot find?
  2. Quiz (3 min). Press Quiz Me and match four findings to the tools.
  3. Plan (4 min). For a resource of yours, list one check you would automate and the human check that must follow it.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer against the poster.

  1. A link checker reports no broken links. What can it not tell you? (Whether a working link leads to the wrong content.)
  2. Can an accessibility scan tell you whether alt text is useful? (No. It finds missing alt attributes, not whether the text is useful.)
  3. What can a readability scan not find? (Undefined terms, dense ideas, and audience fit.)

docs.title: Connection to the OER Evaluator rubric
docs.text: Pairing what each tool finds with what it misses motivates the human check that Chapter 14 formalizes.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Human-in-the-loop - Wikipedia - Describes systems in which a person reviews or corrects an automated process. Background for the chapter's rule that a human checks the agent's evidence before any score is accepted.
  2. Web Accessibility Evaluation Tools List - W3C Web Accessibility Initiative - A filterable directory of accessibility checkers by purpose, platform, price, and standard. Helps readers choose the automated accessibility checks this chapter recommends.
  3. Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA) - U.S. Department of Education - The Student Privacy Policy Office's official FERPA page, with guidance for schools and teachers on education records and disclosure. The primary source for the chapter's privacy rules.

docs.title: Bloom's Ladder: Six Levels, Measurable Verbs
docs.text:
Run the Bloom's Ladder: Six Levels, Measurable Verbs MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 6: Alignment and Readability

To change the content, edit data.json in this folder. The artwork is bloom-ladder.svg, and scripts/posters/specs/ holds the code that draws it.

You can add this MicroSim to any web page with this iframe:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/oer-evaluator/sims/bloom-ladder/main.html"
        height="717px"
        width="100%"
        scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The alignment metric, the outcome verb checks, the quiz bank, and this book's own learning outcomes all use Bloom's levels, so this poster is a reference to come back to. It uses the 2001 revised names. The verbs are the largest text on each step because they are what a writer or auditor actually uses. A side panel shows the mismatch the chapter warns about: an outcome that says "predict" taught by activities that ask only for recall.

This MicroSim is a grid overlay: the poster is a drawing made for this book (SVG), and each zone is a clickable rectangle over it.

Zone What it shows Remember Remember: recall facts and terms. Understand Understand: explain ideas in your own words. Apply Apply: use knowledge in a new situation. Analyze Analyze: break material into parts and see how they relate. Evaluate Evaluate: judge using criteria. Create Create: put parts together into something new. Level mismatch An outcome and its activities should sit at the same level.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
• Explore and Quiz Me buttons: switch modes. Quiz Me starts a new run.
  • The zones: hover over a zone or press it to read its summary and facts in the panel below the poster.
  • Quiz questions: read the question, then press the zone that answers it. A wrong press lets you try again.
  • Try Again: repeats the quiz after the last question.

docs.title: Good to Know
docs.text:
Quiz mode scores each question as you answer it. The MicroSim does not store your answers. The poster prints its own headings, so the sim adds no labels on top of it.

  • The poster is a staircase and not a pyramid. The chapter does not claim that fewer outcomes belong at the top.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can name the six levels of the revised Bloom taxonomy in order and match measurable verbs to their levels. (Bloom level: Remember.)

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Adult learners: teachers (K-12 and college), instructional designers, librarians, and OER coordinators.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 5-10 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • The alignment metric from Chapter 6.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (3 min). Press each step and read its verbs and example objective.
  2. Quiz (3 min). Press Quiz Me and find the level for six verbs or examples.
  3. Audit (4 min). Take one outcome from a resource you use. Circle its verb. Which level is it, and do the activities sit at the same level?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer against the poster.

  1. Which level are "explain", "summarize", and "interpret"? (Understand.)
  2. Which level asks learners to put parts together into something new? (Create.)
  3. An outcome says "predict" and every activity asks only for recall. What is wrong? (The outcome and its activities sit at different levels, so learners never practice the skill the outcome asks for.)

docs.title: Connection to the OER Evaluator rubric
docs.text: An outcome and the activities that teach it should sit at the same level. That is the core of the alignment metric.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Bloom's taxonomy - Wikipedia - Describes the original and revised Bloom's taxonomies and their six cognitive levels with example verbs. Supports the chapter's method of matching a resource's activities to the level of its stated outcomes.
  2. Constructive alignment - Wikipedia - Explains John Biggs's principle that outcomes, teaching activities, and assessment should match one another. The idea behind this chapter's alignment metric and its outcome-to-content mapping.
  3. Learning Objectives - Carnegie Mellon Eberly Center - Explains how to write measurable learning objectives with action verbs and how objectives shape assessment and activities. Helps reviewers judge whether a resource's stated objectives are testable.

docs.title: Can I Publish My Improved Version?
docs.text:
Run the Can I Publish My Improved Version? MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 15: Improving a Resource with AI Agents

To change the content, edit data.json in this folder. The artwork is can-i-publish-my-improved-version.svg, and scripts/posters/specs/ holds the code that draws it.

You can add this MicroSim to any web page with this iframe:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/oer-evaluator/sims/can-i-publish-my-improved-version/main.html"
        height="741px"
        width="100%"
        scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
An agent's edited copy is a derivative work, so the license must be read before the first edit. This poster answers one practical question for each license in the Chapter 15 table: may you publish an improved version, and what must you do? The cards run from most to least permissive. Each has the same rows: the license name, a verdict, and the duties. The verdict has three states, shown with a symbol and a word as well as color: yes, yes with conditions, and no. A footer band covers the last row of the table: with no license, all rights are reserved, so ask the owner first. The poster prints the license names as text and does not redraw the official Creative Commons icons.

This MicroSim is a grid overlay: the poster is a drawing made for this book (SVG), and each zone is a clickable rectangle over it.

Zone What it shows CC0 Yes: Nothing is required, and giving credit is good practice. CC BY Yes, with conditions: Credit the author, link to the license, and say that you changed the work. CC BY-SA Yes, with conditions: The same as CC BY, and release your version under CC BY-SA. CC BY-NC Yes, without commercial use: The same as CC BY, and do not sell or use it for commercial gain. CC BY-NC-SA Yes, without commercial use: The same as CC BY, release under CC BY-NC-SA, and do not use it commercially. CC BY-ND No: You may not share a changed version. You may make changes for your own private use only. No license, all rights reserved No. Ask the owner for permission first.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
• Explore and Quiz Me buttons: switch modes. Quiz Me starts a new run.
  • The zones: hover over a zone or press it to read its summary and facts in the panel below the poster.
  • Quiz questions: read the question, then press the zone that answers it. A wrong press lets you try again.
  • Try Again: repeats the quiz after the last question.

docs.title: Good to Know
docs.text:
Quiz mode scores each question as you answer it. The MicroSim does not store your answers. The poster prints its own headings, so the sim adds no labels on top of it.

  • The chapter's table has no row for CC BY-NC-ND, so the poster has none either. The author decides whether to add that row to the chapter and the poster together.
  • Add the official Creative Commons icons only by following Creative Commons' guidance on its marks. This poster uses text.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can decide whether an improved version of a resource may be published under its license, and state what you must do. (Bloom level: Apply.)

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Adult learners: teachers (K-12 and college), instructional designers, librarians, and OER coordinators.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 5-10 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • The six Creative Commons licenses from Chapter 2 and derivative works from Chapter 15.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (3 min). Press each card from left to right. Where does the answer change from yes to no?
  2. Quiz (3 min). Press Quiz Me and match four situations to the cards.
  3. Apply (4 min). Find the license on a resource you want to improve. Read its card and write the notice you would add to your version.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer against the poster.

  1. A resource is CC BY-ND. May you publish your improved version? (No. You may make changes for your own private use only.)
  2. A resource is CC BY-SA. What must you do? (The same as CC BY, and release your version under CC BY-SA.)
  3. A resource has no license. May you publish an improved version? (No. All rights are reserved, so ask the owner for permission first.)

docs.title: Connection to the OER Evaluator rubric
docs.text: This poster saves effort by stopping work on a resource that cannot be legally shared once improved. Read the license before the first edit.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Derivative work - Wikipedia - Explains how a work based on another is treated in copyright law. Background for the chapter's check of what a license allows before an agent changes a resource.
  2. Marking Your Work with a CC License - CC Public Wiki - Shows how to place a license notice on a work. This is the step needed when a revised version is published.
  3. About CC Licenses - Creative Commons - Official overview of the six licenses, with plain-language summaries of the conditions each carries. The authoritative reference for what BY, SA, NC, and ND permit and require.
  4. Compatible Licenses - Creative Commons - Explains which Creative Commons licenses may be combined in an adaptation and which license the result may carry. Direct support for checking whether two licenses allow a remix.
  5. License Chooser - Creative Commons - An interactive questionnaire that leads a creator to a suitable license and produces the license statement. Good practice for the chapter's license selection exercise.

docs.title: You Can't Reuse What You Can't Find
docs.text:
Run the You Can't Reuse What You Can't Find MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 9: Modularity and Metadata

To change the content, edit data.json in this folder. The artwork is cant-reuse-what-you-cant-find.svg, and scripts/posters/specs/ holds the code that draws it.

You can add this MicroSim to any web page with this iframe:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/oer-evaluator/sims/cant-reuse-what-you-cant-find/main.html"
        height="741px"
        width="100%"
        scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The principle behind the metadata metric is that you cannot reuse what you cannot find. This poster is a mock search results page for the query from Chapter 9, "watershed grade 6 reading open license", with the chapter's three records as result cards. Resource A has a full record and ranks high. Resource B has only the title "Reading 4", and the search cannot find it. Resource C has a title and an author but no subject, grade, or license, so it may be found, yet the teacher cannot tell the grade or whether she may reuse it. Empty fields show as dashed placeholders. The search page is generic and is not any real search engine.

This MicroSim is a grid overlay: the poster is a drawing made for this book (SVG), and each zone is a clickable rectangle over it.

Zone What it shows Resource A: found, ranks high Yes, and it ranks high. Resource B: not found No: no field mentions a watershed. Resource C: found, but unclear Possibly, but the teacher cannot tell the grade or whether she may reuse it.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
• Explore and Quiz Me buttons: switch modes. Quiz Me starts a new run.
  • The zones: hover over a zone or press it to read its summary and facts in the panel below the poster.
  • Quiz questions: read the question, then press the zone that answers it. A wrong press lets you try again.
  • Try Again: repeats the quiz after the last question.

docs.title: Good to Know
docs.text:
Quiz mode scores each question as you answer it. The MicroSim does not store your answers. The poster prints its own headings, so the sim adds no labels on top of it.

  • The three records come from the Chapter 9 worked example and are illustrative.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can explain why a record with missing metadata is found, not found, or found but unclear for the same search. (Bloom level: Analyze.)

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Adult learners: teachers (K-12 and college), instructional designers, librarians, and OER coordinators.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 5-10 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • The six core metadata fields from Chapter 9.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (3 min). Press each card and read which fields are filled. What does the teacher still not know about card C?
  2. Quiz (3 min). Press Quiz Me and match three outcomes to the three cards.
  3. Fix (4 min). Choose one resource of yours and fill in all six fields. How long did it take?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer against the poster.

  1. Why is resource B not found by the search? (No field mentions a watershed.)
  2. Why is resource C found but unclear? (It has no subject, grade level, or license, so the teacher cannot tell the grade or whether she may reuse it.)
  3. Which six fields make up a core record? (Title, author, subject, grade level, license, and description.)

docs.title: Connection to the OER Evaluator rubric
docs.text: Metadata is metric 8. It is also the cheapest fix in Chapter 15, where adding the missing fields takes half an hour in the chapter's example.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Dublin Core - Wikipedia - Describes the fifteen-element Dublin Core metadata set, its history, and its use in libraries and repositories. The basis of the metadata record taught in this chapter.
  2. Metadata - Wikipedia - Surveys kinds of metadata, standards, and uses, from library catalogs to web pages. Background for scoring whether a resource carries complete, useful metadata.
  3. Metadata Basics - Dublin Core Metadata Initiative - The DCMI introduction to metadata and the Dublin Core style, listing the fifteen core elements such as title, creator, subject, and description. The primary reference for the chapter's core fields.
  4. Learning Resource Metadata Initiative (LRMI) - Dublin Core Metadata Initiative - Describes the vocabulary, maintained by DCMI, that adds educational properties such as alignment to standards and typical age range to resource descriptions. Supports scoring education-specific metadata.

docs.title: Creative Commons Element Explorer
docs.text:
Run the Creative Commons Element Explorer MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 2: Open Licenses and Attribution

To edit the sketch, paste the contents of cc-element-explorer.js into the p5.js editor. The learning content (the items, answers, and reasons) is in the CONFIG block at the top of the file.

You can add this MicroSim to any web page with this iframe:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/oer-evaluator/sims/cc-element-explorer/main.html"
        height="690px"
        width="100%"
        scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
A Creative Commons license is a set of elements. BY (Attribution) is always on. You can add SA (ShareAlike), NC (NonCommercial), and ND (NoDerivatives). SA and ND never appear together, because ShareAlike governs adaptations that NoDerivatives forbids anyone to share.

In explore mode, three switches build a license and the screen shows Yes or No for five actions, with the reason for each No. When you are ready, prediction mode asks eight "Allowed?" questions and makes you commit an answer before it is shown.

Action What it asks A1 Post an unchanged copy on your website, with credit. A2 Post a translated version. A3 Sell printed copies for profit. A4 Publish a remix of it under CC BY. A5 Change it privately for your own use and do not share it.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
• SA, NC, and ND switches: turn each element on or off. Turning on SA while ND is on, or the reverse, shows an explanation instead of changing the license.
  • Start the predictions: leaves explore mode.
  • Yes and No buttons: commit a prediction.
  • Back to explore: on the results screen, returns to the switches.

docs.title: Good to Know
docs.text:
Only your first committed answer on the first completed run counts as evidence of mastery. Practice runs give the same feedback but do not change that first-run score. Nothing moves until you act, and the MicroSim does not store your answers.

  • The actions are illustrative examples. The results follow the 4.0 licenses and are a study aid, not legal advice.
  • A1 is Yes for every license, and A5 is Yes for every license, because no license forbids private changes.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can infer whether each of five actions is allowed under a given Creative Commons license by reasoning from its elements, with at least 7 of 8 predictions correct on the first attempt. (Bloom level: Understand.)

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Adult learners: teachers (K-12 and college), instructional designers, librarians, and OER coordinators.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • The four elements Attribution, ShareAlike, NonCommercial, and NoDerivatives, and the six licenses they form, from Chapter 2.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (5 min). Build all six licenses with the switches. For each, say which actions are No and why.
  2. Find the rule (2 min). Find the two licenses where A2 (a translation) is No, and say what they share.
  3. Predict (5 min). Press Start the predictions and answer all eight questions.
  4. Review (2 min). For each miss, go back to explore mode and rebuild that license.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer by using it.

  1. A translation of a CC BY-ND work: allowed to post? (No. ND forbids sharing a changed version, and a translation is a change.)
  2. Can you sell printed copies of a CC BY-NC work? (No. NC forbids use directed toward monetary compensation.)
  3. Can you privately change a CC BY-NC-ND work? (Yes. ND blocks sharing changed versions, not private changes.)
  4. Why can SA and ND not both be on? (SA governs adaptations that ND forbids anyone to share.)

docs.title: Connection to the OER Evaluator rubric
docs.text: The more elements are on, the lower the license sits on the openness spectrum. Chapter 9 shows how the rubric scores a license along that spectrum.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. About CC Licenses. Creative Commons. Plain-language summaries of what each license permits and requires.
  2. Creative Commons license. Wikipedia. The six main licenses and the BY, SA, NC, and ND conditions.
  3. Compatible Licenses. Creative Commons. Which licenses may be combined in an adaptation.
  4. License Chooser. Creative Commons. A questionnaire that leads a creator to a license.

docs.title: Creative Commons License Switches
docs.text:
Run the Creative Commons License Switches MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 2: Open Licenses and Attribution

To edit the sketch, paste the contents of cc-license-switches.js into the p5.js editor.

You can add this MicroSim to any web page with this iframe:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/oer-evaluator/sims/cc-license-switches/main.html"
        height="562px"
        width="100%"
        scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Picture the elements of a Creative Commons license as switches on a panel. The Attribution (BY) switch is always on, because every Creative Commons license requires credit to the creator. Each other switch you turn on takes a freedom away from the person who receives the work.

This MicroSim gives you the three switches that keep a work open for adaptation:

Switch What it does when you turn it on Freedom taken away BY Attribution Locked on. Credit to the creator is always required. None. This is the baseline of every Creative Commons license. SA ShareAlike Adaptations must carry the same license as the original. Picking the license for your remix. NC NonCommercial The work may not be used for commercial advantage or monetary compensation. Using the work commercially.

Two freedoms never change on this panel: sharing the unchanged work and adapting, translating, or remixing it, both with credit. The four switch positions give four licenses:

Switches on License Freedoms kept BY CC BY 4.0 4 of 4 BY, SA CC BY-SA 4.0 3 of 4 BY, NC CC BY-NC 4.0 3 of 4 BY, NC, SA CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 2 of 4

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
• BY switch (locked): click it and a message explains why it stays on.
  • SA switch: turns the ShareAlike requirement on or off.
  • NC switch: turns the NonCommercial requirement on or off.

Clicking a switch or its label flips it, and the keyboard works too: press Tab to reach a switch and Space to flip it. After each flip the license name changes, the freedom that moved flashes, and a message says what was taken away or given back. A screen reader announces the same result.

docs.title: What the panel leaves out
docs.text:
• NoDerivatives (ND) is not on this panel. ND takes away the freedom to adapt, and it cannot be combined with ShareAlike. Chapter 2 covers all four elements and the six licenses they form.
  • CC0 is a public domain dedication, not a license, so it has no switches.
  • The text follows the 4.0 licenses. Earlier versions differ in small ways, and the panel is a study aid, not legal advice. Read the license deed for the exact terms.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can explain how the ShareAlike and NonCommercial elements each narrow what a person receiving a Creative Commons work may do, and can name the license that results from any setting of the switches. (Bloom level: Understand.)

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Adult learners: teachers (K-12 and college), instructional designers, librarians, and OER coordinators.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 5-10 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• The five R permissions from Chapter 1: retain, reuse, revise, remix, and redistribute.
  • The Attribution, ShareAlike, and NonCommercial requirements as defined in Chapter 2.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Predict (2 min). Before touching a switch, write down which freedom you think NonCommercial takes away and which one ShareAlike takes away.
  2. Explore (3 min). Flip SA and NC in all four combinations. For each license, record its name and how many freedoms are kept.
  3. Locate the extremes (2 min). Find the license that keeps all four freedoms and the one that keeps the fewest. Explain in one sentence what the second one costs the person who receives the work.
  4. Try the locked switch (1 min). Click BY. Explain why Creative Commons does not let you turn it off.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer by flipping the switches.

  1. A district wants to sell printed copies of an openly licensed worksheet. Which of the two optional switches must be off? (NC must be off. NC forbids commercial use.)
  2. A teacher translates a CC BY-SA reading. Under which license must she share the translation? (CC BY-SA, the same license. ShareAlike requires it.)
  3. How many freedoms does CC BY-NC-SA keep on this panel, and which two are taken away? (Two of four. Commercial use and picking the license for a remix.)
  4. Why is the BY switch locked on? (Every Creative Commons license requires credit to the creator.)

docs.title: Connection to the OER Evaluator rubric
docs.text: The more switches are on, the fewer freedoms remain, and the lower a license sits on the openness spectrum. Some definitions of openness are strict: the Open Definition accepts CC BY and CC BY-SA, which allow commercial use, and does not accept the NC licenses. Chapter 9 shows how the rubric scores a resource's license along this spectrum.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Creative Commons: About CC Licenses. Plain-language description of the four license elements and the six licenses.
  2. Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0). Commons Deed.
  3. Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International (CC BY-SA 4.0). Commons Deed.
  4. Attribution-NonCommercial 4.0 International (CC BY-NC 4.0). Commons Deed.
  5. Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 4.0 International (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0). Commons Deed.
  6. Open Definition: Conformant Licenses. Open Knowledge Foundation list of licenses that meet the Open Definition.

docs.title: Following a Claim Back to Its Source
docs.text:
Run the Following a Claim Back to Its Source MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 5: Accuracy and Currency

To change the content, edit data.json in this folder. The artwork is claim-source-chain.svg, and scripts/posters/specs/ holds the code that draws it.

You can add this MicroSim to any web page with this iframe:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/oer-evaluator/sims/claim-source-chain/main.html"
        height="670px"
        width="100%"
        scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Confirming that a citation exists is not the same as tracing the claim. This poster shows the worked example from Chapter 5. The claim "Wetlands filter pollutants" appears in a resource's footnote 4, which cites a textbook, which cites a review article, which summarizes several studies. One of those studies reports measurements of pollutant levels before and after water passed through a wetland. The first three links are other people's summaries. The fourth is where the measurement was made. A red flag at the second link marks the early stop that the poster exists to prevent. The sources are invented for the chapter and are illustrative, so there is nothing to look up.

This MicroSim is a callout overlay: the poster is a drawing made for this book (SVG) with no text in it, and every label comes from the numbered markers.

# Part What it shows 1 Footnote 4 of the resource The claim "Wetlands filter pollutants" appears in the resource. Footnote 4 cites a textbook. This link is someone's summary and is not the original. 2 The textbook The textbook says wetlands filter pollutants and cites a review. A reviewer who stops here, at the red flag, has found only that a textbook agrees with the resource. 3 The review article The review article summarizes several studies of wetland filtering. It is another summary, so it is not the original either. 4 The original study One of those studies reports measurements of pollutant levels before and after water passed through a wetland. This is the original, and the claim is supported by it.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
• Explore and Quiz buttons: switch modes.
  • Numbered markers and labels: hover over a marker or a label to read about that part of the poster.
  • Quiz mode: the labels are hidden. Read the prompt, then press the marker it names. A wrong press lets you try again.
  • Try Again: repeats the quiz after the last question.

docs.title: Good to Know
docs.text:
Quiz mode scores each marker as you answer it. The MicroSim does not store your answers. The artwork carries no text, so every name and number you read comes from the overlay.

  • The chapter's sources are invented for illustration. The poster prints no journal names or citations.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can trace a claim through a chain of citations to its original source and explain why stopping at the first link is not enough. (Bloom level: Analyze.)

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Adult learners: teachers (K-12 and college), instructional designers, librarians, and OER coordinators.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 5-10 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Primary and secondary sources from Chapter 5.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (3 min). Hover over markers 1 to 4. Which links are other people's summaries?
  2. Quiz (3 min). Press Quiz and find each link from its description.
  3. Trace (4 min). Pick a claim from a resource you use. How many links can you follow before you reach a primary source?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer against the poster.

  1. A reviewer stops at link 2. What has the reviewer found? (Only that a textbook agrees with the resource.)
  2. Which link is the original source? (Link 4, the study that reports the measurements.)
  3. The further back you trace a claim, what happens to the check? (You can trust the check more.)

docs.title: Connection to the OER Evaluator rubric
docs.text: Chapter 14 warns about invented citations. A reader needs to see that confirming a citation exists is not the same as tracing the claim.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Fact-checking - Wikipedia - Describes how claims are checked before and after publication and the methods professional fact-checkers use. Supports this chapter's procedure for sampling and verifying the facts in a resource.
  2. SIFT (The Four Moves) - Hapgood - Mike Caulfield's own post explaining Stop, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, and Trace claims. A short, usable routine for tracing a citation back to its origin.
  3. Evaluating Sources of Information - Purdue OWL - Explains how to judge a source's author, publisher, date, and evidence. A plain companion for deciding whether a resource's citations are reliable and recent enough.

docs.title: Component in a Box
docs.text:
Run the Component in a Box MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 18: Reusable Components and Publishing OER

To change the content, edit data.json in this folder. The artwork is component-in-a-box.svg, and scripts/posters/specs/ holds the code that draws it.

You can add this MicroSim to any web page with this iframe:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/oer-evaluator/sims/component-in-a-box/main.html"
        height="552px"
        width="100%"
        scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Chapter 18 turns improved resources into reusable components, and packaging is the concrete step that makes the lift-out test from Chapter 9 and the portability checks from Chapter 10 pass. This poster is an exploded view of the quiz package watershed-quiz. Six parts float above the box: the page itself (index.html), the script it needs kept inside the folder (quiz.js), a README that says what the component is and how to use it, a license file, a metadata file, and an image folder. Everything the component needs travels with it. Outside the box a dotted line runs from the page to a folder elsewhere, with a cross on it: the broken link that packaging prevents. The seventh marker sits on the three finished boxes of Watershed Basics v1.1, the reading, the quiz, and the simulation. The artwork has no text, and the file names come from the overlay.

This MicroSim is a callout overlay: the poster is a drawing made for this book (SVG) with no text in it, and every label comes from the numbered markers.

# Part What it shows 1 index.html The quiz page itself. A reuser opens this file to see and use the component. All links in it must be complete addresses or point to files inside the folder. 2 quiz.js The script the page needs, kept inside the folder. If it lived in a sibling folder, it would not travel with the component. 3 README.md What the component is, how to embed it, and how to credit it. 4 LICENSE.txt The license text or a link to it, so a reuser knows what they may do. 5 metadata.json The metadata record of Chapter 9 in a form a program can read, so a catalog can find and describe the component. 6 img/ The images the component uses, kept inside the package with complete addresses or paths inside the folder. 7 Three finished boxes for Watershed Basics v1.1 After splitting, Watershed Basics v1.1 has three components: the reading, the quiz, and the simulation. Each is packaged in its own box with its own license and metadata.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
• Explore and Quiz buttons: switch modes.
  • Numbered markers and labels: hover over a marker or a label to read about that part of the poster.
  • Quiz mode: the labels are hidden. Read the prompt, then press the marker it names. A wrong press lets you try again.
  • Try Again: repeats the quiz after the last question.

docs.title: Good to Know
docs.text:
Quiz mode scores each marker as you answer it. The MicroSim does not store your answers. The artwork carries no text, so every name and number you read comes from the overlay.

  • This book's own MicroSim folders follow the same idea: each has a main.html, an index.md, and its own script, but they also load the shared overlay libraries from docs/sims/shared-libs.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can list the files in a packaged component, say what each is for, and explain why a link that leaves the folder breaks the package. (Bloom level: Understand.)

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Adult learners: teachers (K-12 and college), instructional designers, librarians, and OER coordinators.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 5-10 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Standalone components from Chapter 9 and packaging from Chapter 18.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (4 min). Hover over markers 1 to 7. Which part would stop a reuser from knowing what they may do if it were missing?
  2. Quiz (3 min). Press Quiz and find each part from its description.
  3. Inspect (3 min). Open a folder of yours. Which of the six parts are missing, and where do its links point?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer against the poster.

  1. Where must the script a page needs be kept? (Inside the folder, so it travels with the component.)
  2. Why does the box include a license file and a metadata file? (So a reuser knows what they may do and a catalog can find and describe it.)
  3. What should links inside a package be? (Complete addresses, or point to files inside the package.)

docs.title: Connection to the OER Evaluator rubric
docs.text: Packaging ties together license, metadata, and portability. A component with every part passes the lift-out test and embeds without edits.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Material for MkDocs: Getting Started - Material for MkDocs - Official instructions for installing and configuring the Material theme used by this book. Supports the chapter's steps for building a textbook site.
  2. Creating a GitHub Pages Site - GitHub Docs - Step-by-step instructions for publishing a site from a repository for free. Supports the chapter's walkthrough of publishing an improved OER.
  3. Semantic Versioning 2.0.0 - semver.org - A simple scheme for numbering releases so users can tell a small fix from a breaking change. Useful for keeping a component library's versions clear.
  4. Zenodo - CERN - An open repository that gives uploaded files a DOI and reports views and downloads. One way to publish an OER permanently and begin tracking its reuse.

docs.title: How Fast Does Content Spoil?
docs.text:
Run the How Fast Does Content Spoil? MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 5: Accuracy and Currency

To change the content, edit data.json in this folder. The artwork is content-shelf-life.svg, and scripts/posters/specs/ holds the code that draws it.

You can add this MicroSim to any web page with this iframe:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/oer-evaluator/sims/content-shelf-life/main.html"
        height="717px"
        width="100%"
        scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Currency is half of the accuracy and currency metric, and reviewers often apply one rule to every page. This poster is a market stall with three shelves, taken from the Chapter 5 table of how quickly six kinds of content go out of date. The slow shelf holds content that is checked at each major review. The middle shelf is checked every few years. The fast shelf is checked every year or more often. Every item wears a date stamp with the wording from the chapter.

This MicroSim is a grid overlay: the poster is a drawing made for this book (SVG), and each zone is a clickable rectangle over it.

Zone What it shows Slow shelf Slow shelf: ages very slowly to slowly. Middle shelf Middle shelf: ages moderately. Fast shelf Fast shelf: ages quickly.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
• Explore and Quiz Me buttons: switch modes. Quiz Me starts a new run.
  • The zones: hover over a zone or press it to read its summary and facts in the panel below the poster.
  • Quiz questions: read the question, then press the zone that answers it. A wrong press lets you try again.
  • Try Again: repeats the quiz after the last question.

docs.title: Good to Know
docs.text:
Quiz mode scores each question as you answer it. The MicroSim does not store your answers. The poster prints its own headings, so the sim adds no labels on top of it.

  • The poster keeps the chapter's own wording for how often to check. It does not turn "every few years" into a number.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can match each of six kinds of content to how fast it ages and how often a reviewer should check it. (Bloom level: Understand.)

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Adult learners: teachers (K-12 and college), instructional designers, librarians, and OER coordinators.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 5-10 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • The currency half of the accuracy and currency metric from Chapter 5.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (3 min). Press each shelf and read its two items and their stamps.
  2. Quiz (3 min). Press Quiz Me and place four kinds of content on the right shelf.
  3. Apply (4 min). Pick a page you teach from. Which shelf does most of it sit on? When should you next check it?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer against the poster.

  1. Which shelf holds software screenshots? (The fast shelf, checked every year or more often.)
  2. How often do you check standards, curricula, and guidelines? (Every few years, and when a standard is revised.)
  3. Why not use one currency rule for every page? (The multiplication table does not change, while a software screenshot can change within a year.)

docs.title: Connection to the OER Evaluator rubric
docs.text: Currency is half of metric 1. A quick triage by shelf tells a reviewer where to spend checking time, and supports the link rot and revision history ideas in the same chapter.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Link rot - Wikipedia - Explains how links stop working over time, how common the problem is, and what can be done about it. Background for the currency checks that test a resource's links.
  2. Fact-checking - Wikipedia - Describes how claims are checked before and after publication and the methods professional fact-checkers use. Supports this chapter's procedure for sampling and verifying the facts in a resource.
  3. Wayback Machine - Internet Archive - Lets reviewers retrieve archived copies of pages that have moved or vanished and see what a page said on an earlier date. A practical tool for the broken-link and currency checks in this chapter.

docs.title: Evidence or Opinion Sorter
docs.text:
Run the Evidence or Opinion Sorter MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 3: The Ten-Metric Rubric and Scoring

To edit the sketch, paste the contents of evidence-quality-sorter.js into the p5.js editor. The learning content (the items, answers, and reasons) is in the CONFIG block at the top of the file.

You can add this MicroSim to any web page with this iframe:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/oer-evaluator/sims/evidence-quality-sorter/main.html"
        height="654px"
        width="100%"
        scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
A score needs evidence another reviewer could check. A note is checkable evidence when it gives (1) where the reviewer looked, (2) what the reviewer saw, as a quote, count, or measurement, and (3) the rule it was compared with. This MicroSim shows ten review notes and you place each in one of two bins.

An unchecked claim by an AI agent is always Not evidence yet, because nobody has checked it. Each bin holds five notes.

Bin Meaning Checkable evidence All three parts are present: where, what, and the rule. Not evidence yet One or more parts are missing, so no other reviewer could repeat the check.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
• Two bin buttons: place the note. The placement is final.
  • Next: moves to the next note.
  • Show definitions: on a narrow screen the test and bin definitions move behind this button.
  • Play again and the missed-note review on the results screen.

docs.title: Good to Know
docs.text:
Only your first committed answer on the first completed run counts as evidence of mastery. Practice runs give the same feedback but do not change that first-run score. Nothing moves until you act, and the MicroSim does not store your answers.

  • The notes are illustrative examples in a shuffled order.
  • A note counts as evidence only when all three parts are present.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can judge whether each of ten review notes is checkable evidence or not yet evidence, by looking for a location, an observation, and a rule, with at least 9 of 10 correct on the first attempt. (Bloom level: Evaluate.)

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Adult learners: teachers (K-12 and college), instructional designers, librarians, and OER coordinators.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • The ideas of evidence for a score and evidence citation from Chapter 3.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Learn the test (2 min). Read the three-part test and say which part is missing from "The text seems accurate."
  2. Sort the notes (6 min). Place all ten notes and read each reason.
  3. Repair (4 min). Rewrite two "Not evidence yet" notes so that they pass the test.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer by using it.

  1. "The alt text is probably fine." Evidence? (Not evidence yet. "Probably" shows no one looked.)
  2. "Page 7 link returns an error, tested on 2026-10-12." Evidence? (Checkable evidence. It gives the location, the observation, the rule, and the date.)
  3. "The AI agent said the license is CC BY." Evidence? (Not evidence yet. An agent's claim is a statement to check.)
  4. Why does a count help? (Another reviewer can repeat a count and compare it with yours.)

docs.title: Connection to the OER Evaluator rubric
docs.text: Evidence is how a reviewer defends a score, and how a team spots a biased one. Chapter 14 treats an AI agent's claims the same way: as statements to verify before they count.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Rubric (academic). Wikipedia. Criteria, performance levels, and analytic versus holistic rubrics.
  2. Creating and Using Rubrics. Carnegie Mellon Eberly Center. The parts of a rubric and how to use it.
  3. Inter-rater reliability. Wikipedia. How agreement between independent raters is measured.
  4. VALUE Rubrics. AAC&U. Level-by-level descriptors that different reviewers can apply consistently.

docs.title: Feedback That Teaches
docs.text:
Run the Feedback That Teaches MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 8: Practice and Feedback

To change the content, edit data.json in this folder. The artwork is feedback-that-teaches.svg, and scripts/posters/specs/ holds the code that draws it.

You can add this MicroSim to any web page with this iframe:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/oer-evaluator/sims/feedback-that-teaches/main.html"
        height="789px"
        width="100%"
        scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Feedback is the part of practice that does the teaching. This poster holds the situation constant: the question "Which describes infiltration?" and a learner who chose "water flowing over the ground". It answers the same wrong answer four ways, ordered from least to most helpful, and rates each message against the criteria in Chapter 8: it says the answer was wrong, it explains why, it points toward the right idea, and it does not blame. Only the last message passes all four. Chapter 15 has agents write practice questions, so the same yardstick applies to what they produce.

This MicroSim is a grid overlay: the poster is a drawing made for this book (SVG), and each zone is a clickable rectangle over it.

Zone What it shows Message 1: Wrong. Says the answer failed and says nothing else. Rated weak. Message 2: Good try! Does not say whether the answer was right. Rated weak. Message 3: Incorrect. The answer is A. Gives the answer and no reason. Rated weak. Message 4: Not quite... Corrects, explains, and names the mix-up. Rated strong.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
• Explore and Quiz Me buttons: switch modes. Quiz Me starts a new run.
  • The zones: hover over a zone or press it to read its summary and facts in the panel below the poster.
  • Quiz questions: read the question, then press the zone that answers it. A wrong press lets you try again.
  • Try Again: repeats the quiz after the last question.

docs.title: Good to Know
docs.text:
Quiz mode scores each question as you answer it. The MicroSim does not store your answers. The poster prints its own headings, so the sim adds no labels on top of it.

  • The wording of the messages is exact and not paraphrased. The check and cross marks are rated against the four criteria in the chapter.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can rate a feedback message against four criteria and explain why only one of four messages for the same wrong answer is strong. (Bloom level: Evaluate.)

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Adult learners: teachers (K-12 and college), instructional designers, librarians, and OER coordinators.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 5-10 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • The feedback metric from Chapter 8.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (3 min). Press each message and read what it does. Which criterion does each weak message miss?
  2. Quiz (3 min). Press Quiz Me and find the message that matches each description.
  3. Rewrite (4 min). Take one wrong answer from a quiz you use. Write a message that names the likely mix-up and points to what to review.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer against the poster.

  1. A message says "Incorrect. The answer is A." Is it strong? (No. It gives the answer and no reason.)
  2. What does "Good try!" fail to do? (It does not say whether the answer was right.)
  3. What four things does a helpful message do? (Says the answer was wrong, explains why, points toward the right idea, and does not blame.)

docs.title: Connection to the OER Evaluator rubric
docs.text: Feedback is part of the practice and feedback metric. Because agents write practice questions in Chapter 15, reviewers use the same four criteria on what they produce.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Formative assessment - Wikipedia - Describes assessment used during learning to guide teaching and give feedback, as opposed to grading at the end. Background for judging whether a resource's questions help learners improve.
  2. Testing effect - Wikipedia - Summarizes research showing that retrieving information from memory strengthens it more than rereading. Supports the chapter's sections on quizzes and retrieval practice.
  3. Formative vs Summative Assessment - Carnegie Mellon Eberly Center - Contrasts assessment that guides learning with assessment that measures it, with examples of each. Helps reviewers decide whether a resource's quizzes give feedback or only a grade.

docs.title: Five Ways a Test Can Lie to You
docs.text:
Run the Five Ways a Test Can Lie to You MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 16: Designing an A/B Test with Students

To change the content, edit data.json in this folder. The artwork is five-confounders.svg, and scripts/posters/specs/ holds the code that draws it.

You can add this MicroSim to any web page with this iframe:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/oer-evaluator/sims/five-confounders/main.html"
        height="741px"
        width="100%"
        scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Small classroom tests fail on confounds far more often than on statistics. This poster is a pre-flight checklist for a test plan. Each of the five panels from the Chapter 16 table has a pair of balance scales. The top scale is tilted by a hidden weight, which is how the confounder misleads. The bottom scale is level, which is the defense. The weights are neutral: a confounder is hidden and is not villainous. Before you trust any difference between groups, ask what else is different besides the version.

This MicroSim is a grid overlay: the poster is a drawing made for this book (SVG), and each zone is a clickable rectangle over it.

Zone What it shows Different teachers How it misleads: One teacher's enthusiasm lifts one group. The defense: One teacher for both groups. Different times of day How it misleads: Students are more alert at one time. The defense: Both groups at the same time. Extra help How it misleads: One group gets a review or hints. The defense: The same script and help for both. Different tests How it misleads: The versions are measured in different ways. The defense: The same test and key for both. Student choice How it misleads: Motivated students choose one version. The defense: Random assignment.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
• Explore and Quiz Me buttons: switch modes. Quiz Me starts a new run.
  • The zones: hover over a zone or press it to read its summary and facts in the panel below the poster.
  • Quiz questions: read the question, then press the zone that answers it. A wrong press lets you try again.
  • Try Again: repeats the quiz after the last question.

docs.title: Good to Know
docs.text:
Quiz mode scores each question as you answer it. The MicroSim does not store your answers. The poster prints its own headings, so the sim adds no labels on top of it.

  • The weights are drawn as neutral gray blocks, since a confounder is hidden and is not a villain.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can identify the confounder in a test setup and name its defense. (Bloom level: Analyze.)

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Adult learners: teachers (K-12 and college), instructional designers, librarians, and OER coordinators.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 5-10 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • The control group and the one-difference rule from Chapter 16.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (3 min). Press each panel. What is the hidden weight in each tilted scale?
  2. Quiz (3 min). Press Quiz Me and match four test setups to their confounders.
  3. Preflight (4 min). Take a test plan of your own. Go through the five panels and say which defense you use for each.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer against the poster.

  1. Students choose which version to use. What is the confounder, and what is the defense? (Student choice, because motivated students choose one version. Defense: random assignment.)
  2. One group takes the test in the morning and the other after lunch. Which confounder? (Different times of day. Run both groups at the same time.)
  3. What question should you ask before trusting a difference between groups? (What else was different besides the version?)

docs.title: Connection to the OER Evaluator rubric
docs.text: This is the one-difference rule: arrange everything except the version to be the same, and let random assignment handle what you cannot arrange.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. A/B testing - Wikipedia - Defines A/B testing, how users are split between versions, and how results are compared. The core idea behind comparing an original resource with its improved version.
  2. Randomized controlled trial - Wikipedia - Explains random assignment to treatment and control groups and why it supports causal claims. Background for the chapter's sections on random assignment and control and treatment groups.
  3. How Not To Run an A/B Test - Evan Miller - Explains why checking results repeatedly and stopping when they look good inflates false positives. A caution for anyone running a small test with students.
  4. Identifying and Implementing Educational Practices Supported by Rigorous Evidence - Institute of Education Sciences - A user-friendly guide to what counts as strong evidence in education, with emphasis on randomized studies. Helps teachers judge what their own small test can and cannot show.

docs.title: The 5R Permissions: Five Things You May Do
docs.text:
Run the 5R Permissions: Five Things You May Do MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 1: Foundations of Open Educational Resources

To change the content, edit data.json in this folder. The artwork is five-r-permissions.svg, and scripts/posters/specs/ holds the code that draws it.

You can add this MicroSim to any web page with this iframe:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/oer-evaluator/sims/five-r-permissions/main.html"
        height="741px"
        width="100%"
