docs.title: Description
docs.text:
This poster shows the five permissions that an open license grants, in the order Chapter 1 teaches them: retain, reuse, revise, remix, and redistribute. Every panel has the same structure: a scene, a plain-language meaning, the test question to ask of any resource, and one classroom example. A strip under the panels shows that the permissions build on one another.

This MicroSim is a grid overlay: the poster is a drawing made for this book (SVG), and each zone is a clickable rectangle over it.

Zone What it shows Retain Make, own, and control copies of the resource. Reuse Use the resource in its original, unaltered form. Revise Adapt, adjust, modify, or alter the resource itself. Remix Combine the work with other open material to create something new. Redistribute Share copies of the original, revised, or remixed work with others.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
• Explore and Quiz Me buttons: switch modes. Quiz Me starts a new run.
  • The zones: hover over a zone or press it to read its summary and facts in the panel below the poster.
  • Quiz questions: read the question, then press the zone that answers it. A wrong press lets you try again.
  • Try Again: repeats the quiz after the last question.

docs.title: Good to Know
docs.text:
Quiz mode scores each question as you answer it. The MicroSim does not store your answers. The poster prints its own headings, so the sim adds no labels on top of it.

  • The five panels run in sequence, not in rank. No permission is more important than another.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can identify which of the 5R permissions a classroom action uses, with at least 4 of 5 correct on the first attempt. (Bloom level: Remember.)

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Adult learners: teachers (K-12 and college), instructional designers, librarians, and OER coordinators.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 5-10 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • The meaning of an open license from Chapter 1.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (3 min). Press each panel. Which two permissions are easiest to confuse, and what separates them?
  2. Quiz (3 min). Press Quiz Me and match five classroom actions to their permissions.
  3. Practice (4 min). Write one action of your own for each permission. Swap with a partner and check each other.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer against the poster.

  1. You fix a typo in an open worksheet. Which permission is that? (Revise. Reuse stops where change begins.)
  2. You email an unchanged open worksheet to a colleague. Which permission? (Redistribute.)
  3. Which permission lets you build one unit from chapters of two open textbooks? (Remix, and the licenses must be compatible.)

docs.title: Connection to the OER Evaluator rubric
docs.text: Revise leads to the editable source metric, remix leads to license compatibility, and redistribute leads to ShareAlike. The 5Rs are the vocabulary of every later chapter.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Definition of Open - opencontent.org - David Wiley's own statement of the 5R permissions (retain, reuse, revise, remix, redistribute) and why a license must grant all five. This is the source of the 5R framework used throughout the book.
  2. Open educational resources - Wikipedia - Defines OER, traces the movement's history, and lists the 5R permissions with examples of repositories and national policies. Anchors this chapter's definition of an OER and its distinction between open and merely free materials.
  3. OER Resources for Educators - Creative Commons - A teacher's guide to finding openly licensed images, video, audio, textbooks, simulations, and courses, with pointers to OpenStax, PhET, and OER Commons. Supports the chapter's section on finding OER.

docs.title: Five R Scenario Matcher
docs.text:
Run the Five R Scenario Matcher MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 1: Foundations of Open Educational Resources

To edit the sketch, paste the contents of five-r-scenario-matcher.js into the p5.js editor. The learning content (the items, answers, and reasons) is in the CONFIG block at the top of the file.

You can add this MicroSim to any web page with this iframe:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/oer-evaluator/sims/five-r-scenario-matcher/main.html"
        height="634px"
        width="100%"
        scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
An open license grants five permissions: retain, reuse, revise, remix, and redistribute. This MicroSim gives you ten everyday teacher actions, one at a time, and you name the one permission that each action uses.

You get two tries on each action. If your first answer is wrong, the sim shows the test question for the right permission without naming it. Only a correct first answer counts as evidence of mastery.

Permission Test question Retain Can I make and keep my own copy? Reuse Can I use it as it is? Revise Can I change it? Remix Can I combine it with other open work? Redistribute Can I share copies with others?

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
• Five permission buttons: choose the permission the action uses.
  • Next: moves on after you read the feedback.
  • Previous missed / Next missed: on the results screen, page through the actions you missed.
  • Play again: reshuffles the ten actions for a practice run.

docs.title: Good to Know
docs.text:
Only your first committed answer on the first completed run counts as evidence of mastery. Practice runs give the same feedback but do not change that first-run score. Nothing moves until you act, and the MicroSim does not store your answers.

  • The scenarios are illustrative examples written for Chapter 1.
  • Where a scenario says a step is already done, only the action happening now counts. The MicroSim does not test license conditions such as credit or share-alike.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can apply the definitions of the five R permissions to name the one permission that each of 10 classroom actions exercises, with at least 8 correct on the first attempt. (Bloom level: Apply.)

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Adult learners: teachers (K-12 and college), instructional designers, librarians, and OER coordinators.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • The terms open license and the five permissions retain, reuse, revise, remix, and redistribute from Chapter 1.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Recall (2 min). Write the five test questions from memory, then check them against the table above.
  2. Match the actions (6 min). Work through the ten actions. When a hint appears, answer the test question before you choose again.
  3. Explain (3 min). For each action you needed a hint on, explain in one sentence why the permission you first chose was wrong.
  4. Replay (2 min). Press Play again and try to answer every action correctly on the first try.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer by using it.

  1. You email a colleague an unchanged copy of an open worksheet. Which permission? (Redistribute. Sharing copies with others is redistributing.)
  2. You add alt text to every image in an open chapter. Which permission? (Revise. Adding alt text changes the work.)
  3. You download the editable source files of an open lab manual for safekeeping. Which permission? (Retain. Making and keeping your own copy is retaining.)
  4. What is the difference between revise and remix? (Revise changes one work. Remix combines two or more works into something new.)

docs.title: Connection to the OER Evaluator rubric
docs.text: The five permissions are the vocabulary behind the open license and editable source metrics. Chapter 4 shows why editable source files make revise and remix possible.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Definition of Open. opencontent.org. David Wiley's statement of the 5R permissions.
  2. Open educational resources. Wikipedia. Defines OER and lists the 5R permissions.
  3. Open Educational Resources. UNESCO. The international Recommendation on OER.
  4. OER Resources for Educators. Creative Commons. A teacher's guide to finding openly licensed materials.

docs.title: Five Resources, Five Shapes
docs.text:
Run the Five Resources, Five Shapes MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 3: The Ten-Metric Rubric and Scoring

To change the content, edit data.json in this folder. The artwork is five-resources-five-shapes.svg, and scripts/posters/specs/ holds the code that draws it.

You can add this MicroSim to any web page with this iframe:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/oer-evaluator/sims/five-resources-five-shapes/main.html"
        height="741px"
        width="100%"
        scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
This poster draws the five resources from the Chapter 3 total score example as radar charts, from the lowest total to the highest. Each chart has ten spokes. The five spokes on the right are the quality metrics, drawn as blue circles. The five on the left are the reusability metrics, drawn as purple squares. A dashed ring marks the floor of 5. Watershed Basics and Locked Chemistry E-book both total 65, yet their shapes look nothing alike. All five resources are illustrative examples written for the chapter.

This MicroSim is a grid overlay: the poster is a drawing made for this book (SVG), and each zone is a clickable rectangle over it.

Zone What it shows Thin Material Total 37, Weak band, decision Reject. Quality 14, reusability 23. Watershed Basics Total 65, Fair band, decision Revise. Quality 32, reusability 33. Locked Chemistry E-book Total 65, Fair band, decision Revise. Quality 44, reusability 21. One Gap Total 85, Good band, decision Revise. Quality 45, reusability 40. Open Algebra Total 90, Excellent band, decision Adopt. Quality 43, reusability 47.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
• Explore and Quiz Me buttons: switch modes. Quiz Me starts a new run.
  • The zones: hover over a zone or press it to read its summary and facts in the panel below the poster.
  • Quiz questions: read the question, then press the zone that answers it. A wrong press lets you try again.
  • Try Again: repeats the quiz after the last question.

docs.title: Good to Know
docs.text:
Quiz mode scores each question as you answer it. The MicroSim does not store your answers. The poster prints its own headings, so the sim adds no labels on top of it.

  • The five resources, their scores, and their decisions are illustrative examples from Chapter 3.
  • The bands and the decision rule are this book's starting values, not a standard.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can distinguish resources with the same total score by the shape of their ten metric scores, and name the metric to fix first. (Bloom level: Analyze.)

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Adult learners: teachers (K-12 and college), instructional designers, librarians, and OER coordinators.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 5-10 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • The ten metrics and the 0 to 10 scale from Chapter 3.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (3 min). Press Watershed Basics, then Locked Chemistry E-book. Both total 65. What does each need first?
  2. Quiz (3 min). Press Quiz Me and find each resource from a description of its shape.
  3. Plan (4 min). For each resource, name the one metric you would raise first and say why.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer against the poster.

  1. Two resources total 65. Can you say how they differ from the total alone? (No. A total hides the split between quality and reusability and the weakest metric.)
  2. Which resource has nine metrics of 9 and one of 4, and what is its decision? (One Gap, total 85, Good, and Revise because one metric is below 5.)
  3. What does the dashed ring on each chart mark? (The floor of 5. Any spoke that dips inside it is a metric below the floor.)

docs.title: Connection to the OER Evaluator rubric
docs.text: A shape is learned faster than a table, and the notch in a shape is the first thing to fix. This prepares the improvement rule of Chapter 15: raise the lowest metric first.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Rubric (academic) - Wikipedia - Defines rubrics, their criteria and performance levels, and the difference between analytic and holistic forms. Background for the ten-metric rubric and for how its scoring scales are built.
  2. Not All Rubrics Are Equal: A Review of Rubrics for Evaluating the Quality of Open Educational Resources - IRRODL - Yuan and Recker's peer-reviewed comparison of fourteen OER quality rubrics shows what each one emphasizes. Useful for seeing where this book's ten metrics overlap with, and differ from, earlier tools.
  3. Achieve OER Rubrics - Achieve - Describes eight rubrics for judging how well an OER aligns to standards and meets other quality criteria, delivered through an online evaluation tool on OER Commons. An earlier example of scoring an OER criterion by criterion.

docs.title: 5Rs of OER Workflow
docs.text:
Run the 5Rs of OER Workflow MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 1: Foundations of Open Educational Resources The Sixth R: Regenerate

To change the content, edit the nodeInfo object in main.html. The flowchart itself is the Mermaid text in the same file, and five-rs-oer.js holds the hover and click behavior.

You can add this MicroSim to any web page with this iframe:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/oer-evaluator/sims/five-rs-oer/main.html"
        height="802px"
        width="100%"
        scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
This MicroSim visualizes David Wiley's 5Rs framework for Open Educational Resources (OER) — Retain, Reuse, Revise, Remix, and Redistribute — as a vertical Mermaid.js flowchart, starting from a licensed OER and building cumulatively toward full redistribution rights. A seventh node, styled with a dashed purple border, presents a proposed 6th R: Regenerate — the freedom to recreate an intelligent textbook from its underlying learning graph and reusable agentic skills, not just from its rendered chapters.

Chapter 1 teaches the five permissions in depth. The poster The Sixth R: Regenerate covers the proposed sixth R.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
• Hover over any step in the diagram to see a short, one-sentence tip in a floating tooltip.
  • Click a step to select it (highlighted with an amber border) and read a detailed narrative explanation in the right-hand panel.
  • The color key at the top of the right panel distinguishes the licensed OER starting point, Wiley's original 5Rs, and the proposed 6th R.

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Undergraduate, graduate, and professional development (instructional designers, OER authors, textbook publishers)

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: General familiarity with copyright vs. open licensing (e.g. Creative Commons) is helpful but not required.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Exploration (5 min): Click through each of the 5Rs in order and read the detailed narrative for each, noting the example given for each freedom.
  2. Guided Practice (5 min): Discuss why each R is described as building cumulatively on the one before it (e.g. why you can't Remix a resource you have no right to Revise).
  3. Assessment (5 min): Click Regenerate and discuss whether it should count as a true 6th R or as an implementation detail of the existing 5Rs.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Ask learners to classify a real resource (e.g. a textbook PDF found online) against the 5Rs: which freedoms does its license actually grant?

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Wiley, D. (2014). The Access Compromise and the 5th R. Iterating Toward Openness.
  2. Wiley, D. Defining the "Open" in Open Content and Open Educational Resources.
  3. Creative Commons. About CC Licenses.

docs.title: The Fix Toolkit
docs.text:
Run the Fix Toolkit MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 15: Improving a Resource with AI Agents

To change the content, edit data.json in this folder. The artwork is fix-toolkit.svg, and scripts/posters/specs/ holds the code that draws it.

You can add this MicroSim to any web page with this iframe:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/oer-evaluator/sims/fix-toolkit/main.html"
        height="557px"
        width="100%"
        scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Thirteen fixes in a table are hard to keep in mind, and the improvement plan starts from the lowest metric and asks which fix applies. This poster is that lookup as a pegboard. Eight panels hold the thirteen tools, one panel for each metric a fix mainly raises. Quality metrics hang in blue panels and reusability metrics in purple panels. Each marker's description gives the typical agent mistake and the human check from the chapter, and every tool carries a small person-with-check badge, because nothing is applied without human review. The artwork has no text, so every name comes from the overlay.

This MicroSim is a callout overlay: the poster is a drawing made for this book (SVG) with no text in it, and every label comes from the numbered markers.

# Part What it shows 1 AI alt text generation Mainly raises accessibility. Typical agent mistake: generic text or invented details. The human check: look at each image beside its draft. 2 Caption generation Mainly raises accessibility. Typical agent mistake: mis-heard technical terms. The human check: watch the video while reading the captions. 3 Heading repair Mainly raises accessibility. Typical agent mistake: renamed or merged sections. The human check: compare the outline before and after. 4 Reading level rewrite Mainly raises readability. Typical agent mistake: lost precision or meaning. The human check: run the readability tool and the meaning checks. 5 Glossary generation Mainly raises readability. Typical agent mistake: a definition that differs from the resource's use. The human check: compare with the resource and a trusted source. 6 Link repair Mainly raises accuracy and currency. Typical agent mistake: an invented address. The human check: open every new link. 7 Content update Mainly raises accuracy and currency. Typical agent mistake: a figure from memory. The human check: open the source and confirm the figure. 8 Metadata generation Mainly raises metadata. Typical agent mistake: a guessed author or license. The human check: verify each field against the page. 9 License statement repair Mainly raises open license. Typical agent mistake: a license assigned to someone else's work. The human check: find the owner's terms or replace the item. 10 Chapter splitting Mainly raises modularity. Typical agent mistake: a module that still depends on another. The human check: open each module alone. 11 PDF-to-Markdown conversion Mainly raises editable source. Typical agent mistake: lost tables, headings, or pictures. The human check: compare the output with the pdf. 12 Practice question generation Mainly raises practice with feedback. Typical agent mistake: a wrong key or a leading stem. The human check: answer each question without the key. 13 MicroSim building Mainly raises practice with feedback. Typical agent mistake: wrong science or a failed embed. The human check: use every control and embed it on each platform.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
• Explore and Quiz buttons: switch modes.
  • Numbered markers and labels: hover over a marker or a label to read about that part of the poster.
  • Quiz mode: the labels are hidden. Read the prompt, then press the marker it names. A wrong press lets you try again.
  • Try Again: repeats the quiz after the last question.

docs.title: Good to Know
docs.text:
Quiz mode scores each marker as you answer it. The MicroSim does not store your answers. The artwork carries no text, so every name and number you read comes from the overlay.

  • Thirteen markers are near the readable limit, so some leader lines cross the board. Use the labels in the side panels to follow them.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can match each of the thirteen fixes to the metric it mainly raises, and state the human check for one of them. (Bloom level: Apply.)

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Adult learners: teachers (K-12 and college), instructional designers, librarians, and OER coordinators.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 5-10 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • The ten metrics from Chapter 3 and the improvement plan from Chapter 15.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (4 min). Hover over the markers 1 to 13. Which panel holds the most tools?
  2. Quiz (3 min). Press Quiz and find each tool from its description.
  3. Plan (3 min). Take the lowest metric of a resource you have scored. Which tool on the pegboard would you reach for, and what is its human check?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer against the poster.

  1. Which metric does PDF-to-Markdown conversion mainly raise? (Editable source.)
  2. What is the human check for link repair? (Open every new link.)
  3. What is the typical agent mistake in metadata generation? (A guessed author or license.)

docs.title: Connection to the OER Evaluator rubric
docs.text: The improvement plan starts from the lowest metric and asks which fix applies. The poster is that lookup, and every tool carries the reminder that nothing is applied without human review.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Derivative work - Wikipedia - Explains how a work based on another is treated in copyright law. Background for the chapter's check of what a license allows before an agent changes a resource.
  2. Alt Decision Tree - W3C Web Accessibility Initiative - A decision tree for choosing the right alt attribute for each kind of image. Lets a reviewer judge whether an agent's alt text suits the image's purpose.
  3. Marking Your Work with a CC License - CC Public Wiki - Shows how to place a license notice on a work. This is the step needed when a revised version is published.
  4. Pull Requests - GitHub Docs - GitHub's documentation on proposing, reviewing, and merging changes. The standard way to let a person inspect every change an agent made before accepting it.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Git vocabulary is the hardest part of Chapter 4, and this poster shows what a list cannot: whose copy each step happens in. The top lane is the original repository and its maintainer. The bottom lane is your own copy. The seven steps run left to right, and the arrows cross between the lanes at the fork, the pull request, and the merge. A faint dotted branch shows the other ending, a declined pull request. The pictures are physical: a photocopied binder for the fork, a sticky note for the pull request, and a rubber stamp for the merge.

This MicroSim is a callout overlay: the poster is a drawing made for this book (SVG) with no text in it, and every label comes from the numbered markers.

# Part What it shows 1 Find the repository Find the repository of the resource you want to improve. You cannot copy what you have not found. 2 Fork it to make your own copy Fork the repository to make your own copy. You change your copy, not the original. 3 Make your change and save it with a message Make your change in your copy and save it with a message that says what you did. A pull request needs a change to propose. 4 Open a pull request Open a pull request that proposes your change to the original repository. The maintainer can only review a change that has been proposed. 5 The maintainer reads and comments The maintainer reads your pull request and leaves comments. The review follows the proposal. 6 You answer with more changes You answer any comments by adding more changes to your copy. You respond to what the review found. 7 The maintainer merges The maintainer merges the pull request into the original. Merging is the last step, after the review is satisfied.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
• Explore and Quiz buttons: switch modes.
  • Numbered markers and labels: hover over a marker or a label to read about that part of the poster.
  • Quiz mode: the labels are hidden. Read the prompt, then press the marker it names. A wrong press lets you try again.
  • Try Again: repeats the quiz after the last question.

docs.title: Good to Know
docs.text:
Quiz mode scores each marker as you answer it. The MicroSim does not store your answers. The artwork carries no text, so every name and number you read comes from the overlay.

  • The drawing is a generic interface with no screenshots or logos of a real code-hosting site.
  • The sequence shows the successful path. The faint branch is the other ending.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can order the seven steps of the fork and pull request workflow and say in which copy each step happens. (Bloom level: Understand.)

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Adult learners: teachers (K-12 and college), instructional designers, librarians, and OER coordinators.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 5-10 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • The meaning of a repository, a fork, and a pull request from Chapter 4.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (3 min). Hover over markers 1 to 7 in order. Which steps happen in the top lane and which in the bottom lane?
  2. Quiz (3 min). Press Quiz and find each step from its description.
  3. Discuss (4 min). What does the faint dotted branch show, and what would you do after a declined pull request?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer against the poster.

  1. Where do you make your change? (In your own copy, the fork, never in the original.)
  2. Can a pull request be sent before the change is made? (No. A pull request needs a change to propose.)
  3. Must the maintainer accept every pull request? (No. A maintainer may decline it.)

docs.title: Connection to the OER Evaluator rubric
docs.text: This is how an improved resource finds its way back to its author, which matters again in Chapter 15 (improving a resource) and Chapter 18 (publishing components).

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Git - Wikipedia - Explains Git's distributed model, commits, branches, and history. Background for the chapter's version control section and for reading repository history as evidence when scoring editable source.
  2. Hello World - GitHub Docs - A short tutorial that creates a repository, a branch, a commit, and a pull request. Gives teachers hands-on experience with the version control steps this chapter describes.
  3. Version Control with Git - Software Carpentry - A free lesson for beginners on tracking changes, viewing history, and collaborating with Git, written for people who are not programmers. A gentle companion to the chapter's version control section.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Classifying errors by type is a stated course outcome, because the type tells the reviewer how to catch the error and the prompt writer how to prevent it. This poster is a field guide for the review desk. Each card has the same three parts: what the error looks like, how to catch it, and how to prevent it. The inset at the bottom is the Chapter 14 worked example, "A 9 that should be a 5": the agent reported a 9, and its own evidence supports five passing checks. The tone is gently skeptical and not mocking.

This MicroSim is a grid overlay: the poster is a drawing made for this book (SVG), and each zone is a clickable rectangle over it.

Zone What it shows Factual error A wrong claim about the resource, such as a feature that is absent or a count that is off. License error A wrong reading of the resource's license, or a missed or mismatched license. Citation error A reference that does not exist or does not support its claim. Scoring error A score that does not follow from the agent's own checks, or arithmetic that does not add up. A 9 that should be a 5 The agent reported accessibility 9. Its evidence supports five passing checks, so the score is 5.

  • The "9 that should be a 5" example is from the chapter. The chapter's sources are invented, so the poster prints no real names.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can classify an agent error as factual, license, citation, or scoring, and name the reviewer check and the prompt fix for it. (Bloom level: Analyze.)

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Adult learners: teachers (K-12 and college), instructional designers, librarians, and OER coordinators.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 5-10 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Hallucination and agent error types from Chapter 14.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (3 min). Press each card and read the three parts. Which check needs the least outside information?
  2. Quiz (3 min). Press Quiz Me and match four reviewer checks to the error types.
  3. Apply (4 min). Find an agent report you have. Pick one claim and say which error type it could be, and which check would expose it.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer against the poster.

  1. A reference does not exist. Which error type is it? (A citation error.)
  2. What do you do to catch a scoring error? (Recount the passes, recompute the band, and re-add the total.)
  3. How can a prompt prevent a license error? (Require the license statement quoted word for word, and "not stated" for anything it does not mention.)

docs.text: Agent output is a draft that a person must check. The error type tells the reviewer where to look first.

docs.text:
1. Hallucination (artificial intelligence) - Wikipedia - Explains how AI systems produce confident but false output, including invented citations, and why it happens. Background for the chapter's sections on hallucination and invented citation.
  2. Reduce Hallucinations - Claude Platform Docs - Practical prompt techniques such as letting the model say it does not know, asking for direct quotes, and verifying claims. Supports the chapter's verification steps.
  3. Survey of Hallucination in Natural Language Generation - arXiv - Ji and colleagues' survey sorts hallucinations into types and reviews how they are measured and reduced. Gives vocabulary for classifying an agent's errors.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Most workshops stop at a happy survey, which measures only the first level. This staircase uses the model of Donald Kirkpatrick that Chapter 19 names: reaction, learning, behavior, and results. Each step asks its question and shows the chapter's evidence for a workshop of 20 teachers. All the numbers are illustrative, made up in the chapter to show the form, and the poster marks them that way. An arrow beneath shows that later levels take longer to collect. Without a comparison group a change may have other causes, and counts of reuse are weaker than evidence of learning.

This MicroSim is a grid overlay: the poster is a drawing made for this book (SVG), and each zone is a clickable rectangle over it.

Zone What it shows 1. Reaction Did participants find the day useful? Illustrative evidence for a workshop of 20 teachers. 2. Learning Did they gain the skills? Illustrative evidence for a workshop of 20 teachers. 3. Behavior Do they use the skills afterward? Illustrative evidence for a workshop of 20 teachers. 4. Results Did it change outcomes? Illustrative evidence for a workshop of 20 teachers.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
• Explore and Quiz Me buttons: switch modes. Quiz Me starts a new run.
  • The zones: hover over a zone or press it to read its summary and facts in the panel below the poster.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can place a piece of workshop evidence at the right level of training evaluation and explain why a happy survey is not enough. (Bloom level: Understand.)

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Adult learners: teachers (K-12 and college), instructional designers, librarians, and OER coordinators.

docs.title: Prerequisites

docs.text:
1. Explore (3 min). Press each step. Which level is the easiest to collect, and which is the hardest?
  2. Quiz (3 min). Press Quiz Me and place four pieces of evidence on the right step.
  3. Plan (4 min). For a workshop you run, write one piece of evidence you could collect for each level.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer against the poster.

  1. "17 of 20 teachers earned the certificate" belongs to which level? (Learning.)
  2. "9 components were reused by another teacher" belongs to which level? (Results.)
  3. Why is a count of reuse weaker than evidence of learning? (Without a comparison group, reuse may have other causes.)

docs.title: Connection to the OER Evaluator rubric
docs.text: The staircase is a ready frame for a grant report, alongside the Grant Response and Grant-Period Timeline workshop pages.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Evaluating Professional Development - Thomas R. Guskey - Corwin Press (2000) - Guskey's five levels (participants' reactions, learning, organization support, use of new knowledge, and student outcomes) test whether a workshop changed practice, not only whether people enjoyed it.
  2. Professional certification - Wikipedia - Explains how certifications are awarded after training and assessment, and what makes them credible. Background for the chapter's certificate requirements and submission review.
  3. Open Badges - 1EdTech - The standard for verifiable digital credentials that can carry evidence of what the earner did. A model for a certificate that links to a learner's reviewed work.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Teachers constantly ask how to put a resource into their course, and the wrong method means a broken embed or a gradebook that never updates. This poster shows the same resource and the same generic learning management system (LMS) in four zones. A link opens the resource at its own address. An embed shows it inside your course page. A Common Cartridge import brings a single compressed file with a manifest into the LMS. An LTI tool opens inside the course but runs on another company's server and can send a score back to the gradebook. The arrows show the difference: one-way for the first three, two-way for LTI. The LTI zone carries a small shield because passing learner information raises the privacy questions of Chapter 13. A footer names the barrier that stops all four, platform lock-in.

This MicroSim is a grid overlay: the poster is a drawing made for this book (SVG), and each zone is a clickable rectangle over it.

Zone What it shows Link Students open the resource at its own address. Embed The resource appears on your course page through a frame. Common Cartridge import A whole unit is copied into the LMS as a package. LTI tool An external tool opens inside the LMS and can send results back.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:

  • The poster draws a generic LMS and no vendor logos. 1EdTech is named as the standards group.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can choose the right way to bring a resource into an LMS for each of four teacher needs. (Bloom level: Apply.)

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Adult learners: teachers (K-12 and college), instructional designers, librarians, and OER coordinators.

docs.text: 5-10 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • LMS import, Common Cartridge, and LTI from Chapter 10.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (3 min). Press each zone. Which arrows are one-way, and which is two-way?
  2. Quiz (3 min). Press Quiz Me and match four teacher needs to the zones.
  3. Plan (4 min). Think of a resource you use. Which method would you choose, and what would you test in a real LMS first?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer against the poster.

  1. You want an external quiz tool to send each student's score to the gradebook. Which method? (An LTI tool.)
  2. You want a simulation to appear on your course page. Which method? (Embed.)
  3. You want colleagues with a different LMS to receive the same unit. Which method? (Common Cartridge import.)

docs.text: Portability is metric 10. The chapter's own objective is to choose among exactly these four methods for a given need.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Learning management system - Wikipedia - Describes what learning management systems do, the major products, and how course content is delivered through them. Background for testing whether a resource can be imported into an LMS.
  2. Common Cartridge - 1EdTech - The official page for Common Cartridge, the open package format that lets learning management systems import and exchange course content. The standard behind the chapter's LMS import test.
  3. Learning Tools Interoperability (LTI) - 1EdTech - The official page for the LTI standard, which connects external tools to learning platforms. Useful for understanding how an interactive resource can be launched from many systems.
  4. : The Inline Frame Element - MDN Web Docs - Reference for the HTML element that embeds one page inside another, including attributes and security notes. Directly supports the chapter's iframe embedding test.

docs.title: Inter-Rater Agreement Explorer
docs.text:
Run the Inter-Rater Agreement Explorer MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 3: The Ten-Metric Rubric and Scoring

To edit the sketch, paste the contents of inter-rater-agreement-explorer.js into the p5.js editor. The learning content (the items, answers, and reasons) is in the CONFIG block at the top of the file.

You can add this MicroSim to any web page with this iframe:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/oer-evaluator/sims/inter-rater-agreement-explorer/main.html"
        height="888px"
        width="100%"
        scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Two reviewers can give a resource the same total and still disagree on many metrics. A metric agrees when the two scores differ by 3 or fewer, and it is flagged when they differ by more than 3. Percent agreement is the number of agreeing metrics divided by 10, times 100.

In explore mode, Reviewer 1's ten scores are fixed and ten sliders change Reviewer 2's scores. The differences, flags, percent agreement, and both totals update at once. In practice mode you type the number of agreeing metrics and mark the flagged metrics for three pairs, then press Check.

Term Rule Agrees The two scores differ by 3 or fewer Flagged The two scores differ by more than 3 Percent agreement Agreeing metrics / 10 x 100

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
• Ten sliders: in explore mode, set Reviewer 2's scores from 0 to 10 in whole points. They start equal to Reviewer 1's.
  • Start practice: leaves explore mode.
  • Agreeing metrics box: type a whole number from 0 to 10.
  • Ten metric buttons and None flagged: mark every flagged metric, or choose None flagged.
  • Check: commits the answer. Back to explore is on the results screen.

docs.title: Good to Know
docs.text:
Only your first committed answer on the first completed run counts as evidence of mastery. Practice runs give the same feedback but do not change that first-run score. Nothing moves until you act, and the MicroSim does not store your answers.

  • The three pairs are illustrative examples in the order A, B, C.
  • A pair is correct only when both the count and the flagged set match exactly. Equal totals do not mean agreement.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can calculate the number of agreeing metrics and name the flagged metrics for each of three pairs of reviewer scores, with at least 2 of 3 pairs fully correct on the first attempt. (Bloom level: Apply.)

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Adult learners: teachers (K-12 and college), instructional designers, librarians, and OER coordinators.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 15-20 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • The terms inter-rater agreement, agreeing metric, flagged metric, and percent agreement from Chapter 3.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (5 min). Move one Reviewer 2 slider until a metric is flagged. Then change two scores so the totals match but five metrics disagree.
  2. Calculate (8 min). Work through the three pairs. Find the differences on paper before you type the count.
  3. Interpret (3 min). Explain why case B has 100% agreement even though the totals differ.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer by using it.

  1. Two scores are 5 and 9. Agree or flagged? (Flagged. The difference is 4, which is more than 3.)
  2. Two scores are 7 and 4. Agree or flagged? (Agree. The difference is exactly 3.)
  3. Reviewer totals are both 65. Do the reviewers agree? (Not necessarily. Totals can match when metric scores disagree.)
  4. Seven of ten metrics agree. What is the percent agreement? (70%.)

docs.title: Connection to the OER Evaluator rubric
docs.text: Agreement between reviewers is the first test of whether a rubric is reliable. Chapter 14 measures agreement between an AI agent and human reviewers.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Inter-rater reliability. Wikipedia. How agreement between independent raters is measured.
  2. Reliability (statistics). Wikipedia. Consistency of a measure across repeated use.
  3. Rubric (academic). Wikipedia. Criteria, performance levels, and analytic versus holistic rubrics.
  4. VALUE Rubrics. AAC&U. Level-by-level descriptors that different reviewers can apply consistently.

docs.title: License Compatibility Checker
docs.text:
Run the License Compatibility Checker MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 2: Open Licenses and Attribution

To edit the sketch, paste the contents of license-compatibility-checker.js into the p5.js editor. The learning content (the items, answers, and reasons) is in the CONFIG block at the top of the file.

You can add this MicroSim to any web page with this iframe:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/oer-evaluator/sims/license-compatibility-checker/main.html"
        height="614px"
        width="100%"
        scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
When you combine two openly licensed sources into one work, each source sets conditions on the license of the result. This MicroSim shows ten pairs of source licenses. For each pair you choose the license the combined work may carry, or Conflict when no license satisfies both sources, or Blocked when one source is an ND license.

The rule: the answer is the first license, in the order CC BY, CC BY-SA, CC BY-NC, CC BY-NC-SA, that both sources allow. If the two allowed sets share no license the answer is Conflict. If either source is an ND license the answer is Blocked.

Source Licenses the combined work may carry CC0 and CC BY CC BY, CC BY-SA, CC BY-NC, CC BY-NC-SA CC BY-SA CC BY-SA CC BY-NC CC BY-NC, CC BY-NC-SA CC BY-NC-SA CC BY-NC-SA CC BY-ND and CC BY-NC-ND None: the combination is Blocked

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
• Six outcome buttons: CC BY, CC BY-SA, CC BY-NC, CC BY-NC-SA, Conflict, Blocked.
  • Show requirements table: opens the table above. Opening it is exploration, not evidence. On a narrow screen a long table has page buttons.
  • Next: moves to the next pair.
  • Play again and the missed-pair review on the results screen.

docs.title: Good to Know
docs.text:
Only your first committed answer on the first completed run counts as evidence of mastery. Practice runs give the same feedback but do not change that first-run score. Nothing moves until you act, and the MicroSim does not store your answers.

  • The pairs are illustrative examples, always in the same order. This is a study aid, not legal advice.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can solve ten license-combination problems by finding the license a combined work may carry, or by recognizing a conflict or a blocked combination, with at least 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt. (Bloom level: Apply.)

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Adult learners: teachers (K-12 and college), instructional designers, librarians, and OER coordinators.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • The licenses CC0, CC BY, CC BY-SA, CC BY-NC, CC BY-NC-SA, CC BY-ND, and CC BY-NC-ND and the idea of license compatibility from Chapter 2.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Study the table (2 min). Open the requirements table and say why CC BY-SA and CC BY-NC cannot be combined.
  2. Solve the pairs (8 min). Work through all ten pairs, opening the table only when you need it.
  3. Generalize (3 min). Write a one-line rule for each of the three outcome types: a license, Conflict, and Blocked.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer by using it.

  1. CC BY with CC BY-SA. What may the combined work carry? (CC BY-SA. Only CC BY-SA satisfies the second source, and CC BY accepts it.)
  2. CC BY-SA with CC BY-NC. What is the outcome? (Conflict. CC BY-SA allows only CC BY-SA, and CC BY-NC allows only noncommercial licenses.)
  3. CC BY with CC BY-ND. What is the outcome? (Blocked. The ND source cannot be changed or blended and then shared.)
  4. CC0 with CC BY-SA. What may the combined work carry? (CC BY-SA. CC0 allows any of the four, and CC BY-SA is the only one that satisfies the other source.)

docs.title: Connection to the OER Evaluator rubric
docs.text: A resource built from open parts is only reusable if its license is consistent. Chapter 4 explains why editable source files make remixing practical.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Compatible Licenses. Creative Commons. Which licenses may be combined in an adaptation.
  2. License compatibility. Wikipedia. Why works under different licenses cannot always be combined.
  3. About CC Licenses. Creative Commons. Plain-language summaries of what each license permits and requires.
  4. Creative Commons license. Wikipedia. The six main licenses and the BY, SA, NC, and ND conditions.

docs.title: License Selection Advisor
docs.text:
Run the License Selection Advisor MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 2: Open Licenses and Attribution

To edit the sketch, paste the contents of license-selection-advisor.js into the p5.js editor. The learning content (the items, answers, and reasons) is in the CONFIG block at the top of the file.

        height="686px"

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Choosing a license means choosing which freedoms to give away. Three questions drive the choice: Will you allow commercial reuse? Will you allow others to share changed versions? Must changed versions carry the same license? CC0 applies only when a creator wants no conditions at all.

This MicroSim states seven goals, one for each of seven licenses. For each goal you choose the license that serves it. The three questions are available on request, and opening them is exploration, not evidence.

Commercial reuse? / Shared changes? / Same license? License Yes / Yes / No CC BY Yes / Yes / Yes CC BY-SA No / Yes / No CC BY-NC No / Yes / Yes CC BY-NC-SA Yes / No / not applicable CC BY-ND No / No / not applicable CC BY-NC-ND No conditions at all CC0

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
• Seven license buttons: CC0, CC BY, CC BY-SA, CC BY-NC, CC BY-NC-SA, CC BY-ND, CC BY-NC-ND.
  • Show the three questions: opens the table above.
  • Next: moves to the next goal.
  • Play again and the missed-goal review on the results screen.

docs.title: Good to Know
docs.text:
Only your first committed answer on the first completed run counts as evidence of mastery. Practice runs give the same feedback but do not change that first-run score. Nothing moves until you act, and the MicroSim does not store your answers.

  • The goals are illustrative examples and appear in a shuffled order.
  • Each goal has exactly one correct license, one per license.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can apply the three license-selection questions to choose the license that serves each of seven stated goals, with at least 6 of 7 correct on the first attempt. (Bloom level: Apply.)

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Adult learners: teachers (K-12 and college), instructional designers, librarians, and OER coordinators.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • The idea of license selection and the licenses CC0, CC BY, CC BY-SA, CC BY-NC, CC BY-NC-SA, CC BY-ND, and CC BY-NC-ND from Chapter 2.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Answer the questions (3 min). Read the first goal and answer the three questions for it before you choose.
  2. Choose licenses (6 min). Work through all seven goals. Open the table only if you are stuck.
  3. Create (4 min). Write a goal of your own for a resource you own, answer the three questions, and name the license.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer by using it.

  1. Others may change my lesson noncommercially, and every changed version must carry my license. Which license? (CC BY-NC-SA. NC blocks commercial use, and SA requires the same license on changes.)
  2. Anyone may share my finished report, even for sale, but nobody may share a changed version. Which license? (CC BY-ND. ND forbids changed versions, and there is no NC element.)
  3. When is CC0 the right choice? (Only when the goal asks for no conditions at all, not even credit.)
  4. Name two checks to make before you pick any license. (Check who owns the work, and read any grant terms that require a specific license.)

docs.title: Connection to the OER Evaluator rubric
docs.text: The license a creator picks becomes the license a reviewer scores. Chapter 18 returns to licensing the components you publish.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
A complete license statement does more than show a row of icons. This MicroSim draws the bottom of a lesson web page: a picture with a caption strip above a footer bar. Seven numbered markers point at the parts of a complete license statement. The drawing contains no text, so every label comes from the data in the sim.

In Explore mode you hover or click a marker to read its label, description, and tip. In Quiz me mode you read a hint, such as "A row of four small round icons at the left of the footer", and click the marker that matches. You get two tries.

Marker Part 1 License badge icons 2 License name and version 3 Link to the license 4 Copyright holder and year 5 Scope of the license 6 Notice for third-party content 7 Machine-readable license marking

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
• Explore and Quiz me buttons: switch modes. Quiz me starts a new run.
  • The seven numbered markers: hover, focus with the Tab key, or click.
  • Next: moves to the next hint.
  • Play again: repeats the quiz as practice.

docs.title: Good to Know
docs.text:
Only your first committed answer on the first completed run counts as evidence of mastery. Practice runs give the same feedback but do not change that first-run score. Nothing moves until you act, and the MicroSim does not store your answers.

  • A wrong first click says so and lets you try once more. A second wrong click reveals the marker. Only a correct first click counts as evidence.
  • The drawing is made for this book (SVG) and carries no statistics.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can identify the seven parts of a complete license statement on an annotated page footer from a description of each part, with at least 6 of 7 correct on the first attempt. (Bloom level: Remember.)

docs.text: 5-10 minutes.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:

  2. Quiz (4 min). Press Quiz me and find all seven parts from their hints.
  3. Apply (3 min). Open a real OER page and name which of the seven parts it shows and which it lacks.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer by using it.

  1. Why is "CC BY" with no version an incomplete statement? (Terms differ between versions, so the version must be named or linked.)
  2. Do the license icons alone make a license statement? (No. They are a hint, and the written statement must be confirmed.)
  3. Does a license statement on a page cover every image on it? (No. Treat each image as separately licensed until its caption says otherwise.)
  4. Where can a reader find the machine-readable marking? (In the page source, or through a search tool's license filter.)

docs.title: Model, Assistant, Agent, Skill
docs.text:
Run the Model, Assistant, Agent, Skill MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 12: AI Agents, Prompts, and Rubric Scoring

To change the content, edit data.json in this folder. The artwork is model-assistant-agent-skill.svg, and scripts/posters/specs/ holds the code that draws it.

You can add this MicroSim to any web page with this iframe:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/oer-evaluator/sims/model-assistant-agent-skill/main.html"

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The vocabulary is the first barrier in the AI half of the book, and mixing the terms leads to wrong decisions about what to trust. This poster stacks four layers, each built on the one below. A large language model predicts the next piece of text and does not look facts up. An AI assistant is a program you talk to in ordinary language that answers and waits. An AI agent adds tools, files, and a loop of observe, decide, act, and observe the result. An agent skill is a packaged set of instructions that is the durable, shareable form of a rubric prompt. The poster leaves out product and model names, which date quickly.

This MicroSim is a grid overlay: the poster is a drawing made for this book (SVG), and each zone is a clickable rectangle over it.

Zone What it shows Large language model Predicts the next piece of text, one piece at a time. AI assistant A program you talk to in ordinary language. It answers and waits. AI agent Works toward a goal over several steps, using tools and files. Agent skill A saved set of instructions that an agent loads when a task matches.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
• Explore and Quiz Me buttons: switch modes. Quiz Me starts a new run.
  • The zones: hover over a zone or press it to read its summary and facts in the panel below the poster.
  • Quiz questions: read the question, then press the zone that answers it. A wrong press lets you try again.
  • Try Again: repeats the quiz after the last question.

docs.title: Good to Know
docs.text:
Quiz mode scores each question as you answer it. The MicroSim does not store your answers. The poster prints its own headings, so the sim adds no labels on top of it.

  • The poster leaves out product and model names, which date quickly, and uses no robot or glowing-brain pictures.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can distinguish a language model, an assistant, an agent, and a skill, and say which layer adds tools and a loop. (Bloom level: Understand.)

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Adult learners: teachers (K-12 and college), instructional designers, librarians, and OER coordinators.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 5-10 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • The vocabulary of Chapter 12.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (3 min). Press each layer from the bottom up. What does each step add?
  2. Quiz (3 min). Press Quiz Me and match four descriptions to the layers.
  3. Sort (4 min). Write down three AI tools you have used. Which layer is each one, and what would you need to check?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer against the poster.

  1. Which layer answers and waits? (The AI assistant.)
  2. Which layer plans, acts, looks at what happened, and acts again? (The AI agent.)
  3. What does a language model not do? (It does not look facts up, and it can sound sure when it is wrong.)

docs.title: Connection to the OER Evaluator rubric
docs.text: The difference between an assistant that answers and an agent that acts across steps decides what a reviewer must check in Chapters 13 and 14.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Large language model - Wikipedia - Explains how large language models are trained, how they use tokens and context, and what they can and cannot do. Background for the chapter's sections on models and the context window.
  2. Intelligent agent - Wikipedia - Defines an agent as a system that perceives its environment and acts toward goals, with common agent types. The foundation for the chapter's distinction between an assistant and an agent.
  3. Building Effective AI Agents - Anthropic - Separates workflows from agents and describes patterns such as prompt chaining, routing, and evaluator-optimizer. Helps teachers understand the agent workflow this chapter uses for rubric scoring.
  4. Agent Skills Overview - Claude Platform Docs - Explains skills as packaged instructions and resources that an agent loads when relevant. Shows the format behind the reusable evaluator skills this book teaches readers to build.

docs.title: NonCommercial Gray Area Sorter
docs.text:

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The NonCommercial element is vague on purpose. Creative Commons defines it as use that is not primarily intended for or directed toward commercial advantage or monetary compensation, and reasonable people disagree about some uses. This MicroSim shows ten uses of a CC BY-NC worksheet. You judge each one against that criterion.

The middle bin, Unclear: ask the owner, is a valid answer and not a failure to decide. The bins give a likely reading, not legal advice.

Bin Meaning Clearly allowed No one earns money from the use. Unclear: ask the owner The use touches money in a way reasonable people disagree about. Likely not allowed The use earns money or is directed toward earning it.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
• Three bin buttons: place the use in a bin. The placement is final.
  • Next: moves to the next use.
  • Show definitions: on a narrow screen the criterion and bin definitions move behind this button.
  • Previous missed / Next missed and Play again on the results screen.

docs.title: Good to Know
docs.text:
Only your first committed answer on the first completed run counts as evidence of mastery. Practice runs give the same feedback but do not change that first-run score. Nothing moves until you act, and the MicroSim does not store your answers.

  • The ten uses are illustrative examples written for Chapter 2.
  • Only the Clearly allowed bin means no permission is needed.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can judge whether each of ten uses of a CC BY-NC resource is clearly allowed, unclear, or likely not allowed, with at least 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt. (Bloom level: Evaluate.)

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Adult learners: teachers (K-12 and college), instructional designers, librarians, and OER coordinators.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • The terms NonCommercial requirement, CC BY-NC, and attribution requirement from Chapter 2.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Predict (2 min). Read the criterion. Which of these will be hardest to judge: a paid course, a bookstore sale at cost, or a free class website?
  2. Sort the uses (6 min). Place all ten uses and read each reason.
  3. Discuss (4 min). With a partner, pick one Unclear use and write the email you would send the owner to ask permission.
  4. Replay (2 min). Play again and try to explain each answer aloud before you click.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer by using it.

  1. A blog with paid ads posts the worksheet. Which bin? (Likely not allowed. The advertising income makes the use commercial.)
  2. A nonprofit workshop charges $20 to cover room and printing. Which bin? (Unclear: ask the owner. Cost recovery is not profit but is still payment.)
  3. Is a nonprofit always noncommercial? (No. Judge the use, not the kind of organization.)
  4. Does "free of charge" settle the question? (No. Advertising on a free page can still make the use commercial.)

docs.title: Connection to the OER Evaluator rubric
docs.text: The NonCommercial element lowers a resource on the openness spectrum. Chapter 9 shows how the open license metric scores that.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. About CC Licenses. Creative Commons. Plain-language summaries of what each license permits and requires.
  2. Creative Commons license. Wikipedia. The six main licenses and the BY, SA, NC, and ND conditions.
  3. Recommended Practices for Attribution. CC Public Wiki. Good and weak credit lines for CC-licensed work.
  4. Fair use. Wikipedia. Fair use is a separate permission from an open license.

docs.title: The OER Evaluator Loop
docs.text:
Run the OER Evaluator Loop MicroSim Fullscreen Chapters

To change the content, edit data.json in this folder. The artwork is oer-evaluator-loop.svg, and scripts/posters/specs/ holds the code that draws it.

You can add this MicroSim to any web page with this iframe:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/oer-evaluator/sims/oer-evaluator-loop/main.html"
        height="575px"
        width="100%"
        scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
This poster is a map of the whole book. Eight stations sit on one closed loop. A reader first learns what OER and licenses are, scores a resource by hand with the ten-metric rubric, directs an AI agent to make a first pass, and checks the agent's evidence. The reader then improves the lowest metrics with agents, tests the change with students, calibrates the agent against the test results, and publishes and trains others. The thick arrow that returns from calibration to the agent's first pass is the one that matters: it is how automated scores earn trust.

This MicroSim is a callout overlay: the poster is a drawing made for this book (SVG) with no text in it, and every label comes from the numbered markers.

# Part What it shows 1 Understand OER and licenses Learn what makes a resource open and how the six Creative Commons licenses work. Chapters 1 and 2. 2 Score a resource by hand with the ten-metric rubric Score ten metrics, five for quality and five for reusability, and add them up to a total out of 100. Chapters 3 to 11. 3 Direct an AI agent to make a first pass Write a rubric prompt, run the agent, and collect its scores with evidence. Chapters 12 and 13. 4 Check the agent's evidence Open each quoted source and recompute each score. Look for factual, license, citation, and scoring errors. Chapter 14. 5 Improve the lowest metrics with agents Fix the lowest-scoring metric first, using agents for alt text, readability, metadata, and more, with a human check on every change. Chapter 15. 6 Test the change with students in an A/B test Randomly assign students to the original or the improved version, and compare learning gain. Chapters 16 and 17. 7 Calibrate the agent against the test results Compare the agent's scores with what the students actually learned, then adjust the prompt. Chapters 14 and 17. 8 Publish and train others Package improved components with a license and metadata, publish them openly, and train other teachers. Chapters 18 and 19.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
• Explore and Quiz buttons: switch modes.
  • Numbered markers and labels: hover over a marker or a label to read about that part of the poster.
  • Quiz mode: the labels are hidden. Read the prompt, then press the marker it names. A wrong press lets you try again.
  • Try Again: repeats the quiz after the last question.

docs.title: Good to Know
docs.text:
Quiz mode scores each marker as you answer it. The MicroSim does not store your answers. The artwork carries no text, so every name and number you read comes from the overlay.

  • Chapter numbers come from the chapter list. If chapters move, update the marker descriptions in data.json.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can describe the eight stations of the OER Evaluator loop in order and explain why test results are used to calibrate the AI agent. (Bloom level: Understand.)

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Adult learners: teachers (K-12 and college), instructional designers, librarians, and OER coordinators.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 5-10 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • None. This poster is the overview, so it works before or after any chapter.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (3 min). Hover over each marker in order, 1 to 8. Which station would your team start at?
  2. Quiz (3 min). Press Quiz and find each station from its description.
  3. Discuss (4 min). Marker 7 returns to marker 3. In your own words, what changes in the agent's next pass after calibration?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer against the poster.

  1. Which station comes right after "check the agent"? (Improve the lowest metrics with agents (Chapter 15).)
  2. What does the return arrow from station 7 to station 3 mean? (Test results calibrate the agent, so its next first pass can be trusted more.)
  3. Which chapters teach scoring by hand? (Chapters 3 to 11.)

docs.title: Connection to the OER Evaluator rubric
docs.text: The course description lays out a path from evaluation to improvement to testing, with test results used to check and calibrate the automated scores. This poster is that path in one picture.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Open educational resources. Wikipedia. Background for station 1.
  2. Rubric (academic). Wikipedia. Background for station 2.
  3. Hallucination (artificial intelligence). Wikipedia. Why station 4 checks the agent's evidence.
  4. A/B testing. Wikipedia. Background for station 6.
  5. Calibration (statistics). Wikipedia. Background for station 7.

docs.title: OER or Not Classifier
docs.text:
Run the OER or Not Classifier MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 1: Foundations of Open Educational Resources

To edit the sketch, paste the contents of oer-or-not-classifier.js into the p5.js editor. The learning content (the items, answers, and reasons) is in the CONFIG block at the top of the file.

You can add this MicroSim to any web page with this iframe:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/oer-evaluator/sims/oer-or-not-classifier/main.html"
        height="690px"
        width="100%"
        scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
A resource can cost nothing and still be closed, and it can cost money and still be open. This MicroSim shows eleven described resources, one at a time. You decide whether each is Open (OER), Free but not open, or Not free and not open by checking its license and public-domain status instead of its price.

After each placement the card flies into its correct bin, and you read the reason. The bins stay on screen the whole time, so you can compare a new card with the cards you have already placed.

Bin What it holds Open (OER) The resource is in the public domain or carries an open license, whatever its price. Free but not open The resource costs nothing but is neither in the public domain nor under an open license. Not free and not open The resource costs money and is neither in the public domain nor under an open license.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
• Three bin buttons: place the current card. The placement is final.
  • Next: moves to the next card after you read the feedback.
  • Show definitions: on a narrow screen the bin definitions move behind this button.
  • Previous missed / Next missed: on the results screen, page through the cards you missed.
  • Play again: shuffles the cards for a practice run.

docs.title: Good to Know
docs.text:
Only your first committed answer on the first completed run counts as evidence of mastery. Practice runs give the same feedback but do not change that first-run score. Nothing moves until you act, and the MicroSim does not store your answers.

  • The eleven cards are illustrative examples written for Chapter 1.
  • A card with no license statement counts as all rights reserved, and a price never moves a resource out of the Open bin.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can classify each of 11 described resources as open (OER), free but not open, or not free and not open, by checking its license and public-domain status rather than its price. (Bloom level: Understand.)

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Adult learners: teachers (K-12 and college), instructional designers, librarians, and OER coordinators.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • The terms educational resource, copyright, license, public domain, open license, free resource, and open educational resource from Chapter 1.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Predict (2 min). Read the three bin definitions. Before placing any card, write down which bin you think a free online course with the terms "personal use only" belongs in.
  2. Place the cards (5 min). Place all 11 cards. Read the reason after each one, especially the ones you got wrong.
  3. Review (3 min). On the results screen, page through the missed cards and say aloud what you checked the first time and what you should have checked.
  4. Replay (2 min). Press Play again and aim for a perfect run. Practice runs do not change the first-run score.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer by using it.

  1. A quiz bank under CC0 is sold on a marketplace for $5. Which bin? (Open (OER). CC0 grants the permissions, and the price does not change that.)
  2. A video streams free of charge and shows no license. Which bin? (Free but not open. With no license the default is all rights reserved.)
  3. Why is a photograph taken by a NASA employee as part of their job an open resource? (Works made by U.S. federal employees as part of their duties are in the public domain.)
  4. What single question separates the Open bin from the other two? (Does a license or the public domain grant permission to retain, reuse, revise, remix, and redistribute?)

docs.title: Connection to the OER Evaluator rubric
docs.text: The first question a reviewer asks about any resource is whether it is open. Chapter 9 scores the license metric on how clearly a resource states what others may do.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Open educational resources. Wikipedia. Defines OER and lists the 5R permissions.
  2. Free content. Wikipedia. Separates works that merely cost nothing from works that grant freedoms.
  3. Copyright. Wikipedia. Explains why all rights are reserved by default.
  4. Definition of Open. opencontent.org. David Wiley's statement of the 5R permissions.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
A facilitator can print this poster for the room, and participants can see the logic of the day and what they carry out of it. It is built from the sample agenda in Chapter 19: check-in and setup, the ten metrics, calibration by hand and then with the agent, checking the agent, lunch, the improvement challenge, peer review and publishing, and next steps. Block widths are in proportion to time, so the long improvement challenge looks long and the breaks look short. A token under each block shows what teachers leave with. Two arcs show why the order matters: the rubric comes before calibration, and checking comes before improving. The times live in the overlay data and not in the artwork, so a facilitator can adapt the agenda without redrawing.

This MicroSim is a callout overlay: the poster is a drawing made for this book (SVG) with no text in it, and every label comes from the numbered markers.

# Part What it shows 1 Check-in and setup 8:30 to 9:00. Teachers leave with: a working agent session. 2 The ten metrics 9:00 to 9:45. Teachers leave with: a rubric card. 3 Calibration by hand, then with the agent 9:45 to 10:45. Teachers leave with: hand and agent scores, with gaps explained. 4 Checking the agent 11:00 to 12:00. Teachers leave with: a verified evaluation of the sample. 5 Lunch 12:00 to 12:45. Teachers leave with: no deliverable, just a rest. 6 The improvement challenge 12:45 to 2:15. Teachers leave with: an improved component and its new score. 7 Peer review and publishing 2:30 to 3:15. Teachers leave with: a published, openly licensed component. 8 Next steps 3:15 to 3:30. Teachers leave with: a certificate checklist.

docs.text:
