  • Numbered markers and labels: hover over a marker or a label to read about that part of the poster.
  • Quiz mode: the labels are hidden. Read the prompt, then press the marker it names. A wrong press lets you try again.
  • Try Again: repeats the quiz after the last question.

docs.title: Good to Know
docs.text:
Quiz mode scores each marker as you answer it. The MicroSim does not store your answers. The artwork carries no text, so every name and number you read comes from the overlay.

  • The times are in the overlay data. Edit the descriptions in data.json to adapt the agenda for your own day.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can order the blocks of the one-day workshop and explain why the rubric comes before calibration and checking comes before improving. (Bloom level: Understand.)

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Adult learners: teachers (K-12 and college), instructional designers, librarians, and OER coordinators.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 5-10 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • The sample agenda from Chapter 19 and the Sample One-Day Schedule.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (4 min). Hover over markers 1 to 8. Which block takes the longest, and what do teachers leave with from it?
  2. Quiz (3 min). Press Quiz and find each block from its description.
  3. Adapt (3 min). If your day were two hours shorter, which block would you shorten, and which two blocks must stay in order?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer against the poster.

  1. Which block comes right after calibration and the break? (Checking the agent.)
  2. What do teachers leave with from the improvement challenge? (An improved component and its new score.)
  3. Why does the rubric come before calibration? (You score by hand against the rubric first, so there is a human score to compare the agent with.)

docs.title: Connection to the OER Evaluator rubric
docs.text: This poster pairs with the Sample One-Day Schedule workshop page and gives a facilitator the logic of the day at a glance.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Evaluating Professional Development - Thomas R. Guskey - Corwin Press (2000) - Guskey's five levels (participants' reactions, learning, organization support, use of new knowledge, and student outcomes) test whether a workshop changed practice, not only whether people enjoyed it.
  2. Quality Matters - Quality Matters - A nonprofit that trains peer reviewers and certifies courses against a published rubric. A mature model for training and certifying reviewers, like the local reviewer role in this chapter.
  3. Open Badges - 1EdTech - The standard for verifiable digital credentials that can carry evidence of what the earner did. A model for a certificate that links to a learner's reviewed work.

docs.title: Four Principles, Five Learners
docs.text:
Run the Four Principles, Five Learners MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 7: Accessibility

To change the content, edit data.json in this folder. The artwork is pour-principles-learners.svg, and scripts/posters/specs/ holds the code that draws it.

You can add this MicroSim to any web page with this iframe:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/oer-evaluator/sims/pour-principles-learners/main.html"
        height="789px"
        width="100%"
        scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Accessibility is full of standards language, and teachers need the human reason first. This poster joins two tables from Chapter 7: the four WCAG principles with an example criterion each, and five learners with the feature that lets each one use a resource. Perceivable covers the blind learner, the deaf learner, and the learner with low vision. Operable covers the learner who cannot use a mouse. Understandable covers the learner with a reading disability. Robust covers assistive technology. Some features serve more than one principle, so the pairing is an editorial choice for teaching.

This MicroSim is a grid overlay: the poster is a drawing made for this book (SVG), and each zone is a clickable rectangle over it.

Zone What it shows Perceivable (P) Perceivable: Can users perceive the content? Operable (O) Operable: Can users operate the controls? Understandable (U) Understandable: Can users follow it? Robust (R) Robust: Does it work with assistive technology?

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
• Explore and Quiz Me buttons: switch modes. Quiz Me starts a new run.
  • The zones: hover over a zone or press it to read its summary and facts in the panel below the poster.
  • Quiz questions: read the question, then press the zone that answers it. A wrong press lets you try again.
  • Try Again: repeats the quiz after the last question.

docs.title: Good to Know
docs.text:
Quiz mode scores each question as you answer it. The MicroSim does not store your answers. The poster prints its own headings, so the sim adds no labels on top of it.

  • The learner pairing is an editorial choice. Some features serve more than one principle, and the author confirms the mapping.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can match each learner support to the WCAG principle it serves, and state one example criterion for each principle. (Bloom level: Understand.)

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Adult learners: teachers (K-12 and college), instructional designers, librarians, and OER coordinators.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 5-10 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • The accessibility metric from Chapter 7.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (3 min). Press each letter. Which learners does it protect, and what gets in their way?
  2. Quiz (3 min). Press Quiz Me and place five learner supports under the right principle.
  3. Check (4 min). Open a page you teach from. Pick one support from each zone and test whether the page offers it.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer against the poster.

  1. Which principle do captions for a deaf learner belong to? (Perceivable.)
  2. Which principle asks that all functions work with a keyboard? (Operable.)
  3. What does Robust ask about a custom control? (That it exposes a name and role to assistive technology.)

docs.title: Connection to the OER Evaluator rubric
docs.text: Accessibility is metric 4 in the ten-metric rubric. The rubric starts from the people, so a reviewer knows why each criterion matters.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Web Content Accessibility Guidelines - Wikipedia - Explains the WCAG versions, their four principles, and the A, AA, and AAA conformance levels. The standard behind this book's accessibility metric, which targets WCAG 2.1 AA.
  2. WCAG 2 Overview - W3C Web Accessibility Initiative - The W3C's overview of the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines covering versions 2.0, 2.1, and 2.2, with links to the full standard and quick references. The official starting point for the accessibility metric.
  3. Alternative Text - WebAIM - Explains when and how to write alt text for informative, decorative, functional, and complex images, with examples. Directly supports the chapter's section on images.
  4. Keyboard Accessibility - WebAIM - Explains how people use a page without a mouse, including tab order, visible focus, and skip links. Gives a simple procedure for the chapter's keyboard test.

docs.title: Free Is Not Open: Price and Permission
docs.text:
Run the Free Is Not Open: Price and Permission MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 1: Foundations of Open Educational Resources

To change the content, edit data.json in this folder. The artwork is price-and-permission.svg, and scripts/posters/specs/ holds the code that draws it.

You can add this MicroSim to any web page with this iframe:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/oer-evaluator/sims/price-and-permission/main.html"
        height="765px"
        width="100%"
        scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
This poster is a two-by-two matrix. The columns ask what the resource costs the user. The rows ask whether the user may edit and share it. The four cells use the four examples from Chapter 1. The point is that the two questions are independent: a zero on the price dial says nothing about the permission dial. A resource is OER because of what its license permits, not because of what it costs.

This MicroSim is a grid overlay: the poster is a drawing made for this book (SVG), and each zone is a clickable rectangle over it.

Zone What it shows Free and open Free and open: costs nothing and grants permissions. Open, with a paid print copy Open, with a paid print copy: the license, not the price, makes it OER. Free but closed Free but closed: no price, but no permission to edit or share. Paid and closed Paid and closed: costs money and grants no permissions.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
• Explore and Quiz Me buttons: switch modes. Quiz Me starts a new run.
  • The zones: hover over a zone or press it to read its summary and facts in the panel below the poster.
  • Quiz questions: read the question, then press the zone that answers it. A wrong press lets you try again.
  • Try Again: repeats the quiz after the last question.

docs.title: Good to Know
docs.text:
Quiz mode scores each question as you answer it. The MicroSim does not store your answers. The poster prints its own headings, so the sim adds no labels on top of it.

  • The dollar amounts in the chapter, such as the $15 printed copy, are illustrative and are left off the poster.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can explain why a resource that costs nothing is not necessarily open, using the four cells of the price and permission matrix. (Bloom level: Understand.)

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Adult learners: teachers (K-12 and college), instructional designers, librarians, and OER coordinators.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 5-10 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • The definition of an open educational resource from Chapter 1.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (3 min). Press each of the four zones and read the facts. Which zone surprises you most?
  2. Quiz (3 min). Press Quiz Me and place all four examples.
  3. Apply (4 min). Pick three resources you used this month and say which zone each belongs in. What would you need to check to be sure?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer against the poster.

  1. A library e-book costs the reader nothing but forbids copying. Which zone is it in? (Free but closed.)
  2. A lesson plan licensed CC BY 4.0 is posted on a teacher blog. Is it OER? (Yes. It is open, and the price does not matter.)
  3. A print shop sells an open textbook at cost. Is the printed copy still OER? (Yes. The license grants the permissions even though the paper copy costs money.)

docs.title: Connection to the OER Evaluator rubric
docs.text: Open license is the first reusability metric in the ten-metric rubric. The rubric scores what you may do with a resource, never what it costs, which is why this matrix comes before any scoring.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Open educational resources - Wikipedia - Defines OER, traces the movement's history, and lists the 5R permissions with examples of repositories and national policies. Anchors this chapter's definition of an OER and its distinction between open and merely free materials.
  2. Free content - Wikipedia - Surveys definitions of free and open content, separating works that merely cost nothing from works that grant freedoms to reuse and modify. Supports the chapter's section explaining why free does not mean open.
  3. Definition of Open - opencontent.org - David Wiley's own statement of the 5R permissions (retain, reuse, revise, remix, redistribute) and why a license must grant all five. This is the source of the 5R framework used throughout the book.
  4. Open Educational Resources - UNESCO - UNESCO's OER hub, including the 2019 Recommendation on OER, the first international standard-setting instrument for openly licensed materials. Shows how governments define OER and why they encourage adoption.

docs.title: Quality and Reusability Quadrant Sorter
docs.text:
Run the Quality and Reusability Quadrant Sorter MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 3: The Ten-Metric Rubric and Scoring

To edit the sketch, paste the contents of quality-reusability-quadrant.js into the p5.js editor. The learning content (the items, answers, and reasons) is in the CONFIG block at the top of the file.

You can add this MicroSim to any web page with this iframe:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/oer-evaluator/sims/quality-reusability-quadrant/main.html"
        height="750px"
        width="100%"
        scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
A resource can be good but locked, or open but weak. The rubric separates the two ideas into a quality subtotal (metrics 1 to 5) and a reusability subtotal (metrics 6 to 10), each out of 50. A subtotal is high at 25 or more and low below 25. The threshold is a study aid.

This MicroSim shows eight resource profiles. You place each one in one of four quadrants. Afterward the sim shows the two subtotals and plots the profile on a two-axis chart. The chart doubles as the legend: each quadrant is named and defined in place.

Quadrant Subtotals Strong and open Quality 25 or more and reusability 25 or more Good but locked Quality 25 or more and reusability less than 25 Open but weak Quality less than 25 and reusability 25 or more Weak and locked Quality less than 25 and reusability less than 25

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
• Four quadrant buttons: place the profile. The placement is final.
  • Next: moves to the next profile.
  • Chart: each answered profile appears as a numbered point, green when right the first time and red when missed. On a wide page the results screen shows all eight points.
  • Play again and the missed-profile review on the results screen.

docs.title: Good to Know
docs.text:
Only your first committed answer on the first completed run counts as evidence of mastery. Practice runs give the same feedback but do not change that first-run score. Nothing moves until you act, and the MicroSim does not store your answers.

  • The profiles are illustrative examples in a shuffled order, two per quadrant.
  • The subtotals appear only after you answer.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can differentiate resources that need quality work from resources that need reusability work by placing each of eight profiles in the correct one of four quadrants, with at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. (Bloom level: Analyze.)

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Adult learners: teachers (K-12 and college), instructional designers, librarians, and OER coordinators.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • The ideas of the quality dimension, the reusability dimension, and quality versus reusability from Chapter 3.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Predict (2 min). Read the four definitions. Which quadrant do you expect a commercial e-book to land in?
  2. Place the profiles (6 min). Place all eight profiles, then study the chart.
  3. Plan (4 min). Choose one profile in a "locked" quadrant and name the two metrics you would fix first.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer by using it.

  1. A polished e-book, all rights reserved, PDF only. Which quadrant? (Good but locked. Quality is high, and the license and source pull reusability below 25.)
  2. A CC BY worksheet set with outdated links and no alt text. Which quadrant? (Open but weak. Reusability is high, and the errors and missing descriptions pull quality below 25.)
  3. Which quadrant needs work on both subtotals? (Weak and locked.)
  4. Why report both subtotals and not only the total? (Two resources can share a total and need very different work.)

docs.title: Connection to the OER Evaluator rubric
docs.text: Reporting both subtotals next to the total tells a reviewer which half of the rubric to improve. Chapter 15 shows how an AI agent can help improve a resource.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Rubric (academic). Wikipedia. Criteria, performance levels, and analytic versus holistic rubrics.
  2. Creating and Using Rubrics. Carnegie Mellon Eberly Center. The parts of a rubric and how to use it.
  3. Not All Rubrics Are Equal: A Review of Rubrics for Evaluating the Quality of Open Educational Resources. IRRODL. Compares fourteen OER quality rubrics.
  4. Achieve OER Rubrics. Achieve. Rubrics that score an OER criterion by criterion.

docs.title: Reading an Effect Size
docs.text:
Run the Reading an Effect Size MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 17: Analyzing A/B Test Results

To change the content, edit data.json in this folder. The artwork is reading-an-effect-size.svg, and scripts/posters/specs/ holds the code that draws it.

You can add this MicroSim to any web page with this iframe:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/oer-evaluator/sims/reading-an-effect-size/main.html"
        height="765px"
        width="100%"
        scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Effect size is the hardest idea in the second half of the book for readers without statistics. Overlapping curves give the intuition without algebra. Each panel shows the control group as one curve and the treatment group as the other, with the two means marked and the overlap shaded. The more the curves separate, the larger d. All three panels use the same axes, and the curves are drawn from the normal density. The sizes are rules of thumb, and what counts as important depends on the cost of the change and the setting. The caution strip carries the Watershed Basics pilot: a difference of 7.0 over a pooled standard deviation of about 6.78 gives d of about 1.03, and a big number from a small test deserves a second look.

This MicroSim is a grid overlay: the poster is a drawing made for this book (SVG), and each zone is a clickable rectangle over it.

Zone What it shows Small: d = 0.2 d = 0.2 is called small by convention, a rule of thumb. Medium: d = 0.5 d = 0.5 is called medium by convention, a rule of thumb. Large: d = 0.8 d = 0.8 is called large by convention, a rule of thumb. Caution: a pilot with d about 1.03 A d of about 1.03 from 12 students per group deserves a second look.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
• Explore and Quiz Me buttons: switch modes. Quiz Me starts a new run.
  • The zones: hover over a zone or press it to read its summary and facts in the panel below the poster.
  • Quiz questions: read the question, then press the zone that answers it. A wrong press lets you try again.
  • Try Again: repeats the quiz after the last question.

docs.title: Good to Know
docs.text:
Quiz mode scores each question as you answer it. The MicroSim does not store your answers. The poster prints its own headings, so the sim adds no labels on top of it.

  • The curves are normal densities with equal spread, drawn in code. The d labels are rules of thumb and not cutoffs.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can interpret d values of 0.2, 0.5, and 0.8 as the overlap between two groups, and explain why a large d from a small test deserves caution. (Bloom level: Understand.)

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Adult learners: teachers (K-12 and college), instructional designers, librarians, and OER coordinators.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 5-10 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Means, spread, and effect size from Chapter 17.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (3 min). Press each panel. How much of the control curve is still overlapped at d = 0.8?
  2. Quiz (3 min). Press Quiz Me and match four descriptions to the panels.
  3. Compute (4 min). Use the formula for a difference of 4.0 and a pooled standard deviation of 8.0. Which panel is closest?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer against the poster.

  1. What does d measure? (The difference of the two group means in units of the pooled standard deviation.)
  2. What size is d = 0.5 by convention? (Medium, a rule of thumb.)
  3. Why is the pilot's d of about 1.03 not the number to plan the next test on? (A small pilot gives a noisy estimate, and impressive estimates from small tests tend to shrink when repeated.)

docs.title: Connection to the OER Evaluator rubric
docs.text: Effect size is how Chapter 17 puts a difference on a common ruler. A teacher can compare tests with different spreads.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Effect size - Wikipedia - Explains effect sizes such as Cohen's d, how they are computed, and how to interpret them. Supports the chapter's section on reading the size of a difference, not only whether it exists.
  2. Using Effect Size—or Why the P Value Is Not Enough - Journal of Graduate Medical Education - Sullivan and Feinn explain why a significant p value says little about how large or useful a difference is. A short, readable argument for reporting effect size.
  3. Interpreting Cohen's d - R Psychologist (Kristoffer Magnusson) - An interactive visualization showing how two overlapping distributions change as Cohen's d grows. Helps teachers picture what a small or medium effect looks like.
  4. Statistical Power Analysis for the Behavioral Sciences (2nd ed.) - Jacob Cohen - Lawrence Erlbaum Associates (1988) - Cohen introduced the standardized difference d and offered 0.2, 0.5, and 0.8 as rough small, medium, and large conventions. He also showed how to plan sample size for them. The source of this chapter's effect size convention.

docs.title: Reliability and Validity Targets Poster
docs.text:
Run the Reliability and Validity Targets Poster MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 3: The Ten-Metric Rubric and Scoring

To change the content, edit the DATA block at the top of reliability-validity-targets.js. The drawing is inline SVG in main.html.

You can add this MicroSim to any web page with this iframe:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/oer-evaluator/sims/reliability-validity-targets/main.html"
        height="702px"
        width="100%"
        scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
A rubric can be steady without being right. Reliable means scores land close together, so reviewers agree. Valid means scores land on the bullseye, so they measure what matters. This poster shows four archery targets, each with a bullseye and six shots, one for each combination.

In Explore mode you hover or click a target to read what it means for a rubric. In Quiz me mode you read six scenarios and click the target that matches. The poster is a drawing made for this book (SVG). Its shot positions are fixed and it prints no numbers.

Target Meaning Reliable and valid Scores are consistent and measure the right thing. Reliable but not valid Scores are consistent but miss what matters. Valid on average but not reliable Scores scatter, though their average points the right way. Neither reliable nor valid Scores scatter and miss what matters.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
• Explore and Quiz me buttons: switch modes. Quiz me starts a new run.
  • The four targets: hover, focus with the Tab key, or click. In quiz mode a click is your answer.
  • Next: moves to the next scenario.
  • Play again: repeats the quiz as practice.

docs.title: Good to Know
docs.text:
Only your first committed answer on the first completed run counts as evidence of mastery. Practice runs give the same feedback but do not change that first-run score. Nothing moves until you act, and the MicroSim does not store your answers.

  • Each scenario has one attempt. Only the first completed run counts as evidence.
  • The poster prints its own target titles, so the sim adds no labels over it.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can classify each of six rubric scenarios as reliable and valid, reliable but not valid, valid on average but not reliable, or neither, with at least 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. (Bloom level: Understand.)

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Adult learners: teachers (K-12 and college), instructional designers, librarians, and OER coordinators.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 5-10 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • The terms rubric reliability and rubric validity from Chapter 3.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (3 min). Hover over each target. Which two have shots close together?
  2. Classify (4 min). Press Quiz me and classify all six scenarios.
  3. Invent (3 min). Write a rubric scenario of your own for the "reliable but not valid" target.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer by using it.

  1. Two reviewers always agree, but the scores do not predict learning. Which target? (Reliable but not valid.)
  2. Scores vary widely, but their average tracks student performance. Which target? (Valid on average but not reliable.)
  3. Is a rubric with scattered scores useless? (No. If the average is on target, more reviewers or clearer descriptors can help.)
  4. Can agreement alone prove a rubric is right? (No. Reviewers can agree and still miss what matters.)

docs.title: Connection to the OER Evaluator rubric
docs.text: A trustworthy rubric needs both properties. Chapter 14 measures agreement, and Chapter 17 compares scores with student results.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Reliability (statistics). Wikipedia. Consistency of a measure across repeated use.
  2. Validity (statistics). Wikipedia. What it means for a measure to capture what it claims to.
  3. Inter-rater reliability. Wikipedia. How agreement between independent raters is measured.
  4. Rubric (academic). Wikipedia. Criteria, performance levels, and analytic versus holistic rubrics.

docs.title: Reviewer Bias Spotter
docs.text:
Run the Reviewer Bias Spotter MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 3: The Ten-Metric Rubric and Scoring

To edit the sketch, paste the contents of reviewer-bias-spotter.js into the p5.js editor. The learning content (the items, answers, and reasons) is in the CONFIG block at the top of the file.

You can add this MicroSim to any web page with this iframe:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/oer-evaluator/sims/reviewer-bias-spotter/main.html"
        height="666px"
        width="100%"
        scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Reviewer bias is a systematic tendency in a reviewer's judgment that comes from the reviewer and not from the resource. Biases are not character flaws: everyone has them, and a method works by catching them. This MicroSim shows eight reviewer notes. For each you choose the bias it shows from six named biases or No bias.

After each answer the sim names the bias, says why, and gives the defense. Two of the eight notes show the same bias, and one shows none.

Bias Defense Halo effect Score one metric at a time, across the whole resource Anchoring Score alone, and do not see others' scores first Leniency Score against the descriptors, not against the effort Author or brand bias Run every check, whatever the source Confirmation bias Look for evidence that would change the score Fatigue Take breaks, and review in two sessions

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
• Seven option buttons: the six biases and No bias. The choice is final.
  • Show bias table: opens a table of the six biases, what happens, and the defense. Opening it is exploration, not evidence.
  • Next: moves to the next note.
  • Play again and the missed-note review on the results screen.

docs.title: Good to Know
docs.text:
Only your first committed answer on the first completed run counts as evidence of mastery. Practice runs give the same feedback but do not change that first-run score. Nothing moves until you act, and the MicroSim does not store your answers.

  • The notes are illustrative examples in a shuffled order.
  • The seven options are always offered.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can distinguish the bias shown in each of eight reviewer notes from six named biases and a no-bias option, with at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. (Bloom level: Analyze.)

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Adult learners: teachers (K-12 and college), instructional designers, librarians, and OER coordinators.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • The term reviewer bias and the six biases listed in Chapter 3.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Study the table (2 min). Open the bias table. Which two biases involve the order in which you score?
  2. Spot the bias (6 min). Work through all eight notes and read the defense for each.
  3. Plan (4 min). Choose the bias you are most likely to show and write the defense you will use in your next review.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer by using it.

  1. "The graphics are gorgeous, so I gave every metric an 8 or higher." Which bias? (Halo effect. One strong feature lifted every score.)
  2. "It comes from a famous university press, so I skipped the link check." Which bias? (Author or brand bias. The source led the reviewer to skip a check.)
  3. How does anchoring differ from the halo effect? (Anchoring is pulled by a number seen first. The halo effect is pulled by one strong feature.)
  4. What does a note with no bias look like? (It shows a check, a record, and a score that follows from them.)

docs.title: Connection to the OER Evaluator rubric
docs.text: Naming a bias is the first step in correcting for it. Chapter 14 shows how an AI agent's scores can drift too, as score inflation, and how to check them against human reviewers.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Halo effect. Wikipedia. One striking trait coloring the judgment of every other trait.
  2. Anchoring effect. Wikipedia. The first number seen pulls later judgments toward it.
  3. Confirmation bias. Wikipedia. Looking for evidence that fits an expectation.
  4. Inter-rater reliability. Wikipedia. How agreement between independent raters is measured.

docs.title: Ten-Metric Rubric Map
docs.text:
Run the Ten-Metric Rubric Map MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 3: The Ten-Metric Rubric and Scoring

To change the nodes or the complaints, edit the NODES and COMPLAINTS tables at the top of rubric-structure-map.js.

You can add this MicroSim to any web page with this iframe:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/oer-evaluator/sims/rubric-structure-map/main.html"
        height="562px"
        width="100%"
        scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The Ten-Metric Rubric rates an OER on ten metrics worth 10 points each. This map shows 13 nodes: the root, two dimensions (Quality, 50 points, and Reusability, 50 points), and five metrics under each dimension. Each edge means "is a part of" and points from the child to its parent.

In Explore mode you click a node to highlight its parent and children and to read its definition, the question it answers, and the chapter that teaches it. In Quiz me mode you read a teacher complaint, such as "I only have a PDF, and I need to change one sentence", and click the metric it tests. You get two tries.

Dimension Metrics Quality (50 points) Accuracy and currency, Alignment, Readability, Accessibility, Practice with feedback Reusability (50 points) Open license, Modularity, Metadata, Editable source, Portability

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
• Explore and Quiz me buttons: switch modes. Quiz me starts a new run.
  • Nodes: click a node. The same nodes are reachable by keyboard through a hidden list of buttons, and a screen reader announces each node.
  • +, minus, and Fit: zoom the map. The map does not zoom with the mouse wheel, so it never captures page scrolling. Once zoomed in, drag to pan.
  • Next: moves to the next complaint. Play again repeats the quiz.

docs.title: Good to Know
docs.text:
Only your first committed answer on the first completed run counts as evidence of mastery. Practice runs give the same feedback but do not change that first-run score. Nothing moves until you act, and the MicroSim does not store your answers.

  • Clicking the root or a dimension node during the quiz counts as a wrong attempt.
  • Each complaint has exactly one correct metric, and each metric is the answer to exactly one complaint.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can attribute each of ten teacher complaints to the one rubric metric it tests, with at least 9 of 10 correct on the first attempt. (Bloom level: Analyze.)

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Adult learners: teachers (K-12 and college), instructional designers, librarians, and OER coordinators.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • The ten rubric metrics and the quality and reusability dimensions from Chapter 3.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (4 min). Click each of the ten metrics and read the question it answers. Which two metrics sound most alike?
  2. Quiz (5 min). Press Quiz me and match all ten complaints to metrics.
  3. Distinguish (3 min). For each metric pair you confused, write one complaint that belongs to only one of them.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer by using it.

  1. "A screen reader reads the picture names as image1.png." Which metric? (Accessibility. Missing text descriptions block learners who use screen readers.)
  2. "I cannot tell whether I may translate this." Which metric? (Open license. The reuse permissions are not stated.)
  3. Which dimension holds Editable source? (Reusability.)
  4. Are readability and accessibility the same metric? (No. Readability is about wording for the audience, and accessibility is about learners with disabilities.)

docs.title: Connection to the OER Evaluator rubric
docs.text: Chapters 4 to 10 teach the checks behind these ten metrics, and each node in the map names the chapter that teaches it.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Rubric (academic). Wikipedia. Criteria, performance levels, and analytic versus holistic rubrics.
  2. Creating and Using Rubrics. Carnegie Mellon Eberly Center. The parts of a rubric and how to use it.
  3. Not All Rubrics Are Equal: A Review of Rubrics for Evaluating the Quality of Open Educational Resources. IRRODL. Compares fourteen OER quality rubrics.
  4. Achieve OER Rubrics. Achieve. Rubrics that score an OER criterion by criterion.

docs.title: Anatomy of a Rubric Worksheet
docs.text:
Run the Anatomy of a Rubric Worksheet MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 3: The Ten-Metric Rubric and Scoring

To change the content, edit the DATA block at the top of rubric-worksheet-anatomy.js. The drawing is inline SVG in main.html.

You can add this MicroSim to any web page with this iframe:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/oer-evaluator/sims/rubric-worksheet-anatomy/main.html"
        height="702px"
        width="100%"

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The rubric worksheet is where a reviewer records scores and evidence. This MicroSim draws a printed worksheet lying on a desk, seen from above. Eight numbered markers point at its parts. The drawing contains no text, so every label comes from the data in the sim.

In Explore mode you hover or click a marker to read its label, description, and tip. In Quiz me mode you read a hint, such as "A narrow column marked with a person icon", and click the marker that matches. You get two tries.

Marker Part 1 Resource information block 2 Metric and what-to-check columns 3 Your score column 4 Agent score column 5 Evidence column 6 Quality half 7 Reusability half 8 Totals box

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
• Explore and Quiz me buttons: switch modes. Quiz me starts a new run.
  • The eight numbered markers: hover, focus with the Tab key, or click.
  • Next: moves to the next hint.
  • Play again: repeats the quiz as practice.

docs.title: Good to Know
docs.text:
Only your first committed answer on the first completed run counts as evidence of mastery. Practice runs give the same feedback but do not change that first-run score. Nothing moves until you act, and the MicroSim does not store your answers.

  • A wrong first click says so and lets you try once more. A second wrong click reveals the marker. Only a correct first click counts as evidence.
  • The drawing is made for this book (SVG) and carries no statistics. A blank agent column is correct in a manual review.

docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer by using it.

  1. Which column holds where you looked, what you saw, and the rule you applied? (The evidence column.)
  2. Which half of the sheet is worth 50 points and holds Open license? (The reusability half.)
  3. Is the agent column filled in during a manual review? (No. Leave it blank.)

docs.title: Safe to Send? Student Data and AI Services
docs.text:

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
A privacy mistake cannot be undone, and a teacher new to AI may paste a gradebook without thinking. This poster sorts the items from the Chapter 13 worked example into three chutes. The published text of an open textbook chapter and a rubric prompt template are safe to send. A class's quiz scores with student names need fixing first, because names make the scores personal data. A spreadsheet of grades with student ID numbers, a student's photograph, and an email thread with a parent about a student must never be sent. Shapes and icons carry the meaning as well as color, and a silhouette stands in for the photograph. The poster gives no legal advice.

This MicroSim is a grid overlay: the poster is a drawing made for this book (SVG), and each zone is a clickable rectangle over it.

Zone What it shows Send it Safe to send. Fix it first Anonymize or get approval. Never send it Do not send.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
• Explore and Quiz Me buttons: switch modes. Quiz Me starts a new run.
  • The zones: hover over a zone or press it to read its summary and facts in the panel below the poster.
  • Quiz questions: read the question, then press the zone that answers it. A wrong press lets you try again.

docs.title: Good to Know
docs.text:
Quiz mode scores each question as you answer it. The MicroSim does not store your answers. The poster prints its own headings, so the sim adds no labels on top of it.

  • The poster gives no legal advice. Your school's policy decides what you may send, and FERPA is the U.S. law that protects student education records.

docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can sort six items into send it, fix it first, and never send it, and state why the sorting matters. (Bloom level: Apply.)

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Adult learners: teachers (K-12 and college), instructional designers, librarians, and OER coordinators.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 5-10 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (3 min). Press each chute and read why each item belongs in it.
  2. Quiz (3 min). Press Quiz Me and place six items in the right chute.
  3. Apply (4 min). List three files you would like an AI service to help with. Which chute is each in? Who would you ask if you are not sure?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer against the poster.

  1. Why are quiz scores with names not safe as they are? (Names make the scores personal data, so anonymize or get approval first.)
  2. Can you take back text you pasted into an AI service? (No. It has left your computer, and a deletion request may not undo it.)
  3. What do you do if you are not sure an item is safe? (Ask before you send it.)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA) - U.S. Department of Education - The Student Privacy Policy Office's official FERPA page, with guidance for schools and teachers on education records and disclosure. The primary source for the chapter's privacy rules.
  2. Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act - Wikipedia - Explains the U.S. law that protects the privacy of student education records and when schools may disclose them. The legal basis for the chapter's student data privacy guidance.
  3. Common Sense Privacy Program - Common Sense Media - Evaluates the privacy policies of educational apps and tools and rates them. Helps teachers check an AI service's data practices before sending it any student material.
  4. AI Risk Management Framework - NIST - A voluntary framework for governing, mapping, measuring, and managing the risks of AI systems. Supports decisions about which checks to automate and which need human oversight.

docs.title: Score Descriptor Matcher
docs.text:

        height="614px"

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Every rubric metric uses the same 0 to 10 scale, and each band has a descriptor. The share of the check that is met decides the band: checks passed divided by checks, times 100. This MicroSim states nine observations, such as "Accessibility: 13 of 24 checks pass", and you choose the band that fits.

The six bands are 0 Absent, 1 to 2 Very poor, 3 to 4 Weak, 5 to 6 Adequate, 7 to 8 Good, and 9 to 10 Excellent. A boundary belongs to the higher band, so 25% is Weak, 50% is Adequate, and 75% is Good.

Score Share of the check met 0 Absent 0% 1 to 2 Very poor 1% to 24% 3 to 4 Weak 25% to 49% 5 to 6 Adequate 50% to 74% 7 to 8 Good 75% to 89% 9 to 10 Excellent 90% to 100%

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
• Six band buttons: choose the band. The choice is final.
  • Show descriptor table: opens the table above. Opening it is exploration, not evidence.
  • Next: moves to the next observation.
  • Play again and the missed-observation review on the results screen.

docs.title: Good to Know
docs.text:
Only your first committed answer on the first completed run counts as evidence of mastery. Practice runs give the same feedback but do not change that first-run score. Nothing moves until you act, and the MicroSim does not store your answers.

  • The observations are illustrative examples in a shuffled order.
  • A share that falls between two whole percentages belongs to the band that contains it, so 12.5% is in the 1% to 24% band.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can apply the scoring descriptors to choose the correct score band for each of nine observations about a metric, with at least 8 of 9 correct on the first attempt. (Bloom level: Apply.)

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Adult learners: teachers (K-12 and college), instructional designers, librarians, and OER coordinators.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • The terms score scale, scoring descriptor, and metric score from Chapter 3.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Calculate (3 min). Work out the share for "9 of 12 checks pass" by hand. Which band is it?
  2. Match the bands (6 min). Choose a band for all nine observations.
  3. Edge cases (3 min). Find the three observations that sit exactly on a boundary and explain why the higher band wins.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer by using it.

  1. 3 of 12 components stand alone. Which band? (3 to 4 Weak. 25% is the bottom of the Weak band.)
  2. 18 of 22 checked facts match their sources. Which band? (7 to 8 Good. About 82% is in the 75% to 89% band.)
  3. 0 of 6 required metadata fields are recorded. Which band? (0 Absent. Nothing in the check is met.)
  4. Why does a boundary belong to the higher band? (The rule avoids ties, and a check that is exactly half met earns Adequate.)

docs.title: Connection to the OER Evaluator rubric
docs.text: Descriptors are what make one reviewer's 7 equal another reviewer's 7. Chapter 14 checks whether an AI agent applies them the same way.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Rubric (academic). Wikipedia. Criteria, performance levels, and analytic versus holistic rubrics.

  3. VALUE Rubrics. AAC&U. Level-by-level descriptors that different reviewers can apply consistently.
  4. Achieve OER Rubrics. Achieve. Rubrics that score an OER criterion by criterion.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
This poster puts the six Creative Commons licenses side by side: CC BY, CC BY-SA, CC BY-NC, CC BY-NC-SA, CC BY-ND, and CC BY-NC-ND. Each panel prints its license name, shows its icons, and carries a small pictogram of its main rule.

Panel Main rule CC BY Credit is the only condition. CC BY-SA Credit, and keep adaptations open the same way. CC BY-NC Credit, and no commercial use. CC BY-NC-SA Credit, noncommercial, and the same license on adaptations. CC BY-ND Credit, and share the work unchanged only. CC BY-NC-ND Credit, noncommercial, unchanged only.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
• Explore and Quiz me buttons: switch modes. Quiz me starts a new run.
  • The six panels: hover, focus with the Tab key, or click. In quiz mode a click is your answer.
  • Next: moves to the next question.

docs.title: Good to Know
docs.text:
Only your first committed answer on the first completed run counts as evidence of mastery. Practice runs give the same feedback but do not change that first-run score. Nothing moves until you act, and the MicroSim does not store your answers.

docs.title: Learning Objective

docs.title: Grade Level

docs.title: Prerequisites

docs.text:
1. Explore (3 min). Hover over each panel and read the facts. Which two licenses forbid sharing changed versions?
  2. Quiz (4 min). Press Quiz me and answer all six questions.
  3. Compare (3 min). Pick two panels that differ by one element and say what that element changes.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer by using it.

  1. Which license allows commercial use but forbids sharing changed versions? (CC BY-ND.)
  2. Which license puts no condition on the work beyond credit? (CC BY.)
  3. Which license text does Wikipedia use? (CC BY-SA.)
  4. Does CC BY-NC allow adaptations? (Yes, as long as use stays noncommercial.)

docs.title: Connection to the OER Evaluator rubric

1. About CC Licenses. Creative Commons. Plain-language summaries of what each license permits and requires.
  2. Creative Commons license. Wikipedia. The six main licenses and the BY, SA, NC, and ND conditions.

docs.title: Source Files and Delivery Files
docs.text:
Run the Source Files and Delivery Files MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 4: Open File Formats and Version Control

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Editable source is a reusability metric, and the most common failure is a resource distributed only as a PDF. This poster sorts the formats from Chapter 4 into three zones. Every file is a document tile with its extension printed large and two badges: a round badge for "is the format open?" and a square badge for "is it a good source for editing?". The PDF is the instructive tile. Its format is open, and it is still a poor source because it is built for reading.

This MicroSim is a grid overlay: the poster is a drawing made for this book (SVG), and each zone is a clickable rectangle over it.

Zone What it shows Good source Five formats that are open and good sources for editing. Usually acceptable The Word document is a published standard, but fidelity depends on software. Poor source A PDF is open but built for reading; a design-program file is closed.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
• Explore and Quiz Me buttons: switch modes. Quiz Me starts a new run.
  • The zones: hover over a zone or press it to read its summary and facts in the panel below the poster.
  • Quiz questions: read the question, then press the zone that answers it. A wrong press lets you try again.
  • Try Again: repeats the quiz after the last question.

docs.title: Good to Know
docs.text:
Quiz mode scores each question as you answer it. The MicroSim does not store your answers. The poster prints its own headings, so the sim adds no labels on top of it.

  • The page layout or design-program file is drawn as a generic tile with no program name or logo.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can explain why an open file format is not always a good source for editing, using the PDF as the example. (Bloom level: Understand.)

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Adult learners: teachers (K-12 and college), instructional designers, librarians, and OER coordinators.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 5-10 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • The editable source metric from Chapter 4.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (3 min). Press each zone. Which tile has a round check badge and a square cross badge?
  2. Quiz (3 min). Press Quiz Me and place four formats.
  3. Apply (4 min). List the files you hand out to colleagues. Which zone does each belong in? What would you add so that others can edit them?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer against the poster.

  1. Is a PDF an open format? Is it a good source? (Open, yes. Good source, no, because it is built for reading.)
  2. Why is a Word document only usually acceptable? (It is a published standard, but full fidelity depends on particular software.)
  3. Which formats are good sources for data and for diagrams? (CSV for data and SVG for diagrams.)

docs.title: Connection to the OER Evaluator rubric
docs.text: Editable source is metric 9 in the ten-metric rubric. A resource that ships only a PDF loses points here even if its license is fully open.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Open file format - Wikipedia - Defines file formats whose specifications are published so anyone can implement them without fees, with examples. Background for deciding whether a resource's source files count as open and editable.
  2. Markdown - Wikipedia - Describes the lightweight plain-text syntax, its history, and variants such as CommonMark. Shows why Markdown is this book's recommended editable source format for text.
  3. Markdown Guide: Basic Syntax - Markdown Guide - A clear reference for headings, emphasis, lists, links, and images in Markdown, with side-by-side examples. Enough to read and edit the Markdown source of an OER and to try the chapter's exercises.
  4. Basic HTML Syntax - MDN Web Docs - Introduces elements, tags, and attributes in HTML. Helps teachers recognize HTML as an open, editable source format and read the pages they will adapt.

docs.title: From Ten Scores to One Decision
docs.text:
Run the From Ten Scores to One Decision MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 3: The Ten-Metric Rubric and Scoring

To change the content, edit data.json in this folder. The artwork is ten-scores-to-one-decision.svg, and scripts/posters/specs/ holds the code that draws it.

You can add this MicroSim to any web page with this iframe:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/oer-evaluator/sims/ten-scores-to-one-decision/main.html"
        height="850px"
        width="100%"
        scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
This poster follows the layers of Chapter 3 from left to right. Ten metric scores, each 0 to 10, combine into two subtotals of 50 points, which add to a total out of 100. The total falls into a band, and the band plus a floor of 5 produces a decision: Adopt, Revise, or Reject. The example is Watershed Basics, total 65, Fair, Revise. The inset in the lower right shows the One Gap resource caught at the floor: nine metrics of 9 and one of 4 give a total of 85, which is Good, and the decision is still Revise.

This MicroSim is a callout overlay: the poster is a drawing made for this book (SVG) with no text in it, and every label comes from the numbered markers.

# Part What it shows 1 Ten metric scores Each metric is scored as a whole number from 0 to 10. Metrics 1 to 5 are quality and metrics 6 to 10 are reusability. The dashed line is the floor of 5. The example is Watershed Basics: 7, 6, 8, 5, 6 and 9, 5, 4, 8, 7. 2 Two subtotals of 50 points The quality subtotal is the sum of metrics 1 to 5 and the reusability subtotal is the sum of metrics 6 to 10. Each is out of 50. Watershed Basics has 32 and 33. 3 The total out of 100 The total is the quality subtotal plus the reusability subtotal, from 0 to 100. Watershed Basics totals 65. It is the number people ask for and the least informative number in a report. 4 The score band The total falls into a band: Excellent 90 to 100, Good 75 to 89, Fair 50 to 74, Weak 25 to 49, and Poor 0 to 24. A total of 65 is Fair. 5 The decision Adopt when the total is at least 75 and every metric is at least 5. Reject when the total is below 50. Otherwise Revise. Watershed Basics is Revise, shown by the pencil. 6 The floor gate and the One Gap example One Gap has nine metrics of 9 and one of 4. The total is 85, which is Good, yet the decision is still Revise because one metric is below the floor of 5.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
• Explore and Quiz buttons: switch modes.
  • Numbered markers and labels: hover over a marker or a label to read about that part of the poster.
  • Quiz mode: the labels are hidden. Read the prompt, then press the marker it names. A wrong press lets you try again.
  • Try Again: repeats the quiz after the last question.

docs.title: Good to Know
docs.text:
Quiz mode scores each marker as you answer it. The MicroSim does not store your answers. The artwork carries no text, so every name and number you read comes from the overlay.

  • The thresholds are this book's starting rule, not a standard.
  • Watershed Basics and One Gap are illustrative examples from Chapter 3.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can trace ten metric scores through subtotals, a total, a band, and a decision, and explain why the floor can override a high total. (Bloom level: Understand.)

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Adult learners: teachers (K-12 and college), instructional designers, librarians, and OER coordinators.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 5-10 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • The ten metrics from Chapter 3.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (3 min). Hover over markers 1 to 6 in order and watch what each layer keeps and what it loses.
  2. Quiz (3 min). Press Quiz and find each layer from its description.
  3. Apply (4 min). A resource totals 80 with one metric at 3. Which decision does the rule give, and why?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer against the poster.

  1. What is the Adopt rule? (A total of at least 75 and every metric at least 5.)
  2. What band is a total of 65? (Fair, which runs from 50 to 74.)
  3. A resource totals 85. Is it always Adopt? (No. If any metric is below 5 the decision is Revise.)

docs.title: Connection to the OER Evaluator rubric
docs.text: Chapter 11 applies this same decision rule to real adoption decisions. The thresholds are this book's starting rule, a teaching choice and not a standard.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Rubric (academic) - Wikipedia - Defines rubrics, their criteria and performance levels, and the difference between analytic and holistic forms. Background for the ten-metric rubric and for how its scoring scales are built.
  2. Not All Rubrics Are Equal: A Review of Rubrics for Evaluating the Quality of Open Educational Resources - IRRODL - Yuan and Recker's peer-reviewed comparison of fourteen OER quality rubrics shows what each one emphasizes. Useful for seeing where this book's ten metrics overlap with, and differ from, earlier tools.
  3. Achieve OER Rubrics - Achieve - Describes eight rubrics for judging how well an OER aligns to standards and meets other quality criteria, delivered through an online evaluation tool on OER Commons. An earlier example of scoring an OER criterion by criterion.

docs.title: Total Score Calculator
docs.text:
Run the Total Score Calculator MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 3: The Ten-Metric Rubric and Scoring

To edit the sketch, paste the contents of total-score-calculator.js into the p5.js editor. The learning content (the items, answers, and reasons) is in the CONFIG block at the top of the file.

You can add this MicroSim to any web page with this iframe:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/oer-evaluator/sims/total-score-calculator/main.html"
        height="862px"
        width="100%"
        scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Ten metric scores, each a whole number from 0 to 10, add up to a quality subtotal (metrics 1 to 5), a reusability subtotal (metrics 6 to 10), and a total out of 100. The total falls in a band, and a decision rule turns the scores into Adopt, Revise, or Reject.

In explore mode ten sliders show the subtotals, total, band, and decision at once, and name any metric below the floor of 5. In practice mode you type the total for five scored resources, choose the decision, and press Check. A resource is correct only when both the total and the decision match.

Band Total Excellent 90 to 100 Good 75 to 89 Fair 50 to 74 Weak 25 to 49 Poor 0 to 24

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
• Ten sliders: in explore mode, set each metric score from 0 to 10 in whole points. The start position is 5 for every metric.
  • Start practice: leaves explore mode.
  • Total score box: type a whole number from 0 to 100.
  • Adopt, Revise, Reject buttons: choose the decision.
  • Check: commits the answer. Back to explore is on the results screen.

docs.title: Good to Know
docs.text:
Only your first committed answer on the first completed run counts as evidence of mastery. Practice runs give the same feedback but do not change that first-run score. Nothing moves until you act, and the MicroSim does not store your answers.

  • The decision rule: Adopt when the total is 75 or more and every metric is 5 or more. Reject when the total is below 50. Otherwise Revise.
  • The five resources are illustrative examples. The explanation names the rule that decided each outcome.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can calculate the quality subtotal, reusability subtotal, total score, band, and adoption decision for each of five scored resources, with the total and the decision both correct on at least 4 of 5. (Bloom level: Apply.)

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Adult learners: teachers (K-12 and college), instructional designers, librarians, and OER coordinators.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 15-20 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • The terms quality subtotal, reusability subtotal, total score, score band, and adoption threshold from Chapter 3.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (4 min). Set every slider to 8, then lower one slider to 4. What happens to the decision, and why?
  2. Calculate (8 min). Work through the five resources. Add the scores on paper before you type the total.
  3. Explain (3 min). For the resource whose total is 85, explain why the decision is not Adopt.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer by using it.

  1. A resource totals 85 and one metric is 4. What is the decision? (Revise. The metric is below the floor of 5, even though the total is high.)
  2. A resource totals 37. What is the decision? (Reject. The total is below 50.)
  3. Does a total of 75 always mean Adopt? (No. Every metric must also be 5 or more.)
  4. Does the floor apply only to the license metric? (No. It applies to every metric.)

docs.title: Connection to the OER Evaluator rubric
docs.text: This is the arithmetic behind every total on the rubric worksheet. Chapter 11 uses the decision in a full manual evaluation.

docs.title: References

docs.title: Weak Prompt, Strong Prompt
docs.text:
Run the Weak Prompt, Strong Prompt MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 12: AI Agents, Prompts, and Rubric Scoring

To change the content, edit data.json in this folder. The artwork is weak-and-strong-prompt.svg, and scripts/posters/specs/ holds the code that draws it.

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/oer-evaluator/sims/weak-and-strong-prompt/main.html"

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Writing a rubric prompt is the first hands-on AI skill, and its five parts form a checklist. This poster sets two paper cards side by side, each divided into the same five bands: role, task, input, rules, and output format. The weak card says only "Check accessibility." and the other four bands are empty and hatched. The strong card fills all five. The wording comes from the Chapter 12 worked example. A good prompt does not guarantee a good answer, so Chapters 13 and 14 exist to check what comes back. The prompts are drawn as paper cards and not as a chat window, so the poster shows no brand interface.

This MicroSim is a grid overlay: the poster is a drawing made for this book (SVG), and each zone is a clickable rectangle over it.

Zone What it shows Weak prompt The weak prompt fills only the task band. Strong prompt The strong prompt fills all five bands.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
• Explore and Quiz Me buttons: switch modes. Quiz Me starts a new run.
  • The zones: hover over a zone or press it to read its summary and facts in the panel below the poster.
  • Quiz questions: read the question, then press the zone that answers it. A wrong press lets you try again.
  • Try Again: repeats the quiz after the last question.

docs.title: Good to Know
docs.text:
Quiz mode scores each question as you answer it. The MicroSim does not store your answers. The poster prints its own headings, so the sim adds no labels on top of it.

  • The prompt text is drawn as live text so its wording is exact.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can evaluate a prompt against the five parts of a rubric prompt and name the part that is missing. (Bloom level: Evaluate.)

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Adult learners: teachers (K-12 and college), instructional designers, librarians, and OER coordinators.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 5-10 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Prompts and the parts of a rubric prompt from Chapter 12.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (3 min). Press each card. Which empty band of the weak prompt would cause the worst answer, and why?
  2. Quiz (3 min). Press Quiz Me and match four descriptions to the two cards.
  3. Rewrite (4 min). Take a prompt you have used. Fill in the five bands. Which one was missing?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer against the poster.

  1. Which part tells the model what to do when it cannot tell? (Rules: write "not checkable".)
  2. Why does the strong prompt include the full text of the resource? (The input band supplies the material, so the model does not assume it knows it.)
  3. Does a strong prompt guarantee a correct answer? (No. Answers still need checking, which is why Chapters 13 and 14 exist.)

docs.title: Connection to the OER Evaluator rubric
docs.text: A rubric prompt is how an agent is told to apply the ten metrics and return evidence. The evidence column is what Chapter 14 checks.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Prompt engineering - Wikipedia - Surveys techniques such as few-shot examples and chain-of-thought prompting for steering a model's output. Supports the chapter's guidance on writing prompts and prompt templates.
  2. Building Effective AI Agents - Anthropic - Separates workflows from agents and describes patterns such as prompt chaining, routing, and evaluator-optimizer. Helps teachers understand the agent workflow this chapter uses for rubric scoring.
  3. Prompt Engineering Overview - Claude Platform Docs - Official guidance on writing clear prompts, giving examples, and iterating with tests. Supports the chapter's section on prompt iteration, where a rubric prompt is refined after checking the agent's first results.
  4. Prompt Engineering Guide - DAIR.AI - A free catalog of prompting techniques with examples, including zero-shot, few-shot, and chain-of-thought prompts. A handy reference while building a rubric prompt.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Hearing the result is more persuasive than reading a rule. This poster shows four rows from the Chapter 7 worked example. On the left is what a sighted reader sees. On the right is what a screen reader typically announces. The same photograph appears in every image row, so the only difference is the markup. A real heading is announced with its level. Good alt text is read as the image's description. No alt attribute makes the reader announce the file name, which is useless. An empty alt attribute is announced as nothing, which is correct only for a decorative image. Wording varies between screen reader programs, and the poster shows no real program.

This MicroSim is a grid overlay: the poster is a drawing made for this book (SVG), and each zone is a clickable rectangle over it.

Zone What it shows What is seen Four rows a sighted reader sees: a heading and the same photograph with three kinds of alt markup. What is heard What a screen reader typically announces for each of the four rows.

  • Announcement wording varies between screen reader programs. The poster shows typical announcements and no real program.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can predict what a screen reader announces for a heading and for images with good, missing, and empty alt text. (Bloom level: Understand.)

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Adult learners: teachers (K-12 and college), instructional designers, librarians, and OER coordinators.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 5-10 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Alt text, decorative images, and heading structure from Chapter 7.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (3 min). Press the seen column, then the heard column. Which row would frustrate a blind learner most?
  2. Quiz (3 min). Press Quiz Me and answer which zone shows what is seen and what is heard.
  3. Listen (4 min). Turn on a screen reader on your computer for five minutes and visit a page you teach from. Which row from this poster did you meet?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer against the poster.

  1. What does a screen reader say for an image with no alt attribute? (Often the file name, such as "Image, river.png", which is useless.)
  2. When is an empty alt attribute correct? (Only for a decorative image.)
  3. How does a screen reader announce a real heading? (With its level, such as "Heading level 2, How water moves".)

docs.title: Connection to the OER Evaluator rubric
docs.text: Five minutes with a screen reader changes how you write alt text. This poster gives a taste of that without any software, and supports the accessibility metric.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Screen reader - Wikipedia - Describes how screen readers turn on-screen content into speech or braille and what they need from a page's structure. Helps reviewers understand why headings and alt text are scored.
  2. Alternative Text - WebAIM - Explains when and how to write alt text for informative, decorative, functional, and complex images, with examples. Directly supports the chapter's section on images.
  3. WAVE Web Accessibility Evaluation Tools - WebAIM - A free tool that marks errors and alerts directly on a web page. Shows which accessibility problems automated checks can find and which still need a human reviewer.

docs.text:
Modularity is the seventh metric, and the lift-out test is the practical way to score it. This poster shows the same three pieces, a reading, a quiz, and a simulation, built two ways. On the left they are threads of one cloth, so pulling out the quiz unravels the rest. On the right they are separate blocks, each in its own folder, and the quiz lifts away cleanly. Four rows come from the chapter's table, and a strip along the bottom shows that modularity is a matter of degree.

Zone What it shows Woven design One long page where explanation, quiz, and simulation are threads of one cloth. Modular design A reading, a quiz, and a simulation as separate pieces, each in its own folder.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can apply the lift-out test to decide whether a resource is woven or modular, and place it on the degrees of modularity. (Bloom level: Analyze.)

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Adult learners: teachers (K-12 and college), instructional designers, librarians, and OER coordinators.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 5-10 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • The modularity metric and the standalone component from Chapter 9.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (3 min). Press each side and read its four rows. What changes about reuse?
  2. Quiz (3 min). Press Quiz Me and decide which design each statement describes.
  3. Apply (4 min). Pick one resource of yours. Copy one component into an empty file and read it cold. Does it still make sense?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer against the poster.

  1. A quiz refers to "the diagram above". Does it pass the lift-out test? (No. A component that depends on its surroundings is not standalone.)
  2. How does another teacher reuse a woven page? (Take everything or nothing.)
  3. What is the far end of the degrees of modularity? (Each part packaged with its own license and metadata.)

docs.title: Connection to the OER Evaluator rubric
docs.text: Modularity is metric 7 in the ten-metric rubric. It prepares Chapter 18, where components are packaged with a license and metadata.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Learning object - Wikipedia - Explains the learning object idea of small, self-contained, reusable units of instruction and the standards built around it. Supports the chapter's modularity metric.
  2. Dublin Core - Wikipedia - Describes the fifteen-element Dublin Core metadata set, its history, and its use in libraries and repositories. The basis of the metadata record taught in this chapter.
  3. Metadata - Wikipedia - Surveys kinds of metadata, standards, and uses, from library catalogs to web pages. Background for scoring whether a resource carries complete, useful metadata.

docs.title: OER Evaluator Stories
docs.text:
Short, lighthearted graphic-novel stories that help OER evangelists, librarians, and faculty remember how to evaluate open educational resources, with and without AI agents.

The Story Ideas page lists 29 planned stories. The six stories below have illustrated covers and complete panel artwork. The Cast and Style Sheet keeps the characters looking the same from story to story.

docs.title: Story Cast and Style Sheet
docs.text:
This page is the source of truth for how recurring characters look and how image prompts are written in the OER Evaluator stories. Each image is generated by a separate request that remembers nothing about the other panels, so every image prompt must repeat the full description of each character who appears in it. Copy the text below word for word. Do not paraphrase it, and do not shorten it.

All characters are invented. Campuses are described by type, and no real person, organization, or brand appears in any image.

docs.title: House Style
docs.text:
Paste this sentence into every image prompt, then add the story's genre costume if it has one.

Flat cartoon illustration, modern vector style, clean confident outlines, bold simple shapes, gentle humor, warm cream and soft gray neutrals with indigo (#3949ab) and burnt orange (#b45309) as the two accent colors, wide landscape 16:9 composition.

docs.title: Recurring Cast
docs.text:
Character Description to paste into every prompt where they appear Margie Halvorsen Margie Halvorsen, a calm woman in her late fifties with silver-blond hair in a low ponytail, round tortoiseshell glasses, a freckled face and a patient half-smile, wearing a mustard-yellow cardigan over a white blouse and dark slacks, with a lanyard around her neck holding a laminated card marked with ten small colored squares. Dr. Priya Raman Dr. Priya Raman, a brisk woman in her late forties of South Asian descent with short black hair that has one streak of gray at the front, rectangular dark-framed glasses and one permanently arched eyebrow, wearing a white lab coat over a teal sweater, with a pen behind her ear and a thick battered maroon textbook under her arm. Tomás Reyes Tomás Reyes, an enthusiastic man in his mid-thirties with medium-brown skin, short dark curly hair and a neatly trimmed beard, wearing a navy hoodie with big over-ear headphones around his neck. Bao Vang Bao Vang, a tired but cheerful woman in her early forties of Hmong American heritage with long black hair in a single braid and a pencil stuck in it, wearing an orange fleece vest over a gray shirt, with dark circles under her eyes and a laptop covered in stickers. Nadia Ibrahim Nadia Ibrahim, a practical woman in her mid-thirties of Somali American heritage wearing a deep-green hijab and a gray technician's work jacket with the sleeves pushed up, with safety glasses resting on top of her head and a clipboard in one hand. Gene Lindqvist Gene Lindqvist, a tall thin man in his early seventies with a white beard, wearing a red-and-black plaid flannel shirt with suspenders and reading glasses on a chain, carrying a paper notebook and a mechanical pencil. Devon Devon, a lanky library student worker in their early twenties with tousled dark curls, a green staff lanyard and a baggy oatmeal cardigan, carrying a stack of paper call slips. Dean Pemberton Dean Pemberton, a cheerful round-faced man in his sixties with a white fringe of hair around a bald head and tiny gold-rimmed half-moon glasses, wearing a gray suit with an orange bow tie, always grinning and often holding an oversized pair of ceremonial scissors or a rolled-up banner. Quill Quill, a friendly AI agent drawn as a small rounded cream-white robot about the height of a tall child, with a smooth indigo screen for a face showing two simple round eyes and a wide eager smile (no text on the screen), a tiny orange necktie, a single white feather quill tucked into the top of its head like a plume, and a clipboard held in both hands. Quill has no gender and is always called "they". Echo the Loon A very small loon with a glossy black head, a white belly, a black back with a white checkered pattern, a red eye, a small indigo scarf, and an orange-handled magnifying glass held in one wing. Echo is always tiny and in the background, never the focus.

Devon is a library student worker who first appears in The Citation That Never Was. Devon has no gender and is called "they". Other one-off characters, such as the fair board chairman and the potluck cooks in Blue Ribbon Casserole, are described inside their own story and are not part of the recurring cast.

docs.title: Echo's Cameo
docs.text: Echo appears somewhere in the background of at least one panel of every story, small enough that readers have to look for it. Name the panel and where Echo hides in that panel's prompt. Echo never speaks and never takes part in the action.

docs.title: Prompt Rules
docs.text:
1. Start each prompt body with the panel identifier line from the story template, and end it with the line "Generate the image immediately without asking clarifying questions."
  2. Repeat the house style sentence and the full cast description of every named character in the panel.
  3. Give at least six specific visual details: the setting, the props, the lighting, where each character stands and what they are doing, the facial expression, and one background gag.
  4. Keep text in the picture to a minimum. Image generators garble words. Allow at most one or two short labels per image (for example a sign reading "OPEN" or a stamp reading "NOPE"), quote them exactly in the prompt, and put all dialogue in the narrative text under the panel.
  5. No brand names, logos, or real interface screenshots. Draw generic stand-ins, such as "a generic laptop with a plain gray window". No real people.
  6. No violence, injuries, or anything alarming. The stories are gentle comedies.
  7. Show competence. Students and people who use assistive technology are always the sharpest people in the room, and are never the butt of a joke.
  8. Name the genre costume when the story has one (noir, game show, storybook fable, and so on) in both the cover prompt and every panel prompt.

docs.title: OER Story Ideas
docs.text: A list of fun and engaging mini-graphic novel stories that will help you remember the key strategies in efficiently evaluating OER resources both with and without AI agents.

docs.title: How This List Was Built
docs.text:
The story generator was first written to inspire young readers with profiles of scientists. This book's readers are different: OER evangelists, librarians, instructional designers, and the professors and teachers who choose textbooks for a campus, a department, or a district. They have sat through the committee meeting, defended the textbook budget, and been burned by a "free" PDF. So these ideas are fictional comedies set in places they know: the faculty lounge, the department meeting, the library reference desk, the school board meeting, and the potluck.

Each idea is built on one thing a reader should still remember a month later, and each is tied to the chapters that teach it.

  • Humor comes from the situation, never from the learner. The jokes land on "All rights reserved" footers, the 14th edition, final_FINAL_v7.docx, and committees that score everything an 8. Students, and people who use assistive technology, are always the competent ones in the room.
  • The AI agent is a character, not a villain. Quill is an eager intern who is fast, confident, and sometimes wrong. The lesson is never "AI bad" or "AI good". It is "check the evidence".
  • Stories with and without AI are both here. Part 1 teaches the skills a reviewer needs even with no AI at all. Part 2 adds the agent. Several stories (22, 26, 27, and 29) put the two side by side.
  • Settings cover high school, college, university, and district. The tag in each entry says which.
  • There are no historical profiles. Every character is invented. Campuses are described by type. The Minnesota stories may use the real names of colleges if the participants agree.
