docs.title: The Recurring Cast
docs.text:
A small repeating cast makes the stories feel like one universe and lets readers meet the same people again in a different chapter. None is a real person.

Character Who they are What they are like Margie Halvorsen Campus librarian and OER evangelist Wears a laminated rubric card on a lanyard. Calm. Her catchphrase is "Show me where it says that." Dr. Priya Raman Chemistry professor Has used the 14th edition of the same textbook since 2009. A real skeptic, and usually right. Tomás Reyes Instructional designer Accessibility zealot. Listens to his email at three times normal speed. Bao Vang Community college math instructor Builds MicroSims at midnight and forgets to label them. Dean Pemberton Dean who loves a savings number Wants a banner, a press release, and a ribbon-cutting. Means well. Quill The AI agent An eager intern with a clipboard who never says "I don't know". Uses they/them. Drawn the same way in every story. Echo Echo the Loon, the book's mascot A background cameo in every story, with a small magnifying glass: a Where's Echo? game for readers. In the winter Minnesota story Echo has migrated south and appears only on a postcard.

Students appear by first name (Kiara, Marcus, Noor) and are always sharper than the adults expect.

docs.title: Art Direction
docs.text:
The standard skill picks an art style by historical era. These stories are contemporary, so use one consistent house style and let each story borrow a genre for fun.

  • House style: flat cartoon, modern vector, clean lines, matching Echo's pose set. Palette of indigo (#3949ab) and burnt orange (#b45309) with warm neutrals.
  • Genre costumes: a few stories borrow a look for the joke, such as film noir (7), a game show (2), a home-makeover show (21), a storybook fable (22), a county fair (5), and a forensic procedural (17). Name the genre in the cover prompt.
  • No brand names, logos, or real interface screenshots in any image prompt. Draw generic stand-ins. No real people.
  • Numbers are illustrative unless the entry says it comes from a chapter. A story that shows a score should say "illustrative" in its Narrative Prompt and keep the numbers consistent with the rubric in Chapter 3.

docs.title: Part 1: Evaluating Without AI
docs.text: These stories teach what a reviewer needs even if no AI agent is ever opened. An agent can only check what a person knows to ask.

docs.title: 1. The Free Textbook That Wasn't
docs.text:
Setting Community college faculty lounge, the Tuesday before fall semester (college) Theme Free is not the same as open Connection Chapter 1: OER definition, the 5R permissions, free versus open Panels 6: one technique, one gag per permission Look House style, with a red rubber stamp that recurs

Dr. Raman announces that she has adopted a free chemistry PDF and saved her students $289. Then she tries to do the five things OER allows, and each attempt earns a red "NOPE" stamp: keep a copy, reuse a chapter in class, fix a typo, add a table from another source, and hand the file to a colleague. Margie slides a CC BY chemistry text across the table, and each of the five stamps turns green.

What readers will remember: Price and permission are two separate dials. Open means you may retain, reuse, revise, remix, and redistribute.

docs.title: 2. Adopt, Adapt, or Create: The Game Show
docs.text:
Setting University "Textbook Affordability Week" assembly (university) Theme Match the effort to the need Connection Chapter 1: adopt, adapt, create; Chapter 18: building a component library. See the Adopt, Adapt, or Create Pathway Chooser MicroSim Panels 7: setup, three doors, aftermath Look Game show, with studio lights and a laugh-track banner

Dean Pemberton hosts a game show in which three faculty contestants each pick a door. Door One is Adopt: use it as is, and a sparkling stack of existing books waits behind it. Door Two is Adapt: revise or remix, which means a pleasant afternoon with an editable file. Door Three is Create, and behind it sits one exhausted professor and a calendar showing 800 hours. Margie, as the "phone-a-friend", runs the rubric for each contestant and steers two of them to the cheaper doors. A student in the front row holds up a $289 receipt as the studio audience applauds.

What readers will remember: Look for an existing resource first, change it second, and build from nothing last.

docs.title: 3. The Potluck Label Law
docs.text:
Setting High school staff room, Teacher Appreciation Potluck (high school) Theme Credit where it is due Connection Chapter 2: attribution, the TASL format (Title, Author, Source, License), noting a change Panels 6: one technique, before and after Look House style, with every dish shown with a small index card

A new principal decrees that every dish needs a TASL card. The first cards are a disaster: "Recipe from the internet." "Grandma's." Then the real test arrives, a wild rice hotdish adapted from a 1974 church cookbook with the soup swapped out. The correct card names the title, the author, the source, and the license ("share it, but return the pan"), and adds a line saying what was changed. The principal's own brownies turn out to be a remix too.

What readers will remember: Title, Author, Source, License, and a note when you changed something.

docs.title: 4. License Speed-Dating
docs.text:
Setting Open Education Week mixer in a campus gym (college or university) Theme Not every license can combine with every other Connection Chapter 2: the Creative Commons elements (BY, SA, NC, ND), license compatibility, the NonCommercial gray area. See the License Compatibility Checker and NonCommercial Gray Area Sorter MicroSims Panels 8: five matches, one mismatch, one gray-area interlude, one resolution Look Speed-dating mixer with name tags, a bell, and a snack table

Six licenses wear name tags and take turns at small tables. BY just wants credit. BY-SA will share, but only with those who share alike. BY-ND says "don't change a thing." BY-NC wants nothing commercial. Two matches go well. The BY-SA and BY-NC match ends politely and permanently: irreconcilable differences. A chaperone by the snack table asks whether the PTA selling brownies to fund a course pack counts as commercial, and the whole room goes quiet. Margie closes with a seating chart of what combines with what.

What readers will remember: ND blocks remixes, SA passes its terms on, NC has a gray area, and some pairs simply cannot combine.

Check before drafting

The compatibility pairs must match the rules in Chapter 2 exactly. Check them there before writing the dialogue.

docs.title: 5. Blue Ribbon Casserole
docs.text:
Setting County fair hotdish contest, then Monday on campus (college) Theme Quality and reusability are different questions Connection Chapter 3: five quality and five reusability metrics, reporting two subtotals, not one blend. See the Quality and Reusability Quadrant Sorter MicroSim Panels 8: three contest entries, the verdict, and the Monday echo Look County fair, with ribbons and a judging table

Margie volunteers as a judge at the county fair hotdish contest, and each entry teaches a quadrant. Entry A is the best thing anyone has tasted, but the recipe is "a pinch of this" on a napkin, and the cook will not share it: high quality, low reusability. Entry B has a flawless recipe card with photos and a printable version, and it tastes like wet cardboard: low quality, high reusability. Entry C is delicious and shareable, and takes the ribbon. On Monday Margie opens two chemistry textbooks and sees Entry A and Entry B all over again.

What readers will remember: Report quality and reusability separately. A great resource nobody can reuse and a perfectly portable bad one both need work.

docs.title: 6. final_FINAL_v7_reallyfinal
docs.text:
Setting University department shared drive (university) Theme Open, editable source makes improvement possible Connection Chapter 4: open file formats, Markdown, editable source, version control, fork, pull request Panels 7: a linear fix, from chaos to a clean history Look House style, with a hallway of identical folder icons

The department wants to fix one chapter of a shared syllabus and a PDF-only textbook. The drive holds SyllabusFinal, SyllabusFINAL2, and SyllabusFINAL_USETHIS, and a Track Changes document is a rainbow of seven colors. Dr. Raman refuses to touch anything with the word "code" in it. Margie shows that the open version is a plain text file with some pound signs, and that version control is a time machine with a memory. A "fork" is your own copy, and a "pull request" is politely handing someone your edit with a note. Priya makes her first pull request, with the commit message "fix typo", and then makes it forty more times.

What readers will remember: An editable source plus a history is what lets strangers fix your book.

docs.title: 7. The Case of the Dead Link
docs.text:
Setting University library, 4:55 p.m. on the Friday before finals (university) Theme Accuracy and currency decay, and good citations resist it Connection Chapter 5: fact checking, citation quality, link rot, outdated content, persistent identifiers, archived copies Panels 9: mystery, three clues, a reveal, and a multi-step fix Look Film noir, black and white with a single orange accent

A world-weary narrator (Margie in a trench coat) takes the case of a textbook that cites a web page that has vanished. The victim is a 2011 URL. The clues: a "newest" social network that no longer exists, a sentence about a phone with a physical keyboard, and three other links that return 404. The witnesses: a persistent identifier that still resolves, an archived snapshot, and a newer source that says the number changed. The case closes with a list of what to fix and a note saying why the DOI survived and the plain URL did not.

What readers will remember: Links rot, so cite stable sources, save an archived copy, and check the date.

docs.title: 8. Grade 14 in Room 9
docs.text:
Setting High school ninth-grade biology class (high school) Theme Readability is about fit, not dumbing down Connection Chapter 6: reading level, Flesch-Kincaid grade level, plain language, fit to audience Panels 6: one problem, one fix Look House style, with a sentence stretched down a hallway like police tape

Noor, the student newspaper editor, runs the opening paragraph of the ninth-grade biology textbook through a readability checker. The result: grade 14.2. One sentence runs 74 words and has to be diagrammed across a whole hallway. The author insists this is "rigor". Noor and Margie rewrite the paragraph in plain language, keep every technical term, define each one on first use, and drop the reading level to grade 9. Nobody's science got easier. It just got readable.

What readers will remember: A textbook can have hard ideas and easy sentences. Match the reading level to the reader.

docs.title: 9. What the Screen Reader Said
docs.text:
Setting College instructional design office (college) Theme Accessibility is something you can hear when it fails Connection Chapter 7: alt text, headings, WCAG 2.1 AA, screen readers, automated accessibility checkers Panels 7: a demonstration, a pattern, and a fix Look House style, with sound waves drawn as speech balloons

Kiara, a student who uses a screen reader every day, offers to read the professor's new chapter aloud. The room hears: "Image. Figure underscore three underscore final underscore v2 dot jpg. Graphic. Graphic. Graphic." Next come the headings, which are bold text and not real headings, so the reader announces "no headings found" and navigation is a ten-minute scroll. Tomás hands over a new rule: alt text answers "what does this image do here?" and not "what does it look like?" The same river photo gets alt text mentioning the bends in one chapter and no alt text in another where it is decoration. Kiara reads the fixed page back at triple speed and grades it.

What readers will remember: Alt text says what the image does here, and real headings make a page navigable.

docs.title: 10. The Fluorescent Yellow Textbook
docs.text:
Setting College dorm study room (college) Theme Re-reading feels like learning and often is not Connection Chapter 8: worked examples, formative assessment, retrieval practice, question quality, immediate feedback Panels 6: before, exam, after Look House style, with the page glowing yellow

Marcus highlights every line of his textbook until the page glows like a traffic cone, then fails the exam. His study partner has a different textbook: a worked example first, then a question, then feedback that explains why an answer is wrong. A second textbook, in a gag panel, has a quiz where every answer is C and the feedback is the single word "Incorrect." The partner explains retrieval practice: close the book and try to say it. Marcus's highlighter, now dry, becomes a bookmark.

What readers will remember: Practice with feedback beats highlighting. Feedback should teach, not just grade.

docs.title: 11. The Orphan MicroSim
docs.text:
Setting University library, reference desk (university) Theme You can't reuse what you can't find Connection Chapter 9: metadata, Dublin Core, the six core fields, metadata completeness Panels 7: a loss, a search, and a rescue Look House style, with a lost-and-found bin of sad little objects

Bao built a superb interactive slope simulation in 2022. It lives in a folder named untitled-3 with no description, no subject, no grade level, and no license. A colleague in another state needs exactly that simulation and searches for "interactive slope" for an hour. In the lost-and-found at the library desk, the simulation wears a name tag reading "Hello, my name is: Untitled." Margie fills in six fields of metadata, and the same search now finds it in four seconds. A final panel shows the colleague's course page with the simulation embedded and Bao credited.

What readers will remember: Good metadata is what makes a resource findable, and findable comes before reusable.

docs.title: 12. The Chapter That Wouldn't Lift Out
docs.text:
Setting Community college math department (college) Theme A good component stands alone Connection Chapter 9: modularity; Chapter 10: portability, no-login access, iframe embedding, LMS import, platform lock-in Panels 8: the lift attempt, three snags, the redesign, and a clean lift Look Knitting and craft, with a sweater whose threads stand in for links

Bao pulls one section out of a textbook to drop into her course, and it will not come loose, like a thread in a sweater. The section says "as we saw in Chapter 3" fourteen times. Its images are hotlinked and vanish. The interactive graph needs a login to a platform that has since been acquired and shut down. After the lift test fails three times, the section is redesigned with its own objective, stated prerequisites, local images, and a no-login embed. The last panel is the same section pasted into a course page in one try.

What readers will remember: Apply the lift-out test: can it stand alone, open without an account, and move without breaking?

docs.title: 13. The Floor Beneath the Total
docs.text:
Setting College department meeting, 4 p.m. on a Thursday (college) Theme A high total can hide a failed metric Connection Chapter 3: bands and the adoption threshold; Chapter 11: adopt, revise, or reject, boundary cases Panels 8: the argument, the rule, three boundary cases, and a fix Look Game show, with a limbo bar set at 5

A committee reviews a textbook that scores 88. Dean Pemberton wants to adopt it today. Tomás points out that accessibility scored 4, and a student who uses a screen reader enrolls on Monday. Margie lays out the rule on a flip chart: Adopt needs a total of at least 75 and every metric at 5 or above, which she illustrates with a limbo bar set at 5. The Dean pleads "But it's 88!", and Margie walks him through the boundary cases: 74 is Revise, 75 with every metric at 5 or above is Adopt, 50 is Revise, and 49 is Reject. The cheap fix, alt text and captions, is done by Friday, and the re-score clears the floor.

What readers will remember: Adopt means 75 or more with nothing below 5. Never report a total without the lowest metric.

docs.title: Part 2: Evaluating With AI Agents
docs.text: These stories introduce Quill and the habits that make an agent's report trustworthy. None of them is anti-AI. Each is about checking the evidence.

docs.title: 14. Quill, the Eager Intern
docs.text:
Setting University OER office (university) Theme The agent makes the first pass and the human makes the call Connection Chapter 12: AI assistants, agents, skills, rubric scoring, evidence for a score; Chapter 13: human in the loop Panels 8: an arrival, a miracle, a catch, and a working routine Look House style, with Quill drawn as an eager intern holding a clipboard

Margie hands a 400-page textbook to Quill, and four minutes later there is a ten-metric report with scores and a confident tone. Dr. Raman's eyebrow rises. Margie says her catchphrase and asks for the evidence: every score has to quote the text it came from. Most quotes are exact. One is "paraphrased", and one points at a page that is not in the book. By the last panel the three-step routine is on the wall: the agent proposes, the human checks the evidence, and the human decides.

What readers will remember: The agent is fast, the evidence is what you trust, and you make the decision.

docs.title: 15. Weak Prompt, Strong Prompt
docs.text:
Setting Faculty technology workshop (college or university) Theme A good prompt works like a good order Connection Chapter 12: prompts, rubric prompts, structured output Panels 6: a side-by-side comparison Look House style, split down the middle, with two coffee orders

Two professors sit side by side. One types "Is this textbook good?" and Quill writes a warm essay ending with "a delightful journey!" and no numbers. The other writes a prompt like an order for a very specific coffee: the role, the rubric, the audience, the rule that each score must quote evidence, the output format, and the line "anything untested counts as failed". The first gets a poem, and the second gets a report she can check. The final panel is the two orders on a coffee shop board.

What readers will remember: Rubric, evidence rule, format, and "untested counts as failed" are what a strong prompt contains.

docs.title: 16. The Privacy Officer Has Entered the Chat
docs.text:
Setting High school teachers' room (high school) Theme Review the resource, not the students Connection Chapter 13: student data privacy, FERPA, AI cost, human in the loop Panels 6: a mistake, an apparition, and a rule Look House style, with a gentle ghost gag

A well-meaning teacher pastes the whole grade roster, with names and support notes, into a chatbot to "personalize feedback". A translucent district privacy officer rises from the chat window holding a clipboard. Nobody is shamed. The officer explains the rule in one line: an agent that reviews a resource needs only the resource. The teacher also gets a look at the usage meter, which ticks like a taxi. The last panel is a three-item checklist on the staff-room wall that ends with "when unsure, ask your privacy officer".

What readers will remember: Keep student information out of every prompt. Ask before you send. Mind the meter.

Keep it non-legal

The chapter says this book does not give legal advice. The story should end with a pointer to the school's own privacy officer, and never with a legal conclusion.

docs.title: 17. The Citation That Never Was
docs.text:
Setting University library reference desk (university) Theme If you cannot find it, treat it as false Connection Chapter 14: hallucination and its four forms (feature, quotation, measurement, source), invented citation; Chapter 5: citation quality Panels 9: a mystery, a reveal, and a multi-step fix Look Forensic procedural, with evidence markers numbered like a crime scene

Quill's report praises a textbook as well sourced and cites a journal article by two authors, with volume, issue, and page numbers. It reads perfectly. Margie checks the catalog, the DOI lookup, the publisher's table of contents, and an interlibrary loan request. The journal exists, but volume 14 never had that issue. Quill's defense: "It sounded right." Margie sets out the four ways an agent invents things, adds a column to the report called "found by a human", and tells the class the one-line rule.

What readers will remember: A fluent, confident citation is not evidence. Look it up.

docs.title: 18. The License Quill Misread
docs.text:
Setting Community college OER office (college) Theme A license is what it says, not what it sounds like Connection Chapter 14: license misreading; Chapter 2: reading a license statement. See the Anatomy of a License Statement MicroSim Panels 6: two misreads, one catch Look House style, with a footer shown in close-up

The footer of a textbook reads "© 2019 Creative Commons Learning Network. All rights reserved." Quill sees the words "Creative Commons", declares the book CC0 and public domain, and scores the license metric 10. Dean Pemberton is about to approve a remix. Margie reads the footer aloud. Then Quill reads a CC BY-NC-ND license as "free to remix", and Margie reaches for the license deed. The story ends with a stamp: "Read the license, not the logo."

What readers will remember: Agents pattern-match on names. Verify every license against its actual terms.

docs.title: 19. The Pizza Menu Scores 82
docs.text:
Setting University OER office (university) Theme Calibrate the agent with a decoy Connection Chapter 14: overconfident score, score inflation, calibration against human scores; Chapter 3: score bands Panels 7: a setup, a surprise, a recompute, and a fix Look House style, with a pizza menu treated like a serious academic text

Before trusting Quill with real textbooks, Margie slips in a decoy: a pizza restaurant menu. It has no learning outcomes, one source (a phone number), and a typo in "pepperoni". Quill returns 82 out of 100, praising it as "engaging, accessible, and highly practical". Margie recomputes one metric from Quill's own checks: 6 of 10 passed, which earns a 5 or 6 (Adequate), but Quill reported an 8. The menu's stated learning outcome is "hunger". She adds the rule that untested counts as failed and demands a tool log, and the pizza menu drops to a sensible 31 (illustrative).

What readers will remember: Test an agent with a resource you already know is bad. A high score with thin evidence is overconfident.

docs.title: 20. The Standards Code That Never Was
docs.text:
Setting High school district curriculum office and school board meeting (high school, district) Theme Alignment is checked against the real standards document Connection Chapter 6: learning outcomes, standards alignment, Bloom's levels; Chapter 14: hallucination Panels 7: a request, a table, a public question, and a fix Look House style, with a board room in the evening

The district curriculum coordinator asks Quill to map a biology unit to the state standards, and gets a gorgeous table. At the board meeting a parent asks what one of the codes in the table actually says. Nobody knows, because the code matches nothing in the state's document. A student teacher finds the actual standards document, and the team re-maps the unit against the real text. Along the way they notice the unit's outcomes say "understand", which no one can measure, and swap in verbs a quiz can check.

What readers will remember: Never accept alignment from memory. Check the code against the source, and write outcomes you can measure.

docs.title: 21. The Great Fix-It Weekend
docs.text:
Setting Community college math department, a Saturday and Sunday (college) Theme Improve one metric at a time, then review every change Connection Chapter 15: improvement plan, the Fix Toolkit, controlling the changes, derivative work, re-scoring Panels 10: a before, six fixes in a montage, one near-disaster, and an after Look Home-makeover show, with reveal curtains and a before-and-after score

Bao's 2014 algebra notes PDF scores a modest 52 (illustrative), with no alt text, fake headings, a high reading level, no metadata, and no practice. Over a weekend, Quill and Bao fix them in order of impact, in a makeover montage. In the middle of the montage Quill "improves" an equation and flips a sign. Bao catches it because she reviews every change. Margie checks that the license allows a revised copy and that the credit stays attached. On Sunday evening they re-score, and the reveal curtains open on 78 (illustrative).

What readers will remember: Fix the lowest metric first, re-score, review every change, and keep the credit.

docs.title: 22. The Tortoise, the Hare, and the Rubric
docs.text:
Setting University departments with one deadline (university) Theme Automate what is checkable, judge what is not Connection Chapter 11: manual evaluation; Chapter 12: agent scoring; Chapter 13: automated checks and what they cannot find; Chapter 14: checking output Panels 8: a race, two finishes, and a combined protocol Look Storybook fable, with watercolor edges

Two colleagues must choose among five candidate textbooks by Friday. Dr. Raman, the Tortoise, scores them by hand. Tomás, the Hare, runs an agent and automated link and accessibility checks. Priya finishes only three books, but she catches a subtle chemistry error that only an expert would see. Tomás finishes all five and finds 61 missing alt texts and 9 dead links (illustrative counts), but he misses the chemistry error and trusts one invented citation. Margie ties the two together with a protocol: tools for what can be checked, the agent for a first pass, and a human for judgment and for verifying evidence. Everyone shares the last slice of pie.

What readers will remember: Machines give breadth, people give judgment, and the best review uses both.

docs.title: 23. The Skeptic Is Not Required to Convert
docs.text:
Setting College faculty senate (college) Theme Healthy skepticism is a feature of the process Connection Chapter 13: human in the loop; Chapter 14: classifying errors (factual, license, citation, scoring), logging findings, measuring agreement Panels 7: a debate, a test, and an uneasy truce Look Courtroom comedy, with a gavel and a two-minute timer

A senate debate on whether the campus should use AI to review textbooks. Dr. Raman, the skeptic, argues "it lies", and she is partly right. Instead of a conversion, the story gives her the job she is best at: she writes the checklist that classifies every agent error as factual, license, citation, or scoring, and she logs findings in a shared table. At the next meeting her log shows where the agent was wrong and where it matched the humans. She remains unconvinced about AI and extremely convinced about her checklist, and the senate votes to adopt it.

What readers will remember: You do not have to love the agent. You have to check its work, and a skeptic makes the best checker.

docs.title: 24. Two Sections, One Sneaky Schedule
docs.text:
Setting High school biology department (high school) Theme A test can fool you if you design it carelessly Connection Chapter 16: control and treatment groups, random assignment, confounding variables, sampling bias, pre-test and post-test, learning gain, informed consent Panels 8: a plan, three traps, a redesign, and a clean test Look House style, with a pep rally as the recurring villain

A teacher wants to test an improved Watershed Basics. The first plan: first period uses the old version and seventh period uses the new one. Margie points out that seventh period comes after lunch and a pep rally, which is a confounding variable. The second plan: let volunteers use the new version. Now the eager students are all in one group, and that is sampling bias. The third plan sends the consent letters after the pre-test, which is backward. The final design uses blocked random assignment within each class, consent first, the same pre-test and post-test for both groups, and an equally good activity for students who decline.

What readers will remember: Randomize, get consent first, and watch for anything else that differs between the two groups.

docs.title: 25. Large Effect, Small Sample
docs.text:
Setting College dean's office (college) Theme A big number from a small test deserves a second look Connection Chapter 17: comparing group means, spread, effect size, small-sample caution, checking rubric scores against outcomes Panels 7: a triumph, a hush, and an honest report Look House style, with a banner under construction

The Watershed Basics pilot has 12 students per group, and the effect size comes back at 1.03. Dean Pemberton orders a banner reading "OER IMPROVEMENT: LARGE EFFECT!" Margie and a statistician friend ask the Dean to look at the spread: the control group's gains run from 3 to 22 and the treatment group's from 9 to 33, so they overlap. A few strong students could have moved the averages. The banner is replaced by a modest sign: "Promising. Next: more classes." A last panel shows the two questions the pilot cannot yet answer: would more classes agree, and did the change raise learning or only the rubric score?

What readers will remember: Effect sizes of 0.2, 0.5, and 0.8 are small, medium, and large, and small tests produce noisy numbers.

docs.title: Part 4: The Minnesota Series
docs.text:
Three connected stories about OER evangelists at different Minnesota colleges who join forces to build a workshop on evaluating OER. They draw on the one-day workshop in the grant response and the sample schedule: about 20 teachers, an 8:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. day, hand scoring first, then agents, then an improvement challenge, then publishing under a CC BY license.

The characters are invented composites. They come from different kinds of campuses: a Minnesota State university, a community college, a private liberal arts college, a technical college, and the University of Minnesota. The author can swap in real campus names later, with each person's consent. If a tribal college colleague should be in the cast, invite them to shape that character.

Minnesota touches to use sparingly: the loon (the state bird, and Echo), "Minnesota nice", hotdish, long goodbyes at the door, lake-effect weather, the drive across the state, and a church-basement potluck.

docs.title: 26. Minnesota Nice Is Not a Scoring Method
docs.text:
Setting A statewide video call of five reviewers from five campuses (college and university) Theme Politeness inflates scores Connection Chapter 3: reliability, evidence for a score; Chapter 11: calibration and consensus; Chapter 14: score inflation. See the Reviewer Bias Spotter and Inter-Rater Agreement Explorer MicroSims Panels 7: a polite review, a translation, a standoff, and a rule Look House style, with subtitles that translate what people really mean

Five exceedingly polite reviewers score the same sample textbook. Every score lands between 7 and 9. The comments are "That's... different." "It has a lot of... content." "I'm sure the author tried." Subtitles translate: "interesting" means 3, and "has potential" means 4. Margie points out that this is leniency bias and that the group is inflating scores exactly the way an overconfident agent does. The fix is the book's own: score alone first, quote the evidence, then discuss only gaps larger than 3 points. For the first time, someone says, "I... respectfully... disagree." Then there is the Midwest goodbye, which takes eleven minutes.

What readers will remember: Humans inflate scores too. Calibration needs evidence, blind scoring first, and permission to disagree.

docs.title: 27. The Lake Effect Workshop
docs.text:
Setting Five Minnesota campuses, a Minneapolis venue, and a February blizzard (multi-campus) Theme A good method spreads when colleagues build it together Connection Chapter 19: workshops, the facilitator guide, certificate requirements; Chapter 11: calibration; Chapter 12: agent scoring; Chapter 14: checking the agent Panels 12: a full planning-to-workshop arc Look House style, with a snowy map of Minnesota and the five campuses as dots

A $1,000 grant arrives, enough for one day, 20 teachers, lunch for 24, and a stack of printed rubric cards. Five evangelists, scattered across the state, plan it on a video call where someone is always frozen mid-sentence: Margie (the librarian, from a Minnesota State university in the south), Tomás (the instructional designer, from a private liberal arts college), Bao (the community college math instructor), Nadia (the technical college faculty member who wants rubric cards a mechanic could read), and Gene (a retiring professor who loves paper and is the best fact-checker anyone has met).

Each takes a session. In a trial run the five disagree on a sample score, the Minnesota nice problem from story 26, and they build the calibration exercise from their own argument. On the night before the workshop a blizzard arrives. On the day, 11 teachers arrive in person and 9 join by video, and the improvement challenge runs while the power flickers. Gene catches Quill's invented citation live, in front of the room. At 3:15 the improved components are published under CC BY, and the certificate checklist goes up on the screen. In the final panel the potluck table has TASL cards on every dish (callback to story 3). Echo is not in the background anywhere, because loons leave before the freeze, but there is a postcard from the Gulf coast: "Wish you were here. Check the evidence."

What readers will remember: A repeatable workshop has a run-of-show, a shared worksheet, a live catch of an agent error, and a certificate with clear requirements.

docs.title: 28. A Call Across the Lake
docs.text:
Setting The same campuses, six weeks later (multi-campus) Theme Every trained teacher becomes a local reviewer Connection Chapter 18: publishing to a clearinghouse, tracking reuse, reporting impact; Chapter 19: certificate review, training local reviewers Panels 6: a ripple, spreading Look House style, with a lake at dawn and ripples as the visual thread

Certified teachers start running their own mini-workshops. Nadia trains her technical college department. Gene coaches the first new local reviewer over video. Bao's simulation, now with full metadata, turns up in a nursing course in Duluth, and a reuse counter ticks over. The clearinghouse has its first ten components. The final panel is a map of the state where dots light up one by one and ripples overlap, and a single loon call carries across the water.

What readers will remember: Training, certifying, publishing, and tracking reuse are what turn one workshop into a network.

docs.title: 29. Watershed Basics: The Whole Loop
docs.text:
Setting One resource, one academic year, several campuses (mixed high school, college, university) Theme Evaluate, improve, test, calibrate, publish, train Connection Chapters 1 to 19, using the book's running example, Watershed Basics Panels 16: a synthesis montage, one chapter's idea per one or two panels Look House style, with a loop drawn as a river that returns to its source

The book's own example follows the full loop. A teacher finds it and decides between adopt, adapt, and create. Margie reads the license and writes the credit line. The hand review gives 65, with metadata at 4, which is below the floor, so the verdict is Revise. Quill makes the first pass and a human catches four invented claims. The fix toolkit raises the weak metrics. A 12-and-12 A/B test follows, with consent first, and the effect size is read with caution. The test results are then compared with the agent's scores, which is how the agent is calibrated. The improved version is published with metadata and a CC BY license, and a Minnesota workshop teaches others to repeat it. The river returns to its source and the loop starts again.

What readers will remember: The whole book is one loop, and test results are what make automated scores worth trusting.

Use the chapter numbers

Take every score, count, and threshold from Chapters 3, 11, 14, 16, and 17 and keep them identical. If a chapter changes, update the story.

docs.title: Coverage by Chapter
docs.text:
Every chapter has at least one story, and the hardest chapters (14 and 11) have several.

docs.title: Where to Start
docs.text:
If you generate only a few, these cover the book's main arguments and the Minnesota request. Together they are 52 panels and 58 images. All six are now drafted, with text and image prompts, and are listed on the Stories overview. The images have not been generated yet. The characters' fixed descriptions are on the Cast and Style Sheet.

Order Story Why 1 27. The Lake Effect Workshop The Minnesota collaboration, and the story most readers will share 2 26. Minnesota Nice Is Not a Scoring Method Introduces the cast and the bias lesson that story 27 builds on 3 5. Blue Ribbon Casserole The clearest picture of quality versus reusability 4 13. The Floor Beneath the Total The adoption rule, which is the one decision every reader must make 5 17. The Citation That Never Was The most important thing to know about AI agents 6 22. The Tortoise, the Hare, and the Rubric The "with and without AI" story in one place

docs.title: Held in Reserve
docs.text:
These came up but need fact-checking or a source before drafting, so they are not in the main list.

  • How the Four Rs Became Five. A short history of the 5R permissions and the year "Retain" was added. Needs a verified timeline and citations.
  • Fourteen Rubrics Walk Into a Conference. The rubrics themselves as characters, and who has a scoring guide. The numbers come from the rubric specification, which is still a draft.
  • The Rubric That Ate the Department. A satire on rubric creep, where every committee adds one more indicator until nobody finishes a review. The rubric specification notes that more indicators add burden for users, which gives the joke a real basis.

docs.title: How to Generate a Story
docs.text:
To turn any idea into a full graphic novel with generated images, use:

book-media-generator (story route): {Story Title} --panels {N}

The suggested panel count is in each entry, and --panels N overrides it. At about $0.039 per image the cost is $0.039 × (N + 1). A 6-panel story costs about $0.27 and a 12-panel story about $0.51. All 29 stories together are 252 images, about $9.83.

Before generating any story:

  1. Read CONTENT-GENERATION-GUIDE.md. Student-facing prose follows the book's writing rules.
  2. Keep the cast consistent with the table above, and put Echo in the background of at least one panel.
  3. Keep brand names and logos out of every image prompt.
  4. Generate the cover first and check it before spending credits on the panels.
  5. Add the story to the Stories section of mkdocs.yml, add a card to docs/stories/index.md, and run mkdocs build --strict.

docs.title: Blue Ribbon Casserole
docs.text: Cover Image Prompt (This is the Cover Image. Do not include this label in the image.) Please generate a wide-landscape 16:9 cover image for a graphic-novel comedy titled "Blue Ribbon Casserole". Flat cartoon illustration, modern vector style, clean confident outlines, bold simple shapes, gentle humor, warm cream and soft gray neutrals with indigo (#3949ab) and burnt orange (#b45309) as the two accent colors, wide landscape 16:9 composition. County-fair costume: triangle bunting in indigo and orange strung across the top, hay bales, a long folding judging table with paper plates and plastic forks, a striped tent roof, and a Ferris wheel far in the background. In the center stands Margie Halvorsen, a calm woman in her late fifties with silver-blond hair in a low ponytail, round tortoiseshell glasses, a freckled face and a patient half-smile, wearing a mustard-yellow cardigan over a white blouse and dark slacks, with a lanyard around her neck holding a laminated card marked with ten small colored squares. She holds a blue ribbon rosette high in one hand and looks over her glasses at the viewer, with a gentle raised eyebrow. On the table to her left sits a golden, glowing casserole dish with a small padlock hanging from its handle and a crumpled, grease-stained napkin beside it. On the table to her right sits a flat gray-beige casserole in a spotless glass dish beside a thick, tidy binder with colorful tabs. Behind her, two tall easel scoreboards stand side by side, each with two simple unlabeled bars, one tall and one short on the left board and the reverse on the right board. The title "Blue Ribbon Casserole" is rendered across the top in bold, friendly county-fair poster lettering in indigo with orange outlines; it is the only text in the image. Narrative Prompt This is a fictional comedy for adult readers: OER evangelists, librarians, instructional designers, and the professors and teachers who choose textbooks. It is set at a Minnesota-style county fair and, on the following Monday, in a college faculty office. The central idea comes from Chapter 3 of the book: a resource has two independent halves, quality and reusability, and they must be scored and reported separately. A great dish that nobody can copy is a "good but locked" resource. A flawless recipe card for a bland dish is an "open but weak" resource. The dish that wins both columns is "strong and open".  Characters: Margie Halvorsen, the volunteer judge, is a librarian and OER evangelist. Chet Olson is the fair board chairman, who wants one number. The three contest cooks are Ardis (Entry A, the delicious dish with a secret napkin recipe), Wendell (Entry B, the perfectly documented dish that tastes like cardboard), and Dolores with the church basement committee (Entry C, the winner). On Monday, Dr. Priya Raman, a chemistry professor, compares two chemistry textbooks with Margie. Echo the Loon is a tiny background cameo in several panels.  Illustrative numbers: all scores in this story are illustrative. The fair's score sheet is a playful stand-in for the book's rubric, with a Taste column and a Recipe column of 10 points each; the Recipe column stands in for the five reusability metrics (open license, modularity, metadata, editable source, portability). The casserole scores are 9 and 2 (Entry A), 2 and 9 (Entry B), and 9 and 9 (Entry C). The two textbooks have quality and reusability subtotals of 44 and 12 (Text A) and 20 and 40 (Text B). These mirror the style of the eight profiles in Chapter 3's Quality and Reusability Quadrant Sorter, and each subtotal is out of 50. The totals, 56 and 60, both fall in the Fair band (50 to 74) from Chapter 3. The quadrant boundary of 25 per subtotal is a teaching choice, not a standard.  Visual language: county-fair comic style in the book's flat vector house style, with indigo and burnt orange accents. Keep every character's look identical across panels. The same recurring gags appear throughout: a padlock hanging on anything locked, an open padlock on anything shareable, and two-bar scoreboards that are never merged into one.

docs.title: Prologue – Two Questions Every Judge Gets
docs.text: Every county fair judge hears the same two questions the moment the ribbon goes on: "Is it any good?" and "Can I have the recipe?" Most people think those are one question. Margie Halvorsen, librarian, OER evangelist, and volunteer judge of this year's hotdish contest, knows they are two, and she has brought a lanyard to prove it.

docs.title: Epilogue – What Did Margie Learn?
docs.text:
A county fair and a faculty office turn out to run on the same rule. Quality asks whether a resource does its job for the person using it. Reusability asks whether other people can find it, change it, and use it in their own setting. A resource can win one scoreboard and lose the other, and a single blended number will hide which one needs work.

Challenge How Margie Responded Lesson for Today The fair wanted one number She crossed out Total and drew two columns Keep the quality subtotal and the reusability subtotal separate. A merged number tells you how good a resource is on average and hides what to fix. Entry A: delicious, but locked Scored Taste 9 and Recipe 2, then wrote the recipe down Good but locked: improve the license, metadata, source, or portability. These often change quickly with small actions. Entry B: documented, but bland Scored Taste 2 and Recipe 9 Open but weak: improve accuracy, readability, accessibility, or practice. Quality fixes usually take longer. A tie at 11 and 11 Held up both sheets instead of flipping a coin The same total can mean opposite problems. Report the total with both subtotals and the lowest metric. Two chemistry textbooks on Monday Plotted both on a quadrant Totals of 56 and 60 look alike, but the quadrants called for different plans.

docs.title: Call to Action
docs.text:
The next time someone tells you a textbook is "pretty good," ask which scoreboard they mean. Score the resource on quality, score it on reusability, and keep the two numbers side by side. Then bring a hotdish to the meeting and a recipe card to go with it.

"Taste tells me whether it works. The recipe tells me whether it travels." – Margie Halvorsen

"A handful is three-quarters of a cup. Who knew?" – Ardis

"Folks, a tie is not a result. It is a mystery." – Chet Olson

Across the top of the image a cream banner carries the title in bold friendly indigo letters: "THE CITATION THAT NEVER WAS". No other text appears anywhere in the image. Color palette: cream, soft gray, indigo, and burnt orange. Emotional tone: wry, curious, lighthearted suspense. Generate the image immediately without asking clarifying questions.  Narrative Prompt This is a fictional case study for adult readers: OER evangelists, librarians, and professors who choose textbooks. It is set in a contemporary university library on an ordinary weekday afternoon. The tone is a wry, lighthearted forensic procedural: the reference desk is the crime lab, and the evidence is a citation. The humor comes from the situation, never from a learner, and the AI agent, Quill, is an eager intern and not a villain. All characters, the two authors, the article title, the journal, the volume, issue, and page numbers, and the DOI are made up for this story and are illustrative. Library tools (the catalog, the discovery search, the serials directory, the DOI resolver, the publisher's table of contents, and the interlibrary loan office) are drawn generically, with no brands, logos, or real interface screenshots. Interlibrary loan turnaround is compressed to two days for the story. The four checks follow Chapter 14 of this book: search the exact title, check the journal and the issue, resolve the identifier, and read the passage. The four forms of hallucination (an invented feature, quotation, measurement, and source) also come from Chapter 14. Character consistency: in every image Margie Halvorsen, Quill, Dr. Priya Raman, Devon (the library student worker), and Echo the Loon look exactly as described in their prompts. Echo is always tiny and in the background. Text inside images is limited to one or two short labels per panel, and all dialogue stays in the narrative text below each panel.

docs.title: Prologue – The Most Complete Reference of the Semester
docs.text: Quill's reports always arrive looking finished: ten scores, a table of evidence, and a total at the bottom. This one also carried a citation so tidy that Margie nearly admired it. It had two authors, a year, a title, a journal, a volume, an issue, a page range, and a DOI. The only thing it lacked was an article.

On a quiet Tuesday afternoon, Quill carries a ten-metric report across the reference desk with the pride of an intern delivering a first solo project. Under the accuracy metric, one line says that the claim in Chapter 3, that short chapters raise completion, is "well supported by the literature", followed by a citation. Margie says "Thank you, Quill" in the voice of someone about to ask for the evidence. Dr. Raman, who only came to renew a course reserve, stays to watch.

Margie reads the citation aloud, and it sounds wonderful: two authors named Plumtree and Quimby, a year, a title, a journal, volume 14, issue 3, pages 211 to 230, and a DOI for good measure. A citation has a predictable shape, and a language model can write that shape without any source standing behind it.

Margie's first rule is to search for the exact title. Zero results, zero results, and a polite suggestion about an article on an entirely different topic. "Maybe it is just very new?" Devon offers, and Margie points out, kindly, that a 2021 article is not new.

Next comes the journal itself. The serials directory confirms that it is real, and for one hopeful moment the desk relaxes. Then the publisher's own table of contents shows that volume 14 has exactly two issues, and the second one ends well before page 211. "Issue 3," says Devon, "does not exist."

A DOI is a permanent code that should lead to the article's page, so Margie has Devon type this one in character by character, in case the problem is only a typo. The resolver answers with a plain page and a broken-chain icon: not found. A DOI that leads nowhere, or to a different article, is a strong sign of an invented citation, though a missing one would be only a weak sign. Dr. Raman's eyebrow reaches a new altitude.

When the catalog, the publisher, and the resolver have all shrugged, Margie falls back on the people who can find the unfindable. Devon files an interlibrary loan request, and two days later the office sends back the slip stamped "cannot verify". The last check, opening the article and reading the passage that supposedly supports the claim, cannot even begin, because nobody can read a page of an article that does not exist. Margie sets the slip on the desk like a verdict.

Quill sits under the desk lamp with the clipboard clutched to their chest. "Where did you find it?" asks Margie, gently, because nobody gets scolded at this desk. "It sounded right," says Quill, and the screen face wobbles into a small nervous line. Margie opens the textbook to Chapter 3 and shows the group the truth: the book makes its claim with no citation at all, and Quill, trying to be helpful, filled the gap with the reference that was most likely to come next.

In front of the board, seated on the floor on cushions like an attentive class, are Quill, a friendly AI agent drawn as a small rounded cream-white robot about the height of a tall child, with a smooth indigo screen for a face showing two simple round eyes and a wide eager smile (no text on the screen), a tiny orange necktie, a single white feather quill tucked into the top of its head like a plume, and a clipboard held in both hands, who has no gender and is always called "they", and Devon, a lanky library student worker in their early twenties with tousled dark curls, a green staff lanyard and a baggy oatmeal cardigan, carrying a stack of paper call slips. At the side stands Dr. Priya Raman, a brisk woman in her late forties of South Asian descent with short black hair that has one streak of gray at the front, rectangular dark-framed glasses and one permanently arched eyebrow, wearing a white lab coat over a teal sweater, with a pen behind her ear and a thick battered maroon textbook under her arm, studying the board with one eyebrow slightly lowered in respect. Emotional tone: warm, teacherly, and amused. The only text in the image is the numbers 1 to 4 on the evidence markers. Generate the image immediately without asking clarifying questions.

Margie pins four index cards to the evidence board. An agent can invent a feature (captions the video does not have), a quotation (a sentence found nowhere in the resource), a measurement (a contrast ratio no tool ever ran), or a source, which is today's case. She pins a fifth card for the sneaky cousin: a real source, such as a paper on urban runoff, cited for a claim about wetlands, which only reading the passage will catch. Then she changes the prompt, telling the agent to cite only sources found in the resource or supplied by the reviewer and to write "no source found" instead of guessing, and the report gains a new column: "found by a human".

Quill has no gender and is always called "they". Margie Halvorsen, a calm woman in her late fifties with silver-blond hair in a low ponytail, round tortoiseshell glasses, a freckled face and a patient half-smile, wearing a mustard-yellow cardigan over a white blouse and dark slacks, with a lanyard around her neck holding a laminated card marked with ten small colored squares, tapes a small laminated card to the desk, which shows only a large magnifier icon. Dr. Priya Raman, a brisk woman in her late forties of South Asian descent with short black hair that has one streak of gray at the front, rectangular dark-framed glasses and one permanently arched eyebrow, wearing a white lab coat over a teal sweater, with a pen behind her ear and a thick battered maroon textbook under her arm, gives a grudging thumbs-up with a half-smile, her eyebrow lowered for the first time in the story. Sitting on the brass desk bell, with its tiny magnifying glass raised in salute, is Echo the Loon, a very small loon with a glossy black head, a white belly, a black back with a white checkered pattern, a red eye, a small indigo scarf, and an orange-handled magnifying glass held in one wing. Quill rewrites the report. Beside the Chapter 3 claim the line now reads "no source found", the accuracy score goes down a notch, and a note recommends that the textbook's author add a real citation. Dr. Raman gives the new version the closest thing to a compliment in her vocabulary: "Better." Margie tapes a card to the desk with the rule she wants every reviewer, human or otherwise, to remember: if you cannot find it, treat it as false.

docs.title: Epilogue – What Did the Reference Desk Learn?
docs.text:
The citation never existed, but the afternoon was productive. The desk ran the four checks in the order Chapter 14 teaches them: search the exact title, check the journal and the issue, resolve the identifier, and read the passage. Each check took minutes, and any one of them would have raised the alarm alone. Quill was not punished. They were given a better prompt and a report with a column labeled "found by a human".

Challenge How the Desk Responded Lesson for Today A citation that looked complete and perfect Searched the exact title in the catalog, the discovery search, and the subject index A complete-looking reference proves nothing. Search for it A journal that was real and an issue that was not Checked the publisher's table of contents for the volume Verify the journal and the issue, not just the name A DOI that led nowhere Typed it in carefully and resolved it A DOI that leads nowhere, or to a different article, is a strong sign of an invented citation A source nobody could confirm Filed an interlibrary loan request and waited for the answer When every check fails, treat the source as nonexistent and say so A confident, helpful agent Changed the prompt to "no source found" and added a "found by a human" column The agent proposes. A human finds the source

docs.title: Call to Action
docs.text:
Pick one citation from the last AI-generated report you received, and try to find it before you trust it. Search the exact title, check the journal and the issue, and resolve the identifier. It will take about five minutes, and it is the cheapest quality control in the building.

"Fluent is not the same as found." – Margie Halvorsen

"It sounded right." – Quill

"I would like it noted that the eyebrow was correct." – Dr. Priya Raman

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Wikipedia: Hallucination (artificial intelligence) - How and why language models produce fluent statements that are not true
  2. Wikipedia: Digital object identifier - The permanent identifiers that should lead to a work's page
  3. Wikipedia: Interlibrary loan - How libraries borrow materials from one another and verify requests
  4. DOI Foundation: What is a DOI? - The official explanation of DOIs and how they resolve
  5. ISSN International Centre: What is an ISSN? - The identifier librarians use to confirm that a journal exists

Where this is taught in this book

  • Chapter 14: Checking and Calibrating AI Agent Output: hallucination, its four forms, and the four checks for an invented citation.
  • Chapter 5: Accuracy and Currency: source citation, citation quality, and link rot.
  • Chapter 12: AI Agents, Prompts, and Rubric Scoring: writing a prompt that makes an agent return evidence.

In the foreground a long horizontal limbo pole rests across two stands, marked with a bold orange stripe, and a row of ten tall rectangular score cards stands behind it like contestants: nine are tall and glowing indigo, and one in the fourth position is short and sits sadly beneath the pole. Margie Halvorsen, a calm woman in her late fifties with silver-blond hair in a low ponytail, round tortoiseshell glasses, a freckled face and a patient half-smile, wearing a mustard-yellow cardigan over a white blouse and dark slacks, with a lanyard around her neck holding a laminated card marked with ten small colored squares. Margie stands on the right holding one end of the limbo pole steady and looking calmly at the short card. Generate the image immediately without asking clarifying questions.  Narrative Prompt This is a lighthearted workplace comedy for OER evangelists, librarians, and professors, set in a present-day college department meeting. Dean Pemberton wants to adopt a new economics textbook, *Marketplace Basics*, because it scored 88 out of 100 on the ten-metric rubric. Tomás Reyes reads the lowest metric, accessibility at 4, and Margie Halvorsen shows the committee the adoption threshold from Chapters 3 and 11: Adopt needs a total of at least 75 and every metric at least 5. The story uses a limbo bar set at 5 as a running visual: in this version of limbo nothing gets under the bar. Every score and total in the story is illustrative and was written for this story, not taken from a real review. The made-up scores for *Marketplace Basics*, in rubric order, are accuracy and currency 10, alignment 9, readability 9, accessibility 4, practice with feedback 9 (quality subtotal 41), then open license 10, modularity 9, metadata 9, editable source 10, portability 9 (reusability subtotal 47), for a total of 88 in the Good band. After the fixes in the story, accessibility is 7, the quality subtotal is 44, and the total is 91 in the Excellent band, with 7 as the lowest metric. The boundary cases (75, 74, 50, 49, and 88 with one metric at 4) come from Chapter 11. A student who uses a screen reader is enrolled in Monday's section but never appears in any panel and is never the subject of a joke. Visual style: flat cartoon, modern vector, with a game-show costume (bright bulbs, scoreboards, spotlights). Keep the same four characters looking identical in every panel: Dean Pemberton, Margie Halvorsen, Dr. Priya Raman, and Tomás Reyes, plus two unnamed committee members (a young man in a rust-colored sweater and an older woman with a silver bob haircut and a purple scarf) who sit at the table.

docs.title: Prologue – The Number Dean Loves
docs.text: Every department has a number it loves. For Dean Pemberton the number is 88, the total score of a new economics textbook, which he considers an A-minus worth a ribbon-cutting. What he does not love is the number 4, which sits quietly in one column of the review and is about to spoil his Thursday afternoon. This is the story of a limbo bar, a very polite librarian, and the rule that stops a good total from hiding a bad metric.

"Never report a total without the lowest metric," she says, and the committee repeats it, Dean loudest. His new banner is a little smaller than the first, and this time it includes the small print. Monday's section will open with a book that every learner can use.

docs.title: Epilogue – What Did the Committee Learn?
docs.text:
The committee started the afternoon with a number and ended it with a rule. A total tells you how a resource does on average, and the lowest metric tells you who can use it. The department adopted Marketplace Basics on Friday, and not on Thursday, for the price of a few days of careful work.

Challenge How the Committee Responded Lesson for Today A high total of 88 hid an accessibility score of 4 Tomás read all ten scores aloud instead of just the total Read the lowest metric before you read the total, and report both Dean pleaded that 74 was practically 75 Margie showed the rule at its edges: 74 is Revise, 75 with the floor met is Adopt A threshold is a line, so apply it exactly as written A Revise sounded like a failure The committee listed the cheap fixes: alt text, captions, real headings Revise means promising and needs work, and the work is often small The fix had to be trusted, not assumed Priya, the skeptic, re-ran the accessibility checks herself Re-score with evidence, ideally by a reviewer other than the fixer

docs.title: Call to Action
docs.text:
The next time someone in a meeting quotes you a total, ask one question: what is the lowest metric? Try it yourself with the Total Score Calculator, where you can drag one metric below 5 and watch a Good band total turn into a Revise.

"Read the lowest metric before you read the total." – Margie Halvorsen

"I have never been so happy to be told no by a piece of lumber." – Dean Pemberton

"I will believe the seven when I have counted the checks myself." – Dr. Priya Raman

Narrative Prompt This is a fictional adult workplace comedy for OER evangelists, librarians, instructional designers, and professors. It follows five invented colleagues from five different kinds of Minnesota campuses as they build and run a one-day workshop that teaches 20 teachers to evaluate open educational resources with an AI agent and to check the agent's work. The title puns on lake-effect snow and on ripples spreading across a lake. The humor comes from situations (frozen video calls, polite disagreement, a blizzard, flickering power, a potluck), never from learners. Quill, the AI agent, is an eager intern and not a villain. No real person, campus, or organization appears. The grant is called a small regional OER grant, and the campuses are described only by type: a state university in the south of the state (Margie), a private liberal arts college (Tomás), a community college (Bao), a technical college (Nadia), and a large research university (Gene).  Real figures taken from this book: the $1,000 budget split ($500 stipends, $300 lunch for about 24 people, $120 AI credits, $80 printing); about 20 teachers; the 8:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. schedule and its sessions (setup, the ten metrics, calibration at 9:45, checking the agent at 11:00, lunch, the improvement challenge at 12:45, peer review and publishing, and next steps at 3:15); the sample resource Watershed Basics with a teacher total of 65 and an agent total of 73 (Chapter 19), Accessibility scored 5 by the teacher and 9 by the agent, the agent agreeing within 1 point on 8 of 10 metrics (80 percent) with a bias of +0.8, and the agent's missing tool log and the video with no captions; the flag threshold of more than 3 points (Chapters 11 and 19); the four invented claims in the Chapter 14 draft (a caption feature, a quotation, a contrast measurement, and a link count); the invented journal citation from the Chapter 14 worked example; the four citation checks; and the certificate requirements, including the 30-day window and gains on at least two quality and two reusability metrics under a CC BY license. Echo the Loon is deliberately absent from every winter panel, because loons leave before the freeze. Echo appears only in a framed summer photograph in panel 1 and on a postcard in panel 12. Score cards held up in pictures are blank, with no digits, so the image generator does not garble numbers.

docs.title: Prologue – A Thousand Dollars and a Lot of Lakes
docs.text: Minnesota is a state where five people who care about open textbooks can live hours apart and still be on each other's reminder lists. This is the story of five of them, one small grant, one February blizzard, and a workshop that taught twenty teachers to check an AI agent's work before trusting it. None of the people in it are real. The lake-effect snow, unfortunately, is.

docs.title: Epilogue – What Did the Five Learn?
docs.text:
Five people from five campuses, who had met mostly as frozen rectangles, ran a day that worked even when the weather, the Wi-Fi, and the power did not. They did it by dividing the sessions by strength, practicing the disagreement before the day, and keeping a paper backup for everything that plugged in. The agent was useful and had to be checked, and the checking turned out to be the lesson that stuck. By the end, twenty teachers had a rubric card, an improved component, and a clear list of what to submit within thirty days.

Challenge How the Five Responded Lesson for Today Five colleagues who had never worked in one room Met halfway at a diner and divided the day by each person's strength A shared workshop needs one named owner for every session Five polite reviewers whose scores ran from 3 to 8 Scored alone, stated the evidence, and settled each gap of more than 3 points by the evidence Calibrate by evidence, never by averaging An agent that scored Accessibility 9 with no tool log Flagged the gap, found the uncaptioned video, and trusted the 5 A score with no evidence is only a mood An invented journal citation Ran the four checks, logged the finding as rejected, and added "no source found" to the prompt If you cannot find it, reject it A blizzard, nine remote teachers, and a flickering power grid Planned a hybrid day, paired teachers, printed backups, and kept a paper checklist Plan for the day to go sideways A workshop that could end in a pile of notes Ended with published CC BY components and a short certificate checklist A workshop should end with a product and a path

docs.title: Call to Action
docs.text:
You do not need a large budget to run this workshop. The book's sample schedule, rubric worksheet, and facilitator guidance fit a single day and a handful of friends from different campuses. Pick a sample resource, find your own Gene, agree in advance to disagree out loud, and bring a paper backup.

"If I cannot find it, I do not believe it, and neither should the agent." – Gene Lindqvist

"Decide by the evidence, never by the average." – Nadia Ibrahim

"Show me where it says that." – Margie Halvorsen

Emotional tone: warm, gently comic, and politely tense. Generate the image immediately without asking clarifying questions.  Narrative Prompt This is a fictional workplace comedy for OER evangelists, librarians, instructional designers, and professors. It is the first story in the book's Minnesota series, and it leads into "The Lake Effect Workshop". The setting is a statewide video call in the present day. Five reviewers from five different kinds of campus meet to calibrate their scoring before they teach others: Margie Halvorsen (a librarian at a Minnesota State university), Tomás Reyes (an instructional designer at a private liberal arts college), Bao Vang (a math instructor at a community college), Nadia Ibrahim (a faculty member at a technical college), and Gene Lindqvist (a professor at the state's flagship university). No real campus is named. All five characters are invented and drawn the same way in every panel, as described in the Cast and Style Sheet.  The sample resource is a made-up earth science textbook called Soil and Sky. Every score, count, and page number in this story is illustrative and was invented for the story: the first-round scores (every one between 7 and 9, averaging a total of 84), the 14 figures without alt text, the six dead links, the page 41 citation, the disputed metric (Bao's 8 against Gene's 3), the consensus score of 4 for that metric, and the evidence-based total of 58. The rules and terms are not invented. They come from Chapter 3 (reviewer bias, evidence for a score, the 100-point total and its bands), Chapter 11 (calibration, the rule to discuss only metrics that differ by more than 3 points, consensus by evidence and never by averaging, the Revise decision at a total of at least 50 when the adopt rule is not met), and Chapter 14 (score inflation and bias as the average of the signed differences).  The humor is affectionate. It comes from the situation, in which everyone is too kind to say a number out loud, and never from the characters' backgrounds. The "subtitles" are the main joke: they translate a polite phrase into the score it really means. Keep the style flat, warm, and clean, with indigo and burnt orange accents. Keep readable text inside the images to a minimum. Echo the Loon appears tiny in the background of at least one panel.

docs.title: Prologue – The Complete Sentence
docs.text: In Minnesota, "That's different" is a complete sentence, and everyone in the room knows it means "no". This works beautifully at a church potluck. On a scoring rubric it is a problem, because a rubric asks for a number, and a number has no way of being nice. Five OER evangelists from five campuses are about to find out what happens when the nicest people in the state are asked to score the same textbook.

With the one disputed metric settled, the evidence-based total for Soil and Sky is 58 of 100, in the Fair band, and the decision rule says Revise, a long way from the first round's cheerful Adopt. Margie says, "Well, I should let you go." Then the Midwest goodbye begins: "Oh, I've got a minute." "Tell your sister hi." "Drive safe, it's supposed to ice up." "No, you hang up first." The goodbye lasts eleven minutes, longer than it took to settle the only disputed metric, and nobody scores it.

docs.title: Epilogue – What Did the Panel Learn?
docs.text:
Five generous people produced a score sheet that would have put a weak textbook into a classroom, and not one of them was careless. The fix was a process, not a personality change: each reviewer scored alone, wrote down the evidence, and discussed only the gaps that mattered. The result was a lower number, a more useful report, and an author who now knows exactly which link to repair.

Challenge How the Panel Responded Lesson for Today Every first-round score fell between 7 and 9 although the comments implied 3s and 4s, so the group total of 84 would have meant Adopt Margie named leniency, one of the six biases in Chapter 3 Score against the descriptors, not against the effort Everyone saw the same cluster of numbers at once, which anchors the next score Each reviewer rescored alone with the sheet hidden Finish your own ten scores before you look at anyone else's The scores had no evidence behind them Each score now named where the reviewer looked, what they saw, and the rule they compared it with A score with no evidence cannot be repeated or discussed The first round averaged 84 and the evidence-based total was 58, a bias of 2.6 points per metric (illustrative) The group compared the sheets and discussed only metrics more than 3 points apart Treat consistent upward drift as score inflation, in people as well as in agents Nobody wanted to be the first to disagree Gene disagreed "respectfully" and brought evidence, and the group repeated the check together Decide by evidence, never by averaging, and remember that disagreeing with a score is not disagreeing with a person

docs.title: Call to Action
docs.text:
Before your next review panel, ask everyone to score alone, write the evidence in three parts, and agree in advance that a disagreement about a number is a kindness to the author. An author can fix "the link on page 41" and cannot fix "that's different". Then try the same discipline on an AI agent, because a polite machine inflates scores exactly as a polite colleague does. Practice spotting both with the Reviewer Bias Spotter and the Inter-Rater Agreement Explorer.

"A score without evidence is just a feeling with a number on it." – Margie Halvorsen

"I... respectfully... disagree." – Gene Lindqvist

"I wrote the dead link in my evidence column and still gave it an 8." – Bao Vang

docs.title: Prologue – A Race Nobody Entered
docs.text: Once upon a semester, in a chemistry department with a tight budget and a very loud printer, the Dean announced a contest that nobody had entered. Five open textbooks wanted to be the course book, and the course started in three weeks. One reviewer trusted her red pen. Another trusted his AI agent. A librarian trusted neither until she had seen the evidence.

Dr. Raman did not hurry, because she had learned long ago that a score without evidence is only an opinion. She read each chapter with the rubric beside her, quoted the line behind every score on her worksheet, and fringed the margins with sticky notes. A book took her about three hours (an illustrative figure), so by Wednesday evening she had finished book one, started book two, and listened to a fast keyboard through the wall for two days.

docs.title: Epilogue – What Did the Race Teach?
docs.text:
The race ended in a photo finish, because the race had been the wrong shape. The Hare was fast at everything a tool can see, and the Tortoise was sharp at everything that takes a chemist. Neither alone would have chosen well, and together they chose well by Friday. The moral of this fable: automation gives you breadth, people give you judgment, and the best review uses both.

Challenge How They Responded Lesson for Today Five books and one week Tomás ran an agent and four automated checks; Dr. Raman scored by hand Tools and agents cover many resources quickly, and a careful reader covers fewer resources more deeply. A clean-looking scan Margie asked what the scans could not see A link checker cannot tell whether a working link leads to the right page, and a clean accessibility scan is a starting point and not a pass. A confident accuracy score of 9 with no source Dr. Raman read the worked examples and found a wrong pH A claim that rests on the agent's own memory needs every claim checked, and subject expertise cannot be automated. A reference that reads perfectly Margie went to the source and could not find the journal An invented source cannot be opened, so source verification is the strongest check. Asking the agent whether it is sure proves nothing. Who gets the credit Margie drew the combined protocol on a flip chart Keep a person in the loop for judgment and for the claims that decide the outcome. The agent cannot take responsibility for the decision.

docs.title: Call to Action
docs.text:
Before your next adoption deadline, split the work the way Margie did. Let the tools count what can be counted, let an agent make the first pass with its evidence attached, and give a person the claims that decide the outcome. Then find the one error that matters, fix it, and share the fix.

"A fast answer is a good start. It is not yet a good answer." – Margie Halvorsen

"I did not find more errors than the tools did. I found the one that mattered." – Dr. Priya Raman

"Five books by Tuesday felt like winning. Friday taught me what winning needed." – Tomás Reyes
