docs.title: Grant Response: AI-Assisted OER Evaluation Training for Teachers
Summary
docs.text:
We request $1,000 from the MNOP OER Pathfinder Grant to run a one-day, in-person training in Minneapolis for 20 K-12 and college teachers. Teachers learn to score open educational resources (OER) on 10 quality and reusability metrics from the OER Evaluator textbook, using AI agents to do the first pass. They then use AI agents to improve one existing OER and publish it as a reusable, openly licensed component. Teachers who finish earn a Certificate of OER Quality Evaluation Using AI Agents.

The sections below follow the proposal form field by field.

docs.title: 1. Team Lead
docs.text:
Dan McCreary, author of the OER Evaluator open textbook (dmccreary.github.io/oer-evaluator)

  • Email: dan.mccreary@gmail.com

docs.title: 2. Team Composition
docs.text: Team member Role on the project Dan McCreary, author of the OER Evaluator textbook Team lead; builds the rubric and AI agents; lead facilitator Arun Batchu, AI Strategist and Consultant to Stone Arch Collaborative and the University of Minnesota Planning and Strategy Review Shannon Sever Educator and Founder of the Stone Arch Collaborative

docs.title: 3. Institutional Context
docs.text: The project builds on the OER Evaluator textbook, an open textbook in development (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0) hosted on GitHub. This interactive intelligent textbook are built with the same AI-agent workflow the training teaches: agents draft content, and automated checks score each component. Existing checks score interactive simulations (MicroSims) on a 100-point rubric and test glossary definitions against the ISO 11179 standard for precise, non-circular definitions. The key asset is a highly detailed agent skill that is use to evaluate a textbook. See OER Evaluator Skill.

docs.title: 4. Project Rationale
docs.text:
Teachers can find OER for almost any course, but they lack a fast, shared way to judge its quality or tell whether it can really be reused. A careful manual review of one textbook can take hours, and reviewers using different checklists reach different conclusions. Many OER are also hard to reuse: they ship as one PDF, carry unclear licenses, or bundle content that cannot be lifted into another course.

AI agents change the cost of review. An agent can check a chapter against a rubric in minutes for missing alt text, reading level, broken links, license terms, and alignment to learning outcomes. The same agents can fix much of what they find. But agents also make confident mistakes, such as invented citations or misread licenses, so teachers need training to direct agents, check their output, and decide what to keep.

Why now: AI tools are widely available to teachers, yet OER review is still mostly manual and ad hoc. One day of training on a common rubric gives a cohort of teachers a shared method, a credential that signals it, and a set of improved OER components that any teacher in the region can reuse. Each certified teacher can then lead the same review in their own school or department.

docs.title: 5. Project Plan
docs.text:
Proposed activities

  1. Build and pilot (November 2026 to January 2027). Publish the 10-metric rubric in the OER Evaluator textbook: five quality metrics (accuracy, alignment to learning outcomes, readability, accessibility, practice with feedback) and five reusability metrics (open license, modularity, metadata, editable source, portability). Package AI-agent prompts that score an OER against the rubric and cite evidence for each score. Pilot both with two or three teachers, and recruit 20 participants through the applicant institution and MNOP networks.
  2. Training day (Saturday, February 20, 2027, Minneapolis). Teachers score a sample OER by hand, compare their scores with the agent's, and learn where agents err. In the afternoon improvement challenge, each teacher uses AI agents to raise the score of one component of an OER they already use: adding alt text, splitting a chapter into reusable modules, writing metadata, generating practice questions, or building an interactive simulation. Teachers re-score their work and publish it under a CC BY license.
  3. Certificate and follow-up (February to April 2027). Within 30 days, teachers submit an evaluation of one OER from their own subject, with a human check of every agent finding, and an improved component that gains on at least two quality and two reusability metrics. Completers receive the Certificate of OER Quality Evaluation Using AI Agents. Volunteers compare the original and improved versions with their students in a simple A/B test.
  4. Package and share (May 2027). Publish the training kit and findings to the MNOP Clearinghouse, submit the final report, and present at the wrap-up event.

Deliverables

  1. An open training kit (CC BY 4.0): rubric, agent prompts, slides, facilitator guide, and certificate requirements, ready for any school to rerun.
  2. At least 10 teacher-improved OER components with before-and-after scores, plus a short findings report on how often agent scores matched teacher scores.

Anticipated impact

  • 20 teachers trained; at least 15 earn the certificate.
  • Improved components gain an average of 15 or more points on the 100-point rubric.
  • At least 80% of participants report confidence evaluating OER with AI agents on the exit survey.
  • At least 5 teachers adopt or adapt an OER in a spring 2027 course.
  • Certified teachers become local reviewers who repeat the process in their schools.

Use of funds ($1,000)

  • $500: completion stipends of $50 for up to 10 teachers who publish an improved component
  • $300: lunch and refreshments for about 24 participants and facilitators
  • $120: AI usage credits for the shared evaluation agent on training day
  • $80: printed certificates, rubric cards, and supplies

The applicant institution provides the venue in kind, and the facilitators donate their time. If no institution can be found to host for free we may rent a training room.

docs.title: 6. Previous or Related Work
docs.text: The closest related work is the OER Evaluator textbook and the AI-agent toolchain behind it, which already generates open textbook components and scores them automatically. This grant adds what the toolchain cannot supply on its own: teachers trained to run these agents, check their output, and apply the method to OER they already use.

docs.title: 7. Commitment Statement
docs.text: Our team will attend the virtual kickoff and the check-ins about every two months. We will submit a one-to-two-page final report by May 28, 2027, share the training kit and improved OER through the MNOP Clearinghouse, and present at the regional wrap-up event in late May or early June 2027.

docs.title: Sample One-Day Workshop Schedule
docs.text:
This workshop trains teachers to evaluate open educational resources (OER) for quality and reusability with AI agents, and then to use those agents to improve an OER they already teach with. Teachers arrive with one OER from their own subject and leave with an improved, openly licensed component and a checklist for earning the Certificate of OER Quality Evaluation Using AI Agents.

The day runs 8:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. and is designed for about 20 teachers. Every session uses the Sample Rubric Worksheet.

docs.title: Before the Workshop
docs.text:
Each teacher should:

  • Choose one OER they already use, such as a textbook chapter, a unit, a quiz, or an interactive simulation.
  • Bring a laptop with access to an AI agent tool.
  • Print or download the Sample Rubric Worksheet.

docs.title: Schedule
docs.text: Time Session What teachers leave with 8:30 to 9:00 Check-in and setup: log in to the AI tools and load the OER each teacher brought A working agent session 9:00 to 9:45 Why quality and reusability matter: the 10 metrics and how each is scored Rubric card 9:45 to 10:45 Calibration: pairs score a sample OER by hand, then run the agent and compare Hand and agent scores, with gaps explained 10:45 to 11:00 Break 11:00 to 12:00 Checking the agent: spot invented citations, misread licenses, and overconfident scores A verified evaluation of the sample 12:00 to 12:45 Lunch 12:45 to 2:15 Improvement challenge: use agents to raise one component's score by adding alt text, splitting content into reusable modules, writing metadata, generating practice questions, or building a simulation An improved component and its new score 2:15 to 2:30 Break 2:30 to 3:15 Peer review and publishing: swap and re-score each other's work, then publish under a CC BY license A published, openly licensed component 3:15 to 3:30 Next steps: certificate requirements and exit survey Certificate checklist

docs.title: After the Workshop
docs.text:
Teachers have 30 days to finish the certificate work described at the end of the Sample Rubric Worksheet. A reviewer checks each submission against the rubric before the certificate is issued.

The workshop sits inside a longer program, from building the rubric through the final report. See the Grant-Period Timeline.

docs.title: Sample Rubric Worksheet
docs.text:
This worksheet scores one open educational resource (OER) out of 100 points: 50 for quality and 50 for reusability, with 10 points per metric. Score each metric yourself, then record the AI agent's score beside yours so you can see where you and the agent disagree.

The reusability metrics follow the 5R permissions of open content: the right to retain, reuse, revise, remix, and redistribute. These are sample metrics; they will be aligned with the chapters of this book as they are written.

Use it with the Sample One-Day Workshop Schedule.

docs.title: Calibration: Where You and the Agent Disagree
docs.text:
List every metric where your score and the agent's score differ by more than 3 points, and explain which score you trust and why.

Metric Your score Agent score Explanation

docs.title: Agent Findings Log
docs.text:
AI agents make confident mistakes, such as invented citations, misread licenses, and overconfident scores. Record each agent finding and what you did with it.

Agent finding Accepted, corrected, or rejected Why

docs.title: Certificate Requirements
docs.text:
To earn the Certificate of OER Quality Evaluation Using AI Agents, a teacher:

  1. Attends the full training day.
  2. Completes the calibration exercise and explains every metric where their score and the agent's differ by more than 3 points.
  3. Submits an evaluation of one OER from their own subject, scored on all 10 metrics, with evidence for each score and a note on every agent finding they accepted, corrected, or rejected.
  4. Publishes one improved component under a CC BY license, with metadata, that gains on at least two quality and two reusability metrics.
  5. Submits both within 30 days of the workshop. A reviewer checks each submission against this rubric.
